question: Deputy Darren O'Rourke asked the Minister for Education and Youth if she will review the increasing use of digital devices in secondary schools from an educational outcome's perspective and a cost to parents/guardians perspective given the move away from digital devices in some countries.
reply:
In May 2026, Minister Naughton communicated directly with all schools and boards of management, clarifying the department's position that there is no requirement for a personal device for junior or senior cycle. Minister Naughton requested schools to be cognisant of the views of parents in relation to the use of digital devices and the associated costs. The Minister stressed the need for schools to engage with all parents not just the Parent's Association before deciding on an approach regarding devices.
Minister Naughton will continue engagement with schools, education stakeholders on the impact of digital technologies on educational outcomes and student wellbeing.

The findings from PISA 2025 also provide useful context. Irish students reported spending less time using digital devices in school for learning activities than the OECD average and reported lower levels of digital distraction in classrooms. question: Deputy Peadar Tóibín asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation to provide, for each department, the expenditure levy amount applied from 2027; the specific measures submitted and approved to meet it; the posts to be supressed, programmes reduced and grants to State agencies reduced; the amount classified as efficiencies versus reductions in services; and if proposals by any department were rejected or remain unagreed.
reply:
The achievement of value for money in public expenditure is a Government priority, supported by a strong agenda for reform and efficiency. Public expenditure must be managed to maximise value for money for the taxpayer and support the delivery of Government priorities within the voted allocation, as outlined in Circular 18/2025 (Value for Money Obligations).
Earlier this year, the Government agreed that additional funding of €646 million would be provided to the Department of Education and Youth in 2026. To accommodate this reprioritisation and deliver on the 2027 ceiling agreed under the Medium Term Fiscal Plan, an Expenditure Levy of €446 million has been reflected in all Budget 2027 funding allocations, with the exception the Department of Education and Youth. A breakdown of the expenditure levy for each Vote Group has been provided to the Deputy.
In April, my Department wrote to other Departments highlighting the Government decision to apply an Expenditure Levy for 2027 and emphasise the need to achieve savings. The levy is not intended as an expenditure reduction exercise, rather, it is designed to encourage more efficient and effective delivery of public services.
In designing the levy, Government’s priority has been to protect a number of essential areas. That includes:

question: Deputy Ciarán Ahern asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation if he will give assurances that 100% of revenue collected through the carbon tax will be ringfenced for climate action measures to facilitate a just transition, and that all unspent carbon tax revenue will be carried over to the following year rather than returned to the Exchequer.
reply:
In Budget 2027, and as set out in the Budget Publication "The Use of Carbon Tax Funds", a total of €1,114 million from carbon tax revenue is being allocated to programmes which support climate measures and ensure the most vulnerable are protected from unintended impacts of the tax.
The Programme for Government 2025 – Securing Ireland’s Future commits to using the carbon tax as a key tool to encourage a shift away from fossil fuels and to invest in a sustainable future. It also commits to continue to use carbon tax revenues to fund social welfare measures, agri- environmental schemes and retrofitting.
Between Budget 2020 and Budget 2026, additional carbon tax revenues have been allocated incrementally each year to programmes to insulate the most vulnerable from increases in the carbon tax and to support decarbonisation and energy efficiency programmes across buildings, agriculture and transport.
More recently, in light of the deviation from the previously scheduled increases to the carbon tax rates, carbon tax allocations will remain in line with those made in Budget 2026. While there is no increase in the amount allocated from the carbon tax in 2026, Government is committed to prioritising those key measures which promote a just transition and is increasing the overall expenditure allocations to these measures through wider State funds.

question: Deputy Maurice Quinlivan asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation if he will commit to meaningful public sector pay talks with the unions representing public sector workers.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 50, 55, 64 and 82 together.
I have always been, and remain, committed to meaningful engagement with public service unions and staff associations in relation to a successor Public Service Pay Agreement.
I am very pleased that, following intensive engagement in recent days, industrial action scheduled for 21 October 2026 has been averted.
In this regard, I am appreciative of the efforts of Mr Kevin Foley, as chair, as well as Mr Owen Reidy and Ms Oonagh Buckley in engaging with both parties to identify a pathway back to formal negotiations.
The first formal engagement between the parties took place in the Workplace Relations Commission on 19 October 2026. This represents a constructive step forward and will support efforts to secure a new agreement. There is now a genuine opportunity to make progress through constructive engagement and a shared commitment to dialogue.
I recognise the significant contribution made by public service workers to our society and our country. They are the backbone of our healthcare, social care, education, policing and many other essential services. The Government is committed to negotiating a pay agreement that is fair, affordable and sustainable. However, given the confidential nature of the process, I am not in a position to comment further on the substance of the ongoing discussions or the terms of any potential agreement.

question: Deputy Peter Roche asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation the measures being taken to ensure that the continued digitalisation of public services does not disadvantage older people, people with disabilities or those with limited digital literacy; and the way in which access to in-person and telephone services will be maintained where needed.
reply:
The strategic goal to digitalise public services carries with it a risk of excluding people from participating fully with these services, if their individual needs and preferences are not factored in to the design of these digital-first, but not digital-only, services.
Work to develop the Life Events model for Irish public services so far has included engagement across a range of users with amplified needs when engaging with public services. This has included research with older adults and adults with intellectual disabilities to understand their preferences, challenges and needs when engaging digitally with the State. Understanding the experience of such users is the primary starting point for building out public services, recognising that access is dependent on having the requisite skills, and knowledge, and also the availability of material resources and connectivity.
This approach has allowed the work to move beyond merely increasing digitisation and toward a more holistic set of digitally enabled services that can be accessed across multiple channels, including over the telephone and are centered on the needs of the user, proactively mitigating exclusion.
Through the process of design the human journey of using a service is mapped out end to end based on real insight helping to highlight shared challenges and opportunities for improvement. question: Deputy Cathy Bennett asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation the basis on which it was decided to award excessive salary increases to the CEOs of many State bodies.
reply:
On 27 June 2023, the Minister for Public Expenditure National Development Plan Delivery and Reform published the final review of the Report of the Independent Review Panel on Senior Public Service Recruitment and Pay Processes. The Panel made a range of findings and 38 recommendations. Among these recommendations was the establishment of a Review Body on Higher Remuneration to advise the Minister on total remuneration arrangements for senior posts in the Public Service and for Chief Executive Officers (CEOs) of CSBs. It further recommended that the CEOs of CSBs be prioritised for review by the recommended Body arising from the lack of an agreed mechanism to review rates and their exclusion from national pay agreements.
The Government subsequently established the Senior Post Remuneration Committee (SPRC) in March 2024 on an administrative footing and, as per the recommendations of the Report of the Independent Review Panel, the first task of the Committee was to perform a review of the remuneration arrangements for the CEOs of CSBs. In doing so Government was conscious of the scale, complexity and commercial responsibilities associated with leading major State companies, and their role in the management of critical national infrastructure and the delivery of significant investment programmes.

question: Deputy Cathal Crowe asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation if he will provide an update on plans to develop flood mitigating measures in the vicinity of Shannon town and Shannon Airport in County Clare.
reply:
Shannon Town and its Environs are at risk of flooding from both coastal and fluvial (stream/river) sources. The main sources of coastal flooding risk are wave water overtopping of the embankment crest driven by strong winds during high tide periods and also through any potential breaches of the embankments. The main sources of fluvial flooding risk are the inadequate capacities of the existing drainage systems (surface water channels/culverts and pumping systems) and limited outflow capacities of the tidally affected outfall systems
The design options for the Shannon Town & Environs Flood Relief works are being progressed to protect 1,400 properties, including 1,237 residential and 163 commercial properties. A Value Engineering Review Workshop was held in January 2026 to consider all potential options for the Scheme. Meetings with the National Parks and Wildlife Services are also informing the potential options.
An additional Public Consultation Day took place in Q3 2026 where the emerging preferred Option was presented to the public, prior to the submission of a planning application.
On completion of the review and the feedback from the public consultation day, an emerging preferred option will be agreed by the project Steering Group, with the final report expected at the end of 2026. An Environmental Impact Assessment Report for the Scheme is projected to be completed by Q2 2027.
Clare County Council can apply to the OPW's Minor Flood Mitigation Works and Coastal Protection

question: Deputy Pádraig O'Sullivan asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation the growth in public service numbers since 2021, by sector and by frontline and non-frontline grades, in tabular form; and how this data is informing his approach to the next public service pay agreement.
reply:
The table below sets out the number of public service employees, in full time equivalent terms, by sector since 2021. The figures for 2026 are the latest available and reflect the position at end-June. A breakdown by frontline and non-frontline grades is not available, as the classification of such grades varies across sectors and individual bodies.

question: Deputy Matt Carthy asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation the measures he has introduced to ensure value-for-money in respect of public capital projects.
reply:
My Department is responsible for the Infrastructure Guidelines. These set the value for money requirements and guidance for evaluating, planning and managing Exchequer-funded capital projects to ensure that vital infrastructure projects will be delivered on time and in a manner that ensures value for money through detailed evaluation, appraisal and planning. Management and delivery of investment projects and public services within allocation and the national frameworks, including the Infrastructure Guidelines, is a key responsibility of every Department, Accounting Officer and Minister.
Under the Accelerating Infrastructure Action Plan, a number of reforms to the Infrastructure Guidelines have been progressed and implemented under Action 23. In February, the following changes were implemented:
• In relation to Major Projects, the threshold will increase from €200m to €500m for sectors with a well established track record of delivery (Transport, Energy and Water)
• For all sectors, the External Assurance Process (EAP) will be replaced with a streamlined and time-bound internal review by the relevant Vote section in DPER; and
• Major projects at Approval Gate 2 will no longer need Ministerial approval and may now be approved solely by the Accounting Officer of the Government Department that is funding the proposed project.

reply:

question: Deputy Naoise Ó Muirí asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation whether the Government plans to move beyond annual capital investment targets and introduce a strategic framework, as recommended in the Future Forty report, with medium and long-term goals for infrastructure provision across housing, transport, energy and water services.
reply:
The Government is fully committed to providing financial certainty for infrastructure projects needed to transform our housing, energy, water, transport, and health infrastructure over the next 10 years to ensure we meet the needs of our growing population.
The Review of the National Development Plan (NDP), published in July 2025, set out a €275 billion public capital investment programme to 2035, the largest in the history of the State. The plan set out Exchequer funded sectoral capital allocations of €102.4 billion for the years 2026 to 2030; and a further €100 billion for the period 2030 to 2035. In addition, an estimated total of €63 billion in non-Exchequer funding by commercial semi-state bodies, will be invested in capital expenditure. A further €10 billion, equity funding, has also been provided for the period 2026 to 2030 to support the delivery of large projects, such as electricity grid capacity, water and transport infrastructure.
The review increased overall allocations by an additional €34 billion relative to the previous 2021-2030 NDP.
This is the largest ever capital investment plan in the history of the State and will enable the delivery of thousands of new homes, increase Ireland's competitiveness, improve transport services, provide more childcare and school places, invest in children’s disability services and ensure better healthcare for all.

question: Deputy John Connolly asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation for an update on the Clifden flood relief scheme.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 32 and 74 together.
Clifden has a long history of flooding including in 2020 and more recently in November 2024.
The Catchment Flood Risk Assessment and Management Programme, (CFRAM), was the largest study of flood risk and was completed by the Office of Public Works (OPW), in 2018. Since 2018, and working with local authorities, the OPW has trebled, to some 100, the number of flood relief schemes at design and construction. As part of the CFRAM Programme a potential flood relief scheme was recommended for Clifden, Co. Galway. The OPW engaged with Galway County Council (GCC) and confirmed that the OPW would fund the costs of developing and implementing a scheme to alleviate flooding in Clifden, through the Government’s €1.3bn investment in flood measures under the National Development Plan.
Galway County Council, is the lead authority for the Clifden Flood Relief Scheme, with funding from the OPW, for one full time Engineer. The Council appointed Engineering and environmental consultants to design a scheme for Clifden in 2021.
The final Options Report for a viable flood relief scheme to manage the flood risk within Clifden for some 24 properties has been delivered by the appointed consultant and is being discussed with Galway County Council.

question: Deputy Willie O'Dea asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation the way in which he will enhance public trust in how the public sector uses AI.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 54 and 73 together.
My Department is taking a proactive and coordinated approach to enabling the responsible and effective adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) across the Public Service, both to improve service delivery and to maintain public trust, in line with the policy objectives and targets set out in the Better Public Services Strategy, the Digital Public Services Plan, and the National Digital and AI Strategy.
My Department is ensuring the roll out generic AI capability across Government over 2027 to ensure that all public service bodies can avail of shared, trusted AI digital building blocks. This will provide interoperable AI platforms and services that will include tools for virtual assistants, summarisation and analysis of documents, as well as translation, transcription and efficient knowledge management. These technical tools will be supported by an AI Advisory Unit that will provide advice and expertise to guide effective deployment.
As part of Budget 2027, an additional €17 million was provided for the Digital Transformation Fund to help design and deliver effective and efficient digital public services that utilise AI in a responsible and trustworthy way. This funding is in addition to ongoing investment of €9 million in Government digital infrastructure to support the transformation of public services to ensure the delivery of Better Public Services.

question: Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation the position regarding the work he is doing to ensure that all OPW owned buildings, structures and monuments are fully accessible.
reply:
The Office of Public Works endeavours to prioiritise accessibilty across its owned buildings, structures and monuments a) as far as is practicable in the case of protected structures and b) in compliance with the Technical Guidance Documents of the Building Regulations in circumstances relating to accessibility of the modern estate.
New government department office buildings, garda stations, coast guard stations, cultural facilities and visitor centres are designed to Part M of the current building regulations across the OPW portfolio unless exemptions are in place.
In addition, existing buildings are modified on a phased basis in accordance with the terms set out in the OPW Universal Access Programme. This Programme targets access solutions for all OPW owned sites or leased buildings and facilities. Schedules of works typically involve site specific solutions which can consist of adjustments to entrance areas, easing of circulation routes by automation of doors, alterations to sanitary facilities and customer services areas. Access audits are undertaken by qualified personnel and lead to a solution informed by the end users and clients of the facility or service. Compliance with the Disability Act 2005 forms the basis of accessibility where a service is provided to the public. Co-designed solutions which involve all stakeholders are applied as far as possible and in consultation with experts from the Centre of Excellence Unit of the National Disability Authority. reply:

question: Deputy Micheál Carrigy asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation his plans for the Corlea Trackway; the timeline of implementation; the funding available; and to confirm a start date for the project.
reply:
Corlea Trackway is an Iron Age roadway, or togher, located near Keenagh in County Longford and dating from approximately 148 BC. It is one of the most significant surviving examples of an Iron Age wooden trackway in Europe, with an 18-metre section of the original structure preserved and displayed at the Visitor Centre. This National Monument is cared for and managed by the Office of Public Works. The Visitor Centre provides an important opportunity for the public to experience and learn about this exceptional archaeological monument. It opens seasonally each year from March to November and welcomed 19,537 visitors in 2024, and 22,082 visitors in 2025, an increase of 13% on the previous year.
In 2024, the Office of Public Works made an application under the European Union Just Transition Fund programme for funding to develop potential options for the future development of Corlea Trackway and Visitor Centre. Grant funding of up to €262,500 was subsequently awarded under the Fund to support a feasibility assessment exploring options for the future development of the site and its interaction with the wider destination. This is development funding and is not a capital allocation for the construction of a new or redeveloped visitor centre.

question: Deputy Seán Kyne asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation his plans to review capital expenditure allocation; and whether consideration is being given to increasing the level of capital funding available to the Department of Education and the Department of Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science.
reply:
As part of the NDP Review 2025, Government set out annual sectoral allocations for 2026 to 2030, and overall Government capital expenditure ceilings to 2035. This leads to a total public capital investment of €275.4 billion over the period to 2035. This comprises €202.4 billion in Exchequer Voted capital expenditure from 2026 to 2035.
Of this, €102.4 billion is being allocated for the next five years – an additional €23.9 billion on what was previously allocated in the NDP. A further €10 billion in equity and fund releases is being provided for megaprojects in water, energy and transport. This brings the total additional capital investment to €33.9 billion for the period to 2030.
The agreement of five-year annual sectoral allocations provides multi-year certainty to departments as to their level of capital funding over the next five years. This multi-year certainty has enabled Departments to plan for the delivery of their capital investment priorities through to 2030. It also provides visibility on the investment pipeline to enable construction firms to scale capacity and prepare commercial bids to deliver on the planned investment.
The Department of Education have been allocated a capital budget of €7.5 billion over the period 2026 to 2030, which represents a significant increase of 73% over their 2021 to 2025 NDP allocation of just under €4.4 billion.

question: Deputy Louis O'Hara asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation if his Department has been involved in any discussions in relation to the future of Dunguaire Castle, Kinvara, County Galway; and if OPW staff have assessed the condition of the castle.
reply:
The Office of Public Works is responsible for the conservation, maintenance and presentation of over 780 National Monuments and 33 Historic Properties nationwide.
Dunguaire Castle was built around 1520, it is believed to have been built on the site of the Dún (or fort) of Guaire, a 6th century King of Aidhne. This gives the castle its name, Dún Guaire. The 16th-century castle is thought to have been a seat of the Ó hEidhin (O’Hyne) family, who were the regional rulers.
By the early 17th century, the castle was owned by the Martyn family, one of the wealthy and famous merchant ‘Tribes’ of Galway. The family owned the castle up until the 20th century.
In 1924, Dunguaire was bought and repaired by Oliver St. John Gogarty, the famous surgeon and literary figure and in 1954 the castle was acquired by Christobel, Lady Ampthill who completed the restoration started by Oliver St. John Gogarty.
Subsequently the castle became the property of the Shannon Development Company and it was an important feature of its tourism offering, giving an insight into the lifestyle of the people who lived from 1520 to modern times.
As the Deputy is already aware, the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage is responsible for the designation of National Monuments and the decision as to what properties come into care. question: Deputy Michael Cahill asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation if he will provide funding for urgently required flood protection works at Rossbeigh and Cromane in Kerry.
reply:

Local Authorities may apply to the Office of Public Works (OPW) for funding for flood mitigation and coastal protection works under the OPW Minor Flood Mitigation Works and Coastal Protection Scheme (Minor Works Scheme). Since its introduction in 2009, some €70 million has been approved under the Scheme for 930 local authority led projects that are delivering flood mitigation and coastal protection for some 8,000 properties.
In May this year, I was pleased to announce that the revised criteria for the Minor Works Scheme are available and greatly increase the scope of the Scheme and provides local authorities with a greater opportunity to address localised flooding and coastal erosion risk within their administrative areas. The revisions include an increase in the upper threshold in funding for projects from €750,000 to €2 million and an increase in the OPW contribution from 90% to 95% for approved funding above €300,000. I have also expanded the Scheme to include interim flood mitigation measures for communities where a major flood relief scheme is planned, but not complete. Further revisions include the relaxing of some economic criteria.

question: Deputy Brian Stanley asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation the timeline for completion of the flood defence in Portarlington and Mountmellick.
reply:

The Government has committed €1.3 billion to the delivery of Flood Relief Schemes through the National Development Plan to protect some 23,000 properties, identified in the Flood Risk Management Plans in those 150 communities that are under threat from river and coastal flood risk.
Since 2018, and constrained by available specialised engineering resources, nationally, the OPW in partnership with Local Authorities has trebled the number of flood relief schemes at design, planning or construction to some 100 schemes at this time. question: Deputy Naoise Ó Muirí asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation if he will provide an update on progress delivering the commitments set out in the Accelerating Infrastructure Action Plan.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 27 and 58 together.
The Programme for Government established a clear priority for the National Development Plan Review: to maximise investment in the strategic infrastructure required to support Ireland’s future development. This includes the energy, water and transport networks that underpin housing delivery, economic growth and regional development. These sectors were subsequently identified as critical infrastructure in the Accelerating Infrastructure Actions Report and Action Plan.
The Plan sets out 30 targeted actions across four pillars of reform. Measures include increasing exemption thresholds for critical infrastructure projects, streamlining processes involving agencies and regulators, advocating for reforms at EU level, and establishing a duty on State bodies to cooperate in making land available for nationally significant projects.
Implementation continues to maintain strong momentum, with delivery on track across all 30 actions and major reforms progressing from policy development into implementation. As of the end of Q3 2026, two-thirds of the overall Action Plan has been implemented, with 85% of commitments due by end-Q3 complete.

reply:
Cork County Council with funding from the Office of Public Works (OPW), for nine staff for flood projects across the county, is leading the delivery of a flood relief scheme for Carrigaline.

Since 2018, and working with local authorities, the OPW has trebled, to some 100, the number of flood relief schemes at design and construction.
The OPW completed a Flood Relief Pre-Feasibility Investigation for Carrigaline in 2020. There are 89 properties in the town of Carrigaline deemed at risk of a 100 year return period fluvial event or a 200 year tidal event (36 residential properties and 53 non-residential properties).
Cork County Council has advised the OPW that it is preparing the procurement documentation for the Carrigaline Flood Relief Scheme. The OPW has reaffirmed to Cork County Council its funding commitment for a viable flood relief scheme for Carrigaline and is available to provide assistance to the Council as it prepares documentation to appoint a consultant engineer to design a scheme.
Pending the completion of a flood relief scheme, the Council can apply for funding for interim measures in Carrigaline through the OPW’s Minor Flood Mitigation Works and Coastal Protection Scheme. question: Deputy Mairéad Farrell asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation to give an update on the impact of Budget 2027 on infrastructure investment in the west of Ireland.
reply:
As part of the budgetary process each year, my Department sets overall expenditure ceilings for each Ministerial Vote Group. These are laid out at Vote level in the Budget Day Expenditure Report published in October with further detail provided in the Revised Estimates for Public Services published in December.
Following the allocation of each Ministerial Expenditure Ceiling, it is a matter for each Minister to assign funding as appropriate at programme and subhead level for their Departments and the agencies under their remit, accounting for the demands for services in different areas and regions and having regard to demographics and other relevant factors. Within this process, both current and capital expenditure are allocated on a Departmental basis and not a geographic basis.

question: Deputy Richard Boyd Barrett asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation if he will meet with unions and address public sector pay issues as a matter of urgency.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 50, 55, 64 and 82 together.
I have always been, and remain, committed to meaningful engagement with public service unions and staff associations in relation to a successor Public Service Pay Agreement.
I am very pleased that, following intensive engagement in recent days, industrial action scheduled for 21 October 2026 has been averted.
In this regard, I am appreciative of the efforts of Mr Kevin Foley, as chair, as well as Mr Owen Reidy and Ms Oonagh Buckley in engaging with both parties to identify a pathway back to formal negotiations.
The first formal engagement between the parties took place in the Workplace Relations Commission on 19 October 2026. This represents a constructive step forward and will support efforts to secure a new agreement. There is now a genuine opportunity to make progress through constructive engagement and a shared commitment to dialogue.
I recognise the significant contribution made by public service workers to our society and our country. They are the backbone of our healthcare, social care, education, policing and many other essential services. The Government is committed to negotiating a pay agreement that is fair, affordable and sustainable. However, given the confidential nature of the process, I am not in a position to comment further on the substance of the ongoing discussions or the terms of any potential agreement.

I propose to take Questions Nos. 54 and 73 together.
My Department is taking a proactive and coordinated approach to enabling the responsible and effective adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) across the Public Service, both to improve service delivery and to maintain public trust, in line with the policy objectives and targets set out in the Better Public Services Strategy, the Digital Public Services Plan, and the National Digital and AI Strategy.
My Department is ensuring the roll out generic AI capability across Government over 2027 to ensure that all public service bodies can avail of shared, trusted AI digital building blocks. This will provide interoperable AI platforms and services that will include tools for virtual assistants, summarisation and analysis of documents, as well as translation, transcription and efficient knowledge management. These technical tools will be supported by an AI Advisory Unit that will provide advice and expertise to guide effective deployment.
As part of Budget 2027, an additional €17 million was provided for the Digital Transformation Fund to help design and deliver effective and efficient digital public services that utilise AI in a responsible and trustworthy way. This funding is in addition to ongoing investment of €9 million in Government digital infrastructure to support the transformation of public services to ensure the delivery of Better Public Services.

question: Deputy Grace Boland asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation further to his announcement in Budget 2027 of a Public Spending Efficiency Taskforce, when its terms of reference will be published; the way in which will its membership and work programme will be determined; and the way in which recommendations, expected savings and impact on public services will be reported to Dáil Éireann.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 19, 53 and 71 together.
Public expenditure must be managed to maximise value for money for the taxpayer and support the delivery of Government priorities within the voted allocations.
Achieving value for money in public expenditure is a key Government priority. Over the past two years, a number of initiatives have been introduced to strengthen the focus on value for money and drive efficiencies across the public service.
This work is underpinned by the Government’s objective of ensuring that investment in public services and infrastructure improves living standards for the people of Ireland, both now and in the future.
To support this objective, my Department has developed robust guidance and comprehensive frameworks. These are intended to ensure that every public body and official treats public funds with due care and places financial responsibility at the heart of the discharge of their public duties.
Value for money is achieved through the efficient and effective use of public funds and resources to deliver better public services and improved outcomes.
Budget 2026 placed greater emphasis on reform, efficiency and the outputs and outcomes supported by public spending. This ensures a clearer link between investment and service levels being delivered for the population.

question: Deputy Aindrias Moynihan asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation the up-to-date position on advancing the Crookstown flood relief scheme; if the local authority has contacted the OPW in relation to securing the additional funding required for this project.
reply:
The River Bride overtops its banks both upstream and downstream of Crookstown Bridge during flood events, affecting residential properties and local and regional roads. The 2014 Lee Catchment Flood Risk Assessment and Management (CFRAM) Programme examined the flood risk at Crookstown but did not identify a viable major flood relief scheme.
In 2021, the OPW approved funding of €295,027 to Cork County Council under the Minor Flood Mitigation Works and Coastal Protection Scheme for interim mitigation works at Crookstown. These works included drainage improvements, a storm water pumping station and associated works, and were intended to mitigate flood damage pending consideration of further options.
Cork County Council has advised that it was engaging with its consultants to develop further works at Crookstown. While the OPW has not received a request from Cork County Council for additional funding in relation to the proposed further works, any future application would be considered in accordance with the revised criteria for this Scheme, that I announced in May this year. The revised criteria has relaxed some of the previous qualifying criteria, including economic benefits and has increased the funding thresholds to €2m and OPW’s contribution to 95% for funding amounts greater than €300,000.

question: Deputy Noel McCarthy asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation to provide an update on the rollout of the east Cork individual property protection scheme to date.
reply:
In October 2024, the OPW approved €5.8m in funding for Cork County Council to make Individual Property Protection (IPP) (i.e. flood barriers/gates) available free of charge to an estimated 923 home and business owners who were so badly impacted by Storm Babet in Midleton (749) and East Cork (174), including Castlemartyr, Mogeely, Killeagh, Rathcormac and Youghal.
The scheme opened for applications on 7th October 2024 to all households and businesses in the affected areas. Applications for the scheme were accepted until 18th November 2024. Cork County Council received a total of 721 valid applications.
Cork County Council arranged for an independent assessment by engineering consultants of the suitability of the properties for IPP and subsequently the type of IPP products required (e.g. expandable flood gates, slot in flood gates, etc.). These property surveys were completed for all properties deemed eligible for inclusion in the scheme early in 2025.
Delivery of flood gates to suitable properties began in mid-April 2025. Ancillary building works have been carried out by contractors working on behalf of Cork County Council since June 2025. This is the largest such scheme ever delivered in Ireland. The delivery programme has experienced some scheduling challenges arising from procurement and supply chain factors. Cork County Council continues to work closely with contractors and suppliers to progress the scheme and maintain momentum towards completion.

question: Deputy John Connolly asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht if there are any proposals under consideration to review, revise or expand the current statutory Gaeltacht boundaries; whether any assessment has been undertaken of communities located immediately adjacent to existing Gaeltacht areas which have significant Irish-speaking populations or strong Irish-language educational provision.
reply:
Both my Department and its agencies, Foras na Gaeilge and Údarás na Gaeltachta, remain committed to promoting and strengthening the Irish language both within and outside designated Gaeltacht areas through a range of policies and initiatives aimed at supporting the use of the language.
In accordance with the provisions of the Gaeltacht Act 2012, the Gaeltacht is now divided into 26 Language Planning Areas. In addition, the Act provides for the recognition of towns serving Gaeltacht communities as Gaeltacht Service Towns. Sixteen of these towns have been identified following a public consultation process, 2 of which are situated within the Gaeltacht boundaries with the remaining 14 situated outside the Gaeltacht. In addition, there are currently 3 statutory Irish Language Networks recognised under the Act with a further 2 recognised under a non-statutory scheme administered by Foras na Gaeilge north of the border. The Deputy should be aware that I recently approved a proposal by Foras na Gaeilge to seek expressions of interest from a further 3 language communities for recognition as statutory Irish Language Networks.
I can confirm that I, as Minister, do not have the authority, under the Act, to extend the boundaries of the Gaeltacht.

question: Deputy Liam Quaide asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht the number of vacant or derelict buildings have been acquired and brought back into productive community use through the town and village renewal scheme and Rural Regeneration and Development Fund since 2022, broken down by county and year; the number of acquired buildings that remain vacant or awaiting redevelopment; and the additional funding being provided in 2027 to accelerate their redevelopment.
reply:

Rather than being specific to the acquisition of vacant and derelict buildings, both the TVRS and the RRDF provide funding to support a range of town centre regeneration works. Where this entails the upgrade of buildings, broadly speaking, it is for buildings already in the ownership of our County Councils or their communities at the time of funding application.
Since 2022, almost €62 million in funding has been approved under the TVRS ‘Main Scheme’. This included funding for projects which have seen varying degrees of renovation and upgrade of buildings already in the ownership (or long term leasehold) of the applicants. It has also included other works such as public realm works and streetscape improvements.
In 2022, a TVRS ‘Building Acquisition Measure’ was introduced to enable local authorities to acquire vacant or derelict buildings. In 2025 the Measure was expanded to include land acquisition, becoming the Building and Land Acquisition Measure (BLAM), which continued in 2026. question: Deputy Liam Quaide asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht the assessment that has been undertaken of the effectiveness of the Social Inclusion and Community Activation Programme (SICAP) in reaching people experiencing poverty, social isolation and disadvantage in rural communities; the proportion of the programme funding has been allocated to rural areas in each of the past three years, broken down by county; and the additional measures and resources planned for 2027 to address rural disadvantage.
reply:
The Social Inclusion and Community Activation Programme (SICAP), is our country’s primary social inclusion intervention.
SICAP has 2 programme goals. Goal one is supporting communities, which involves supporting local community groups representing disadvantaged communities and target groups. Goal two involves supporting individuals who have been identified as being in need, to improve their life through lifelong learning and training, labour market supports to improve work readiness, or working with people in broader and more holistic ways so that they can improve their quality of life and general well-being.
Under each of these goals, Programme Implementers (PIs) and their relevant Local Community Development Committees (LCDCs) are required to set and meet Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) based on indicative Department data on an annual basis. Information on KPI outputs as well as beneficiary progress and results are captured through the Integrated Reporting and Information System (IRIS).
The 2025 SICAP Annual Report highlights the significant impact of the programme, which has a renewed focus on targeting those who are most disadvantaged in Irish society. By the end of 2025, KPIs for the programme were exceeded by 22%, indicating strong programme reach among marginalised individuals and communities.

question: Deputy Liam Quaide asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht the assessment his Department has undertaken of the financial sustainability of community and voluntary organisations, particularly those facing increased insurance, energy, staffing and premises costs; and whether additional core funding will be made available in 2027 to support their ongoing operations rather than solely capital projects.

question: Deputy Barry Heneghan asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht the reasons for the exclusion of Darndale/Priorswood from the SÍOL programme despite its recognised levels of deprivation; the specific criteria and weighting used to select eligible areas; whether the decision to exclude Darndale/Priorswood will be reviewed; and whether additional areas will be considered for inclusion in 2027.
reply:

SÍOL means ‘Seed’ in English and SÍOL stands for Scéim Infheistíochta ag Obair Le Chéile, which translates to ‘Working Together Investment Scheme’. Capital funding of €31.5 million has been secured up to 2030 in the National Development Plan to support the new programme. Funding of €5m has been allocated to the programme for 2026 and Budget 2027 allocated an additional €1m for next year's programme.

question: Deputy Eoghan Kenny asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht if the streetscape enhancement grant will reopen again for 2027.
reply:
The Town and Village Renewal Scheme (TVRS) is part of a range of measures under my Department’s Rural Development Investment Programme to support the revitalisation of rural Ireland. This scheme places particular emphasis on projects which support sustainable employment creation, town centre resilience and regeneration, enhance streetscapes, and bringing derelict and vacant buildings and sites back into use as multi-purpose community spaces.
Since 2016, over €217 million has been approved for almost 2,000 projects across the country, of this over €11.3 million has been awarded to County Cork for 104 projects.

Under the 2025 TVRS Main Scheme funding of over €24.3 million was announced for 77 successful projects and this included projects to enhance streetscapes.

question: Deputy James O'Connor asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation the status of the Midleton flood relief scheme; and he timeline for when the planning application will be submitted to the relevant authorities.
reply:

Funding for this scheme is part of the Government’s €1.3bn commitment for the delivery of flood relief measures over the lifetime of the National Development Plan.

question: Deputy Gillian Toole asked the Minister for Health if the HPRA (Health Product Regulatory Authority) warning system will be inspected and upgraded in light of findings from the Food and Drug Administration in the United States where warnings about adverse events relating to Messenger RNA Covid vaccines were not on alerts.
reply:
The Health Products Regulatory Authority (HPRA) is the national competent authority responsible for monitoring the safety of medicines, including vaccines, in Ireland.
In Ireland, the HPRA participated in vaccine safety surveillance through the European Medicines Regulatory Network.
The safety of COVID-19 vaccines authorised for use in Ireland was monitored through this European network, which brought together the national competent authorities (NCAs) of European Member States under the coordination of the European Medicines Agency (EMA). Coordinated action ensured that COVID-19 vaccines and treatments were closely monitored and used as safely as possible.
This work began with preparations for intensified safety monitoring of COVID-19 vaccines prior to the commencement of immunisation campaigns. In November 2020, before the first vaccines were authorised, EMA and NCAs in EU Member States published a dedicated intensified safety monitoring plan. The plan established a framework with refined methodologies suitable for the rapid collection and review of the high volume of safety data expected from the planned vaccination campaigns.
During 2021 and 2022, people in the EU and EEA received almost 1 billion doses of COVID-19 vaccines, making this the largest vaccination programme in history. question: Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Health if there are proposals to take private maternity care away as an option for women with high risk pregnancies; and the alternatives that will be put in place to give women the option of choosing private maternity care on health grounds such as high risk pregnancies.
reply:
As the Deputy will be aware, the Public Only Consultant Contract was introduced in March 2023 as a key step towards a universal, single-tier health service in which access to care is based on clinical need rather than ability to pay.
The POCC is applicable to all specialities, not just to maternity care. The transition to POCC will take place progressively as consultants are recruited to, or move to, the new contract. Consultants choosing that contract cannot continue to provide private practice in public hospitals after 31 December 2025. Consultants who remain on earlier contracts may continue to provide private care in public hospitals in accordance with their contractual arrangements. Accordingly, the change does not involve an immediate cessation of private maternity care. Private maternity care in public hospitals will therefore reduce gradually over time.
I recognise that this change may cause concern for some private patients. However, this reform supports equitable access to care based on clinical need.
Maternity care in Ireland is provided in line with the National Maternity Strategy (NMS).
The National Maternity Strategy sets out a Model of Care for maternity services, with three care pathways tailored to the clinical needs and risk profile of each woman and her baby:

question: Deputy Brendan Smith asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation if he will report on the progress to date in establishing a successor programme to the PeacePlus Programme.
reply:
The €1.1 billion PEACEPLUS programme (201-2027) supports peace and prosperity across Northern Ireland and the border counties of Ireland in sectors such as health, education, transport, and socio-economic regeneration. It is an important European Union Cohesion Policy programme. PEACEPLUS continues the work of previous EU PEACE and INTERREG programmes which began in the 1990s. I have joint responsibility for the PEACEPLUS programme along with the Minister of Finance Northern Ireland.
The implementation of the PEACEPLUS programme is managed by the Special EU Programmes Body (SEUPB) and is progressing well. €993 million has been awarded to projects to date. This represents 94% of the programme value. Ringfenced funding for reserve projects and small grant awards brings the total commitment to 100% of the programme’s value. Small grants are awarded through the Changemakers Fund, which supports people-to-people projects that strengthen cross-community and cross-border relationships.
In March 2025, the Taoiseach and the UK Prime Minister issued a Joint Statement outlining their shared commitment to the successful delivery of the 2021-2027 PEACEPLUS programme and their agreement in principle to a successor programme. In July 2025, the European Commission included legislative provision for a successor to the PEACEPLUS programme in its draft Multi-annual Financial Framework proposals for 2028-2034.

question: Deputy Cathal Crowe asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation if he will provide an update on plans to remediate the defective concrete blocks in the structure of Shannon Garda, Station, County Clare.
reply:
Between 2022 and 2025, the Office of Public Works engaged a consultant engineer to undertake monitoring and preliminary testing of the cracking that was observed in the external walls of Shannon Garda Station, to ensure that there were no safety issues with the building.
The outcome of this monitoring and preliminary testing determined that a detailed assessment (desktop study, inspections, testing, analysis) and design would be necessary to enable potential remedial solutions to be determined.
In September 2025 the Office of Public Works prepared a public tender for the services of a consultant structural engineer to undertake the necessary detailed assessment, design and provide remedial options, to enable the Office of Public Works to evaluate and determine the optimum remedial solution.
In November 2025 a consulting structural engineer was appointed by the Office of Public Works.
The consultant has advised the Office of Public Works that their inspections do not raise any structural concerns at present and that they do not anticipate the need for structural remedial works within the next five years.

question: Deputy Ruth Coppinger asked the Minister for Health to address the gaps in the assisted human reproduction legislative framework that continue to affect LGBTQ+ families, including the lack of recognition for international surrogacy arrangements, the exclusion of some same-sex female couples from parental recognition pathways, the limited routes available to gay men seeking to become parents, and the absence of definitions that reflect the lived realities of transgender parents.
reply:
The Health (Assisted Human Reproduction) Act 2024 was signed into law by the President in July 2024, having passed all stages in both Houses of the Oireachtas.
The primary purpose of this complex and far-reaching legislation is to regulate fertility clinics providing treatment and ensure that assisted human reproduction (AHR) practices and related areas of research are conducted in a more consistent and standardised way and with the necessary oversight. The 2024 Act encompasses the regulation of a wide range of practices undertaken in Ireland, including: the use and donation of gametes and embryos for AHR and research; pre-implantation genetic testing of embryos; and embryo and stem cell research. The establishment of the Assisted Human Reproduction Regulatory Authority (AHRRA), as provided for in the legislation, is a vital component for the effective regulation of this sector.
Prior to this, the Children and Family Relationships Act 2015 introduced a regulatory framework for the legal parentage for children born in Ireland as a result of a donor-assisted human reproduction (DAHR) procedure which takes place in an authorised Irish DAHR facility. This allows for the birth of a donor conceived child to be registered as such by an tArd-Chláraitheoir (the Chief Registrar). This applies equally to single women, same-sex female couples and heterosexual couples, when they have undertaken a DAHR procedure in full accordance with the 2015 Act.

question: Deputy Mairéad Farrell asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation if he intends to build upon the national procurement strategy, released in August 2026, with legislative action that delivers real reform to the public procurement system.
reply:
Procuring for our Future: National Public Procurement Strategy 2026-2030 represents a transformational milestone for public procurement in Ireland and a significant step towards delivering meaningful reform across the procurement system. For the first time, it sets out a shared vision, values and objectives for public procurement, establishing a clear strategic direction for the next five years.
The Strategy is both ambitious and practical. It is firmly grounded in the challenges and opportunities identified during the extensive consultation process that my officials carried out. This included public bodies, suppliers and other stakeholders with an interest in the future direction of public procurement in Ireland. Reflecting this engagement, the Strategy contains fifty-one actions across five strategic pillars focused on investing in our enterprise base, incorporating social, green, innovation and resilience considerations into procurement, safeguarding public trust, strengthening procurement capability across the public sector and reducing complexity for buyers and suppliers alike.
The Strategy provides a comprehensive roadmap for change and is underpinned by a robust implementation framework, including clear actions, key performance indicators and reporting arrangements to ensure progress is monitored and delivered. question: Deputy Thomas Gould asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation the actions he has taken to ensure regional counterbalancing and fair funding shares to Cork under the National Development Plan.
reply:
As Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation, I am responsible for setting the overall capital allocations across Departments and for monitoring expenditure at Departmental level.
The National Development Plan (NDP) Review 2025 was published in July 2025 and set out overall Government capital expenditure ceilings to 2035 alongside annual sectoral capital expenditure ceilings for the period 2026 to 2030.
Following the agreement of annual sectoral capital allocations for the period out to 2030, each Department had to develop a Sectoral Investment Plan. These Plans were published throughout November and December 2025 and outlined the specific capital projects and programmes to be prioritised and delivered within their five-year allocation.
The responsibility for the management and delivery of individual projects within these Sectoral Investment Plans rests with the individual sponsoring Department in each case. Each Minister is responsible for deciding on the priority programmes and projects that will be delivered under their remit within the NDP. Expenditure is therefore allocated and monitored on a Departmental basis and not a geographical basis.

question: Deputy Brian Brennan asked the Minister for Health further to Parliamentary Question No. 41437/26, without response from the HSE, if she will provide an update on the request made to ensure the HSE and primary care networks fully transition from an outdated medical model of disability to a human rights-based social model as mandated by Ireland's ratification of the UNCRPD.
reply:
The Government is committed to implementing the United Nations Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (UNCRPD) and to advancing a human rights-based approach to disability across all public services. The National Human Rights Strategy for Disabled People 2025-2030 provides the overarching framework for this work and commits all relevant Departments and agencies to embedding the principles of equality, participation, inclusion and respect for the rights of disabled people.
The First Programme Plan of Action 2025-2026 clearly sets out how the priority actions under each commitment will be delivered, identifying lead Departments and agencies, delivery timelines and the indicators against which progress will be measured. It is the first of three two-year Programme Plans of Action that will guide implementation of the Strategy and support the effective delivery of its commitments.
The Department of Health is working closely with the Department of Children, Disability and Equality and the Health Service Executive to support the implementation of the Strategy. Through the governance structures established under the National Human Rights Strategy for Disabled People, Departments and agencies are accountable for delivering actions that improve access, inclusion, autonomy and participation for disabled people.

question: Deputy Micheál Carrigy asked the Minister for Health the steps she will take to address the 107-day waiting time for urgent outpatient paediatric referrals at Regional Hospital Mullingar; if she will intervene in the case of a 5-month-old infant (details supplied) who has been waiting four weeks for an urgent chest assessment following repeated hospitalisations for respiratory issues; if she is aware the referral hasn't been accepted yet.
reply:
It is acknowledged that many patients are still waiting too long for hospital appointments and treatments. I am conscious of the burden that this places on patients and their families.
The multi-annual Action Plan approach initiated in September 2021 is focused on improving waiting times for patients, and the Waiting Time Action Plan (WTAP) 2026, embodies the Government’s commitment to reducing waiting times for patients, thereby improving access to hospital care. Significant progress has been made under this approach in reducing the length of time patients are waiting.
With the 2026 plan, we will continue to build upon the progress delivered to date under the multi annual action plan approach, moving towards the ultimate vision of a public healthcare service in which everyone has timely access to high-quality scheduled care, where and when they need it.
Under the Health Act 2004, the Health Service Executive (HSE) is required to manage and deliver, or arrange to be delivered on its behalf, health and personal social services. question: Deputy Séamus McGrath asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation the status of a minor flood mitigation works scheme at Lower Adamstown, Ballinhassig, County Cork.
reply:
Localised flooding issues are a matter, in the first instance, for each Local Authority to investigate and address, and a Local Authority may carry out flood mitigation works using its own resources. Local Authorities may apply to the Office of Public Works (OPW) for funding for flood mitigation and coastal protection works under the OPW Minor Flood Mitigation Works and Coastal Protection Scheme.
In May this year, I was pleased to announce that the revised criteria for the Minor Flood Mitigation Works and Coastal Protection Scheme are available and greatly increase the scope of the Scheme. The revised scheme provides local authorities with a greater opportunity to address localised flooding and coastal erosion risk within their administrative areas. The revisions include an increase in the upper threshold in funding for projects from €750,000 to €2 million and an increase in the OPW contribution from 90% to 95% for approved funding above €300,000. I have also expanded the Scheme to include interim flood mitigation measures for communities where a major flood relief scheme is planned, but not complete.
Since 2009, the OPW has approved some €8.5 million in funding for Cork County for some 74 projects under the Scheme. In 2026 the budget for medicines is increased by over €200 million with €30 million ringfenced to support access to new medicines. • The first to allocate additional funding to the Department of Education and Youth in relation to increased supports and staffing in the sector.

reply:

www2.hse.ie/services/schemes-allowances/lti/about/.

While there are currently no plans to extend the list of conditions, it is important to remember that the LTI Scheme exists within a wider eligibility framework.

• In circumstances where an applicant is still over the income limit for a medical card, they are then assessed for a GP visit card, which entitles the applicant to GP visits without charge.

question: Deputy Colm Burke asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality if she will permit the extension of a sponsored claim through the national childcare scheme to August 2027, which is due to expire on the 13 December 2026 for a child (details supplied).

Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality if her attention has been drawn to concerns related to the lack of flexibility under Section 8.2/8.3.2 of the national childcare scheme, specifically for children that are neurodiverse and benefit particularly from afterschool activities; and her views the current scheme acts as a disincentive for families to include their children in sporting or other afterschool activities.
reply:
The National Childcare Scheme (NCS) provides financial support to help families with their early learning and childcare costs. The families of almost 247,000 children availed of National Childcare Scheme (NCS) subsidies in 2025 to help offset the costs of early learning and childcare. Up to 277,000 children are expected to avail of the Scheme this year.
The NCS is designed to be flexible, recognising that childcare needs are different for each family. Under the NCS, subsidies are awarded as an hourly rate, up to a maximum number of 45 hours a week for which the subsidy applies.
The Department designed the NCS to also be flexible around children’s attendance, recognising that children’s attendance may vary from week to week. If a child is occasionally picked up early or misses an occasional day, this will not impact on a family’s subsidy. This is outlined in Section 8.3.2 of the NCS policy guidelines under “Occasional under-attendance”, which is the section highlighted by the Deputy in their question.
Section 8.3.2 also states that ‘If a child is not using the hours registered on a consistent basis the under-attendance rules will apply. This happens when a child under attends every week for 8 consecutive weeks.’ If the pattern of under-attendance continues past the 8 consecutive weeks, then persistent under-attendance rules apply which can result in a reduction of subsidised hours in line with a child's actual attendance. Persistent under-attendance rules are detailed in Secti

question: Deputy Cian O'Callaghan asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality to examine the current age eligibility rules for the Early Childhood Care and Education (ECCE) scheme; and if she accepts that children born in January are at a distinct educational disadvantage as they will not be 2 years and 8 months old by the time September comes around.
reply:
The ECCE programme provides up to two years of pre-school free of charge to families and is based on the National Practice Frameworks - Aistear and Síolta. Currently, children are eligible for ECCE starting at 2 years and 8 months to an upper age limit of 5 years and 6 months. The current ECCE eligibility criteria were set based on a number of considerations, including national experience and a review of international practice. The lower age range is informed by Tusla regulations for minimum adult-to-child ratios for children in early learning and childcare settings. These regulations take account of the needs and developmental stages of children such as toilet training and sleeping arrangements. The current arrangements also ensure that all children have the same eligibility for 2 years of ECCE.
The Department recognises that the use of age limits in programmes such as ECCE can result in some children narrowly falling outside the eligibility range in a given year. However, in the interest of fairness and consistency, the Department must apply a clear and fixed age threshold, and cannot make exceptions. The current arrangements ensure that all children have the same entitlement of 2 years of ECCE regardless of their birth date. Some parents may prefer for their children to start school at age 4 rather than 5 years. These parents may therefore choose to avail of 1 year of ECCE only. question: Deputy Ruairí Ó Murchú asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality the reason the Disability (Amendment) bill 2025 is continuing its passage through the Oireachtas given that a review of the parent act, the Disability Act 2005, is currently underway.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 391 and 392 together.
The National Human Rights Strategy for Disabled People 2025-2030 commits to a broad legislative programme that recognises the need to review and update existing disability legislation, and to consider where a need for new legislation may exist, particularly following Ireland’s ratification of the United Nations Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (UNCRPD). The Programme for Government also commits to reform of the Disability Act 2005 in consultation with stakeholders. The Department's review of the Disability Act is in line with these commitments.
The Disability Act is a wide-ranging piece of legislation that relates to the definition of disability, the Assessment of Need process, accessible public buildings, universal design, the use of genetic data, public sector employment and more.
However, improvements to the Assessment of Need process are required as soon as possible; this cannot wait for the review of the Act as a whole. Accordingly, the Disability (Amendment) Bill 2026 is now progressing through the Oireachtas. The Bill makes specific and targeted changes to Part 2 of the Disability Act 2005 which sets out the Assessment of Need process. These targeted changes aim to make the Assessment of Need process more efficient and effective for children and their families.

question: Deputy Naoise Ó Muirí asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality whether she is aware that some children born shortly after the ECCE eligibility cutoff date may receive only one year of ECCE before commencing primary school; and if she has assessed the educational and financial impact of this on affected families.
reply:
The ECCE programme provides up to two years of pre-school free of charge to families and is based on the National Practice Frameworks - Aistear and Síolta. Currently, children are eligible for ECCE starting at 2 years and 8 months to an upper age limit of 5 years and 6 months. The current ECCE eligibility criteria were set based on a number of considerations, including national experience and a review of international practice. The lower age range is informed by Tusla regulations for minimum adult-to-child ratios for children in early learning and childcare settings. These regulations take account of the needs and developmental stages of children such as toilet training and sleeping arrangements. The current arrangements also ensure that all children have the same eligibility for 2 years of ECCE.
The age eligibility criteria for ECCE have evolved significantly over the lifetime of the programme. When first introduced in 2010, eligibility was limited to children aged between 3 years and 2 months and 4 years and 7 months and provided one year of pre-school. In 2016, the eligibility criteria for the Programme changed with children eligible to enrol in the Programme at age three and remain in Programme until they transitioned to primary school. question: Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine the total value of both the BISS and CRISS payments that were subject to delayed payment due to the recent industrial action.
reply:
My Department recently confirmed that there was to be a delay to the issuing of payments under the BISS and CRISS schemes which were scheduled to commence from Friday 16 October as a result of the Industrial Action that is currently underway across the public sector.
Processing of applications is ongoing and the issuing of payments on time and to the maximum number of farmers is one of my key priorities and every avenue has been explored to date to ensure payments are made. question: Deputy Mairéad Farrell asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine to outline the regulations for deer hunting licenses issued by Coillte; the way in which license holders are required to engage with privately owned land and neighbouring landowners; the steps that Coillte takes in the event that these regulations are breached by license holders; and if there is a mechanism for landowners to complain to Coillte regarding the behaviour of deer hunting license holders.
reply:
Coillte was established as a commercial state company with private limited status under the Forestry Act, 1988, to become custodian and manager of the national forest estate. question: Deputy Maurice Quinlivan asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine the steps being taken by his Department to ensure equine chip and pin legislation is enforced.
reply:
The rules relating to equine traceability are set down in EU Regulation 2016/429 and its delegated and implementing acts, known collectively as the Animal Health Law.
I have invested significantly in improving equine traceability, with a particular focus on maximising the potential of digital technology to keep our equine traceability system accurate. A new Central Equine Database was launched in October 2025, linking horses to the premises where they are kept and to a responsible operator. This represents a significant step forward and strengthens accountability across the sector.
My Department has designed the new equine traceability system so that enforcement with traceability rules is built into the day-to-day operation of the industry. The database is now supported by nine key traceability checkpoints at which an active equine premises number or database check is required, helping to ensure compliance and that records are kept up to date. These include registrations, accessing veterinary medicines, registration updates, access to grant aid, export checks, inspections, entering sales catalogues, the census and death notification. This systematic enforcement makes it more difficult for operators to operate outside of the rules and prompts engagement and compliance.

question: Deputy Maurice Quinlivan asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine for an update on the online portal launched in July 2023 which allows members of the public to check whether an equine is recorded on the central equine database.
reply:
The online equine chip checker can be found at: https://equine-chipcheck.apps.services.agriculture.gov.ie/ and is an important tool in strengthening equine identification, traceability and transparency across the sector.
This portal allows members of the public to check whether an equine UELN (passport number) or an equine microchip number is valid and listed on the central equine database, empowering horse owners, purchasers and others involved in the industry to satisfy themselves that an animal is appropriately identified and registered.
Since July of this year, the portal has been further enhanced to allow users to verify the validity of an equine premises registration number (EPRN), which is mandatory for premises keeping equines in Ireland, or an Equine Establishment Number (EEN) which is mandatory for premises in Northern Ireland. This new functionality represents an important step forward in promoting greater transparency and accountability, enabling individuals to verify not only the registration status of an animal but also that of the premises where it is being kept or traded from.
The growing use of the portal is encouraging with over 92,000 hits on the website up to the end of September this year, representing a 41% increase on the corresponding period in 2025. question: Deputy Tony McCormack asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation the way in which he is facilitating SMEs to participate in public procurement processes.
reply:
The Programme for Government includes a commitment to review the public procurement process to make it more transparent and to ensure greater participation from SMEs. As part of this review, my Department engaged extensively with the broad spectrum of Irish enterprise through a public consultation process, stakeholder meetings, a dedicated supplier webinar and three regional roadshows. This culminated in the publication of Procuring for our Future: National Public Procurement Strategy 2026-2030, which sets out a clear ambition to optimise the use of public procurement as an investment mechanism while making it easier for SMEs, particularly micro-enterprises, start-ups and social enterprises, to participate in public procurement. In doing so, the Strategy aims to enhance competition, deliver better value for money and support better public services.

question: Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration further to Parliamentary Question No. 72780/26, the precise reasons the regulations and contribution model as laid down in the relevant Statutory Instrument have never been implemented before now; if this was a political or policy decision by his Department or by Cabinet; and if implementation of the S.I. has been objected to by any advocacy group in the migration or asylum space.
reply:
IPAS Accommodation is provided for in EU regulations and transposed into Irish law. Statutory Instrument No 230/2018, European Communities (Reception Conditions) Regulations 2018, provides that all IP applicants are entitled to Material Reception Conditions.
The Regulations further provide that where a resident is in receipt of an income above a certain level, they may be required to make a contribution to the cost of providing reception condition services. The contribution rates are set out in a Schedule to the Regulations and are proportionate to the amount that people earn.
The 2025 Programme for Government included a commitment to introducing a contribution model for people in international protection accommodation.
Recommendations for Government on a contribution model for people in international protection accommodation were originally developed by the then Department of Children, Equality, Disability, Integration, and Youth (DCEDIY) in 2024.
A proposal for working international protection applicants to contribute to the cost of their IPAS accommodation was then considered by Government in November 2025 and is now being progressed by the Department of Justice, Home Affairs, and Migration.
The Department and I are not in receipt of any formal objections to the implementation of this contribution model since its announcement in November 2025, as outlined in the Deputy's question.
