question: Deputy Peadar Tóibín asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade if she can detail any step that has been taken by Ireland in its position of EU Presidency to try to facilitate peace between Ukraine and Russia.
reply:
Ireland remains steadfast in our support for Ukraine. We all want to see peace in Ukraine.
However, Russia’s aggression continues, and while a deadly stalemate is maintained on the frontline, there has been a clear escalation in Russia's wider missile and drone attacks on Ukraine's towns and cities and on its energy infrastructure. These have targeted civilians and have caused extensive damage to Ukraine’s critical infrastructure and Ukraine's economic capacity. Attacks on Ukraine's Black Sea grain facilities are having an impact not only on Ukraine, but are contributing to a wider crisis on food security.
Russia’s illegal war in Ukraine is deadlier today for civilians than at any point since the start of the full-scale invasion. In the first eight months of 2026, more civilians were killed and injured in Ukraine than during the whole of 2025.
Russia can halt its brutal attacks any time, yet it refuses to do.
We maintain our call for a ceasefire and for Russia to cease its illegal aggression and engage in meaningful negotiations.
Ireland and EU Member States remain united in our resolve to support the people of Ukraine in the face of Russia's continuing aggression. Along with our EU partners, Ireland welcomes efforts to achieve a just, lasting and comprehensive peace agreement. It is crucial that any agreement that might be reached upholds the fundamental principle that borders cannot be changed by force.
Ukraine is a horizontal priority for our EU Presidency; we are pursuing

question: Deputy Paul McAuliffe asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage to provide an update on the progress of a review of HAP limits.
reply:
The HAP scheme plays a vital role in housing eligible families and individuals. At the end of Q1 2026, over 133,100 HAP tenancies had been set up since the scheme commenced, of which there were 48,355 households actively in receipt of HAP support nationally.
Maximum rent limits for HAP were set for each housing authority area in 2016 in conjunction with the Department of Social Protection. Since 11 July 2022, each local authority has statutory discretion to agree to a HAP payment up to 35% above the prescribed maximum rent limit. Discretion can be increased up to 50% above the prescribed maximum rent limits for Homeless HAP tenancies in Dublin. Local authorities also have additional flexibility to apply a couple HAP rate to single-person households.
I gave my approval for a review of the current HAP rent limits to be undertaken to ensure there is sufficient support under the HAP scheme to assist eligible households in accessing accommodation in the private rental sector.
As part of this review, the Housing Agency carried out an analysis of the rental market and submitted its report to my Department on 16 July. This helped inform my Department’s review of the HAP rent limits, which has now concluded. I am currently considering its findings before setting out the next steps.

question: Deputy John Clendennen asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport for an update on his engagement with Coimisiún na Meán regarding the broadcasting levy on independent radio stations.
reply:
There is a long-standing principle that costs of regulation are met by regulated sectors themselves, and therefore, the Broadcasting Act provides for the imposition by Coimisiún na Meán of levies to meet the costs of its full range of statutory functions and duties.
Furthermore, the Act vests authority and responsibility for such a levy in Coimisiún na Meán, and as such as Minister, I have no role in approving the proposed income or expenditure of Coimisiún na Meán, or importantly in the setting of the annual levy for any category of regulated entities, including that of sound broadcasting.
I have, however, met Coimisiún na Meán in order to seek clarity regarding their approach to implementing their statutory responsibilities in this regard. It was also an opportunity for me to impress upon them the need to take the opportunity to more clearly communicate such matters to their stakeholders and the wider public, and also consider how the levy can in future be formulated to avoid placing an unnecessary burden on the sector.
In formulating its annual levies, Coimisiún na Meán is required to ensure that the levies are such an amount so as to meet all expenses properly incurred in the period, and is also required to ensure proportionality in attribution of expenses and application of levies across relevant categories of regulated service providers or entities. An Coimisiún must also have regard to a number of factors in setting the levy including the financing of a service provide

question: Deputy John Clendennen asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport whether consideration will be given to establishing a formal funding pathway for Irish athletes competing at international level in codes outside those traditionally supported through Sport Ireland.
reply:
Sport Ireland, which is funded by my Department, is the statutory body with responsibility for the development of sport, increasing participation at all levels and raising standards, including the allocation of funding across its various programmes.
Accordingly, I have referred the Deputy's question to Sport Ireland for direct reply. I would ask the Deputy to inform my office if a reply is not received within 10 days.

question: Deputy Daniel Ennis asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport whether security and transport costs are included in the €14.275 million operational budget for hosting an event (details supplied); and when a full, updated estimate of the total cost to the State will be published.
reply:
Major international sporting events can play a key role in increasing sporting participation, boosting domestic and international tourism and promoting Ireland as a destination for education and business opportunities. They present a wonderful opportunity to showcase the island of Ireland and our world-class tourism and sport offering to Europe and the world.
When the Government took the decision in 2019 to proceed with hosting this event, it agreed to an allocation of €14.275 million for the operational budget to support the event's staging. These costs included transport, security, local authority costs, ceremonies and fanzones.
The operational budget for the event was estimated in 2019 prior to COVID-19 and recent international conflicts that have led to global supply chain pressures and significant cost of living increases. It is therefore reasonable to presume that the costs associated with the operational budget would have increased, in line with the potential benefits from hosting the event. A continuous review of the operational budget (transport, security, local authority costs, etc) is taking place in parallel with the strategic planning to host the event which is governed by the Government Steering Group.
A full economic analysis/assessment will be conducted post-event to evaluate the total economic impact of this event once it has concluded.

question: Deputy Peter 'Chap' Cleere asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport when applicants can expect to be notified of the outcome of the selection process for the basic income for arts scheme; when the first payments are expected to actually reach successful applicants.
reply:
In February this year I announced that the Government had approved a permanent successor to the Basic Income for the Arts pilot scheme and that 2,000 artists would be provided with funding of €325 per week for three years. This is a major milestone for the arts in Ireland and I am particularly pleased that the research my Department conducted provided Government with a clear evidence base upon which to make that decision.
The deadline for application to the Basic Income for the Arts 2026 - 2029 was 5pm on Tuesday 12th May, with over 10,000 applications received by the deadline.
I appreciate that applicants are eager to know the outcome, however, in order to protect the integrity of the scheme the assessment process is by necessity very intensive and time consuming. No two professional arts practices are the same and therefore the proofs supplied vary considerably. The Department has commenced communication to applicants invited to participate in the scheme on Thursday 15 October. Due to the volume involved, successful applicants will be notified in tranches as assessments are completed.
My Department is processing the applications as promptly as possible and I anticipate that payments will commence shortly. All successful candidates will receive the full allocation of €325 per week for three years.

question: Deputy Pat the Cope Gallagher asked the Minister for Education and Youth when she expects her Department to conclude its assessment of the accommodation requirements at a school (details supplied) given that students and staff continue to work in prefabricated accommodation dating back to the 1980s which has been described as damp, mould-ridden and unsuitable for a modern educational environment; if she will outline a timeline for the delivery of a permanent accommodation solution.
reply:
I can confirm that my department is in receipt of an application, under the Additional School Accommodation (ASA) scheme, from the school referred to by the Deputy. In 2022 the department approved Modular accommodation for a classroom for students with special educational needs and a further application was submitted for reconfiguration to create additional special educational needs accommodation.
A department-led prioritisation process will continue over the course of 2026 and 2027 to assess and evaluate the progression of individual projects through the design pipeline having regard to the continual need to maximise existing capacity and determine the prioritised needs going forward. This process will involve engagement with key stakeholders and individual schools and will ultimately inform the next tranches of programme rollout to tender. The Department led Energy and Condition Survey of the school estate, which will be finalised later in 2026, will provide an additional evidence base for assessing priorities and will give a good picture of the nature of accommodation at all schools. This will facilitate good strategic overview and decision-making on relative priorities between schools for further investment in the existing school estate. A decision on this application will be communicated to the school authority in due course based on this information.

question: Deputy Emer Currie asked the Minister for Education and Youth if she will review the circumstances of a staffing appeal submitted by a school (details supplied); and if consideration will be given to retaining the teaching post concerned for the remainder of the 2026/2027 academic year.
reply:
The key factor for determining the level of staffing resources provided at individual school level is the staffing schedule for the relevant school year and pupil enrolments on the previous 30 September. The staffing schedule operates in a clear and transparent manner and treats all similar types of schools equally.
The staffing process also contains an appeals mechanism for schools to submit a staffing appeal to an independent Primary Staffing Appeals Board. The school referred to by the Deputy has submitted an appeal which will be considered by the Appeals Board at their meeting this week. The Primary Staffing Appeals Board operates independently of the Department and its decision is final.

question: Deputy Charles Ward asked the Minister for Education and Youth whether there is Government funding, grant assistance or a transport subsidy available to small rural schools that are forced to travel significant distances, including across the border, to access swimming facilities.
reply:
The purpose of my Department's School Transport Scheme is, having regard to available resources, to support the transport to and from school of children who reside remote from their nearest school.
Children are eligible for school transport where they satisfy the distance criterion and are attending their nearest national school or post primary education centre, having regard to ethos and language.
In accordance with the terms of my Department's School Transport Scheme, school transport services operate during the standard school year and facilitate a child's attendance during normal school opening and closing times. Transport to extracurricular activities is outside the remit of the scheme.

question: Deputy Paul Murphy asked the Minister for Education and Youth the steps she is taking to facilitate school patronage change on foot of the national parents’ survey.
reply:
The Primary School Survey gathered the views of both parents of children currently attending primary school and parents of children yet to enter the school system. It explored preferences regarding school patronage/ethos, language (education through Irish or English) and single-sex or co-educational school provision.
In early June, my department issued primary schools with their school-specific results and explanatory information.
Boards of Management have been asked to share their survey results and explanatory information with their school communities, to review their survey results and to engage with their communities (including parents), and the local community (including parents with children not yet in school), before deciding on their next steps.
The future direction of primary schools arising from the Primary School Survey work should be led by school communities themselves, who should then engage with their patron and my department. It is important that schools are given the time and space to reflect carefully on their results and to engage fully with parents and their wider school communities.
My department has published all school-level reports, survey results, guidance documents and supporting materials on www.gov.ie/PrimarySchoolSurvey. These resources are designed to support Boards of Management in sharing results and engaging openly with parents, staff, patrons and the wider school community. My department will continue to support and engage with schools as the

question: Deputy Catherine Callaghan asked the Minister for Education and Youth when schools will be notified of and receive payment under the minor works grant scheme and the ICT infrastructure grant scheme for the 2027-2028 school year; and if her Department remains committed to the December/January payment schedule announced in December 2025.
reply:
As part of the NDP Sectoral Plan published in January 2026, and in line with Programme for Government commitments, clarity and certainty has been provided for school system on annual grant payment timeline which is now set at December/January each year.
The next payment of Minor Works Grant for school year 2027/2028 will issue in either December 2026 or January 2027. Since 2020, close to €340 million in Minor Works Grants and Enhanced Minor Works Grants, have been allocated to schools. This includes the payment of Minor Works Grants totalling almost €30 million for the school year 2026/2027 which has issued in December 2025.
Primary and special schools need not apply for Minor Works Grant aid. Under the scheme, funding is made available to all primary and special schools on the following basis:
€5,500 basic grant plus €18.50 per mainstream pupil and €74 per special needs pupil enrolled in the school on the 30th of September of the year prior to the issue of the grant. The €74 rate applies to a special needs pupil attending a special school or attending a special class attached to a mainstream school.
The Digital Strategy for Schools to 2027 and its associated implementation plan is underpinned by funding of €200m over the course of the strategy, committed to under Ireland’s National Development Plan. question: Deputy Paul Nicholas Gogarty asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade the pathways that exist for students at relevant third level courses in Ireland to secure an internship with her Department or related agency in order to gain experience in diplomacy, international relations and Irish foreign policy; the positions are advertised and where, if there is an email address or a point of contact to make applications.
reply:
The Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade has a number of established paid graduate internship programmes which run from 6 to 22 months depending on the role. These internships are in the areas of human rights, conflict resolution, legal affairs, communications and development. Recruitment to these internship opportunities is carried out by means of a competitive selection process which usually attracts strong interest from well qualified applicants.
All graduate internships in the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade are advertised on our career page on www.gov.ie.
The Department also facilitates the placement of four University of Limerick students under the University's Cooperative Education Programme each year. These placements run for 6 months and recruitment is carried out by a competitive selection process in conjunction with the university.

question: Deputy John Clendennen asked the Minister for Education and Youth for an update on the additional school accommodation project for a school (details supplied), including details of any recent review and the current status of the project.
reply:
The school referred to by the Deputy was approved to enter the Department’s pipeline of school buildings under the Additional School Accommodation Scheme for a project providing one special educational needs classroom and one central activities space. This project is devolved to the school authority for delivery.
The Stage 2b (post planning) report was submitted to my Department. Following a review, Department officials requested clarifications and these were recently received. This project remains under review from a technical and cost perspective. All school building projects, as they progress through the pipeline, must undergo the necessary due diligence outlined in the Infrastructure Guidelines and Capital Works Management Framework.
The timing of a project moving from one stage to the next requires careful planning and takes account of factors such as compliance with all scope, design and cost requirements; timing of affordability; and the prioritisation necessary for the school building programme to remain within agreed annual funding allocations. Therefore, all school building projects are subject to the National Development Plan review.
It is expected that the next tranche of projects to proceed to tender will be published in 2027. Prioritisation will continue over the coming months to identify this next tranche of projects. question: Deputy John Clendennen asked the Minister for Education and Youth for an update on the recent application for a modular build for a school (details supplied).
reply:
The school to which the deputy refers was approved to enter the Department’s pipeline under the SEN Repurposing scheme for a project providing one SEN classroom.
The school has been sanctioned to open a special class for 2026/2027 by the National Council for Special Education (NCSE). The school received the €30,000 Start Up Grant and was advised additional funding was available if required.
The school submitted an application for additional funding under the SEN Repurposing Small Scale Works Scheme. The application was reviewed by the Department’s Professional & Technical Unit and based on the information provided the application was approved for €70,000. The project has now been devolved to the school authority for delivery.
Officials at my Department will continue to engage with the school to provide practical assistance for the delivery of this project.
There is no modular build application noted for this school.

question: Deputy John Clendennen asked the Minister for Education and Youth the number of school capital projects completed in 2021 to 2025 inclusive and to date in 2026, where the final design team fees exceeded the original contracted fees; the average percentage increase in such cases; and the total additional expenditure incurred, broken down by reason for these increases, in tabular form.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 70 and 71 together.
Since 2021 my department has invested over €6.8 billion in our schools throughout the country under the National Development Plan. This has facilitated the completion of over 1,500 school building projects, along with over 4,100 small-scale improvement works to meet priority maintenance needs and advance energy efficiency and climate goals.
Design Team appointments are governed by the Department's published Design Team Procedures and associated conditions of engagement. Any increase in Design Team fees are done in accordance with contractual provisions and conditions of engagement and typically arise due to factors such as where the nature of the project evolves to cater for example for additional accommodation requirements for mainstream or special education needs or where additional works arise due to planning conditions, site specific issues, decarbonisation etc.

If the Deputy wishes to provide details of a specific project, my Department will examine further and provide the information available.

question: Deputy Ruth Coppinger asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade the measures her Department is taking, through its foreign policy and Irish aid programme, to respond to the growing influence of anti-rights movements globally, particularly those seeking to undermine gender equality and women's rights; and whether additional policy or funding measures are being considered to support women's rights organisations and movements responding to these threats.
reply:
The Government remains firmly committed to advancing gender equality and protecting human rights internationally. We recognise gender equality and the empowerment of women and girls as a fundamental human right and a strategic imperative.
The global pushback against gender equality poses a significant challenge to strengthening gender perspectives and women’s empowerment globally. It threatens an unacceptable rollback of core values and progress towards the Sustainable Development Goals, while making it increasingly difficult to advance a rights-based approach in external action.
As human rights and gender equality face serious levels of opposition globally, leadership is needed now more than ever in defending and promoting fundamental human rights, including gender equality, women’s and girls’ empowerment, and sexual and reproductive health and rights. Ireland is deeply concerned by growing global challenges in these areas and continues to advocate internationally for them.
Reductions in international development budgets risk undermining progress on gender equality. We believe it is important to protect resources for gender equality, including support for women-led and women's rights organisations at the frontline of humanitarian and development responses. In line with the Government's international development policy, A Better World, we provide direct funding for gender equality programmes to ensure integration of gender and women’s rights across all interventions.

reply:

The study of Modern Foreign Languages is optional at Junior and Senior Cycle. However, it should be noted that schools may have their own rules in relation to the study of a foreign language and higher educational institutions may require a foreign language to be studied for matriculation purposes.

question: Deputy Darren O'Rourke asked the Minister for Education and Youth the number of NEPS posts currently filled and unfilled, respectively.
reply:
The National Educational Psychological Service (NEPS) provides educational psychological support to all schools. Due to a national shortage of suitably qualified educational psychologists not all schools have an assigned educational psychologist. For those schools without an assigned educational psychologist, the school will be supported by NEPS through the Advisory Support Service. All schools continue to have support in the event of a critical incident through the local NEPS office and has access to training and support from NEPS for school staff.
Through the NEPS Advisory Support Service, schools have an opportunity to access responsive support and advice from a NEPS psychologist. The educational psychologist can provide advice and support and where the need is established can sanction an assessment through the Scheme for the Commissioning of Psychological Assessments (SCPA). Schools can contact the service as needed throughout the school year.
There are currently 242 educational psychologists employed in NEPS with 56 maingrade vacancies. The Department is making every effort to recruit additional educational psychologists to address the shortage. question: Deputy Darren O'Rourke asked the Minister for Education and Youth the way in which she plans to address the ongoing costly issue of school uniforms.
reply:
Ultimately, decisions on school uniforms are a matter for individual schools and Boards of Management. Under the Education Act 1998, all recognised schools are managed by school Boards of Management. Individual school authorities are responsible for the drawing up of a school policy in relation to the wearing of uniforms. Decisions on changes to school uniform polices are a matter for schools at local level. Schools are advised to consult with parents and students when drafting a policy on uniforms.
My department’s Circular 0032/2017 is currently being reviewed. In addition to a focus on reducing costs for parents, the review is looking at the comfort and sustainability of school uniforms. My officials will continue to engage with the education partners, including the National Parents Council, as we progress this important work.
The Education (Charter and Miscellaneous Provisions) Bill 2019 includes provisions to enhance financial transparency within school communities and support greater awareness of school-related costs. The Bill provides that charter guidelines may require schools to make available information on school finances, including details of income and expenditure, and extend this transparency to funds raised and spent by parents’ associations. The amendments also provide that such information may be made available to teachers and other school staff, in addition to parents and students.

reply:
The Department of Education and Youth, along with other Departments across the public service, implemented the outcome of the public service-wide review of allowances and premium payments (September 2012) by the Department of Public Expenditure, National Development Plan Delivery and Reform (DPENDPDR). This meant that many allowances were no longer payable to “new entrants” including Teachers.

reply:

reply:

In addition, part of the forward planning process as to where new classes, schools or expansion is required looks at how far students are travelling to access an education that meets their needs. question: Deputy Cathal Crowe asked the Minister for Education and Youth if she will intervene in the case of a constituent (details supplied) facing an unfair duplicate €440 registration fee from the Teaching Council due to protracted administrative delays; if the council has the power to issue manual fee waivers in such instances.

The Teaching Council register teachers under the Teaching Council Act 2001-2015 and in line with the Teaching Council Registration Regulations 2025. Per the legislation, my department has no role in the registration of individual teachers.

question: Deputy Mairéad Farrell asked the Minister for Education and Youth the work her Department is doing to ensure that school pupils in single-sex schools have access to a range of subject choices, and that subject choices available to pupils are not influenced by gender-stereotypes.
reply:
My Department is committed to providing an education system that is inclusive, equitable, and empowering for all. Every learner deserves the opportunity to thrive. Our focus is on high standards, inclusive practices, and strong supports to ensure no one is left behind.
My Department’s work in this area includes the STEM Education Policy Statement 2017–2026, which aims to improve STEM experiences and outcomes for all learners, from early learning and care through to post-primary level. It acknowledges that there is a need to increase the uptake of STEM subjects and to enhance STEM learning for learners of all backgrounds, abilities and gender, with a particular focus on uptake by females
In addition, I announced the publication of subject and career information leaflets in September this year supports learners at the key transition to post-primary schools with information on subject choices, including STEM.
The range of subjects offered depends on each school’s resources, staffing, and student needs. Each school retains autonomy to design timetables and determine which programmes and subjects to provide. Schools aim to balance available resources with student demand. Any issues arising on the matter of subject provision and subject choice should be addressed to the principal of the school in question in the first instance.

question: Deputy Niamh Smyth asked the Minister for Education and Youth the supports available to schools experiencing significant educational disadvantage that do not currently have DEIS status; the options for such schools to access additional supports and resources; and the status of previously approved school building projects.
reply:
Addressing educational disadvantage in all schools is a key priority for me as Minister for Education and Youth. The DEIS programme is targeted at schools with the highest levels of concentrated disadvantage. Schools that were included in the most recent expansion of the programme in 2022 were those with the highest levels of concentrated disadvantage as identified through the refined DEIS identification model. Schools were not required to apply for inclusion in the DEIS programme, and the model was applied fairly and equally to all schools. A detailed paper on the refined DEIS identification model is available on gov.ie.
Earlier this year, I announced the DEIS Strategy to 2035 which is the first long-term, whole-system approach to addressing educational disadvantage. This strategy recognises education as central to breaking cycles of disadvantage, expanding opportunity, and ensuring long-term security. It sets out a more flexible model of support, so that resources are aligned with each school’s level of need as it changes over time.
The strategy also acknowledges that students at risk of educational disadvatage are present in all schools. It therefore focuses on improving outcomes, encouraging innovation, and ensuring schools can access the right supports when needed. question: Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Minister for Education and Youth for an update on her Department's plans for the piece of vacant land adjacent to the primary school in the Hollywoodrath estate, Hollystown, Dublin 15; if she can share a potential timeline for the outcome of discussions within her Department in relation to this.
reply:
My department has determined that the Minister-owned site at Hollywoodrath will be the permanent location of Ériu Community College.
The school building on that site is currently occupied by two primary schools while refurbishment works are being carried out on their permanent school buildings. Once these schools return to their refurbished accommodation, the vacated building at the Hollywoodrath site will provide part of the permanent accommodation required for pupils attending Ériu Community College. This is not expected to occur before September 2028.
My department will keep the school authority and patron body informed of progress in relation to this project.

question: Deputy Charles Ward asked the Minister for Education and Youth whether any new Irish-medium schools are planned for Donegal for the period 2026 to 2031; and her plans to keep up with the demand for Irish-medium schools in Donegal.
reply:
My department establishes new school entities on the basis of identified demographic demand for school places. Demographic requirements in an area determine the need or otherwise for establishing new schools, and the resources available for school infrastructure must be prioritised to meet the needs of areas experiencing significant population growth so as to ensure that every child has access to a school place. Based on current demographic analysis, there are no new school entities currently being established, either Irish-medium or English-medium, in County Donegal. This position is kept under ongoing review by my department.
In planning for school provision, my department divides the country into 314 school planning areas and uses a geographical information system informed by a range of data sources, including Census data, child benefit records, school enrolment trends, residential planning and construction activity, and engagement with local authorities and the construction sector. This enables my department to identify current and future demand for school places and to ensure that school infrastructure planning keeps pace with demographic change.

question: Deputy Ruth Coppinger asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade the specific actions Ireland has taken, and intends to take during its Presidency of the Council of the European Union, to deliver on its stated commitment to shepherd an ambitious European agenda on gender equality and the rights and empowerment of all women and girls, strengthening the Union’s role as a principled global actor.

Ireland has a comprehensive set of employment rights that apply to part-time workers through our existing legislation and Statutory Codes of Practice.
The Protection of Employees (Part-Time Work) Act 2001 and the Employment (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 2018 provide important provisions to improve job security and working conditions for part-time workers and for employees in precarious or variable-hour roles.
The Protection of Employees (Part-Time Work) Act 2001 is accompanied by a recently revised Workplace Relations Commission Code of Practice on Access to Part-Time Work which states that, as far as possible, employers should give consideration to requests by employees to transfer from full-time to part-time work; and requests by employees to transfer from part-time to full-time work or to increase their working time should the opportunity arise.
The Employment (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 2018 represented a major step forward in strengthening employment protections for workers, particularly those in precarious forms of employment or with variable working hours.
The 2018 Act inserted banded hours provisions into the Organisation of Working Time Act 1997. question: Deputy Robert Troy asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation if there are plans to treat oncology appointments the same way as maternity leave, whereby if a civil servant with cancer was to exceed their yearly number of sick days attending essential oncology appointments they would still be able to obtain their yearly increment.
reply:

The Scheme provides the framework for sick leave in the Civil and Public Service, including paid sick leave and supports during periods of ordinary and critical illness. The provisions of the Scheme are set out at: www.irishstatutebook.ie/eli/2014/si/124/made/en/printas amended

Maternity leave is a statutory protected period of leave from work, with entitlements set out in the Maternity Protection Acts 1994 and 2004.
Maternity leave and sick leave are distinct forms of leave with separate legislative and policy basis. Maternity leave is a statutory entitlement associated with pregnancy and childbirth, whereas absence arising from illness, including where applicable absence associated with oncology treatment, is dealt with in accordance with the provisions of the Public Service Sick Leave Scheme.

reply:

Following intensive engagement in recent days, and with the assistance of a Government-appointed group, a pathway has been established to formal negotiations at the Workplace Relations Commission, which commenced on 19 October 2026. I welcome this positive outcome.

reply:

question: Deputy Cian O'Callaghan asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance if his Department has assessed the position of retired members of private sector pension schemes whose pensions were permanently reduced to meet the 2011 to 2015 pension levy, and whose cumulative losses now substantially exceed the levy amounts attributable to them; if he accepts that a levy described as temporary has had a permanent effect on these pensioners and their surviving spouses.
reply:
The pension fund levy was introduced in 2011 in the wake of a severe economic and financial crash. To preserve and boost jobs, all sectors of the economy had to contribute to the recovery. In this context, the pension levy was designed to claw back a small amount of the very significant tax relief that those contributing to pension arrangements had benefitted from over many years. It is worth noting that pensions continued to benefit from a range of tax relief benefits even at a time of serious economic difficulty.
Specifically, the levy funded the tax reductions and expenditure measures introduced in the then Jobs Initiative, including, for example, the lowering of the VAT rate for the tourism sector to 9%. For the years 2011, 2012 and 2013 the rate was 0.60% of the pension scheme assets. For the year 2014 the rate was 0.75% of the assets and for the year 2015, the final year of the levy, the rate was reduced to 0.15%.
Under the relevant legislation, the payment of the levy was treated as a necessary expense of a pension scheme. Scheme trustees or insurers, as appropriate, were entitled to adjust current or prospective benefits payable under a scheme to take account of the levy. It was at the discretion of those trustees or insurers to decide whether, when, and how the levy should be passed on, and to what extent, given the particular circumstances of the pension schemes for which they are responsible.

question: Deputy Emer Currie asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance the number of homes purchased with assistance from the help to buy scheme, broken down per year from 2016 to date in 2026, in tabular form.
reply:
The Help to Buy (HTB) incentive, is a tax-based scheme to assist first-time purchasers with the deposit they need to buy or build a new house or apartment. It also aims to encourage additional supply of new houses by supporting demand.
HTB provides a refund of Income Tax and Deposit Interest Retention Tax (DIRT) paid in Ireland over the previous four years, subject to limits outlined in the legislation.
The level of support available to first time buyers under the HTB scheme, is whichever is the lesser of:
• €35,000 (from 07 October 2026); or
• 10 per cent of the purchase price of the new property; or
• the amount of Income Tax and DIRT paid in the four years before application for the relief.
For a property to qualify for the HTB scheme, it must be new or converted for use as a dwelling, having not previously been used as a dwelling. Additionally, the purchase value/approved valuation of the property must not exceed €500,000.
Based on the latest available data (30 September 2026), the scheme has supported over 70,000 individuals or couples to buy or build their own home.

question: Deputy Barry Ward asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance if a calculation has been made regarding the rate of capital gains tax if deemed disposal was removed and ETFs moved to a CGT regime instead of an exit tax regime; and whether this has been given consideration.
reply:
An exchange-traded fund (ETF) is an investment fund whose units are traded on a regulated stock exchange. There is no separate tax regime for ETFs. The domicile of an ETF generally determines the applicable funds taxation regime, specifically whether the ETF falls within the domestic fund regime (gross roll-up), or the offshore funds regime. There are different rules applicable under the offshore funds regime dependent on the domicile and regulatory status of the fund.
The gross roll-up regime for Irish domiciled investment funds allows the monies invested in these funds to grow on a tax-free basis. Tax is payable when value transfers, or is deemed to arise, from the fund to the investor. Investment undertaking tax (IUT) must be deducted on the occurrence of a ‘chargeable event’. In the case of an Irish domiciled investment fund, a chargeable event includes –
• the making of relevant payments,
• the redemption of the investment,
• the transfer by an investor of their investment, and
• the ending of an eight-year period following the acquisition of the investment and then every eight years thereafter. This is commonly referred to as the eight-year deemed disposal.
The rate of IUT applying to chargeable events is currently 38% but, as recently announced in the Budget, the rate is due to decrease to 35% for chargeable events occurring on or after 1 January 2027. A chargeable event does not attract a liability to Pay Related Social Insurance (PRSI) or Universal Social Charge (USC

question: Deputy Barry Ward asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance the position regarding the total level of funding brought in by the deemed disposal tax for each of the years 2022, 2023, 2024 and 2025.
reply: I am informed by Revenue that the information available to them does not allow them to isolate the tax returned due to the deemed disposal rule from other events which give rise to a tax liability. Therefore, it is not possible to directly identify the tax revenue arising from the application of the deemed disposal rule. For Budget 2027, an estimate was made of the fiscal impact of removing the deemed disposal rule, based on overall levels of tax paid over the previous eight years and information received from some providers regarding the proportion of that tax that was paid under the deemed disposal rule. It was estimated that, based on the 38% rate of tax, removing deemed disposal would have an Exchequer cost of approximately €149 million in 2027.

question: Deputy Réada Cronin asked the Minister for Health whether any plan or pathway is under consideration to enable clinical embryologists to obtain CORU registration; whether she is aware that the current eligibility criteria for andrology posts in the HSE Regional Fertility Hubs exclude experienced clinical embryologists from applying.
reply:
Work is ongoing in my department to develop a framework to guide policy on the regulation of health and social care professionals into the future. The framework will modernise our approach to professional regulation both in terms of how decisions are made regarding professional regulation and the ways in which we regulate professions. The framework will be informed by an evidence and risk-based approach to regulation in line with requirements set out in the EU Proportionality Test Directive.
The issues to be considered regarding the proportionate degree of regulatory force required to protect the public are complex and this is therefore a significant project requiring considerable research and engagement with relevant stakeholders.
It should be noted that statutory regulation forms a part of a system of assurance that the Department utilises to mitigate risk posed to the public by the practise of health and social care professions. Many professions employed in the health service, including in the HSE and the publicly funded sector, are not subject to statutory regulation. For example, audiologists, clinical measurement physiologists, medical physicists, play therapists and play specialists, and perfusionists are among the non-regulated groups which are currently employed by the HSE.
Regulation of additional individual professions, including clinical embryologists, is not planned until the risk-based assessment framework is place in compliance with best practice, international

question: Deputy John Clendennen asked the Minister for Health the assessment undertaken of geographical loss of private maternity choice; and the impact that this may have on how a woman experiences her pregnancy.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 223 and 226 together.
As the Deputy will be aware, the Public Only Consultant Contract was introduced in March 2023 as a key step towards a universal, single-tier health service in which access to care is based on clinical need rather than ability to pay.
The POCC is applicable to all specialties, not just to maternity care. The transition to POCC will take place progressively as consultants are recruited to, or move to, the new contract. Consultants choosing that contract cannot continue to provide private practice in public hospitals after 31 December 2025. Consultants who remain on earlier contracts may continue to provide private care in public hospitals in accordance with their contractual arrangements. Accordingly, the change does not involve an immediate cessation of private maternity care. Private maternity care in public hospitals will therefore reduce gradually over time.
I recognise that this change may cause concern for some private patients. However, this reform supports equitable access to care based on clinical need.
Women with complex pregnancies will continue to receive appropriate consultant-led care. Care for women with high-risk pregnancies is led by a named consultant within the multidisciplinary team.
Maternity care in Ireland is provided in line with the National Maternity Strategy (NMS).

question: Deputy John Paul O'Shea asked the Minister for Health the position regarding the roll-out of the shingles vaccine for the over-65s as announced in budget 2027.
reply:
Ireland’s immunisation programme is informed by the advice of the National Immunisation Advisory Committee (NIAC). NIAC considers the prevalence of the relevant disease in Ireland as well as international best practice in relation to immunisation when developing its advice.
The current NIAC guidelines state that the shingles vaccine may be considered for those aged 65 years and older, due to the greater burden and severity of disease in this age group and in those aged 18 years and older at increased risk of shingles.
I can confirm that I have approved the introduction of a Shingles Vaccination Programme, in line with NIAC advice, to be implemented on a phased basis over 5 years, for immuno-compromised groups and persons aged 65 and over.
The programme is expected to commence in 2027, initially offering shingles vaccines to immuno-compromised groups. This will be followed by the 80 years and older cohort. The programme will conclude with the 65–69-year-old cohort.
It is expected that the vaccine will be administered in the main by GPs and Pharmacists. Further programme details will become available in due course.

question: Deputy Holly Cairns asked the Minister for Health to detail the location of all dedicated stem-cell transplantation units; whether her Department would consider the establishment of a dedicated unit in Cork; and to outline the work conducted by her Department to date on the matter.
reply:
The Government is committed to improving cancer care, ensuring better prevention, maintaining improvements in cancer survival rates, and facilitating timely access to treatments. This includes through the increased provision of access to advanced cellular therapies. Advanced cellular therapies are highly specialised treatments used in the management off a range of malignant and non-malignant diseases. These therapies require specialist multidisciplinary teams, dedicated laboratory facilities, tissue establishment infrastructure, specialised inpatient facilities and robust regulatory and accreditation arrangements.
Cellular therapies currently available in Ireland include autologous stem cell transplantation, allogeneic stem cell transplantation and chimeric antigen receptor T-cell (CAR-T) therapy. Adult Autologous Stem cell transplantation services are currently provided in St James's Hospital, University Hospital Galway and St Vincent's University Hospital. Adult allogeneic stem cell transplantation is currently provided through St James's Hospital.
The Government continues to progress the expansion of advanced cellular therapies nationally. In 2026, Beaumont Hospital was designated as an additional autologous stem cell transplantation and CAR-T Centre, working towards commencement of services in 2027.

question: Deputy Barry Heneghan asked the Minister for Health the current status of the HSE's full health technology assessment of budesonide orodispersible tablets (Jorveza, NCPE HTA ID 24014) for eosinophilic oesophagitis, commissioned on 25 June 2024; the reason no outcome has been published in over two years; and the expected date of a reimbursement decision.
reply:
Under the Health (Pricing and Supply of Medical Goods) Act 2013, the Health Service Executive (HSE) has statutory responsibility for decisions on the pricing and reimbursement of medicines.
The HSE received a complete application for pricing and reimbursement of budesonide (Jorveza®) on the 10th May 2024 from Dr Falk Pharma UK Ltd. (the applicant) for the treatment of eosinophilic esophagitis (EoE) in adults (older than 18 years).
The first step in the process is the submission of a Rapid Review dossier (a clinical and economic dossier) to the National Centre for Pharmacoeconomics (NCPE) for assessment. The HSE commissioned the Rapid Review process on the 15th May 2024.
The NCPE Rapid Review assessment report was received by the HSE on the 7th June 2024. The NCPE advised the HSE that a full health technology assessment (HTA) was recommended to assess the clinical effectiveness and cost effectiveness of budesonide compared with the current standard of care, on the basis of the proposed price relative to currently available therapies.
The HSE commissioned a full HTA on the 25th June 2024 as per agreed processes. The NCPE publishes details of medicines where the HSE has commissioned a Rapid Review assessment and / or a full HTA on their website. The website is updated at regular intervals and includes assessment outcomes and updates on reimbursement for each individual medicine and indication listed. Details of the assessment of budesonide (Jorveza®) are available at: www.ncpe.i

reply:

question: Deputy Pa Daly asked the Minister for Transport the reason provisions for the regulation of rickshaws have not been fully implemented; the regulations that currently govern the operation of rickshaws and similar passenger vehicles; the passenger safety requirements, insurance obligations and enforcement mechanisms that are presently in place; whether his Department intends to introduce a comprehensive licensing and regulatory regime for rickshaws; and the immediate steps that are being considered following the tragic circumstances of an event (details supplied).
reply:
For the Deputy's information, if a rickshaw is fitted with a small engine or electric motor of any kind, it is considered to be a mechanically propelled vehicle (MPV). Under road traffic law, if an MPV is used in a public place it is subject to all of the regulatory controls that apply to other vehicles i.e., it must be roadworthy, registered, taxed and comply with the following regulations:
• SI 190 of 1963 – Road Traffic Construction, Equipment and Use of Vehicles Regulations 1963.
• SI 189 of 1963 – Road Traffic Lighting of Vehicles Regulations 1963.
• SI 5 of 2003 – Road Traffic Construction and Use of Vehicles Regulations 2003.
The drivers of all vehicles on public roads, including motorised rickshaws, are required to comply with road traffic legislation and to behave in a safe manner paying due care to other road users. The enforcement of such road traffic legislation is a matter for An Garda Síochána.
A provision was contained in section 31 of the Road Traffic Act 2016, which was aimed at amending section 20 of the Taxi Regulation Act 2013, to allow the National Transport Authority (NTA) to make regulations for “non-motorised passenger transport” in towns and cities which includes rickshaws propelled by pedal cycle. It is important to note that the section 31 provision does not allow for the regulation of rickshaws with an electric motor, only non-motorised rickshaws. Section 31 was subsequently found not to be legally permissible and could not be commenced.

reply:
As Minister for Transport, I have responsibility for policy and overall funding in relation to public transport. The National Transport Authority has responsibility for the regulation of fares charged to passengers in respect of public transport services provided under public service obligation (PSO) contracts.
Third level students travelling from the South to third level institutions in Northern Ireland can avail of the 50% student/YAC reduction on the proportion of the journey carried out in the South. This means, for example, if 90% of the journey is through the South and the remaining 10% is through Northern Ireland, then the 50% discount will just apply to the 90% of the journey that is carried out within the State. The discount does not apply to the element of the journey that is carried out outside of the State.
The Young Adult Card initiative is an opt-in Scheme, meaning that while the discount is available on all PSO services, it is only available on those commercial bus operators that have decided to participate in the Scheme.
It is also important to note the National Transport Authority (NTA) has statutory responsibility for the regulation and approval of fares on public transport services operated under Public Service Obligation (PSO) contracts, within Ireland only. This includes determining fare structures and available ticket products for eligible passengers, such as those using Student Leap Cards and Young Adult (YAC) Leap Cards, across PSO-funded services.

question: Deputy Micheál Carrigy asked the Minister for Health the progress on the changing of the reimbursement process for new medicines.
reply:
Delivering timely access to medicines for patients is a priority for Government.
Two new Framework Agreements on the Supply and Pricing of Medicines (FASPM) between the State and Medicines for Ireland and the Irish Pharmaceutical Health Association respectively were signed on the 3rd of March for the period 2026-2029.
These Agreements include a commitment and a structured process towards achieving a 180-day timeline for reimbursement decisions by Q1 2029, accelerating patient access to new treatments.
In line with these agreements the Minister for Health commissioned a strategic end to end review of the Irish medicines pricing and reimbursement process and its functioning.
The review is considering every stage of the pricing and reimbursement process, including periods prior to application to the HSE and following reimbursement decision. The tender process for the end-to-end review has now concluded with Deloitte LLP identified as the successful applicant with the aim to have the review completed within an anticipated completion timeframe of 9 months following the start of the contract. Engagement between Deloitte LLP and all stakeholders in the process have now commenced and this work is ongoing.
Along with the other measures outlined in the Framework Agreements, implementation of recommendations arising from the end-to-end review will contribute to enabling faster reimbursement decisions for new medicines.

question: Deputy Pat Buckley asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality to increase funding and staff assessment of need teams and children’s disability network teams to eliminate the backlogs that delay formal diagnosis (details supplied).
reply:
Demand for Assessment of Need has increased significantly in recent years, with applications increasing from 4,700 in 2020 to over 13,000 in 2025, and some 7,100 applications received in the first six months of 2026. The level of demand has exceeded the capacity of the system to meet it and there were 23,282 AON reports overdue for completion by the end of June, according to the most recent data provided by the HSE to the Department.
However, there has also been progress over the past two years with a noticeable increase in the number of completed applications. reply:
I wish to thank the Deputy for the question in relation to the transposition of EU Directives that fall under the Department.
Gender Balance on Listed Corporate Boards.
At a European level, EU Directive 2022/2381 (on improving the gender balance among directors of listed companies and related measures) stipulates that at least 40% of the non-executive director positions in listed companies should be held by members of the under-represented sex by 2026. If Member States choose to apply the new rules to both executive and non-executive directors, 33% of all director positions should be held by under-represented sex by 2026.
This Department has fully transposed this EU Directive through the European Union (Gender Balance on Boards of Certain Companies) Regulations 2025 [S.I. No. 215/2025]. The Regulations applied the objective of relevant Boards having 40% of all non-executive Directors from the under-represented sex. Relevant companies will also need to set individual quantitative objectives to improve the gender balance on their executive director level.

There is no centralised waiting list for Early Learning and Care (ELC) or School-Age Childcare (SAC). As part of the early years sector profile survey, providers are asked whether they operate a waiting list and, where applicable, the number of entries on a waiting list for a place for their service. While this data can be used to give an indication of demand, it should not be used as a measure of overall demand for ELC or SAC places as it is vulnerable to overestimating the actual number of children requiring a place. An individual child may be on multiple waiting lists in different services and may remain on one or multiple service lists after taking up a place.

Data for the Early Years Sector Profile is typically captured in May/June of each programme year. question: Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Defence if she would consider the use of EU SAFE loans to amortise the costs of defence investment over the 30-year life of the equipment, as is done in other EU states, including France and Spain.
reply:
Since entering into force on 29 May 2025, the Security Action for Europe (SAFE) instrument has become a significant new EU mechanism, providing Member States with access to up to €150 billion in EU-backed loans to support national defence investment. A decision was taken in August 2025, in conjunction with the Department of Finance and the Department of Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation that Ireland would not draw down funding via the loan mechanism. However, Ireland is fully committed to taking advantage of joint procurement opportunities available under SAFE, where these projects are aligned with our capability development plans.
Any decision on Ireland drawing down SAFE loans would require the support of both the Department of Finance and the Department of Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation. In that context, any decision to avail of SAFE funding mechanisms will be considered as part of a broader assessment of defence investment priorities, including those set out under the forthcoming Capability Development Programme (2028-2040).

question: Deputy Naoise Ó Muirí asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality the number of families who avail of core funding, by band, in tabular form.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 153 and 154 together.
The National Childcare Scheme (NCS) is designed to substantially reduce costs to families using eligible early learning and childcare. It is designed to be flexible, recognising that early learning and childcare needs are different for each family.
The NCS is designed to fit around the needs of families. The family agrees the number of hours to be used with provider and (within overall scheme limits) these hours are registered with the scheme administrator. Those hours can be used over any number of days within the week. There are no restrictions on the attendance pattern of families or the number of days they use. The family only needs to agree with the provider the number of hours.
It is however a matter for the provider to decide their service offer. The different fee “bands” correspond to different numbers of hours per week. The “Band F” fee cap applies solely to places that are provided for 50 or more hours per week. Providers respond to parental choice, and a provider’s decision to offer a “Band F” fee may respond to parental demand for places for 50+ hours.
Providers offer a diverse range of service offers and many offer options in different Fee Bands. Some services offer both early learning and care and school age childcare, some services offer early learning and care only and some offer school-age childcare only. Some services operate in term only, while others are year-round and their fee options vary - in term

question: Deputy Paul Nicholas Gogarty asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality whether she has considered extending statutory paid paternity leave from the current entitlement of two weeks to at least eight weeks; if her Department has undertaken any assessment of the social, economic and family benefits associated with longer periods of paternity leave, including impacts on child development, maternal wellbeing, gender equality and workforce participation; and his plans or a timeline for increasing paternity leave entitlements in line with best practice in other European countries.
reply:
There have been significant developments in entitlements for parents of working families in recent years. The Government is committed to supporting workers, including by extending paid leave for parents to allow them to spend more time with their child during their earliest years.
The Paternity Leave and Benefit Act 2016 provides the relevant parent (other than the mother of the child) with 2 weeks paid Paternity Leave. Ireland's statutory Paternity Leave arrangements are fully aligned with the requirements of the EU Work-Life Balance Directive, which introduced a minimum standard for Paternity Leave across EU Member States.
Under the Parent’s Leave and Benefit Act 2019, working parents are also entitled to nine weeks of paid Parent's Leave for each relevant parent, to be taken in the first two years after the birth or adoptive placement of a child. Parent's Leave is an individual separate entitlement and is non-transferable between parents.
Under the Parental Leave (Amendment) Act 2019, an employee who is a relevant parent in respect of a child under the age 12 is entitled to 26 weeks’ unpaid Parental Leave for each child. Where a child has a disability or long-term illness, the entitlement can continue until the child is 16. A relevant parent is a parent, an adoptive parent, or a person acting in ‘loco parentis’. Both parents have an equal, separate entitlement to Parental Leave.

question: Deputy Pearse Doherty asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine if assistance can be provided to a returning emigrant (details supplied) to locate a suitable location in Dublin Port to offload personal items from a container.
reply:
My Department carries out Sanitary and Phytosanitary (SPS) checks on certain goods and machinery imported into the EU from third countries at designated Border Control Posts (BCPs). This consignment, which entered Dublin Port under a Transfer of Residence (TOR), contained a used tractor/part and wood packaging material (WPM), which are regulated and pose a plant health risk.
A valid phytosanitary certificate must accompany used machinery/parts; no certificate was furnished for the tractor. Wood Packaging Material must comply with International Standards for Phytosanitary Measures No. 15 (ISPM 15); the markings which indicate compliance were absent.
The options available for rejected consignments are re-export to a third country or destruction. My Department's BCP team and Revenue have engaged with the individual in question to arrange the detention of the controlled goods while facilitating the release of the remainder of the consignment. It was agreed that a Customs Bonded Warehouse (CBW) could be used to complete this process. My Department is currently awaiting receipt of a selected CBW and an application for a plant health registration to progress this matter and bring it to a conclusion. My Department remains ready to assist the individual in question with any clarifications they may require.

question: Deputy Mattie McGrath asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine his views on the impact of high aluminium levels in the public water supply in South Tipperary which has found to be as high as 12 times the prescribed EU level; the impact that this may have on animals and our food systems as animals have been drinking this water for some period of time; the guidance available from his Department in relation to the safe levels of aluminium for livestock; if he will examine this matter; and issue guidance on the matter for farmers who are seeking guidance.
reply: My Department has reviewed the concentrations of aluminium identified in water in this case, and the conclusion is that the current risk to animal health, and the food chain, is negligible . Additionally, my Regional Veterinary Laboratory Service has not received any reports of an increase in specific animal health problems over the same period (September to October) that could be related to this matter.

question: Deputy Michael Healy-Rae asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine the work carried out in relation to the formulation of a new forestry programme; and the engagement that has been carried out at an EU level.
reply:
The formulation of the Forestry Programme post-2027 is currently underway. My Department is working actively to ensure the inclusion of diverse stakeholder perspectives across the forestry sector, and that future forestry policy and programme design are informed by robust evidence. To date, this has included deliberate engagement with key stakeholder groups, behavioural analysis of landowner decision-making, and structured workshops.
My Department has published a Public Attitudes Survey on Forestry 2026 which built on our 2021 benchmark study.
Ireland’s Forestry Programmes requires State Aid approval from the European Commission. My Department will continue to engage with the Commission in this regard.
In respect of ongoing consultation with stakeholders my Department will facilitate a series of focussed regional stakeholder workshops planned in the coming weeks.
I am focussed on building on the potential contained in our current Forestry Programme 2023-2027 for the post 2027 period, so that we can continue to deliver lasting multifunctional benefits from forest for climate change, biodiversity, wood production, economic development alongside quality of life.

reply:

The modular units delivered under the Rapid Build Programme, were developed in the first instance to temporarily accommodate people fleeing the war in Ukraine. In total, 654 homes were built across 11 locations, accommodating 2,640 people in family units of four, with children.

question: Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if it is part of his Department's strategy to reduce numbers in IPAS accommodation by moving persons who have been given leave to stay into homeless accommodation.
reply:
The International Protection Accommodation Service (IPAS) is currently accommodating nearly 32,000 residents, including just over 4,500 people who have completed their application process and have received a positive decision. This means they have a legal status that allows them to remain in Ireland.
It also means that they are no longer entitled to IPAS accommodation. However, they are now able to access the full range of social protection schemes and housing supports available to all Irish residents. These housing supports are not available to people who are still going through the international protection application process.
The IPAS accommodation system receives new applicants on a daily basis. It is not sustainable for the system to continue accommodating individuals indefinitely who have already been granted status while new applicants are arriving who require accommodation under the State’s legal obligations. IPAS must prioritise accommodation for international protection applicants who are entitled to accommodation under the International Protection Act 2026.
People who have held status for a considerable period - generally six months for single people and couples, and twelve months for families - are supported and encouraged to secure accommodation in the community. If they are unable to do so they may be transferred to IPAS emergency accommodation, where necessary. This approach ensures that IPAS accommodation can remain available for newly arriving applicants.

question: Deputy Ruairí Ó Murchú asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of fully qualified, active registered intermediaries currently available to assist vulnerable or non-speaking victims during Garda interviews and court proceedings; and the specific target date by which a mandatory, nationwide panel will be fully operational.
reply:
Section 14 of the Criminal Evidence Act 1992, as amended, provides for the appointment of intermediaries to assist vulnerable victims and witnesses in giving evidence where the court considers such assistance necessary in the interests of justice.
In response to recommendations of the Review of Protections for Vulnerable Witnesses in the Investigation and Prosecution of Sexual Offences (the O'Malley Review), carried out in 2020, and the commitments set out in Supporting a Victim's Journey, my Department partnered with the University of Limerick (UL) to establish a pilot project for the training of registered intermediaries. The project was initially established for a three-year period, was subsequently extended for a further year, and is now complete.
As part of the project, UL developed and delivered the Professional Diploma in Intermediary Studies, a one-year, part-time programme designed to provide suitably qualified professionals with specialist intermediary training.
The programme has supported the establishment of a nationwide Registered Intermediary Panel, which is now operational. The national Register of Intermediaries is maintained by the Courts Service and currently lists 23 intermediaries. The register is publicly available on the Courts Service website. To be included on the register, applicants must have successfully completed the UL Diploma and have at least three years' practice experience as a CORU-registered Speech and Language Therapist, Occupational Therap

question: Deputy Ruth Coppinger asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration to expediate the appeals students from Palestine have brought forward to challenge the decision of his Department to refuse visas for these students.
reply:
I am aware of the exceptionally difficult circumstances facing applicants from Gaza and the profound disruption caused by the ongoing conflict.
Visa and preclearance applications provide legal avenues for people moving to Ireland and to facilitate visitors who wish to travel for business and/or tourism. These are important screening processes, designed to establish that a person has a legitimate reason to come to Ireland prior to travel. Verifying an application is an important part of our immigration system. Each visa application is assessed on its own merits, taking all relevant information into consideration at that time.
Where a visa application is refused, the reasons for refusal are set out in the decision letter issued to the applicant. Applicants may appeal a refusal, and information on how to submit an appeal is provided with the decision letter. The visa appeal process involves a full consideration of the application. This provides applicants with an opportunity to address the reasons for refusal and to submit additional information or supporting documentation for consideration. Appeals are examined having regard to all information available, including any new material submitted in support of the appeal.
My Department is conscious of the importance of these applications for the students concerned and will continue to process appeals as expeditiously as possible. Decisions are communicated directly to applicants as soon as full consideration of an appeal has been com

question: Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the position regarding the number of prosecutions brought forward under Section 2 (2) of the Criminal Law (Suicide) Act, 1993 since this Act was signed into law.
reply:
The Criminal Law (Suicide) Act, 1993, de-criminalised suicide itself but the offence of assisting suicide was retained and put on statutory footing. Under section 2(2) of the 1993 Act, it is an offence for a person to aid, abet, counsel or procure the suicide or an attempt at suicide of another person. The offence has a maximum penalty of 14 years imprisonment on conviction on indictment. The severe penalty was to cover situations where a person deliberately procured the suicide of another for his or her own motives.
Prosecutions are a matter for the Director of Public Prosecutions (DPP). The DPP is wholly independent in her functions under Section 2(5) of the Prosecution of Offences Act 1974 (as amended). As Minister I have no role in the operations, functions, oversight or governance of the Office of the DPP, which is an independent statutory agency that does not come under my remit. As such I am unable to provide any statistical information on the work of the Office of the DPP.

question: Deputy Natasha Newsome Drennan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration when regulations for drug testing of serving Garda members will be finalised and introduced.
reply:
The vast majority of members of An Garda Síochána serve the State with distinction, professionalism and integrity throughout their careers. It is essential that the culture within any disciplined organisation, including An Garda Síochána, is one that promotes the highest standards of conduct and makes clear that inappropriate behaviour has no place within the organisation.
Professionalism, integrity and accountability are core values that are instilled from the earliest stages of Garda training and reinforced throughout every rank and grade of the organisation. Maintaining public trust and confidence requires a continued commitment to these values at every level of An Garda Síochána.
Officials from my Department are working closely with An Garda Síochána and with drafters in the Office of the Attorney General to finalise the Regulations which will underpin testing for controlled drugs and psychoactive substances. The Regulations are complex and have required thorough consideration but are now at an advanced stage of drafting.
It is hoped that the Regulations will soon be finalised and it will then be open to An Garda Síochána to fully implement this new testing regime.

question: Deputy Peadar Tóibín asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of applications for citizenship granted for the last 15 years for whom there were no checks of financial self sufficiency at all.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 117, 122 and 123 together.
All applications for a certificate of naturalisation are considered individually in accordance with the Irish Nationality and Citizenship Act 1956, as amended.
Applicants are required to have five years' reckonable residence in the State prior to making an application, except for spouses of Irish nationals, for whom the requirement is three years. In all cases, the final 12 months must be continuous residence in the State, with up to 70 days allowed to facilitate foreign travel for business, family or holiday purposes.
All applicants are required to satisfy the good character criterion under section 15 of the Irish Nationality and Citizenship Act 1956, as amended. Adult applicants must undertake the Garda e-Vetting process, or such other police-vetting processes as may be deemed necessary. As part of the good character assessment, An Garda Síochána is requested to make enquiries into an applicant's background, the detail and extent of which are matters for An Garda Síochána.
There is currently no statutory requirement for an applicant for naturalisation to undergo a verbal interview or to satisfy a financial self-sufficiency test. Accordingly, the Department does not compile statistics in the form sought by the Deputy.

reply:
Peace Commissioners are appointed by the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration in accordance with section 88 of the Courts of Justice Act 1924. The appointment of a Peace Commissioner is entirely at the discretion of the Minister. The fact that an applicant or nominee may be suitable for appointment does not, in itself, provide any entitlement to appointment as a Peace Commissioner; other factors, such as the need for appointments in particular areas at a specific point in time, may be taken into account.

question: Deputy Mairéad Farrell asked the Minister for Social Protection if he is aware of Irish citizens, who have worked abroad, draw their pensions from abroad and therefore are excluded from supports such as the living alone Increase and certain age-related benefits on the grounds that they do not qualify for an Irish State pension or related contributory payments are also; and if he plans to change this.

reply:

reply:

School Meals suppliers are subject to the same high standards, inspection regimes and enforcement measures as all other registered food businesses.
The Department of Health advised my Department on 24 September 2026 that a Closure Order has been served by the HSE National Environmental Health Service on a food business operator in Timahoe GAA, Páirc Mochua, Cremorgan, Timahoe, Portlaoise, Co. Laois.

Officials from my Department contacted the supplier who advised only one school was being served from the affected premises and that food provision for this school has been moved to a neighboring Heating hub.
Closure Orders and Improvement Orders remain listed in the enforcement reports on the Food Safety Authority website for a period of three months from the date of when a premises is adjudged to have corrected its food safety issue.

• Having entered the Social Insurance system 10 years before drawdown of the SPC.
• Having a minimum of 520 paid social insurance contributions (i.e., 10 years reckonable PRSI contributions).
