question: Deputy Ciarán Ahern asked the Minister for Social Protection his views on a policy matter (details supplied); and the reason his Department will not accept a letter from a hospital as proof of illness for illness benefit claims.
reply:
Illness Benefit is a scheme to support applicants if they cannot work in the short term due to illness. Illness must be certified by a doctor.
The Department primarily accepts medical certification from general practitioners on the department’s certifier panel in the form of a Med1/eCert. The institution that a general practitioner works for is not a deciding factor on whether they can join the panel. All panelists must be registered with the Irish Medical Council, sign a declaration confirming that they have received and read the Medical Certifiers Guide, the Closed Certification Guidelines issued to them, and that they will adhere to the policies and procedures outlined in the two documents when issuing medical certificates.
The acceptance of non-electronically submitted medical certificates requires significant manual intervention and can cause delays in deciding claims and awarding payment to customers. For this reason, it is the strong preference of the department to receive medical certificates in electronic format via secure means (HSE Healthlink). In general, medical certification must be submitted on the department’s official forms (either electronic or physical).
Following a review in 2025, the acceptance criteria was expanded to include short-term certificates of incapacity from hospital doctors for both inpatients and outpatients. It should be noted that the department has a large team of medical practitioners, who were involved in the consultative process.

question: Deputy Michael Healy-Rae asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage his plans to review the terms and conditions for long term tenants living in a Part V local authority house who want to purchase their property under the tenant purchase scheme.
reply:
The Tenant (Incremental) Purchase Scheme 2016 is open to eligible tenants of local authority houses that are available for sale under the scheme. The scheme is underpinned by the Housing (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 2014 and the Housing (Sale of Local Authority Houses) Regulations 2015, as amended by the Housing (Sale of Local Authority Houses) (Amendment) Regulations 2023.
The regulations provide for a number of specified classes of houses to be excluded from sale, including those provided to local authorities under Part V of the Planning and Development Act 2000. The Part V provisions seek to promote social integration and secure mixed tenure, sustainable communities. Accordingly, Part V properties are excluded from the scheme to ensure the original policy goals of the legislation are not eroded over time and the properties remain available for people in need of social housing support.
Several other classes of house are excluded from sale within the regulations underpinning the scheme, including, for example, houses specifically designed for occupation by older people, group traveller housing and houses provided for persons with disabilities moving from congregated settings to community based living.

question: Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Taoiseach to provide an update, including the publication date, of the National Security Strategy.
reply:
The Government is committed to the delivery of a National Security Strategy in the coming months. Work is ongoing in finalising drafting the strategy, integrating inputs from a range of relevant stakeholders, including the Departments of Foreign Affairs and Trade; Defence; Justice, Home Affairs and Migration; An Garda Síochána; the Defence Forces and National Cyber Security Centre. This work is co-ordinated by the National Security Secretariat in my Department.
The preparation of a draft strategy covers a broad range of national security issues. There will be a focus on the State’s internal security, including the evolving challenges we face from terrorism and extremism and from cyber threats, and a focus on the need to increase investment in security and to modernise our legislation in the security field, notably in the investigatory powers available to our security services. The ongoing implementation of the Report of the Commission on the Defence Forces and the modernisation of key aspects of our defence legislation are also included in the preparations.

reply:
I am aware of recent commentary regarding the Understanding Management & Adult ADHD Programme (UMAAP) delivered by ADHD Ireland. Following direct engagement with the Chief Executive Officer of ADHD Ireland, I can clarify that there has been no reduction in Government or HSE funding for the UMAAP programme.
ADHD Ireland has confirmed that it will receive the same level of HSE funding for UMAAP in 2026 as it has received in previous years. While the organisation recently issued a fundraising appeal, I am advised that this was not the result of any reduction in State funding. I am a strong supporter of ADHD Ireland and of the vital role the UMAAP programme plays in providing information, education and peer support to adults with ADHD and their families. I previously secured recurring annual funding for the programme, and that funding has been ringfenced since 2024 in recognition of the programme's value and impact.
Based on my Office's engagement with ADHD Ireland, I understand that the organisation remains committed to the delivery of UMAAP and to supporting those who rely on its services and participants will be able to join the programme as normal in November and December. reply:
The development of Specialist Mental Health Services, including for adults with ADHD, has been a priority since my appointment as Minister for Mental Health in 2020. Deputy Paul Murphy asked the Minister for Health the reason children with neurological issues who had hip dysplasia operations are being excluded from the proposed commission of inquiry; the number of children who are being excluded on this basis; and the percentage of the total number of affected children.
reply:
I appointed Mr. Remy Farrell, Senior Counsel, as the independent facilitator of the CHI Inquiry into Spina Bifida and Complex Scoliosis Scoping Exercise and he commenced his work on 3 March. During the process, Mr. Farrell wrote to me requesting that hip dysplasia be included within his terms of reference and I agreed to this request.
Mr. Farrell’s independent report was published by me on 28 September. Mr. Farrell recommends a Commission of Investigation covering four defined modules on waiting lists, spinal surgery, hip dysplasia and the cohort of children who were not transferred to Temple Street post 2008.
Mr. Farrell recommends that a Commission would examine the threshold used for hip dysplasia surgery in Temple Street and Cappagh between 2019-2025 and whether surgery was recommended appropriately, whether thresholds differed from accepted practice, whether management knew of any divergence, and why it occurred. The report recommends that the hip dysplasia module of the Commission be informed by the External Expert Review Panel which is expected to offer broad expert assessment on surgical thresholds and help define the key issues that the Commission should examine.
I have asked the HSE to reply directly to the deputy in relation to which groups of patients are included in the External Expert Panel.

question: Deputy Naoise Ó Cearúil asked the Minister for Health whether any pathway is under consideration to enable clinical embryologists to obtain CORU registration or otherwise permit suitably qualified clinical embryologists to be employed in andrology roles within the HSE; whether her Department or the HSE has reviewed the eligibility criteria currently applied to andrology posts in the regional fertility hubs.
reply:
Work is ongoing in my department to develop a framework to guide policy on the regulation of health and social care professionals into the future. The framework will modernise our approach to professional regulation both in terms of how decisions are made regarding professional regulation and the ways in which we regulate professions. The framework will be informed by an evidence and risk-based approach to regulation in line with requirements set out in the EU Proportionality Test Directive.
The issues to be considered regarding the proportionate degree of regulatory force required to protect the public are complex and this is therefore a significant project requiring considerable research and engagement with relevant stakeholders.
It should be noted that statutory regulation forms a part of a system of assurance that the Department utilises to mitigate risk posed to the public by the practise of health and social care professions. Many professions employed in the health service, including in the HSE and the publicly funded sector, are not subject to statutory regulation. For example, audiologists, clinical measurement physiologists, medical physicists, play therapists and play specialists, and perfusionists are among the non-regulated groups which are currently employed by the HSE.
Regulation of additional individual professions, including clinical embryologists, is not planned until the risk-based assessment framework is place in compliance with best practice, international

question: Deputy Ivana Bacik asked the Minister for Health further to Parliamentary Question No. 774 of 29 September 2026, if forthcoming amendments to assisted human reproduction legislation will apply retrospectively to children born prior to the commencement date of that legislation.
reply:
As outlined to the Deputy in my reply to PQ No. 774 the Health (Assisted Human Reproduction) (Amendment) Bill contains amendments to the Children and Family Relationships Act 2015.
It is proposed that the amendments will address the circumstances where a donor-conceived child has been born abroad following a donor assisted human reproduction (DAHR) procedure undertaken in a DAHR facility in Ireland and in accordance with Parts 2 and 3 of the Children and Family Relationships Act 2015.
While drafting of the amending Bill is at an advanced stage, as the process has not yet been completed, and as the provisions contained in the final draft of the amending Bill will ultimately be a matter for the Oireachtas, it is not possible to state definitively at this time how they will apply in practice.
I would like to assure the Deputy that I remain committed to enacting these provisions which will provide legal certainty for families undertaking DAHR in the circumstances described.

question: Deputy Peadar Tóibín asked the Minister for Health the supports available to patients who experience complications arising from treatment obtained under the Cross-Border Healthcare Directive or the treatment abroad scheme; the body responsible for assisting patients where difficulties arise in accessing follow-up care in Ireland after such treatment; and whether any advocacy or support groups are funded or recognised by the HSE for persons in these circumstances.
reply:
Under the terms of the EU Cross Border Directive (CBD), where a patient has received healthcare abroad, in another EU/EEA country under the provisions of the CBD, and medical follow-up proves necessary the home country (in this case Ireland) is obliged to provide the patient with the same follow-up treatment it would have provided had the treatment taken place on its territory. In relation to the Treatment Abroad Scheme (TAS), in general once a patient is discharged from an approved specific episode of care abroad, their care immediately reverts to their referring public consultant based in Ireland.
As this is a service matter, I have asked the Health Service Executive to respond to the Deputy directly, as soon as possible.

question: Deputy Paul Murphy asked the Minister for Health to provide details about the new dual diagnosis team in Dublin South-West to support people experiencing both mental health difficulties and addiction, which was announced in the context of budget 2027 (details supplied); including whether it will be provided in a hospital setting or within the community; and when it will be operational.
reply:
Dual diagnosis means a person experiences both a substance abuse problem and a mental health issue such as depression or an anxiety disorder.
Dual Diagnosis services must address both issues, and as such the HSE have developed a Model of Care which recommends the development of 12 Adult Specialist Dual Diagnosis Community Teams nationally, 4 Adolescent Hub Community Teams, and a National Dual Diagnosis Rehabilitation Centre. To date funding of over €5 million has resulted in the roll out of the Dual Diagnosis teams. Five Dual Diagnosis teams are being recruited into and developed at present – adult teams in Limerick and Cork commenced treatment services in 2024, and two further teams in are in recruitment. Two Adolescent hub teams in Dublin have also been developed, supported by funding from HSE Social Inclusion. Funding was also provided for a Dual Diagnosis Day Programme in Dublin.
Under Budget 2027, funding has been allocated for an additional Dual Diagnosis team for Dublin South West.
As occurs each year following the Budget, discussions will now take place with the HSE on the detailed allocation of resources and implementation of specific service initiatives through the HSE National Service Plan 2027, including mental health services.

question: Deputy Albert Dolan asked the Minister for Health the status of access to an insulin pump (details supplied) for children with type 1 diabetes; the engagement the HSE has had with the organisation for access; the barriers that remain to a pricing and reimbursement application; the way these are being addressed; whether an interim or exceptional access pathway could be considered for very young children where clinically appropriate; and the specific steps and indicative timeline that can be provided for access in Ireland, having regard to planned launches elsewhere in Europe.
reply:
For a product to be considered for addition to the Reimbursement List, the company must submit a pricing and reimbursement application to the HSE under the Health (Pricing and Supply of Medical Goods) Act 2013. To date, an application has not been made for Omnipod® 5 by the company to the HSE.
Clinical and cost-effectiveness assessments are carried out after a company submits a pricing and reimbursement application to the HSE. As such no such assessment has been carried out.
The HSE has advised that the company has not yet launched the product to the Irish market. Omnipod® 5 is being rolled out world-wide on a phased basis due to constraints in manufacturing capacity versus demand and the company has informed the HSE that they do not yet have a timeline for launch in Ireland.
On the 21st of May, The Diabetes Policy and Services Review: A Strategy for Better Care was launched by the Minister for Health.
This is Ireland’s first national strategy for diabetes. It sets out recommendations for action in relation to type 1 diabetes, type 2 diabetes, diabetes in pregnancy and paediatric diabetes. The strategy marks a major milestone in diabetes care in Ireland, representing the development of a unified approach to the delivery of diabetes care.

reply:
The Long-Term Illness (LTI) Scheme was established under Section 59(3) of the Health Act 1970 (as amended). Regulations were made in 1971, 1973 and 1975, prescribing 16 conditions to be covered by the Scheme. Further information, including the list of conditions, can be found at:
www2.hse.ie/services/schemes-allowances/lti/about/
Under the LTI Scheme, patients receive drugs, medicines, and medical and surgical appliances directly related to the treatment of their illness, free of charge. While there are currently no plans to extend the list of conditions, it is important to remember that the LTI Scheme exists within a wider eligibility framework.
Individuals and families in Ireland may be entitled to the following schemes:

• In circumstances where an applicant is still over the income limit for a medical card, they are then assessed for a GP visit card, which entitles the applicant to GP visits without charge.

question: Deputy Barry Heneghan asked the Minister for Health her plans to introduce free shingles vaccination for people aged 65 and over; and the expected timeline for its introduction.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 882 and 1039 together.
Ireland’s immunisation programme is informed by the advice of the National Immunisation Advisory Committee (NIAC). NIAC considers the prevalence of the relevant disease in Ireland as well as international best practice in relation to immunisation when developing its advice.
The current NIAC guidelines state that the shingles vaccine may be considered for those aged 65 years and older, due to the greater burden and severity of disease in this age group and in those aged 18 years and older at increased risk of shingles.
I can confirm that I have approved the introduction of a Shingles Vaccination Programme, in line with NIAC advice, to be implemented on a phased basis over 5 years, for immuno-compromised groups and persons aged 65 and over.
The programme is expected to commence in 2027, initially offering shingles vaccines to immuno-compromised groups. This will be followed by the 80 years and older cohort. The programme will conclude with the 65–69-year-old cohort.
It is expected that the vaccine will be administered in the main by GPs and Pharmacists. Further programme details will become available in due course.

question: Deputy Robert Troy asked the Minister for Health if she will expedite an appointment for surgery, for a person (details supplied), or refer this patient through the treatment purchase fund.
reply:
The National Treatment Purchase Fund (NTPF) works with public hospitals, as opposed to with patients directly, to offer and provide the funding for treatment to clinically suitable long waiting patients who are on a public hospital waiting list.
The key criteria of the NTPF is the prioritisation of the longest waiting patients first. While the NTPF identifies patients eligible for NTPF treatment, it is solely on the basis of their time spent on the Inpatient/Daycase Waiting List. The clinical suitability of the patient to avail of NTPF funded treatment is determined by the public hospital. The availability of capacity for the specific procedure required by the patient is a factor in an offer of treatment being made and in the selection of treatment provider.

question: Deputy Darren O'Rourke asked the Minister for Health if a GP is entitled to charge a patient for, and only for, referring them to a private hospital or public hospital for a consultation.
reply:
GPs are private practitioners, most of whom hold a GMS contract with the HSE for the provision of GP services without charge to medical card and GP visit card holders.
Under the terms of the GMS contract, GPs are required to provide eligible patients, medical card and GP visit card holders, with ''all proper and necessary treatment of a kind usually undertaken by a general practitioner and not requiring special skill or experience of a degree or kind which general practitioners cannot reasonably be expected to possess". Persons who hold a medical card or a GP visit card are not subject to any co-payments or other charges in respect of such services.
Patients who do not hold a medical card or GP visit card attend their GP on a private basis. Services provided outside of the GMS contract are a matter of private contract between patient and the GP concerned.
Following a medical consultation, the decision to refer a patient for further medical services or to a consultant is a clinical determination made by the medical practitioner concerned based on an evaluation of the patient's symptoms and medical history.

reply:

question: Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality the position regarding any review of the national childcare scheme particularly in relation to the lack of flexibility afforded to parents who choose not to take the full-time allotted due to differing working arrangements outside the traditional 9-5pm pattern.
reply:
The NCS is designed to be flexible, recognising that early learning and childcare needs are different for each family. Under the NCS, subsidies are awarded as an hourly rate, up to a maximum number of 45 hours a week for which the subsidy applies.
The hours-based nature of the NCS is designed to fit around the needs of families and ensure that the effectiveness of funding is maximised for all. The NCS enables families to agree the number of hours to be used with their service provider within overall scheme limits. The number of hours can be altered week to week so, for example the subsidy can be increased during a school midterm where a parent requires more hours of care.
The Department designed the NCS to also be flexible around children’s attendance, recognising that children’s attendance may vary from week to week. If a child is occasionally picked up early or misses an occasional day, this will not impact on a family’s subsidy.
This combination of flexibility and accountability provides an appropriate balance of supporting parents and providers while also ensuring the efficient use of Exchequer funding.
In relation to the independent evaluation of the National Childcare Scheme (NCS), the review commenced in March 2026 following a procurement tendering process which launched in late 2025. question: Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality the position regarding any review of section 8.2/8.3.2 to allow certified extracurricular activities to count toward registered attendance hours under NCS attendance rules; and if she believes the current scheme disincentivises families to include their children in sporting or other afterschool activities.
reply:
Many families avail of the National Childcare Scheme (NCS) as a way to reduce the cost of their early learning and childcare. NCS subsidies are awarded as an hourly rate, along with a maximum number of weekly hours that the subsidy will be paid for. It is between the parent and provider to agree on the hours of childcare based on the family's requirements and what sessions the provider can offer.
The accurate recording of a child’s attendance is a core obligation under the Child Care Act 1991 (Early Years Services) Regulations 2016 for early years providers and is one of the conditions set out in the NCS funding agreement.
This said, the rules of the Scheme are designed to be very flexible. Children can under-attend services for a consecutive 12 weeks before action is taken. The Department recognises that there are many reasons why a child’s attendance may be occasionally less than their agreed hours. For instance, a parent may be able to collect their child earlier than usual because of the child's extracurricular schedule. It is only if continual under-attendance is recorded for a consecutive 12 weeks that the award will be revised to reflect the child’s actual hours.
In full detail, if a child attends fewer than their agreed hours for a consecutive 8 week period, the provider must notify the scheme administrator and a warning will issue to the parent alerting them to the situation. question: Deputy Micheál Carrigy asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality whether she will direct the Decision Support Service to establish regional, in-person support clinics and paper-based application streams to reduce administrative barriers for adults with intellectual disabilities and their families, as highlighted in a report (details supplied).

question: Deputy Micheál Carrigy asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality the mandatory interim safeguarding directives or circulars issued by her Department to the Health Service Executive to protect vulnerable residents in congregated disability settings from abuse and communication barriers, pending the enactment of comprehensive adult safeguarding legislation.
reply:
This Government is committed to ensuring that residential services for people with disabilities provide a good quality service that is safe, effective, and provides a home from home environment for residents.
In respect of congregated settings, Article 19 of the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (UNCRPD) states that all individuals have the right to live independently and be included in the community, it is an equal right of all persons to live in the community and have choices equal to others. Article 19(c) states that all individuals must have the opportunity to choose their place of residence and where and with whom they live, they are not obliged to live in a particular living arrangement such as a residential institution.
In line with the UNCRPD and the Transforming Lives Policy, Disability Services are being reformed, developed and reconfigured to support and enable people with disabilities to live in their own homes and communities, through services, supports and environments designed and adapted as necessary to meet their needs.
Time to Move on from congregated settings was established under the Transforming Lives Programme. It is a model of support where people with disabilities are supported to move from congregated settings, often large institutions to their own homes in the community, with the supports they need.
This Government is committed to the implementation of Time to Move on, as outlined in the Programme for Government and Budget 2027

question: Deputy Emer Currie asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality the timing and publication of the review on the work life balance Bill provisions for flexible working, including consideration of extending the right to request flexible work to everyone.
reply:
The Work Life Balance and Miscellaneous Provisions Act 2023 complements existing family leaves by providing additional flexibility to ensure that workers are supported in balancing their work and private lives.
The Act introduced important entitlements for workers, including five days leave for medical care purposes and an extension to the entitlement to breastfeeding breaks. It also introduced the right to request remote working for all employees and the right to request flexible working for parents and carers in line with Article 9 of the Directive EU 2019/1158.
Remote, hybrid and flexible working represent a significant opportunity for creating a more inclusive labour market and society, particularly for people with caring responsibilities, people returning to the workforce, older people, people with disabilities and people facing long commutes in the context of high fuel costs. This in turn provides employers with access to a larger talent pool, with remote and hybrid options representing powerful tools for staff recruitment and retention which improves economic performance and labour market access overall.

question: Deputy Cian O'Callaghan asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality the steps her Department will take to protect families whose childcare providers do not participate in core funding; whether alternative affordability measures or incentives could be introduced to encourage providers to rejoin the core funding scheme; and if her Department has considered ways in which parents can be protected from substantial fee differences when they have limited practical alternatives for childcare.
reply:

This is to ensure that the State’s significant investment through the Scheme is not absorbed by unnecessary fee increases.
These fee management conditions of the Core Funding Scheme apply exclusively to Partner Services who have signed a Core Funding Agreement. These regulations are not applied to services which remain outside of the Core Funding scheme.

The Department, through the local Childcare Committees, engages directly with any such service to highlight the benefits of staying in Core Funding, not only for their services but also for the families who avail of them. I am hopeful that the providers may reconsider their decision.

question: Deputy Colm Burke asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality to confirm that the entirety of funding for a person (details supplied) to attend an adult disability day placement will urgently be made available, due to the needs of the person and that a start date has not yet been provided to date.
reply:
HSE-funded day programmes for people with intellectual disabilities, autism, or complex physical disabilities include a range of centre-based and community-based activities. Access to services is based on an individual’s needs rather than on their diagnosis. The focus is on supporting people to participate in the mainstream activities and in the life of their community, in line with their wishes and needs.
Day services are a vital support for adult with disabilities to participate in the life of their community and to realise their own ambitions and desires. The majority of young people due to leave school in a given year that require a HSE funded day service have been profiled by the end of the previous year to establish their support needs. Once needs are identified, referrals are made to the service provider of choice, funding is committed and negotiations are concluded with providers by end of May to confirm placements to young people and their families. In many instances young people due to leave school at end of June are introduced to their day services for trialling purposes during April, May and June so there is a natural transition into day services in September.

reply:
Under the rules of the National Childcare Scheme (NCS), it is the responsibility of the parent to provide the CHICK to their early learning and childcare once an award has issued. The Provider can then register the CHICK and create an associated claim, which must be confirmed by the parent before subsidy payments can commence.
Where a CHICK is not supplied to the childcare provider, a registration is not created and the subsidy cannot be applied to the family's childcare fees.
While I understand that the applicant sought to pursue a review after becoming aware of the issue, the review process is generally intended to consider matters relating to eligibility, assessments or award decisions. The issue outlined in the correspondence arises from the fact that the subsidy was not activated with the childcare provider, rather than from an incorrect assessment or award etc. This said, Department officials are investigating the matter with the Scheme Administrator, Pobal, and a more in-depth reply will issue to the applicant within the next 28 days.
It is important to note that generally the backdating of NCS subsidies is not permitted where a CHICK was not registered with a childcare provider. There are limited exceptions to this rule. Under the Scheme rules, subsidy payments cannot be made for periods prior to the completion of a valid registration. As no registration was in place for the period concerned, generally the subsidy would not be applied retrospectively.

question: Deputy Emer Currie asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality the proposed fee-setting arrangements for childcare services established under the State-led capital programme; whether these services will be subject to the same maximum fee caps as existing core funding providers; and whether her Department intends to establish a separate or lower fee structure for State-led facilities.

Operators in State-led services will be required to participate in the Core Funding Scheme. As a result, they will be subject to the fee-setting rules of that scheme, like all other Partner Services.

question: Deputy Emer Currie asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality for an update on the independent evaluation of the national childcare scheme.
reply:
The independent evaluation of the National Childcare Scheme (NCS) commenced in March 2026 following a procurement tendering process which launched in late 2025. It is expected that the evaluation will run for approximately 18 months with a final report expected to be published in Q3 2027. This evaluation aims to assess the performance of the NCS to date and its operation within the wider early learning and childcare funding and policy environment.
The evaluation will examine whether the NCS, as part of the wider funding model, is making high-quality early learning and childcare more accessible and affordable, particularly for families in the lowest income groups and the most disadvantaged households. It will also identify any improvements that could be made to enhance accessibility and affordability and to ensure that the NCS is working for as many families as possible.
The evaluation will include consultation and engagement with parents, educators, practitioners, providers and representative organisations. Any changes to the NCS will be carefully considered in light of the findings of this evaluation.

reply:

question: Deputy Michael Healy-Rae asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine whether he will support Felix's Law and reclassify pets as sentient beings under Irish Law, making pet theft a standalone offence with appropriate penalties for animal cruelty.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 802 and 804 together.
Animal welfare is a key priority for me as Minister and for the Government. My Department has lead policy responsibility within Government for animal welfare and takes this matter most seriously.
I am committed to the policy that animal welfare standards are vigorously applied in a fair and even-handed manner and remain committed to the continued robust enforcement of the Animal Health and Welfare Act 2013, which provides a modern framework for regulating and applying standards in the area of animal health and welfare.
All reports of alleged animal cruelty or neglect received by my Department are investigated. My Department and authorised officers appointed under the Animal Health and Welfare Act 2013, including An Garda Síochána, customs agents, local authorities, and the National Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals (NSPCA), undertake appropriate enforcement action, where breaches or shortcomings are identified.
Offences under the Act may be prosecuted in the District Court by me as Minister, by local authorities and members of An Garda Síochána. Matters tried on indictment are the remit of the Director of Public Prosecutions in the normal manner. My Department does not hold records on prosecutions taken by An Garda Síochána and local authorities.
My Department keeps the Act under review in light of key developments in the areas of animal welfare, the law and having regard to the practical lessons learnt fro

question: Deputy Michael Cahill asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine to address an issue (details supplied) where TB was found in two animals which were sold.
reply:
Under EU and Irish rules relating to the control of bTB my Department is required to suspend the Disease Free Status (DFS) of the herd where a suspected case of bTB occurred until further investigation and an epidemiological enquiry are concluded.
As part of the investigation, backward tracing of animals that fail a TB skin/blood test or confirm TB at slaughter takes place. If such a backward traced animal left the herd of origin more than six weeks prior to disclosure of infection in the subsequent herd, the DFS of the original herd is suspended until it has carried out cleansing and disinfection and completed one clear herd test, at least 42 days after the animal left the herd.
In this case the animals left the herd of origin more than six weeks prior to disclosure of infection in the subsequent herd and did not have a herd test at least 42 days after these animals were sold. Therefore, the Disease Free Status of the herd was suspended pending another herd test. The herdowner was notified by my Department's local regional veterinary office of this Backward Trace herd level test and informed to complete this herd level test.
My Department cannot comment on other herds referred to in the question.

question: Deputy Michael Murphy asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine whether a review is being undertaken of the thresholds and screening requirements governing hedgerow removal under the Environmental Impact Assessment (Agriculture) Regulations; and whether consideration is being given to strengthening protections for mature hedgerows and assessing the cumulative impact of hedgerow removal.
reply:
A commitment to review the European Communities (Environmental Impact Assessment) (Agriculture) Regulations S.I. 456 of 2011 (as amended) was made under Ireland’s previous programme for government, (2020-2024). This review is ongoing.
Hedgerows provide vital ecosystem services and landscape connectivity across the Irish farming landscapes. My Department introduced stronger protection for hedgerows under Conditionality. Under the Good Agricultural and Environmental Conditions (GAEC 8), a greater emphasis was placed on the retention of designated landscape features, such as hedgerows. They cannot be removed apart from limited exceptional circumstances, namely building work and road/farm safety. This strengthening has acted as a deterrent for the removal of hedgerows, and other designated landscape features as the EIA screening application rates decreased by 54 percent between 2022 to 2023. The number of EIA screening applications has continued to reduce year-on-year since.
My Department has several voluntary schemes that support hedgerows. The Eco-scheme has two agricultural practices which aim to retain hedgerows under space for nature and by planting native trees and/or hedgerows. Under the Agri-Climate Rural Environmental Scheme (ACRES), Ireland’s flagship scheme supporting 53,000 farm families, approximately 2,300 kilometres of new hedgerows have been planted, with ongoing efforts to maintain and rejuvenate existing hedgerows. question: Deputy Robert O'Donoghue asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine whether he will confirm the number of cattle and pregnant heifers exported aboard a vessel (details supplied); the veterinary checks that were conducted regarding fitness for transport, vessel suitability and weather conditions; the safeguards monitor animal welfare during the voyage and after arrival; and whether he will consider suspending live exports to destinations where adequate animal welfare standards cannot be verified.
reply:

All animals intended for live export are assessed for their fitness to travel by my Department's Veterinary Inspectors prior to certification and approval for transport.
For a dedicated livestock vessel to be allowed load and transport animals out of Ireland, it must be approved by my Department in accordance with the provisions of S.I. No. 356/2016 - Carriage of Livestock by Sea Regulations 2016. The vessel referred to by the Deputy is approved in accordance with the provisions of this Regulation. question: Deputy Michael Murphy asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine whether additional funding can be made available to facilitate a further intake under the organic farming scheme in 2026 or 2027; the number of prospective applicants who have completed approved organic farming training but cannot enter the scheme; whether particular consideration will be given to dairy farmers seeking to convert to organic production; and the earliest anticipated reopening date.
reply:
Under the CAP Strategic Plan 2023-2027, €256 million was committed to developing the organic farming sector in Ireland. Based on current and approved members of the Scheme and associated 5-year contracts, this funding is fully committed.
Under CSP 2023-2027 the growth in organics has been exceptional. Between 2023 and 2026 the number of farmers in the Organic Farming Scheme (OFS) grew from 2,090 to 5,573, an increase of 266%, which includes over 260 new entrants in 2026. Currently approximately 248,000 hectares or 5.5% of utilisable agricultural land is under organic production.
My Department does not hold records on the numbers of people who have completed organic farming training, as they may do this and never be a part of a scheme. It is only required by my Department when they are accepted onto the Organic Farming Scheme.
Work is ongoing to plan for the Organic Farming Scheme under the next CAP programming period post 2027. This includes a focus on supporting growth in organic production across all sectors including the dairy sector.

question: Deputy Michael Murphy asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine the reason for the decision not to reopen the organic farming scheme to new applicants in 2026; whether this decision is consistent with the Government's targets of 7.5 per cent of agricultural land under organic farming by 2027 and 10 per cent by 2030; the current percentage and total hectares of agricultural land under organic production; and whether revised projections have been prepared for achieving these targets.
reply:
I am fully committed to the development and growth of the organic sector in Ireland, in line with our targets set out in the National Organic Strategy and Climate Action Plan.
Under CSP 2023-2027 the growth in organics has been exceptional. Between 2023 and 2026 the number of farmers in the Organic Farming Scheme (OFS) grew from 2,090 to 5,573, an increase of 266%, which includes over 260 new entrants in 2026. Currently approximately 248,000 hectares or 5.5% of utilisable agricultural land is under organic production.
Under the CAP Strategic Plan 2023-2027, €256 million is committed to developing the organic farming sector and based on current and approved members of the Scheme and associated 5-year contracts, this funding is fully committed.
I am aware that the demand for organic food in major export markets continues to grow. My Department is continuing to engage with the Organic Strategy Forum to ensure that Ireland’s processing capabilities and marketing strategies are in place so that organic production reaches the end consumer in Ireland or overseas. I have provided new funding for the Organic Processing Investment Grant in Budget 2027.
In addition work is ongoing to plan for the Organic Farming Scheme under the next CAP programming period post 2027, and this includes a focus on supporting growth in organic production across all sectors.

question: Deputy Michael Cahill asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine if his Department will review the inspection findings of a BISS conditionality inspection appeal (details supplied) given the supporting evidence regarding farming activity, extensive grazing and biodiversity benefits; the status of the appeal; the expected timeframe for a decision.
reply:
The named applicant had a 2024 Conditionality inspection on 4th December 2024. Conditionality inspections are a requirement as part of the EU regulations governing all EU area-related Schemes. Conditionality inspections cover three main areas namely Climate and Environment, Public, Animal and Plant Health and Animal Welfare. The results of those checks were clear as conveyed to the applicant in a letter dated 16th January 2025.
In addition to the above controls, my Department is required to carry out land eligibility checks to ensure an agricultural activity is taking place on the lands applied for and also that area deductions have been made for artificial surfaces such as buildings, house sites and farm roadways. At this inspection it was determined that no farming activity had taken place in respect of eight land parcels. This was notified to the applicant on 12th December 2024.
The applicant subsequently submitted a review request, through his agricultural advisor, in May 2025. Review requests are dealt with in chronological order and the district inspector will be dealing with his review request shortly.

question: Deputy Michael Healy-Rae asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine the position regarding a forest (details supplied).
reply:
My Department administers a felling licence system whereby the felling of trees generally requires a licence, as per Section 7 of the Forestry Act 2014.
Reforestation after felling is essential to prevent deforestation, which, amongst other things, would counteract the benefits of Ireland’s afforestation programme and associated public expenditure on afforestation.
My Department’s ‘Felling and Reforestation Policy’ (2017) document sets out the procedures and requirements where conversion to agriculture is being proposed. Table 5 and section 5.7 of the document identifies where grants and premiums are to be repaid and where alternative lands are required.
My Department also notes that the EU Deforestation Regulation 23/1115 entered into force in June 2023.
Within the context of the above, my Department will re-examine all the details of this particular case and will revert to the landowner as soon as possible.

question: Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine whether his Department has assessed the impact of the current differential between the livestock VAT rate and the farmer flat-rate addition on livestock marts; whether a reduction in mart throughput has been identified since the change was introduced.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 785 and 788 together.
VAT is a policy matter in the first instance for my colleague the Tánaiste and Minister of Finance and an operational matter for the Revenue Commissioners.
The VAT Flat Rate Addition is calculated on an annual basis by the Revenue Commissioners based on macroeconomic data provided through the CSO. The Tánaiste announced in Budget 2027 that on the basis of the most recent calculation, the flat rate addition paid to unregistered farmers will increase from 4.5% to 4.8% from 01 January 2027.
It has been stated that the reduction of the VAT Flat Rate Addition to 4.5% created an anomaly for livestock marts as the “Livestock Rate" of VAT is fixed at 4.8%. Revenue state that both rates are independent of each other.
I can confirm that I received a number of submissions in this regard in the context of the Budget 2027. However, the increase in the Flat Rate addition ends any perceived anomaly.
Regarding mart throughput, my Department maintains cattle traceability records on a central database known as the Animal Identification and Movement System (AIM). AIM Bovine Statistics Reports provide comprehensive data on calf births, farm-to-farm and mart movements as well as details of cattle slaughtered in Department approved and Local Authority approved slaughter plants, live exports and on-farm bovine deaths. These are available on the Department’s website at: www.gov.ie/en/department-of-agriculture-food-and-the-marine/publications/cat

question: Deputy Michael Murphy asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine whether an assessment has been undertaken of the damage to Coillte forestry on Slievenamon following the July and August 2026 wildfires; the extent of the damage identified; what restoration and wildfire prevention measures are proposed; and whether targeted agri-environmental supports can be made available to upland farmers outside ACRES Co-operation Project areas.
reply:
Coillte was established as a commercial state company with private limited status under the Forestry Act, 1988, to become custodian and manager of the national forest estate. The company is currently managing 440,000 hectares of land (7% of the total land area of Ireland), and its day-to-day operations, such as the management of its forest estate, are a matter for the company. I have directed those parts of the question related to Coillte to them for direct reply to the Deputy.
In relation to targeted agri-environmental supports the Agri-Climate Rural Environment Scheme (‘ACRES’) is Ireland’s national agri-environment climate measure provided under Ireland’s CAP Strategic Plan 2023-2027, with some 53,000 farmers currently participating in it. While the Scheme is currently closed, upland farmers outside the ACRES Co-operation zones were eligible to apply for the General approach within ACRES, with this approach offering a range of General Actions including commonage. The availability of this action in ACRES was to incentivise farmers to help ensure that habitats on commonage lands are maintained/restored to good condition through appropriate management practices. Commonage generally tends to be less productive farmland but is highly beneficial from an environmental point of view as it can contain a mosaic of peatland, heath and upland grass.

reply:

The Act provides for a range of penalties that may be imposed. On summary conviction, an offender may be fined up to €5,000 (a Class A fine) and/or be sentenced to a term of imprisonment of up to 6 months. On conviction on indictment, a fine of up to €250,000 and or a term of 5 years imprisonment may be imposed.

However primary responsibility for protecting the welfare of animals rests with the owner or keeper.

question: Deputy John Paul O'Shea asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine when the areas for the ANC scheme will be reviewed; and if he can give some guidance to potentially eligible landowners.
reply:
The Areas of Natural Constraints (ANC) scheme provides financial compensation to farmers in recognition of the additional cost they incur in farming land that is designated as disadvantaged/constrained.
In 2019, Ireland was required under Articles 31 and 32 of Regulation (EU) No 1305/2013, to change the approach used to designate land as eligible for payment under the scheme. Up to that point, Ireland had been identifying eligible areas using a range of socio-economic indicators, including family farm income, population density, percentage of working population engaged in agriculture and stocking density.
From 2019, eligible areas were instead required to be designated using the following list of bio-physical criteria:
• Low Temperature
• Dryness
• Excess oil moisture
• Limited soil drainage
• Unfavourable texture and stoniness
• Shallow rooting depth
• Poor chemical properties
• Steep slope
Where a townland displayed one or more of the listed criteria at a level above the threshold of 60%, as set out in the regulation, the townland was identified as constrained.
It was then necessary to ‘fine tune’ areas by reference to the following three categories:
District Electoral Divisions (DEDs) that displayed a stocking density over a 3-year average at a level above 1.8 livestock units (LU) per hectare.
DEDs that displayed an average level of above 15% of the agricultural area taken up by arable crops.

reply:

The Multi-Unit Developments Act 2011 provides the statutory framework for important aspects of the ownership and management of common areas in multi-unit developments and the operation of owners' management companies (OMCs). Under the Programme for Government, Securing Ireland's Future, responsibility for the Multi-Unit Developments Act 2011 and the regulation of owners' management companies is to transfer from my Department to the Department of Housing, Local Government and Heritage.

Following the commencement of the Act, the remaining arrangements required to complete the transfer of functions, including the making of a Transfer of Functions Order, are being progressed. question: Deputy John Connolly asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration to clarify the obligations on licensed bookmakers and gambling operators regarding self-exclusion facilities; whether all licensed operators are legally required to provide a self-exclusion facility to customers who request it; whether there is a statutory requirement for operators to offer a lifetime self-exclusion option.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 764 and 765 together.
The Gambling Regulation Act 2024 (the ‘2024 Act’) establishes a comprehensive framework for the licensing and regulation of betting, gaming, and certain lotteries, including activities provided online to persons in the State. It also establishes a new, independent statutory body, the Gambling Regulatory Authority of Ireland (GRAI). Last year, I signed orders to commence the first provisions of the 2024 Act and establish the GRAI from 5 March 2025.
The provisions of the 2024 Act and the powers of the GRAI are being rolled out on a phased basis, with the provisions regarding the licensing of betting operators commencing on 5 February 2026. Existing betting licensees will continue to operate under licenses issued by the Office of the Revenue Commissioners until their expiry dates, namely 30 June for remote (online) bookmakers and betting intermediaries, and 30 November for in-person bookmakers.
Once commenced, Chapter 3, Part 2 of the 2024 Act provides that the GRAI shall establish and maintain a National Gambling Exclusion Register. The Register, which represents an important public health protection measure, will allow individuals to request exclusion from remote gambling indefinitely and will prevent all Business to Consumer licensees from:

question: Deputy John Connolly asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the current status of the proposed National Gambling Exclusion Register; the expected timeline for its implementation; whether a person who self-excludes through the register will be excluded across all licensed gambling operators in the State.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 764 and 765 together.
The Gambling Regulation Act 2024 (the ‘2024 Act’) establishes a comprehensive framework for the licensing and regulation of betting, gaming, and certain lotteries, including activities provided online to persons in the State. It also establishes a new, independent statutory body, the Gambling Regulatory Authority of Ireland (GRAI). Last year, I signed orders to commence the first provisions of the 2024 Act and establish the GRAI from 5 March 2025.
The provisions of the 2024 Act and the powers of the GRAI are being rolled out on a phased basis, with the provisions regarding the licensing of betting operators commencing on 5 February 2026. Existing betting licensees will continue to operate under licenses issued by the Office of the Revenue Commissioners until their expiry dates, namely 30 June for remote (online) bookmakers and betting intermediaries, and 30 November for in-person bookmakers.
Once commenced, Chapter 3, Part 2 of the 2024 Act provides that the GRAI shall establish and maintain a National Gambling Exclusion Register. The Register, which represents an important public health protection measure, will allow individuals to request exclusion from remote gambling indefinitely and will prevent all Business to Consumer licensees from:
• providing gambling services to persons entered in the Register,
• accepting payments from them, and
• communicating with them in a manner that invites (or has the effect of inviting)

question: Deputy Emer Currie asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration for an update on work undertaken to progress the 15 recommendations outlined in the Staines Review, including that legislation should be introduced allowing the member in charge of a Garda station to attach conditions to a station bail bond and that this legislation should set out the factors which must be considered by the member in charge in deciding whether to grant station bail.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 756 and 757 together.
Last year, I appointed Senior Counsel Lorcan Staines to undertake an assessment of the current operation of bail in Ireland, both legal and practical. The report completed by Mr Staines, ‘An Assessment of the Efficacy of Bail Laws in Ireland’, was published by my Department in November 2025.
While bail laws in Ireland are comprehensive and the Bail Act 1997 has been revised and strengthened several times, this examination of our bail laws and subsequent proposals underlines the need for additional actions to be considered, to ensure the criminal justice system effectively mitigates against risks that may be associated with individuals on bail.
Among the recommendations of the Staines Report was that legislation should be introduced allowing the member in charge of a Garda station to attach conditions to a station bail bond and that such legislation should set out the factors which must be considered by the member in charge in deciding whether to grant station bail. This recommendation is currently under consideration in my Department.
A number of other recommendations are also under consideration, in progress or have been completed by my Department. It is proposed that a further Memorandum for the Government will be brought on any further implementation of the recommendations in due course.

reply:

However, it is important to note that there is no automatic entitlement to family reunification, which is dependent on a number of key criteria, including that a sponsor must have the means to be able to provide for their family without recourse to state supports. The economic benefits that migration brings, including through the significant contribution to the State through work and taxation, must be balanced with the substantial costs to the State in areas such as education, childcare, housing, healthcare and welfare that may arise from family migration.
It is a core principle of the Policy that a sponsor must assume primary financial responsibility for any joining family members, thereby minimising the risk of reliance on State resources. question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration whether, where a person convicted of a sexual offence is an asylum seeker, if the confidentiality provisions of international protection legislation prevent that person being named in reports, even in cases where the victim has requested that they be named; and the legal basis for the position.
reply:
It is a central priority of this Government that our immigration laws are robust and effectively enforced. Since taking office, I have worked to ensure integrity, efficiency and public confidence in our migration system.
The confidentiality principle is a fundamental principle of asylum law and is reflected in both the Asylum Procedures Regulation and domestic legislation, namely the International Protection Act 2015, which applies to applications made before 12 June 2026, and the International Protection Act 2026, which applies to applications made on or after that date.
An asylum-seeker's claim is based on a fear of persecution by the authorities in their home country. As a result, family members or friends who remain in that country may be placed at risk if the applicant's personal information is not kept confidential.
Therefore, my officials and I are legally obliged to ensure that the identity of any person who has applied for international protection is kept confidential. For applicants whose applications were made prior to 12 June 2026, section 26(1) of the 2015 Act provides that:
"the Minister and the Tribunal and their respective officers shall take all practicable steps to ensure that the identity of applicants is kept confidential".

reply:

Currently, there are over 900 people subject to deportation orders residing in IPAS accommodation. The allocation for IPAS accommodation and supports for 2025 was €1.2 billion and this reduced to an allocation of over €1.1 billion for accommodation and supports in 2026. This was the first time that the budget allocation has been less than the previous year for over five years. The allocation for 2027 has reduced by a further 250m compared to 2026.

question: Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of applicants for international protection who have made more than one application in Ireland or elsewhere within the European Union, insofar as such information is available through Eurodac or other systems.
reply:
People who apply for international protection are subject to initial security and identity checks and will be registered on the Eurodac system.
The Eurodac database, which began operation in 2003, is used to enable the comparison of fingerprints and assist in determining the country responsible for the assessment of an asylum claim presented in one of the Member States.
The Eurodac Regulation (Regulation (EU) 2024/1358) expands the data collection requirements to individuals aged six and over. It broadens data collection beyond fingerprints to include facial images and travel documents.

question: Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of international protection applicants whose whereabouts are currently unknown to the authorities following registration of their claim.
reply:
It is a central priority for me that Ireland's immigration system is robust and rules-based.
Each application is examined individually on its own merits, in line with national and international asylum law. The relevant national legislation giving effect to the EU Pact on Migration and Asylum is the International Protection Act 2026. This Act sets out the procedures for making, registering and lodging an application for international protection.
All new applicants for international protection since 12 June 2026 undergo screening at the Citywest National Reception Centre, where applicants may also be accommodated under the Asylum Border Procedure and the Asylum and Migration Management Regulation. During the screening procedure, which may take up to seven days, applicants are subject to a restriction on freedom of movement, which requires them to report to immigration authorities daily. If an applicant does not report as required, on three occasions, their application may be deemed to have been implicitly withdrawn.
Those permitted to reside in private accommodation are obliged to notify the International Protection Office (IPO) of any change of address.
Section 65(2)(b) of the International Protection Act 2026 requires applicants to notify the IPO of any change of address within 48 hours, providing a clear statutory timeframe for compliance.

question: Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of Garda National Immigration Bureau personnel assigned specifically to deportation enforcement duties in each year since 2020.
reply:

They are responsible for the enforcement of deportation and removal orders. They also provide assistance, advice and support to Immigration Officers located in Garda Divisions around the country. In addition to the members of GNIB, there are Gardaí who are certified Immigration Officers deployed across the country who fulfil immigration functions as the need arises.

It is a central priority for me that Ireland's immigration system is robust and rules based. Effective enforcement of our immigration laws, including the implementation of deportation orders, is essential to maintaining confidence in the integrity of the system and ensuring that our legislation is applied consistently.
Deportations are often costly and complex to carry out. Consequently, voluntary return is the preferred option wherever possible. My Department operates a voluntary return programme to assist individuals who wish to leave the State before a deportation order is issued. As access to this programme is only available prior to the making of a deportation order, I have increased the resources available to support those who choose to return voluntarily at an earlier stage.
Where a person does not leave the State following the issuance of a deportation order, enforcement action may be required. In recent years, my Department has taken significant steps to strengthen immigration enforcement and increase the number of removals carried out.

question: Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration whether his Department or the Government possesses estimates of the number of unlawfully present migrants currently residing in the State; and if so, the basis for those estimates.
reply:
Where a non-EEA national is present in the State without a current immigration permission to reside, they are considered to be an undocumented migrant.
It is not possible to accurately quantify the number of undocumented migrants residing in the State. Such individuals do not ordinarily make themselves known to officials of Immigration Service Delivery (ISD) in my Department, nor is their lack of permission to remain generally known to the authorities.
Where persons without a valid immigration permission are encountered by An Garda Síochána, including during joint operations with other State authorities, they are referred to ISD for processing. ISD will then take the appropriate action in accordance with the legislation, which may include the issuance of a Deportation Order.

question: Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of persons granted permission to remain in the State on humanitarian or exceptional grounds following a failed international protection application in each of the past five years, together with the grounds relied upon in each case.
reply:
It is a central priority for me that Ireland’s immigration system is robust and rules based.
Each application is examined individually on its own merits, in line with national and international asylum law. The relevant national legislation applicable is the International Protection Act 2015, for applications lodged prior to 12 June 2026, and the International Protection Act 2026, for applications lodged thereafter.
Under the 2015 Act, a person only had to make one application for international protection. During that single process, an international protection officer considered:
• Whether the person qualified for refugee status.
• Whether they qualified for subsidiary protection.
• Whether they should be granted permission to remain in Ireland.
The International Protection Office (IPO) makes the first decision on applications for refugee status and subsidiary protection. Under the 2015 Act, it also made decisions on permission to remain.
It is important to note that the 2026 Act does not include a permission to remain process.
All applicants refused international protection have a right to appeal to the International Protection Appeals Tribunal (IPAT) for applications lodged prior to 12 June 2026, and the Tribunal for Asylum and Return Appeals (TARA) for applications lodged after 12 June 2026. These bodies must then consider if the earlier IPO determinations on refugee status and subsidiary protection should be affirmed or set aside.

question: Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration whether RTÉ or any other media outlets or platforms has received any guidance, formal or informal, from his Department, regarding reporting of migration, asylum or deportation matters.
reply:
My Department engages regularly with media organisations through its press office, to ensure that accurate information is made available to the public about all aspects of the Department's work.
The Department does not provide guidance regarding reporting on migration; the Department's press office provides responses to queries and briefings to media organisations or individual correspondents. They also provide information and background in relation to policy developments, legislative changes or operational updates.
From January 2025 to September 2026, my Department responded to nearly 900 migration-related queries from members of the media, including queries on migration, asylum and deportation as outlined in the Deputy's question. The Department also publishes regular statistics and reports of activity on migration services on our website.

question: Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of residential properties that have been removed by his Department from the private rental market for use as international protection accommodation since January 2022.
reply:
The International Protection Accommodation Service is currently accommodating nearly 32,000 residents in 294 international protection accommodation centres around the country. The Department does not collate reports on IPAS Accommodation Centres in relation to their previous use as outlined in the Deputy's question.
In contracting or purchasing accommodation over recent years, despite significant pressures on accommodation supply, the Department has worked in the main to avoid competing with the residential property market. The Department does not currently accept offers of residential properties for appraisal as international protection accommodation.
The great majority of IPAS accommodation capacity, whether contracted or State-owned, is located in group settings in larger properties, like former hotels, guesthouses, commercial and institutional buildings. A small proportion of more vulnerable applicants may be accommodated in smaller scale residential-type properties.
A total of 37 in-community properties were purchased by the Department of Children, Equality, Disability, Integration and Youth for the accommodation of more vulnerable applicants, for whom group accommodation would not be suitable. It is not my intention as Minister to purchase any further properties of this type.

question: Deputy Frankie Feighan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if he is considering raising the current prize winnings threshold from the current €365,000 under the current lotteries Act.
reply:
Section 28 of the Gaming and Lotteries Act 1956 as amended (the ‘1956 Act’) provides that a lottery licence may be granted by the District Court and may be subject to certain conditions. One of those conditions, included in subsection 28(10), is that the maximum total value of prizes for a once-off lottery in any year shall not exceed €360,000. Subsection 28(13) provides that I, as Minister, may vary the amounts specified in subsection 28(10). Currently, I am not considering raising the amount specified in subsection 28(10).
The regulation of the gambling sector, including certain lotteries, is being overhauled through the phased commencement of the Gambling Regulation Act 2024 (the ‘2024 Act’). The Act establishes an independent agency to regulate the gambling sector, the Gambling Regulatory Authority of Ireland (GRAI), and ensures that the GRAI can respond appropriately to ongoing and future developments in the gambling sector.
The 2024 Act, once the relevant provisions are commenced, will repeal the 1956 Act. The 2024 Act provides for a similar type of licence to allow once-off lotteries (to be operated once every 12 months) with prizes of up to €360,000 for both commercial and charitable/philanthropic purposes. Schedule 3 to the 2024 Act provides for the maximum relevant payments and maximum winnings for certain gambling activities. These limits may be varied by the GRAI, with my consent as Minister, as provided for in section 83(2) of the Act.

question: Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the measures being taken to ensure that the conditions under which interpreters are engaged for court and other justice-sector services support the availability and retention of suitably qualified interpreters, particularly in light of the State’s obligations concerning access to justice and fair proceedings.
reply:
The right to fair procedures is a central tenet of our criminal justice system. Ireland opted in to the EU Directive on the right to interpretation and translation in criminal proceedings and it was subsequently transposed into Irish law. This was done via two Statutory Instruments, one of which relates to Interpretation and Translation in Criminal Proceedings, which concerns the arrangements to be put in place by the Courts Service in respect of the conduct of court proceedings.
Article 5 of the Directive reads that Member States are required to take ‘concrete measures’ to ensure the quality of the interpretation and translation services. A 2018 European Commission report on the implementation of Directive did not flag any issues of concern regarding Ireland’s approach to same. The manner in which these instruments are implemented in practice is an operational matter for An Garda Síochána and the Courts. As the Deputy will appreciate, as Minister, I have no role in individual court proceedings, nor can I intervene in operational Garda matters that fall under the Garda Commissioner’s remit, including the processes by which translation and interpretation services are provided.
Management of the courts is the responsibility of the Courts Service, which is independent in exercising its functions under the Courts Service Act 1998 and the Constitution. question: Deputy Ruth Coppinger asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration to consider introducing flexibility for the income threshold for the temporary protection transition scheme when the person applying is a carer, a lone parent or is a person with disabilities.
reply:
The Temporary Protection Transition Scheme opened for applications on 30 September 2026.
An applicant must demonstrate that they have been in employment or self-employment for at least six months immediately prior to the opening date of the Scheme, with average gross earnings of €29,432, and must continue to be in employment both at the date of application and at the date a decision is made on their application. This rate is set to reflect full-time minimum wage employment.
It is important to note that the Temporary Protection Transition Scheme is not intended to replace Temporary Protection, but to provide an additional pathway for those who are eligible and who wish to remain in Ireland on an independent basis. Persons who do not satisfy the eligibility criteria will continue to benefit from Temporary Protection and its associated rights and entitlements while the Temporary Protection Directive remains in effect. Temporary Protection is currently in place across the EU until March 2028. People in Ireland will continue to have access to the associated rights of the Directive for the duration of Temporary Protection to include the right to reside in Ireland and the right to access to social welfare, education, and employment.

question: Deputy Shónagh Ní Raghallaigh asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration when the current temporary protection contract for the accommodation of Ukrainian citizens at the former Sacred Heart Convent in Roscrea will end; and if it is planned to renew this contract.
reply:
On 26 May 2026, the Government agreed to commence a phased withdrawal of state-contracted commercial accommodation for people fleeing the war in Ukraine with Temporary Protection status who arrived in Ireland prior to 14 March 2024. This forms part of a wider transition program to support people towards greater independence, while ensuring continued support for those who remain in need of state accommodation.
The phased withdrawal of some commercial accommodation is being implemented on a region-by-region basis. These providers will receive notice of termination in due course, if they have not yet already.
Certain suitable and/or accessible properties are being retained to facilitate the accommodation of people with barriers to independence.
A list of all properties whose contracts are being terminated is available on: www.gov.ie/en/department-of-justice-home-affairs-and-migration/news/accommodation-centres-returning-to-original-or-alternative-use/
In line with Government policy, the accommodation in question is being retained to facilitate the accommodation of people with barriers to independence. My Department offers such contracts on a rolling three month basis. As with any such contract, the future use of the accommodation beyond that period will be dependent on the Department’s requirements.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the terms of reference and terms of appointment of the special rapporteur on racial equality and racism; whether the office holder is subject to a code of conduct or standards regarding public commentary; the mechanism for reviewing or ending the appointment before its scheduled end in mid 2028.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 694, 698 and 699 together.
I refer to the response I provided to the questions asked by the Deputy on 24 September 2026 (67965/26; 67966/26; 67967/26; 67968/26, 67969/26).
The role of the Special Rapporteur on Racial Equality and Racism was established as part of the monitoring, oversight and review framework of the National Action Plan Against Racism (NAPAR) 2023-2027. Dr Ebun Joseph was appointed as the Special Rapporteur for Racial Equality and Racism on 2 July 2024 for a four-year term following an open competition which was publicly advertised and managed by the Public Appointments Service.
As with all other public appointments, the Special Rapporteur is required to comply with the applicable Terms of Reference of the role, high standards of integrity and professionalism. Views expressed by the Special Rapporteur in a personal capacity, rather than in her official role, are not governed by the Terms of Reference and fall within the scope of freedom of expression.
In relation to costs to the Exchequer, total cost to date was provided to the Deputy on 7 September 2026 (60899/26). Regarding future expenditure, the Special Rapporteur will receive an annual stipend of €25,000 until the post expires in mid-2028.

question: Deputy Emer Currie asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration when the National Cyber Security Bill 2024 will be published and the timeline for transposition of the NIS2 Directive.
reply:
The National Cyber Security Bill will transpose the Revised Network and Information Systems Directive (NIS2) into Irish law. This legislation represents a significant step in strengthening the State’s cyber security and resilience. It will enhance cyber security risk management in Ireland bringing with it significant improvements in our capacity to protect against, recover from and respond to major incidents.
In anticipation of having the legislation in place and to ensure that Ireland is ready to fully implement the directive, we have taken significant steps to ensure that various implementing measures are in place. This includes a robust approach to sectoral regulation for the Directive with the designation of National Competent Authorities to carry out enforcement and supervision. National Competent Authorities are already undertaking significant preparations to take on these new functions.
The National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) is engaging with its constituents and stakeholders to ensure the requirements of the Bill are communicated ahead of time and has produced resources and guidance for entities that fall within the scope of NIS2. The NCSC has also prepared a media campaign for launch when the Bill is enacted.
