question: Deputy Ivana Bacik asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the status of a visa application by a person (details supplied).
reply:
The visa appeal application referred to by the Deputy is awaiting examination and processing. As there are now judicial review proceedings before the Courts in relation to study visa applicants, the Department cannot comment further on those proceedings.
Each visa application, regardless of nationality, is assessed on its own merits, taking all relevant information into consideration. All visa applicants are advised that the responsibility is on them to provide as much information in support of their applications as they feel is necessary. Guidelines in this regard are posted on our website. The reason(s) for a refusal are outlined in the decision letter issued to the applicants.
Visa and preclearance applications provide legal avenues for people moving to Ireland and to facilitate visitors who wish to travel for business and/or tourism. These are important screening processes, designed to establish that a person has a legitimate reason to come to Ireland prior to travel. Verifying an application is an important part of our immigration system. Each visa application is assessed on its own merits, taking all relevant information into consideration at that time.
My Department is conscious of the importance of these applications for the students concerned and will continue to process appeals as expeditiously as possible. Decisions are communicated directly to applicants as soon as full consideration of the appeal has been completed.

As with all other public appointments, the Special Rapporteur is required to comply with the applicable Terms of Reference of the role, high standards of integrity and professionalism. Views expressed by the Special Rapporteur in a personal capacity, rather than in her official role, are not governed by the Terms of Reference and fall within the scope of freedom of expression.
In relation to costs to the Exchequer, total cost to date was provided to the Deputy on 7 September 2026 (60899/26). Regarding future expenditure, the Special Rapporteur will receive an annual stipend of €25,000 until the post expires in mid-2028.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of requests made by him to the Police Ombudsman under section 205(2); and the number of referrals made under section 205(3), of the Policing, Security and Community Safety Act 2024 since the commencement of the Act on 2 April 2025, by year; the number of occasions on which the Police Ombudsman notified him under section 205(8) of a decision not to investigate a matter referred under section 205(3).
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 691 and 692 together.
Section 205 of the Policing, Security and Community Safety Act 2024 provides for investigations in the public interest.
An investigation under section 205 of the 2024 Act may be undertaken by the Police Ombudsman on their own initiative or at the request of the Minister, the Policing and Community Safety Authority, or the Garda Commissioner of a “relevant cause of concern”.
A relevant cause for concern is defined as a concern that a member of Garda personnel may have committed an offence or behaved in a manner that constitutes misconduct that would justify the bringing of conduct proceedings.
There is no requirement under the Policing, Security and Community Safety Act 2024 for a written procedure to be developed to support the operation of section 205.
I have not made a request to Fiosrú under section 205 since the commencement of the Policing, Security and Community Safety Act 2024 on 2 April 2025.

reply:

question: Deputy Matt Carthy asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the procedures in place to ensure that victims and affected family members are informed of deportation-related decisions where they have indicated a wish to receive such information, given that the victim liaison service does not provide information on the deportation process.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 670 to 672, inclusive, 679 and 680 together.
It is a central priority for me that Ireland's immigration system is robust and rules-based. Effective enforcement of our immigration laws, including the implementation of deportation orders, is essential to maintaining confidence in the integrity of the system and ensuring that our legislation is applied consistently.
The removal of people involved in criminality, and those who pose a risk to public safety, is a priority for me as Minister. My Department works closely with An Garda Síochána and the Irish Prison Service to ensure that high-risk individuals are prioritised for removal from the State.
My Department is responsible for the issuing of deportation orders. The enforcement of deportation orders is an operational matter for the Garda National Immigration Bureau. However, to assist the Deputy, officials in my Department have sought information from An Garda Síochána as to whether procedures are in place for liaising with victims of crimes committed by a person who is being deported. I will write to the Deputy directly once this information is available.
As previously advised to the Deputy, the Irish Prison Service engages with victims of crime through its Victim Liaison Service.
It is important to note that the Irish Prison Service Victim Liaison Service is a voluntary, opt-in service. Victims may register with the Service if they wish to be informed of significant developments in a prisoner'

question: Deputy Sean Fleming asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration to respond to correspondence (details supplied).

question: Deputy Gary Gannon asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration whether his commitment to implement “key civil legal aid reforms” will include the removal of the means test for victims of domestic violence applying for civil legal aid.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 645 to 648, inclusive, 657, 662, 663 and 665 together.
The Legal Aid Board is the statutory, independent body responsible for the provision of civil legal aid and advice to qualifying individuals. Eligibility for the Civil Legal Aid Scheme is determined by reference to a financial assessment and the merits of the case being taken. Civil legal aid and advice is provided primarily through a network of law centres by solicitors employed by the Board. The Board operates a total of 34 full-time law centres and dedicated units along with three part-time centres, and three specialist legal offices. The Board also operates 19 family mediation centres with a number of law centres and family mediation offices co-located. In addition, the Board engages private solicitors to supplement the services provided by Board solicitors in certain areas of law on a case-by-case basis. These areas include District Court family law matters, Circuit Court judicial separation and divorce cases, international protection cases, and cases arising under the Abhaile scheme.
In June 2022, a Civil Legal Aid Review Group under the chairmanship of former Chief Justice Frank Clarke SC was established to review the current operation of the Scheme. An extensive review was undertaken by the Group, including a comprehensive consultation process, to ensure that its work was informed by a broad range of views and experiences. The Review's majority and minority reports were published i

question: Deputy Micheál Carrigy asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the timeline for the procession of Ukrainian Crisis Temporary Accommodation Team, UCTAT, applications; and if a person (details supplied) has an active application for temporary accommodation.
reply:
The application window for people with Temporary Protection currently residing in state-contracted commercial accommodation, to demonstrate a need for continued accommodation was open from 4 August to 11 September 2026.
The process of assessing applications and determining eligibility for continued accommodation is ongoing and is expected to continue for several more weeks.
My officials have confirmed that no application was received for the person to whom the Deputy refers.
Since 8 September 2025, a change in policy means that people granted Temporary Protection who arrived in Ireland before March 2024 and who are not already in state-contracted commercial accommodation, are no longer be eligible to take up new state-contracted commercial accommodation.
This means that people who may have been in accommodation but have since left cannot avail of a second offer of state-contracted commercial accommodation. This also applies to people who arrived before March 2024 and who may not have availed of state-contracted commercial accommodation to date.
I wish advise the Deputy that this person to whom he refers was discharged from state-contracted commercial accommodation in December 2024 and was therefore not eligible to apply under the now closed process outlined above.

question: Deputy Robert O'Donoghue asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the transitional arrangements planned for persons already resident in the State who have not yet applied for naturalisation (details supplied); whether consideration has been given to the position of British citizens, who are not treated as aliens in Irish law and whose reciprocal rights are protected under the common travel area; and which social protection payments will count against the proposed self-sufficiency requirement and over what period.
reply:
The Government recognises and values the significant contribution that migrants make to Irish society, communities and the economy.
Citizenship represents the fullest expression of membership of Irish society, and it is important that the legislative framework governing access to citizenship is robust, fair and sustainable.
The Programme for Government contains a commitment to continue to implement a firmer and more sustainable migration system which protects the integrity of the State's immigration framework. In that context, the General Scheme of the Irish Nationality and Citizenship Bill 2026 proposes a number of reforms to the citizenship process.
The General Scheme is available on the Departmental pages of the Gov.ie website here:
www.gov.ie/en/department-of-justice-home-affairs-and-migration/publications/general-scheme-of-the-irish-nationality-and-citizenship-amendment-bill-2026
While the proposals may affect the timeframe within which some individuals become eligible to apply for citizenship, they do not affect a person's entitlement to reside, work, study, establish a business or establish a life in Ireland in accordance with the terms of their immigration permission.
The proposals do not affect the residency rights of UK nationals in Ireland, nor their access to any rights or entitlements outside of the naturalisation process.
I can also advise the Deputy that these proposals will be subject to detailed scrutiny through the legislative process in the Oireachtas.

question: Deputy Marie Sherlock asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration when his Department expects to have the roles of chief assessor and court delays assessors filled and in place; and can he commit to making operational the Court Proceedings (Delays) Act 2024 as soon as such personnel are in place.
reply:
The Court Proceedings (Delays) Act 2024 provides parties with a right to conclusion of proceedings within a reasonable time. It provides for the establishment of an independent assessment process, to assess claims for breach of that right, and where appropriate, an award of compensation.
Arrangements to operationalise the requirements of the Act are currently being finalised with a view to the Act being commenced shortly. Implementation continues to be advanced.
Earlier this month I made an appointment to fill the role of the Chief Court Delays Assessor and I expect to make further appointments in the coming weeks (including additional Court Delays Assessors) as necessary to give effect to the Act.

question: Deputy John Paul O'Shea asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration for an update on the rate of progress regarding the reduction in the number of Ukrainian beneficiaries of temporary protection in State-supported accommodation; the current total number of persons remaining in such accommodation; and whether the initial tranche and capacity of designated accommodation centres are projected to provide sufficient spaces to accommodate all qualifying new and transitional beneficiaries.
reply:
As of 15 October 2026 there were 14,768 beneficiaries of temporary protection residing in state supported accommodation. This figure includes the 2,809 people that are residing in rapid build and modular accommodation and 11,959 people that are residing in state contracted accommodation.
My Department is not yet in a position to release a final figure on those who will qualify for ongoing State accommodation. The process to determine who meets the criteria for the provision of such accommodation is currently underway and is expected to continue for several weeks. Preliminary indications, at this juncture, indicate that my Department has sufficient contracted accommodation settings to meet the expected need for ongoing accommodation.
My Department remains committed to ensuring that those affected by these changes are provided with information, guidance, and appropriate supports throughout the transition process.
More information can be found at: www.gov.ie/en/department-of-justice-home-affairs-and-migration/campaigns/ukraine-updates-en/

question: Deputy Michael Healy-Rae asked the Minister for Social Protection the reason people who have private pensions cannot sign up for the MyFutureFund pension and therefore do not receive the same supports (details supplied).
reply:
The Programme for Government contained a commitment to introduce the Automatic Enrolment Retirement Savings System (AE). The aim of introducing AE was to address the pension coverage gap that exists in Ireland and to provide workers with greater comfort and security regarding their retirement income.
The new system - known as MyFutureFund - commenced on the 1 January 2026 and it is overseen by the National Automatic Enrolment Retirement Savings Authority (NAERSA), which is a separate statutory body, independent of my Department and directly responsible for all operational elements of MyFutureFund. There are currently over 835,000 participants in MyFutureFund.
MyFutureFund is designed to complement rather than replace existing retirement savings provision. Employees who contribute to a qualifying occupational scheme, PRSA, trust RAC or a PEPP via payroll are not automatically enrolled into MyFutureFund and that employment is deemed to be exempt from MyFutureFund participation. Such employments will continue to be deemed exempt provided that the scheme meets a set of standards related to minimum contribution rates, (i.e. that they are at least as good as the rates in MyFutureFund).

question: Deputy Paul Lawless asked the Minister for Social Protection if he will examine the financial disadvantage faced by retired CIÉ pensioners who pay USC on their occupational pensions but do not have access to a range of supports available to State pension recipients, including the living alone increase and certain medical and household benefits; whether he considers this equitable; and if he will consider introducing measures to address this anomaly.
reply:
Primary weekly social welfare payments are intended to enable recipients to meet their basic day-to-day income needs. In addition to these primary payments, my Department also provides a range of other payments on a weekly, monthly, or less frequent basis. These payments are considered secondary in nature with each of them having their own individual qualifying criteria.
The Living Alone Increase is one of those secondary payments. It is not a scheme or a stand-alone payment, but it is a supplement to a primary social protection payment of €22 per week, rising to €25 per week from January 2027, made to people aged 66 years or over, who are in receipt of certain social welfare payments and who are living alone.
For those aged 66 or over, payments eligible for the Living Alone Increase include State Pension (Contributory), State Pension (Non-contributory), Bereaved Partner’s (Contributory) Pension, Bereaved Partner's Pension under the Occupational Injuries Benefit Scheme, Incapacity Supplement under the Occupational Injuries Benefit Scheme and Deserted Wife's Benefit. The Living Alone Increase is also paid to people aged under 66 who live alone and are in receipt of Disability Allowance, Invalidity Pension, Incapacity Supplement or Blind Pension.

question: Deputy Michael Healy-Rae asked the Minister for Social Protection the status of a person's application for Carer's Benefit (details supplied).
reply:
The person concerned submitted an application for Carer’s Benefit, which was received by the Department on 22 June 2026.

reply:

All schemes operated by my department are subject to ongoing control reviews and continuing eligibility checks. During 2025, my department carried out approximately 716,500 control reviews across a range of schemes.
All recipients are required to notify my department of any changes in circumstance which may impact their payment. This includes plans to be absent from the State. Claimants are informed of this requirement when their payment is awarded and on an ongoing basis.

question: Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Social Protection the amount paid in supplementary welfare and exceptional needs payments to international protection applicants since 2020.
reply:
The Supplementary Welfare Allowance scheme is the safety net within the overall social welfare system in that it provides assistance to eligible people in the State whose means are insufficient to meet their needs and those of their dependents.
Under the Supplementary Welfare Allowance scheme, my department may make Additional Needs Payments to help meet essential expenses that a person cannot pay from their weekly income or other personal and household resources. This also includes supplements to assist with ongoing or recurring costs that cannot be met from the customer’s own resources, and which are deemed to be necessary.
The Habitual Residence Condition is a social welfare condition that a person must satisfy to receive a social assistance payment. Generally, international protection applicants who have not yet been granted protection will not qualify for social welfare payments that are subject to the Habitual Residence Condition, which includes Supplementary Welfare Allowance and Supplements. The Habitual Residence Condition does not apply to Additional Needs Payments. Eligibility for Additional Needs Payments is determined having regard to the applicant's circumstances, income, resources and essential need presented.

question: Deputy Emer Currie asked the Minister for Social Protection whether the public consultation on pay-related parent’s benefit, which he committed to launching in autumn 2026, has commenced; if not, the date it will launch; and whether its scope will include extending a pay-related approach to maternity, paternity and adoptive benefits.
reply:
The Programme for Government commits to introducing Pay-Related Parent's Benefit and exploring other payments where a similar model could be applied.
A pay-related model, which moves away from flat rates of payment, would provide a stronger financial cushion to new parents while reflecting the contributory and solidarity principles of the social insurance system. I intend to issue a public consultation document on a pay-related approach to Parents' Benefit over the coming months.
This consultation will also help to inform decisions about other family and related benefits as referred to by the Deputy.

question: Deputy Sinéad Gibney asked the Minister for Social Protection the outline his Department's position regarding workers and their pension rights (details supplied).
reply:
This issue relates to a group of former workers who left the service of Waterford Crystal between 1990 and 1992 under a redundancy arrangement. At the time of the redundancy, the workers received a refund of their pension contributions relating to their service in the relevant company pension schemes up to that time. As a result, they then ceased to be members of the pension scheme and no longer had any rights or entitlements under the schemes.
Separately, in 2010, a legal action was taken by a group of former Waterford Crystal workers against the State following the insolvency of the Waterford Crystal Factory and Staff pension schemes. The case (known as the Hogan Case) related to the failure of the State to transpose into Irish law the provisions of the Insolvency Protection Directive. The Directive requires Member States to ensure that necessary measures are taken to protect employees’ occupational pension scheme benefits where an employer becomes insolvent.
In 2015, a mediated settlement was reached between the parties to that legal action. The mediated settlement applied to all persons who were members of the Waterford Crystal Staff and Factory pension schemes on the date of wind-up of the schemes (31st March 2009). In total, 1,774 scheme members are covered by the agreement. The total costs to the Exchequer arising from the mediated agreement were estimated at €253 million.

question: Deputy Paul Lawless asked the Minister for Social Protection the reason recipients of disablement benefit are excluded from eligibility for the cost of disability payment while recipients of other long-term disability payments are included; the rationale for this distinction; and if he will consider extending eligibility for the cost of disability payment to people in receipt of disablement benefit, many of whom have long-term disabilities and incur significant additional disability-related costs.
reply:

Disablement Benefit is a compensation payment and can be paid alongside other social welfare payments. People in receipt of Disablement Pension, without another payment, can work, full or part-time. Those who are unfit for work may qualify for Illness Benefit or another social welfare payment based on their social insurance contributions (PRSI). Alternatively, they may qualify for Incapacity Supplement and/or Constant Attendance Allowance. There are no limits to the amount that recipients can earn from work.

reply:
Generally, self-employed workers with incomes of €5,000 or more a year pay PRSI under class S. The PRSI rate applicable to this class from October 1st 2026 onwards is 4.35%, subject to a minimum annual payment of €650. Self-employed contributors now have access to over 90% of the value of all benefits available to employees, even though the PRSI contribution rate for the self-employed is 11.40 percentage points lower than the combined 15.75% made in respect of employees. The only benefits that the self-employed do not currently have access to are Illness Benefit, Occupational Injuries Benefit and Health and Safety Benefit.

question: Deputy Ryan O'Meara asked the Minister for Social Protection the progress made to date on the programme for Government commitment to explore extending access to illness benefit to self-employed workers in return for an increased PRSI contribution; whether his Department has completed an actuarial or financial assessment of the cost of introducing such a scheme; the estimated additional PRSI contribution that would be required from self-employed workers to qualify for illness benefit; when he expects to bring forward proposals in this regard.
reply:
Illness Benefit is the primary short term income support provided by the Department of Social Protection to those who are unable to work due to illness of any type and who are covered by social insurance. Eligibility for Illness Benefit depends on the person’s PRSI record and class.
The person must have made the required number of contributions under class A, E, H or P to qualify. In general, self-employed people make PRSI contributions at class S.
Self-employed contributors pay class S PRSI at a rate of 4.35%. This is 11.40 percentage points lower than the combined employer and employee contribution of 15.75% made in respect of employed contributors. However, self-employed contributors do have access to over 90% of benefits available to employed contributors.
The only benefits that class S PRSI does not provide access to are Health and Safety Benefit, Illness Benefit and Occupational Injuries Benefits. Self-employed contributors who are ill may qualify for Invalidity Pension which is also based on a person’s PRSI record.
In circumstances where people are ill but do not qualify for a contributory payment, my Department provides means tested supports under the Disability Allowance scheme and the Supplementary Welfare Allowance scheme. An Additional Needs Payment may also be available to people who have expenses that they cannot pay from their weekly income.

question: Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Social Protection if his attention has been drawn to the significant level of negative feedback in relation to the €3 increase to the living alone allowance announced in Budget 2027; and the actions he is taking to specifically support recipients of this payment in the context of a very high cost of living.
reply:
The State Pension is the bedrock of the pension system in Ireland. It is very effective at ensuring that our pensioners do not experience poverty. This Government is committed to ensuring that this remains the case for current pensioners, those nearing State Pension age and today’s young workers including those who are only starting their careers.
Over €13 billion was allocated to State Pensions in Budget 2027, which is an increase of nearly one billion on Budget 2026. From January next year, the weekly State Pension is increasing by €10. This means the maximum rate of the State Pension (Contributory) will be €309.30 per week.
By January 2027, the State Pension (Contributory) will have increased by €61 per week since 2021. This shows continued commitment to supporting older people and this will remain a priority for Government.
It is recognised that the cost of living for a person living alone is greater than the individualised cost of two or more people living together. That is why a weekly Living Alone Increase is payable to all pensioners living alone who are in receipt of a State Pension from my Department. As part of Budget 2027, the LAI is increasing to €25 per week from next January. This payment has increased by nearly 178% since 2019, when it was just €9 per week.
I was also able to confirm that a Christmas bonus will be paid to almost 1.4 million long-term social welfare recipients in December 2026, including pensioners.

question: Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Social Protection to confirm that community welfare officers are now described as designated persons; the reason this title change occurred; and who recommended it.
reply:
The delivery of locally based community welfare services to meet the needs of citizens across the country is a priority for me and for my Department. Community Welfare Officers provide a flexible service to meet the different needs of people, who may find themselves in a financially difficult or vulnerable situation and it is important that this service is easily accessible and responsive to people's needs.
The Supplementary Welfare Allowance scheme, administered by my Department through the local Community Welfare Service, is the safety net within the overall social welfare system in that it provides assistance to eligible people in the State whose means are insufficient to meet their needs and those of their dependents.
While the legislation underpinning Supplementary Welfare Allowance refers to a Designated Person, it is a generic term to distinguish those officers who are granted powers in the legislation to make decisions on claims under the scheme.
I trust this clarifies the matter for the Deputy.

question: Deputy John Connolly asked the Minister for Social Protection to outline the changes to the seaweed harvesting disregard announced as part of budget 2027.
reply:
In Budget 2027, I announced an increase in the amount of income derived from seaweed harvesting which will be disregarded in the means assessment for Jobseeker’s Allowance, Fish Assist and Farm Assist. The maximum annual disregard in respect of income earned by a claimant or their spouse derived from seaweed harvesting will increase from €1,270 per year to €2,500.
This measure will take effect from July 2027 and will require amendments to the Social Welfare Consolidation Act, 2005, as well as the Social Welfare (Consolidated Claims, Payments and Control Provisions) Regulations 2007 SI No 142 of 2007, as amended.
The increase will enable individuals engaged in seaweed harvesting to retain a greater proportion of their earnings without affecting their entitlement to Jobseeker's Allowance, Farm Assist, or Fish Assist, thereby providing enhanced support to those living and working in rural and coastal communities.

question: Deputy Aidan Farrelly asked the Minister for Social Protection the grades of staff within his Department that have the authority to issue penalty rate on receipt of social welfare payment where that person has failed to engage with Intreo employment services; and the number of sanctions issued for same in each of the years 2023, 2024, 2025 and to date in 2026.
reply:
A Jobseeker payment is conditional on the recipient being available for, capable of and genuinely seeking work. This reflects the concept of ‘rights and responsibilities’ whereby people who are unemployed have the right to an income support from the State and a right to be supported in their efforts to secure employment but also have a responsibility to seek employment and to engage with the employment services offered by the State.
Jobseekers who do not engage with the Intreo Employment Service or who fail to participate in appropriate employment interventions can have their jobseeker’s payment reduced and subsequently be disqualified from their payment for up to 9 weeks. They may also have their entitlement to a Jobseekers payment reviewed based on a failure to genuinely seek work.
Decisions to apply a reduced rate of payment or disqualification are made by Deciding Officers appointed by me as Minister under Section 299 of the Social Welfare Consolidation Act 2005. For this purpose, the role of Deciding Officer is typically carried out by Clerical Officer and Executive Officer grades within my Department.
A reduced rate is a final step in a process to encourage a jobseeker to avail of the employment supports on offer and once a jobseeker resumes engagement with the employment support service, the reduced rate is lifted immediately.

question: Deputy George Lawlor asked the Minister for Social Protection if he will respond to matters raised in correspondence (details supplied) on 22 September 2026, requesting him to review arrangements for transferring private pension savings from Australia to Ireland for Irish citizens who have worked in Australia and have returned to reside and work in Ireland.
reply:
Transfers of pension benefits into Ireland are governed by a combination of tax law, and, where applicable, pensions law in respect of EU cross-border pension rules.
For an overseas pension transfer to be accepted into an Irish pension arrangement, the receiving Irish scheme must generally be a Revenue-approved arrangement, such as:
• an occupational pension scheme
• a Personal Retirement Savings Account (PRSA)
• a Personal Retirement Bond (Buy-Out Bond), where permitted
The scheme administrator in Ireland overseeing the transfer must ensure that the transfer complies with Revenue rules.
Aside from any applicable Irish rules or conditions on transfer, it is important to note the conditions concerning pension savings in a country outside of Ireland will be determined by the rules and regulations of that country. question: Deputy Claire Kerrane asked the Minister for Social Protection if a rural resident in their early 30s, who has completed a Tús placement and is not a qualifying farmer or fisher can currently access the RSS under any existing provision; if not, if he will consider extending the Rural Dweller Pilot to younger rural residents who have completed Tús, particularly where a recognised community organisation can demonstrate a genuine need for their services; and if he will consider introducing a limited discretionary mechanism or pilot arrangement to facilitate such participation, subject to appropriate eligibility criteria and eligibility.
reply:

The RSS aims to provide part-time employment opportunities for eligible participants who are underemployed in their primary farming or fishing enterprise, while also supporting the delivery of valuable services in rural communities. The scheme is primarily targeted at low-income farmers and fishers who satisfy the prescribed eligibility conditions.
In January 2026, the eligibility criteria for the RSS was amended to broaden the definition of a person with a defined connection to a farming or fishing enterprise and also to include spouses, civil partners, and cohabitants jointly engaged in farming or fishing activities. In Budget 2027, I was delighted to increase the number of partipants place on the Rural Dweller Pilot from 250 to 500.

reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 551 to 554, inclusive, 559, 560 and 613 together.
Tailte Éireann is an independent Government agency and provides a property registration system, property valuation service, and national mapping and surveying infrastructure for the State. Tailte Éireann is independent in the exercise of its valuation functions under the Valuation Act 2001, as amended (the Act).
Tailte Éireann has overall responsibility under the Act for the maintenance of all Valuation Lists used by Local Authorities in the calculation of rates liability. Under the Act, all property is rateable unless it falls into one of the exempt categories listed in Schedule 4 of the Act.
Under Irish law there is a distinct separation of functions between the valuation of rateable property and the setting and collection of commercial rates. The commercial rates payable on a particular property is a product of the valuation of that property determined by Tailte Éireann multiplied by the “Annual Rate on Valuation” (ARV) which is set annually by the elected members of the local authority as part of its budgetary process. question: Deputy Eoin Ó Broin asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage to confirm whether responsibility for the MUD Act and PSRA has transferred to his Department; and, if so, to confirm when he intends to initiate a review of the legislation underpinning both multiple unit developments and the property services regulatory authority.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 589, 594, 607 and 612 together.
At present, the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration and his Department continues to have responsibility for the oversight of OMCs and related legislation including the Multi-Unit Developments Act, 2011.
The Programme for Government committed to moving the responsibility for the MUDs Act to my Department to streamline support for OMCs and improve oversight and it is expected to transfer in due course.
I set out my priority with regard to a review of the MUDs Act to strengthen the operation of management companies in the 2025 National Housing Plan, "Delivering Homes, Building Communities 2025-2030".
The proposed review will commence, once responsibility has moved to my Department.
On 1 August 2025, the Property Services Regulatory Authority (PSRA) transferred functions from the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration (DJHAM) to my Department.
A review of the Property Services (Regulation) Act, 2011 is currently underway. This is in response to European Commission infringement proceedings initiated prior to the transfer of functions for the Property Services Regulatory Authority (PSRA) from the DJHAM to my Department. This legislative review seeks to make amendments to aspects of the control and supervision of the providers of property services and to take into account Directive 2006/123/EC in so far as it relates to property services.

question: Deputy Eoin Ó Broin asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage if he plans to include targets for Traveller-specific accommodation in housing delivery action plans.
reply:
The Housing (Traveller Accommodation) Act 1998 provides that the role of my Department is to ensure that there are adequate structures and supports in place to assist housing authorities in providing accommodation for Travellers, including a national framework of policy, legislation and funding.
The Act provides that housing authorities have statutory responsibility for the assessment of the accommodation needs of Travellers and the preparation, adoption and implementation of multi-annual Traveller Accommodation Programmes (TAPs) in their areas.
Under Delivering Homes, Building Communities, each local authority is preparing a Housing Delivery Action Plan (HDAP) setting out their planned delivery of social and affordable housing to 2030. Local authorities will reflect local need to ensure the right mix of homes to respond to need and priorities, including targets for group housing for Traveller households which will be informed, in particular, by their TAPs. It is expected that new HDAPs will be in place by Q4 2026.

question: Deputy Eoin Ó Broin asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage if his Department has formally instructed local authorities to include specific targets for UD+ (wheelchair liveable) dwellings within their Housing Delivery Action Plans; whether annual and five-year targets for universally designed housing, including wheelchair liveable homes, are mandatory within the HDAP framework; if his Department will require local authorities to revise and resubmit plans that do not contain such targets; and the way in which his Department plans to monitor and report on the delivery of wheelchair liveable homes during the lifetime of the plans.
reply:
Under Delivering Homes, Building Communities, the Government is targeting the delivery of 300,000 new homes by 2030. The plan commits to ensuring that the increased supply of social and affordable homes includes homes that reflect universal design principles, fostering inclusivity.
Under the Housing Plan, each local authority will prepare a Housing Delivery Action Plan (HDAP) setting out their planned delivery of social and affordable housing to 2030 in line with targets set by my Department to ensure the 72,000 social homes will be delivered by 2030. In preparing their HDAP, each local authority will reflect local need to ensure the right mix of homes to respond to local need and priorities including the needs of disabled people and older people.
Accordingly, in allowing local authorities to respond local needs, I have not mandated them to meet a specific percentage of social homes to be UD+ within their HDAP and it remains a matter for each local authority to set out the number of such homes required based on local needs. Subsequently, targets for the delivery of new build housing for older people and disabled people for the period 2027 – 2030 will be agreed as part of the HDAP review process. This phase of the process is underway and HDAPs will be finalised through an iterative process as various elements of the plans are agreed.

question: Deputy Naoise Ó Muirí asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage further to Parliamentary Question No. 66731/26, whether his Department has assessed housing demand using the 2022 Census data; if so, the estimated level of housing demand identified; and if he will provide the figures in tabular form.
reply:
Increasing the supply of new homes is critical to alleviating pressures in the housing market – in this regard, supply has increased significantly over recent years. Over the last five years, to end Q2 2026, more than 156,600 new homes have been delivered. This compares with 87,819 in the previous five-year period and just 29,855 in the five-years before that (Q2 2012 – Q2 2016).
The Government's housing plan, Delivering Homes, Building Communities, seeks to build on this momentum and deliver at least 300,000 new homes by 2030. The Government’s target is based on a realistic, broad assessment of the housing system, including factors such as population growth. As outlined in the plan, 300,000 homes is a baseline target, not a ceiling, and will be a cumulative result of the number of homes delivered during the lifetime of the plan.
Alongside this, the revised National Planning Framework (NPF) approved in April 2025 is a major step forward, and will help increase capacity and accelerate home building across the country as our population changes and further grows.
As outlined in Parliamentary Question No. 66731/26, as part of the First Revision of the NPF, the Economic and Social Research Institute (ESRI) was engaged to provide updated population projections to 2040, based on demographic modelling, and having regard to the results of Census 2022 including fertility, mortality and migration trends. reply:

question: Deputy Alan Kelly asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage when his Department last reviewed its policies, operations and handling of protected disclosures under all relevant protected disclosures legislation.
reply:
My Department’s policies, procedures and practices relating to the receipt, assessment and handling of protected disclosures are kept under ongoing review to ensure compliance with the Protected Disclosures Act 2014, as amended by the Protected Disclosures (Amendment) Act 2022. My Department’s current policy was finalised and circulated to all staff in June 2023, with minor updates in September 2025.
I can confirm a formal review of this policy is underway to ensure it continues to reflect legislative requirements and best practice and is expected to be completed no later than end January 2027.

question: Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage to provide the number of full-time equivalent staff within the climate action unit or division of his Department from 2020 to 2026 to date, broken down by year, in tabular form.
reply:
My Department continues to work hard on achieving our Climate Action Plan goals. While my Department does not have a specific climate action unit, there are units within my Department that have a role in climate action.
The Climate and Construction Innovation Unit takes a lead in developing and co-ordinating my Department’s Climate Action Policy and on climate matters relevant to all Divisions, across all Departmental structures, business units, and bodies and agencies under the aegis of my Department.
In addition to Climate and Construction Innovation unit a number of staff are employed across the Department working directly on Climate related programmes including Built and Archaeological Heritage Sectoral Adaptation Plan; Water Quality and Water Services Infrastructure Sectoral Adaptation Plan (Water SAP); Planning and Development Act 2024; the social housing energy efficiency retrofit programme and the Public Sector Climate Action mandate. A full list of Climate Action initiatives DHLGH staff are supporting can be found in the Government’s Climate Action Plans available at: www.gov.ie/en/department-of-climate-energy-and-the-environment/publications/climate-action-plan/

question: Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage whether the Government maintains a model estimating the impact of net migration on annual housing demand; and if so, the projected figures used by his Department in policy planning.
reply:
Increasing the supply of new homes is critical to alleviating pressures in the housing market – in this regard, supply has increased significantly over recent years. Over the last five years, to end Q2 2026, more than 156,600 new homes have been delivered. This compares with 87,819 in the previous five-year period and just 29,855 in the five-years before that (Q2 2012 – Q2 2016).
The Government's housing plan, Delivering Homes, Building Communities, seeks to build on this momentum and deliver at least 300,000 new homes by 2030. The Government’s target is based on a realistic, broad assessment of the housing system, including factors such as population change and migration trends.
My Department works with the Economic and Social Research Institute to undertake and publish projections of structural housing demand, and these projections include international migration under several scenarios. This research has also informed the revised National Planning Framework (NPF) that was approved in April 2025.
My Department continues to monitor several factors, including changing migration patterns, that may impact the demand and supply of housing on an ongoing basis. As part of this, following the publication of the final results of Census 2027, there will be an opportunity to further evaluate and consider a review of the National Planning Framework.

question: Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage whether Irish citizens and persons granted international protection status are treated identically for the purposes of social housing allocation; and where differences arise, to specify them.
reply:
Social housing support is intended to address a household’s long-term housing need. Therefore, households applying for such support have a long-term permission to reside in the State. It is the responsibility of the local authority to make a decision in each individual case with regard to qualification for social housing support, in accordance with the eligibility and need criteria set down in section 20 of the Housing (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 2009 and the associated Social Housing Assessment Regulations 2011, as amended, and associated Housing Circulars.
Persons granted refugee status, subsidiary protection status or permission to remain are eligible to be considered for social housing support, from the date of granting of such status, on the same basis as an Irish citizen. The residency requirements governing access to social housing support arise from the State's constitutional, European Union and international legal obligations. These requirements seek to ensure that social housing supports are available to persons who have a lawful and sufficient right to reside in the State, while complying with Ireland's obligations under domestic law, EU law and international protection frameworks.

As I understand it, the issue has previously been the subject of correspondence between Tailte Éireann and the parties and was addressed in full.

question: Deputy Peadar Tóibín asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage the cost to date of developing the Lough Erne by-laws, including the cost of the 2015 public consultation that could not be relied upon; and the reason a new consultation was required.
reply:
In 2015, Waterways Ireland commenced a review of the Lough Erne Bye-Laws and undertook a public consultation process. As this work was carried out largely in-house, no significant external costs were incurred.
Subsequently, with the commencement of the review of the Shannon and Canal Bye-Laws, a decision was taken to defer the revision of the Lough Erne Bye-Laws until the updated Shannon and Canal Bye-Laws had been finalised and brought into force.
Given the passage of time since the 2015 consultation, the Department for Infrastructure (NI) advised Waterways Ireland that the views obtained at that time can no longer be relied upon as the sole basis for progressing revised Erne Bye-Laws. Accordingly, a further targeted consultation process will be required to supplement the previous engagement.

question: Deputy James O'Connor asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage if he will consider including an estate (details supplied) in the interim remediation scheme or any related scheme under his Department's remit.
reply:
Drafting of the Apartment and Duplex Defects Remediation Scheme Bill is at an advanced stage and it is listed for publication this session. The statutory scheme will be in place as soon as possible following its passage through the Dáil.
The Scheme will provide supports for the remediation of relevant fire safety, structural safety and water ingress defects in purpose-built apartment buildings, including duplexes, constructed between 1991 and 2013. It is envisaged that 100% of eligible remediation costs will be funded.
The Interim Remediation Scheme ('Scheme') has been in place since December 2023, to provide an acceptable level of fire safety in buildings pending introduction of the Statutory Scheme and completion of the full remedial works. The Scheme is for the funding of emergency fire safety defect works in apartments and duplexes constructed between 1991 and 2013. Eligibility is determined by reference to the scope of the scheme as approved by Government. The Scheme is administered by the Housing Agency. Applications can be made via the Housing Agency’s website at: www.housingagency.ie
The management and operation of the Scheme, including application processing, eligibility assessments and engagement with applicants, is a matter for the Housing Agency. Details on individual applications are not held by my Department. The Housing Agency is responsible for the administration of the Scheme and the associated operational data.

question: Deputy Peadar Tóibín asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage the reason Waterways Ireland operates without a board, unlike other agencies (details supplied); whether a board will be established; and the governance arrangements currently in place.
reply:
Waterways Ireland is North-South Body under the British-Irish Agreement Act, 1999, and as such was established without a Board. The functions of the Agency are exercised by a Chief Executive under the direction of the North South Ministerial Council.
In 2021, the North South Ministerial Council agreed that officials from the Sponsor Departments, in consultation with the Joint Secretariat of the NSMC would explore options for the establishment of a Board to oversee the work of Waterways Ireland. This matter remains under consideration, with a view to bringing proposals to a future meeting of the Council.

question: Deputy Peadar Tóibín asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage the estimated cost of the planned relocation of Waterways Ireland's Tullamore premises to a new purpose-built depot; the original and current cost estimates for the Ulster Canal restoration project; and the completion timeline for each.
reply:
The construction cost for Waterways Ireland's operational depot at Tullamore is €8.2m (VAT inclusive). It is expected that the relocation will occur in mid-2027 when the buildings fit out and equipment commissioning are completed. There are no relocation costs associated with moving the location of the Tullamore depot to the new site as it is within the 45km limit for staff relocation.
The restoration of the Ulster Canal is a major cross-border project principally funded by the Shared Island Fund, which when completed will provide approximately 13.5 km of new navigation and will connect Clones, Co. Monaghan with Upper Lough Erne, Co. Fermanagh. The project is being delivered by Waterways Ireland in three phases. Phase 1 from Upper Lough Erne to Castle Saunderson (c. 2.5 km) was completed in 2019. Phase 2 from Clones to Clonfad (new marina in Clones plus 1 km of canal) was completed June 2024).
Phase 3 Castle Saunderson to Clonfad (c. 10 km) is currently underway. I am not in a position to give the estimated cost of Phase 3 until such time as the tender process is completed and contracts have been awarded.
The project remains on target for completion by the end of 2029, subject to successful land acquisition and procurement of delivery partners.

question: Deputy Ivana Bacik asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage if he is satisfied by the adequacy of Part V of the Planning and Development Acts 2000 to 2024 in view of a situation (details supplied).
reply:

The Ministerial Guidelines on Part V, issued to local authorities under section 28 of the 2000 Act, emphasise the need for consultation with developers regarding the delivery of appropriately located properties at the earliest stage possible, preferably in advance of planning.
This early consultation allows local authorities to consider the need, and the likely future need, for housing for persons who have different levels of income, as well as the need to ensure that a mixture of unit types and sizes are developed to reasonably match the requirements of different categories of households, as may be determined by the local authority.

question: Deputy Ivana Bacik asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage when the review of the Code of Practice for an Approved Housing Body will be complete; if he will ensure that social tenants of AHBs and local authorities can keep pets.
reply:
The national housing plan, Building Homes, Delivery Communities, commits to reviewing the CCMA Code of Practice - Approved Housing Body (AHB) Allocation Process (the Code). A Working Group, including local authority and AHB representatives, has been established by my Department to examine the Code and its implementation.

reply:

The relevant provisions of the Planning and Development Act 2024 are contained in Chapter 2 of Part 7 of that Act. Those provisions have not yet commenced. Accordingly, the Part V agreements and housing delivery referred to in this reply arise under Part V of the Planning and Development Act 2000, as amended.
As noted in the National Housing Plan - Delivering Homes, Building Communities, Part V of the Planning and Development Act 2000 requires private developers to ensure that 20% of land zoned for residential and other uses is reserved for social housing and starter homes. Local authorities negotiate Part V agreements with developers in line with a range of guidelines and supports aimed at assisting them in maximising the benefits of Part V, in the context of their housing needs. The allocation of the Part V component of any development between social houses and starter homes and the negotiations of such Part V agreements is therefore, in the first instance, a matter for each Local Authority to determine. As such, my Department does not report on the number of Part V agreements that are unresolved or under negotiations.
Guidance on the preparation and execution of Part V agreements is available in Circular 5/2017, ‘Part V of the Planning and Development A

question: Deputy Robert O'Donoghue asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage given the recent confirmation that homes in Dublin Fingal are now to be included in the defective concrete blocks grant scheme, whether Fingal County Council have been instructed on the implementation on the scheme by his Department; and when applications can be made from residents in Dublin Fingal.
reply:

question: Deputy Paul McAuliffe asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage the preparatory work undertaken by his Department regarding the transfer of responsibility for the Multi-Unit Developments Act 2011; and the timeline for establishment of a regulatory framework for owners' management companies following the transfer.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 589, 594, 607 and 612 together.
At present, the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration and his Department continues to have responsibility for the oversight of OMCs and related legislation including the Multi-Unit Developments Act, 2011.
The Programme for Government committed to moving the responsibility for the MUDs Act to my Department to streamline support for OMCs and improve oversight and it is expected to transfer in due course.
I set out my priority with regard to a review of the MUDs Act to strengthen the operation of management companies in the 2025 National Housing Plan, "Delivering Homes, Building Communities 2025-2030".

reply:

question: Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage to provide details of the change proposed to the local authority borrowing envelope in Budget 2026; and provide timelines for when it will be implemented.
reply:
Local Authorities are the key stakeholders in the delivery of social and affordable housing. They are also key in delivering on other Government priorities such as infrastructure, urban regeneration and energy policies.
Under Section 106 of the Local Government Act 2001, local authority borrowing is a reserved function requiring both a resolution of elected members and Ministerial sanction.
Both expenditure of their own resources and borrowing by local authorities has a negative impact on the general government balance. Since 2013, local authorities have been required to have a neutral impact on the general government balance, which has impacted on the amount local authorities can borrow. In recent times, revision of the borrowing framework has been recommended in a number of reports.
On 24 June 2025, Government noted and approved the overall approach set out in the Report and Roadmap for Delivery on Dublin City Centre Taskforce Report, including a recommendation that the Department of Finance consider options in changing the borrowing approach, in terms of the overall envelope for the Local Government sector.
Action 7.4 in Delivering Homes, Building Communities is to “provide greater access to more affordable tenancies by accelerating the growth of the cost rental sector, streamline funding support schemes for cost rental delivery and explore increasing debt ceiling levels for local authority borrowing.”

question: Deputy Robert Troy asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage If he can provide an update on the National planning guidelines; when they will be introduced; and if the guidelines will contain a clear and consistent national framework on the development, location and scale of large scale solar and BESS projects.
reply:
In line with commitments in the Programme for Government 2025, my Department is working with the Department of Climate, Energy and the Environment (DCEE), which holds policy responsibility for renewable energy matters, in respect of the introduction of a number of National Planning Statements related to Ireland's Climate Action Plan target to increase the share of electricity generated from renewable sources up to 80% in 2030. This includes the preparation of a National Planning Statement in relation to Solar Energy Development and scoping the need for a Planning Statement in respect of BESS projects.
Further to the commencement of Chapter 3 of Part 3 of the Planning and Development Act 2024 on 2 October 2025, provisions for National Planning Statements have been introduced to replace the provisions for Ministerial guidelines issued under section 28 of the Planning and Development Act 2000. All existing Section 28 guidelines will, over time, be revoked and replaced with new National Planning Statements. Any current section 28 guidelines will however remain in force until revoked or replaced by a corresponding National Planning Statement. The timing of the issuing of National Planning Statements will be based on Government priorities.

question: Deputy Pearse Doherty asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage the position regarding the review of the defective concrete block grant scheme legislative review.
reply:
The Remediation of Dwellings Damaged by the use of Defective Concrete Blocks Act 2022 as amended by the Act of 2025 sets out the framework under which the Grant Scheme which provides grant funding to people whose homes have been affected by Defective Concrete Blocks operates.
A number of amendments contained in the 2025 Act came into operation on 25 February 2026 and more recently further provisions commenced on 27 May 2026.
As per Section 51 of the 2022 Act (as amended), a review of the operation of the Act has now been commenced and is being carried out by my Department with the assistance of external expertise.
The review will make recommendations regarding several aspects of the Act and their interaction with the Defective Concrete Blocks Grant Scheme.
The review is progressing. Following its completion, I will report to each House of the Oireachtas, setting out the findings and conclusions arising from the review, in accordance with the requirements of the Act.
It is not possible to provide a timeframe for its completion at this point in time. However, the work will continue to be progressed as quickly as possible.

question: Deputy Barry Heneghan asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage whether his Department has examined or plans to introduce mandatory standards for residential property advertisements, including verified floor areas, accurate property descriptions and transparent asking prices.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 579 to 582, inclusive, together.
I wish to advise the Deputy, with regard to standards for residential property advertisements, including use of AI-generated or digitally altered images, that Regulation 10(2) of the Property Services (Regulation) Act 2011 (Minimum Standards) Regulations 2020 states that “a licensee shall not knowingly produce, publish or circulate, or cause to be produced, published or circulated, by whatever means, misleading information in respect of land or property other than land, advertised for auction, sale or to let.”
In relation to transparent asking prices, Section 55 of the Property Services (Regulation) Act 2011 requires a licensee to provide a statement of the advised market value of a property to the property vendor. Section 56 prevents the licensee from stating the estimated selling price as “a price that is less than the advised market value of the land provided by the licensee to the vendor under section 55 or, where such advised market value is expressed as a relevant price range, a price that is less than the lower limit of that range”, orally or in writing:
(a) in any advertisement in respect of the land;
(b) in the particulars or conditions of sale of the land;
(c) to a prospective purchaser of the land; or
(d) at the time of the auction of the land.
The Property Services Regulatory Authority's (PSRA) remit in oversight of licensed estate agents is to ensure that agents operate in compliance with the Prope

question: Deputy Michael Murphy asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage whether the National Parks and Wildlife Service has undertaken an ecological assessment of the damage caused by the July and August 2026 wildfires on Slievenamon, including Slievenamon Bog NHA (Site Code 002388); the findings of any such assessment; and whether Slievenamon has been identified for consideration under Ireland's National Nature Restoration Plan.
reply:
Following the fire in Slievenamon in July the NPWS did a preliminary site inspection of the privately owned NHA (Natural Heritage Area Site Code 002388) but no formal ecological assessment has been carried out to date.
In relation to the second part of the question, Ireland submitted a draft Nature Restoration Plan Template, in the format mandated by the EU, on 1 September, the deadline set out in the EU Nature Restoration Regulation. This template is an early-stage, technical draft, focused mainly on setting out baseline information, available data and existing measures rather than a final programme of restoration actions or specific sites.
A phased process will now commence to develop the final plan, including dialogue with the EU, together with extensive stakeholder engagement and public feedback helping to shape the final document for submission to European Commission in 2027.

question: Deputy Albert Dolan asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage whether the measures contained in the European Affordable Housing Plan have been incorporated into the review or amendment of regional and local planning and housing strategies; and, if so, to identify the relevant measures and implementation timelines.
reply:
The European Commission published its European Affordable Housing Plan on 16 December 2025. My Department engaged proactively last year with the Commission in the development of the Plan and has continued to do so in the period since in relation to its implementation, including with regard to revised state aid rules, the proposal for an Affordable Housing Act, the housing simplification package and the Pan European Investment Platform.
Noting the principle of subsidiarity, the European Affordable Housing Plan intends to complement the efforts of Member States in addressing the lack of affordable housing across the EU. It recognises that housing remains a national competence, but that the EU can play a supportive role in helping Member States to deliver affordable, sustainable and good quality housing for citizens.
Housing strategies and regional and local planning strategies are set by the respective authorities in Ireland.
The National Planning Framework is the long-term, 20-year strategy for strategic planning and sustainable development of our urban and rural areas to 2040. Following a revision process which began in June 2023, the National Planning Framework was updated in April 2025.
Further to the approval of the Revised NPF, the NPF Implementation: Housing Growth Requirements Guidelines were issued in July 2025. These guidelines set out the housing demand scenario to 2040 for each local authority by translating the NPF housing requirements into estimated average annual

question: Deputy Albert Dolan asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage whether national housing targets for 2026 to 2030 include targets for the delivery of starter homes; if so, to provide those targets by year and by local authority or county, broken down between rural areas and villages, towns and cities, in tabular form.
reply:
The housing action plan, Delivering Homes Building Communities, reinforces and expands the range of existing affordable housing measures being implemented by the Government. In particular, a new Starter Homes Programme, which is a central component of the plan, aims to deliver an average of 15,000 affordable housing supports annually to 2030, including starter homes for purchase and cost rental homes.
This expanded delivery will build upon the significant progress already made under our previous plan, Housing for All. In 2025 alone, over 9,300 supports were delivered across the Starter Homes Purchase Scheme (formerly the Local Authority Affordable Purchase Scheme), Cost Rental, the First Home Scheme and the Vacant Property Refurbishment Grant.
In order to further drive the delivery of starter homes under the plan, local authorities are now preparing their new Housing Delivery Action Plans (HDAPs), replacing those published in 2021. The purpose of these new HDAPs is to disaggregate the overall delivery requirement for starter homes for purchase and Cost Rental supports to local authority level.
My Department is currently examining the draft HDAPs submitted by the local authorities to ensure that they provide for delivery in line with the Housing Plan, and are engaging with local authorities, as necessary, before the plans are finalised.
My Department publishes comprehensive programme level statistics on a quarterly basis, tracking starter home delivery activity by local author

question: Deputy Albert Dolan asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage the amount of European Union and European investment bank financing which is planned, targeted or anticipated to support housing and housing-related infrastructure in Ireland for each year from 2026 to 2030, broken down by region where available, in tabular form; and the measures being taken to maximise the use of such financing under relevant EU affordable housing initiatives.
reply:
The European Commission published its European Affordable Housing Plan on 16 December 2025.
A specific commitment of the European Affordable Housing Plan is the establishment of a Pan-European Investment Platform for Affordable and Sustainable Housing. The objective of the Platform will be to provide a single framework to support investment in affordable and sustainable housing. Work on the Platform is ongoing within the Commission, in close dialogue with partners like the European Investment Bank (EIB) and other partners, including national and regional promotional banks and international financial institutions. It is expected that the Commission will launch the Platform later this year.
The European Affordable Housing Plan identifies that national and regional promotional banks will aim to invest €375 billion by 2029 into social, affordable and sustainable housing across the EU.
The Plan also commits to mobilise new investment in housing under the current Multiannual Finance Framework (MFF) and to offer new opportunities to scale up housing investments under the new MFF.
From a national perspective, specific schemes co-funded by the EU and other EU Structural and Investment funds include the Town Centre First Heritage Revival Scheme via the European Regional Development Fund (ERDF) for urban regeneration. Ireland is investing €880 million through the ERDF for the 2021–2027 programming period.
The ERDF has two Managing Authorities in Ireland: the Northern and Western Regiona

question: Deputy Pádraig O'Sullivan asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage if his Department has assessed the feasibility of using anonymised or aggregated utility consumption data, including electricity, gas and water usage, to improve the identification of vacant residential properties; and if such an assessment has been undertaken.
reply:

While there are varying indicators of vacancy based on different sources and methodologies, with resulting differing data, the overall trend in vacancy levels is downwards.

In March 2026, the CSO released data for 2024 which details a national vacancy rate of 3.2%, 70,149 dwellings at the end of 2024, down from 3.3%, 72,254 dwellings at the end of 2023. Commentary on the CSO's methodology and a full break down of the resulting data can be reviewed in their publication, www.cso.ie/en/releasesandpublications/fp/fp-rvmec/residentialvacancybasedonmeteredelectricityconsumption2024/keyfindings/
While this data does not identify specific vacant properties, it is used by my Department as an indicator of vacancy and housing stock efficiency.
This data is also beneficial to the work of local authorities in tackling vacancy an

question: Deputy Pádraig O'Sullivan asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage the criteria local authorities use when determining whether a residential property is derelict; and if written national guidance exists to ensure consistency of assessment between local authorities.
reply:
Working to end vacancy and dereliction is a key priority in the Government's housing plan, Delivering Homes, Building Communities. The Plan aims to ensure that the activities and resources used to address vacancy and dereliction are co-ordinated and effective and that legislative powers are used proactively to work to bring vacancy and dereliction to an end.
The Derelict Sites Act 1990 imposes a general duty on every owner and occupier of land to take all reasonable steps to ensure that land does not become, or continue to be, a derelict site as defined in the Act. The Act also imposes a duty on local authorities to take all reasonable steps, including the exercise of appropriate statutory powers, to ensure that any land within their functional area does not become, or continue to be, a derelict site.
Each local authority maintains a Derelict Sites Register under section 8 of the Act for sites which they consider are derelict under the Act. Sites entered on the Derelict Sites Register are subject to an annual derelict sites levy of 7% of market value which will continue to apply until the site is rendered non-derelict.
A property can be placed on the derelict site register where it is deemed by a local authority to satisfy the criteria of a derelict site under the terms of section 3 of the Act:

question: Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage his views on whether the current housing legislation is sufficiently prescriptive in terms of directing local authorities to the criteria which they must consider when allocating available council housing.
reply:
The legislative framework governing the allocation of social housing is set out in the Housing (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 2009, as amended (the Act), and in the Social Housing Allocation Regulations 2011, as amended.
This legislation requires all local authorities, as a reserved function, to make an allocation scheme determining the order of priority to be accorded in the allocation of dwellings to households qualified for social housing support and to households approved for a transfer, the allocation of which would, in the opinion of the authority, meet the accommodation needs and requirements of the households.
This statutory framework allows local authorities flexibility to respond to local housing need, with the allocation of dwellings a matter for the local authority concerned, in accordance with their allocation scheme made under section 22 of the Act. The regulations also require authorities to have regard to factors such as housing need and the accommodation requirements of households and also provides for the operation of choice-based letting systems in the allocation of social housing.
Notwithstanding this, I am conscious of the need to ensure that allocation schemes continue to support broader housing policy objectives, particularly in relation to homelessness. question: Deputy Eoin Ó Broin asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage the number of premature deaths of people experiencing homelessness recorded in each year from 2020 to 2025, either by the Dublin Region Homeless Executive or across all homeless regions; and the steps that have been taken on each of the ten recommendations of the interim report on mortality in single homeless population 2020.
reply:
My Department does not collate the information sought. The Department of Health commissioned the Health Research Board (HRB) to collect data on all deaths which occur among people who are homeless nationally. The HRB collects data directly from coronial files and provides analysis of patterns of premature mortality. The purpose of the report is to improve understanding of premature mortality of people who are homeless and to inform healthcare services for this cohort. Information recently released by the Dublin Region Homeless Executive in relation to deaths in service in 2025 by location and service type has not been subject to HRB analysis.
The most recent HRB report is in respect of deaths that occurred in 2022. The Health Research Board report identified 124 deaths among persons who were homeless that were sudden and unexpected in 2022. The median age of death was 48 years. I extend my sympathies to the families and friends of the deceased and also acknowledge the important work carried out by those on the frontline.
My Department continues to work closely with the Department of Health, the Health Service Executive (HSE) and Local Authorities to deliver the appropriate measures to support all individuals experiencing homelessness including those with complex needs.
Housing First is a key government policy to reduce homelessness, especially for the most vulnerable people. Housing First is a key policy response to The Housing First approach to addressing homelessness places

question: Deputy Conor Sheehan asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage for an update on the preparations and timeline for the statutory review of the operation and effectiveness of the Local Government (Mayor of Limerick) and Miscellaneous Provisions Act 2024, as required under section 7 of the Act; and the status of consultations with the Mayor of Limerick, Limerick City and County Council, and the Limerick Mayoral and Government Consultative Forum.
reply: The Local Government (Mayor of Limerick) and Miscellaneous Provisions Act 2024 provides for a directly elected Mayor of Limerick with executive functions and the new arrangements in Limerick City and County Council. Section 7 of the Act provides that the Minister conduct a review of the operation and effectiveness of the Act no later than three years after the establishment of the mayoral office. The period of three years was viewed as the appropriate balance between needing a mechanism to assess the new office in a timely way, while also allowing time for the new arrangements to become established in Limerick. In conducting the review, the Minister must consult with the Mayor, the members of Limerick City and County Council, the Limerick Mayoral and Government Consultative Forum and any other relevant persons. The Minister must report on the findings of the review and conclusions to both Houses of the Oireachtas. Preparations are currently underway for the review to begin before the end of 2026.

In this regard, supply has increased significantly over recent years. Over the last five years, to end Q2 2026, more than 156,600 new homes have been delivered. This compares with 87,819 in the previous five-year period and just 29,855 in the five-years before that (Q2 2012 – Q2 2016).
Data on New Dwelling Completions are published by the Central Statistics Office on a quarterly basis at: data.cso.ie/table/NDQ05. CSO data show overall housing delivery in Laois has significantly increased in recent years.


Some 2,751 new homes completed in the period 2022 to 2025, an increase of 129% on the previous four year period. This momentum continued into the first half of this year, some 451 new homes have been delivered in H1 2026, up 22% year on year and the highest H1 total since the CSO data series began in 2011.
Supply continues to be the focus of the Government's housing policy. While my Department does not forecast new housing completions for a particular year, delivery in 2026 is likely to be strong.
