reply:
Tailte Éireann is a Government agency under the aegis of my Department and is independent in the exercise of its valuation functions under the Valuation Act 2001, as amended.
The making of valuations for rating purposes is the responsibility of Tailte Éireann and I, as Minister, have no function in decisions in this regard.
Schedule 3, paragraphs 1(a) and (b), of the Valuation Act 2001 provide that all buildings and lands used or developed for any purpose are rateable. The Act provides for a limited range of exemptions under Schedule 4 and Tailte Éireann has no discretion to grant exemptions other than those expressly provided for in legislation. In carrying out its functions, Tailte Éireann examines each property on its own facts and circumstances, having regard to the relevant statutory provisions.
Local authorities are under a statutory obligation to levy rates on properties entered on the valuation lists prepared by Tailte Éireann. The levying and collection of rates are matters for each individual local authority.
Local authorities may support ratepayers through schemes made under Section 15 of the Local Government Rates and Other Matters Act 2019 and Part 9 of the Local Government Act 2001. Decisions on such schemes are reserved functions of the elected members and provide local authorities with flexibility to address local priorities and support community, social and economic development, urban planning and rural regeneration objectives.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport the statutory powers of TV licence inspectors under the Broadcasting Act 2009; the circumstances in which they may enter residential premises; the requirements regarding identification and production of appointment certificates; whether householders may refuse entry.
reply:
The legislative basis for the television licence is set out in Part 9 of the Broadcasting Act 2009.
Section 145 of the Act assigns An Post as the issuing agent for the television licence. Under this section, An Post is empowered to, on behalf of the Minister, issue licences, collect fees, identify persons with television sets who have not paid their television licence, and to bring summary proceedings and prosecute persons for the offence of keeping a television set without a television licence.
Section 146(1) of the Broadcasting Act 2009 provides that An Post as the issuing agent may appoint authorised officers ('TV licence inspectors'). In accordance with section 146(2) of the Act, TV licence inspectors must be issued with certification of their appointment and, when undertaking an inspection, must produce this certification if requested by any person affected by the inspection.
Section 146(3) of the Act provides that a TV licence inspector may enter at any reasonable time any premises for the purposes of ascertaining whether there is a television set there and a television licence is for the time being in force in respect of the premises.
In terms of the other statutory powers of a TV licence inspector:

question: Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport the number of successful Community Sport Facilities Fund applicants that subsequently failed to draw down their allocations in full in each of the years 2022 to 2025 and to date in 2026; the value of unspent grants involved; and the reason funding was not utilised.
reply:
In the period in question, there was one round of allocations under the Community Sport Facilities Fund (CSFF) made in 2024 in respect of the 2023 round. The allocations totalled €277,863,166 and were awarded to 3,046 community sports clubs and facilities.
858 organisations have drawn down their allocations from that 2023 round in full, amounting to €55,267,764.
A further 1,452 organisations, with allocations totalling €146,215,310, have drawn down €58,118,155 to date, with €88,097,155 yet to be drawn down.
The remaining 736 organisations, with allocations totalling €76,380,092, have not yet drawn down any funding.
Accordingly, 2,188 organisations have yet to draw down their allocations in full, with a total outstanding balance of €164,477,247. These figures represent the current drawdown position for the 2023 round.
An allocation that has not yet been drawn down in full should not, on that basis alone, be regarded as funding that will not be utilised. Projects may be at different stages such as obtaining formal approval, completing works or submitting payment claims.
My Department recently advised organisations that had not yet sought formal approval for their 2023 grant that they have until 1 October 2027 to demonstrate substantial progress. This is a deadline for demonstrating progress, rather than a requirement to draw down the grant in full by that date.

question: Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport the number of meetings held by his Department, Coimisiún na Meán or agencies under his remit with technology companies where the subjects of misinformation, harmful content, content moderation or fact-checking were discussed since January 2023.
reply:
The regulation of online platforms for harmful and illegal content is provided for under the Online Safety Framework, comprising the Online Safety and Media Regulation Act 2022, the EU Digital Services Act, the EU AI Act and the Terrorist Content Online Regulation. Coimisiún na Meán is lead regulator for that framework. Under Section 10 of the Broadcasting and Other Media Regulation Acts, 2009 and 2022, Coimisiún na Meán is independent in the exercise of its functions.
In relation to disinformation as part of the process of developing the National Counter Disinformation Strategy, on 29 November 2023, my Department arranged an in-person consultation event. The Strategy was published in April 2025 and information on the development process and progress on implementation is available on the Strategy webpage.

question: Deputy John Lahart asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport if consideration has been given to the late opening of the National Gallery and other state buildings such as the National Writer's Museum and the National Library, other than on a Thursday evening at least once a month; and the obstacles that are in the way of such an arrangement.
reply:
The potential expansion of opening hours for National Cultural Institutions is primarily a question for each National Cultural Institution itself, and decisions regarding opening hours cannot be made by my Department on their behalf.
There are numerous factors which can impact on the feasibility of extending the opening hours of a National Cultural Institution, including, for example, additional staff costs in the form of overtime payments or the necessity to increase overall staff numbers to maintain an equal level of service to evening visitors to a National Cultural Institutions. There are also additional non-pay costs that may be incurred as a result of longer opening hours, such as cleaning and maintenance, energy consumption, and other ancillary costs.
The National Concert Hall and the Abbey Theatre already remain open to 10PM or later on numerous occasions during the year to facilitate the holding of concerts, plays and similar events.
In relation to the museum described by the Deputy as the National Writers Museum, I am assuming that this refers to the Museum of Literature Ireland. This is a subsidiary company of University College Dublin and any decision on opening hours is a matter for the company in question.

These awards support artists at different career stages, enabling research, experimentation, creation, touring, professional development and engagement with communities.

question: Deputy Holly Cairns asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport further to Parliamentary Question No. 69926/26, the estimated timeframe for when applicants to the basic income for the arts will be informed as to whether or not they will receive the payment; and to provide an estimated timeframe for the issuing of the first payment.
reply:
In February this year I announced that the Government had approved a permanent successor to the Basic Income for the Arts pilot scheme and that 2,000 artists would be provided with funding of €325 per week for three years. This is a major milestone for the arts in Ireland and I am particularly pleased that the research my Department conducted provided Government with a clear evidence base upon which to make that decision.
The deadline for application to the Basic Income for the Arts 2026 - 2029 was 5pm on Tuesday 12th May, with over 10,000 applications received by the deadline.
I appreciate that applicants are eager to know the outcome, however, in order to protect the integrity of the scheme the assessment process is by necessity very intensive and time consuming. No two professional arts practices are the same and therefore the proofs supplied vary considerably. The Department has commenced communication to applicants invited to participate in the scheme on Thursday 15 October. Due to the volume involved, successful applicants will be notified in tranches as assessments are completed.
My Department is processing the applications as promptly as possible and I anticipate that payments will commence shortly. All successful candidates will receive the full allocation of €325 per week for three years.

question: Deputy Seán Ó Fearghaíl asked the Minister for Education and Youth if her Department is aware that a child with special educational needs (details supplied) was verbally refused enrolment by a school and did not receive any written notification of the decision or information regarding their right of appeal; and the steps being taken to secure an appropriate school placement for the child.
reply:
The National Council for Special Education (NCSE) is the statutory body responsible for the provision of special education and allocating supports for students with special educational needs.
It is the responsibility of the managerial authorities of all schools to implement an admissions policy in accordance with the Education Act, 1998 and the Education (Admission to Schools) Act 2018.
Under the provisions of this act, all schools are required to have admissions policies which have been approved by the patron following consultation with staff and parents of students who are attending the school. It is a key requirement of the act that all school admission policies are fair and transparent.
Parents may apply to enrol their child in a school of their choosing and where the school has places available for the relevant year, the student should be admitted. However, in schools where there are more applicants than places available, a selection process will be necessary. This selection process and the enrolment policy on which it is based must be non-discriminatory and must be applied fairly in respect of all applicants. Nonetheless, it may result in some students not obtaining a place in the school of their first choice.
The NCSE is, in the first instance, the primary body responsible for the matter the Deputy has raised. I will arrange for your query to be forwarded to the NCSE for their attention and direct reply. Deputies are also welcome to raise such queries with the NCSE dir

question: Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Education and Youth the position regarding the number of schools in the Dublin region that have one or more students with a therapy dog for any part of the school day.
reply:
This government is fully committed to supporting students with special educational needs to fulfil their full potential and the Programme for Government makes a number of commitments to deliver on this objective.
The provision of assistance dogs within a school is a matter for each individual school. As a health support, any guidance required by a school in relation to this provision should be sought from the HSE.
My department and the NCSE are committed to delivering an education system that is of the highest quality and where every child and young person feels valued and is actively supported and nurtured to achieve their full potential.

question: Deputy Alan Kelly asked the Minister for Education and Youth when her Department last reviewed its policies, operations and handling of protected disclosures under all relevant protected disclosures legislation.
reply:
Since the introduction of the Protected Disclosures (Amendment) Act 2022, my department has regularly reviewed its policies and procedures. A 2025 internal audit of protected disclosure practices evaluated the effectiveness of our management and control systems, resulting in several minor recommendations that my department implemented to strengthen its processes.
As a member of both the Protected Disclosure National Advisory Group and Transparency International Ireland’s Integrity at Work (IAW) programme, my department is committed to adopting best practice.
Under section 22 of the Act, my department publishes its protected disclosure annual reports and they are available at gov.ie.

question: Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Minister for Education and Youth to provide the number of full-time equivalent staff within the climate action unit or division of her Department from 2020 to 2026 to date, broken down by year, in tabular form.
reply:

This performance has been recognised at both National and International level with sustainable energy awards for excellence in design, specification and delivery. The content of the School Sector Climate Action Mandate strongly reflects the requirements of the Public Sector Climate Action Mandate.

question: Deputy Ann Graves asked the Minister for Education and Youth to introduce free period products in schools.
reply:
The Programme for Government, Securing Ireland’s Future, includes a commitment to provide free period products in schools to ensure no student is held back due to period poverty.
I was pleased to include funding for free period products to all qualifying schools in the DEIS Plus Scheme for the 2026/27 school year. Payments have now issued to these schools.
My department is working to ensure the Programme for Government commitment is progressed.

reply:

Overall, approximately €230 million is invested in the DEIS programme. This includes the additional €48 million secured under Budget 2026 to support the implementation of the DEIS Strategy to 2035 and the introduction of the DEIS Plus scheme. Budget 2027 provides a further €6 million to support the expansion of DEIS Plus.

question: Deputy Pearse Doherty asked the Minister for Education and Youth to confirm that all public schools can apply for insurance through the Irish Public Bodies Mutual Insurance Ltd., IPB; and to outline the process for schools to apply for insurance through the IPB.
reply:
Many Irish public-sector education bodies, including ETBs and some schools, obtain insurance through IPB.
Responsibility for procurement of insurance and payment of same rests with Boards of Management and the Education and Training Boards (ETBs) in respect of schools operated by them.
Boards of Management and ETBs should take a proactive approach when it comes to sourcing insurance in order to ensure best value is obtained and to ensure compliance with public procurement procedures.
The department does not have any oversight over the Irish Public Bodies Mutual Insurance Ltd (IPB) and cannot provide information on their processes.
The Schools Procurement Unit (www.spu.ie), funded by the department, has a national remit and is available to advise and assist schools in relation to procurement matters.

question: Deputy Peadar Tóibín asked the Minister for Education and Youth the procedures followed where an applicant for international protection who has been enrolled in second-level education as a child is subsequently found not to be a minor following an age assessment; whether such persons remain enrolled in second-level schools or are removed from those settings; the number of cases arising in each of the past five years; and the number of individuals removed from second-level education as a result.
reply:
Under the provisions of the Education Act, 1998 the Board of Management is the body charged with the direct governance of a school on behalf of the patron, and the principal is responsible for the day-to-day management of the school.
Where a Board of Management decides to expel a student from a school, the parent/guardian, or in the case of a student who has reached the age of 18 years, the student themselves, may appeal that decision under Section 29 of the Education Act 1998 (as amended). An independent appeals committee is appointed to consider such appeals.
Any decision to suspend or exclude a student must be taken in accordance with the school’s code of behaviour, as required under Section 23 of the Education (Welfare) Act and would be subject to the appeal mechanisms described above.
Details on Separated children seeking international protection is available at www.tusla.ie/services/alternative-care/separated-children/. The Department of Children, Disability and Equality may have additional information in this regard.
The Department does not have or maintain the information requested by the Deputy.

reply:
The key factor for determining the level of staffing resources provided at individual school level is the staffing schedule for the relevant school year and pupil enrolments on the previous 30 September. The staffing schedule operates in a clear and transparent manner and treats all similar types of schools equally.
Class sizes in schools are affected by a variety of factors including enrolment fluctuations and available accommodation. Schools are best placed to determine the appropriate numbers in any class and so the configuration of classes and the deployment of classroom teachers are done at local school level. question: Deputy Cathal Crowe asked the Minister for Education and Youth if she will clarify the eligibility and timeline for access to the next primary supplementary redeployment panel for a teacher (details supplied) whose contract concluded at the end of August; the review mechanisms available when panel options exceed reasonable commuting distances.
reply:
The current eligibility criteria for the Supplementary Panel, as agreed with the education partners, are set out in Circular 74/2025. Teachers must hold appropriate Teaching Council registration, have achieved a certain point on the payscale and meet the earnings requirement set out in order to access the Supplementary Panel.
Arrangements for next year's Supplementary Panel will be finalised next month and the eligibility criteria and application form will be published on my Department's website.
In general, teachers must accept the first offer of a position from the Supplementary Panel or they will forfeit their panel rights. However, where a teacher on the Supplementary Panel receives an offer of a permanent position from a school which is more than 45km from her base school, the teacher may refuse that offer and still remain on the Supplementary Panel.

question: Deputy Pearse Doherty asked the Minister for Education and Youth the average cost per student for insurance cover with a company (details supplied) of the 304 ETB schools and 187 other schools.
reply:
Insurance cover for ETB schools is arranged as part of the overall insurance cover of the ETB concerned which is provided to the ETB through Irish Public Bodies Mutual Insurance Ltd (IPB). Such insurance encompasses ETB schools, head offices and other educational settings.
ETBs are members of IPB insurance, which is an indigenous mutual general insurance company in the Irish market, specialising in bespoke insurance solutions within core public service, education and health.
The total insurance premium payable by the ETB reflects the risk profile of the entire ETB and is not broken down by individual school or other setting. As a result, it is not possible to provide an average insurance cost per student.
Outside of the ETB sector, insurance is a matter for the boards of management of individual schools.
Schools are required to ensure best value in the procurement of all services, including insurance.
Details of individual schools' insurance cover arrangements are a matter between the schools concerned and their insurer and are not available to my department.

question: Deputy Aindrias Moynihan asked the Minister for Education and Youth the number of primary schools that have contacted her Department regarding a change of school ethos, language status, or co-educational/single-sex status since completion of the national survey on school patronage, including the current status of each request by county, in tabular form; to outline the process applicable to schools seeking such changes.
reply:

It explored preferences regarding school patronage/ethos, co-educational or single-sex provision and language (education through Irish or English).
In early June, my department issued primary schools with their school-specific results and explanatory information.
Boards of Management have been asked to share their survey results and explanatory information with their school communities, to review their survey results and to engage with their communities (including parents), and the local community (including parents with children not yet in school), before deciding on their next steps.

question: Deputy Denise Mitchell asked the Minister for Education and Youth the guidance that exists for parents in the event of a change of patronage of one of two linked schools while a transitional admissions arrangement is in place; and the account her Department would expect to be taken of families who have a binding allocation under such an arrangement.
reply:
As part of the Primary School Survey process, schools have been asked to reflect on their survey results, engage with their school community and inform their patron and my department by 31 October if they request to be included in the first group to change configuration arising from this process.
If a school informs their patron and my department that it wishes to request to be included in the first group of school to change configuration arising from this process, my department will assess the potential outcomes on overall school places in the area. My department will also assign a point of contact to offer guidance, as appropriate, to help schools in considering the practicalities and timeframe for a change in configuration.
Schools are expected to engage with and communicate with their school communities in the normal way regarding any significant changes to admissions arrangements. Good coordination between schools can help ensure that this is managed and worked through at the earliest possible stage. The patron's consent is needed for any changes to take place.
My department is committed to helping schools who wish to introduce changes arising from the preferences of their parents and guardians as expressed through the Primary School Survey results and their subsequent engagement with their community.

question: Deputy Michael Cahill asked the Minister for Education and Youth the reason rural schools are allocated significantly fewer resources, purely because of the label “DEIS Rural” (details supplied).
reply:
Addressing educational disadvantage in all schools remains a key priority for me as Minister for Education and Youth. The DEIS programme is targeted at schools with the highest levels of concentrated disadvantage.
At primary level schools are assigned to DEIS Plus, DEIS Urban Band 1, DEIS Urban Band 2 or DEIS Rural based on the location of the school and based on its level of disadvantage.
Research published by the Education Research Centre has shown that educational outcomes for pupils in DEIS Rural schools are more positive than outcomes for pupils in DEIS Urban schools. DEIS Rural primary schools performed on par with urban non-DEIS schools in Testing under the National Assessment of Mathematics and English Reading (NAMER).
The DEIS Strategy to 2035 sets out a long-term plan to address educational disadvantage in all schools and work to ensure that any child or young person experiencing educational disadvantage is supported through their education journey.
The DEIS Strategy implementation plan 2026-2028, under the strategic objective 2.2, sets out to develop an agile resource allocation model to support children and young people at risk of educational disadvantage in all primary and post-primary schools.
These actions focus on the continued enhancement of the data available to measure school level disadvantage and for the development of a more flexible resource allocation model that can react to change in school needs and provide the right resources at the right time.

question: Deputy Mairéad Farrell asked the Minister for Education and Youth if her attention has been drawn to issues regarding the transparency of recruitment and interview processes for primary school teaching positions; and if her Department has carried out work to increase transparency in the recruitment process for primary school teachers.
reply:
This Government is committed to ensuring that every child has a positive school experience, with access to qualified and engaged teachers who are dedicated to supporting their learning.
The recruitment and appointment of teachers to fill teaching posts is a matter for individual school authorities, subject to procedures agreed under Section 24(3) of the Education Act 1998 (as amended by the Education (Amendment) Act 2012).
In accordance with Department Circular 0044/2019, schools are required to employ appropriately qualified teachers and ensure that unemployed teachers should be offered employment in preference to those who have retired.
As school authorities are the employer of teachers, a central facility for teacher recruitment has not been provided. However, following on from the Department’s Action Plan on Teacher Supply, the Irish Primary Principals’ Network (IPPN) operates an online portal for the recruitment of teachers to long-term teaching positions. The portal facilitates the matching of demand and supply, and provides an efficient and user-friendly recruitment process for both schools and teachers.

question: Deputy Micheál Carrigy asked the Minister for Education and Youth if she will consider establishing a mechanism within the school transport scheme to allow families to access in-principle eligibility information prior to enrolling their children in a post-primary school; if she is aware that school enrolments typically take place late in the preceding year (details supplied); if a forward-looking process will be introduced to provide parents with this necessary clarity during their planning phase.
reply:
The School Transport Scheme is a significant operation managed by Bus Éireann on behalf of the Department of Education and Youth.
As the Deputy will be aware, children are eligible for transport at post primary level where they reside not less than 4.8 kilometres from and are attending their nearest post primary school/education centre as determined by the department/Bus Éireann, having regard to ethos and language.
Children who are eligible for school transport and who complete the application process on time are accommodated on school transport services where such services are in operation. Children who are eligible for school transport but for whom no service is available may be offered the Remote Area Grant towards the cost of making private transport arrangements. The Remote Area Grant is also payable for eligible children who may have to travel 3.2kms or more to or from a designated pick up/set down point.
Families are required to register their details on the Bus Éireann Family Portal to have their eligibility for transport assessed and to make applications under the scheme: buseireann.ie/schooltransport/
The family portal generally opens in the spring before the start of each school year, and following the closing date for payment or entering medical card details, the portal closes to give Bus Éireann time to assess all applications and plan for routes and services for the next school year.

question: Deputy Eamon Scanlon asked the Minister for Education and Youth the evidence, safety data and recommendations arising from the Road Safety Authority review of upper age limits for school transport drivers that informed Bus Éireann's decision to retain the maximum age of 70 years for drivers of minibuses, medium buses and large school buses.
reply:
The School Transport Scheme is a significant operation managed by Bus Éireann on behalf of the Department of Education & Youth.
The retirement age for school bus drivers has been set by Bus Éireann at 70 years of age, which also applies to all Bus Éireann road passenger services.
The Road Safety Authority, under the remit of the Department of Transport, committed to reviewing the upper age limit of drivers as it relates to larger vehicles/school buses. This review is now complete and is available on the Oireachtas website link below. Bus Éireann has no plans to amend the driver age limit for larger vehicles.
An independent review of the upper age limit of drivers as it relates to smaller vehicles has been completed. Following this review, Bus Éireann has announced an extension to the upper age limit of drivers of small public service vehicles (max 8 seats and driver) contracted by Bus Éireann under the School Transport Scheme, from age 70 to 72, for a trial period. This extended age limit will only apply to existing nominated drivers operating school transport services or to drivers who retired from school transport during the 2025/2026 school year.
This decision follows extensive research, stakeholder engagement and a thorough safety review undertaken by Bus Éireann.
The trial period for this extension of the driver age limit is for two years, commencing from the start of the new school year in September 2026 and ending at the conclusion of the 2027/2028 school year in June

question: Deputy Emer Currie asked the Minister for Education and Youth the rules regarding secondary schools giving priority or allocating a set amount of school places to relatives of past pupils; and whether these rules apply to fee paying schools.
reply:
The overall objective of the Education (Admission to Schools) Act 2018 is to provide a framework for school enrolment that is designed to ensure that every child is treated fairly and that the way in which schools decide on applications for admission is structured fair and transparent. The act applies to all recognised schools, including fee charging schools.
Parents have the right to choose which school to apply to and where the school has places available for the relevant year, the student should be admitted. However, in schools where there are more applicants than places available, a selection process will be necessary. This selection process and the enrolment policy on which it is based must be non-discriminatory and must be applied fairly in respect of all applicants. However, this may result in some students not obtaining a place in the school of their first choice.
In accordance with the provisions of the Act 2018, schools are required to clearly set out their selection criteria in their admission policies. The criteria to be applied by schools and the order of priority are a matter for the schools themselves. It is an important feature of the act that schools can only make a decision on an application for admission that is based on the school’s admission policy.

It does so by ensuring the availability of funding for urgent works to those schools that are in need of resources as a result of an emergency situation.
An emergency is deemed to be a situation which poses an immediate risk to health, life, property or the environment, which is sudden, unforeseen and requires immediate action, and in the case of a school, if not corrected would prevent the school or part thereof from opening.
The EWS operates on the basis of a minimal scope works to address the emergency situation. An emergency is deemed to be a situation which poses an immediate risk to health, life, property or the environment, which is sudden, unforeseen and requires immediate action, and in the case of a school, if not corrected would prevent the school or part thereof from opening.
The EWS operates on the basis of a minimal scope works to address the emergency situation. The EWS is intended to remedy an emergency situation and usually provides only an interim measure until a permanent solution can be delivered under the Summer Works Scheme (SWS) which deals with upgrade works to the school.

reply:

My department has been notified that the patron of the school referred to by the Deputy has decided to close the school. question: Deputy Cathy Bennett asked the Minister for Education and Youth to detail the amount that has been set aside within her Department to increase capacity on school bus transport system for the 2027/8 school year.
reply:
The expenditure on the scheme has more than doubled over a six-year period from over €200 million in 2018 to €537 million in 2025 (included a cost-of-living advancement for 2025 of €58m). The allocation in 2026 is estimated at €641m.
The increasing cost of the scheme over the past number of years is due to increased pupil numbers, COVID cleaning and increased distance measures, cost of living measures, provision of transport for children from Ukraine and increased contractor rates for operators under contract to Bus Éireann for the provision of services.
Transport for pupils with special educational needs continues to represent the largest area of expenditure within the scheme, accounting for just under 60% of the total spend in 2025, while serving approximately 13% of the total overall pupils on transport.
School Transport budget will increase to €687 million in 2027. This equates to over €3.7 million on school transport alone per school day. Extra funding will provide for the additional demand for specialised transport and increased transport running costs.

question: Deputy Cathy Bennett asked the Minister for Education and Youth the reason a school (details supplied), the largest rural DEIS primary school in County Cavan, was not included in the home school community liaison pilot initiative introduced earlier this year; the criteria used for this decision; and if there is an appeals process.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 461 and 463 together.
Addressing educational disadvantage in all schools remains a key priority for the Department of Education and Youth. A pilot project was recently introduced to extend Home-School-Community-Liaison (HSCL) provision to 130 schools that are in the DEIS Rural band and outside the DEIS programme, with 4 schools in Cavan included in this pilot initiative. This pilot provides an important opportunity to trial the extension of this support to additional schools and to inform future policy development in relation to the scheme.
The HSCL scheme is a core element of the DEIS programme and forms part of the wider Tusla Education Support Service (TESS). HSCL coordinators are teachers assigned to work directly with parents, guardians, school staff and community services to strengthen engagement between home, school and community. The overarching aim of HSCL is to improve attendance, participation and retention, particularly for children and young people experiencing educational disadvantage.
Schools included in the HSCL pilot project were identified using nationally available data relating to concentrations of educational disadvantage. Operational factors, including clustering feasibility and regional capacity requirements, were also considered to support implementation of the pilot at this stage.

question: Deputy Louis O'Hara asked the Minister for Education and Youth if support will be given to secure a school place for a 17-year-old student (details supplied).
reply:
The National Council for Special Education (NCSE) is the statutory body responsible for the provision of special education and allocating supports for students with special educational needs.
It is the responsibility of the managerial authorities of all schools to implement an admissions policy in accordance with the Education Act, 1998 and the Education (Admission to Schools) Act 2018.
Under the provisions of this act, all schools are required to have admissions policies which have been approved by the patron following consultation with staff and parents of students who are attending the school. It is a key requirement of the act that all school admission policies are fair and transparent.
Parents may apply to enrol their child in a school of their choosing and where the school has places available for the relevant year, the student should be admitted. However, in schools where there are more applicants than places available, a selection process will be necessary. This selection process and the enrolment policy on which it is based must be non-discriminatory and must be applied fairly in respect of all applicants. Nonetheless, it may result in some students not obtaining a place in the school of their first choice.
The NCSE is, in the first instance, the primary body responsible for the matter the Deputy has raised. I will arrange for your query to be forwarded to the NCSE for their attention and direct reply. Deputies are also welcome to raise such queries with the NCSE dir

question: Deputy Aidan Farrelly asked the Minister for Education and Youth whether schools can still apply for funding under the minor works scheme for projects, such as re-surfacing or re-marking the school yard.
reply:
Primary and special schools need not apply for Minor Works Grant aid. Under the scheme, funding is made available to all primary and special schools on the following basis:
€5,500 basic grant plus €18.50 per mainstream pupil and €74 per special needs pupil enrolled in the school on the 30th of September of the year prior to the issue of the grant. The €74 rate applies to a special needs pupil attending a special school or attending a special class attached to a mainstream school.
Schools have the autonomy to use this funding for maintenance and small-scale improvements to school buildings and grounds. Given that each school setting is different, individual schools are best placed, to decide how best to use this funding to address their particular needs.
The works that can be undertaken under the minor works scheme include maintenance and small-scale improvements to school buildings and grounds, fencing, repairs and painting, replacement of flooring, improvement or replacement of mechanical and electrical services, the purchase or repair of standard furniture and PE equipment, the purchase of IT equipment, ventilation improvements, and enhancements to outdoor learning environments. Please refer to www.gov.ie/en/department-of-education/circulars/grant-scheme-for-minor-works-to-national-school-properties/ for further details regarding the scheme.

question: Deputy Conor D. McGuinness asked the Minister for Education and Youth the reason there is no school bus for a school (details supplied) and her plans to provide this service.
reply:
The School Transport Scheme is a significant operation managed by Bus Éireann on behalf of the Department of Education and Youth.
Under the current terms of the mainstream scheme, children are eligible for transport at primary level where they reside not less than 3.2 kilometres from and are attending their nearest national school, and at post primary level where they reside not less than 4.8 kilometres from and are attending their nearest post primary school/education centre as determined by the department/Bus Éireann, having regard to ethos and language.
The scheme is a demand led scheme based on the number of eligible children who apply.
A minimum number of 10 eligible children residing in a distinct locality, as determined by Bus Éireann, are required before consideration may be given to the establishment of school transport services, provided this can be done within reasonable cost limits.
Officials from the School Transport Section of my Department are engaging with Bus Éireann who will reply directly to the Deputy as soon as further information is available.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Education and Youth the procedures available to parents who believe that a post-primary school has refused to consider reasonable accommodation for a student with dyslexia in relation to the study of a modern foreign language; whether her Department can review or investigate the application of school policies in such circumstances; and whether she will issue national guidance clarifying the respective responsibilities of schools and the Department.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 456 and 457 together.
Under the Education Act 1998, the School Board of Management (BOM), appointed by the school’s patron, is the body charged with the direct governance of a school and the principal manages the school on a day-to-day basis. Each school has the autonomy to design its own timetables and decide which subjects and programmes to offer based on the educational needs and interests of its students as well as considerations such as classroom space, staffing, time limitations etc.
The study of Modern Foreign Languages is optional at Junior and Senior Cycle. However, it should be noted that schools may have their own rules in relation to the study of a foreign language and higher educational institutions may require a foreign language to be studied for matriculation purposes.

A key action of the policy is to promote the importance of foreign language learning and to provide supports to schools and teachers in this regard.

question: Deputy Michael Healy-Rae asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment to provide details on the €15 million package for rural pubs; and the way in which the package will work.
reply:
Budget 2027 provided €15m for the provision of support for pubs, in recognition of the challenges faced by the sector. The cultural and economic importance of rural pubs to many local communities across the country was recognised by the Tánaiste in his Budget speech. I welcome this scheme, which aligns with the Programme for Government commitment to bring forward measures to support SMEs operating in the hospitality sector.
The details of this scheme are currently being worked on by my officials and officials at the Department of Finance. I have also been engaging with stakeholder groups to ensure that support is provided by the most effective means, insofar as is possible. This scheme should support those who need it most, and should be introduced in a straightforward manner that does not place an undue burden on claimants. In this regard, I believe it is best that the qualifying criteria be guided by information that is readily available. By focusing on turnover and prioritising pubs in lower turnover bands, it is my understanding that smaller rural pubs would represent a large proportion of those deemed eligible. By limiting the scheme in this manner, it can ensure that the resources will be allocated in such a way as to support smaller pubs.
I and my officials, in conjunction with the Department of Finance, are working to consider the best approach to proceed with this scheme and will be working to finalise the details of this scheme in the near term.

question: Deputy Grace Boland asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment whether the Competition and Consumer Protection Commission has made any recommendations to his Department in relation to improving transparency in the pricing and benefits of private health insurance policies; and if so, if he will provide details of any such recommendations.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 450 and 453 together.
Officials from my Department engage regularly with the Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (CCPC) which is the independent statutory body that enforces competition and consumer law under the remit of this Department.
In the insurance market, both the Central Bank of Ireland and the Health Insurance Authority perform regulatory functions.
That CCPC has advised that, in 2023, it published its Compare and Switch report, which examined consumer behaviour in private health insurance and other regulated markets. The report indicated that a significant proportion of consumers inform themselves, shop around, negotiate and switch provider. However private health insurance had the second-lowest level of shopping around among the products examined, and switching levels were also relatively low.
In relation to transparency, the CCPC highlighted that the presentation of information by service and product providers online can, in some cases, cause confusion for consumers.
With specific regard to the health insurance market a survey published by the Health Insurance Authority of Ireland (HIA) in 2022 indicated that difficulties in comparing plans, together with concerns about losing existing benefits, were among the principal factors influencing consumers’ decisions not to switch health insurance providers.
The CCPC has continued to engage with the Health Insurance Authority, including through participation in a roundtable in

question: Deputy Alan Kelly asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment when his Department last reviewed its policies, operations and handling of protected disclosures under all relevant protected disclosures legislation.
reply:
My Department has in place a Protected Disclosures Policy, which was last updated in September 2023 to incorporate the provisions of the Protected Disclosures (Amendment) Act 2022.
A review of the Department's compliance with its obligations under protected disclosures legislation was carried out by the Department's Audit Unit and approved by the Audit Committee in October 2025.
The review assessed the adequacy of the Department's Protected Disclosures Policy and associated oversight arrangements; training and awareness initiatives to encourage the reporting of wrongdoing; internal reporting channel procedures; investigation procedures; review mechanisms; arrangements relating to confidentiality and protection from penalisation; records management practices; and reporting processes. The review concluded that an adequate and effective system of governance, risk management and control is in place.
A revised Protected Disclosures Policy is currently being prepared to take account of the review's findings and will be considered by the Department's Management Board in due course.

question: Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment if he will consider the introduction of a statutory framework and protection for collective bargaining, noting that an IHREC report (details supplied) found that there are no conflicting rights in the Irish Constitution that would prevent the Government from introducing such a framework.
reply:
I am aware of the report published by the Irish Human Rights and Equality Commission. It is important to note that the report represents the academic analysis and conclusions of its authors. The Government’s current priority is the implementation of Ireland’s Action Plan to Promote Collective Bargaining 2026–2030. The question of whether additional legislative measures are required will be considered in the context of the implementation of the Action Plan and informed by ongoing consultation, research and engagement with the social partners. No decision has been taken by Government at this stage regarding the introduction of a statutory right to collective bargaining or trade union recognition. In addition, ongoing engagement between ICTU, Ibec and officials of my Department through the Labour Employer Economic Forum (LEEF) Technical Sub-Group is intended to identify practical measures to strengthen awareness, capacity, workplace engagement and the effective functioning of Ireland’s industrial relations system.
Ireland’s industrial relations system is founded on voluntarism, under which collective bargaining is conducted voluntarily between employers and workers and their representatives. While employees have a constitutional right to form and join trade unions, employers are not generally required to recognise or negotiate with a trade union.
Ireland’s industrial relations framework provides mechanisms to support collective bargaining where an employer does not engage in dir

question: Deputy Emer Currie asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment the terms of reference and membership of the new National AI Literacy Taskforce established under the Intelligence:Applied Programme.
reply:
The Government on October 13th announced the launch of a new programme, Intelligence: Applied. The programme aims to accelerate AI adoption across the economy and public sector, and to position Ireland as one of the world’s leading locations for responsible, applied AI. This programme will see 35 impactful initiatives implemented over the period to 2030 under the themes of People, Economy, Infrastructure and Ecosystem, building on the ambition set out in the National Digital & AI Strategy, Digital Ireland.
One of these initiatives is the establishment a new National AI Literacy Taskforce by the AI Office of Ireland. Work has commenced on this project and will continue over the coming months.
The establishment of a National AI Literacy Taskforce will form part of the Office’s wider scope of work to support trusted AI adoption and strengthen understanding of AI, its opportunities, and risks.

question: Deputy Emer Currie asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment the plans for enhanced AI and digital vouchers proposed as part of the Intelligence:Applied Programme; and the way in which this initiative relates to the review of the grow digital voucher scheme and any proposals for enhancements to that scheme.
reply:
The Intelligence:Applied programme was recently launched by the Government to accelerate AI adoption across the economy and public sector, and to position Ireland as one of the world’s leading locations for responsible, applied AI. The programme will see 35 impactful initiatives implemented over the period to 2030 under the themes of People, Economy, Infrastructure and Ecosystem, building on the ambition set out in the National Digital & AI Strategy, Digital Ireland.
In late 2025, my Department commissioned an external report of the full suite of supports provides by the LEOs to small businesses. Results of the report indicated that the digital supports provided by the LEOs are contributing to improved understanding of digital opportunities, improved efficiency within the business, improved use of digital tools, and development of new products, services, and processes.
One of the key strategic priorities for my Department, is to accelerate the adoption of digital and AI technologies across enterprises, particularly SMEs, to improve productivity, competitiveness and resilience. question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment the number of employment permits issued to the HSE as employer in respect of medical practitioners in each of the years 2022 to 2025 and to date in 2026, by permit type.
reply:

question: Deputy Eamon Scanlon asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment whether a person (details supplied) who transferred from employment under a critical skills employment permit to a position with an organisation in 2025 required a new employment permit; and the options available to regularise their position if a permit was required but not obtained.
reply:
The Employment Permits System is governed by the provisions of the Employment Permits Act 2024. Under that legislation, both employers and permit holders are required to comply with the conditions attaching to an employment permit and with the relevant statutory requirements governing employment pursuant to an employment permit.
The individual concerned was granted a Critical Skills Employment Permit in October 2024 in respect of a specific employer and occupation. Employment permits are employer-specific and cannot be transferred from one employer to another. Where a permit holder wishes to change employer, a change of employer application must be submitted through the Departments employment permits online system.
The employment permit concerned was cancelled earlier this month. The cancellation of a permit does not preclude the submission of a subsequent permit application.
If the individual wishes to work for a new employer, a new employment permit application must now be submitted. Any application received will be assessed in accordance with the Employment Permits Act 2024 and the relevant eligibility criteria.
It should be noted that a person may not undertake employment unless they hold a valid employment permit in respect of that specific employment, or another immigration permission that permits them to work without an employment permit. Responsibility for compliance with these requirements rests with both the employer and the employee.

question: Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment if he will clarify who made the formal decision to wind down the medical device certification division within the National Standards Authority of Ireland; the date it was approved; the specific mandate or Ministerial oversight that guided this action; and where is the impact assessment on MedTech contractors in rural Ireland.
reply:
The National Standards Authority of Ireland (NSAI) is an independent agency, under the aegis of my Department. On 31 July 2026, I received notification that the Board of NSAI had decided, on 30 July 2026, to begin an orderly exit from the provision of medical product certification services. I understand that the decision followed extensive consideration by the Board of the financial viability of the service. The service has faced sustained challenges, including staff recruitment and retention, maintaining designation by the competent authority, the HPRA, productivity issues, and market competition.

question: Deputy Sean Fleming asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment to respond to matters raised in correspondence (details supplied).
reply:
The Organisation of Working Time Act 1997 (OWTA), as amended, transposes the EU Working Time Directive (2003/88/EC) into Irish law and sets out minimum rest periods, maximum working time limits, annual leave entitlements and other miscellaneous issues.
The OWTA provides for essential employment rights which aim to ensure employees have sufficient health and safety standards in terms of working time, and it is important for all employers to ensure they are in compliance.
There are both general and limited exemptions contained both in the Act itself and in Regulations made on foot of the primary legislation. Section 4 provides for specific exemptions and also allows the Minister to exempt by Regulation defined classes of activities from particular Part II obligations.
There is no application process for seeking exemptions from the requirements of the OWTA. Where the Regulations apply to a particular activity, their provisions must be complied with by the employer and, in the event of a dispute or complaint under the Organisation of Working Time Act, the correct referral body is the Workplace Relations Commission (WRC).
It is outside the functions of my Department to provide legal advice on the applicability of the legislation to specific cases. Independent legal advice should be obtained by the employer should the need arise.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation whether the Office of Public Works flood maps show the Woodford and Monksfield estates, Clondalkin as at risk of flooding from the River Camac; the date those maps were last updated; and whether they take account of any flood defence works carried out nearby.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 428 and 429 together.
Dublin City Council and South Dublin County Council, with funding provided by the Office of Public Works, are leading the development and design of the River Camac Flood Alleviation Scheme (RCFAS) to manage the flood risk within the catchment of the River Camac.
The River Camac is an unusually complex river system, and has presented significant challenges during the modelling of the flood risk and the designing options for a flood relief scheme to protect 413 properties.
The scheme is currently at Stage 1 where the source of the flood risk and the design of the flood relief scheme are under development. It is programmed to have identified a preferred option in 2027 and then extensive environmental assessments will be required to support an application for planning consent to An Coimisiún Pleanála scheduled for 2029. The timing for the commencement of construction will be dependent upon receipt of consent from ACP, and the successful completion of a tender process to appoint a contractor.
The areas of Woodford and Monksfield Housing Estates in Clondalkin are predominantly within the River Camac catchment boundary and are being assessed as part of the scheme's design. Mapping for the area is being developed by the consultant engineers to inform the options for the scheme’s design.

reply:
I would like to thank the Deputy for his question.
The Protected Disclosures Act 2014 provides the basis for Ireland’s national 'whistleblower' framework. A major amendment to the 2014 Act - the Protected Disclosures (Amendment) Act 2022 (the amended Act) - was signed into law on 21 July 2022, and was commenced on 1 January 2023.

Section 2A of the amended Act provides for a statutory review as follows:
“The Minister shall -
(a) not later than the end of the period of 5 years beginning on the passing of the Protected Disclosures (Amendment) Act 2022, commence a review of the operation of this Act, and

I welcome this positive development and look forward to a constructive process aimed at reaching a fair and sustainable agreement that properly rewards public service workers and delivers for our country.

question: Deputy Emer Currie asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation the proposed structure, governance arrangements and operational remit of the public spending efficiency taskforce; the criteria and methodology that will be used to identify potential expenditure efficiencies; whether the Taskforce will undertake systematic reviews of existing expenditure programmes across Departments and public bodies; the ways its work will interact with the existing spending review process and the annual Estimates process; the mechanisms through which its recommendations will be implemented/monitored; and whether quantified savings targets and timelines will be established.
reply:
Public expenditure must be managed to maximise value for money for the taxpayer and support the delivery of Government priorities within the voted allocations.
The achievement of value for money in public expenditure is a Government priority, with an agenda for spending efficiency emphasised in the context of Budget 2026. For Budget 2027, all Departments were required to identify lasting reforms and efficiencies that will embed the value for money agenda over the years 2028-2030.
Building on this work, it is my intention to establish a new Public Spending Efficiency Taskforce whose mandate will be to scrutinise day to day public spending. The Taskforce will identify key areas across the public service where there is scope to achieve greater efficiency and will recommend specific actions to improve service delivery and secure better value for money.
The work of this taskforce will inform the approach to Budget 2028 and subsequent Budgets over the lifetime of the Government, supporting greater economy, efficiency and effectiveness across day-to-day public spending.
The work of the Taskforce will complement, rather than replace, the wide range of policy and expenditure analysis undertaken and published annually by Government Departments. Departments will remain responsible for conducting detailed policy analysis and expenditure evaluations within their respective sectors. They will also continue to contribute sector-specific evidence and insights to the policymaking process.

question: Deputy Emer Currie asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation further to Parliamentary Question No. 62586/26 of 7 September 2026, to outline when the parking strategy is expected to be completed; and to provide a timeline as to when the OPW will submit for planning permission.
reply:
The draft Phoenix Park Parking Strategy examines approaches to parking within the Phoenix Park set against the broader context of a transport and mobility strategy which places a strong emphasis on provisions for pedestrians, cyclists and those with mobility issues who are reliant on their cars to access the park.
Many of the key actions recommended in the draft strategy have already been implemented, including increased cycle parking provision and cycle hire and the introduction of accessible cycle parking across the Park.
One of the key recommendations proposed in the draft Parking Strategy is the introduction of a new car park near the North Road / Chesterfield Avenue Junction near Castleknock Gate. This proposal will require planning permission and detailed design. Once the strategy has been finalised, the Office of Public Works will move to the permission stage of this project. question: Deputy John Lahart asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation on behalf of very local newspapers in Dublin (details supplied), that do not seem to be allowed to apply to host public service, public appointment, or HSE advertisements, his plans to remedy the situation; the rules governing State bodies, semi-State agencies, and NGOs in terms of advertising in local newspapers.
reply:
There is no central Government policy that prohibits State bodies, semi-State bodies, or publicly funded organisations from placing advertisements in local newspapers.
Responsibility for advertising arrangements rests with the individual public body concerned. In discharging this responsibility, public bodies must ensure that expenditure on advertising is justified, delivers value for money, is appropriate to the intended audience, and complies with all applicable statutory, regulatory, and governance requirements. Decisions relating to the placement of advertising should be informed by transparent, objective, proportionate, and non-discriminatory considerations.
The responsibility for ensuring compliance with public procurement rules and procedures rests with the Accounting Officer of each organisation. Accordingly, Accounting Officers must satisfy themselves that procurement and related expenditure decisions, including those concerning advertising, are undertaken in accordance with the relevant legislative, regulatory, and governance frameworks.
In the case of public service recruitment campaigns, advertising is generally coordinated through the Public Appointments Service (PAS), which determines the most appropriate advertising channels on a case-by-case basis. In doing so, the PAS has regard to a range of factors, including the nature of the position, the target audience, the anticipated reach of the campaign, and considerations of cost-effectiveness and value for money.

question: Deputy Emer Currie asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation the way in which the Critical Infrastructure Bill 2026 will enable the development of Ireland's offshore wind capacity.
reply:
The Critical Infrastructure Act 2026 allows the Government to designate certain infrastructure projects developed by or on behalf of the State as being of critical national importance. This provides a statutory basis for accelerating decision making in respect of designated projects and programmes.
In announcing the enactment of the legislation, I stated that my initial focus would be on identifying a small number of projects so that the new framework could be implemented effectively and its operation monitored. The Government approved this first tranche of designated projects in July 2026. These projects were drawn from the transport, energy and water sectors, reflecting the strategic importance of these sectors to the delivery of wider national priorities, including housing and economic development.
In particular, the three electricity projects selected for designation are all crucial for the development of a robust electricity transmission system. This is necessary to meet rising electricity demand and to provide for the accommodation of a greater amount of electricity from renewable sources, including offshore wind.
Any further decision to designate a project remains a matter for Government.
The construction of offshore wind capacity is the responsibility of those companies who are the developers of these projects. These projects are not being developed by or on behalf of the State and hence are not eligible for designation.

question: Deputy Catherine Callaghan asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance if he will urgently review the exclusion of HGV driving schools from the diesel rebate scheme in view of the substantial fuel costs incurred by these businesses, the essential service they provide in training HGV and bus drivers, and the potential impact on driver supply to the transport industry.
reply:
The Diesel Rebate Scheme (DRS) is a State aid that operates under Article 7(2) of Council Directive 2003/96/EC (Energy Tax Directive/ETD).
Article 7(2) explicitly allows EU Member States to apply a differentiated rate of excise duty to gas oil (auto diesel) used for commercial purposes, provided that the EU minimum levels of taxation are respected.
The ETD limits the scope of "commercial gas oil" to auto diesel used by specific segments of road transport. In line with this, the scope of Ireland’s DRS is defined by reference to road transport licensing criteria and includes licensed road haulage (goods transport) and passenger transport operators (such as bus and coach services).

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance whether the Department has assessed the share of new build homes purchased in each of the years 2023 to 2025 by first-time buyers who had been resident in the State for fewer than five years; whether any such analysis has informed the Department's position on the extension and increase of the help to buy scheme.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 389 and 406 together.
The Help to Buy (HTB) incentive, is a tax-based scheme to assist first-time purchasers with the deposit they need to buy or build a new house or apartment. It also aims to encourage additional supply of new houses by supporting demand.
Based on the latest available data (30 September 2026), the scheme has supported over 70,000 individuals or couples to buy or build their own home.
The level of support available to first time buyers under the HTB scheme, is whichever is the lesser of:
€35,000 (from 07 October 2026); or
10 per cent of the purchase price of the new property; or
the amount of Income Tax and DIRT paid in the four years before application for the relief.
For a property to qualify for the HTB scheme, it must be new or converted for use as a dwelling, having not previously been used as a dwelling. Additionally, the purchase value/approved valuation of the property must not exceed €500,000.
HTB provides a refund of Income Tax and Deposit Interest Retention Tax (DIRT) paid in Ireland over the previous four years, subject to limits outlined in the legislation. Consideration of the matters raised in the Deputy's questions did not form part of the Budget 2027 process, nor has it formed part of TSG or other Department of Finance analyses, in relation to HTB.

reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 404 and 405 together.
The Government is taking a comprehensive and proactive approach to improving the affordability and availability of flood insurance in the Irish insurance market with the implementation of refoms under the Action Plan for Insurance Reform 2025-2029.
The decision on whether to offer home insurance, level of premiums charged, and the policy terms applied are matters for individual insurers based on an actuarial assessment of the risks they are willing to accept. The Solvency II Directive restricts Member States in terms of intervening in insurers’ pricing or underwriting decisions. Insurers rely on their own claims’ histories, risk assessments, and cost projections when deciding whether to provide cover. Factors such as inflation in building materials and labour are also influencing premium levels across the sector.
In terms of flood insurance, the Central Bank of Ireland has undertaken extensive research into the nature and scale of the flood insurance protection gap in Ireland. They found that 1 in 20 buildings (approximately 5%) have limited access to flood insurance; and that 54% of this gap is concentrated in Dublin, Cork, Louth, Clare, and Kildare. Neither my Department nor the Central Bank of Ireland hold data on the refusal of home insurance or flood insurance.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance whether an insurer is required to tell a customer the basis on which their property has been classified as at risk of flooding; whether any process exists for a homeowner with no recorded flood history to have that classification reviewed; and, if not, whether he will consider requiring one.
reply:
The Government remains committed to protecting Ireland’s present and future generations by investing in climate adaptation measures to manage the impacts of extreme weather. Accordingly, €1.3 billion has been committed to the delivery of flood relief schemes over the lifetime of the National Development Plan (NDP) to 2030. This will protect approximately 23,000 properties across various communities from river and coastal flood risk.
In terms of flood insurance, the Central Bank of Ireland has undertaken extensive research into the nature and scale of the flood insurance protection gap in Ireland. They found that 1 in 20 buildings (approximately 5%) have limited access to flood insurance; and that 54% of this gap is concentrated in Dublin, Cork, Louth, Clare, and Kildare.
In terms of assessing flood risk, insurers use a variety of different flood data models (both internally developed models and flood models procured from third party vendors). Insurers will generally utilise (i) flood risk maps licenced from a third-party consultancy; (ii) bespoke flood maps based on individual historical claims experience/risk surveys undertaken of locations, and (iii) other information such as the flood defence benefit area data provided to Insurance Ireland by the OPW under the terms of the MOU, if applicable.
Insurance undertakings are bound by the provisions of the Central Bank’s Consumer Protection Code (the Code) in their dealings with consumers for the provision of financial services.

question: Deputy Albert Dolan asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance whether he has considered increasing the VAT registration threshold for service providers; whether his Department has assessed the extent to which the threshold acts as a disincentive for small businesses and agricultural contractors seeking to expand their turnover; and whether any review of the threshold is planned.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 385, 386 and 401 together.
As the Deputy will be aware, no change was made to the VAT registration thresholds in Budget 2027.
VAT registration thresholds are subject to the requirements of EU VAT law, with which Irish VAT law is obliged to comply. In general, the EU VAT Directive requires that all businesses supplying taxable goods and services are registered for VAT, charge VAT on those supplies to their customers, and file returns and remit the VAT to the relevant national tax authority.
Within the framework of the Directive, Ireland has operated VAT registration thresholds for goods and for services for many years. Following increases applied in Finance Act 2024, the levels are now €85,000 for supplies of goods and €42,500 for supplies of services. Generally, a business whose turnover is below the relevant threshold is not obliged to register for VAT and can supply its customers exempt from VAT; when its turnover reaches the threshold, the business is obliged to register for and operate VAT in accordance with normal rules. Businesses whose turnover is below the threshold are entitled to elect to register should they so wish. Separate to the turnover rules, as required under EU law, there are also other circumstances where businesses are required to register for VAT, for example, when making intra-community acquisitions or when accounting for VAT under the reverse charge mechanism because of receiving taxable services from a supplier outside

reply:

question: Deputy Pádraig O'Sullivan asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance whether his Department has assessed Poland's decision to apply an 8% VAT rate to petrol and diesel from 3 October 2026; whether such a measure is compatible with the EU VAT Directive; whether he has sought greater flexibility on fuel VAT at EU level; and the estimated cost to the Exchequer of each one percentage point reduction in VAT on petrol and diesel.
reply:
The EU VAT Directive which Irish VAT law is obliged to comply, generally holds that all goods and service are liable for VAT at the standard rate which Member States must set at a minimum of 15%. Ireland currently charges a standard rate of 23%.
If a good or service is included in a list of goods and services under Annex III of the Directive, a reduced rate of VAT or exemption may be applied. Member States are permitted to apply up to two reduced rates at a minimum of 5%. Ireland currently has two reduced rates of VAT of 13.5% and 9%. Member States may also avail of a derogation under the terms of the Directive that allows for a reduced rate of VAT be applied to specific goods and services that have historically been charged below the standard rate and not included under Annex III. Reduced rates applied because of a derogation cannot be moved lower than 12%.
As auto fuels are not included under Annex III there is no legal basis to apply a VAT rate below 15%. As such the standard rate of VAT, currently 23%, applies to auto fuels. This rate can be reduced as low as 15% but would require all goods and services at 23% to be moved to 15%. The estimated cost of a 1% reduction in the standard rate of VAT is €707m. The full year cost of the standard rate of VAT being reduced from 23% to 15% is estimated to be €5.7 billion.
It should be noted that any VAT reduction may not be passed to consumers.

question: Deputy Darren O'Rourke asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance if he is aware of the excessive and disproportionate customs charges and administrative fees being imposed on everyday purchases and deliveries, which are adding to the cost-of-living burden on ordinary families; and whether any review or engagement with relevant bodies is planned to address this situation.
reply:
Revenue, as Ireland’s Tax and Customs administration, is responsible for managing the importation of goods in accordance with EU Customs. It is a legal requirement across the EU that electronic customs import declarations are required for all parcels / packages coming from non-EU countries including those coming through the postal system regardless of the value of the goods being sent. VAT and Customs Duty are also payable unless there are reliefs available.
In certain circumstances, Gift Relief may apply meaning that Customs Duty and VAT on importation is not payable. However, this only applies where the value of the gift is €45 or less. Where the gift is valued in excess of €45, then VAT and Customs Duty apply on the full value of the gift. In the instance referenced by the Deputy, the value of the gift was €48 which is greater than the gift threshold and as a result, tax and duties apply.
The fees charged by An Post for completing the Customs declaration and collecting the tax and duty owed, is a contractual arrangement between An Post and its customers. Revenue has no role in relation to the fees charged.
Customs rules are standard across the EU and Ireland cannot unilaterally change these rules and this includes the thresholds for Gift Relief.

question: Deputy Pearse Doherty asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance to provide an update on the corporate taxation matters currently under discussion at European Union level, including those being considered by the Economic and Financial Affairs Council, ECOFIN, during Ireland's Presidency of the Council of the European Union; to identify the relevant legislative and non-legislative proposals, including proposals concerning corporate tax transparency, taxation of multinational enterprises and implementation of the EU Minimum Tax Directive; to outline the position of the Irish Government on each of these matters.
reply:
At European Union (EU) level, discussions on corporate taxation are currently focused on a number of legislative and non-legislative initiatives, primarily aimed at simplifying the EU corporate tax framework and improving tax transparency standards.
As part of Ireland's Presidency of the Council of the EU, my officials are focused on progressing the European Commission's Tax Simplification Package, published on 24 June 2026, through Council. This package comprises two principal legislative proposals: a Tax Omnibus and a recast of the Directive on Administrative Cooperation (DAC).
The Tax Omnibus proposal seeks to amend a number of existing corporate tax directives, including the Anti-Tax Avoidance Directive (ATAD), the Parent-Subsidiary Directive (PSD), the Interest and Royalties Directive (IRD), the Tax Merger Directive (TMD), the Tax Dispute Resolution Mechanism Directive (DRM) and the FASTER Directive, with the stated objective of simplifying rules, reducing administrative and compliance burdens and strengthening competitiveness of companies operating in the EU.
The DAC Recast proposal seeks to consolidate the existing DAC framework into a single instrument, streamline administrative cooperation between tax authorities and reduce reporting obligations where these are no longer considered necessary or proportionate.
