question: Deputy Daniel Ennis asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport the steps he will take to address the lack of a full-sized sports pitch in Dublin 1.
reply:
The provision of land for recreational purposes including sports facilities is primarily a matter for local authorities in accordance with their functions under the Planning and Development Act.
Once lands are acquired for sporting purposes, applications for capital investment (including equipment) on those lands can be supported via the Community Sports Facilities Fund (CSFF) or the Large Scale Sports Facilities Fund.
On 2 October, my Department published the Information Guide for the 2026 round of the CSFF. The 2026 round introduces increased maximum grant amounts, allowing local project applications to apply for up to €250,000 and regional Tier 1 projects to apply for up to €550,000.
The 2026 CSFF also introduces, on a pilot basis, a new Regional Tier 2 Grant category with a maximum funding amount of €750,000 with either a local authority or National Governing Body of Sport (NGB) as the project development lead. It is intended that this category will encourage a particular focus on the development of full-sized multisport all-weather pitches.

question: Deputy Joanna Byrne asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport to detail the supports for independent radio broadcasters included in budget 2027.
reply:
Commercial and independent radio broadcasters are eligible to apply for funding under a number of schemes operated by Coimisiún na Meán which support the capacity of the media sector to produce and distribute high quality, independent and trustworthy public service content.
Total support for broadcast and media funding schemes is being maintained in Budget 2027. €5M will be made available for the News Reporting Scheme, with €3M ringfenced for independent radio. Independent radio will also be able to seek funding under the Digital Transformation Scheme (to which €4M is being allocated) and Local Democracy and Courts Reporting Schemes (to which €6M is being allocated), which are administered by Coimisiún na Meán on a platform neutral basis. In addition, 7% of net TV Licence Fee receipts will be allocated to Coimisiún na Meán's longstanding Sound and Vision Scheme under which independent radio can also lodge applications for funding. In 2026, over €7M was awarded by Coimisiún na Meán through the various media funding schemes to support the commercial radio sector, at a local, regional and national level.
I am aware of the challenges facing our independent radio stations in the current climate in an increasingly competitive market. The independent radio sector plays an important role in providing valuable public service content to the Irish public, contributing to diversity and a plurality of voices.

I mí na Bealtaine i mbliana cheadaigh an Rialtas foilsiú an Bhille Craolacháin (Leasú), 2026. Ceann de ghnéithe an Bhille is ea foráil maidir le sásra feabhsaithe chun measúnú a dhéanamh ar fheidhmíocht RTÉ agus TG4 agus ar an maoiniú is cuí dóibh.

question: Deputy Shónagh Ní Raghallaigh asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport the measures he is taking to protect children and young people from the negative effects of frequent AI use, harmful content in online spaces and platforms designed to be addictive.
reply:
Ireland's Online Safety Framework comprises the Online Safety and Media Regulation Act 2022, the EU Digital Services Act, the EU AI Act, and the Online Safety Code.
With respect to protecting minors from the uses of AI, the EU AI Act was recently amended to add new prohibited practices. One of the new prohibited practices is the placing on the market of systems that can generate child sexual abuse material. Another new prohibited practice is the generation of non-consensual sexually explicit or intimate content, such as “nudification apps”.
These provisions will take effect on 2 December 2026. The implementation of the EU AI Act is within the remit of the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment.
More recently, the European Commission published a Proposal for the new EU KIDS Act. That Proposal includes provisions on AI chatbots and companions in the context of protecting children and young people online.
The Proposal provides that AI companions and chatbots that are accessible to minors may not use designs that simulate human relationships in ways likely to create emotional dependency. They will not be able to carry a child’s conversations into later ones, by default. They must be tested for risks to children before being launched onto the market and monitored for harm afterwards. Children under 13 can only use them through parental control tools. Where an AI chatbot is built into a platform or game, it must not switch on automatically, may not be promoted to children

reply:

It provides breeding services and studbook services to the Department of Agriculture, Food and the Marine (DAFM) under contract, and it also leads the development of the sports side of the sport horse sector. Sport Ireland, as the statutory body with responsibility for the development of sport, increasing participation at all levels and raising standards, allocates annual funding under its various programmes to HSI.
My officials, and Sport Ireland, are in contact with colleagues in DAFM regarding the ongoing examinership process, and the outcome of that process is awaited with keen interest. While Sport Ireland plays an important role in promoting, supporting, and strengthening good governance practices across the sector, all NGBs, including HSI, are independent, autonomous bodies and are responsible for their own governance procedures.

question: Deputy Richard Boyd Barrett asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport whether he will withdraw or amend legislation which proposes that 25% of RTÉ's budget should be redirected to the independent sector, and provide that any policy of support for the latter sector should come from dedicated funding streams, rather than from the budgetary allocation for RTÉ as proposed.
reply:
Section 116 of the Broadcasting Act 2009 currently provides that RTÉ shall pay a fixed index-linked sum into the RTÉ independent programme account for the purpose of commissioning programmes from the independent sector.
The Future of Media Commission examined the independent programme account and highlighted that RTÉ’s investment in new programming plays a vital role in supporting the wider creative economy in Ireland. The Commission recommended (Recommendation 5 – 10) the funding level of RTÉ’s Independent Programme Account should be increased to 25% of RTÉ’s public funding, and in the longer-term to a proportion to be recommended by Coimisiún na Meán.
Section 46 of the Broadcasting (Amendment) Bill gives effect to this recommendation by providing that RTÉ’s annual contribution to the independent programme account shall be a minimum of 25% of public funding and that Coimisiún na Meán may increase this minimum percentage, subject to the approval of the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport.

question: Deputy Sinéad Gibney asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport to provide an update on his Department's plans to ensure a more proactive approach to online safety, particularly regarding the use of recommender systems and their impact on social media users.
reply:
It is a Government priority to ensure a robust framework for online safety, in particular for children and young people.
The recent Proposal for a new EU KIDS Act includes new provisions on recommender systems that are specifically designed to protect minors. For example, social media services will have to prioritise the clearly expressed preferences of children instead of implicit ones that are inferred from the behaviour of a child online. Personalisation based on tracking must be off by default. Social media will have to prominently display tools that enable minors to modify or control elements of a recommender system, including making it easy to delete previous preferences. At least one option of a system not based on profiling must be easily available. There are also measures to avoid the “rabbit hole” effect of recommending similar content repeatedly, where the cumulative effect can be harmful.
The EU KIDS Act has other provisions intended to make safer the overall design of social media and other digital services available to minors. These include provisions addressing addictive design, such as infinite scroll, and safeguards against contact from strangers.
As online safety, especially for children and young people, is a key theme of Ireland’s EU Presidency, we are giving priority to the negotiations on the EU KIDS Act and those discussions are advancing.

The International Sports Diplomacy Strategy 2026-2030, which was published earlier this year by my Department and the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade, seeks to enhance the many related activities already underway to maximise the value of significant government investment in both Ireland’s international footprint and in sports at every level, to support stronger coordination among key stakeholders and to identify and support new international sports diplomacy initiatives in line with the goals of this Strategy.
The four goals of the strategy include promoting Ireland as a Sporting Nation; using Sport including Gaelic Games to deepen our diaspora’s connection to Ireland; supporting international sporting partnerships and cooperation in line with Ireland’s values and interests and maximising the economic value of international sports diplomacy and engagement in major sporting events.
An implementation group, jointly chaired by my Department and the Department of Foreign Affairs has recently been established, and it is anticipated that proposals to establish the first round of the International Sports Diplomacy Fund will brought forward soon. This fund, will have an annual budget of €200,000, jointly funded by both Departments. Once established, a targeted call for applications will be published and I look forward to publishing more information in this regard in due course.

question: Deputy Peter Roche asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport the further measures he intends to take to strengthen the protection of children and young people using social media and online platforms; and the way in which the Government intends to progress age restrictions and effective age-assurance measures.
reply:
The protection of children and young people online is a whole of Government priority.
The Online Safety Framework, which includes the Online Safety and Media Regulation Act 2022, the Online Safety Code, the EU Digital Services Act, and the EU AI Act, already provides protections for minors online.
With respect to age restrictions, the Government supports an EU wide approach to support compliance and effective enforcement. Therefore, we welcome the recently published Proposal for a new EU KIDS Act, which provides new age thresholds for access to social media and video sharing platforms. The Proposal takes a graduated approach, starting with measures to prohibit under 13 year olds from having accounts on those services. Children aged between 13 and 15 will be able to have limited accounts, opened and managed by parents, while those over 15 may open their own accounts provided they are on services that are safe for minors.
As part of Ireland’s EU Presidency, we have given priority to the negotiations on this Proposal, to advance the discussions in the Council as efficiently as possible.
Effective enforcement of obligations on digital services is another important aspect of protecting children online. The Broadcasting (Amendment) Bill 2026 provides a new binding information gathering power for Coimisiún na Meán to use as regulator for the Online Safety Framework.

reply:

question: Deputy Eamon Scanlon asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht further to Parliamentary Question No. 1590 of 20 March 2024, if the BDO report commissioned by his Department in 2023 on the cost and availability of public liability insurance for the community and voluntary sector has been finalised; when the final report was received, if applicable; if outstanding, the reason for the delay and expected completion date; whether the report has been or will be published; and if so, when and where it may be accessed.
reply:
Action 23 of the National Volunteering Strategy 2021-2025 was to “Represent the views of the sector in relation to the impact of the cost and availability of public liability insurance on volunteering through engagement with the Insurance Reform Sub-group of the Cabinet Committee on Economic Recovery and Investment, which was established to implement the Government’s insurance reform agenda”.
In furtherance of this action, independent research was commissioned to investigate the impact of insurance costs and liability on the Community and Voluntary Sector in Ireland. Undertaken following a competitive tendering process, the purpose of the research project was to understand and represent the views of the national and international Community and Voluntary sectors in relation to the impacts of the cost and availability of public liability insurance.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science whether the AIReady.ie course content addresses the energy use and carbon emissions associated with AI services, and the guidance, if any, given to learners; and whether any assessment of the environmental impact of the programme was carried out or considered.
reply:
The current AI Ready courses focus on foundational AI literacy, practical every day and workplace use, online safety and scams, career support, and the safe and responsible use of Artificial Intelligence (AI)
As part of the responsible-use content, learners are introduced to the environmental considerations associated with AI. The courses explain that the data centres used to provide AI services consume electricity and require resources for cooling, including water, and that the use of generative AI services therefore has an associated environmental footprint. The material also provides practical guidance on using AI thoughtfully and responsibly.
A standalone environmental impact assessment of the AI Ready programme was not considered necessary as the programme is delivered online through short, self-paced courses and does not itself develop, host or operate AI models or the computing infrastructure on which commercial AI services run.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science the measures, if any, taken or planned to offset or mitigate the additional energy use and emissions arising from the AIReady.ie target of upskilling one million people; and how the programme is consistent with the Government’s legally binding climate targets.
reply:
AIReady.ie is an upskilling and awareness initiative designed to demystify artificial intelligence (AI). The platform is focused on building AI skills and capability and does not involve the development, provision or operation of digital infrastructure.
AIReady.ie does not have responsibility for energy consumption, emissions or climate policy. Measures to manage, mitigate or offset energy use and emissions arising from digital infrastructure do not form part of the programme and are generally matters for the relevant Departments, agencies and regulatory bodies within their respective remits.
More broadly, the Government's wider approach to ensuring that digitalisation and decarbonisation progress together is reflected in the Government Statement on the Role of Data Centres in Ireland's Enterprise Strategy (2022). This sets out the Government's policy principles for the sustainable development of data centre infrastructure in the context of Ireland's climate and energy objectives.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science whether the AI Ready courses direct learners to specific commercial AI products (details supplied), without referring to alternative providers; the criteria by which any such products were selected; and whether he considers this consistent with neutrality between competing providers.
reply:
The AI Ready courses are introductory AI literacy courses intended to help learners understand and make practical use of commonly available artificial intelligence tools. The course materials refer to ChatGPT and Google Gemini as practical examples of generative AI tools. These examples were selected because they are widely recognised, readily accessible through free versions, and suitable for demonstrating the relevant learning outcomes to beginners.
Learners are not required to purchase software or premium subscriptions, nor are they required to use these tools. Learners may simply follow the examples provided, and the skills and principles taught can be applied to alternative AI tools.
The inclusion of named products is therefore illustrative and does not constitute an endorsement of the providers concerned. The content-development approach focuses on the purpose and use of AI tools rather than on the companies providing them, and no commercial consideration formed part of the selection of the examples.
The programme is designed to teach transferable skills, including understanding AI, writing effective prompts, critically assessing AI-generated material, protecting personal information, and using AI safely and responsibly. The use of recognisable examples to support introductory learning is considered consistent with provider neutrality, as the material does not promote or recommend one commercial provider over another and the learning is applicable across different AI to

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science whether SOLAS, his Department, or the National Skills Council has any commercial, sponsorship or data-sharing arrangement with any AI provider in connection with AI Ready; whether any AI provider contributed to the course content; and whether a procurement process was held for its content or tools.
reply:
My Department, SOLAS or the National Skills Council have no commercial, sponsorship or data sharing arrangement with any AI-product provider in connection with the AI Ready courses.
Learners are not required to purchase an AI product, and AI Ready does not sell learner data or share learner data with advertisers, AI providers or other third parties.
The course content was developed with reference to the European Digital Competence Framework (DigComp), with individual course learning outcomes mapped against relevant DigComp 3.0 competence areas, including information and data literacy, communication and collaboration, digital content creation, safety and problem solving.
Pre-existing SOLAS frameworks for online learning services including content development, platform and technical services were used and were subject to the applicable public procurement and financial governance requirements.
No commercial AI tool was procured for use by learners. Where commercial AI products are referenced in learning activities, they are used as illustrative examples and learners can follow the activities without purchasing or subscribing to those products.

question: Deputy Paul Murphy asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science whether he is concerned that it appears Irish universities have spent hundreds of thousands of euros on animal testing outside the jurisdiction (details supplied).
reply:
The Health Products Regulatory Authority (HPRA), a state body under the aegis of the Department of Health, is the competent authority in respect of the use of animals for scientific purposes within Ireland. Any project on animals conducted in Ireland must be evaluated by the HPRA in accordance with Directive 2010/63/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council on the protection of animals used for scientific purposes. The latter Directive seeks to replace the use of live animals for scientific and educational purposes as soon as it is possible to do so. This legislation applies throughout the European Union and is transposed into Irish law by the European Union (Protection of Animals used for Scientific Purposes) Regulations 2012 (S.I. No. 543 of 2012). Projects must be justified from a scientific point of view or required by law, and must be conducted in the most humane and environmentally sensitive manner possible.
Further information in relation to this Directive, and concerning the scope and remit of the HPRA, can be obtained via the Department of Health. In terms of research institutions which are responsible for ensuring the planning and implementation of research which may involve the use of animals, these are individually liable for ensuring all such research is in accordance with all relevant regulations and legislation.

question: Deputy Grace Boland asked the Minister for Health the measures her Department is taking to ensure that private health insurance products are presented to consumers in a clear, transparent and easily comparable manner.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 1104 to 1106, inclusive, together.
As Minister for Health, I am responsible for the legal framework governing the health insurance market in Ireland. This is a voluntary market that operates under the principles of community rating, open enrolment, lifetime cover and minimum benefits. These protections are designed to support fairness and keep health insurance as affordable as possible for all consumers.
The Health Insurance Act 1994 (Minimum Benefit) Regulations 1996 require insurers to provide a minimum level of cover to every insured person, regardless of what insurance policy has been purchased. Private health insurers operate as commercial entities within a competitive market, and where a procedure or service is not designated as a minimum benefit under the Regulations, insurers may determine themselves whether to include it on particular plans.
Beyond the scope of this legislation, I do not have a role in the commercial decision making of any private health insurer and therefore cannot direct any insurer to provide cover for any particular procedure or service, or direct how that cover is to be provided.
The statutory framework governing private health insurance provides for a number of independent oversight and consumer protection mechanisms to ensure that consumers are treated fairly and in accordance with the relevant legislation and regulatory requirements.

question: Deputy John Connolly asked the Minister for Health the progress made to date on the delivery of the new surgical hub at Merlin Park University Hospital under the Elective Care Programme; the forthcoming stages of the project; the expected timelines for those stages; when the surgical hub will become operational; the estimated cost range attributable to the project.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 1093 and 1096 together.
The Government’s Elective Care Programme is being delivered in two phases: a national network of Surgical Hubs in the first instance to meet medium term demand and capacity, and then a national network of Elective Treatment Centres (Elective Hospitals) in Cork, Galway and Dublin.
The new elective facilities enable the separation of scheduled (elective) from unscheduled care. This will mean fewer cancellations and fewer delays for elective care caused by seasonal surges, localised outbreaks, and surges in emergency attendances. Reducing waiting times for elective cases can help to avoid patient conditions from deteriorating further while waiting for treatment. Providing additional elective care capacity will therefore lead to better health outcomes and improved quality of life for those individuals being treated and for their families. Developing increased elective care capacity will also release capacity in existing hospitals, allowing them to focus on non-elective, acute and other inpatient activity.
All efforts are being made to ensure the swift and safe delivery of the new Surgical Hub in Galway. Once fully operational the new Surgical Hub will provide significant additional elective care capacity, including more than 8,100-day case procedures and 5,700 minor ops procedures every year.

question: Deputy Erin McGreehan asked the Minister for Health to outline Ireland’s position on proposed EU maximum permitted levels for vitamins and minerals in food supplements; which bodies represent Ireland in the relevant PAFF Committee discussions; and the timetable for consideration and adoption of these measures.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 1079 and 1080 together.
I am aware of the ongoing work of the European Commission on the possible establishment of harmonised maximum amounts for vitamins and minerals in food supplements and fortified foods.
It is important to note that the European Commission has not yet presented final proposals and no binding limits have been agreed at EU level. The Commission is continuing its preparatory work and has indicated that stakeholders will have opportunities to provide evidence and feedback through forthcoming consultation processes.
As the Commission has not yet published proposed maximum levels, a comprehensive assessment of the impact on consumer access to individual food supplements currently available in Ireland has not been completed. However, the Department is actively monitoring the process and will carefully consider any future proposals, including their potential implications for consumers, public health and access to appropriate food supplements in Ireland.
The Department will closely be monitoring developments and engaging with the European Commission, the FSAI and relevant stakeholders. The Department has not yet finalised a national position on this matter. question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Health whether the Pharmaceutical Society of Ireland and the Nursing and Midwifery Board of Ireland collect data on registrants whose qualifications were obtained outside the State and on fitness to practise complaints concerning them; and, if so, the most recent figures for each.
reply:
I thank the Deputy for his question.
My department have engaged with both the Pharmaceutical Society of Ireland (PSI) and the Nursing & Midwifery Board of Ireland (NMBI) who have provided the following information
The Pharmaceutical Society of Ireland (PSI) collects information on the country in which a pharmacist obtained their qualification as part of the qualification recognition and registration process.
As of 15 October 2026, there are 7,997 pharmacists registered in Ireland. Of these, 4,032 (50.4%) presented a pharmacist qualification obtained outside Ireland during the registration process.
The PSI also manages fitness to practise complaints relating to registered pharmacists. However, complaint data is not routinely categorised or reported by the country in which a pharmacist obtained their qualification.
The Nursing & Midwifery Board of Ireland (NMBI) have said there are approximately 92,000 nurses and midwives on the NMBI Register, of whom 51% obtained their qualifications outside the state.
In 2024, NMBI received 109 complaints about the fitness to practise of a registered nurse or midwife. This represents 0.12% of the total number on the Register. Of the 109 complaints received, 57 registrants obtained their qualifications outside the state (including the United Kingdom).
The NMBI annual State of Complaints report gives an overview of the fitness to practise process and is published on their website.

reply:

The framework will modernise our approach to professional regulation both in terms of how decisions are made regarding professional regulation and the ways in which we regulate professions. The framework will be informed by an evidence and risk-based approach to regulation in line with requirements set out in the EU Proportionality Test Directive.
The issues to be considered regarding the proportionate degree of regulatory force required to protect the public are complex and this is therefore a significant project requiring considerable research and engagement with relevant stakeholders.

question: Deputy Mairéad Farrell asked the Minister for Health to provide an update on the implementation of the recommendations outlined in the Diabetes Policy and Services Review: A Strategy for Better Care, in particular the increased access to continuous glucose monitors in cases where there is a clinical indication outside of patients with T1D.
reply:
The Diabetes Policy and Services Review: A Strategy for Better Care (www.assets.gov.ie/static/documents/a41e7d5d/Diabetes_Policy_and_Services_Review_-_A_Strategy_for_Better_Care.pdf) was launched on the 21st of May.
This is Ireland’s first national strategy for diabetes, marking a major milestone in diabetes care in Ireland. It provides a detailed assessment of our current diabetes services and sets out series of recommendations and actions to improve diabetes care delivery. This includes access to diabetes technology based on clinical need, such as continuous glucose monitoring.
The recommendations cover four key themes:
• Service Development
• Affordability and Access to care
• Better support for people living with diabetes
• Digital Healthcare
The recommendations are marked in the strategy as either short, medium or long-term goals. Short-term refers to recommendations which can be implemented within three years. Medium term recommendations can be implemented within five years, and long-term recommendations are those that will take longer than five years to fully implement.
The HSE is currently working to develop an implementation plan to ensure that the recommendations are followed through at national level and throughout the Health Regions.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Health Whether CORU or her Department has carried out a review, audit or evaluation of CORU’s processes for assessing qualifications obtained outside the State; if so, the date and findings of each; and, if not, whether one is planned.
reply:
CORU’s role is to protect the public by regulating the health and social care professions designated under the Health and Social Care Professionals Act 2005 (as amended).
CORU promotes high standards of professional conduct, education, training and competence through statutory registration, and by setting clear and robust standards for entry to regulated health and social care professions. All registrants are required to practise in accordance with those standards and their profession’s Code of Conduct and Ethics.
CORU constantly strives to improve its processes, including those for assessing overseas qualifications. My officials maintain regular engagement and oversight of CORU and receive monthly updates and reports on qualification assessment activities and associated timelines.
CORU has advised that their Recognition department, which oversees the processing of applications from international applicants, was audited in 2025 by an external auditor. This audit included an evaluation of the full assessment process for international applicants. The findings were presented to the CORU audit committee and only housekeeping breaches of process were found, and have been addressed. The next audit is due in 2027.

question: Deputy Peter 'Chap' Cleere asked the Minister for Health her plans to implement a shingles vaccination programme for those who are immunocompromised and those aged 65+ as announced in Budget 2027; and the expected timeline for the programme to commence.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 882 and 1039 together.
Ireland’s immunisation programme is informed by the advice of the National Immunisation Advisory Committee (NIAC). NIAC considers the prevalence of the relevant disease in Ireland as well as international best practice in relation to immunisation when developing its advice.
The current NIAC guidelines state that the shingles vaccine may be considered for those aged 65 years and older, due to the greater burden and severity of disease in this age group and in those aged 18 years and older at increased risk of shingles.
I can confirm that I have approved the introduction of a Shingles Vaccination Programme, in line with NIAC advice, to be implemented on a phased basis over 5 years, for immuno-compromised groups and persons aged 65 and over.
The programme is expected to commence in 2027, initially offering shingles vaccines to immuno-compromised groups. This will be followed by the 80 years and older cohort. The programme will conclude with the 65–69-year-old cohort.
It is expected that the vaccine will be administered in the main by GPs and Pharmacists. Further programme details will become available in due course.

question: Deputy Ivana Bacik asked the Minister for Health if legislation to provide a legislative underpinning for adult safeguarding in the health and social care sector will be published this quarter; and if preparations are underway to give effect to proposed legislative commitment, including ensuring that safeguarding structures within the HSE are independent.
reply:
A National Policy Framework for Adult Safeguarding in the Health and Social Care sector was published in December 2025, in line with the commitment in the Programme for Government. The policy framework will extend across all public, private and voluntary health and social care services.
Included are a range of both legislative and non-legislative measures that will significantly expand and strengthen existing supports and protections for adults at risk of harm across the health and social care sector. The Government has also approved the development of legislation to underpin these commitments. Key legislative commitments include:
• The Health Service Executive (HSE) will have responsibility for leading and coordinating adult safeguarding across the sector and will have statutory functions, duties, and powers to underpin this role.
• Current safeguarding structures within the HSE will be strengthened and legislation will provide that they will operate independently in the performance of their functions.
• New powers of entry for safeguarding and protection teams and powers to obtain court protection orders.
• The Health Information Quality Authority's (HIQA’s) remit will be extended to include independent oversight and monitoring of adult safeguarding services for the Health and Social care sector delivered by the HSE.

question: Deputy Pa Daly asked the Minister for Health the measures that have been taken to provide nursing home support for survivors of Industrial and Reformatory Schools under the agreement concluded on 10 November 2025; the number of survivors who have benefited from such measures to date.
reply:
The Department of Education and Youth’s Supports for Survivors of Residential Institutional Abuse Act 2025 was signed into law in July 2025. The Act makes available - amongst other supports - the provision of health services without charge to survivors of residential institutional abuse, in the form of a medical card administered by the HSE.
The health supports to be provided under the 2025 Act are similar to those under the standard medical card but with some additional benefits. The supports include, a general practitioner service, approved prescribed drugs, medicines, medical and surgical appliances, home nursing, home support services, dental, aural, ophthalmic and chiropody services. In addition, the survivors’ medical card will be for life and will not be subject to review or means-testing. Holders of this medical card will not be required to pay prescription charges and will also have improved access to counselling and physiotherapy services. The HSE will also appoint dedicated liaison officers for survivors.

question: Deputy Colm Burke asked the Minister for Health whether her Department supports the key recommendations in the European Commission’s recent proposals for a council recommendation on health checks for cardiovascular diseases, including the screening actions for specific age groups, blood pressure and blood glucose assessments and vaccination status assessments.
reply:
Cardiovascular disease (CVD) encompasses a range of conditions including heart attack and stroke, remains one of the most significant public health challenges facing Europe. It is the leading cause of death across the EU, claiming approximately 1.7 million lives each year, while in Ireland it accounts for around 10,000 deaths annually and remains a major contributor to ill health and hospitalisation.
Although substantial progress has been made in reducing mortality, more people are living longer with cardiovascular disease and require ongoing care and support. Cardiovascular disease also places a significant economic burden on society.
As up to 80% of cardiovascular disease are preventable, there is a strong focus in both Ireland and the EU on prevention, early identification and timely intervention to reduce avoidable illness, improve outcomes and lessen its health, social and economic impact.
Last December, I welcomed the publication of the EU Cardiovascular Health Plan, known as the Safe Hearts Plan. The plan aims to support Member States in reducing the burden of cardiovascular disease by strengthening national policies across prevention, health promotion, early detection and screening, and treatment, while also driving innovation.
One of the Plan's ten flagship initiatives is the proposed Council Recommendation on cardiovascular health checks, which was published on 28 September to coincide with the EU's first Screening Week.

question: Deputy Pádraig Rice asked the Minister for Health the actions the HSE and Health Products Regulatory Authority are taking regarding a current supply shortage (details supplied).
reply:
The HPRA has advised that Jorveza holds a centralised European Union marketing authorisation; however, the marketing authorisation holder (MAH) has confirmed that the product is not currently marketed in Ireland.
While Jorveza is authorised for use within the European Union, its availability in Ireland depends on the marketing authorisation holder placing the product on the Irish market. The MAH has advised that a full health technology assessment would be required before the product could be introduced to the Irish market. Information on this process is available from the National Centre for Pharmacoeconomics (NCPE) at NCPE Jorveza HTA information (www.ncpe.ie/budesonide-jorveza-hta-id-24014/). Neither the Department of Health nor the HPRA can require a company to market an authorised medicine in Ireland.

Menopause has been highlighted as a key priority area by the Women’s Health Taskforce. It is a key action in the Women’s Health Action Plans. A number of measures have been implemented in recent years to improve the experience of menopause for women in Ireland, including this HRT arrangement.

question: Deputy Pádraig Rice asked the Minister for Health the funding provided to implement the National Maternity Strategy in Budget 2027; and to provide a detailed breakdown of this allocation.
reply:
The National Maternity Strategy is in its final year. The Strategy has delivered significant reform since 2016, with the majority of actions now completed or well underway. Work is ongoing to ensure completion of the remaining actions of the Strategy in 2026.
Since 2016, €28 million in development funding has been invested through the Strategy, supporting the recruitment of more than 567 additional whole-time equivalent staff, including 44 consultants and over 390 nurses and midwives.
Over €130 million of capital investment has been directed into maternity services over the lifetime of the strategy. This has modernised facilities, delivering refurbishments to wards, and home-from-home birthing rooms across the country.
More than €20 million capital funding has also advanced our information sharing infrastructure, with the Maternal and Neonatal Clinical Management System now live in Cork, Kerry, Limerick, the Rotunda, the National Maternity Hospital, and the Coombe.
Budget 2027 provides a significant increase of €1.6 billion (6.2%) in current funding and €160 million (10.3%) in capital funding for the health service in 2027.
While there is no specific ringfenced allocation for the National Maternity Strategy arising from the Budget, the overall additional funding will support the continued delivery and development of services across hospital and community care settings.

Deputy Pádraig Rice asked the Minister for Health if an issue with glass on the new National Children’s Hospital has been identified; to outline, in detail, the nature of this issue; the date at which it became known; the amount of glass involved; the delay incurred; the cost of remedial works; and the name of the supplier.
reply:
Opening the National Children’s Hospital Ireland (NCHI) is a Government priority. Everything possible is being done to ensure this world-class hospital will open as quickly as possible, on behalf of children, young people, and their families.
I have been clear that the responsibility for committing to, resourcing, and delivering this project sits squarely with the project’s main contractor, BAM Ireland. The State will not reduce the pressure or dilute that accountability.
BAM is responsible for the supply and installation of the glass in the NCHI. I am aware that there are a small number of glass panes that have yet to meet the required compliance standards. BAM is also responsible for rectifying all defects, and this defect will be rectified to the required standard by substantial completion.
Over the last 18 months, significant rework has impacted BAM’s progress. BAM has closed c.200,000 defects, with c.1,900 outstanding. Defects continue to be identified and closed through the ongoing inspection process, including the panes of glass in question. These defects are the responsibility of the contractor BAM.
The National Paediatric Hospital Development Board (NPHDB), on behalf of the State, will only accept completed work that meets contractual standards. Normal room inspection on projects such as this is sampling 10-20%, whereas the Design Team is inspecting 100% of rooms to ensure standards are met. In some instances, the Design Team has had to re-inspect some rooms 6 times.

question: Deputy Louis O'Hara asked the Minister for Health whether she will review the income thresholds that apply as part of the medical card scheme especially in the context of planned increases to the minimum wage.
reply:
Medical Card provision is primarily based on financial assessment. In accordance with the Health Act 1970 (as amended), eligibility for a medical card is determined by the HSE, which assesses each application on a qualifying financial threshold. This is the amount of money that an individual can earn a week and still qualify for a card. It is specific to the individual's own financial circumstances.
Every effort is made by the HSE, within the framework of the legislation, to support applicants in applying for a medical card - in particular, to take full account of difficult circumstances in the case of applicants who may be in excess of the income guidelines. In such circumstances, the HSE may exercise discretion and grant a medical card, for example:
• Discretionary medical cards issued to patients with significant medical expenses, but who do not satisfy the means test.
• Emergency medical cards are issued to patients that are terminally ill, or are seriously ill, and in urgent need of medical care that they cannot afford.
I can assure the Deputy that, in order to ensure the medical card system is responsive and sensitive to people's needs, my Department keeps medical card issues under review and any proposals are considered in the context of any potential broader implications for Government policy, the annual budgetary estimates process and legislative requirements arising.

question: D'fhiafraigh Deputy Aengus Ó Snodaigh den Aire Forbartha Tuaithe agus Pobail, agus Gaeltachta cé mhéad go sonrach atá le baint ó bhuiséad caipitil na nOileán agus cé mhéad atá le baint ó bhuiséad caipitil na Gaeltachta sa chiorrú atá leagtha amach sa Bhuiséad ar airgead caipitil na Gaeltachta agus na nOileán ó €55,362,000 in 2026 go €50,362,000 in 2027.
reply:
Tá leithdháileadh iomlán de €628 milliún faighte ag mo Roinn i gCáinaisnéis 2027, lena n-áirítear leithdháileadh caiptil de €273 milliún. Foilseofar leithdháileadh mionsonraithe de réir fomhír san Imleabhar Meastachán Athbhreithnithe (REV) roimh dheireadh na bliana.
Tá pleananna fíor-uaillmhianacha ag mo Roinn d'fhorbairtí caipitil chun tacú le pobail Ghaeltachta, pobal na Gaeilge agus pobail na n-oileán araon. Maoinítear na forbairtí seo as Clár C de bhuiséad na Roinne - An Ghaeltacht, an Ghaeilge agus na hOileáin. Is fiú a mheabhrú gur tháinig ardú ar an mbuiséad caipitil do Chlár C ó €30 milliún in 2025 go beagnach €55 milliún in 2026. Bhain cuid mhaith den ardú sin le trí phríomhthionscadal infreastruchtúir:
• Cé Inis Oírr,
• An tIonad Gaeilge agus Cultúir ar Shráid Fhearchair, agus
• athfhorbairt shuíomh Choláiste Lurgan in Indreabhán mar Ionad Oideachais agus Óige do Ghaeltacht Chonamara.
Rinneadh gealltanas i leith na dtionscadal seo sa Phlean Forbartha Náisiúnta, agus is cúis áthais dom an maoiniú a fháil chun iad a thabhairt i gcrích anois. Táim den tuairim mheáite go mbeidh an t-allúntas caipitil atá faighte ag mo Roinn leordhóthanach le freastal ar riachtanais chlár na Gaeltachta, na Gaeilge agus na nOileán i 2027 agus sna blianta ina dhiaidh sin.

question: Deputy William Aird asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht when the next round of the Local Enhancement Programme will be announced; and the level of funding that will be available for community groups.
reply:

I was delighted to secure current funding of €2 million for the LEP in Budget 2027 to assist community organisations in easing the pressure of rising operating costs. This is in addition to €5 million in capital funding that is available for LEP 2027. My Department is currently considering the detailed design of the LEP for 2027 and I hope to announce the new programme before the end of this year.

question: Deputy William Aird asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht the level of funding remaining under the LEADER Programme 2023-2027; and the measures being taken to ensure that funding is fully utilised.
reply:
The LEADER Programme is co-funded by the European Union and is delivered through Local Action Groups (LAGs) across rural Ireland. A feature of the LEADER programme is that it is based on a community-led, bottom-up approach to rural development.
The 2023-2027 LEADER programme has total funding of €180 million, with 75% or €135 million available to support projects being completed by rural groups and businesses.
The funding is allocated in advance to LAGs to provide them with greater flexibility to manage their budgets over the programming period. Funding is then paid out by my Department as costs are incurred and claims for payment are submitted.
Using this allocation, LEADER LAGs have approved funding of over €76.8 million for some 1,537 LEADER projects countrywide. This means that c. 57% of the overall project allocation is committed, with some €58 million or 43% remaining. Of these, 551 projects have been completed to date, with the remainder due to be completed over the coming months and years. There are an additional 172 projects progressing through the approval stages across all sub-regional areas.
The €180 million also includes €45 million (or 25%) which is available to support the administration and animation costs of the LAGs involved in running the programme. Of this, €20.1 million has been drawn down to date, with some €24.9 million remaining. question: Deputy William Aird asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht the funding allocated to the Social Inclusion and Community Action Programme (SICAP) for 2027.
reply: The Social Inclusion and Community Activation Programme (SICAP) is Ireland's primary social inclusion programme, which aims to reduce poverty and promote social inclusion and equality by supporting disadvantaged individuals and communities across the country. The programme works with individuals and local community groups to address barriers to participation and strengthen community capacity. I am pleased to have secured almost €74 million for SICAP and other social inclusion supports in Budget 2027. Just under €65 million of that allocation is for SICAP providing greater long-term funding stability for the programme and enabling the continuation of important work across the country. It should be noted that the final estimated allocations for each area will be confirmed in the Revised Estimates Volume which will be published in December, and considered by the relevant select committees. A particularly welcome development is the provision of long-term funding certainty, with previously temporary funding for new arrivals made a permanent part of the core SICAP allocation. This represents an important step towards ensuring that community integration supports can be delivered on a more sustainable, long-term basis. This provides greater certainty for those planning and delivering services and helps sustain integration supports in communities. reply:

This approach is designed to underpin effective delivery of high quality projects for rural communities, and sees applications assessed in a fair and consistent manner, informed by considerations such as suitability against scheme criteria, geographical spread and the quality of the projects.
The Rural Regeneration and Development Fund is a key element of the Rural Development Investment Programme which supports large-scale, ambitious capital projects that can achieve sustainable economic and social development in rural areas. The focus of the RRDF is on rural towns and villages with a population of less than 10,000 people. To date, it has allocated over €611 million to 271 projects located across the country, including over €43.2million to 27 projects in Co. Cork.
I was delighted to open a Call for Category 1 proposals under the Fund in February this year, which sought applications for strategically important, large-scale capital projects that have full planning and other consents in place and are ready to commence. question: Deputy John Paul O'Shea asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht the additional supports in place for social enterprises as a result of Budget 2027.
reply:
The Government recognises the important contribution that social enterprises make to communities across Ireland by delivering social, environmental and economic benefits, while also creating employment opportunities and supporting inclusive local development.
My Department supports social enterprises under a number of different funding streams and I am pleased to note that these supports have been maintained or increased as a result of Budget 2027.
Regarding the delivery of Trading for Impact, the national social enterprise policy, a significant increase in funding to support this was delivered under Budget 2026, and I expect that this funding will remain unchanged. This will support a range of measures to deliver on the objectives of the policy, including verification of social enterprises, awareness and capacity building and impact measurement.
My Department's Community Services Programme (CSP) currently supports the delivery of 453 services nationally via 434 community organisations to provide local social, economic, and environmental services through a social enterprise model, with a budget of €59.4m in 2026. This Programme provides an annual co-funding contribution towards each full-time equivalent (FTE) position being supported and, where warranted, towards the cost of employing a manager. The CSP Programme currently provides funding towards 1,723 FTEs and 354 manager positions.

question: Deputy Colm Burke asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science the steps his Department is taking to assist students following the unexpected and immediate closure of a language college in Cork (details supplied) given that the abrupt closure of the college has left students who rely on it for their immigration status in a uncertain and distressing situation.
reply:
My Department is aware of the closure of the English language education provider in question.
As a private provider, it does not come under the remit of my Department. Nor does my Department have a role in issues arising from a private contract between a student and a provider.
However, such a closure creates uncertainty which has a significant impact on the learners, prospective students, and staff of that provider.
For a provider to be eligible to recruit students from non-EEA countries, the provider’s courses must be included on the Interim List of Eligible Programmes (ILEP). The ILEP is administered by the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration in conjunction with my Department. The provider in question was an ILEP listed provider.
ILEP listed providers are required to have arrangements in place for the protection of enrolled learners. These arrangements are to protect learners in the event that a provider fails, closes or is unable to deliver an ILEP-listed programme. In this case, the provider has had arrangements in place via an insurance product with Arachas.
The provider has been in contact with Quality and Qualifications Ireland (QQI) and advised that arrangements are being made to place learners with other providers in Cork and Dublin to enable them to complete their studies. Learners will be contacted by the provider directly.

question: Deputy Donna McGettigan asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science to give a breakdown of how the €150m unlocked from the NTF in the Budget will be spent over the next three years.
reply:
Budget 2027 provides for a multiannual investment of €150 million from the National Training Fund over the next three years, with €50 million to be provided in 2027.
The investment is intended to strengthen Ireland's capacity to anticipate and respond to emerging skills needs arising from technological, economic and labour market change, including the impact of artificial intelligence and the transition to a low-carbon economy.
The package responds directly to recommendations of the National Skills Council and will strengthen Ireland’s capacity to anticipate and respond to these changes. Funding will support curriculum renewal, educator capability, specialist and emerging skills needs, technology adoption, and expanded opportunities for upskilling, reskilling and lifelong learning.
It will also build on www.aiready.ie, the national gateway for AI skills. Following the launch of Phase 1 earlier this year, the offering will be expanded to enable more people to access training and develop the skills required in a changing workplace.
Meeting future skills needs is essential to ensuring people can access quality employment, and businesses can continue to innovate and grow. This investment package will strengthen Ireland’s skills infrastructure, support labour market participation, help address skills shortages, and enhance productivity and competitiveness.

question: Deputy Emer Currie asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science to provide further detail on the way in which employers will be able to access the National Training Fund funding announced as part of Budget 2027; the eligibility criteria that will apply; the expected timeline for the introduction of the application process.
reply:
In Budget 2027, I secured a €150 million package over three years from the NTF to strengthen Ireland's capacity to anticipate and respond to technological, economic and labour market change in the age of AI. This package will support curriculum renewal, educator capability, specialist and emerging skills needs, technology adoption, and lifelong learning opportunities across the economy. My officials are currently working through the details of the package.
This additional NTF funding will be delivered through existing NTF-supported programmes and mechanisms. It is important to note that the NTF is not a direct grant mechanism for businesses. This means that businesses do not apply directly to the NTF for grants in the way they might access enterprise supports through Enterprise Ireland. Rather, the NTF primarily funds education and training provision delivered primarily through the publicly funded education and training system, as well as employer-focused training programmes delivered through Skillnet Ireland's contracted training model. Therefore, as the funding will be delivered through established NTF-supported channels, employers will generally access supports through existing programmes operated through agencies such as SOLAS, the Higher Education Authority and Skillnet Ireland. question: Deputy Mark Wall asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science if a person (details supplied) in County Kildare can resume a chosen career given the previous issues that forced them to withdraw from the apprenticeship that they had commenced.
reply:
The apprenticeship system supports individuals in developing the skills, knowledge and qualifications required to build a successful career in their chosen field.
Where a registered apprentice has previously withdrawn from an apprenticeship due to personal or other circumstances, this does not necessarily prevent them from resuming their apprenticeship or pursuing a career in that occupation.
In general, a person who has withdrawn from an apprenticeship may be able to resume their apprenticeship, subject to meeting the relevant requirements, including securing an approved employer.
The options available will depend on the individual's specific circumstances, including the stage they had reached in their apprenticeship and the time elapsed since withdrawal.
The person concerned may wish to contact their Training Advisor to discuss their circumstances and the pathways available to re-engage with apprenticeship training. My Department and SOLAS are committed to supporting participation in apprenticeship and ensuring that individuals have access to appropriate information and guidance on available options.
The Apprenticeship Code of Practice for Employers and Apprentices sets out the rights and responsibilities of apprentices, employers and training providers, including arrangements relating to training, mentoring, progression and supports. The Code provides a framework for addressing issues and supporting engagement with the apprenticeship system.

question: Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science to clarify if household or parental income thresholds with respect to accessing SUSI grants have increased in Budget 2027.
reply:
The Government is committed to reducing the cost of participation in further and higher education.
Budget 2027 delivers a €34 million package of student supports which will provide for a €150 reduction in the student contribution in the current academic year and significant improvements to the Student Grant Scheme from September 2027.
The Student Grant Scheme improvements include a 4.5% increase in SUSI maintenance grant rates for 54,000 students, an increase in the special rate of maintenance grant, and enhanced student contribution grant supports for families with more than one dependant student in tertiary education. These maintenance grant improvements will take effect on a pro-rata basis from January 2027.

question: Deputy Pádraig Rice asked the Minister for Health to provide a detailed breakdown of the additional funding provided for in Budget 2027 in relation to the cost of maintaining existing levels of service, demographic growth and inflation; and separately, funding for new services, expanded services and reform.
reply:
Budget 2027 provides an additional €1.6 billion in current funding for health services. Of this increase, €155 million additional pay funding is being provided for workforce growth, equivalent to approximately 2.2% growth in staffing over the course of 2027, while €94 million additional non-pay funding is being allocated to support new and expanded services, reform initiatives and other Ministerial priorities.
The remaining €1.351 billion is being provided primarily to maintain existing levels of service and to meet underlying demand and cost pressures, including demographic growth, inflation, the full-year cost of existing commitments and pay-related costs.
The impact of demographic growth and inflation varies across different service areas. For example, demographic pressures are generally higher in areas such as Older Persons Services, reflecting population growth and ageing.
Similarly, inflationary pressures vary across care groups depending on the particular mix of non-pay expenditure. Funding requirements are therefore assessed on a service-by-service basis, taking account of the particular cost and demand drivers affecting each care group, rather than applying a single demographic or inflation assumption across the health system.
Detailed allocations by Health Region and care group will be set out in the Department's Letter of Determination and the HSE National Service Plan for 2027.

reply:

The Community Centre Investment Fund (CCIF) was introduced to provide high quality, accessible community spaces that are available to all groups in communities in both rural and urban areas. Since 2022 some €112 million has been allocated for the enhancement and refurbishment of existing facilities and the construction of new centres where such a need has been identified.
Earlier this year, I launched the latest round of CCIF for enhancement and refurbishment of existing centres. The closing date for applications has now passed and I look forward to announcing successful projects before year-end.

I have indicated previously that the 2027 scheme will focus on new build centres and the eligibility criteria and funding limits that will apply will be announced when that scheme is launched next year.

question: Deputy David Cullinane asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht the dedicated funding that will be provided to implement the successor to Our Rural Future; when the new policy will be published; and the way in which its objectives will be delivered without dedicated implementation funding.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 62, 73 and 83 together.

question: Deputy Réada Cronin asked the Minister for Health when a comprehensive endometriosis national service and strategy will be established.
reply:
Last October I launched the National Framework for the Management of Endometriosis. Developed by the HSE's National Women and Infants Health Programme (NWIHP), the Framework reflects the voices of patient advocates and aims to transform how endometriosis is recognised and treated across the country. Central to the Model of Care is the principle of presumed diagnosis, acknowledging that women are always the most reliable narrators of their own symptoms and pain.
The Framework marks the first step in developing a more holistic and comprehensive approach to care for women with endometriosis in Ireland.
Regional Specialist Centres for moderate cases have been established in the Rotunda Hospital, the Coombe Hospital, and University Hospital Limerick, with clinics under further development in University Hospital Galway and the National Maternity Hospital.

question: Deputy Seán Ó Fearghaíl asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht the funding available for the LEADER Programme under Budget 2027.
reply:
The LEADER programme is delivered by LEADER Local Action Groups in rural areas across the country.
For the 2023-2027 LEADER programme, €180 million was allocated in advance to these Local Action Groups to provide them with greater flexibility to manage their budgets over the programming period. Funding is then paid out by my Department as costs are incurred and claims for payment are submitted.
Given the structure of the programme, expenditure is not evenly spread over each year. For example, in certain years expenditure can be lower as Local Action Groups focus on engaging with applicants to develop and progress project applications. In other years, expenditure can be higher as projects are delivered and costs are incurred.
To ensure there is sufficient funding available to deliver the 2023-2027 LEADER programme, Budget 2027 provides for funding of €43 million for LEADER for 2027, an increase of €11 million relative to the 2026 allocation.
I am committed to ensuring that the LEADER programme continues to be well funded into the future.

question: Deputy Duncan Smith asked the Minister for Health the reason reimbursement applications under the HSE Cross Border Directive dating back to November 2025 remain outstanding (details supplied); the number of applicants waiting six months or longer for reimbursement; whether sufficient funding has been allocated to clear the current backlog; the reason applicants are receiving conflicting information regarding the status of their claims; the urgent measures being implemented to support patients experiencing financial hardship as a result of prolonged delays; and if sufficient funding has been secured for future reimbursement demand.
reply:
The Cross Border Directive (CBD) allows public patients to access necessary healthcare, which they would have been entitled to access in the public healthcare service in Ireland, in another EU or EEA country. The patient pays upfront for the treatment and is reimbursed upon return to Ireland.
The HSE is responsible for the operation of the Cross Border Directive and has a dedicated office for that purpose.
The continued growth in use of the scheme has placed additional demands on the HSE CBD office and given rise to a build-up of applications. The increased activity is evidenced by the number of treatments reimbursed increasing by approx. 75% between 2020 and 2024.
It is important that this service operates in a responsive way and that reimbursement applications are processed within a reasonable timeframe. The HSE advises it usually aims to repay patients within 30 working days of receipt of all completed documents. The HSE advise the CBD office is currently processing applications received in early April 2026. A 6-month delay for reimbursement is clearly unacceptable. To address this the HSE has advised my Department that additional resources are being assigned to manage this increase in demand with the aim of restoring processing times to expected levels. I have set the HSE a specific target of getting back to the 30-day target by the end of 2026.

Article 22 of the Cosmetics Regulation requires the HPRA to monitor compliance with the Regulation through in-market controls. The NEHS’ role involves the sampling of products at retail/salon level as a part of the annual market surveillance plan.

question: Deputy Pádraig Rice asked the Minister for Health to provide further details regarding her plans for the €7 million allocation for general practice reform in Budget 2027; and if the Strategic Review of General Practice will conclude by year end.
reply:
The Programme for Government includes a commitment to publish the Strategic Review of General Practice, and bring forward a new, modern GP contract.
The review is a comprehensive examination of issues affecting general practice, focusing on GP training, GP capacity, Out of Hours services reform, the eHealth Agenda, and the financial support model for general practice. Significant progress has been made under the review, and the review is to be completed this year.
The review will identify the arrangements necessary to improve the current system of GP care as part of a primary care-focused health service and when completed will make recommendations for a more sustainable general practice into the future.
Budget 2027 provides for €7 million for the reform of GP services, ensuring funding is available for appropriate recommendations to be progressed early after the review is completed. It is expected the focus of the funding will be the reform of GP out of hours services, for better and more equality of access for patients.
The implementation of the recommendations from the review will build on the progress already made under the 2019 and 2023 GP Agreements in improving and better supporting our GP services, as well the progress in increasing GP training places in recent years and in recruitment of GPs from abroad, to improve GP capacity and access to GP services.

question: Deputy Edward Timmins asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht if he will commit to expanding the local improvement scheme, given the benefits to rural Ireland.
reply:
The Local Improvement Scheme (LIS) funds the upgrade of non-public rural roads and laneways, which are not usually maintained by local authorities. My department reinstated the Scheme in 2017, and it is a central element of the overall Rural Development Investment Programme. Since 2017, over €201 million has been allocated to local authorities, resulting in the improvement of over 5,500 roads.
Eligible road projects include works on non-public roads which provide access:
• to parcels of land, of which, two or more are owned/occupied by different persons, one of which must be for agricultural purposes, or
• for harvesting purposes (including turf/seaweed) for two or more persons, or
• to at least one parcel of land owned/occupied by a person engaged in agricultural activities and which separately provides access for harvesting purposes (including turf/seaweed) for at least one other person
In addition, works can be carried out on amenity roads, which are non-public roads leading to important community amenities such as graveyards, beaches and piers.
The scheme’s provision were last expanded in 2024, when the requirement for 2 landowners/occupiers to be involved in separate agricultural activities was reduced to one, and has resulted in an increase in applicants applying for works under the scheme.

question: Deputy George Lawlor asked the Minister for Health when publicly funded donor assisted reproduction services, including donor sperm IUI and IVF will be made available to same sex female couples or others who require donor gametes, if the Government has a specific timeline for the provision of this service including programmes of donor assisted treatment including sperm donation and if funding for this service have been provided for in the 2027 Estimates for her Department.
reply:
The Model of Care for Fertility was developed by the Department of Health in conjunction with the Health Service Executive (HSE) National Women and Infants Health Programme to ensure that fertility-related issues are addressed through the public health system at the lowest level of clinical intervention necessary.
The Model of Care comprises three stages of care. These begin in primary care (GPs), progress to secondary care through the six HSE-run Regional Fertility Hubs located across the country, and, where clinically indicated, advance to tertiary care.
Referrals for publicly-funded, privately-provided assisted human reproduction (AHR) treatment – including IVF (in-vitro fertilisation), ICSI (intra-cytoplasmic sperm injection) and IUI (intrauterine insemination) – commenced in September 2023, subject to patients meeting the criteria agreed by my Department and the HSE. The access criteria were developed by a multidisciplinary group, with reproductive medicine expertise and followed consultation with experts in the field along with a review of the international evidence. These criteria are in keeping with those applied in other jurisdictions.
The terms of the publicly-funded AHR treatment initiative are underpinned by the primary policy principle of supporting couples experiencing fertility issues and, most specifically, those who have been trying unsuccessfully to conceive naturally at the time in question.

reply:
The State Claims Agency (SCA) does not record information in respect of these claims in a manner which allows a response to the question, in a readily extractable format.
The SCA has been notified of 78 claims involving Members of the Public or Service Users relating to the National Ambulance Service between 01/01/2022 & 01/10/2026, as recorded on the National Incident Management System (NIMS). These claims are recorded under a variety of hazard categories on NIMS, including Crash/Collision (motor), Clinical Care, Exposure to Physical Hazards, Exposure to Psychological Hazards, and Exposure to Biological Hazards.
Of the 78 claims, 31 are finalised and 47 remain active as at 01/10/2026. A total of €1.775m has been paid out on the 31 finalised claims in the period.

question: Deputy John Paul O'Shea asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht if he or his Department has any plans in place to address the long waiting times for the local improvement schemes; and if he will make funding available to local authorities as soon as possible for 2027.
reply:
The Local Improvement Scheme (LIS) funds the upgrade of non-public rural roads and laneways, which are not usually maintained by local authorities. My department reinstated the Scheme in 2017, and it is a central element of the overall Rural Development Investment Programme. Since 2017, over €201 million has been allocated to local authorities, resulting in the improvement of over 5,500 roads.
The 2026 scheme was launched in February with subhead funding of €17 million. While the Department provides LIS funding, local authorities administer the scheme and are responsible for managing waiting lists, selecting and prioritising roads and managing works undertaken. The manner in which each local authority manages its LIS application and administration process is decided by the local authority itself and is not prescribed centrally by the Department.
Demand for the scheme nationally remains high. My officials are closely monitoring scheme spending and working with local authorities to ensure that funding is fully utilised and that as many road improvements as possible are completed under the scheme this year. I note, however, that many factors affect the ability of local authorities to meet increasing demand, not just available funding. Factors such as weather conditions, costs and availability of contractors and labour are also relevant.

question: Deputy Paul Lawless asked the Minister for Health the measures being taken by her Department and the HSE to ensure that newly qualified nurses can secure employment within the public health service on graduation; whether additional posts are being approved to facilitate the recruitment of 2026 nursing graduates.
reply:
I thank the Deputy for their question.
Attracting and retaining newly qualified nurses and midwives is central to building a sustainable health workforce and supporting the delivery of high-quality patient care. The HSE is aware of the expected number of graduates each year and plans recruitment accordingly, matching graduates to services and locations where need is greatest.
The latest information provided by the HSE indicates that 974 graduate nurses and midwives have confirmed start dates. Of these, approximately 834 are expected to commence employment before the end of this year, with a further 140 due to commence from January onwards.
To be clear, there is no recruitment embargo in the HSE and recruitment has not ceased. Enhanced controls are currently in place in four Health Regions to ensure appointments are affordable, appropriately prioritised and aligned with areas of greatest patient and service need. Essential posts continue to be filled.
An important element of this approach is the recruitment of permanent staff to fill vacancies currently met through agency staffing. This can provide additional opportunities for graduates, support a more stable workforce, strengthen continuity of care and deliver better value for the taxpayer.

reply:

Earlier this year, I was delighted to launch the latest round of funding for enhancement and refurbishment of existing community centres. The funding under CCIF 2026 is being delivered across two categories, with maximum funding levels of €25,000 and €100,000 respectively. A minimum of 5% of the total project budget was required by the applicant as match funding under Category 1 applications and a minimum of 10% of the total project budget was required by the applicant as match funding under Category 2 applications. My department supports successful applicants through phased payments and ongoing engagement through the project delivery period. Indeed, 90% of the funding is provided in advance for projects approved under category 1.
As part of CCIF 2026, a number of online information events and check-in clinics were held during April to July 2026.
