question: Deputy Mark Wall asked the Minister for Social Protection if there is a facility currently, or plans for the future, to allow employees pay more than the set percentages under the national auto enrolment scheme.
reply:
The Programme for Government contained a commitment to introduce the Automatic Enrolment Retirement Savings System (AE). The aim of introducing AE was to address the pension coverage gap that exists in Ireland and to provide workers with greater comfort and security regarding their retirement income.
The new system - known as MyFutureFund - commenced on the 1 January 2026 and it is overseen by the National Automatic Enrolment Retirement Savings Authority (NAERSA), which is a separate statutory body, independent of my Department and directly responsible for all operational elements of MyFutureFund. There are currently over 835,000 participants in MyFutureFund.
The current focus of NAERSA is on ensuring all employers comply with their obligations and participants realise the value and benefit of participation in MyFutureFund. In the medium term, officials from my Department and NAERSA will begin to look at various policy measures in relation to MyFutureFund, which may include options for individual participants to make additional contributions to their savings fund.
I hope this clarifies matters for the Deputy.

question: Deputy Joe Cooney asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht his plans to the clear the backlog of the Local Improvement Scheme, whether there will be an additional allocation in 2026; and the amount that will be allocated to Clare in 2027.
reply:
The Local Improvement Scheme (LIS) funds the upgrade of non-public rural roads and laneways, which are not usually maintained by local authorities. My department reinstated the Scheme in 2017, and it is a central element of the overall Rural Development Investment Programme. Since 2017, over €201 million has been allocated to local authorities, resulting in the improvement of over 5,500 roads.
The 2026 scheme was launched in February with voted funding of €17 million. Clare County Council received an allocation of over €941,790. This brings the total amount allocated to Clare County Council since 2020 to over €7.7 million.
While the Department provides LIS funding, local authorities administer the scheme and are solely responsible for managing waiting lists, selecting and prioritising roads and managing works undertaken. The manner in which each local authority manages its LIS application and administration process is decided by the local authority itself and is not prescribed centrally by the Department.
Demand for the scheme nationally remains high and my officials are closely monitoring scheme spending and working with local authorities to ensure that 2026 funding is fully utilised and that as many roads as possible are completed under the scheme this year.
The next round of funding that will be made available to local authorities has been secured as part of Budget 2027. This will see €17 million made available to local authorities under the 2027 Local Improvement Scheme.

question: Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Social Protection the number of appeals submitted to his Department with respect to carers allowance and carers benefit in 2025 and to date in 2026; and the number of such appeals that were allowed and the number disallowed.
reply:
The number of appeals relating to Carers Allowance and Carers Benefit processed by the Social Welfare Appeals Office for the year 2025 and 2026 (up to end of Quarter 3) is broken down in the following table:
When an appeal is registered it is referred back to the relevant scheme area of the Department for review. Appeals may be revised in favour of the appellant at this early stage. Therefore, appeals that are Allowed and Partially Allowed by Appeals Officers along with those revised by DSP are considered to have a successful outcome for the appellant. Appeals which are Disallowed are considered to be unsuccessful.
Where an appeal is successful it does not always indicate that the original decision was incorrect. question: Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Social Protection to outline the benefits of the wage subsidy scheme; and his plans to promote awareness of the scheme to ensure a greater uptake by employers.
reply:
The Wage Subsidy Scheme is a key disability employment support provided by my Department. It aims to encourage employers to offer substantial and sustainable employment to disabled people through a subsidy, where their role or tasks have had to be adapted.
In September 2026, there were 1,601 employers availing of the scheme and 2,674 employees supported through the scheme. Expenditure on the scheme in 2025 was €22.1 million.
There are many benefits to the scheme, for both the employer and the employee.
The scheme creates employment opportunities for disabled people and enables them to take on roles, with adaptations in place. For the employee, it creates the space for them to discover their strengths, build confidence and gain independence, both socially and financially.
There is a positive financial aspect for employers as they are provided with a subsidy. The base wage subsidy paid to employers who employ disabled people is €7.50 per hour. This is paid to employers with one to six employees on the scheme. Employers receive €8.50 per hour when they employ seven to 16 employees and €10 when they employ 17 or more employees on the scheme.
Often, after taking on one employee on the scheme, employers hire more disabled employees as a result. It also gives them access to a wider talent pool.

question: Deputy Louis O'Hara asked the Minister for Social Protection if a person in receipt of disability allowance can inherit ownership of their current residence without it effecting their eligibility for the payment (details supplied).
reply:

In addition, the person must be substantially restricted from doing work that would otherwise be suitable for a person of their age, experience, and qualifications. Eligibility for the payment is also subject to a habitual residency requirement.

This recognises the fact that couples operate as a single household and can share living expenses in a manner not available to a single person.

Whether an inheritance has an impact on a person’s means-tested payment such as Disability Allowance, depends on a number of factors such as the level of the inheritance and whether or not the person has any other means. question: Deputy Ciarán Ahern asked the Minister for Social Protection the average time it takes to process EU social insurance contribution records for people returning to Ireland; whether he would consider introducing interim social protection supports for those returning who have met PRSI contribution records in the years preceding that in which they emigrated, subject to a time-bound cut-off point.
reply:
It takes five to seven working days for EU Records to send a request to another EU country on behalf of a benefit area. It is not possible to give an average response time as it differs from country to country.
The Social Insurance Fund operates on a pay-as-you-go basis. When PRSI contributions do not cover benefit payouts, the Exchequer covers the shortfall. The Fund is mainly financed by contributions from employees, employers, and the self-employed, creating a direct link between what people pay in and the benefits they receive. Consequently, individuals returning from abroad, where they may or may not have paid foreign social insurance, may not immediately be eligible for benefits in Ireland.
However, returning individuals may be able to combine their foreign social insurance records with their Irish PRSI history under EU regulations to qualify for social welfare payments. Under EU social security coordination frameworks—specifically Regulation (EC) No 883/2004—mobile workers are protected by two core principles: the aggregation of contributions across member states to secure social security access, and the export of benefits to guarantee that earned financial rights are fully transportable across borders. My Department is fully compliant with these regulatory obligations.

question: Deputy Ciarán Ahern asked the Minister for Social Protection if he will consider introducing a savings disregard in the jobseeker's allowance means test for those saving for their first home.
reply:
The system of social assistance supports provides payments based on an income need. The use of means tests in the social welfare system is a method of targeting limited resources to those with an identified financial need. The means test plays a critical role in determining whether an income need arises as a consequence of a particular contingency – such as disability, unemployment or caring. This ensures that the recipient has a verifiable income need and that resources are targeted to those who need them most.
Social welfare legislation provides that means tests take account of the income and assets of the person (and their spouse or partner) applying for the relevant scheme, including Jobseeker’s Allowance. The means assessment includes income from sources such as employment, self-employment, and occupational pensions. It also includes property owned, other than the family home, and capital such as savings, shares, and other investments.
For Jobseeker's Allowance, the formula used to assess the weekly value of capital is as follows:
• the first €20,000 of capital an applicant holds is fully disregarded;
• the next €10,000 is assessed at €1 per thousand,
• the next €10,000 is assessed at €2 per thousand,
• with the remainder assessed at €4 per thousand.

question: Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Social Protection the number of persons who currently hold a verified MyGovID account; the estimated number of adults who do not; and whether his Department has assessed the risk of exclusion from the European Digital Identity Wallet for persons who are unable or unwilling to obtain a verified MyGovID account.
reply:
Currently there are over 3.7 million verified MyGovID accounts, relating to around 3.4 million unique individuals. It is not possible to estimate how many people do not hold a verified MyGovID account.
The European Digital Identity Wallet is voluntary and is not intended to be the sole means of accessing services. The Digital Wallet is intended to complement, rather than replace, existing channels for accessing services, including online Government services. Responsibility for implementing the Wallet rests with my colleague the Minister for Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation.
The Digital Wallet will enable people to store various credentials, such as driving licence or EU Health Insurance Card, securely on their mobile phone and produce them, at their own discretion, to evidence entitlement to services and benefits across the EU. A key benefit of the wallet is that the personal data will be held and controlled by the citizen. The citizen will decide whether they want to use the wallet, what credentials to hold in the wallet and where and to whom to provide any credential. Any person who does not use the Digital Wallet will be able to evidence entitlement to services and benefits in the EU, through other means.
I hope this clarifies the matter for you.

question: Deputy Louis O'Hara asked the Minister for Social Protection if an exceptional needs payment will be awarded to a person (details supplied).
reply:
Under the Supplementary Welfare Allowance (SWA) scheme, my Department may provide an Additional Needs Payment (ANP) to assist people with essential expenditure, which an eligible person could not reasonably be expected to meet out of their weekly income, and household or personal resources.
SWA payments are administered by Community Welfare Officers who consider the provisions of the legislation and all the relevant circumstances of the case. The purpose of an ANP is to assist with immediate and essential expenses in situations of exceptional or urgent need, which cannot be met by any other source. The ANP does not cover non-essential household or personal expenses. Each application for an ANP is considered on a case-by-case basis, based on the circumstances and the need presenting.
If the person concerned is experiencing financial difficulties, it is open to them to make an application for assistance by completing a SWA1 form and providing all necessary supporting documentation. If the Deputy wishes to provide my Department with the details of the person concerned, an ANP application pack can be sent to them directly. Alternatively, if the person has a verified MyGovID account, they can apply for an ANP at www.MyWelfare.ie.

This is a 20% increase in the allowable means and will allow more single pensioners to qualify for the Fuel Allowance payment.

question: Deputy Mairéad Farrell asked the Minister for Social Protection to provide an update on her Department's plans to end the means test for carer's allowance; the timeline for this process; and the evidence a self-employed person should provide to show their current income after starting to provide care.
reply:
Carer’s Allowance is the main income support for carers, with 112,000 people receiving the payment at an estimated cost of over €1.4 billion this year.
The Programme for Government commits to significantly increasing the income disregards for Carer’s Allowance, with a view to phasing out the means test during the lifetime of this Government.
We are well on our way to achieve this commitment and the changes announced as part of Budget 2027 shows the Government's determination to further deliver to carers.
From July 2026, I increased the weekly income disregard by 60% from €625 to €1,000 for a single person, and from €1,250 to €2,000 for carers who are part of a couple. These disregards are now by far the highest in the social welfare system.
These changes mean that a carer in a two-adult household with an income of €110,000 can retain their full Carer’s Allowance payment and receive a partial payment with a household income up to €139,000. Some 2,700 carers received an increase in their payment as a result of this measure. Almost everyone on the scheme is now being paid at their maximum weekly rate.
As part of Budget 2027, I announced that the disregard will increase by a further €150 to €1,150 for a single carer and by €300 to €2,300 for a carer who is part of a couple. This will mean that a couple household can earn in excess of €126,000 annually and retain a full Carer's Allowance payment. question: Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Social Protection if he will review Schedule C, paragraph 4 of S.I. 312 of 1996, which treats Reserve Defence Forces service of up to 21 consecutive days as subsidiary employment, in light of Supplemental Military Service of up to 100 days a year and the 14-consecutive-day limit on reserve service.
reply:
I understand that membership of the Reserve Defence Force is a part-time voluntary role that can be carried out alongside a person's normal employment, that is subject to social insurance contributions.
Reservists who undertake up to 21 consecutive days service are considered as Class M for Pay-Related Social Insurance (PRSI) purposes and therefore have no PRSI liability.
For those who undertake more than 21 consecutive days service, they are liable to pay PRSI under Class H. Class H contributions can be used to qualify for most of the social insurance benefits available.
I have no plans to review these rules as matters relating to the terms and conditions for members of the Reserve Defence Force are the responsibility of my colleague the Minister for Defence.
I trust that this clarifies the position for the Deputy.

question: Deputy Paul Lawless asked the Minister for Social Protection the number of young people with type 1 diabetes who have transitioned from domiciliary care allowance to disability allowance in each of the past three years; if his Department has examined the financial impact on families arising from the cessation of DCA at age 16; and if he will outline any proposals under consideration to support families caring for young people with lifelong conditions such as type 1 diabetes during this transition.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 529 and 530 together.
Domiciliary Care Allowance is a non means tested payment to a parent or guardian in respect of a child under 16 who has a severe disability and requires continuous care and attention, substantially more than what is typically required by a child of the same age. Eligibility is not based on the disability or diagnosis such as type 1 diabetes, but on the impact of the disability in terms of the level of care and attention required by the child.

reply:
Domiciliary Care Allowance (DCA) is a monthly payment made in respect of a child aged under 16 years who has a severe disability and requires continual or continuous care and attention substantially in excess of that normally required by a child of the same age. The child must also be likely to require this level of care and attention for at least 12 consecutive months. Such care and attention may relate to areas including mobility, personal care, feeding, communication, behaviour, safety, sleep and sensory needs.
Eligibility for DCA is not determined solely by a child's diagnosis or disability. Rather, entitlement is assessed primarily on the basis of the impact of the child's condition and the extent of the additional care and attention required compared with that required by a child of a similar age who does not have such a disability.
An application for DCA in respect of the child concerned was received by my Department on 10 July 2026. Following consideration of the application, including the supporting medical evidence provided and the opinion of a Departmental Medical Assessor, a Deciding Officer determined that the child did not satisfy the qualifying conditions for DCA. The claim was disallowed on 15 September 2026 and the applicant was advised accordingly.

question: Deputy Michael Cahill asked the Minister for Social Protection to allow for a swap to regular jobseekers benefit from seasonal jobseekers benefit for a person (details supplied).
reply:
Jobseeker’s Pay-Related Benefit (JPRB) is a social insurance-based income support for people who become fully unemployed and who satisfy the qualifying conditions of the scheme.
People who are working on a part-time, casual or seasonal basis, including those who have a recurring pattern of employment and unemployment aligned with the academic year continue to be supported under the Jobseeker’s Benefit scheme.
Teachers and other workers in the education sector who are out of contract during the school holidays continue to claim the PRSI-based Jobseeker’s Benefit scheme or the means-tested Jobseeker’s Allowance.
The person concerned is currently in receipt of the PRSI based Jobseeker’s Benefit as they are categorised as an Education Sector Worker. If the person concerned is fully unemployed and has left the education sector, they can make an application for JPRB. Please note that, although JPRB is a qualifying payment for accessing such supports, it does not guarantee approval of the Back to Work Enterprise Allowance or the Short Term Enterprise Allowance.
I trust this clarifies the matter for the Deputy.

reply:
The State Pension is the bedrock of the pension system in Ireland. It is very effective at ensuring that our pensioners do not experience poverty. This Government is committed to ensuring that this remains the case for current pensioners, those nearing State Pension age and today’s young workers including those who are only starting their careers.
Over €13 billion was allocated to State Pensions in Budget 2027, which is an increase of nearly one billion on Budget 2026. From January next year, the weekly State Pension is increasing by €10. This means the maximum rate of the contributory State Pension (Contributory) will be €309.30 per week.
By January 2027, the State Pension (Contributory) will have increased by €61 per week since 2021. This shows continued commitment to supporting older people and this will remain a priority for Government.
It is recognised that the cost of living for a person living alone is greater than the individualised cost of two or more people living together. That is why a weekly Living Alone Increase is payable to all pensioners living alone who are in receipt of a State Pension from my Department. As part of Budget 2027, the LAI is increasing to €25 per week from next January. This payment has increased by nearly 178% since 2019, when it was just €9 per week.
I was also able to confirm that a Christmas bonus will be paid to almost 1.4 million long-term social welfare recipients in December 2026, including pensioners.

question: Deputy Seán Kyne asked the Minister for Social Protection the specific evidential criteria used by deciding officers when determining which parent has care of a child for the majority of the time in shared-care arrangements (details supplied); the types of documentary evidence considered; and whether both parents are routinely afforded an opportunity to review and respond to information gathered by a social welfare inspector before a determination is made.
reply:
Child Benefit is a monthly payment payable to a qualified person in respect of qualified children. In a shared-care arrangement, if the care is shared on a 50/50 basis, the legislation deems the mother to be the qualified person. Otherwise, legislation states that where the child’s parents reside in separate households, the qualified person is the parent with whom the child resides the majority of the time.
Where conflicting information is received from both parents regarding the child’s care arrangements, a Social Welfare Inspector may be tasked with collecting further relevant information, often through an arranged interview, to assist in the determination of whom the child resides the majority of the time. There is no prescribed methodology used for this assessment; the Deciding Officer must use all relevant information available at that time to determine the outcome.
Customers can request a review or an appeal of the decision.
I hope this clarifies matters for the Deputy.

question: Deputy James O'Connor asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage the grants available for properties with residential units above shops in town centres.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 505 and 519 together.
Tackling vacancy and dereliction is at the heart of the Government's housing plan Delivering Homes, Building Communities.
The Vacant Property Refurbishment Grant, funded under the Croí Cónaithe Towns Fund, has been a key measure in addressing vacancy and dereliction across the country. To the end of Q2 2026, over 18,800 applications have been received, over 14,300 approved, with more than 6,300 grants paid out following completion of works, totalling almost €349 million.
The Grant provides up to €50,000 for the refurbishment of vacant properties for occupation as a principal private residence and for properties which will be made available for rent. A top-up grant of up to €20,000 is available where the property is derelict, bringing the total grant available for a derelict property up to €70,000. In order to qualify for the grant, the property must be vacant for two years or more at the time of application.
Applications for the grant can only be made by individuals and sole traders. The grant is not available to registered companies, developers, undertakings etc. Applicants may transfer a property from company ownership into their individual ownership in order to apply for the grant.

question: Deputy Conor Sheehan asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage to provide an update on the Department's review of a draft final report (details supplied).
reply:
Working to end vacancy and dereliction is a key priority in the Government's housing plan, Delivering Homes, Building Communities. The report referred to, submitted to my Department last month, will be considered in this context.
My Department supports this Governmental priority through measures such as the Vacant Property Refurbishment Grant (including a Vacant Above the Shop Grant and an Expert Advice Grant), the CPO Activation Programme, the Repair and Lease Scheme and funding for Vacant Homes Officers across all 31 local authorities.
These measures and more are working. While there are different data sources and definitions, the overall trend in vacancy levels is downwards.
I firmly believe the commitment Government has made to addressing vacancy and dereliction and the actions under Delivering Homes, Building Communities will continue to play a vital role in delivering homes across the country.

question: Deputy Mattie McGrath asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage the reason retained and full-time firefighters who continue to pass annual medical and fitness assessments are required to retire upon reaching 62 years of age; whether he will review this policy in light of increased life expectancy and ongoing recruitment and retention difficulties within the fire service; whether consideration is being given to permitting firefighters who continue to meet all occupational health and fitness standards to remain in service until at least the State pension age of 66.
reply:
The Courts, Civil Law, Criminal Law and Superannuation (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 2024 amended, among other matters, the law in relation to the age at which certain public servants are required to retire.
Part 11 of the Act provided the then Minister for Public Expenditure National Development Plan Delivery and Reform (M/PENDR), to make orders, enabling line ministers – Justice, Defence, and Housing – to make regulations regarding the retirement age of uniformed services. My predecessor made these regulations in August 2024, with the consent of then M/PENDR, raising the mandatory retirement age to 62.
Given this was addressed two years ago, in consultation with fire service staff representative organisations, there are no plans to revisit this matter presently.
Regarding recruitment to and retention in the fire service, since the Workplace Relations Commission (WRC) agreement of 1 September 2023, 749 recruit firefighters have entered the system. In 2026 alone, 120 new recruits have completed the initial QQI Firefighting skills recruit course as of 21 August.

question: Deputy Mark Wall asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage the number of school wardens employed by the State over each of the past three years; and the number per county, in tabular form.
reply: Under Section 159 of the Local Government Act 2001, each Chief Executive is responsible for the staffing and organisational arrangements necessary for carrying out the functions of the local authority for which he/she is responsible. My Department oversees strategic workforce planning for the local government sector, including the monitoring of local government sector employment levels. To this end, my Department gathers aggregate quarterly data on staff numbers in each local authority on a whole time equivalent basis. However, granular data, in terms of the number of staff assigned to specific work areas in each local authority, is not collected and consequently is not available in my Department. The relevant information would be available from each local authority.

question: Deputy Pádraig O'Sullivan asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage whether his Department collects data on the number of residential units granted planning permission in flood zones A and B under the Planning System and Flood Risk Management Guidelines for Planning Authorities (November 2009); if so, the number for each of the years 2022 to 2025; whether the flood mitigation measures required as conditions of such permissions are recorded centrally; and whether his Department intends to update the 2009 guidelines to reflect current climate projections.
reply:
The Planning System and Flood Risk Management Guidelines for Planning Authorities (2009) were prepared jointly by my Department and the Office of Public Works (OPW) and were issued under section 28 of the Planning and Development Act 2000. They continue in force pursuant to section 27 of the Planning and Development Act 2024.
The Guidelines provide for the incorporation of flood risk identification, assessment and management in the planning process. Planning authorities and An Coimisiún Pleanála are required to have regard to the Guidelines in the performance of their planning functions.
The Guidelines are also cited in National Policy Objective 78 of the Revised National Planning Framework (2025) and in Regional Policy Objectives contained in the three Regional Spatial and Economic Strategies. Local authority development plans are required to be consistent with the policy objectives of the NPF and relevant RSES.
The Flood Risk Management Guidelines advocate for a sequential approach to development that incorporates flood risk assessment involving identification of flood zones (i.e. A, B, and C) and classification of the vulnerability of different types of development to flooding (i.e. Highly Vulnerable, Less Vulnerable, or Water Compatible).

reply:

My Department remains committed to supporting the regeneration, re-use or re-purpose of existing buildings and sites for the delivery of social housing, including for persons with disabilities, noting that the range of social housing capital programmes funded by the Department support local authorities and AHBs to acquire and redevelop vacant and derelict buildings and sites where it is feasible and cost effective to do so. Such projects often present additional complexity and challenge. As a result, costs tend to be beyond what we would see with more straightforward projects. This is accepted and factored into our considerations, with a somewhat higher cost tolerance applied to these projects, where appropriate.
That said, it can never be a case of delivery at any cost when it comes to deploying tax-payer money. We must ensure costs remain reasonable and value-for-money can be achieved, particularly if more cost effective options and mechanisms can deliver the same outcomes.
Any revised funding proposal submitted by Monaghan County Council will be considered in this context.

question: Deputy Louis O'Hara asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage the reason recipients of compensation payments under the cessation of turf cutting compensation scheme are being contacted by his Department in relation to being offered advance payments under the scheme (details supplied).
reply:
The Cessation of Turf Cutting Compensation Scheme (CTCCS) was established following engagement with stakeholders in 2011 for active domestic turf cutters arising from the restrictions on turf cutting on 53 raised bog special areas of conservation (SAC) and was extended in 2014 to include 36 raised bog natural heritage areas (NHA).
This scheme has compensated those impacted by restrictions on turf-cutting on protected sites, and over its 15-year term has helped to ensure the conservation of important peatland sites of unique ecological value.
There are now 414 applicants under the scheme who were originally scheduled to receive their final payments in 2028, 2029, 2030 or 2031.
As there are now a small number of remaining recipients, the proposal to provide advance payments to applicants is intended to simplify the administration of the scheme as it approaches completion, and to streamline the process. My Department has previously used this approach on SACs when the CTCCS was reaching completion on those sites.

question: Deputy Duncan Smith asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage the purpose and intended operation of the Cost Rental Allocation Plan Regulations 2025; when he intends to commence the provisions enabling cost rental landlords to apply additional allocation criteria under section 31A of the Affordable Housing Act 2021, as inserted by the Housing (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 2024; and if these regulations will facilitate the introduction of a defined local priority category within cost rental allocations, similar to the priority arrangements permitted under section 8 of the Affordable Housing Act 2021.
reply:
Section 31A of the Affordable Housing Act 2021 took effect in December 2024, and on foot of this legislative change, I made the Affordable Housing Act 2021 (Cost Rental Allocation Plan) Regulations 2025 in July 2025.
These Regulations allow Cost Rental landlords to submit Allocation Plans for specified Cost Rental homes for my approval. Once approved, these plans govern the allocation of those homes in place of the standard provisions that apply to the Cost Rental sector.
Allocation Plans allow applicants to be prioritised where there is a link to the local area through residence, place of employment, or if a member of the household is attending a local educational institution. The locality will generally be defined as a certain distance around the specified Cost Rental homes. These provisions will support people to live and work in their local area.
I have so far approved two Allocation Plans for Cost Rental developments, in Dublin City and Monaghan town. These Plans were developed and proposed by the Cost Rental landlords which, in these cases, were Tuath Approved Housing Body and Monaghan County Council. As well as being publicised by the Cost Rental landlords, these Plans are published online by my Department at:
https://www.gov.ie/en/department-of-housing-local-government-and-heritage/collections/cost-rental-allocation-plans/

question: Deputy Sorca Clarke asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage whether his Department is aware of the documented condition of Carrigglass Manor, County Longford, including its inclusion on An Taisce’s Buildings at Risk Register; whether his Department has engaged with Longford County Council or the owner regarding the conservation of the building and associated demesne; what heritage grants, conservation supports or technical assistance may be available; and whether he will engage with the relevant parties to explore options for the building’s long-term preservation and reuse.
reply:
The role of my Department with regards to the protection and management of our architectural heritage is set out in the provisions of the Planning and Development Act 2000 (as amended), as are the roles of local authorities and the responsibilities of owners.
Part IV of the Planning and Development Act 2000, as amended, gives primary responsibility to local authorities to identify and protect the architectural heritage of their area by including structures of special interest on the Record of Protected Structures (RPS), and by designating areas of special interest as architectural conservation areas (ACAs). Responsibility for this structure therefore falls to Longford County Council in the first instance.
Under my Department, the National Built Heritage Service (NBHS) provides two main grant schemes to support for the protection of eligible heritage buildings and historic structures. These include capital grants for conservation works as well as financial assistance for owners to obtain conservation advice for their historic structures. The Built Heritage Investment Scheme (BHIS) and the Historic Structures Fund (HSF) are, in the main, administered by the local authorities.
The BHIS provides capital funding of between €2,500 and €50,000 for repair or conservation works to the following types of buildings:
Protected structures
Proposed protected structures
Structures in Architectural Conservation Areas (ACAs)
Vernacular buildings

question: Deputy Pat Buckley asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage to establish whether the development at a location (details supplied) can qualify for the interim remediation scheme or any related remediation scheme; if not, the reason for its exclusion; and if a review or alternative route to support is available to ensure homeowners are not left facing potentially substantial remediation costs without access to appropriate financial assistance.
reply:
Drafting of the Apartment and Duplex Defects Remediation Scheme Bill is at an advanced stage and it is listed for publication this session. The statutory scheme will be in place as soon as possible following its passage through the Dáil.
The Scheme will provide supports for the remediation of relevant fire safety, structural safety and water ingress defects in purpose-built apartment buildings, including duplexes, constructed between 1991 and 2013. It is envisaged that 100% of eligible remediation costs will be funded.
The Interim Remediation Scheme ('Scheme') has been in place since December 2023, to provide an acceptable level of fire safety in buildings pending introduction of the Statutory Scheme and completion of the full remedial works. The Scheme is for the funding of emergency fire safety defect works in apartments and duplexes constructed between 1991 and 2013. The Scheme is administered by the Housing Agency. Applications can be made via the Housing Agency’s website at www.housingagency.ie .
The management and operation of the Scheme, including application processing, eligibility assessments and engagement with applicants, is a matter for the Housing Agency. Details on individual applications are not held by my Department. The Housing Agency is responsible for the administration of the Scheme and the associated operational data.
Elected member queries regarding individual applications may be addressed to the Housing Agency at oireachtas@housingagency.ie.

question: Deputy Peadar Tóibín asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport the organisations, agencies, companies and Departments that participated in or observed the joint Ireland-UK subsea telecommunications resilience exercise known as Eastern Pearl on 30 September 2026.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 489, 490 and 492 together.
The purpose of the joint Ireland-United Kingdom exercise which was held on 30 September was to validate and enhance Ireland and the UK’s co-ordination and response capabilities to a realistic scenario affecting subsea telecoms cables. This exercise, Eastern Pearl, involved a range of participants and observers, including representatives from the Department of Defence, the Department of the Taoiseach, the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade, the Department of Climate, Energy and the Environment, the Department of Finance, the Department of Transport, the National Cyber Security Centre, the Commission for Communications Regulation and the Central Bank of Ireland.
Eastern Pearl focused on how my Department would react to unexpected disruption to subsea telecoms cables, and how we would coordinate with the United Kingdom in the event that the disruption related to our shared critical undersea infrastructure. It was a realistic scenario that took into account the emergency planning structures in place across Government.

question: Deputy Peadar Tóibín asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport the protocols governing information sharing between Ireland and Britain under the joint framework for responding to disruption of subsea telecommunications cables.
reply: Ireland and the United Kingdom have developed a joint framework formalising how both governments will share information, coordinate decisions and respond jointly to disruption affecting subsea telecoms cables connecting both nations. The framework has been designed to allow for the development of operational arrangements over time. As such the framework sets out the principles of cooperation within which flexible arrangements are being developed to address specific scenarios which we wish to jointly tackle.

question: Deputy Edward Timmins asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht the funding available for community spaces and recreational facilities for young people in West Wicklow; and the way in which his Department will engage with young persons to identify and assess the needs.
reply:
My department provides a range of schemes which support the development of community spaces and recreational facilities for young people nationwide, including in West Wicklow.
The Community Centre Investment Fund (CCIF) was introduced to provide high-quality community facilities that are available to all groups in both urban and rural communities. To date, some €112 million has been allocated for the enhancement and refurbishment of existing community centres and the construction of new centres where such a need has been identified.
Since 2022, 25 projects have been approved under CCIF in County Wicklow with associated funding of over €1.3 million, including over €148K allocated under CCIF 22 to fund the replacement of the roof of the Imaal Hall, Dunlavin.

This includes walking trails, cycleways, mountain access routes and facilities at rivers, lakes and beaches. Since 2020 €5.3 million has been allocated to 63 projects in Wicklow.

question: Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport the date on which the general scheme of the digital identity framework regulation Bill will be published; whether it will be referred for pre-legislative scrutiny and to which committee; which provisions of Regulation (EU) 2024/1183 it will give national standing to; if an eIDAS steering group has been established; and the Departments which will participate on same.
reply:
The Digital Identity Framework Regulation Bill is currently under development within my Department, in collaboration with the Department of Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation and the Department of Social Protection. The Bill is on the Government Legislative Programme and work is ongoing to prepare the General Scheme of the Bill having regard to the requirements of Regulation (EU) 2024/1183, which amended Regulation (EU) No. 910/2014 (eIDAS). It is intended that the General Scheme will be submitted to Government for approval in the coming months. This timeline is subject to any policy or legal issues that remain to be teased out.

question: Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport the total amount drawn down in funds to date under the Large Scale Sporting Infrastructure Fund announcement of October 2024; the proportion of the overall funds awarded that this represents; and the reason funds have not been distributed.
reply:
The Large-Scale Sport Infrastructure Fund (LSSIF) was established under the National Sports Policy to provide Exchequer support for larger sports facility projects. The total allocation made under LSSIF under the 2018 round (allocations announced in early 2020) and the 2024 round is €297 million across 68 projects.
Grants totaling €173 million, benefiting 35 individual projects, were allocated under the second round of the LSSIF in 2024. No payments have yet been made under the 2024 round as projects step through the approval gates set out by the Infrastructure Guidelines published by the Department of Department of Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation.
Two projects from the 2024 are currently at construction stage, with the rest at various stages of the approval gates process as mandated by the Infrastructure Guidelines. My Department continues to focus on supporting the delivery of projects approved under the first two LSSIF rounds and regularly engages with the various grantees to help them to progress their projects.

question: Deputy Johnny Mythen asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport the position regarding the basic income for artists; if the full 2000 allocations been filled; to provide a breakdown by region of number of the successful applicants; the numbers pertaining to each category of artists involved, musicians, writers, painters and so on; and if he make a statement on the matter.
reply:
In February this year I announced that the Government had approved a permanent successor to the Basic Income for the Arts pilot scheme and that 2,000 artists would be provided with funding of €325 per week for three years. This is a major milestone for the arts in Ireland and I am particularly pleased that the research my Department conducted provided Government with a clear evidence base upon which to make that decision.
The deadline for application to the Basic Income for the Arts 2026 - 2029 was 5pm on Tuesday 12th May, with over 10,000 applications received by the deadline.
Like the pilot scheme selection is via an anonymous random selection process, this is considered the fairest method where there is not enough funding for all eligible applicants. The eligibility assessment process is ongoing to determine the final 2,000 applicants who will receive the BIA as a result I am not in currently in a position to provide the requested information.
I appreciate that applicants are eager to know the outcome, however, in order to protect the integrity of the scheme the assessment process is by necessity very intensive and time consuming. No two professional arts practices are the same and therefore the proofs supplied vary considerably.
My Department will begin informing successful applicants in batches from this week and that process will continue until all 2,000 places are filled. All successful candidates will receive the full allocation of €325 per week for three years.

question: Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport the measures he will put in place to offset the carbon footprint of an event (details supplied); and the way in which sustainability will be promoted at the event.
reply:
The event in question is expected to be one of the largest sporting events ever held in Ireland. It is intended that a key sustainability initiative for this event will be a major planting scheme of native Irish trees (within Adare and across the county of Limerick) which will significantly offset the carbon footprint generated by the hosting of the event.
My Department is currently engaging with an Irish philanthropist and with the Department of Agriculture in relation to this initiative and both the local authority and the host venue have identified suitable lands for tree planting. It is envisaged that up to 100 acres in total could be planted using a combination of conventional planting methodologies and a pilot planting scheme using the Miyawaki method, a dense planting approach. With a view to making this event a more sustainable one, I intend to allocate up to €500,000 towards this tree planting initiative, once an agreed approach has been reached with all relevant stakeholders.
It is the ambition of government that this event will be the most sustainable edition in its long history, supported by green initiatives, government funding, and corporate partnerships. In this regard, the event organisers are currently preparing a sustainability plan for the event.

question: Deputy Sinéad Gibney asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport whether any consideration was given to expanding the basic income for the arts scheme in Budget 2027.
reply: The introduction of the Basic Income for the Arts scheme on a permanent basis is a major milestone for the arts in Ireland and has been a priority for me as Minister since taking office. Under this scheme, 2,000 artists will be provided with funding of €325 per week for three years. My priority in the context of Budget 2027 was to secure the necessary substantial resources to fund the full year cost of the scheme which was announced earlier this year.

question: Deputy John Connolly asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport if he will consider an extension to the deadline to register with the SPRAOI system.
reply:
The Department's new SPRAOI grant management system went live on Monday 28 September for registrations in advance of the 2026 round of the Community Sport Facilities Fund (CSFF) and clubs and organisations not previously registered with the Department are encouraged to register on SPRAOI.
Approximately 8,000 clubs and organisations that were registered on the previous grant management system have been transferred into SPRAOI.
The 2026 CSFF funding round will open for applications on 19 October 2026 and will remain open until 26 February 2027. Registrations on SPRAOI will be possible until shortly before the latter closing deadline.

question: Deputy Naoise Ó Muirí asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht his views on the results of the Social Inclusion and Community Activation Programme (SICAP) Annual Report 2025.
reply:
The Social Inclusion and Community Activation Programme (SICAP) is Ireland’s primary social inclusion programme, which aims to reduce poverty and promote social inclusion and equality by supporting disadvantaged individuals and communities.
SICAP is a national programme delivered in both rural and urban areas by Local Development Companies (LDCs), providing targeted supports to those experiencing poverty, disadvantage and social exclusion.
I was very happy to launch the SICAP Annual Report 2025 in September with my colleague Minister Chambers. The Report provides a comprehensive overview of programme delivery, detailed analysis of programme beneficiaries, supports provided and progress achieved in 2025.
The 2025 report highlights the impact of the current programme, which has a renewed focus on targeting those who are most disadvantaged in Irish society. To support this objective, resources are targeted locally based on local needs and local knowledge. By the end of 2025, key performance indicators (KPIs) for the programme were exceeded by 22%, indicating strong programme reach among marginalised individuals and communities.
In 2025, 3,097 Local Community Groups and 33,714 individuals were supported by the programme, with significant levels of new participation. question: Deputy Holly Cairns asked the Minister for Education and Youth if her attention has been drawn to shortfalls at a school (details supplied) resulting in graduates being unable to have their diplomas recognised by an organisation; if this issue has been satisfactorily resolved; and if not, if a process has been put in place to allow graduates of this course to gain recognition.
reply:
The Teaching Council is the body with the statutory authority and responsibility for the regulation of the teaching profession in Ireland including the registration of teachers in the State.
The Teaching Council register teachers under the Teaching Council Act 2001-2015 and in line with the Teaching Council Registration Regulations 2025. As set out in the Schedule of the Regulations, the Council registers teachers under five routes of registration: Route 1 - Primary, Route 2 - Post-primary, Route 3 - Further Education, Route 4 - Other and Route 5 - Student Teacher. The qualification requirements for each route are set out in the Schedule of the Regulations. Per the legislation, my department has no role in the registration of individual teachers.
As the independent regulator of the teaching profession in Ireland, the Teaching Council’s role is to protect the public by promoting and regulating professional standards in teaching. This is carried out through the statutory registration of teachers, ensuring a highly qualified teaching profession whose members meet and uphold high standards of professional competence and conduct.
The qualification requirements for Route 2 (post-primary) can be summarised as follows:
Completion of an undergraduate degree in teacher education, accredited by the Teaching Council which satisfies the requirements for at least one curricular subject:
or
Completion of a post-primary programme of teacher education (ITE) accredited by the Teaching Council

question: Deputy Darren O'Rourke asked the Minister for Education and Youth the amount her Department paid in abortive fees related to capital projects in each of the past five years to date in 2026, in tabular form.
reply:
Between 2020 and the end of August 2026, over 1,600 Large Scale, Additional Accommodation and Modular projects were completed across the school system, providing additional and modernised accommodation for school communities nationwide parallel, the Department has prioritised the optimisation of the existing school estate to support the timely delivery of school places and special educational provision.
Repurposing and optimisation of existing accommodation has been a key enabler in expanding special class capacity, with over 85% of new special classes established in the 2025/26 school year facilitated within existing school accommodation. The Department also continues to invest significantly in the upkeep and improvement of the existing school estate. Since 2020, over 4,300 small-scale projects have been delivered to address priority maintenance requirements, improve accessibility, enhance energy efficiency and support the achievement of climate action objectives. This extensive programme reflects the Department's continued investment in expanding capacity, modernising school infrastructure, supporting inclusion and ensuring that school buildings remain safe, sustainable and fit for purpose for students and staff.
It is important to note that a fundamental tenet of the approach outlined in the government’s Infrastructure Guidelines is the incremental approvals process. To prevent lock-in, protect scarce Exchequer resources and ensure maximum value for money, proposals are ap

question: Deputy Darren O'Rourke asked the Minister for Education and Youth the changes to school transport fees planned for 2027-2028 arising from budget 2027.
reply:
The School Transport Scheme is now larger than ever, with 181,000 children and young people using school transport to get to and from school every day.
In line with the Programme for Government commitment to ensure the financial sustainability of the scheme, the school transport fees will be restored to the original 2021 rates for the 2027/28 school year.
This means €100 per primary level pupil, which equates to 55 cent per school day. There is a family cap of €220 per year for primary school.
While at post primary, it will be €350 per pupil, or €2.11 per school day, with an overall family cap of €650.
€3.92 is the maximum daily cost to a family, no matter how many children per family use the service.
Based on an estimated transport cost of between €1,400 and €1,500 per pupil, the State funds the vast majority of the cost of school transport. For primary pupils, where families contribute €100, the State subsidy is over 92%. For post-primary pupils, where families contribute €350, the State subsidy is over 75%.
Importantly, school transport remains free for the 46,000 pupils with specialised transport needs and medical card holders.

question: Deputy Darren O'Rourke asked the Minister for Education and Youth the impact the additional teachers provided for in budget 2027 will have on class sizes and the pupil-teacher ratio.
reply:
Budget 2027 provides for a record investment of €14.435 billion in our school-level education. This is an increase of €5.3 billion (58%) since 2021.
Funding for approximately 1,600 new teachers has been provided for in Budget 2027. This brings the total number of teachers in our school system to circa. 82,000. Of these 1,600 new teachers, 1,353?are special education teachers working in special classes, special schools and mainstream, to further support children with special educational needs. Additional Home School Community Liaison coordinators are being provided for in our DEIS Plus schools. Increased school leadership supports are also being provided, increasing the number of deputy principals in our schools. These additional teachers will improve the primary pupil teacher ratio which, in 2025/26, stood at 12.6:1, comparing favourably with the OECD average of 14:1.
The primary staffing schedule has improved from an average allocation ratio of 26:1 five years ago to 23:1 for the current school year, the lowest ever at primary level. More favourable staffing arrangements apply in DEIS Urban Band 1 and DEIS Plus schools. Average class sizes have fallen from 24.1 to 21.9 pupils in that time.

question: Deputy Johnny Mythen asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht the total capital funding allocated in Budget 2027 for Gaeltacht development, Irish-language infrastructure and Irish-language organisations, compared with 2026; the reasons for any reduction in capital expenditure; and the way in which his Department intends to ensure that investment is sufficient to support the sustainability of Gaeltacht communities and the objectives of the Government's Irish-language policy.
reply:
My Department has received a total allocation of €628 million in Budget 2027, including a capital allocation of €273 million. A breakdown by sub-head of the allocation will be published in the Revised Estimates Volume (REV) before the end of the year.
My Department has very ambitious plans for capital developments to support Gaeltacht communities, the Irish language community and island communities alike. These developments are funded under Programme C of the Department’s budget – The Gaeltacht, the Irish Language and the Islands. It is worth noting that the capital budget for Programme C increased from €30 million in 2025 to almost €55 million in 2026. A significant portion of that increase related to three key infrastructure projects:
• Inis Oírr Pier,
• The redevelopment of the Conradh na Gaeilge headquarters on Harcourt Street as a language and cultural hub, and
• The redevelopment of the Coláiste Lurgan site in Indreabhán as an Education and Youth Hub for the Connemara Gaeltacht.
A commitment regarding these projects was made in the National Development Plan, and I am pleased to have secured the necessary funding to bring them to completion. It is my considered view that the capital allocation secured by my Department will be sufficient to meet the requirements of the Gaeltacht, the Irish Language, and the Islands programme in 2027 and beyond.

reply:

question: Deputy Emer Currie asked the Minister for Education and Youth to provide a detailed breakdown of the €687 million allocated to the school transport scheme in budget 2027; the amount allocated to existing school transport services, service expansion, fleet investment; the new initiatives or pilots to help operators meet increased bus contractor running costs.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 465 and 466 together.
The expenditure on the scheme has more than doubled over a six-year period from over €200 million in 2018 to €537 million in 2025 (included a cost-of-living advancement for 2025 of €58m). The allocation in 2026 is estimated at €641m.
The increasing cost of the scheme over the past number of years is due to increased pupil numbers, COVID cleaning and increased distance measures, cost of living measures, provision of transport for children from Ukraine and increased contractor rates for operators under contract to Bus Éireann for the provision of services.
Transport for pupils with special educational needs continues to represent the largest area of expenditure within the scheme, accounting for just under 60% of the total spend in 2025, while serving approximately 13% of the total overall pupils on transport.
School Transport budget will increase to €687 million in 2027. This equates to over €3.7 million on school transport alone per school day. Extra funding will provide for the additional demand for specialised transport and increased transport running costs.

question: D'fhiafraigh Deputy Shónagh Ní Raghallaigh den Aire Oideachais agus Óige cad iad a pleananna chun an liúntais do mhúineadh trí Ghaeilge a thabhairt ar ais do mhúinteoirí meánscoile chun aitheantas a thabhairt do na dúshláin a bhaineann leis an obair sin.
reply:
Foráiltear le Comhaontú na Seirbhíse Poiblí 2024 – 2026 go bhféadfaidh fostóirí agus ceardchumainn/comhlachais athruithe breise ar rátaí pá agus/nó ar choinníollacha fostaíochta a idirbheartú suas go 1% ar a mhéad den chostas bunphá, lena n-áirítear liúntais de chineál pá, a bhaineann leis an ngrád, leis an ngrúpa nó leis an gcatagóir fostaí ar leith nó leis an aonad margála ar leith. Féadfaidh go n-áireofar leis sin tograí a bhfuil athruithe ar struchtúir, ar chleachtais oibre nó ar choinníollacha eile seirbhíse i gceist leo.
Roghnaigh Cumann Múinteoirí Éireann (INTO) an Ciste Margála Áitiúla a úsáid chun roinnt éileamh a shocrú de réir théarmaí an Chiste agus laistigh den teorainn cistiúcháin Státchiste atá i bhfeidhm. Leagtar amach i gCiorclán 54/2026 an toradh a comhaontaíodh le INTO i ndáil le roinnt éileamh atá á socrú don earnáil bunscoile.
Ós rud é go bhfuil roinnt ceardchumann ag déanamh ionadaíocht do mhúinteoirí, is faoi gach eagraíocht ionadaíoch atá sé idirbheartú thar ceann a comhaltaí féin.
Ní fhéadfar leasuithe breise ar Théarmaí agus Coinníollacha múinteoirí, lena n-áirítear pá agus liúntais, a bhaint amach ach amháin trí idirchaidreamh agus comhaontuithe cómhargála idir an Rialtas agus na ceardchumainn Seirbhíse Poiblí. Ní fhéadfar athruithe den sórt sin a dhéanamh ach amháin faoi na próisis sin, agus ba ghá don Roinn, don Roinn Caiteachais Phoiblí agus Athchóirithe agus do na ceardchumainn iomchuí mionbhreithniú a dhéanamh ar aon tograí dá leithéid.

question: Deputy Barry Heneghan asked the Minister for Education and Youth whether her Department has the authority to direct a primary school Board of Management to review or remove a designated liaison person (details supplied) where concerns have been formally substantiated; and the procedures in place to address such matters while ensuring fair procedures for all involved.
reply:
Tusla is the agency of the State with the statutory responsibility to assess all reports of child welfare and protection concerns and as such my Department does not have powers to investigate child protection concerns.
My Department has no role in employer/employee matters. The Education Act, 1998 sets out the legal framework for schools and their patrons. The act provides that the board of management is the body charged with the direct governance of a school on behalf of the patron and is the employer of school staff. In the case of schools established or maintained by an ETB the ETB in the employer of school staff. Any actions in relation to the school employee, in relation to employment matters, are exclusively a matter for the employer.
My Department's Child Protection Procedures for Schools set out the reporting requirements for school personnel, including the Designated Liaison Person. Where any member of school personnel fails to report a matter to Tusla where advised by Tusla to do so, or otherwise fails to comply with the procedures, this is to be reported to and dealt with separately by the employer in accordance with the relevant disciplinary procedures. The procedures are available on the gov.ie website: www.gov.ie/en/department-of-education/policy-information/child-protection-procedures-in-schools/.

question: Deputy Naoise Ó Muirí asked the Minister for Education and Youth the mandatory items that must be on every agenda of a Board of Management meeting for primary schools in Ireland as required by law and under the School Governance Manual 2023-2027.
reply:
The Education Act, 1998 sets out the legal framework for schools and their patrons. The act provides that the board of management is the body charged with the direct governance of a school on behalf of the patron.
The agreed procedures for the appointment of boards of management of primary schools and the rules under which these boards operate are set out in the department’s publication ‘Governance Manual for Primary Schools 2023-2027’.
Boards of management are required to comply with the provisions of the Education Act 1998, and all other relevant legislation and department circulars relating to the operation of boards.
A primary school board of management must hold a minimum of one meeting per school term and not less than five meetings in any school year.
The agenda for every board of management meeting should include the following, the minutes of the previous board meeting, matters arising from the minutes, correspondence, treasurer’s report, principal’s report, principal’s child protection oversight report, health and safety, and the agreed report. The agreed report is the decision reached at the end of each board meeting on the information to be disclosed to the school community and on the manner in which this information is to be communicated. The agreed report shall not include details of any issues which must remain confidential to board members.

UBU Your Place Your Space (UBU) is the largest youth services scheme funded by the department. question: Deputy John Lahart asked the Minister for Education and Youth the educational campaigns that are being implemented in schools to inform teenagers about the harms of recreational nitrous oxide use.
reply:

reply:

reply:

Bus Éireann manages the procurement tender process and contract management arrangements to include services provided by contractors. The STG is also payable on an interim basis while a family is waiting for a service to commence or in the case of any disruptions to their service.

reply:
The School Transport Scheme is a significant operation managed by Bus Éireann on behalf of the Department of Education and Youth.

The school transport scheme has expanded significantly over the past six years. In that time, the numbers of children and young people using the service have grown from under 120,000 pupils in 2018 to over 180,000 pupils in 2025, which equates to an increase of close to 50%.

question: Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Education and Youth to provide an update on the work of the AI in Schools External Advisory Taskforce; to list its membership; the number of meetings to date; and to indicate when it expects to report.
reply:
The AI in Education External Advisory Taskforce has been established to support the Department in developing a coherent national approach to the safe, responsible and effective use of AI across the school system at primary and post-primary level. Two AI Taskforce meetings have been held to date, 14 May and 21 September. The list of members will be published on gov.ie in the coming weeks.
Meetings are attended by teacher unions, management bodies and other stakeholders such as teachers, parents and students representative groups and research bodies and other relevant agencies. Its membership ensures a broad range of perspectives and expertise are brought to the discussion.
To support its work the Taskforce has established two working groups. The first is focused on assessment, including both summative and State-certified assessment, with the second Working Group focusing on teaching, learning and formative assessment.
The current phase of the taskforce is expected to operate over an initial 18-24 month period with outputs delivered on a rolling basis. Quarterly reports will be published on gov.ie in due course. These publications will provide greater transparency regarding the Taskforce's work programme and priorities.
The taskforce will help ensure that the department’s response is informed by practical experience, ongoing work across the education system, and emerging national and international developments.

question: Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Education and Youth the number of children in Ireland who are home-educated; and the measures in place to assess the quality of that education.
reply:
The Constitution of Ireland acknowledges the family as the primary and natural educator of the child and sets out the rights and duties of the State in the matter of education. The Constitution makes explicit that the State does not oblige parents to send their children to any particular type of school. Parents are free to provide education in their homes, in private schools, or in schools recognised or established by the State.
Tusla’s Alternative Education Assessment and Registration Service (AEARS) is under the remit of my department. AEARS is responsible for the regulation of provision for education in places other than recognised schools, including children who are home schooled or who are enrolled in a non-recognised independent school.
Parents who wish to educate their child in a place other than a recognised school are required to make an application to AEARS to have their child included on the Section 14 Statutory Register. AEARS will then carry out an assessment of the educational provision to determine if the child is eligible to be placed on the register. Assessments are carried out by an authorised person in line with the ‘Guidelines on the Assessment of Education in Places other than a recognised School’, issued by my department and which is available to view at the following link: Guidelines on the Assessment of Education in Places Other Than Recognised Schools (File Format PDF 1.3MB). www.tusla.ie/uploads/content/Guidelines_on_Assessment_of_Education.pdf

Cuireadh maoiniú comhaontaithe de €20 milliún ar fáil d'Fhoras na Gaeilge agus do Ghníomhaireacht na hUltaise i mbliana. Ardaíodh maoiniú Chlár na Leabhar Gaeilge go €2 milliún in 2026, an leibhéal is airde riamh. question: Deputy Cian O'Callaghan asked the Minister for Education and Youth if the design team has submitted the tender report in relation to the new school building project for a school (details supplied) to her Department; and if construction is still due to commence in Q4 2026.
reply:
The large-scale capital project for the school referred to by the Deputy is for the provision of a new 600 pupil school building including all associated ancillary accommodation, with the inclusion of additional classrooms for children with Special Educational Needs configured within the existing layout.
The invitation to tender issued in late Q4 2025. The Design Team recently submitted the tender report to my Department and a detailed review is currently ongoing. It is envisaged that construction will commence in the coming months.
I would like to advise the Deputy, since 2020, the Department of Education has provided over €2 billion in capital funding for Dublin schools. Over this period, a total of 300 schools have been upgraded through provision of either a new school building, extension, modular accommodation or climate pathfinder projects. 20 school projects to go to tender or construction in 2026 and 2027 were included in the NDP Implementation Plan including Gaelcholaiste Reachrann.
There are currently 47 large-scale, extension, modular or climate pathfinder projects in Dublin under construction.
There are also 53 projects underway through the Climate Action Summer Works Scheme.
In addition, since 2020 a total of 541 special classes have been sanctioned in Dublin, of which 140 were sanctioned for September 2026.

question: Deputy Naoise Ó Muirí asked the Minister for Education and Youth the way in which the proposed common enrolment system will operate where linked schools have different patrons; whether parents will have an opportunity to vote on a specific proposal; the way in which the transition will accommodate pupils already enrolled; and the options that will be available to schools that do not join the initial group by 31 October 2026.
reply:
As a first step towards implementing a commitment in the Programme for Government for a nationwide common applications system, my department launched the Apply to School pilot scheme in October 2025 and this scheme was expanded for the 2026/2027 admissions cycle. The expanded pilot covers 22 post-primary schools in ten school planning areas and represents a significant step towards improving the school admissions system. It provided families with a single online application process for first year places and introduced synchronised and streamlined timelines for schools to manage admissions and issue offers. Participating schools retain full control of their own individual admissions policies and associated legal responsibilities under the Education (Admission to Schools) Act 2018. Under the pilot arrangements, parents submit one application through a central portal and may apply to multiple participating schools, with applications processed in accordance with the admissions criteria of each school concerned. Where schools in the same area have different patrons, the operation of the Apply to School system will not alter the patronage or ethos of any participating school. Each school will continue to apply its own admissions policy, approved by its board of management and patron, and any arrangements between schools will be implemented in a manner that respects the governance and patronage structures of the schools concerned.

question: Deputy Donnchadh Ó Laoghaire asked the Minister for Education and Youth the process for applying for a new Gaelcholáiste; to outline such a process; and if applications for new Gaelcholáistí will be considered other than if it this is the outcome of the public voting process which has been in place in various locations in recent years.
reply:
New schools are established in areas of demographic growth, as the resources available for school infrastructure have to be prioritised to ensure that every child has a school place.
Demographic requirements in an area determine the need or otherwise for establishing new schools and while there are no Irish medium or English medium schools planned currently (other than new special schools) this position is kept under constant review by my department.
The Programme for Government 2025, Securing Ireland’s Future, includes a commitment to establish Gaelscoileanna and Gaelcholáistí where there is demand and support parents choosing Irish-medium education for their children.
In November 2025 my department published a ‘Policy for Irish-medium Education outside of the Gaeltacht’ and established a Taskforce on Models of Provision for Irish-medium Education.
The role of the taskforce is to provide a platform for collaboration between my department and key stakeholders to develop a pathway to increase provision of Irish-medium education nationally. The taskforce's work is expected to be completed by the end of the year. It will make recommendations to my department on areas such as the criteria for Irish-medium education provision, how to support schools transitioning to Irish-medium and mechanisms to facilitate expansion of provision.

question: Deputy Catherine Callaghan asked the Minister for Education and Youth if she will review the criteria governing the recognition of overseas teaching service for incremental credit and pensionable service purposes; the number of years of overseas teaching service that may currently be recognised; and whether consideration is being given to recognising all teaching service completed abroad where it can be verified.
reply:
The criteria for the award of incremental credit are set out in the Department of Education & Youth’s Circulars 10/2001, for primary teachers, and 29/2007 and 29/2010, for post-primary teachers. These circulars provide for the award of incremental credit in respect of prior teaching service, including overseas teaching service, both within and outside the EU.
There is no separate scheme in the Department to recognise overseas teaching service for pensionable service purposes alone and under the Department Pension schemes, service given in countries outside Ireland does not constitute pensionable service.
Teaching service given outside the Republic of Ireland by a qualified teacher in a school or college must be deemed to be equivalent to teaching service given in a primary or post primary school in the Republic of Ireland. This includes teaching service given in a public or private primary or secondary school abroad.
Criteria such as whether the school is subject to state funding, which can be of relevance when examining claims relating to private teaching schools, and the length of time the school has been in existence, must be satisfied for service at that school to be recognised for incremental credit. Where a school satisfies the criteria set out in the circulars to have service at that school recognised for incremental credit, an award of incremental credit can be made.

question: Deputy Ciarán Ahern asked the Minister for Education and Youth further to Parliamentary Question No. 65501/26, for an update on the implementation of the SC L1\L2 programmes for special schools.
reply:

Since its initial introduction in 2024, there has been strong uptake of the programmes across both mainstream and special schools. Following a programme of work, SCL1/SCL2 LPs have now been integrated on the Post-Primary Online Database (PPOD) and the Primary Online Database (POD), allowing students in mainstream and special schools to have their programmes registered for the 2026/27 school year as part of the annual October Returns process. Separately, students register with the State Examinations Commission (SEC) via their assessment portal to obtain certification.

reply:
The Primary School Survey gathered the views of both parents of children currently attending primary school and parents of children yet to enter the school system. It explored preferences regarding school patronage/ethos, co-educational or single-sex provision and language (education through Irish or English).
In early June, my department issued primary schools with their school-specific results and explanatory information.
Boards of Management have been asked to share their survey results and explanatory information with their school communities, to review their survey results and to engage with their communities (including parents), and the local community (including parents with children not yet in school), before deciding on their next steps.

It is important that schools are given the time and space to reflect carefully on their results and to engage fully with parents and the wider school communities before making decisions.
My department has published all school-level reports, survey results, guidance documents and supporting materials on www.gov.ie/PrimarySchoolSurvey.
