question: Deputy Peter 'Chap' Cleere asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht for an update on CCIF applications for Carlow and Kilkenny.
reply:
The Community Centre Investment Fund (CCIF) was introduced to provide high quality, accessible, community spaces that are available to all groups in all communities in both rural and urban areas. Some €112 million has been allocated since 2022 for the enhancement and refurbishment of existing community centres and the construction of new centres where such a need has been identified.
Since 2022, I am pleased to confirm that 15 projects in County Carlow have been approved for funding under the CCIF representing a total investment of over €5.1 million. This includes an allocation of over €4.1 million under CCIF 2023 towards the development of a new community centre at Tullow Road, Carlow. County Kilkenny has received over €2.5 million for 35 projects under the CCIF.
I was delighted to launch the latest round of funding under CCIF 2026 on the 26th of March for enhancement and refurbishment of existing community centres. The fund will be delivered across two categories with maximum funding levels of €25,000 and €100,000 respectively. The closing date for the CCIF 2026 has now passed.
Applications are currently being assessed, including those received in respect of centres in Carlow and Kilkenny. I look forward to announcing the successful projects under category 1, which provides funding of up to €25,000, in the coming weeks. The successful projects under category 2, which provides funding of up to €100,000, will be announced before year-end.

question: Deputy Mark Wall asked the Minister for Transport the eligibility criteria for a disabled person parking permit for a person (details supplied) in county Kildare.
reply:

Disabled parking permits are available to an individual with permanent conditions or disabilities that severely restrict their ability to walk. Eligibility is thus defined on the basis of mobility impairment rather than on the basis of a specific medical condition. An individual who is certified as blind may also qualify for a permit.
The websites of the issuing bodies, the Irish Wheelchair Association and the Disabled Drivers Association of Ireland, which issue disabled parking permits on behalf of the State, have details of the application process and eligibility criteria (www.iwa.ie and www.ddai.ie).
The Deputy may also wish to note that neither I, nor my Department, can intervene in any individual Disabled Parking Scheme application or appeals process.

question: Deputy Paul Lawless asked the Minister for Transport if he has considered amending the Railway Safety Bill 2026 to strengthen the preventative role of the Railway Accident Investigation Unit (RAIU); if the reporting, recording and investigation of near miss incidents, including incidents at level crossings, will form part of the statutory framework under the Bill; if the RAIU will have powers to make recommendations on emerging safety risks before serious accidents occur; and if annual reports on railway safety recommendations and trends will be submitted to the Minister and laid before the Houses of the Oireachtas.
reply:
The statutory powers of the Railway Accident Investigation Unit (RAIU) for reporting and investigations are set out under the European Union (Railway Safety) (Reporting and Investigation of Serious Accidents, Accidents and incidents) Regulations 2020 (SI No. 430 of 2020). These Regulations of 2020 which are based on the EU Railway Safety Directive apply to the Iarnród Éireann network. The equivalent provisions will be provided for other railways in Part 2 of the Railway Safety Bill 2026.
The legislation already has a preventative goal. The Regulations of 2020 state that the objective of an investigation is to improve, where possible, railway safety and the prevention of accidents. The purpose of RAIU investigations is to make safety recommendations in order to prevent accidents and incidents in the future and improve railway safety. During an investigation, if the RAIU make some early findings on safety issues that require immediate attention, the RAIU will issue a Safety Advice Notice (SAN) or an Urgent Safety Advice Notice) (USAN) outlining the associated safety recommendations.
I can confirm that the reporting of accidents and incidents at present to the RAIU includes near miss incidents and incidents at level crossings. In that regard, the Regulations of 2020 state that in addition to the investigation of a serious accident, the RAIU may also investigate those accidents and incidents which under slightly different conditions might have led to serious accidents.

question: Deputy Conor Sheehan asked the Minister for Transport if he will introduce legislation to extend existing requirements for priority seating on public transport to explicitly include elderly and vulnerable passengers; and if he will consider creating a legal requirement for passengers who do not require priority seating to vacate such seats when they are needed by an elderly, disabled or vulnerable passenger.
reply:
As Minister for Transport, I have responsibility for policy and overall funding in relation to public transport; however, I am not involved in the day-to-day operations of public transport.
Under the Dublin Transport Authority Act 2008 and the Public Transport Regulation Act 2009, the Oireachtas assigned statutory responsibility to the National Transport Authority (NTA) for promoting the development of an integrated, accessible public transport network and public transport infrastructure. A sustainable fare policy helps support these objectives.

question: Deputy Matt Carthy asked the Minister for Transport if his Department has been informed of the specific economic baseline and calculations used by the National Transport Authority to justify fare increases of up to 30% on regional bus routes servicing Cavan and Monaghan.
reply:
As Minister for Transport, I have responsibility for policy and overall funding in relation to public transport; however, I am not involved in the day-to-day operations of public transport.

reply:

question: Deputy Ruairí Ó Murchú asked the Minister for Transport if the disabled parking permit scheme provides any mechanism for exceptional cases to be assessed according to the child's actual functional ability, mobility requirements and safety risks, including the need for a special-needs buggy, rather than physical walking ability alone.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 300 and 302 together.
As Minister of State for International & Road Transport, Logistics, Rail & Ports, I wish to advise that neither I, nor officials within my Department, can intervene in any individual application or appeals process for a disabled parking permit.
The day to day responsibility of the Disabled Parking Scheme, including issuance and refusal of permits, falls under the remit of the issuing bodies, the Irish Wheelchair Association and the Disabled Driver's Association of Ireland.
Disabled parking permits are available to an individual with permanent conditions or disabilities that severely restrict their ability to walk. Eligibility is therefore defined on the basis of mobility impairment, rather than a specific medical condition. An individual who is certified as blind may also qualify for a permit.
The Deputy may wish to note, however, that my Department is currently undertaking a review of the Disabled Parking Scheme, including the eligibility criteria.

reply:

The Programme currently provides funding towards the employment of over 1,723 FTE positions and 354 manager posts.
In line with a Programme for Government commitment, nine organisations that had been waitlisted following the 2023 Open call, joined the CSP Programme in April this year. Additionally, an Open Call for organisations join the Programme was launched on 30 March. The closing date for receipt of preliminary applications was 08 May and the review process is ongoing. Further details of the Open Call can be found on Pobal's web-site www.pobal.ie, under the community services programme link.

question: Deputy Louis O'Hara asked the Minister for Transport if he supports the transfer of responsibility for alcohol and psychoactive substance testing from State authorities to individual airlines or other private entities under the Irish Aviation Authority's proposed Employer-Led Drug and Alcohol Testing Framework; and whether his Department will make a submission to the IAA's ongoing consultation regarding the proposed framework.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 292, 293, 294, 295, 323 and 324 together.
On 29 September the Irish Aviation Authority (IAA) commenced a public consultation on the future regulatory approach to drug and alcohol testing in the Irish aviation sector. The consultation seeks the views of aviation stakeholders, employees, industry representative bodies, public authorities and members of the public on the most appropriate means of introducing a comprehensive framework to manage the safety risks associated with impairment arising from alcohol and other psychoactive substances. The deadline for submissions is 31 October 2026.
While the IAA is seeking views on a proposed Employer-Led Testing Framework with IAA Oversight, no decision has been taken yet on state policy in this area. The purpose of the consultation is to gather evidence, perspectives and views of all relevant stakeholders to inform future policy development.
My department will be engaging with the IAA following completion of the consultation process.

question: Deputy Emer Currie asked the Minister for Transport whether the ICE2EV scrappage scheme has been fully exhausted; and whether his Department plans to launch a second round of funding.
reply:
The ICE2EV Pilot Scrappage Scheme was designed and launched as a capped pilot initiative. The full €17 million allocated from the Climate Action Fund has been committed, comprising €10 million for the scrappage grant and €7 million for the associated EV purchase grant.
The strong level of interest in the scheme is encouraging and highlights increasing consumer engagement with the transition to electric vehicles. This positive response aligns with Ireland’s broader Climate Action objectives, including the ambition to increase the uptake of electric vehicles to 30% of the national car fleet by 2030.
The policy purpose of the capped initiative was to test the effectiveness of scrappage as a tool to stimulate EV uptake among those who may not otherwise transition in the near term, with the ultimate goal of delivering additional emissions reductions necessary for our climate targets.
While the pilot scheme has closed for new applications, validation and payment processing remains ongoing. A post-completion evaluation of the scheme will be undertaken to assess its effectiveness, emissions impact and overall value for money, and to inform future policy decisions in this area. The evaluation will consider a range of factors, including the drawdown of available funding, participation across different geographic areas, the characteristics of vehicles being scrapped, and the types of electric vehicles supported under the scheme.

question: Deputy Frankie Feighan asked the Minister for Transport if there is an appeal process under the fuel support scheme.
reply:
My Department received over 4,400 applications, in respect of approximately 31,500 vehicles, for the Road Transporters Support Scheme (RTSS). As of 06 October 2026, all applications received during the original application window have been assessed and approved for payment.
The appeals portal is being finalised and will open shortly. Officials in my Department are engaging with trade representative bodies to ensure the portal and information documents relating to appeals are clear and comprehensive to support applicants in completing the appeals process. Information will be published on the Department’s website once this feedback has been received.
Once the appeals portal launches, all applicants will be contacted directly by the Department with instructions on how to submit an appeal. Please note, only applicants who have a valid RTSS application ID will be permitted to submit an appeal.
Queries that are not answered by the website material can be sent to rtss.appeals@transport.gov.ie.

As Minister for Defence, I am fully committed to increasing and strengthening recruitment and supporting retention in the Permanent Defence Force.

Last year saw a growth in the overall strength of nearly 200, with a total of 790 inductions achieved- the highest in twenty years - while the number of personnel who discharged was at its lowest level in more than five years. I am determined to build on this and have set a target of more than 800 inductions for 2026.
Interest in a career in the Defence Forces remains robust with a total of 16,510 applications received in 2025 and over 14,000 applications received to the end of August of this year. The challenge now for the Defence Forces is to convert this high level of applications to inductions. A draft Strategic Workforce Plan prepared by the Defence Forces is being considered by a Civilian/ Military Working Group. As the Deputy will be aware, the aim of this process is to provide a pathway to the achievement of an overall strength of 11,500, inclusive of civilian personnel, commensurate with Level of Ambition 2.

question: Deputy Erin McGreehan asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht if his Department will consider providing Gaeltacht funding to Omeath.
reply:
My Department provides funding to Foras na Gaeilge to fund and deliver various programmes to help develop and promote the Irish Language across the island.
My Department is not aware of any Irish language groups in Omeath. However, I am advised that two groups located in the wider area currently receive funding under Foras na Gaeilge's Irish Language Networks Development Scheme, namely Gaeláras Mhic Ardghail in Newry and Craobh Pheadair Ó Dhubhda in Dundalk.
The scheme aims to promote, protect and engrain the Irish language in particular areas with an emphasis on the development and implementation of comprehensive language plans.
Other supports are available to groups outside of the Irish Language Networks Development Scheme. Glór na nGael, nominated by Foras na Gaeilge as its lead organisation for community development, offer many practical supports in enabling and empowering local community groups to encourage the use of the Irish language.
I would recommend to the Deputy that any groups interested in promoting the use of the language in Omeath contact Foras na Gaeilge, in the first instance, to discuss the various supports available both from the agency itself and from its lead organisations.

question: Deputy Seán Ó Fearghaíl asked the Minister for Defence further to Parliamentary Question No. 69615/26, if she will address the specific matters raised in further correspondence (details supplied), including the rationale for the withdrawal of a proposed property sale, apparent inconsistencies in correspondence issued by her Department regarding occupancy of the property, and the application of current disposal policies in light of previous sales of similar properties in the same estate.
reply:
With regard to the specific property referred to by the Deputy, officials in my Department have, over the years since the original offer was made, engaged with the parties subject to the original sale offer and the current occupant on this matter. In that regard, the Department advised on the 24 October 2005, that if the then Contract for Sale was not received within a specified period of time then the Department will be obliged to consider the offer withdrawn. In addition, the Department also went on to advise that it would also be obliged to apply current market values should there be any future offers of sale. Subsequently, I am advised that, the current occupant was advised on the 13 March 2022 that the Department could not proceed with the sale. This remains the case.
The Deputy may wish to note that it has been a long-standing policy that long term residential married quarters are no longer provided. There is no immediate plan to reverse this long-standing policy, which was introduced in the early 1990’s and was implemented on a gradual basis in recognition of the sensitivities involved for military personnel and their families then occupying Department properties. In this particular instance, the offer of a licence to the occupant to regularise their occupation of the premises remains open.

question: Deputy Michael Cahill asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment if he has evaluated the concerns of the liquid fuel sector that the proposed obligation rates in the forthcoming renewable heat obligation scheme are too low to provide any additional renewable fuel and will consequently have no impact in reducing carbon emissions.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 265 and 267 together.
Decisions made in relation to the Renewable Heat Obligation (RHO) scheme design, including initial obligation rates and level increases as the scheme progresses, were based on a full examination of the scale of obligation required to meet Ireland’s renewable heat targets, and encompassed extensive engagement with key industry stakeholders, including the liquid fuel sector. The scheme is considered appropriate and effective to support market participation and achievement of our energy and climate targets.
Priority drafting of the RHO Bill is now at an advanced stage and nearing completion. Once finalised, I intend to submit the final scheme to Government seeking approval to publish.

question: Deputy Pearse Doherty asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment when the NORA levy will be reapplied to relevant fuels.
reply: The NORA levy is a charge of 2 cent per litre applied to most petroleum products sold in the market, for the purpose of funding the operations of NORA and the Climate Action Fund (CAF). The levy has been reduced to a nominal amount, with the reduction coming into effect from 1 April 2026. In Budget 2027, it was announced that the levy reduction, which was due to expire on 31 October 2026, will be extended until 31 December 2026.

question: Deputy Sinéad Gibney asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment when his Department will bring forward legislation to fully implement the Energy Efficiency Directive.
reply:
The Recast Energy Efficiency Directive (EU) 2023/1791 (EED) is a wide-ranging European directive that seeks to enhance energy efficiency across all EU Member States and forms a key component of the EU's Fit for 55 package. The Recast EED replaces the 2012 EED, as amended in 2018, which Ireland has previously fully transposed and implemented.
The new Directive entered into force in October 2023, with a transposition deadline of 11 October 2025, and contains a range of new measures aimed at further improving energy efficiency across society. The Government has an ambitious programme in place to enhance energy efficiency across all sectors as a key part of its efforts to decarbonise the economy and achieve national climate targets. The Government remains fully committed to implementing the EED and recognises the significant benefits arising from increased energy efficiency, including reduced energy costs for households, businesses and the Exchequer; enhanced competitiveness and job creation; reduced fossil fuel consumption and greenhouse gas emissions; reduced energy poverty; improved health outcomes; and greater energy security.
The Government has invested significantly in promoting energy efficiency across all sectors. This includes residential energy efficiency grant schemes administered by the Sustainable Energy Authority of Ireland (SEAI), investment in transport measures that support greater use of public transport, active travel and electric vehicles, and a range of initi

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment further to Parliamentary Questions Nos. 70575/26 and 70577/26, whether the feasibility study on transitioning household waste collection to a franchise model, described in those replies as recently completed, will be published; the date of publication; whether the National Waste Collection Permit Office study on incentivised charging structures will also be published.
reply:
It is the Department’s intention to publish the report titled, Study to Explore the Feasibility of Transitioning Ireland’s Waste Collection Market from its Current Side-by-Side Licensing System to a Franchise Tendering System, in the coming weeks. The report is intended to inform policy development and stakeholder engagement. It should be noted that its findings and recommendations remain under consideration by the Department and publication should not be interpreted as indicating any final decision on future policy direction.
The National Waste Collection Permit Office Report on Incentivised Charging will also be published in due course. Together, these reports represent important evidence-based inputs to the development of the next iteration of the Waste Action Plan for a Circular Economy. Their development reflects the Department’s commitment to ensuring that future waste policy is informed by robust analysis, stakeholder perspectives, and international best practice.

question: Deputy John McGuinness asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment the policy changes if any he is considering to provide greater transparency and oversight relative to the deposit return scheme for plastic bottles and cans; if the unclaimed cash can be estimated with a view to the State taking control of part of the sum for use in the public interest.
reply:
Re-turn is a producer-led and owned, not-for-profit company established by beverage producers to meet their obligations under the Separate Collection (Deposit Return Scheme) Regulations 2024 (S.I. No. 33 of 2024).
The framework for governance and oversight of the scheme is set out in the Regulations, the Ministerial Approval issued under those Regulations, and the Code of Corporate Governance for Compliance Schemes. While Re-turn is responsible for the operational and financial management of the scheme, officials from the Department closely monitor its performance through monthly meetings with Re-turn, supported by quarterly engagements on strategic priorities and governance matters. I have also met with representatives of the company on a number of occasions.
Under Regulation 4(3) of the Separate Collection (Deposit Return Scheme) Regulations 2024 (S.I. No. 33 of 2024), unredeemed deposits are one of the sources of funding for operation of the scheme. These funds generated must be re-invested in its operation. I am, however, considering whether future unredeemed deposits could be used to fund other activities that promote and support Ireland’s transition to a Circular Economy.

question: Deputy Ivana Bacik asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment the projected increased cost of the Dublin District Heating Project; if his Department has met with Dublin City Council since the cost projected was revised upwards; if the council has sought further grants from his Department to fund the development; and his views on the need for sustainable district heating options in urban centres, and Dublin in particular.
reply:
National policy in Ireland has recognised the contribution that district heating can make to Ireland’s energy and climate goals and is underpinned by the findings of the Sustainable Energy of Ireland's National Heat Study 2022. Therefore, the deployment of district heating at scale, particularly in densely populated areas with ready-made heat sources located nearby, is a key Government objective under the Climate Action Plan and a component in meeting the built environment sectoral emissions ceiling.
Although district heating, as a sector in Ireland, is in its infancy, progress is being made. The first efficient district heating project operational in Ireland is in Tallaght. It was developed by South Dublin County Council and supported through the Climate Action Fund. Phase 2 of this project is now being planned and evaluated by South Dublin County Council.
In addition, I have allocated up to €5 million to support the pre-construction costs of nine efficient district heating projects across Ireland, including in Dublin. This pilot funding is designed to help projects move from concept to delivery by supporting the critical development work required before construction can begin.
Through the Climate Action Fund €50 million has been allocated to the Dublin District Heating Project. question: Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment to outline the legal and site specific measures that were taken in respect of Dunsink dump-landfill following the decision of the European Court of Justice in Case C-494/01; which of these measures are still being implemented; and can he confirm whether the European Commission continues to monitor the measures Ireland is taking with respect to the Dunsink dump-landfill.
reply:
Following a comprehensive multi-year structural transformation of Ireland’s waste regulatory framework, the European Commission formally closed Case C-494/01 in 2015. The Department is not aware of any ongoing monitoring by the European Commission in relation to this specific site.
The Department provided financial support to Fingal County Council under the Landfill Remediation Grant Scheme for remediation works at the Dunsink site which was directed towards the remediation of the former landfill and associated measures to address environmental risks and facilitate the site's long-term management.

Details of the site's environmental management are available through the EPA's Licence and Enforcement Access Portal (LEAP) (https://leap.epa.ie/confirm?returnUrl=https%3A%2F%2Fleap.epa.ie%2F%3F_gl%3D1*1dtauhg*_ga*Njk2ODk5ODk0LjE3Njc2OTY4ODk.*_ga_TPK2CK9KEX*czE3OTIwNDkxMjkkbzMwJGcwJHQxNzkyMDQ5MTI5JGo2MCRsMCRoMA..) under Waste Licence W0127-01. The EPA continues to oversee compliance with the conditions of the waste licence throughout the aftercare phase.

question: Deputy Emer Currie asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade the position on Armenia's accession to EU membership.
reply:
Ireland strongly supports EU enlargement which is a key priority of our EU Presidency.
Ireland and Armenia have strong bilateral relations and we work together in the Council of Europe and the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe. The Taoiseach visited Yerevan in May to attend the eighth European Political Community Summit.
Ireland welcomes the strengthening relationship between the EU and Armenia. On 8 October, alongside President of the European Parliament, Roberta Metsola, Minister of State for European Affairs and Defence, Thomas Byrne T.D. signed a measure on the temporary trade-liberalisation of Armenian products to the EU market. These measures were passed to support the Armenian economy following the imposition of severe economic trade restrictions by Russia, limiting imports of Armenian goods.
On 5 May, the first EU-Armenia summit was held. The Joint Declaration that was issued following that meeting acknowledges the European aspirations of the Armenian people, rooted in the adoption of the Law on Launching Armenia’s EU accession process of March 2025. The Joint Declaration also states that any decision on EU membership is a matter for the people of Armenia to decide freely and democratically.

question: Deputy Emer Currie asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade the latest position on Georgia's accession to EU membership.
reply:
Georgia applied for EU membership in 2022 and obtained candidate status in 2023. However, in 2024 its EU progress was de facto halted following the Georgian government's adoption of the ‘Law on Transparency of Foreign Influence’ and Prime Minister Kobakhidze's statement that Georgia would not pursue the opening of EU accession negotiations until 2028.
In the European Commission's 2025 Enlargement Report – which is an annual analysis prepared by the European Commission of the reform progress made by candidate countries over the year – the Commission stated that it considered Georgia to be “a candidate country in name only”. The European Commission's 2026 Enlargement Reports will be published in the coming weeks and will provide an updated analysis of Georgia's EU accession process.
As underlined by the European Council in December 2024, the EU stands ready to support the Georgian people’s European aspirations and the country’s path towards accession, should the authorities reverse their current course of action. Ireland has consistently supported and aligned with the EU’s position on Georgia.

question: Deputy Emer Currie asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade her Department's views on Montenegro's capacity to translate all EU law accurately; and the implications this has on potential accession in 2028.
reply:
EU Enlargement is a key priority of Ireland’s EU Presidency. Ireland aims to advance the candidacies of all candidate countries, provided that necessary reforms are implemented and once conditions allow. In particular, we aim to advance the candidacies of the four front-runners of Montenegro, Albania, Ukraine and Moldova. Montenegro applied for EU membership in December 2008 and was granted EU candidate status in December 2010. Montenegro's EU accession negotiations commenced in June 2012.
Montenegro has expressed a desire to close all negotiating chapters during Ireland’s EU Presidency. Montenegro have also expressed a desire to join the EU in 2028. Ireland's EU Presidency will seek to facilitate Montenegro's ambition of closing all remaining chapters before the end of the year. However, this will depend on the implementation by Montenegro of necessary reforms and the agreement of all EU Member States to allow the closure of remaining chapters. Officials in my Department are working closely with Montenegro, the European Commission and all other Member States to seek to complete the technical negotiations with Montenegro by the end of the year.
Over the first half of our Presidency, Ireland has already secured significant progress on Montenegro’s candidacy. question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade to set out the precise wording of Ireland's position on Taiwan as agreed when diplomatic relations with the People's Republic of China were established in 1979; if Ireland's One China Policy differs from the One China Principle as stated by the People's Republic of China; if Ireland has ever formally accepted that Taiwan is part of the People's Republic of China.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 247, 248, 250, 251, 252, 253 and 254 together.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade the Irish mission that provides consular services to Irish citizens resident in or visiting Taiwan; her Department's estimate of the number of Irish citizens residing there; the number of consular cases handled in each of the years 2022 to 2026; her views whether these arrangements are adequate without an Irish presence in Taipei.
reply:
Ireland, along with our EU partners, adheres to the One China Policy. This means that we do not have diplomatic relations with Taiwan and that we recognise the People's Republic of China as the sole legal government of China.
This does not preclude the provision of consular assistance to Irish citizens in Taiwan. Should an Irish citizen in Taiwan require consular assistance, they will be assisted by my Department’s Consular Assistance Unit, based at our headquarters in Dublin. Moreover, in line with Council Directive 2015/637 of the European Union, Irish citizens may receive consular protection from other Member States of the European Union in locations where Ireland is not represented.
I can confirm that there were no consular cases recorded involving Irish citizens in Taiwan between 2022 and 2024. A small number of citizens sought consular assistance in 2025 and to date in 2026; in line with best practice on small data sets we will not publish the number to protect the confidentiality of those persons.
There are currently 56 Irish citizens registered with my Department’s Citizen Registration service as being in Taiwan. It is important to note that registration is not mandatory and that we offer this as a service to citizens who wish notify us voluntarily of their location. Data from Citizen Registration is not, therefore, a definitive measure of numbers of citizens in a given location.

question: Deputy Emer Currie asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade the number of EU member states Ireland maintains a resident diplomatic presence, including embassies, consulates-general and other diplomatic missions.
reply: Ireland has a resident bilateral Embassy in all 26 EU Member States. Since the launch of Global Ireland, Ireland has also opened Consulates-General in Frankfurt and Munich in Germany, Lyon in France, Milan in Italy and, most recently, in Malaga in Spain.

question: Deputy Emer Currie asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade the number of EU membership candidate states Ireland maintains a resident diplomatic presence, including embassies, consulates-general and other diplomatic missions.
reply: Ireland maintains resident Embassies in five candidate countries for EU membership. Ireland has had a resident Embassy in Turkiye since 1999. Since Global Ireland, Ireland has opened resident Embassies in Bosnia and Herzegovina, Moldova, Serbia and Ukraine. Ireland is accredited on a non-resident basis to the other four EU candidate countries for EU Membership.

question: Deputy Emer Currie asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade her Department's position on an issue (details supplied).
reply:
I am aware of the reports concerning a laboratory incident in Irkutsk, Russia, in which one person is reported to have died following a suspected infection with plague.
The European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) is closely monitoring the situation and in a statement on 6 October said that based on the limited information currently available, there are no reports of secondary cases and no evidence of sustained human-to-human transmission that would cause further spread of the disease.
It added that the ECDC continues to monitor the event and is proactively in contact with WHO Europe to discuss the situation.
We will continue to monitor developments very closely from Ireland’s perspective and will also liaise with our EU colleagues in the matter.

question: Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade if officials from her Department participate in UNWRA Advisory Commission proceedings; and if so if she will publish all statements made to the commission on Ireland's behalf by these officials since 2023.
reply:
Ireland is a member of UNRWA’s Advisory Commission, along with 28 other member states. We are represented at the twice-yearly meetings of the Advisory Commission by officials from the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade. The Advisory Commission engages with UNRWA on the fulfilment of its mandate, its commitment to neutrality and integrity, and the crucial processes of reform, including those outlined in the Colonna Report.
Support for Palestinian refugees is a longstanding priority for Ireland and annual funding to UNRWA is a key component of our continued support for the people of Palestine. In 2026, I announced €42 million in support of the people of Palestine, with €20 million to be provided as core funding for UNRWA. This support was provided to UNRWA by June 2026, bringing funding to UNRWA since January 2023 to €78 million.
For more than 75 years, UNRWA has delivered essential services to Palestinian refugees, now reaching 5.9 million across Palestine, Jordan, Syria and Lebanon, including 1.5 million of the 2 million people in Gaza, and more than 900,000 in the West Bank.
In Gaza, UNRWA and its 10,000 staff have been the backbone of humanitarian action. On a fortnightly basis UNRWA continues to provide around 73,000 health consultations from 35; supply drinkable water for 800,000 people; remove around 4,000 tonnes of solid waste; and teach approximately 47,000 children in temporary learning spaces. This work continues despite the loss of more than 390 of its employee

question: Deputy Michael Healy-Rae asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade if an application for foreign births will be expedited (details supplied).
reply:
Foreign Birth Registration (FBR) applications are currently being processed within the turnaround time of 12 months from receipt of supporting documents. Applications which require further supporting documents will take longer to process.
Foreign Birth Registration, by its nature, is a detailed and complex process, often involving official documentation relating to three generations and issued by several jurisdictions. Such documents take considerable time to validate.
The FBR service operates a transparent general policy of processing applications in order of receipt except in cases of exceptional urgency, such as expectant parents, or stateless persons. With regard to the specific FBR application about which the Deputy has enquired, the applicant does not meet these criteria.
The supporting documents and application form for this application were received in the FBR office on 7 April 2026. Therefore this application is within the normal turnaround time. The Passport Service will contact the applicant directly if any further documents are required.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade the amount of the €1,500,000 paid to an organisation (details supplied) between 2020 and 2024 that was State membership fees; the amount that was project funding, with a breakdown of the projects funded.
reply:
The Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade, through the Embassy in Tanzania, has provided funding to the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) to implement a programme on the blue economy. As part of the overall bilateral development programme in Tanzania, this programme was aimed at building the capacity of people and nature in coastal regions in the country to adapt to the challenges of climate change. It focused on conservation of the marine ecosystem by establishing mangrove restoration zones, strengthening governance networks and undertaking research. It also worked on expanding sustainable livelihood options for coastal communities, particularly in relation to access to finance.
Over the period 2021-2024, we provided a total of €2,600,000 to IUCN to implement this programme. The funds were fully used to implement programme activities and none of the funds were used for State membership fees.

reply:

Last year I approved over €14m million for 238 projects under the programme, the highest amount since the scheme was reintroduced 10 years ago. This funding included almost €536,000 for 10 projects in Co Longford.
The CLAR programme provides funding for community facilities and amenities such as community centres, sport facilities, playgrounds, walking tracks, sensory gardens and much more. The programme invests in community vehicles used by our first responders, by meals on wheels groups and by organisations transporting people with mobility issues to vital services. In December 2021, the Reconciliation Fund awarded Cambridge University €300,000 for a three-year lectureship in Modern Irish History. Dr Niamh Gallagher took up the position in January 2022.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade the purpose of the €1,600,000 paid to an organisation (details supplied) between 2020 and 2024; the objectives and measured outcomes of this funding; whether an independent evaluation was carried out; and whether funding to the organisation continues.
reply:
Funding is provided to Straight Talk Foundation as part of Ireland's bilateral development programme in Uganda, to deliver the Irish Bursary Scheme in the Karamoja region of the country. The objective of this funding partnership is to promote equitable access to quality education for marginalised learners across Karamoja. The bursaries provide school fees, school material and expenses for the most disadvantaged, vulnerable and bright girls and boys at both post-primary and tertiary level institutions. Between 2020 and 2024, Ireland provided a total of €4.2 million in funding to Straight Talk Foundation.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade the purpose of the €700,000 paid to an organisation (details supplied) between 2020 and 2024; the countries and projects funded; the outcomes achieved; the reason Irish public funds were directed to a charity linked to a UK public broadcaster.
reply:
As part of Ireland's bilateral development programme in Tanzania, funding has been provided through the Embassy in Dar Es Salaam to the organisation BBC Media Action to deliver a project to strengthen civic participation by facilitating a dialogue in on policy issues including gender equality and climate change.
A total of €1,550,000 was provided to BBC Media Action over the period 2021-2024 -


Radio continues to be the most widely accessed form of media and information in Tanzania, particularly in rural areas. BBC Media Action is an international charity which was chosen as a partner due to its established presence in the Tanzanian media space, its reach across the country, and its capacity to carry out specialised work, including training and building the capacity of radio stations.
In the period 2021-2024 BBC Media Action delivered significant results in line with Ireland’s priorities. As a result of the funding, up to 40 radio stations across Tanzania broadcast programmes covering governance, gender equality, climate change, and public accountability issues. These reached up to 5 million listeners nationwide. The programme successfully served as a platform for citizens to engage in public dialogue with decision-makers. It also led to increased women’s participation in public decision-making and promoted the inclusion of persons with disabilities and other marginalised groups.

question: Deputy Cian O'Callaghan asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade the reason the revised allocation for Vote 27 – International Cooperation for 2026, announced yesterday as €855 million, falls €11.4 million below the Budget 2026 allocation of €866.4 million as published in the Revised Estimates for Public Services; if she will clarify how this reduction aligns with the Government’s stated commitments on Ireland’s international development programme (details supplied).
reply:
The Programme for Government commits to annual increases in Official Development Assistance (ODA), working towards the UN target of providing 0.7% of Gross National Income.
I am very pleased that Budget 2027 has provided an increased allocation of €855 million for the international development programme, Irish Aid, managed by the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade. This is a €14 million increase on the Budget 2026 allocation.
The allocation announced in Budget 2026 was €841 million. A once-off provision of €25 million was subsequently agreed to support Ukraine's energy infrastructure in response to damage being caused by Russia's aggression, which is counted as ODA. This was then included in the 2026 Revised Estimate of €866.4 million.
At a time of great uncertainty internationally, when some other countries are cutting their international development budgets, the increase in the allocation for 2027 is an important demonstration of the Government's commitment to Ireland's work on long term development and life-saving humanitarian assistance, with a focus on reaching the furthest behind first. The Government has increased the allocation for the Irish Aid programme every year since 2020.

reply:

question: Deputy Colm Burke asked the Minister for Health to confirm that medical card income thresholds will be increased at least in line with recent social protection increases announced in Budget 2027, in order that those receiving these payments will not be disadvantaged in applying for a medical card.
reply:
Medical Card provision is primarily based on financial assessment. In accordance with the Health Act 1970 (as amended), eligibility for a medical card is determined by the HSE, which assesses each application on a qualifying financial threshold. This is the amount of money that an individual can earn a week and still qualify for a card.
However, every effort is made by the HSE, within the framework of the legislation, to support applicants in applying for a medical card - in particular, to take full account of difficult circumstances in the case of applicants who may be in excess of the income guidelines. In such circumstances, the HSE may exercise discretion and grant a medical card
In addition, where a person's sole household income is derived from a social protection payment, they will be awarded a medical card.
I can assure the Deputy that, in order to ensure the medical card system is responsive and sensitive to people's needs, my Department keeps medical card issues under review and any proposals are considered in the context of any potential broader implications for Government policy, the annual budgetary estimates process and legislative requirements arising.

reply:

Access to convalescent care, rehabilitation or follow-up therapies is determined under the eligibility arrangements and service criteria applying to the particular service, following an assessment of the person’s clinical and care needs.

question: Deputy John Lahart asked the Minister for Health the plans for the establishment of the new dual diagnosis team in Dublin south-west, based in Tallaght; the proposed staffing and timeline for the team to become operational; the pathway by which patients will access the service.
reply:
Dual diagnosis means a person experiences both a substance abuse problem and a mental health issue such as depression or an anxiety disorder.
Options must address both issues, and as such the HSE have developed a Model of Care which recommends the development of 12 Adult Specialist Dual Diagnosis Teams nationally, 4 Adolescent Hub Teams, and a National Dual Diagnosis Rehabilitation Centre. To date funding of over €5 million has resulted in the roll out of the Dual Diagnosis teams. Five Dual Diagnosis teams are being recruited into and developed at present – adult teams in Limerick and Cork commenced Treatment services in 2024, and two team including Waterford are in recruitment. 2 Adolescent hub teams in Dublin have also been developed, supported by funding from HSE Social Inclusion. Funding was also provided for a Dual Diagnosis Day Programme in Dublin.
Under Budget 2027, funding has been allocated for an additional Dual Diagnosis team for Dublin South West .
Discussions will now take place by my Department with the HSE on the detailed allocation of resources and implementation of specific service initiatives through the HSE National Service Plan 2027, including mental health services.

question: Deputy Naoise Ó Muirí asked the Minister for Health the details of the delivery of a new shingles vaccine for adults aged 65+.
reply:
Ireland’s immunisation programme is informed by the advice of the National Immunisation Advisory Committee (NIAC). NIAC considers the prevalence of the relevant disease in Ireland as well as international best practice in relation to immunisation when developing its advice.
The current NIAC guidelines state that the shingles vaccine may be considered for those aged 65 years and older, due to the greater burden and severity of disease in this age group and in those aged 18 years and older at increased risk of shingles.
I can confirm that I have approved the introduction of a Shingles Vaccination Programme, in line with NIAC advice, to be implemented on a phased basis over 5 years, for immuno-compromised groups and persons aged 65 and over.
The programme is expected to commence in 2027, initially offering shingles vaccines to immuno-compromised groups. This will be followed by the 80 years and older cohort. The programme will conclude with the 65–69-year-old cohort.
It is expected that the vaccine will be administered in the main by GPs and Pharmacists. Further programme details will become available in due course.

question: Deputy David Cullinane asked the Minister for Health the projected supplementary estimate which will be needed for the health budget in 2026; the steps she has taken to achieve savings targets; the extent to which savings targets were missed; the reasons.
reply:
The HSE is under significant financial pressure in 2026. At the end of September, it had a cash deficit of €781 million. The final position will depend on expenditure over the remainder of the year and the impact of the savings measures and expenditure controls now being implemented.
My Department is working closely with the HSE and the Department of Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation to keep any additional funding requirement as low as possible.
There are genuine pressures on the health service, including population growth and ageing, rising demand for services, inflation and higher medicines costs. However, those factors do not fully explain the financial position.

question: Deputy Seán Ó Fearghaíl asked the Minister for Health the expanded older persons and community supports, including additional home-support hours, dementia services and community-based care that will be provided under Budget 2027.
reply:
Budget 2027 strengthens the supports that enable older people to live independently, safely and with dignity in their own homes and communities. Budget 2027 is the largest ever for older persons services, with over €3.4 billion allocated to maintain and further enhance services in 2027.
Budget 2027 provides an additional €123m in funding, for an increase of 1.8 million hours of home support, increasing the target from 26.7 million hours in 2026 to a record 28.5 million hours in 2027. This investment will give more people access to care at home, support families and carers, and help address waiting lists. A minimum of 24% of all new home-support hours will support people with dementia.
An additional €1.4 million will expand community-based dementia services. This funding will provide eight new or expanded dementia day-care services, additional day care at home, five young-onset dementia activity clubs and five additional dementia advisers. These services will help people with dementia remain active, connected and supported at home for longer.
Budget 2027 will also invest €2m in Meals on Wheels, €2m in a new Community Supports Grant Scheme, and €627,500 for five new Care and Repair locations. Funding is also being provided for five additional Healthy Age Friendly Homes coordinators. Together, these measures will improve access to practical, locally delivered services and strengthen support for older people, families and carers across the country.

question: Deputy Shay Brennan asked the Minister for Health the way in which Budget 2027 will support a new programme to move clinically appropriate cancer monitoring and follow-up from acute hospitals into community settings.
reply:
The total health allocation for 2027 is €29.1 billion, comprising €27.39 billion in current expenditure and €1.72 billion in capital investment. This represents increases of €1.6 billion in current expenditure and €160 million in capital investment compared with 2026.
Following the announcement of the annual budget allocation for my Department, I will shortly be issuing a Letter of Determination to the HSE which will outline the my specific policy priorities, service expectations and strategic funding allocations for the upcoming year. This will be the basis on which the HSE will draw up its National Service Plan (NSP) for 2027.
Prior to the issue of the Letter of Determination, I have asked all six HSE Regions, working with the HSE's National Cancer Control Programme, to develop a practical programme for 2027 to expand cancer care in community settings under appropriate clinical oversight and where safe to do so. This will ensure that treatment, monitoring and follow-up care can be delivered closer to home while protecting acute hospital capacity for patients who require specialist treatment.
The development of these services will be an important step towards cancer treatment that is more accessible, integrated and organised around patients’ lives.

question: Deputy Cormac Devlin asked the Minister for Health her plans for a major expansion of community crisis mental health supports.
reply:
A key priority for myself as Minister in Budget 2027 is a further €10 million investment in crisis supports and suicide prevention, building on the significant expansion of crisis services over recent years. We are continuing to shift services into communities and investing in earlier intervention to make sure more people can access appropriate, timely support, as close to home as possible.
Budget 2027 includes funding to establish the Suicide Crisis Assessment Nurse (SCAN) service in every county. SCAN teams provide rapid assessment, safety planning and follow-up support for people who present to their GP experiencing suicidal ideation or severe emotional distress. Twelve additional teams will be established across eight counties, ensuring national coverage of the programme for the first time.
The Budget will also fund two new Crisis Resolution Teams in Wexford and North Tipperary. These multidisciplinary teams provide intensive short-term support in people's homes and communities as an alternative to admission to hospital, helping individuals experiencing acute mental health difficulties to remain connected to family, work and local supports while receiving treatment.
Six new Solace Crisis Cafés will be established in Wexford, North Tipperary, Carlow, Louth, Dublin Mid-West and Dublin North Inner City. Operated in partnership with the community and voluntary sector, Solace Cafés offer out-of-hours support for people experiencing emotional distress, providing a safe space to

question: Deputy David Cullinane asked the Minister for Health the extent to which Budget 2027 provides for the full cost of maintaining existing levels of services and accounts for demographic and inflationary pressures; the funding available for genuinely additional services and capacity; the measures she will take to prevent further recruitment and service restrictions arising from budgetary overruns.
reply:
Budget 2027 provides an additional €1.6 billion in current funding for health services. Of this increase, €155 million additional pay funding is being provided for workforce growth, equivalent to approximately 2.2% growth in staffing over the course of 2027, while €94 million additional non-pay funding is being allocated to support new and expanded services, reform initiatives and other Ministerial priorities.
The remaining €1.351 billion is being provided primarily to address underlying demand and cost pressures, including demographic growth, inflation, the full-year cost of existing commitments, pay-related costs and other underlying costs associated with maintaining existing service provision.
The impact of demographic growth and inflation varies across different service areas. For example, demographic pressures are generally higher in areas such as Older Persons Services, reflecting population growth and ageing. Similarly, inflationary pressures vary across care groups depending on the particular mix of non-pay expenditure. Funding requirements are therefore assessed on a service-by-service basis, taking account of the particular cost and demand drivers affecting each care group, rather than applying a single demographic or inflation assumption across the health service.
The HSE will be required to manage service delivery and expenditure within the funding levels approved by Government for 2027. Expenditure and performance will continue to be monitored through the establi

question: Deputy Pádraig Rice asked the Minister for Health to provide an update on the development of a new model of care for trans healthcare; the current timeline being worked towards; and the allocation provided for trans healthcare in Budget 2027.
reply:
The Deputy will be aware that, as outlined in the Programme for Government 2025, the Government are committed to ensuring a transgender healthcare service that is based on clinical evidence, respect, inclusiveness and compassion.
The provision of proper, appropriate and integrated gender healthcare services is something that I want to ensure is in place for those who are questioning their gender identity or are experiencing gender incongruence or dysphoria.
A new clinical programme for gender healthcare has been initiated by the HSE and an updated clinical model for gender healthcare services is being developed. The Clinical lead is in place and recruitment is ongoing for the rest of the multidisciplinary team.
The expected completion date for the HSE Model for Gender Healthcare is 2026. This work will also inform an implementation plan for its delivery.
Funding for the HSE is approved by the Oireachtas as part of the annual Budget and Estimates process. My department will thoroughly review all funding requests, whether for new or ongoing initiatives. I am committed to supporting measures that bring meaningful and positive improvements to gender healthcare.

question: Deputy Sean Fleming asked the Minister for Health the way in which Budget 2027 will result in improved access to oral health and orthodontic services for children,.
reply:
The Government recognises that significant challenges continue to affect the delivery of public dental services, including orthodontics. Addressing this will require a multifaceted approach requiring a mix of shorter-term interventions and meaningful strategic reform. My Department and the HSE are finalising a focused two-year Oral Health Action Plan to deliver real improvements on the ground in the near term.
The Plan will responds to sustained service pressures and long waiting lists—particularly for children and for people with additional needs, including people with disabilities.
It will focus on a small number of clear priorities:
• Tackling waiting lists in the School Dental Programme and Orthodontics.
• Improvement and expansion of the access programme to oral healthcare for people who have additional needs including those with disabilities.
• Commencing a reform of the Dental Treatment Services Scheme.
• Supporting recruitment, education and training.
• Supporting innovation and new ways of delivering care.
Over the next two years, the aim is to stabilise services, reduce waiting times, and make access measurably better for patients—while laying the groundwork for longer-term reform. The Plan will be overseen by a dedicated governance group, with progress monitored closely and aligned to wider Department and HSE priorities.

question: Deputy Peter Roche asked the Minister for Health the measures her Department is taking, in conjunction with the HSE, to ensure the timely restoration of healthcare services and the rescheduling of appointments affected by the planned industrial action.
reply:
The Department of Health, in conjunction with the HSE, continues to engage routinely with relevant stakeholders in relation to the management of industrial relations issues and the maintenance of healthcare services.
The HSE is responsible for the operational management and delivery of health services, including the implementation of appropriate arrangements to mitigate the impact of planned industrial action on service provision.
Engagement with relevant parties takes place through established channels, with a view to minimising disruption to services and facilitating the restoration of normal service delivery as soon as practicable. The HSE also works to ensure that patients affected by service disruptions are appropriately prioritised for the rescheduling of appointments.

question: Deputy George Lawlor asked the Minister for Health the services available to pregnant women who require psychiatric or mental health care during their pregnancy; and if these services are available at all maternity hospitals.
reply:
The Specialist Perinatal Mental Health Services (SPMHS) is now available in all 19 maternity hospitals nationwide, providing support to pregnant women and women with a baby up to one year old, with an existing or new mental health problem. Funding of €5 million annually has established 6 consultant led multidisciplinary teams across major maternity hospitals (Coombe, NMH, Rotunda, Galway, Cork, Limerick), and 13 spoke sites staffed by perinatal mental health midwife posts. There are now over 75 funded posts in SPMHS nationally.
Under Budget 2026, I secured an additional €640,000 to recruit two additional consultant psychiatrists for the Programme’s busiest sites, the Rotunda and Holles Street, to meet growing demand for the service.
The HSE are progressing a review of the Model of Care for SPMHS, with a refreshed model to be published in due course. The key objective of this refresh is the provision of equivalent service to the major hospital sites as for the other 13 spoke sites, and this will be the focus of this second phase of the Model of Care.
A key priority under this Model of Care is to develop a Perinatal Mother and Baby Unit (PMBU). Work is ongoing by the HSE to progress the development of an PMBU for Ireland, an inpatient mental health service with relevant maternity support to allow women to stay with their babies during their mental health treatment.

question: D'fhiafraigh Deputy John Connolly den Aire Forbartha Tuaithe agus Pobail, agus Gaeltachta cad é líon na n-iarratas ar ceadaíodh maoiniú dóibh faoin gClár Tacaíochtaí Pobail agus Teanga in 2024 agus in 2025; cén dáta a fuair an Roinn gach iarratas ar éirigh leis; agus an bhfuil na leithdháiltí uile tarraingthe anuas go hiomlán ag na grúpaí pobail ar bronnadh maoiniú orthu.
reply:
Is é príomhaidhm An Clár Tacaíochtaí Pobail agus Teanga ná tacú le pobail sna ceantair Ghaeltachta, áiseanna pobail a fhorbairt chomh maith le tacaíocht bhreise a sholáthar don phróiseas pleanála teanga agus d’fheidhmiú iomlán na Straitéise 20 Bliain don Ghaeilge 2010-2030. Tá bileog eolais faoin gclár agus na coinníollacha éagsúla a bhaineann leis ar fáil ar shuíomh mo Roinne.
Tá ciste caipitil an chláir oscailte ó cheann ceann na bliana agus tagann iarratais chun cinn de réir mar a éiríonn le coistí Gaeltachta iarratais a ullmhú. Maidir leis na blianta 2024 agus 2025, ceadaíodh 22 deontas sa bhliain 2024 ar luach iomlán níos mó ná €1.7 milliún. Sa bhliain 2025, ceadaíodh 14 deontas ar luach níos mó ná €2 mhilliún san iomlán.
Éilítear íocaíochtaí de réir mar a chuirtear tograí i gcrích bunaithe ar chaiteachas deimhnithe. Braitheann minicíocht na n-éileamh seo ar an togra féin agus baineann cuid de na deontais le céim deartha nó le tréimhse ullmhaithe le haghaidh togra caipitil níos mó. Mar gheall air seo, is minic nach n-íocfar an deontas iomlán go dtí go bhfuil an togra iomlán curtha i gcrích.

question: Deputy Peter 'Chap' Cleere asked the Minister for Health her plans on the rollout of a national shingles vaccination programme.
reply:
Ireland’s immunisation programme is informed by the advice of the National Immunisation Advisory Committee (NIAC). NIAC considers the prevalence of the relevant disease in Ireland as well as international best practice in relation to immunisation when developing its advice.
The current NIAC guidelines state that the shingles vaccine may be considered for those aged 65 years and older, due to the greater burden and severity of disease in this age group and in those aged 18 years and older at increased risk of shingles.
I can confirm that I have approved the introduction of a Shingles Vaccination Programme, in line with NIAC advice, to be implemented on a phased basis over 5 years, for immunocompromised groups and persons aged 65 and over.
The programme is expected to commence in 2027, initially offering shingles vaccines to immunocompromised groups. This will be followed by the 80 years and older cohort. The programme will conclude with the 65–69-year-old cohort.
It is expected that the vaccine will be administered in the main by GPs and Pharmacists. Further programme details will become available in due course.

question: Deputy Mark Wall asked the Minister for Health if her Department is committed to the introduction of a no wait card for people who have invisible and chronic illnesses that require urgent access to a toilet, given her commitment to the introduction of such a card.
reply:
The Department of Health recognises the challenges faced by people living with chronic and invisible medical conditions, including those which may require urgent access to toilet facilities. For many individuals, timely access to appropriate facilities is essential to maintaining dignity, independence and full participation in daily life.
‘No Wait Cards’ are currently issued by a number of patient advocacy organisations to support individuals in requesting access to toilet facilities where required. While these cards do not have a statutory basis, they can assist in raising awareness and facilitating understanding of the needs of people living with certain medical conditions.
The provision and management of toilet facilities in private establishments is generally a matter for the premises concerned, subject to relevant equality and health and safety legislation.
The Department of Health remains supportive of initiatives that promote accessibility, inclusion and reasonable accommodation for people with health conditions. The Department will continue to engage with relevant stakeholders and organisations in relation to measures that may support improved awareness and access for those affected.

question: Deputy Paul McAuliffe asked the Minister for Health if there are unexpected delays for hip operations at the National Orthopaedic Hospital, Cappagh as result of changes to funding allocated to the hospital.
reply:
The National Orthopaedic Hospital Cappagh (NOHC) is a voluntary hospital which provides services to the HSE under Section 38 of the Health Act (2004). NOHC is under the remit of the HSE Dublin and North East Region (DNE).
There has been significant investment in NOHC in recent years, its budget increasing from €41m in 2020 to €63m for 2026 and staff levels increasing from 427 in 2020 to 552 in June 2026.
Core activity in the hospital is based on this funding allocation received from the HSE. In previous years the National Treatment Purchase Fund (NTPF) funded specifically identified and appropriate insourced waiting list activity in the Hospital.
There has been engagement between the HSE, DNE, NTPF and NOHC on funding procedures for 2026, having regard to the NTPF’s budgetary position and its obligations to deliver additional activity equitably across the system. The HSE has advised that NOHC is prioritising clinically time-sensitive inpatient surgical cases to ensure patients with the greatest clinical need continue to receive timely treatment.
This sustained progress in reducing the number of patients and improving the length of time they are waiting on both OPD and IPDC waiting lists in NOHC and the commitment to prioritising care for the patients who need it most, will help us move towards our goal of ensuring timely access to care for everyone, where and when they need it.

question: Deputy Louis O'Hara asked the Minister for Health to provide an update on the employment of newly graduated nurses and midwives.
reply:
Attracting and retaining newly qualified nurses and midwives is vital to building a sustainable workforce and supporting high-quality patient care. The HSE knows how many graduates are expected each year and must plan their recruitment accordingly, matching graduates to the services and locations where the need is greatest.
The latest information provided by the HSE indicates that 974 graduate nurses and midwives have confirmed start dates. Approximately 834 are expected to commence before the end of this year, with a further 140 due to start from January onwards.
To be clear, there is no recruitment embargo in the HSE and recruitment has not been stopped. Strengthened controls are in place in four Regions to ensure that appointments are affordable, properly prioritised and directed to areas of greatest patient and service need. Essential posts can continue to be filled.
A key part of this approach must be to prioritise direct recruitment where vacancies are being filled through sustained agency usage. This can provide permanent opportunities for graduates, build a more stable workforce, support safe care and deliver better value within the overall pay bill.
This is against a backdrop of sustained investment in the health workforce. HSE staffing has increased by almost 30,000 WTE since December 2020, including an increase of 9,924 nursing and midwifery WTE.

question: Deputy Peter Roche asked the Minister for Health the measures being taken to address waiting lists for home support services in Galway; and the way in which the shortage of home care workers, particularly in rural areas, is being addressed.
reply:
The Government is committed to supporting older people to live independently in their own homes for as long as possible and has significantly increased investment in home support services in recent years. Home support funding has more than doubled since 2018. Budget 2027 provides for an increase of approximately 1.8 million hours for the delivery of home support.
In Galway and Roscommon, the HSE has held 12 rounds of interviews since November 2022 for home support staff. The HSE is currently running a rolling campaign in Galway and will continue to fill vacancies as they arise. HSE Home Support regularly attends recruitment fairs and colleges that provide training to carers. The HSE is also communicating and liaising on an ongoing basis with the approved providers on the Authorisation Scheme to recruit additional staff.
Preliminary data from the HSE indicates that at the end of August 2026, the waiting list for home support stands at 5,361. This is a substantial reduction since the start of 2020, when over 9,000 people were waiting for home support, and a reduction from the 2025 year-end position when 5,600 people were waiting.
Although waiting list data has been collected and monitored for many years, for the first time, the HSE’s National Service Plan 2026 includes home support waiting lists as a Key Performance Indicator. question: Deputy Aisling Dempsey asked the Minister for Health the way in which continuity of consultant care will be provided in maternity hospitals as private care is phased out.
reply:
The Public Only Consultant Contract began on 8 March 2023. Consultants choosing that contract cannot continue to provide private practice in public hospitals after 31 December 2025.
Consultants remaining on previous contracts may continue private practice until retirement. Private maternity care in public hospitals will therefore reduce gradually over time.
I recognise that this change may cause concern for some private patients. However, this reform supports equitable access to care based on clinical need.
Women with complex pregnancies will continue to receive appropriate consultant-led care.
Maternity care in Ireland is provided in line with the National Maternity Strategy. The model provides three pathways, reflecting each woman’s individual clinical needs. Within public maternity services, continuity of care is generally delivered through multidisciplinary teams rather than being guaranteed through the same individual consultant or midwife throughout pregnancy, birth and the postnatal period.
The Supported Care Pathway is intended for women with normal-risk pregnancies. It is midwife led, with care provided by a multidisciplinary team. The Assisted Care Pathway provides obstetric led care for women with medium-risk pregnancies. The Specialised Care Pathway supports women assessed as having high-risk pregnancies. Their care is led by a named consultant with the multidisciplinary team. Women are supported through the pathway appropriate to their individual clinical needs.

question: Deputy Peadar Tóibín asked the Minister for Health the assessment that has been undertaken of the potential patient safety implications arising from findings that evidence of English language competency, Garda vetting and overseas police clearance was absent or incomplete in a number of cases involving internationally recruited doctors.
reply:
The HSE recently published an Internal Audit report examining the recruitment of internationally recruited consultants and non-consultant hospital doctors (NCHDs).
The audit identified weaknesses in the evidence and retention of certain mandatory pre-employment documentation in a sample of personnel files. These included documentation relating to English language competency, Garda vetting, overseas police clearance and occupational health clearance.
Importantly, the audit found that all doctors included in the sample were registered with the Medical Council and authorised to practise medicine in Ireland. The audit findings therefore related to governance, documentation and consistency in the application of recruitment processes rather than professional registration.
Patient safety is paramount. While the audit did not identify concerns regarding Medical Council registration, it highlighted deficiencies in the recording and retention of documentation relating to a number of mandatory pre-employment checks. Such checks are an important safeguard for patients and the public, and it is essential that they are completed, evidenced and consistently applied across all healthcare settings. The HSE has advised that no specific patient safety incidents were identified through the audit; however, the findings underline the importance of robust recruitment controls and oversight arrangements.

question: Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Health for an update on the National Children's Hospital, including projected opening date, costs to date, and projected final costs.
reply:
Opening the National Children’s Hospital Ireland (NCHI) is a Government priority. Everything possible is being done to ensure this world-class hospital will open as quickly as possible, on behalf of children, young people, and their families.
I have been clear that the responsibility for committing to, resourcing, and delivering this project sits squarely with the project’s main contractor, BAM Ireland. The State will not reduce the pressure or dilute that accountability.
Ultimately, realising substantial completion is dependent on BAM’s execution and delivery of its own programme. BAM has shifted its Substantial Completion date 20 times over the last 6 years. On 13 July, BAM issued an updated programme to the Employer’s Representative (ER - independent third party responsible for administering the contract). The ER subsequently wrote to BAM for further detail to inform that review. That updated programme is still awaited from BAM.
In June, Children’s Health Ireland (CHI) gained early access to Level 1 where the critical care beds are, and this is welcome. However, access to Level 2 remains outstanding due to BAM’s repeated failure to deliver as committed. Achieving substantial completion is essentially a ‘volume exercise,’ to complete over 5,728 rooms. There has been a continued reduction in resources on site and while 5,135 of the 5,728 (89%) rooms have been delivered to the contractual standard, this is still falling behind BAM’s own completion targets.

question: Deputy Peter Roche asked the Minister for Health if she can provide an update on the availability of mental health services, particularly the current waiting times for adults and young people seeking access to mental health and psychology services.
reply:
Adult Services are provided in a variety of settings to best meet the need of people experiencing mental health difficulties.
There is a nationwide network of Adult Mental Health Teams. Through these teams, adults with mental health difficulties can access multi-disciplinary supports. There are 112 Community Adult Mental Health Teams operating nationwide with over 1,800 staff, and 34 Psychiatry of Later Life Teams with 404 staff operational.
Approximately 1,200 adults are supported in community residences, supervised residential settings that have varying levels of supervision and support. There are around 118 such residences, and they are due to be regulated under the Mental Health Act.
Public mental health inpatient care is provided in 66 approved centres nationwide, with a current capacity of 2,604 beds. Care in these services is regulated by the independent Mental Health Commission. The HSE are currently considering future capacity needs for inpatient services.
Talk therapies
Expanding access to community-based talk therapy supports is a key objective under Sharing the Vision, our national mental health policy, and Connecting for Life, the self-harm and suicide reduction strategy.
Talk therapies are becoming a core component of mental health service provision across all levels of care, with medical card holders eligible for free counselling through CiPC, and with significant funding for NGO partners to deliver supports to priority groups.
