question: Deputy Aindrias Moynihan asked the Minister for Health when women who are medically unable to take hormone replacement therapy can expect a decision on the reimbursement of a medication (details supplied); the factors are contributing to the duration of the process to date.
reply: Under the Health (Pricing and Supply of Medical Goods) Act 2013, the Health Service Executive (HSE) has statutory responsibility for decisions on the pricing and reimbursement of medicines. To commence this process, a pharmaceutical company must submit an application for a new medicine or a new use of an existing medicine, which has been granted European Medicines Agency (EMA) or Health Products Regulatory Authority (HPRA) authorisation, to the HSE’s Corporate Pharmaceutical Unit. Applicants must continue to engage throughout the process to ensure that the necessary evidence is available for the HSE to carry out its statutory role as a decision-maker with respect to the reimbursement of new medicines, in accordance with the Act. The Act specifies nine criteria which must be considered. These include the health needs of the public and the clinical need for the medicine. All these factors, taken together, allow the HSE to make an informed decision on new medicines. The Drugs Group is the national committee which the HSE has in place to make recommendations on the pricing and reimbursement of medicines. The membership of the HSE Drugs Group includes public interest members. Pharmacoeconomic reports are reviewed by the HSE Drugs Group along with the outputs of commercial negotiations, and any patient group submission(s) received. The HSE Drugs Group considers all of the evidence and makes a recommendation to the HSE Senior Management Team. The decision-making authority in the HSE

question: Deputy Tony McCormack asked the Minister for Health the measures being taken to address shortages of occupational therapists, particularly in counties where children and adults face prolonged delays in accessing services; and whether a national workforce recruitment and training strategy is being developed.
reply:
The recruitment and retention of Occupational Therapists remains a priority for the health service.
The Department of Health is developing policy on Advanced Practice in Health and Social Care Professions (HSCP). Occupational Therapists (OTs) form part of the HSCP group and introducing Advanced Practice HSCP in the Irish context will enable OTs to work at a higher level of practice, with enhanced critical decision making, competencies and level of education. This will facilitate advanced and efficient delivery of care to the population of Ireland in the most appropriate setting, with improved outcomes and overall patient experience.
It is anticipated that expanding the development pathway for HSCP will contribute to a more sustainable HSCP workforce and support recruitment and retention of HSCP, including OTs.
To support implementation, 30 Candidate Advanced Practice in Health and Social Care Professions posts have been allocated and aligned with clinical service areas to address specific patient and service need. Occupational Therapy is included in this initial roll out alongside other disciplines such as Dietetics, Speech and Language, Physiotherapy, Radiography and Radiation Therapy.
In addition, the HSE National HSCP Office is implementing a range of measures to support recruitment and retention, including funding for postgraduate education, specialist training and professional development, practice education supports and initiatives to increase student placement capacity

question: Deputy David Cullinane asked the Minister for Health the measures she is taking in Budget 2027 to make health care more affordable for workers and families; if she will extend eligibility for medical cards or reduce the drug payment scheme threshold.
reply:
Medical card provision is primarily based on financial assessment. In accordance with the Health Act 1970 (as amended), eligibility for a medical card is determined by the HSE, which assesses each application on a qualifying financial threshold. The amount of money that an individual can earn per week and still qualify for a card and is specific to their individual financial circumstances.
As of 1st September 2026, 1,568,218 people hold a medical card, and 816,507 people hold a GP visit card. This means that 43% of the population have access to free GP care.
There has been a significant focus, in recent budgets, on improving access to and the affordability of healthcare services. In 2023, eligibility for GP visit cards was expanded to all children under 8 years old, and to all individuals earning up to the median household income. It was estimated that 78,000 six and seven year olds, and 430,000 individuals under the median income-based expansion would be eligible. While uptake among children under 8 has been very strong, with the majority of those eligible having signed up, only around 40% of those eligible for GP visit cards under the median income expansion have signed up.
In response to the low uptake under the median income expansion, my Department conducted behavioural research in relation to the GP Visit Card application process, which found that some people may face unnecessary barriers when trying to determine their eligibility for a GP visit card or complete an appl

question: Deputy Paul Murphy asked the Minister for Health if she will review her decision to establish a private Commission of Investigation into Children's Health Ireland rather than a public inquiry.
reply:
I published the independent report of the Children's Health Ireland Inquiry into Spina Bifida and Complex Scoliosis Scoping Exercise on 28 September following engagement with patients and families. Mr Farrell, the independent facilitator of the scoping exercise, recommended a Commission of Investigation covering four defined modules; waiting lists, spinal surgery, hip dysplasia and the cohort of children who were not transferred to Temple Street post 2008.
Government has accepted the report's recommendations in full and have agreed to the initiation of drafting the Terms of Reference (ToR) for the proposed Commission of Investigation. Officials in my Department will work in close consultation with the Office of the Attorney General on drafting the Terms of Reference. There will be a call for input from advocacy groups on the ToR.
The final ToR will be submitted to Government for approval.

question: Deputy Willie O'Dea asked the Minister for Health the way in which Budget 2027 will provide more evening and weekend activity across operating theatres, outpatient clinics and diagnostics, making better use of existing staff, facilities and equipment.
reply:
Since 2020, overall health spending has increased by €8.3 billion, or 47%, while the health workforce has grown by more than 30,000 staff, an increase of 30%. The Government has also made substantial investment through the Public Only Consultant Contract and wider health service reforms. The challenge now is to ensure that patients see the full benefit of that investment.
Budget 2027 supports the continued rollout of those reforms. The objective is not simply to spend more, but to make better use of the staff, facilities and equipment already available across the health service. This includes increasing activity in operating theatres, outpatient clinics and diagnostics, including in the evenings and at weekends where appropriate.
We are already seeing this approach deliver results. Tallaght Hospital is running Saturday pain theatre sessions for long-waiting patients, St James's has introduced Saturday urology clinics, Cavan is operating evening and weekend cardiology sessions, Galway is providing evening and weekend gynaecology clinics, and Children's Health Ireland is running additional Saturday theatre sessions.
Budget 2027 will allow us to build on this progress. We are continuing to expand the Surgical Hub programme and will move to six-day operations across the Surgical Hub network. The existing hubs have already treated almost 14,000 patients this year and, with additional capacity coming on stream, are expected to undertake approximately 85,000 procedures next year.

question: Deputy Richard Boyd Barrett asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht the proportion of his Department's funding allocation for 2027 that will go to community development for the Traveller community.
reply:
My Department is committed to promoting inclusion and equal opportunities for Traveller communities and addressing the barriers they experience. The Social Inclusion and Activation Programme (SICAP) 2024-2028 is an important part of this work, with Travellers identified as one of its 12 pre-defined target groups.
Through SICAP, Programme Implementers work with Traveller individuals and community organisations to identify local needs, strengthen participation, and improve access to education, training, employment and other supports. Delivery is overseen by Programme Implementers, with oversight from Local Community Development Committees. Annual plans take account of local needs and supports are tailored accordingly.
I am pleased to have secured almost €74 million for SICAP and other social inclusion supports in Budget 2027. Just under €65 million of that allocation is for SICAP, providing greater long-term funding stability for the programme and enabling the continuation of important work across the country.
A particularly welcome development is the provision of long-term funding certainty, with previously temporary funding for new arrivals made a permanent part of the core SICAP allocation. This represents an important step towards ensuring that community integration supports can be delivered on a more sustainable basis.
As the programme supports a range of target groups, it is not possible to identify the precise proportion of the 2027 Budget allocation for SICAP that will

question: Deputy Matt Carthy asked the Minister for Health the proposals in place to expand CT and MRI scanners in Cavan and Monaghan, specifically any proposals to locate CT or MRI scanners at the Monaghan hospital site; the envisaged timeframe and costs associated with these proposals.
reply:
Cavan General Hospital and Monaghan Hospital operate as a single entity with integrated management, care pathways, and support functions. The budget for Cavan and Monaghan for 2026 is over €167m which has increased by over 53% since 2020. The budget for Monaghan Hospital alone has doubled since 2020. WTEs at both sites have increased by almost 50% since 2020. Bed numbers have also increased in Cavan and Monaghan in the same period.
I am advised by the HSE that a Strategic Healthcare Investment Framework (SHIF) for a proposed MRI at Monaghan General Hospital has been approved. It is anticipated a Design Team for this project will be appointed by year end.
A preliminary business case, a project scope and brief will then be developed following which the proposal will progress through approval gates in line with Infrastructure Guidelines. Until the scope and brief of the proposal have been determined and the proposal reviewed in line with Infrastructure Guidelines it is premature to establish a definitive timeframe.
The provision of an MRI scanner at Monaghan Hospital will provide additional diagnostic capacity for the region. Currently, Cavan and Monaghan Hospital has one MRI scanner which is located at Cavan General Hospital, with access prioritised according to clinical need.
Patients have access to CT services in Cavan General Hospital which currently operates two high-throughput CT scanners. I am advised that there are no plans to seek additional CT modality at Cavan and Mon

question: Deputy Aengus Ó Snodaigh asked the Minister for Health the number of times the national hearing care plan working group has met since it were set up in 2014; when the group's work will be concluded; and the timeframe for action to be taken on its findings.
reply:
The National Hearing Care Plan Working Group, established in August 2024, is jointly chaired by the Department of Health and the Health Service Executive (HSE). Membership of the Working Group is drawn from relevant stakeholders, including clinicians, representative bodies, and other agencies.
The Working Group has been tasked with developing recommendations for a holistic model of hearing care in Ireland. The Working Group and associated subgroups have met 25 times to date, with significant progress being made.
An important milestone in progressing the development of the Plan was a public consultation process. The views and opinions gathered through this process are directly informing the development and finalisation of the National Hearing Care Plan, which is at an advanced stage.
The draft Plan produced by the Group will be presented to the Minister in quarter 4 for approval. Recommendations arising from the Plan will then be implemented on a phased and priority basis.

question: Deputy Ryan O'Meara asked the Minister for Health if Budget 2027 contains funding for the establishment of a sexual assault treatment unit in the Mid-West.
reply: The Department provides funding to the HSE through the annual Estimates, Letter of Determination and National Service Plan processes. Decisions regarding the development of individual services, including Sexual Assault Treatment Units, are operational matters for the HSE and the relevant Health Region, which are responsible for planning and prioritising services within the overall funding available to them. The assessment of service need and any decision regarding the establishment of a Sexual Assault Treatment Unit in the Mid West is an operational matter for HSE Mid West in the context of the overall funding resources available to them.

question: Deputy Colm Burke asked the Minister for Health to provide an update on the proposed elective hospital for Cork; and whether the project can proceed to planning.
reply:
An application for planning permission for the new Elective Treatment Centre (also referred to as Elective Hospital) at the site of St Stephen’s Hospital in Cork was submitted to Cork City Council by the HSE on 12th October 2026. The proposal includes 9 day-case theatres, 10 minor operation rooms, and 7 endoscopy suites, with a total floor area of 16,243sqm. It also includes new road access for the St. Stephens Hospital campus.
The HSE will continue its constructive engagement with statutory authorities including Cork City Council and Transport Infrastructure Ireland to progress the planning application.
The timeline for the remaining design process and for delivery through the construction phase will become clearer following approval of planning permission, relevant regulatory consents and market engagement.
The Elective Care Programme is being delivered in two phases: a national network of Surgical Hubs in the first instance to meet medium term demand and capacity, and then a national network of Elective Treatment Centres (Elective Hospitals) in Cork, Galway and Dublin. The HSE South West Surgical Hub at Cork University Hospital opened to patients last month.
The new elective facilities enable the separation of scheduled (elective) from unscheduled care. This will mean fewer cancellations and fewer delays for elective care caused by seasonal surges, localised outbreaks, and surges in emergency attendances. question: Deputy Peter Roche asked the Minister for Health the measures being taken to address staffing and operational pressures within Child and Adolescent Mental Health Services in Galway; the way in which continuity of care is being ensured for young people who age out of CAMHS at 18 years-of-age, particularly where appropriate adult mental health services are limited or unavailable.
reply:
All aspects of mental health care, including the specialist Child and Adolescent Mental Health Service (CAMHS), are being enhanced and delivered in accordance with the implementation of our mental health policy Sharing the Vision 2020-2030, our suicide reduction policy Connecting for Life: 2026-2035, and the HSE national service plans.
The Government continues to demonstrate its commitment to the provision of adequate and equitable mental health services through the allocation of increased annual funding to the sector, with record funding of almost €1.6 billion provided for mental health in 2026. CAMHS alone receives approximately €191 million annually, an increase of almost 40% over the last four years. A further €127 million is provided to NGOs, many of which focus on young people. In Budget 2026, €10 million was provided to improve youth mental health services, including CAMHS.
As the Deputy will be aware, HSE mental health supports range from prevention and early intervention to the specialist CAMHS service, which is for those under the age of 18 with moderate to severe mental health difficulties. Access to CAMHS nationally is based on clinical assessment, in accordance with the CAMHS Operational Guidelines. For young people attending CAMHS, if they still require psychiatric support as they turn 18, they move to the Adult Mental Health Service (AMHS) in their area. This transition begins approximately six months before the person turns 18 years old. During this time, CAMH

question: Deputy Brian Brennan asked the Minister for Health for an update on the progress of the proposed Gorey primary health care centre.
reply:
Primary Care Centres form a critical part of our healthcare infrastructure, ensuring primary care services are delivered as close as possible to people in their own homes and in their own communities.
As you are aware, the need for a Primary Care Centre in Gorey has previously been identified and a tender process was undertaken.
However, this process concluded unsuccessfully, and I fully recognise that it is disappointing that the Primary Care Centre in Gorey has been delayed and that a new tender process had to be commenced.
Following advertisement on the E-tenders procurement platform, I am pleased to confirm that the HSE has advised that the tender process has now completed stage two – which is a priced offer.
The tenders received have been evaluated and HSE Board approval for a preferred developer was given on 25th September 2026, with letters issued to all developers in relation to the outcome of the process.
Following that approval, there is a 2-week standstill period after which the HSE can formally engage with the preferred developer.
Thereafter, a definitive projected timeline for construction and opening of the Primary Care Centre in Gorey will become available.
When completed, the Gorey Primary Care Centre will accommodate a range of services, including a GP practice, nursing services, dental, disability, CAMHS, and other primary care therapies.
I want to assure the Deputy that my Department will continue to actively engage with the HSE in relation to the developme

question: Deputy Marie Sherlock asked the Minister for Health her plans to commence the remaining sections of the Health (Assisted Human Reproduction) Act 2024.
reply:
The Deputy will be aware that the Health (Assisted Human Reproduction) Act was enacted, having passed all stages in both Houses of the Oireachtas and been signed into law by the President, in July 2024.
While the 2024 Act was progressing through the Houses of Oireachtas, issues were identified which required further consideration and consultation with the Office of the Attorney General. The formal drafting process for the Health (Assisted Human Reproduction) (Amendment) Bill is in its final stages, led by the Office of Parliamentary Counsel, along with officials from my Department, the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration, and the Department of Children, Disability and Equality. I hope to be in a position to introduce the published Bill to the Dáil during the current term.
The AHR Amendment Bill is a very substantive piece of legislation. It is largely concerned with outstanding issues of parentage and citizenship, particularly in respect of children born as a result of a donor-assisted human reproduction (DAHR) procedure or surrogacy arrangement undertaken abroad by Irish resident parents or undertaken by Irish citizen parents living abroad. It also seeks to make other necessary amendments to various other sections of the 2024 Act.
Some sections of the 2024 Act relating to the administrative functions of the Assisted Human Reproduction Regulatory Authority (AHRRA) were commenced to formally establish the body. I also signed an Order in April to commence three su

question: Deputy Sean Fleming asked the Minister for Health her plans to reduce waiting lists in the school dental programme and to improve access to more complex dental treatment.
reply:
At present, the HSE Oral Healthcare Service aims to provide an oral examination and necessary treatment for children at up to three intervals, targeting ages approximating to second and sixth class and, in some cases, fourth class. Emergency care is provided for children of all ages up to 16. The Dental Treatment Services Scheme provides dental care, free of charge, to medical card holders aged 16 and over. The HSE Orthodontic Service provides treatment to those children with the most severe and complex orthodontic treatment needs. Referral for orthodontic assessment is usually made at the 6th Class oral health examination. Children whose treatment need is assessed as being in Grade 4 or Grade 5 of the modified index are offered treatment free of charge.
I am determined to improve access to the public oral healthcare system. My Department and the HSE are finalising a focused two-year Oral Health Action Plan to deliver real improvements on the ground.
The plan will be driven by a dedicated governance group, with progress monitored closely and aligned to wider HSE and Department priorities. It responds to sustained service pressures and long waiting lists—particularly for children. €18 million has been allocated in Budget 2027 to commence implementation of the Plan which will focus on a small number of clear priorities:
• Cutting waiting lists in the School Dental Programme and orthodontics
• Improvement and expansion of the access programme to oral healthcare for people who ha

question: Deputy Naoise Ó Cearúil asked the Minister for Health whether her Department has assessed the adequacy of the €2 million allocated to the women’s health applied partnership scheme for 2026 and 2027 in light of the evidence gaps identified by the Health Research Board; and whether a review of future funding requirements is planned.
reply:
I have approved funding for the Health Research Board (HRB) Applied Partnership Awards Scheme for Women’s Health, with up to €2 million being made available from the Department of Health’s Women’s Health Fund.
This funding supports the Women’s Health Action Plan 2026–2027commitment to strengthen the evidence base underpinning women’s health policy, service development and implementation.
The research themes for the scheme were informed by Ministerial priorities, engagement, listening to women, the work of the Women’s Health Taskforce, and the findings of the HRB report Women’s Health Outcomes: An Evidence and Gap Map Review, commissioned by the Department of Health and published in 2025.
The response to the funding call was very encouraging, demonstrating the growing strength of women’s health research in Ireland and the significant interest among researchers and healthcare partners in contributing to improved outcomes for women and girls. The quality and volume of applications submitted highlights both the appetite and capacity within the research community to support evidence-informed policy and service delivery in women's health.
The HRB operates an open and competitive funding process, with applications assessed through a robust international peer-review process. Funding is awarded only to proposals that meet the highest standards of scientific excellence, relevance and potential impact. reply:
Budget 2027 provides an additional €1.6 billion in current expenditure for the Health Vote, bringing the total current allocation to €27.4 billion. The budget does not, and never has, set out the number of WTE allocated to any care service within the HSE. The Department is currently preparing the Letter of Determination to the HSE, which will set out the priorities for 2027 based on this funding level.
Following receipt of the Letter of Determination, the HSE will prepare its National Service Plan 2027, which will outline how the HSE will operationalise the priorities funded under Budget 2027. Further information on specific initiatives to be advanced in 2027, including workforce and training developments, will be available following completion and approval of the National Service Plan.

question: Deputy Edward Timmins asked the Minister for Health in light of the recent changes to the day care services for older people in Blessington, County Wicklow, the plans to maintain and expand the service.
reply:
The HSE have confirmed that the Day Care Service in Blessington continues to operate four days each week and currently supports 40 registered service users. The service has operated on this four day basis since 2023, with no reduction in its capacity or level of provision.
In July 2026, the HSE relocated the service from the Blessington Coimin Parish Centre to the Blessington Primary Care Centre as the Parish Centre would only be available for two days per week going forward. The HSE therefore secured alternative accommodation to protect the existing service and ensure that older people could continue to access four days of day care each week within Blessington.
The relocation maintained continuity for service users without reducing capacity or requiring alternative service arrangements. It resulted from accommodation requirements and did not relate to staffing, funding or any reduction in local demand.
The HSE operates and directly funds the Blessington service as part of its wider Older Persons Service provision.
The HSE remains committed to maintaining day care services for older people in Blessington. These services give older people opportunities to remain active, connected and independent within their own community. The move to the Primary Care Centre has secured the existing four-day service locally and provides a basis for the HSE to continue supporting the needs of older people in the area.

question: Deputy Emer Currie asked the Minister for Health if she is aware that same-sex female couples accessing IVF may be refused medical-expense tax relief where neither partner has a diagnosed fertility condition; whether she will engage with the Minister for Finance to address this apparent inequality in the tax treatment of IVF.
reply:
It is my understanding that individuals who have undertaken assisted human reproduction (AHR) treatment may be in a position to avail of tax relief in respect of medical expenses incurred during the course of that treatment.
My officials engaged with colleagues in the Office of the Revenue Commissioners with a view to seeking clarity on issues relevant to AHR treatment. Any such claim for tax relief is considered and granted by the Office of the Revenue Commissioners if it is satisfied that the criteria as set out in relevant legislation and guidance documents have been met.
I also understand that my officials and officials from the Department of Finance are to meet in the coming weeks in relation to this issue.
You will appreciate that I cannot comment on the operation of tax relief schemes as this matter is the responsibility of the Office of the Revenue Commissioners, which comes under the remit of the Department of Finance.

question: Deputy Brian Brennan asked the Minister for Health to provide an update on when skyclarys will be available for patients with Friedreich’s ataxia.
reply:
Under the Health (Pricing and Supply of Medical Goods) Act 2013, the Health Service Executive (HSE), through its Senior Management Team (SMT) has statutory responsibility for decisions on the pricing and reimbursement of medicines and medical devices. It decides, based on all competing demands across the health service, whether a new medicine—or a new use of an existing medicine—can be funded within the resources available, in line with the Health (Pricing and Supply of Medical Goods) Act 2013.
Following extensive engagement between the HSE and Biogen, the HSE’s SMT approved the reimbursement of Skyclarys for patients over 16 years of age with Friedreich’s Ataxia, on the 25th August 2026.
Subject to supply by Biogen , from the 1st October 2026, omaveloxolone (Skyclarys®) is approved to be added to the list of reimbursable items under the High-Tech Drug Arrangements for the treatment of Friedreich’s ataxia in adults and adolescents aged 16 years and older. Prescribing of omaveloxolone (Skyclarys®) is through the High-Tech Hub and is restricted to designated approved consultants.
Before patients can begin treatment with Skyclarys, they must undergo a suitability assessment as per the European medicines marketing authorisation. This includes a neurological review, cardiology review, blood tests, a recent echocardiogram and education about the medication.
Tallaght University Hospital has put in place additional clinics, commencing from October 2nd, to progress the assessment and

question: Deputy Martin Kenny asked the Minister for Health for an update on the orthopaedic surgical theatre in Sligo University Hospital in relation to the recent leak in the roof; and the way in which this is affecting the orthopaedic surgical waiting list in Sligo University Hospital.
reply:
There has been a history of leaks coming through the roof the orthopedic surgical theatre in Sligo University Hospital over the last number of years resulting in cancellation of surgical schedules.
The HSE has informed my Department that an upgrade was completed at the end of last year and as a result of these works there have been no further roof-related leaks.
Separately, the Air Handling Units for the Orthopedic Theatre are due to be replaced and a tender process is underway to procure replacement Units. The HSE advises that, in recent weeks, a small amount of water from an existing Unit leaked, due to a blocked condensation pipe which overflowed. This was repaired within 24 hours, and falling out from this cleaning and air sampling took place resulting in elective activity being deferred.
Efforts are made to resolve these infrastructure issues as quickly as possible in order to resume services as soon as possible. Patients are being rescheduled as early as possible following such situations and this is being monitored on an ongoing basis to minimize delays for patients.
There is a proposal under review for 2 orthopedic theatres at Sligo University Hospital and this is at the early stages of initiation.

question: Deputy Richard Boyd Barrett asked the Minister for Health her plans to reduce waiting lists for specialist endometriosis care.
reply:
Last October, I launched the National Framework for the Management of Endometriosis. I also mandated an action plan to accelerate development of our endometriosis services. This includes the recruitment of additional colorectal surgeons in Cork and Tallaght. This will increase capacity for more complex surgical treatments.
Over €5 million was invested in endometriosis services between 2021 and 2025. From this, the two supra-regional specialist centres in Cork and Tallaght have been established. These centres provide for the management of complex endometriosis cases. Regional Centres for moderate cases have been established in the Rotunda, the Coombe, and Limerick. Clinics in Galway and the NMH are under further development.
A further 65.5 WTEs have been prioritised through the HSE National Service Plan 2026. This will provide additional consultants and other healthcare professionals. This represents more than €11m in further investment between 2026 and 2027. The HSE has advised that this recruitment may take up to 18 months.
Last year over €0.5m was provided to increase surgical activity and reduce waiting lists. The HSE carried out 142 additional surgeries in Q4 2025. This was against a target of 100 additional surgeries by the end of 2025.
2026 has seen increased referrals, clinics, new patients and surgeries across the network.
I am fully committed to the continued expansion of these essential services.

question: Deputy Michael Cahill asked the Minister for Health if she plans to ensure all cancer patients receive medical cards.
reply:
Eligibility for a medical card is generally determined by residency and means under the Health Act 1970, having regard to a person's income and circumstances. In accordance with the Act, eligibility for a medical card is determined by the HSE, which assesses each application on a qualifying financial threshold. This is the amount of money that an individual can earn per week and still qualify for a card.
Every effort is made by the HSE, within the framework of the legislation, to support applicants in applying for a medical card - in particular, to take full account of difficult circumstances in the case of applicants who may be in excess of the income guidelines. In such circumstances, the HSE may exercise discretion and grant a medical card.
Cancer patients may also benefit from a range of existing supports, including medical cards where they meet the relevant criteria, GP visit cards, the Drugs Payment Scheme, and other health service supports.
It should be noted that previous expert consideration of condition-based eligibility concluded that granting medical cards on the basis of illness or a disability should not pursued. The expert Group concluded that it was not feasible, desirable, nor ethically justifiable to list medical conditions in priority order for medical card eligibility. In following the Expert Group’s advice, a person’s means remains the main qualifier for a medical card.
Furthermore, I can advise the Deputy that, since 2015, medical cards are awarded witho

question: Deputy Peter 'Chap' Cleere asked the Minister for Health for an update on the progress on Ballyhale Health Centre.
reply:
I would like to thank Deputy Cleere for giving me the opportunity to provide an update to the House on the Ballyhale Health Centre.
The expansion of primary care infrastructure in Ballyhale was included on the HSE Capital Plan 2026. The HSE is in the process of appointing a Design Team for this project, it is expected that a Design Team will be appointed in Q4 2026.
Design development will follow thereafter. An overall programme for the expansion of infrastructure in Ballyhale will be determined once the design has progressed.
The purpose of health infrastructure is to enable service delivery. Prioritisation of capital investment and capital investment decisions must be driven by evidence-based service needs, and on the basis that existing assets are fully utilised. This means that all additional infrastructure will depend on the full utilisation of existing HSE facilities in the area.
The objective must be to ensure that new capital developments are aligned with service needs, enable the delivery of Sláintecare/Universal Healthcare and deliver optimum value for money.

reply:

question: Deputy Brendan Smith asked the Minister for Health if she will amend the criteria for the nursing homes support scheme to ensure that payment under the fair deal scheme is effective from the date the application is submitted on behalf of the patient.
reply:
The Nursing Homes Support Scheme (NHSS – or Fair Deal) is a procedure encompassing the gathering of detailed clinical and financial information, and its administration is governed by the 2009 Act. As set out in the Act, an applicant’s contribution to the cost of their care is calculated based on the financial assessment of their income and assets on the date they first make an application under the Nursing Homes Support Scheme. In addition, transferred assets and income, defined as assets or income transferred to another person up to five years before a person's first application to the scheme, are also assessed.
The programme for Government includes commitments to including increased funding for the Fair Deal Scheme to ensure that the wait for funding does not exceed four weeks after approval. Applicants who transfer from acute settings to a nursing home can, under certain circumstances, avail of Transitional Care Funding provided by the HSE.
The Department of Health consistently seeks to identify improvements and introduce enhancements to the scheme, where feasible, which aims to ensure that long-term nursing home care remains sustainable, accessible and affordable for everyone and that people continue to be cared for in the most appropriate settings. Given the size, complexity and cost of the NHSS, implementation is complex and any changes in policy direction need to be carefully assessed and kept under review. There are currently no plans to amend the application process.

question: Deputy Shay Brennan asked the Minister for Health her plans to increase virtual care capacity.
reply:
Virtual Care is clinically led, digitally-enabled care, that allows patients to receive safe, high-quality care in their homes or communities. It supports more effective use of healthcare resources and reduces pressure on hospital services.
Significant progress has already been made through the rollout of Virtual Wards focused on earlier discharge. These enable patients who would otherwise require a hospital bed to recover at home, helping reduce occupancy and improve patient flow. There are currently 147 Virtual Ward beds of this kind available. While we have yet to reach 100% occupancy of these beds, I would like to acknowledge the significant progress made to date, with particular increases in occupancy across sites in Cork and Drogheda recently. To date, over 5,100 patients have been admitted to Virtual Wards, delivering over 47,000 bed days.
In 2027 we will continue to expand capacity. Each Region will work towards providing an additional virtual care option, enabling services to reach people earlier and help avoid Emergency Department attendances or hospital admissions.
My Department is also progressing a National Virtual Care Policy, which will launch in coming weeks. This will support additional virtual pathways in each region, increased telehealth and remote-monitoring initiatives, and enhanced workforce capability.
Through these measures, we are ensuring that more patients receive appropriate care in the right place, at the right time.

question: Deputy Rose Conway-Walsh asked the Minister for Health the reason for the continued delays, in some cases extending over months and years, in transitioning agency staff to permanent positions within the Health Service Executive.
reply:
Agency staff have long played an important role in keeping health services running safely, covering vacancies and absences, and helping services respond to short-term increases in demand. However, what should be a flexible support has become too significant a feature of the workforce. The health service remains overly reliant on agency staffing, which is more costly and provides less continuity and workforce stability than direct employment. With agency expenditure expected to exceed €800 million in 2026, this level of reliance is not sustainable.
It has always been my clear direction to the HSE that they need to reduce agency use while supporting direct recruitment into approved and funded posts. Direct employment offers better value for the health service, greater job security, improved continuity of care for patients and a more stable workforce, while retaining skills and experience within the public system rather than repeatedly purchasing the same capacity through external agencies.
A national Agency Conversion Framework has been in place in the HSE since 2024 with over 900 posts converted from agency between 2024 and 2025. Efforts have ramped up in 2026 and to date this year a further 1,492 agency staff have already converted to direct employment, representing 57.8% of the HSE’s 2026 target of 2,581 conversions. question: Deputy Aidan Farrelly asked the Minister for Transport if he will provide an update on the development of legislative changes to the Taxi Regulation Act 2013 with respect to cross-Border taxi services.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 92 and 96 together.
The regulation of the small public service vehicle (SPSV) industry is a matter for the independent transport regulator, the National Transport Authority (NTA), under the provisions of the Consolidated Taxi Regulation Acts 2013 and 2016. Under section 6(2) of this Act, An Garda Síochána is responsible for the granting of SPSV driver licences. I have no role in the day-to-day operations of the SPSV sector.
Under the provisions of the Taxi Regulation Act 2013, operators are required to hold an SPSV licence and an SPSV driver licence to carry persons for hire or reward in the State. The 2013 Act and its requirements only apply to services provided in the State - it does not provide for services across a border. The legislative position in Northern Ireland is similar. Thus, under current legislation, a taxi operator wishing to operate cross-border services, would have to apply for and obtain SPSV licences on each side of the border. Unlike other areas of transport - such as bus and road haulage operations - taxi services are not subject to EU harmonisation, so arrangements for regulating taxi services remain a matter for the relevant authorities in each EU Member State, in respect of services that operate in their jurisdiction.

question: Deputy Ivana Bacik asked the Minister for Transport the position regarding so-called rickshaw vehicles carrying passengers for monetary reward; the adequacy of measures to enforce a ban on motorised rickshaws announced in 2018; the number of enforcements taken against operators of mechanically propelled rickshaws carrying passengers for reward under existing SPSV legislation in each year since 2016, in tabular form; his plans to further review guidance to An Garda Síochána or new legislation, following recent road traffic incidents involving rickshaws.
reply:
For the Deputy's information, if a rickshaw is fitted with a small engine or electric motor of any kind, it is considered to be a mechanically propelled vehicle (MPV). Under road traffic law, if an MPV is used in a public place it is subject to all of the regulatory controls that apply to other vehicles i.e., it must be roadworthy, registered, taxed and comply with the following regulations:
• SI 190 of 1963 – Road Traffic Construction, Equipment and Use of Vehicles Regulations 1963.
• SI 189 of 1963 – Road Traffic Lighting of Vehicles Regulations 1963.
• SI 5 of 2003 – Road Traffic Construction and Use of Vehicles Regulations 2003.
The drivers of all vehicles on public roads, including motorised rickshaws, are required to comply with road traffic legislation and to behave in a safe manner paying due care to other road users. The enforcement of such road traffic legislation is a matter for An Garda Síochána. Therefore, statistics on the number of enforcement actions taken against operators of mechanically propelled rickshaws, would be a matter for An Garda Síochána.
A provision was contained in section 31 of the Road Traffic Act 2016, which was aimed at amending section 20 of the Taxi Regulation Act 2013, to allow the National Transport Authority (NTA) to make regulations for “non-motorised passenger transport” in towns and cities which includes rickshaws propelled by pedal cycle. It is important to note that the section 31 provision does not allow for the regulation of ricks

question: Deputy Michael Healy-Rae asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht when decisions on applications under the Community Centre Investment Fund be made.
reply:
The Community Centre Investment Fund (CCIF) was introduced to provide high quality community facilities that are available to community groups in both urban and rural communities. Through the CCIF, some €112 million has been allocated for the enhancement and refurbishment of existing community centres and the construction of new centres where such a need has been identified.
I launched the latest round of funding under CCIF 2026 on the 26th March for enhancement and refurbishment of existing community centres. The fund will be delivered across 2 categories with maximum funding levels of €25,000 and €100,000 respectively. The closing date for the CCIF 2026 has now passed.
Applications are currently being assessed and I look forward to announcing the successful projects later in the year.

question: Deputy Michael Healy-Rae asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht when decisions on recent CLAR applications be announced.
reply:
The CLAR programme provides funding under a number of different measures for small-scale infrastructural projects in designated rural areas. Last year I approved over €14m million for 238 projects under the programme, with funding being provided under a number if measures for community facilities and amenities, community vehicles and specific support for island communities.
On the 10th of March I launched the 2026 CLAR programme with 3 funding measures that were broadly similar to last year. On 1 October 2026 I was delighted to announce funding of €2.5 million for 44 vehicles nationwide under measure 2 of the 2026 CLAR programme.
My officials are currently assessing applications under measures 1 and 3 of the 2026 CLAR programme and I expect to announce the successful projects in the coming months.

question: Deputy Michael Healy-Rae asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht if a further allocation for the local improvement scheme will be made to Local Authorities before the end of 2026.
reply:
The Local Improvement Scheme funds the upgrade of non-public rural roads and laneways, which are not usually maintained by local authorities. My department reinstated the Scheme in 2017, and it is a central element of the overall Rural Development Investment Programme. Since 2017, over €201 million has been allocated to local authorities, resulting in the improvement of over 5,500 roads.
The 2026 scheme was launched in February with voted funding of €17m million. This represents an increase on base funding allocated to the scheme in previous years. Kerry County Council received an allocation of €1.133 million.
While the Department provides funding for the Scheme, it is administered by each local authority, who retain responsibility for the selection and prioritisation of roads and management of waiting lists. It should be noted that the ability of local authorities to meet demand under the scheme is not purely a function of available funding, as other factors such as weather conditions, rising costs and the availability of contractors and labour are also relevant.
Local authorities are in the process of preparing their funding drawdown requests for works completed this year. My department officials will monitor this process closely and work with each local authority to ensure funds are fully utilised and that as many roads as possible are completed under the scheme.
The next round of funding that will be made available to local authorities has been secured as part of Budget 2

question: Deputy Michael Healy-Rae asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht if funding has been secured to reopen the scéim na mBóithre áise scheme in 2027.
reply:
The current Programme for Government includes a commitment to restoring Scéim na mBóithre Áise during this Government's term. The mechanism and approach related to reintroducing this scheme are currently being examined by officials in my Department.
In the meantime, funding is available through my department under the Local Improvement Scheme (LIS) to assist local authorities in carrying out improvement works on private roads and on roads that are not normally publicly maintained.
The 2027 Local Improvement Scheme has a budget of €17 million for repairs and improvement works on non-public rural roads and laneways.
Further information on the Local Improvement Scheme (LIS) is available on my Departments website.

question: Deputy Albert Dolan asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht the additional supports he intends to provide for community infrastructure and recreational facilities in rapidly growing rural towns and villages; and the way in which his Department will ensure that investment in community facilities keeps pace with population growth in areas such as Galway east.
reply:
The Town Centre First Policy (TCF) is a major government initiative supporting the regeneration of Irish towns and villages, intended to help ensure they can become vibrant, viable and attractive places to live, work, visit and invest in. To help deliver on the objectives of TCF at local level, my Department provides funding to local authorities, including Galway County Council, for dedicated Town Regeneration Officers who work closely with communities and multi-disciplinary regeneration teams.
In addition, over €7m in dedicated TCF support funding has been provided nationally. This has included funding for the development of 52 TCF Town Plans nationally, including in Gort and Athenry and funding to support the establishment of over 100 Town Teams nationwide, including in Headford, An Cheathrú Rua, and Oranmore. These initiatives aim to support local communities in identifying and addressing the key issues in their own towns and communities.
Separately, a range of capital funding streams is available across my department to support delivery on TCF objectives. Calls for Proposals under these funds are structured to allow local authorities prioritise needs using a place based local development approach and to themselves select the priority areas for applications.

question: Deputy Conor Sheehan asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht the projects funded under the town and village renewal scheme in Limerick in 2025 and to date in 2026, in tabular form.
reply:
The Town and Village Renewal Scheme (TVRS) was introduced in 2016 and is one of a number of measures designed to rejuvenate rural towns and villages throughout Ireland. Since the launch of the scheme over €217 million has been allocated to almost 2,000 projects across the country and of this, over €9.2 million has been allocated to 78 projects in County Limerick.
This scheme places particular emphasis on projects which support sustainable employment creation, town centre resilience and regeneration, enhance streetscapes, and bringing derelict and vacant buildings and sites back into use as multi-purpose community spaces.
A TVRS Call for Proposals was issued to local authorities on 16 September 2026. There are two funding streams available under this Call: The Main Scheme and the Project Development Measure and further details are available on my department's website. The closing date for the submission of applications is 22 January 2027.
A separate Call for Proposals under the TVRS ‘Building and Land Acquisition Measure’ (BLAM) issued earlier this year. Under BLAM, local authorities can apply for funding of up to €500,000, which can be used to purchase up to three buildings or sites to re-develop into multi-purpose community facilities or infrastructure. question: Deputy Aidan Farrelly asked the Minister for Transport the extent to which he and or his officials have engaged with the Department of Infrastructure in Northern Ireland in respect of a reciprocal arrangement for smaller passenger vans (details supplied) and so on, to operate in each other's jurisdictions; and if he has consulted with Tourism Ireland in respect of same.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 92 and 96 together.
The regulation of the small public service vehicle (SPSV) industry is a matter for the independent transport regulator, the National Transport Authority (NTA), under the provisions of the Consolidated Taxi Regulation Acts 2013 and 2016. Under section 6(2) of this Act, An Garda Síochána is responsible for the granting of SPSV driver licences. I have no role in the day-to-day operations of the SPSV sector.
Under the provisions of the Taxi Regulation Act 2013, operators are required to hold an SPSV licence and an SPSV driver licence to carry persons for hire or reward in the State. The 2013 Act and its requirements only apply to services provided in the State - it does not provide for services across a border. The legislative position in Northern Ireland is similar. Thus, under current legislation, a taxi operator wishing to operate cross-border services, would have to apply for and obtain SPSV licences on each side of the border. Unlike other areas of transport - such as bus and road haulage operations - taxi services are not subject to EU harmonisation, so arrangements for regulating taxi services remain a matter for the relevant authorities in each EU Member State, in respect of services that operate in their jurisdiction.

question: Deputy Robert Troy asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht if his Department can provide clarity on the recruitment panel which has been put in place to serve on the board of Pobal; and the length of time the panel will remain in place to fill any upcoming positions on the board.
reply:
Pobal works on behalf of Government to support communities and local agencies in their work to achieve social inclusion and support community development. Pobal operates under the aegis of the Department of Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht.
Pobal is governed by a voluntary Board of Directors. Members of the Board are appointed by Government, on the nomination of the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht, in line with the Guidelines for Appointments to State Boards. The Minister requests the Government to appoint Directors to the Board of Pobal to fill vacancies arising from the ordinary rotation of the Board, and, when required, to fill casual vacancies arising.
Where upcoming vacancies on the board of Pobal are identified, my Department initiates the State Boards appointments process at least six months before the current member’s term of office expires. The process is managed by the Public Appointments Service (PAS).
The PAS public jobs website is the portal through which all State Board vacancies are advertised, and information is provided there on the appointments process. When expressions of interest are received, an assessment panel is convened by PAS to consider the applications received. A shortlist of suitable candidates is put forward for the Minister's consideration. The Minister then nominates the chosen candidate(s) for appointment by Government.
Successful appointees are issued with letters of appointment from the Minist

question: Deputy Cian O'Callaghan asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht the funding streams for local authorities such as Fingal Country Council to progress an upgrade to Howth library.
reply:
The provision of library services, including the upgrading of library buildings and services, is primarily a matter for local authorities in their capacity as library authorities under the Local Government Act 2001.
As the Deputy will be aware, the Libraries Capital Programme for the period 2023-2027 was announced in April 2024. I am advised that no application was received from Fingal County Council for a library project in Howth at that time and the programme is now fully committed. My Department will be developing a successor Libraries Capital Programme to the 2023-2027 programme, setting out the terms and conditions including eligibility, and all Local Authorities will be invited to submit applications in due course.
On 26 June 2026, under the Libraries Capital Programme, Minister Calleary and I announced €3m in funding for targeted Small-scale Capital Investment in public libraries. This funding will provide sensory equipment, accessibility infrastructure, ICT hardware upgrades to increase broadband speed, and modern furniture and operational equipment for public libraries across the country. Fingal County Council was awarded €147,505 under this fund.
These strategic investments and targeted initiatives demonstrate my Department’s commitment to ensuring public libraries remain accessible, inclusive and dynamic spaces that empower individuals and communities alike.

question: Deputy Eoghan Kenny asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht if the Charities Regulator has been notified of any changes in the trusteeship, senior management or governance structure of a registered charity (details supplied) since 2020; whether all changes requiring notification were notified within the appropriate timeframe.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 906, 907, 908, 909, 910, 911, 912 and 913 together.
The Charities Regulator, under the aegis of my Department, is the statutory body responsible for registering and regulating Ireland’s charities, with a mandate to promote good governance practice. While the Regulator is under the aegis of my Department, it is important to note that the Regulator is fully independent in the performance of its statutory functions.
Any concerns, complaints and correspondence relating to financial or governance matters in specific charities are a matter for the Charities Regulator to manage. Where breaches of charity legislation are identified, the entity is contacted by the Regulator with a view to addressing such breaches. In the event that serious breaches of charity legislation are identified, the Regulator may commence a statutory investigation.

Any correspondence between the Regulator and a charity is a matter for the two bodies and does not involve my office or my officials.

question: Deputy Erin McGreehan asked the Minister for Transport whether he plans to review the vehicle price ceiling under the SEAI electric vehicle purchase grant scheme; whether a tapered reduction in grant assistance above the ceiling has been assessed as an alternative to the immediate loss of eligibility.
reply:
The Government is fully committed to supporting the transition to zero-emission and the ambitious target to have 30% of private car fleet switched to electric by 2030.
Regarding the EV Purchase Grant, the maximum eligible vehicle price threshold for the grant will now be €50,000, rather than €60,000. This change has been made to target funding for EV transition towards lower price bracket cars and enables a greater proportion of the funding available within the National Development Plan to support the roll-out of charging infrastructure. The amended price threshold came into place for new applications received after 31 July 2026, and will be kept under review in 2027.
The EV grant system is continually reviewed to optimise EV purchasing with a view to replacing older, polluting vehicles. It should be noted that decisions on financial incentives, including EV grants, must be taken in the context of overall financial sustainability.

question: Deputy John Connolly asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science for an update on the provision of a borrowing framework for the technological universities.
reply:
The National Student Accommodation Strategy 2026-2035 recognises the important role that higher education institutions, including Technological Universities, can play in increasing student accommodation capacity.
Building on the Programme for Government commitment, my Department is working with the Higher Education Authority and the sector to examine the financing arrangements required to support future student accommodation projects.
As Minister, I am committed to ensuring that Technological Universities have the tools to support strategic investment and expand accommodation provision. One model which is widely used internationally is a nomination agreement. These provide institutions with guaranteed beds for their students while giving developers the occupancy certainty needed to secure finance and deliver new accommodation.
At present, Technological Universities do not have approval to enter into nomination agreements. My Department is working with the Departments of Finance, Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation, and the Higher Education Authority, to develop an appropriate mechanism, with the necessary safeguards and controls, to allow Technological Universities to enter into such agreements on a strictly limited basis. As part of this work, NewERA has agreed to undertake a financial assessment.
I will continue to advance this work to support the delivery of student accommodation while protecting institutional and Exchequer finances

question: Deputy John Lahart asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science if there has been consideration given to enhancing graduate entry medicine tuition support or a state-backed finance scheme; and the future plans for same.
reply:
I am committed to ensuring that financial circumstances do not present an undue barrier to participation in higher education and tertiary education. This is particularly important in disciplines where Ireland faces significant skills shortages, including healthcare professions.
In Budget 2027, the Government further strengthened these supports through a €34 million student support package, including increases in SUSI maintenance grants, enhanced student contribution grant supports for families with multiple students in tertiary education, expanded eligibility for certain supports, and measures to assist students with the cost of attending college.
The question of introducing an interest-free student loan scheme has been considered in a variety of policy contexts over the years. Any proposal of this nature would require careful consideration of its affordability, overall cost to the Exchequer, administrative arrangements, repayment mechanisms, impact on student participation and interaction with the existing student support framework. It would also need to be assessed in the context of wider Government priorities and value-for-money considerations.
There may, however, be circumstances where alternative financing models could assist students who face significant education costs but who are not eligible for existing grant supports. question: Deputy Robert Troy asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science the appeal process available for third level students in relation to free fee's for Irish students in circumstances (details supplied).
reply:
The State pays tuition fees, under the Free Fees Initiative, exclusive of the student contribution, on behalf of eligible students attending approved full-time undergraduate courses. To qualify for funding under the Department's Free Fees Initiative, students must meet the criteria of the scheme including the residency requirements in their own right.
To meet the residency criteria a student must have been ordinarily resident in an EU/EEA/Swiss/UK state for at least three of the five years preceding their entry to an approved third level course.
All students are required to meet the residency criteria of the scheme preceding their entry to an approved third level course. Under EU law, nationals of other EU jurisdictions are entitled to access education on the same basis as Irish citizens. Therefore, it would not be feasible to provide an exemption for persons of Irish nationality only.
The three out of five-year rule takes cognisance of students who wish to take time out to travel or work abroad. Such students can still meet the residency requirement if they have not been outside the countries referenced above for more than two of the previous five years. Similar, and in some cases more restrictive residency criteria apply in other countries. For example, in the UK, a student must be resident for the three years immediately preceding his/her commencement in college.

question: Deputy Maeve O'Connell asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science the projected increase of student enrolments over the next five years; and the anticipated additional funding that will be required to meet this demand.
reply:
In June, my Department published “Projections of Demand for Higher Education 2025–2045”, highlighting strong expected growth in demand for full-time higher education places over the coming years.
The report shows that overall student numbers are projected to rise significantly over the next five years, increasing by up to 18% from current levels, from 211,540 in the 2024/25 academic year to between 243,750 and 250,260 in the 2031/32 academic year, depending on the scenario considered.
The main drivers of this growth are a projected increase in undergraduate enrolment demand from Irish school leavers (demographic increase) and growth in postgraduate enrolment demand, with continued growth in non-EU postgraduate enrolment
Ireland experienced high annual births of over 70,000 between 2007 and 2012 (provisional number of births in 2025 was 54,125) – these individuals, who have been going through primary and secondary education, are now reaching higher education age. These trends have potential implications for funding for the higher education sector and will inform policy development and investment planning over the coming decade.
I am committed to supporting the higher education sector to meet this increasing demographic demand. The total allocation to higher education in Budget 2027 is €2.85 billion.

question: Deputy Thomas Gould asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science the reasons ICOT have been removed from the Interim List of Eligible Programs.
reply:
The Department does not comment on individual cases.
Inclusion on the Interim List of Eligible Programmes (ILEP) is necessary for a Higher Education or English language education provider to be eligible to recruit learners from non-EEA countries on Stamp 2 immigration permissions. The ILEP is administered by the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration in conjunction with the Department of Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science.
To have its programmes listed for this purpose, a provider must meet the relevant ILEP criteria on an ongoing basis. Where issues of non-compliance are identified and brought to the attention of the ILEP, these issues are reviewed and considered by a Committee comprised of officials from both Departments. Subject to its deliberations, this Committee may decide that the provider and its programmes are to be removed from the ILEP given the nature of non-compliance with established criteria. When such a decision is made and communicated, the provider may appeal within five working days and this shall be considered by the ILEP appeals committee.
It should be noted that the ILEP is in the process of being superseded by the TrustEd Ireland statutory quality mark. question: Deputy Seán Ó Fearghaíl asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science if he will address the concerns raised in correspondence (details supplied) regarding a university student who has been refused progression to fourth year.
reply:
I am sorry to learn of the difficulties experienced by the student concerned.
Higher education institutions are statutorily independent and autonomous bodies with responsibility for the management of their own academic and administrative affairs. Decisions concerning a student’s academic progression are therefore matters for the institution concerned, and neither I nor my Department has a role in reviewing or intervening in individual cases.
A student who wishes to challenge such a decision should, in the first instance, engage with the institution and avail of any relevant internal review, appeal or complaints procedures. Information on these procedures should be available directly from the institution.
Publicly funded higher education institutions come within the remit of the Office of the Ombudsman. Where a student has exhausted the institution’s internal procedures and remains dissatisfied, it is open to them to contact the Ombudsman. The Ombudsman may examine complaints concerning administrative actions or procedures, including alleged unfair treatment, a failure to provide clear reasons for a decision, undue delay or a failure to deal properly with a complaint. However, the Ombudsman cannot examine matters involving academic judgement.
Further information on making a complaint is available at www.ombudsman.ie or by contacting the Office of the Ombudsman at 6 Earlsfort Terrace, Dublin 2, D02 W773, or on 01 636 5600.

question: Deputy John Lahart asked the Minister for Health if there has been a provision in Budget 2027 for medical cards to be issued to lung fibrosis patients as a matter of routine care.
reply:
Medical card provision is primarily based on financial assessment. In accordance with the Health Act 1970 (as amended), eligibility for a medical card is determined by the HSE, which assesses each application on a qualifying financial threshold. This is the amount of money that an individual can earn per week and still qualify for a card. It is specific to the individual’s own financial circumstances.
People under 70 are assessed under the general means tested medical card thresholds which are based on an applicant’s household income after deduction of tax, PRSI and Universal Social Charge. Certain expenses are also taken into account. Detailed guidelines are available at: www2.hse.ie/services/schemes-allowances/medical-cards/applying/assessment/. People aged 70 or older are assessed under medical card income thresholds which are based on gross income. However, those aged over 70 can also be assessed under the general means tested scheme where there are particularly high medical costs. Details are available at: www2.hse.ie/services/schemes-allowances/medical-cards/other-types-of-medical-card/over-70s/.
The issue of granting medical cards on the basis of illness or a disability was previously examined in 2014 by the HSE Expert Panel on Medical Need and Medical Card Eligibility. The Group concluded that it was not feasible, desirable, nor ethically justifiable to list medical conditions in priority order for medical card eligibility. question: Deputy Seán Ó Fearghaíl asked the Minister for Transport if he will address the concerns raised in correspondence (details supplied) regarding the driver testing system, including matters relating to testing standards, consistency and the appeals process.
reply:
Under the Road Safety Authority Act 2006, the Road Safety Authority (RSA) has statutory responsibility for the National Driver Testing Service, including all operational matters. The RSA conducts the driving test to a standard that complies with the EU Driving Licence Directive. Given the RSA's responsibility in this matter, I have referred the Deputy's question to the Authority for direct response. Please contact my office if a reply is not received within ten days.
Pending this response, the RSA provides an appeals process whereby, if an applicant is unhappy with how a driving test was conducted or they believe they were unfairly treated, they can appeal the decision or raise a complaint.
Under section 33(6)(a) of the Road Traffic Act 1961, a person aggrieved by a test decision may also appeal to the District Court. The court will then examine whether or not the test was conducted properly. If the court determines that the tester did not conduct the test in accordance with procedures, a further test would be offered to the applicant free of charge.

question: Deputy Conor D. McGuinness asked the Minister for Transport if he has examined correspondence received by the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht regarding speed signage in Gaeltacht areas that continue to display speed limits in English only; and the steps he will take to overturn the rules laid out by his Department on the matter.
reply:
My Department received correspondence from the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht on the 16 February 2026. I issued a reply to the Minister on 25 May 2026.
The Official Languages Act 2003 at (Section 9) Regulations 2008 (SI 391/2008) at Section 3.3 exempts road signage from the requirement under the Act. However, the Traffic Signs Manual at Section 1.1.52 states:
It is a statutory requirement that place names on information signs be in both Irish and English, except:
For names of destinations in Gaeltacht areas where there is a direction by statute that only the Irish language version of the placename shall be used; and where the spelling of a place name is similar in both languages, in which case only the Irish form of the name should be shown.
I wish to assure you that at all times, especially within Gaeltacht areas, roads authorities are aware of their obligations under the provisions of the Traffic Signs Manual. It must be noted that a significant amount of traffic signage has the same display in both Irish and English. In addition, speed limit signs in the Republic of Ireland are language independent; hence no Irish or English text is used with them. They display a number along with the abbreviation km/h. Abbreviations such as ‘m’, ‘km’ and ‘km/h’ are Système International units and, as such, are not in any particular language. The abbreviation km/h is used because on the Island of Ireland the speed limits in the Republic are set in kilometres

question: Deputy John Lahart asked the Minister for Health for an update with regard to the regulation of vapes; and if she plans to restrict retail vaping outlets.
reply:
The focus of policy and legislation regarding nicotine inhaling products is on reducing youth use.
The Public Health (Tobacco Products and Nicotine Inhaling Products) Act 2023 introduced domestic regulation of nicotine inhaling products including:
• A minimum age of sale of 18
• Further advertising restrictions in cinemas, on public transport and near schools
• Prohibition on the sale of nicotine inhaling products by self-service, at events aimed at children, and from temporary or moveable premises.
A significant provision in the Act was the licensing system for the retail sale of tobacco products and nicotine inhaling products, which became operational for all retailers on 2 August 2026. Previously, there was a once-off registration system for tobacco retailers, and no register for retailers of nicotine inhaling products.
Those who wish to sell these products must now apply for a licence, pay the required fee and renew that licence annually. The licensing system will give the HSE's National Environmental Health Service robust oversight of who is selling nicotine inhaling products. The legislation allows for increased penalties for offences such as selling to minors, including revocation of a licence. In addition, licences will not be granted to temporary or moveable premises such as those at festivals, and the sale of these products at events aimed at children is also prohibited.

As Minister for Transport, I have responsibility for policy and overall funding in relation to public transport. However, I am not involved in the day-to-day operations of public transport. The National Transport Authority (NTA) has responsibility for the regulation of fares charged to passengers in respect of public transport services provided under public service obligation (PSO) contracts.
The Young Adult Card (YAC) provides individuals aged 19 to 25 with 50% off adult fares across the entire Transport for Ireland (TFI) network and for participating commercial operators. question: Deputy Barry Heneghan asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade the number of Irish election observers to be deployed to Serbia for the upcoming OSCE/ODIHR election observation mission; the number who have previous election observation experience; and if she will consider increasing the size of the Irish contingent and the proportion of experienced observers.
reply:
The Government is committed to supporting democratisation, human rights, and the rule of law, as a key element of our foreign policy. Support to election observation is central to this commitment and Ireland has contributed observers to international election observation missions since the 1990s.
The Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade maintains and administers a roster enabling Ireland to respond to calls to participate in election observation missions coordinated by the OSCE and the EU. The current five-year Roster commenced on 1 January 2024 and has 169 members.
In response to OSCE calls for nominations for positions on an Election Observation Mission to the Serbian Parliamentary Elections scheduled for 25 October 2026, one Irish Roster member has been selected and deployed as a Long-Term Observer. Ten further Roster members will shortly fill Short-Term Observer positions, all of whom have previous election observation mission experience.
The window for nominations to this mission is closed, with logistical planning for arrival of Short-Term Observers underway. The participation of 11 Irish observers is consistent with the level of participation in other OSCE missions in 2026.

reply:
The HSE, through National Doctors Training and Planning (NDTP), funds postgraduate specialist training in Psychiatry delivered by the College of Psychiatrists of Ireland at both Basic Specialist Training (BST) and Higher Specialist Training (HST) level.
For the 2026/2027 training year, 80 doctors commenced Basic specialty training (BST) and a further 47 commenced higher speciality training (HST) within Psychiatry. Planning for the July 2027 intake is continuing with the College of Psychiatrists of Ireland and the final HST intake will depend on the training posts and associated WTE/funding available.
Psychiatry operates a streamlined training pathway, whereby trainees who successfully complete BST and meet the College’s requirements for progression can progress to Higher Specialist Training. To support this progression, additional Psychiatry Senior training posts are being considered as part of plans to continue expansion of Postgraduate Medical Specialty Training Posts in 2027.
There has been significant expansion in postgraduate medical training capacity over the last five years, with the number of doctors enrolled in postgraduate medical training increasing by 21% over that period (HSE National Doctors Training and Planning (NDTP) Medical Workforce Report 2025–2026). This includes expansion in Psychiatry training posts in recent years, with BST intake in Psychiatry having increased by approximately 30% since 2021 and this increased cohort now progressing through to HST.
