question: Deputy Michael Healy-Rae asked the Minister for Social Protection the timeline for a decision to be made on a carer's allowance (details supplied) review.
reply:
Carer's allowance, CA, is a means-tested social assistance payment made to a person who is habitually resident in the State and who is providing full-time care and attention to a child or an adult who has such a disability that, as a result, they require that level of care.
An application for CA was received from the person concerned on 14 May 2026.
It is a condition for receipt of CA that every claimant shall furnish such certificates, documents, information, and evidence as may be required for the purposes of deciding their claim. A request to provide additional information issued to the person concerned on 26 June 2026. As the person concerned failed to supply all of the information requested, the claim was disallowed on 18 July 2026.
The person concerned was notified of their right to have the decision reviewed (where further information is available) or to appeal the decision to the Social Welfare Appeals Office (SWAO).
A subsequent review was initiated on foot of further documents received on 05 October 2026 and, following this review, CA was awarded from 14 May 2026.
The first payment will issue to the nominated bank account of the person concerned on 15 October 2026. Any arrears due will issue shortly.
The person concerned was notified of this decision in writing on 08 October 2026.
I hope this clarifies the position for the Deputy.

The €10 rate increase to pension payments is a 3.3% increase on 2026 rates. The increase will come into effect in January 2027. This increase is greater than the forecasted inflation for 2027 and means that, for the first time, the State Pension (Contributory) will exceed €300 per week, increasing to €309.30. The €10 rate increase to working age schemes represent a 3.9% increase on 2026 rates.
The across the board rate increase announced in Budget 2027 will assist in mitigating the prices increase for both pension and working age recipients.
In determining Budget rates, consideration is given not only to the headline rates but also targeted secondary supports. That is why, as part of Budget 2027, I also announced an increase to the Living Alone Allowance of €3 per week, the Child Support Payment of €6 and an increase of €5 to the weekly rate for Fuel Allowance. An initial Cost of Disability payment of €500 for recipients of long-term disability payments will also be paid in the first quarter of 2027.
Changes to social welfare rates, are based on a wide range of inputs used by my Department, most notably CSO data including the survey of income and living conditions, SILC, the labour force survey, the monthly CPI and HICP releases and the CSO earnings and hours in employment surveys. question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Social Protection the number of international protection applicants who, while in receipt of a social welfare payment or dependent-related payment, entered prison in each of the past five years; what happened to each payment during imprisonment; the number transferred to a spouse, partner or other dependent; and the total annual cost involved.
reply:
My department administers the Daily Expenses Allowance which is paid to International Protection Applicants who reside in, or are waiting for, accommodation provided by the International Protection Accommodation Services. The current weekly rates of payment are €38.80 per adult and €29.80 per child. In addition there is an increased rate of €113.80 per week for an adult applies where a person is unaccommodated and is on a waiting list for International Protection Accommodation Service.
Where an International Protection Applicant enters prison, their Daily Expenses Allowance claim is closed, as they no longer satisfy the conditions for payment
Daily Expense Allowance is paid on an individual basis, meaning that each eligible adult has their own payment and couples are not paid together. Where there are children in the family, the other parent can apply to have the children added to their Daily Expense Allowance payment.
The Department does not compile statistics on recipients of Daily Expenses Allowance who enter prison, nor does it maintain records of the number of child payments transferred to the other parent. Consequently, the statistical information requested is not available.
I trust this clarifies the issue for the Deputy.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Social Protection the number of persons who became Irish citizens in each of the past five years who subsequently received social welfare payments and were subsequently imprisoned; what payments they were receiving immediately prior to imprisonment; whether those payments ceased, were suspended or continued for dependants; and the total value of payments made to their dependants during their imprisonment.
reply: The Department of Social Protection does not collect or maintain data on persons becoming Irish citizens, or on customers' legal status. Statistics on welfare payments to and legal status of naturalised citizens are not available.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Social Protection the number of persons whose social welfare payment was suspended or terminated following imprisonment in each of the past five years; the number whose qualified adult or child increases continued to be paid to another person; the number of such cases involving non-Irish nationals; and the number involving persons who had previously acquired Irish citizenship.
reply:
Statistics on suspension or termination of welfare payments due to imprisonment are not available. My Department operates over 90 schemes and services, operated across a number of different operational systems, and claim closure reasons are not always populated; in other cases multiple reasons for a closure could apply but only one reason is recorded.
The Department of Social Protection does not collect or maintain data on persons becoming Irish citizens, or on customers' legal status. Statistics on welfare payments to and legal status of naturalised citizens are not available.

question: Deputy Paul Lawless asked the Minister for Social Protection if consideration is being given to providing additional pension protections for parents who have provided lifelong care to a son or daughter with a disability and who may have reduced pay related social insurance contribution records as a consequence of their caring responsibilities.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 488, 489, 490, 491, 492 and 493 together.
My Department provides State Pension payments through the State Pension (Contributory), which is a contributory payment based on a person's social insurance record, and the State Pension (Non-Contributory) which is a means-tested social assistance payment.
The State Pension (Contributory) (SPC) is funded from the Social Insurance Fund through the contributions paid by workers and employers. The rate of payment reflects the number of social insurance contributions paid over a working life. Eligibility for the SPC is based on a number of criteria:
• Being aged 66 or over.
• Having entered the Social Insurance system 10 years before drawdown of the SPC.
• Having a minimum of 520 paid social insurance contributions (i.e., 10 years reckonable PRSI contributions).
This Government acknowledges the important role that carers play and is fully committed to supporting them in that role. Accordingly, carers are not excluded from access to the SPC. Once a person has met the minimum requirement of 520 paid contributions, the State Pension system gives significant recognition to those whose work history includes extended periods outside of paid employment, often to raise families or in a full-time caring role including:
• PRSI credits (which include Credits for Carer's Benefit and Carer's Allowance), and
• Homemaking Disregards and HomeCaring Periods to recognise caring periods of up to 20 years outside of paid empl

question: Deputy Conor D. McGuinness asked the Minister for Social Protection if he has considered extending the age limit for domiciliary care allowance from sixteen to eighteen-years-of-age.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 486 and 487 together.
Domiciliary Care Allowance is a non-means tested payment to a parent or guardian in respect of a child under 16 who has a severe disability and requires substantially more care and attention than would normally be needed by a child of the same age.
From January 2026, the monthly rate of Domiciliary Care Allowance increased from €360 to €380. More than 65,950 families currently receive the payment in respect of approximately 75,496 children, with estimated expenditure of almost €359 million in 2026.
Domiciliary Care Allowance stops being paid when a child turns 16 years of age. If the young person has a disability that significantly impacts their daily living activities, they can then apply for a Disability Allowance payment in their own name of €254 per week. question: Deputy Donnchadh Ó Laoghaire asked the Minister for Social Protection the length of time it is currently taking for reviews of disability allowance applications to be undertaken.
reply:
Disability Allowance is a weekly allowance paid to people with a specified disability who are aged 16 or over and under the age of 66. This disability must be expected to last for at least one year and the allowance is subject to a medical assessment, means test and Habitual Residency conditions.
Processing times for new applications vary across schemes, depending on the differing qualification criteria. Schemes that require a high level of documentary evidence from the customer, particularly in the case of illness-related schemes, can take longer to process.
Currently the average number of weeks to award a Disability Allowance claim in September 2025 is 5 weeks. The average processing time for an appeal on Disability Allowance, from date of appeal to the last decision on the appeal, was 12.7 weeks.

question: Deputy Colm Burke asked the Minister for Social Protection if his Department will consider an increase in the secondary dinner rate with a drink in the school meals programme to €3,20 from €2.50 to equalise it with the hot schools meal and backdate it to the beginning of this school year, as providers are finding it difficult to maintain services with the costs incurred.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 478 and 483 together.
All 3,200 primary schools and 550,000 children are eligible for hot school meals. Across all meal types there some 3,700 schools and 682,000 children are eligible for support. This equates to the distribution of up to 3.4 million school meals per week. The budget for 2026 is €286 million.
The Hot School Meals Scheme introduced in 2019 was specifically developed for Primary Schools. Recognising that the vast majority of primary schools do not have catering facilities the funding model is calibrated to allow for off-site preparation and delivery to the schools. In contrast, the dinner option available under the School Meals Programme for DEIS Secondary schools was developed and tendered on the basis that meals would be prepared on-site, utilising the canteen facilities available in those schools.
Secondary schools issued requests for tenders based on the payment rates available, rates that were well known among interested food business operators within the food services industry.
The rate for the dinner model was increased in 2023 when there was an increase for all options under the School Meals Programme. There are no plans for a further increase at this time.
I trust this clarifies the matter for the Deputy.

question: Deputy Frankie Feighan asked the Minister for Social Protection if the mechanism to pay suppliers under the current school meals programme has been modified; and if the Minister is satisfied that all suppliers will be paid within 30 days of invoices having been submitted.
reply:
Under the School Meals Programme, the primary relationship is between the school and supplier. My department provides the funding for the meals directly to the school and it is the responsibility of each school board to administer the Programme in their school including managing the procurement process. All schools are responsible for choosing their school meals supplier on the open market, in a fair and transparent manner in accordance with public procurement rules. These rules clearly define the successful tenderer's responsibilities and obligations, including adherence to the nutritional standards.
The payment mechanism for the School Meals Programme has not been modified. Funding is awarded on receipt of a fully completed and signed application form which includes all supporting documentation. These include a signed service level agreement with the Department, a menu compliant with the Programmes Nutrition Standards, details of income and expenditure including banks statements and invoices.
Schools as independent public bodies are responsible for paying suppliers invoices.
I trust this clarifies the position for the Deputy.

question: Deputy Willie O'Dea asked the Minister for Social Protection if he will give consideration to removing the mandatory certificate of benefit comparison requirement for straightforward defined contribution-to-PRSA transfers, where there is an identifiable fund value; in situations where the consumer is receiving appropriate regulated financial advice, including the material benefits being surrendered and the reasons the transfer is considered suitable, given this would remove an unnecessary cost and administrative barrier for ordinary defined contribution pension savers seeking to consolidate their pensions.
reply:
Under section 113 of the Pensions Act 1990, as amended, when assets are transferred from an occupational pension scheme to a PRSA, the PRSA provider is required to furnish the individual with a Certificate of Benefit Comparison (CBC), which compares the possible benefits of the scheme with the possible benefits from the PRSA.
The report of the Inter-Departmental Pensions Reform and Taxation Group in November 2020 recommended that the Pensions Authority reconsider the requirements in relation to the provision of CBCs, in particular in relation to transfers to PRSAs from defined contribution pension arrangements and make recommendations to my Department for legislative change where necessary.
My Department has worked in conjunction with the Pensions Authority to examine the requirements for CBCs and has developed policy and draft legislative proposals to simplify the requirements in the case of transfers from defined contribution schemes to PRSAs.
It is anticipated that these proposals will be submitted to Government in the near future for approval and referral to the Office of the Parliamentary Counsel of the Government for drafting.
I trust this clarifies the matter for the Deputy.

question: Deputy Seán Ó Fearghaíl asked the Minister for Defence if she will examine the possibility of extending access to the swimming pool at the Curragh Camp to residents of the Curragh, Newbridge and surrounding areas; if any assessment has been carried out regarding wider community use of the facility; and the measures that would be required to facilitate public access.
reply:
I am advised that while the swimming pool in the Defence Forces Training Centre, Curragh Camp is primarily for the training and exercise of Defence Forces personnel, my Department positively engages with local schools and community groups in allowing the use of this facility. Taking into account Defence Forces usage, the limited availability that remains has now being allocated to local National Schools and a community group located in the immediate vicinity of the camp.
Permission for the use of the pool is subject at all times to Defence Forces requirements and signed conditions, which includes the requirement for the schools and organisations to have appropriate insurance.

reply:

question: Deputy Ruairí Ó Murchú asked the Minister for Social Protection the number of applications for fuel allowance refused to date in 2026.
reply:
Fuel Allowance is a payment to help with the cost of heating a person's home during the winter months, and is usually paid as an additional amount on top of a person's underlying payment. The 2026/2027 Fuel Allowance began to be paid from 28 September 2026. I was pleased to announce as part of Budget 2027 that Fuel Allowance will increase to €43 per week from January 2027.
Due to the way Fuel Allowance operates as an additional payment on top of an underlying qualifying scheme, this involves multiple different operational systems. Fuel Allowance processing statistics, including refusals, are collected on an annual, rather than monthly, basis due to the complexity involved, and are subsequently published in the Departments Annual Statistics Report, available from gove.ie/dsp/statistics.
In 2025, 39,521 Fuel Allowance claims were awarded and 12,099 claims for Fuel Allowance were rejected.

question: Deputy Michael Healy-Rae asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage his plans for funding to be made available to local authorities through the Housing Activation Office for projects to unlock housing.
reply:
The Housing Activation Office (HAO) is responsible for managing the €1 billion Housing Infrastructure Investment Fund (HIIF), which was launched by Government in January 2026 to support the delivery of housing-enabling infrastructure.
Under the first funding call opened in January 2026, I invited applications from local authorities and the Land Development Agency. Following assessment of the applications received, 82 infrastructure projects were accepted onto the HIIF programme in June 2026.
These projects relate to sites where infrastructure deficits have been identified as barriers to housing delivery. The approved projects span transport, water, wastewater, electricity and other housing-enabling infrastructure and will support the activation of housing sites at both a local level and a number of strategically important locations.
The HAO team is working directly with local authorities and the Land Development Agency to progress the 82 projects and with critical utilities such as Uisce Éireann and ESB Networks to ensure complementary investment in water and energy in tandem with the delivery of the 82 projects.

question: Deputy Albert Dolan asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage the actual and projected number of residential dwellings and population for each local authority for 2020, 2025 and 2030 under the assumptions used for national and regional planning; and the resulting number of dwellings per 100 persons in each local authority for each of those years, in tabular form.
reply:

The Revised NPF strategy sets out the need to plan for a projected population of at least 6.1m people in Ireland by 2040. Taking into account ‘pent-up’ demand, the strategy sets out a need to plan for the delivery of approximately 50,000 additional housing units per annum nationally, to 2040.
As part of the revision process, the Economic and Social Research Institute (ESRI) were engaged to update their previous projections relating to population growth to 2040, based on demographic and econometric modelling and having regard to the results of Census 2022 and other factors with potential to influence fertility, mortality and migration trends.
The ESRI projections published in July 2024 estimated that the population of Ireland will increase by around one million people or by 20% over 2022 levels, to around 5.7m by 2030 and approximately 6.1 million people by 2040, with higher figures of 5.9m and 6.3m people respectively in a ‘high-migration’ scenario.
To ensure that local authority development plans reflect the requirements of the NPF in respect of housing as soon as possible, I issued the NPF Implementation: Housing Growth Requirements Guidelines under section 28 of the Planning and Development Act 2000 in July 2025. question: Deputy Albert Dolan asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage if targets have been established for the number of vacant residential properties to be returned to use for each year from 2026 to 2030; if so, to provide those targets, by local authority, in tabular form; and, if not, the reason progress in reducing residential vacancy is to be measured and assessed.
reply:

My Department also provides annual funding to local authorities to strengthen their capacity to tackle vacancy and dereliction. This includes funding for Vacant Homes Officers and the Compulsory Purchase Order Activation Programme, which assists local authorities identify and bring vacant and derelict properties back into use.
While the Vacant Property Refurbishment Grant aims to support the delivery of 20,000 homes, annual targets are not set for the return of residential properties to use.
The management and maintenance of local authority social homes is the responsibility of respective local authorities under s.58 of the Housing Act 1966. Local authorities must ensure, in line with these responsibilities, that all tenanted properties comply with the Housing (Standards for Rented Houses) Regulations 2019 and that they make adequate budgetary provision for repairs and cyclical maintenance, drawing on housing rental income as part of their annual budget process.

The timing of the issuing of National Planning Statements will be based on Government priorities.

question: Deputy Seán Kyne asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage whether motions passed and agreed by elected members of local authorities who opposed wind farm or solar farm developments and seeking moratoriums on future developments can be taken into account by planning authorities and by An Coimisiún Pleanála when determining planning applications.
reply:
Public participation is a crucial element of all substantive decision-making processes under the Planning and Development Act 2000, and the Planning and Development Act 2024. It is likely that both of the proposed draft National Planning Statements on Wind Energy and Solar Energy development will be subject to Strategic Environmental Assessment and that a public consultation will be held as part of this process, whereby individuals and stakeholders – including the local authorities and their elected members – will have the opportunity to make observations on the draft National Planning Statements.
In addition, it is open to any member of the public to make an observation or submission on a planning application, including in relation to solar energy developments, and the planning authority is statutorily obliged to consider such submissions before making a decision on the application. Persons who make submissions are also entitled to be notified of any significant further information provided to the planning authority by the applicant and to be notified of the authority’s decision on the application.
Furthermore, any person who made a submission on a planning application may appeal the planning authority’s decision on the application to An Coimisiun Pleanála or may make a submission to the Board in relation to an appeal of that decision.

question: Deputy Niall Collins asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage his views on correspondence (details supplied).
reply:
In the first instance, the management and delivery of the development contribution scheme waiver is a matter for the local authorities concerned, and Local Authority officials will determine locally if a waiver applicant has complied with the terms and conditions of the scheme.

In line with commitments in Delivering Homes, Building Communities, my Department is currently developing a revised social housing estate remediation and regeneration programme. question: Deputy Eoin Ó Broin asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage for an update on the review of HAP rates; and if changes will be made to the rates or levels of discretion in 2026.
reply:
The HAP scheme plays a vital role in housing eligible families and individuals. At the end of Q1 2026, over 133,100 HAP tenancies had been set up since the scheme commenced, of which there were 48,355 households actively in receipt of HAP support nationally.
Maximum rent limits for HAP were set for each housing authority area in 2016 in conjunction with the Department of Social Protection. Since 11 July 2022, each local authority has statutory discretion to agree to a HAP payment up to 35% above the prescribed maximum rent limit. Discretion can be increased up to 50% above the prescribed maximum rent limits for Homeless HAP tenancies in Dublin. Local authorities also have additional flexibility to apply a couple HAP rate to single-person households.
I gave my approval for a review of the current HAP rent limits to be undertaken to ensure there is sufficient support under the HAP scheme to assist eligible households in accessing accommodation in the private rental sector.
As part of this review, the Housing Agency carried out an analysis of the rental market and submitted its report to my Department on 16 July. This helped inform my Department’s review of the HAP rent limits, which has now concluded. I am currently considering its findings before setting out the next steps.

question: Deputy Eoin Ó Broin asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage for an update on the child homelessness strategy; when it will be published; and the additional funding for homeless prevention that will be allocated for 2027.
reply:
Supporting individuals and families experiencing or at risk of experiencing homelessness is a priority for my Department and Government. Our housing plan, ‘Delivering Homes, Building Communities: An Action Plan on Housing Supply and Targeting Homelessness’ is an integrated housing and homelessness plan. The Plan is based on two key pillars: activating the supply of 300,000 more homes; and supporting people to have a home of their own.
Increased supply is key to addressing homelessness. Government is focused on making sure that everyone has access to good quality, affordable and secure homes that suit their needs.
Our Plan recognises that homelessness is the single most pressing social issue that we face and introduces a number of key measures to address homelessness.
Addressing family homelessness is a key priority for Government. Our housing plan commits to the development of a Child and Family Homelessness Action Plan. This has brought together key stakeholders to drive the continued focus on preventing children and families entering emergency accommodation, providing enhanced supports for children experiencing homelessness, as well as measures to accelerate exits and reduce the time spent by children and their families in homeless emergency accommodation. It is intended it that the plan will be published shortly.
Prevention of homelessness in the first instance is an absolute priority. There are many prevention initiatives already underway in my own Department and across G

question: Deputy Brian Brennan asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage if he will consider a review of the commercial rates for an industry (details supplied).
reply:
Tailte Éireann is an independent Government agency and provides a property registration system, property valuation service, and national mapping and surveying infrastructure for the State. Tailte Éireann is independent in the exercise of its valuation functions under the Valuation Act 2001, as amended (the Act). Tailte Éireann has overall responsibility under the Act, for the maintenance of all Valuation Lists used by Local Authorities in the calculation of rates liability.
Schedule 3 of the Act paragraphs 1(a) and (b), provides that all buildings and lands used or developed for any purpose, are rateable. The starting premise under the Act is that all interests (including buildings) and all developed land are rateable unless expressly exempted under Schedule 4. There is a very specific range of exemptions that can be applied, and Tailte Éireann has no discretionary latitude to grant exemptions not covered by Schedule 4.
Paragraph 5 of Schedule 4 provides that ‘farm buildings’ are an exempt category of property. question: Deputy Maeve O'Connell asked the Minister for Defence if her Department has considered expanding the structures of the Defence Forces reserves to allow people with critical skills such as cybersecurity to contribute to the Defence Forces knowledge base.
reply:
My key priority as Minister for Defence is the modernisation of our Defence Forces and revitalising our Reserve Defence Force is a vital part of that transformation process.
In July 2024, the Defence Forces Office of Reserve published the RDF Regeneration and Development Plan which contains 27 actions across four objectives [(i) Recruitment & Retention, (ii) Resourcing, (iii) Training & Education, and (iv) Integration & Deployment, designed to operationalise the recommendations contained in the CoDF Report, for the RDF.
One action, ‘Specialist Reserve Capabilities’, references the exploration of mechanisms for the development of specialist capabilities to augment and support PDF operations. The military authorities advise that development of this action will proceed following consideration of wider Defence Design proposals.
Additionally, the Detailed Implementation Plan Recommendation #75 requires ‘Specific Skillset Profiling’ of the RDF to be completed. The Defence Forces are currently engaging with key stakeholders throughout the Defence Organisation in relation to the creation of a bespoke solution to capture such data.
The Reserve Defence Force currently has personnel with specialist cyber skills serving within its establishment. These members provide valuable cyber expertise to the Defence Forces and regularly participate in Defence Forces-led and international cyber exercises, contributing essential specialist capability in this important domain.

question: Deputy Cian O'Callaghan asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage to provide an update on the development of the Apartment and Duplex Defects Remediation Bill 2024; when the Bill will come before the Houses of the Oireachtas; and if the remediation scheme will cover balcony defects.
reply:
Drafting of the Apartment and Duplex Defects Remediation Scheme Bill is at an advanced stage and it is listed for publication this session. The statutory scheme will be in place as soon as possible following its passage through the Dáil.
The Scheme will provide supports for the remediation of relevant fire safety, structural safety and water ingress defects in purpose-built apartment buildings, including duplexes, constructed between 1991 and 2013. It is envisaged that 100% of eligible remediation costs will be funded. The content of the final Bill will be a matter for the Government to agree in due course.
It is expected that applicants to the current Interim Remediation Scheme will transfer seamlessly over to the new statutory scheme, which will be managed by the Housing Agency. My Department and the Housing Agency will work to ensure that applications under the statutory scheme are progressed as quickly as possible.

question: Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage the number of households on social housing waiting lists in November 2025 that had entered the State within the previous ten years; and if he will provide a breakdown by immigration category.
reply:
My Department does not collect data on households qualified for social housing support by date of entry to the State. Accordingly, the information requested is not available.
Details on the number of households qualified for social housing support in each local authority administrative area is provided in the annual statutory Summary of Social Housing Assessments (SSHA).
The most recently published summary for all counties, conducted in November 2025, is available on my Department's website, along with all summaries since 2011 at www.gov.ie/en/collection/62486-summary-of-social-housing-assessments/.
Details of the citizenship of the main applicant qualified for social housing support for each local authority are included in tables 2.9 and A1.9 in the report.

question: Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage if persons granted refugee status, subsidiary protection status or permission to remain are subject to the same social housing waiting list rules and prioritisation criteria as Irish citizens; and if he will provide details of the exemptions that apply.
reply:
Social housing support is intended to address a household’s long-term housing need. Therefore, households applying for such support have a long-term permission to reside in the State. It is the responsibility of the local authority to make a decision in each individual case with regard to qualification for social housing support, in accordance with the eligibility and need criteria set down in section 20 of the Housing (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 2009 and the associated Social Housing Assessment Regulations 2011, as amended, and associated Housing Circulars.
Persons granted refugee status, subsidiary protection status or permission to remain are eligible to be considered for social housing support, from the date of granting of such status, on the same basis as an Irish citizen. The residency requirements governing access to social housing support arise from the State's constitutional, European Union and international legal obligations. These requirements seek to ensure that social housing supports are available to persons who have a lawful and sufficient right to reside in the State, while complying with Ireland's obligations under domestic law, EU law and international protection frameworks

question: Deputy Willie O'Dea asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage the number of people who have applied for the enhanced defective concrete blocks grant scheme in Limerick; the estimated total number of applicants in Limerick in the future; the reason the cost of demolition and the removal of asbestos is not allowed under the scheme; and his views on whether it is unfair that an individual may have to pay significantly more than the grant awarded to rebuild their house.
reply:
The total number of applications received by Limerick City and County Council under the Defective Concrete Blocks Grant Scheme, as at 31 August 2026, is 100. reply:

question: Deputy Pádraig O'Sullivan asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage further to the Budget 2027 Expenditure Report, which states that €5.6 billion in capital expenditure is being provided to Programme A – Housing in 2027, the reason the Estimates for Public Services 2027 set out in the same report provide capital of €5,201 million for Programme A, compared with €5,218 million in 2026; and a reconciliation of the two figures.
reply:
The difference between the figures published in the Estimates for Public Services 2027 and those set out in the Vote Chapter arises for technical reasons. Certain capital subheads previously managed within the Department's Planning Division are now under the remit of the Housing Activation Office within the Department's Housing Division, and are included in the NDP Sectoral Plan for Housing. This transfer is not yet reflected in the subhead structure used for the Estimates for Public Services 2027.
The updated subhead structure will be reflected in the Revised Estimates Volume (REV) to be published later this year. Under the revised structure, Programme A capital will amount to €5.6 billion and Programme D capital will reduce to €45 million (both net of apportioned administrative costs), as indicated in the Budget 2027 Expenditure Report. This is a presentational change only and does not affect the overall level of funding provided.

question: Deputy Pádraig O'Sullivan asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage the reason the number of housing assistance payment and rental accommodation scheme tenancies provided for falls from some 61,000 in the Budget 2026 Expenditure Report to approximately 56,000 in the Budget 2027 Expenditure Report, notwithstanding provision for over 8,000 new tenancies in each year.
reply:
The figures in the Budget Expenditure Reports reflect estimates of the number of Housing Assistance Payment (HAP) and Rental Accommodation Scheme (RAS) tenancies requiring continued support in the relevant year.
The lower combined estimate for 2027 reflects the net reduction in active HAP tenancies during 2026, whilst active RAS tenancies have increased slightly. It should be noted that both schemes are demand led.
My Department is satisfied that funding provided for 2027 is sufficient to support the number of existing and new tenancies under both schemes. Demand and expenditure will continue to be monitored throughout the year.

question: Deputy Pa Daly asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment further to Parliamentary Question No. 69365/26, (details supplied) if he is aware of concerns that data centres are putting the delivery of housing at risk; the measures he is taking to ensure that he delivers housing targets in light of these concerns.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 33 and 43 together.
Section 9 of the Electricity Regulation Act 1999 (as amended) sets out the responsibilities of the CRU with regard to electricity security of supply, which includes ensuring that supply and demand growth remain in balance. CRU have a dedicated email for queries via oireachtas@cru.ie.
EirGrid complement this role in their function as Transmission System Operator (TSO) through developing, managing and operating the transmission grid in Ireland. They balance supply and demand on an on-going basis, while also planning for Ireland’s long-term electricity needs. As part of its role in planning the electricity system, EirGrid publishes an annual All-Island Resource Adequacy Assessment (AIRAA) which provides a forecast for supply and demand on the all-island electricity grid over the next ten years. Ireland’s electricity security of supply is improving year on year. Overall, the AIRAA 2026-35 shows marked progress on the outlook for security of supply over the last five years.
The Government continues to work with electricity system operators to assess the various expected future demands on the system including from economic and population growth, housing, electric vehicle and heat pump targets in addition to data centre growth as part of their network development plans to ensure medium and long term future demands on our electricity system continue to be supported.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage the national guidance issued to local authorities regarding the retention, termination and reallocation of social housing where the tenant is imprisoned.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 426 and 427 together.
The management and administration of local authority housing tenancies is, in the first instance, a matter for each local authority in the exercise of its statutory functions under the Housing Acts 1966 - 2026.
My Department does not issue specific guidance or policy to housing authorities dealing with tenancy arrangements or the termination of tenancies solely on the basis that a tenant has received a custodial sentence. Any decision regarding the continuation, management or termination of a tenancy is a matter for the local authority concerned, having regard to the relevant legislative provisions, the terms and conditions of the tenancy agreement, the circumstances of the individual case, and the local authority's own policies and procedures.
Local authorities act in accordance with the provisions of the Housing Acts 1966 - 2026, fair procedures and their broader responsibilities in relation to tenancy and estate management. Accordingly, responsibility for decisions affecting individual tenancies rests with the relevant local authority.

• Applicant(s) that previously purchased or built a residential dwelling/dwellings, but has been divested of this through insolvency or bankruptcy proceedings, are eligible to apply. question: Deputy Réada Cronin asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage whether his Department is considering applying a rent pressure zone to older persons' accommodation.
reply:
The Residential Tenancies Acts 2004 to 2026 (RTA) regulate the landlord-tenant relationship in the residential rental sector and set out the rights and obligations of landlords and tenants.
On 1 March 2026, the Residential Tenancies (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 2026 came into operation. The Act provides for a national rent control and significantly strengthens security of tenure for tenants, while also encouraging more private investment in the rental market. The new national rent control limits rent increases to inflation as measured by the Consumer Price Index (CPI), up to a maximum of 2%. For new build apartments and student-specific accommodation, however, rent increases are capped at the level of inflation (CPI) only.
In order to stimulate investment and keep existing landlords in the market, the resetting of rents to market value is now allowed, as part of the reform of rent controls for new tenancies created on or after 1 March 2026, with certain exceptions. The linking of rent control to a property, rather than a tenancy, under the previous Rent Pressure Zone (RPZ) system of rent control made investment in rental accommodation less attractive in Ireland. By allowing rent resetting for new tenancies from 1 March 2026, existing and new landlords, who are vital for the sector, can ensure that their investment remains viable.

question: Deputy Michael Healy-Rae asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment the efforts being made to decrease waiting times for those waiting for the warmer home scheme.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 25, 31 and 42 together.
The Warmer Homes Scheme (WHS) aims to improve the energy efficiency and warmth of homes owned by people at risk of energy poverty by providing fully funded retrofits. The scheme is operated by the Sustainable Energy Authority of Ireland (SEAI) on behalf of my Department and is funded through carbon tax revenues and the European Regional Development Fund.
The scheme targets support to those on the lowest incomes who are living in the least efficient homes so that the resources available can have the greatest impact in addressing energy poverty. Over 8,100 homes were upgraded last year, 109% of the annual target.
Applications to the scheme are assessed on the basis of when they first apply to the SEAI. Homes with the worst Building Energy Ratings also known as BER (E, F or G) are then prioritised for works. No other prioritisation takes place under the scheme.
Under the WHS, a pre-works BER is an obligation mandated for EU funding via the ERDF. The BER rating enables the SEAI to prioritise the worst performing homes and it is also key in determining the increase in energy efficiency as a result of the works upon completion.
Over 8,060 upgrades were completed under the scheme to end September 2026, an increase of 34.5% on the same period last year. At the same time, 11,823 applications have been received to the WHS to end September compared to 7,905 in the same time window last year, an increase of 49.6%.

question: Deputy Natasha Newsome Drennan asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage for an update on the review of the 2006 wind energy development guidelines; and when new guidelines will be published.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 419, 443 and 457 together.
In line with commitments in the Programme for Government 2025, my Department is working with the Department of Climate, Energy and the Environment (DCEE), which holds policy responsibility for renewable energy matters, in respect of the introduction of a number of National Planning Statements related to Ireland's Climate Action Plan target to increase the share of electricity generated from renewable sources up to 80% in 2030. This includes the preparation of a National Planning Statement in relation to onshore wind energy development, following a review of the existing 2006 Wind Energy Development Guidelines.
Further to the commencement of Chapter 3 of Part 3 of the Planning and Development Act 2024 on 2 October 2025, provisions for National Planning Statements have been introduced to replace the provisions for Ministerial guidelines issued under section 28 of the Planning and Development Act 2000. All existing Section 28 guidelines will, over time, be revoked and replaced with new National Planning Statements. Any current section 28 guidelines will however remain in force until revoked or replaced by a corresponding National Planning Statement. The timing of the issuing of National Planning Statements will be based on Government priorities.

question: Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage the engagements by him or officials in his Department concerning the failure of Wicklow County Council to commence any social or affordable housing schemes in Arklow, County Wicklow; and the pressure he may be able to place on the council to develop housing in the town.
reply:

Accordingly, the development and implementation of individual housing projects is a matter for the relevant local authority, in this case Wicklow County Council.
My Department engages regularly with local authorities, including Wicklow County Council, regarding housing delivery and the achievement of national housing targets. However, decisions relating to the identification, prioritisation and progression of specific housing schemes within a local authority area are matters for the local authority concerned.
Local authorities, including Wicklow County Council, are currently finalising their Housing Delivery Action Plans (HDAPs) for the period 2027-2030. When published, these plans will set out the local authority's projected social and affordable housing delivery programme. These plans will be supported by the significant investment being made under Delivering Homes, Building Communities, the Government's national housing plan.
In 2026 alone, more than €9 billion is being provided in capital investment for housing, including investment through the Land Development Agency and Housing Finance Agency lending. This is supplemented by over €2 billion in current expenditure funding to support housing need and housing delivery. In addition to funding provided directly to local authorities, my Department also supp

question: Deputy John Connolly asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage the number of approvals under the local authority home loan scheme for each local authority in 2024 and 2025 and to date in 2026; and the resources provided to each local authority under the local authority home loan scheme in 2024, 2025 and to date in 2026, in tabular form.
reply:
Applications for a Local Authority Home Loan are made through individual local authorities and the final decision on loan approval is a matter for the relevant local authority and its Credit Committee on a case-by-case basis. Decisions on all housing loan applications must be made in accordance with the Regulations establishing the scheme and the Credit Policy that underpins the scheme, in order to ensure prudence and consistency in approach in the best interests of both borrowers and local authorities.
My Department publishes information on the number and value of (i) local authority loan approvals and (ii) local authority loan drawdowns. Local authority approval means that an official letter of offer has been sent to a borrower (and therefore relates to a specific property and loan amount). Information on drawdowns, approvals, average drawdowns, and average approvals for Local Authority Home Loans are available on my Department’s website at the following link: www.gov.ie/en/collection/42d2f-local-authority-loan-activity/#local-authority-loans-approvedpaid.
Each year, my Department allocates Local Authorities a limit for new lending approvals under the Local Authority Home Loan schemes. The allocations for 2024, 2025 and 2026 are set out in the table below.

question: Deputy John Connolly asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage whether his Department, the National Monuments Service, the National Parks and Wildlife Service, or an agency under his remit has assessed, or intends to assess, the suitability of High Island (Ardoileán), Claddaghduff, County Galway, for acquisition by the State in light of its archaeological and cultural significance (details supplied); whether the site has previously been considered for State acquisition; whether any discussions have taken place with the current owner regarding its future protection and stewardship.
reply: My Department acquires heritage structures and monuments, which are either of national or strategic importance, from time to time as resources and opportunities permit. In all cases, the Department assesses potential acquisitions carefully, taking into consideration similar existing properties within the State portfolio, gaps in the State portfolio, the conservation and maintenance needs, and the short and long-term cost of acquisition/maintenance to the Exchequer. It is on this basis that the Department is only ever in a position to make a very limited number of acquisitions in any given fiscal year.

question: Deputy Albert Dolan asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage to outline the Government’s plans for the wind-down of the cessation of turf cutting compensation scheme; the number of participants whose entitlement under the scheme is due to expire in each of the next five years; whether a replacement or successor scheme is being considered; the arrangements that will apply to affected landowners and turbary right holders once their current compensation period ends; the consultation that will take place with those affected; and the next steps and timeline for decisions in this regard.
reply:
The Cessation of Turf Cutting Compensation Scheme (CTCCS) was established following engagement with stakeholders in 2011 for active domestic turf cutters arising from the restrictions on turf cutting on 53 raised bog special areas of conservation (SAC) and was extended in 2014 to include 36 raised bog natural heritage areas (NHA).
In 2026, 986 qualified CTCCS applicants received their final annuity payments. The below table shows the number of qualified CTCCS applicants where their entitlement will end in the coming years, and it is dependent on when they entered the CTCCS.
This scheme has compensated those impacted by restrictions on turf-cutting on protected sites, and over its 15-year term has helped to ensure the conservation of important peatland sites of unique ecological value.
It has enabled progress in the achievement of national and European conservation targets and supports UN Sustainable Development Goals (target 15.1 relating to the conservation of terrestrial ecosystems, Target 15.3 relating to combating land degradation, and SDG Target 15.5 relating to natural habitats and the loss of biodiversity).
Recent reporting on the status of protected habitats and species showed that the extent of Active Raised Bog (a priority habitat under the Habitats Directive) in Ireland has shown a 7.0% increase since 2018. This is the first time such increases in the habitat have been recorded since Ireland commenced assessing the conservation status of this habitat in 2007. The C

question: Deputy Michael Cahill asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage if the Castleisland Housing Project (details supplied) will be expedited; the status of the issues raised.
reply:
As of January 2026, all new proposals for new?build social housing projects up to €200 million have moved to a single approval process.
The new single approval process, which replaces the 4-Stage and existing Single Stage approval process, removes the requirement for additional detailed submissions for review and approval throughout the project lifecycle. It is designed to align particular requirements related to the delivery of social housing, providing a more seamless approval process, with a clear and intentional focus on embedding standardisation and value for money.
This new process covers all social housing new build and major refurbishment projects up to a value of €200 million, funded via the Social Housing Investment Programme (SHIP) incorporating regeneration and remedial works schemes; and the Approved Housing Body (AHB) Capital Assistance Scheme (CAS).
My Department is aware an Approved Housing Body is working on a Proposal for Capital Assistance Scheme funded social housing development and is in direct contact with the AHB to resolve some outstanding issues in progressing the proposal.

question: Deputy Sinéad Gibney asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage to provide a schedule of EU Presidency events being hosted by his Department broken down by name of the event, location, date, State agencies or other departments involved in the organising of the event; and cost or budgeted cost of same (including costs borne by state agencies under its aegis), in tabular form.
reply:
Ireland’s Presidency of the Council of the European Union is an important opportunity for Ireland to shape Europe’s policy direction, lead important aspects of the EU’s work, and showcase Ireland’s engagement, expertise and values at the heart of the European Union.
Over the course of Ireland’s Presidency, my Department will host 14 meetings/events in Dublin, Wicklow, Westmeath and Cork, including an Informal Meeting of Housing Ministers on 25-26 November 2026 in Dublin Castle.
The Revised Estimates for 2026 published in December 2025 included allocations to individual Government Departments for Presidency related costs. This included an allocation of €5.6m for my Department. Of this €1.053m has been allocated to pay-related costs, while €4.547m has been allocated to meet anticipated travel and related costs associated with international meetings, as well as the cost of meetings and events in Ireland.
My Department has undertaken significant planning to ensure that costs are appropriately managed and prudent financial management will continue to ensure value for money is achieved.
The final costs of the Irish Presidency will not be known until 2027, once all the work is complete and the final bills are paid. In the meantime, every effort is being made to ensure costs are being well managed across all areas.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment if his Department has assessed the impact of standing charges and minimum service charges on single occupancy households and low waste producing households; if his Department holds data on average annual household waste collection charges broken down by household size.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 38, 40 and 41 together.
Waste management is a statutory executive function of individual local authorities. Under the Waste Management Act, responsibility for the permitting and regulation of waste collection activities rests with the National Waste Collection Permit Office (NWCPO).
The waste collection market is serviced by competing private companies, where prices charged are matters between those companies and their customers, subject to compliance with all applicable legislation, including contract, consumer and competition legislation. The Minister has no power to set prices in a private competitive market. The Department does not hold data on collection charges, broken down by household type.
All waste collectors are required to hold a permit from the NWCPO in order to collect waste. A standard set of conditions are attached to the permits. Under the conditions, collectors must charge fees which encourage their customers to segregate their waste. All permits are available to view on www.nwcpo.ie.
Waste collectors are obliged to provide their customers with a 3-bin system to allow for waste segregation. However, there is no requirement on households to avail of a door-to-door collection service. Where a household chooses not to avail of a collection service, they may home compost, use local waste compactors, bring their waste to a local authority recycling facility (Civic Amenity Site) or bin share, subject to local authority waste bye-la

question: Deputy Pa Daly asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage the way in which he has allocated the €2 billion allocated to his Department under the ICNF; the amount that has been spent to date; the amount that has been allocated to date; and the amount that has yet to be allocated, in tabular form.
reply:
The National Development Plan allocated €650 million from 2026 to 2030 under the ICNF to my Department.
I designated 10 Uisce Éireann wastewater treatment plant upgrade projects under the ICNF in 2026 with a funding allocation of €105m. The designation of projects under ICNF including funding allocations will be an annual process out to 2030.

question: Deputy Cathal Crowe asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport if groups applying for the Arts Capital Investment Fund must strictly furnish audited accounts, even if the groups are exempt from requiring same on an annual basis.
reply:
Under the Arts Capital Investment Fund Guidelines, for Category 1 and 2 applicants, the organisation must submit one year’s audited accounts or financial statements at application stage.
For Category 3 applicants, one year’s signed annual accounts or financial statements are required but where formal accounts are not prepared, a signed annual Income and Expenditure Statement and a Balance Sheet must be provided.
The Department recognises that certain organisations, particularly smaller community and voluntary organisations, may be exempt from the statutory requirement to have their annual accounts audited. Where an organisation is exempt from the statutory requirement to have its accounts audited, the Department will accept unaudited financial accounts for the purposes of an application under the Arts Capital Investment Fund.

question: Deputy Ivana Bacik asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport the way in which the fifteen million euro committed to supporting the post office network in Budget 2027 will be allocated; the portion of those funds that will be committed to retaining and expanding in-person postal services; the mechanisms in place to ensure that community input will be sought and heeded in allocating such funds; if he acknowledges that funding must ensure no selling off of publicly owned assets in the postal network; and his plans to ensure funding supports vulnerable postal service users who require face-to-face services because online services are inaccessible to them.
reply:
The Government is committed to a sustainable An Post and post office network as a key component of the economic and social infrastructure throughout Ireland. The Programme for Government states that the Government will continue to provide the nationwide network of post offices with funding to ensure their sustainability and enhance the value they bring to local communities.
In that regard, on 13 January 2026, Government approved renewed funding for the Post Office Network over the next 5 years (2026-2030), at an enhanced amount of €15m per annum from my Department.
In line with the Programme for Government, the funding will support the stability and sustainability of the nationwide network of post offices, protecting and nurturing a commercially-focused Post Office Network. It will also support access for citizens to the key social benefits of the Post Office Network and help citizens access services effectively and equitably.
The Government also agreed the principles on which the funding model will operate, which include:
• maintaining access to the network across urban and rural Ireland, ensuring no community is left behind.
• aligning individual funding with criteria including the degree of isolation and the sustainability of each post office.
• ensuring a minimum revenue threshold for post offices; and
• recognising offices of cultural or geographic significance—such as those on inhabited islands or in Gaeltacht areas.
It should be noted that An Post is a commercial State

question: Deputy Catherine Callaghan asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport for an update on the roll-out and implementation of the basic income for the arts scheme.
reply:
In February this year I announced that the Government had approved a permanent successor to the Basic Income for the Arts pilot scheme and that 2,000 artists would be provided with funding of €325 per week for three years. This is a major milestone for the arts in Ireland and I am particularly pleased that the research my Department conducted provided Government with a clear evidence base upon which to make that decision.
The deadline for application to the Basic Income for the Arts 2026 - 2029 was 5pm on Tuesday 12th May, with over 10,000 applications received by the deadline.
Like the pilot scheme selection is via an anonymous random selection process, this is considered the fairest method where there is not enough funding for all eligible applicants. The selection process took place in May with independent oversight by EY. The selection ranked all applications from 1 - 10,000 and eligibility checks then started from the first selected applicant to determine if those selected were eligible. That assessment process is ongoing to determine the final 2,000 applicants who will receive the BIA.
I appreciate that applicants are eager to know the outcome, however, in order to protect the integrity of the scheme the assessment process is by necessity very intensive and time consuming. No two professional arts practices are the same and therefore the proofs supplied vary considerably.
My Department is processing the applications as promptly as possible and I anticipate that payments

question: Deputy Pádraig O'Sullivan asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport the total current funding for Sport Ireland in 2027, given that the Budget 2027 expenditure report states €122 million in one section and €164.9 million in another; and for a reconciliation of the two figures.
reply:
Under Budget 2027, I have secured current funding in 2027 of €121.872 million for Sport Ireland.
The total allocation of €164.872 million for Sport Ireland in 2027 comprises the current funding plus €43 million in capital funding.

question: Deputy Pádraig O'Sullivan asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport the 2027 allocation for the large scale sport infrastructure fund; the amount drawn down under the fund in 2025 and in 2026 to date; and whether a new call for applications is planned.
reply:
The Large-Scale Sport Infrastructure Fund (LSSIF) was established under the National Sports Policy to provide Exchequer support for larger sports facility projects. The cumulative investment under the LSSIF since 2020 is €297 million across 68 projects.
Payments to grantees amounted to €25.776 million in 2025 and €19.5 million to date in 2026.
Details of LSSIF payments from 2019-2025 are available on the Department’s website at: www.gov.ie/en/department-of-culture-communications-and-sport/services/large-scale-sport-infrastructure-fund-lssif-2018/#payments.
While I anticipate that a third round of the fund will take place in the coming years, no decision has yet been taken on the timing of a future call for applications. The immediate priority is to support the delivery of projects approved under the first two rounds. My officials continue to work closely with grantees to help them progress their projects.

question: Deputy Pádraig O'Sullivan asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport the total funding available under the community sport facilities fund 2026 round, for which applications open on 19 October 2026 and close on 26 February 2027; the amount provided for the round in the 2027 allocation; the expected profile of expenditure on the round over 2027 to 2029; and the expected date for the announcement of grants.
reply:
The National Development Plan provides a significant level of capital investment in sport in the period 2027-2030 with over half a billion euro allocated for that period. Specific allocations for each year, including the CSFF, are published as part of the Revised Estimates Volume.
The amount of funding available for allocations arising from the 2026 round will be determined following an assessment of the level of demand and in consultation with the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation. The timing of funding announcements will be reviewed next Spring following the closure of the application window on 26 February 2027 and a thorough assessment of the time likely to be needed to assess all applications.

question: Deputy Cathal Crowe asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport if he will consider expanding the regional tier 1 pilot initiative under the Community Sport Facilities Fund to allow sports clubs from County Clare who are similarly affected by defective concrete blocks to apply for the pilot funding stream.
reply:
On 2 October, my Department published the Information Guide for the 2026 round of the Community Sport Facilities Fund (CSFF) and confirmed that the window for applications will run from Monday 19 October 2026 to Friday 26 February 2027.
As a pilot initiative, sports clubs in Donegal and Mayo with premises / infrastructure severely impacted by defective concrete blocks can apply for funding under the 2026 CSFF round. The maximum grant available will be set at the Regional Grant rate maximum of €550,000 and payable at a maximum funding rate of 95%. The pilot initiative will employ assessment criteria similar to those used in relation to the Defective Concrete Blocks Grant Scheme operated by the Housing Agency. It is envisaged that up to 5 clubs could be supported under this pilot initiative. Specific rules and procedures for this pilot scheme will be published before the end of the year, providing impacted clubs with sufficient time to make an application before the 26 February 2027 deadline.
While there are currently no plans to extend the pilot initiative beyond Donegal and Mayo, any clubs similarly affected by defective concrete blocks can engage with the department on the issue.

question: Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport if there is a contingency support mechanism for a sports club drawing down a community sports infrastructure grant where a contractor fails to deliver, or goes out of business.
reply:
Neither of my Department's sport capital funding schemes, the Community Sport Facilities Fund (CSFF) and the Large-Scale Sport Infrastructure Fund (LSSIF), provide a contingency mechanism in the event of a contractor going out of business or failing to deliver agreed works. Any contract for works is between the grantee and the contractor, and my Department is not a party to such contracts. Any breach of such contracts is a civil matter between the grantee and the contractor.
However, my Department’s officials can assist clubs impacted by either scenario in identifying how approved projects may proceed within the terms and conditions of their grants.
Where no grant funding has been drawn down, any impacted club should contact my Department regarding a proposed change of contractor and provide the relevant quotation and supporting documentation. Any change must comply with the applicable grant conditions and procurement requirements.
Where some works have already been completed, a club may submit a claim for eligible expenditure on those works, supported by invoices, proof of payment and any other required documentation. Such claims will be assessed in accordance with the terms and conditions of the grant.

question: Deputy Sinéad Gibney asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport to provide a schedule of EU Presidency events being hosted by his Department broken down by name of the event, location, date, State agencies or other departments involved in the organising of the event; and cost or budgeted cost of same (including costs borne by state agencies under its aegis), in tabular form.
reply:

question: Deputy Ivana Bacik asked the Minister for Education and Youth the portion of funding announced in Budget 2027 that will be committed to special education in Dublin bay south; the number of new places in mainstream and special schools that will result from that allocation in Dublin bay south, respectively; and her plans to ensure that pupils with additional needs will be required to leave their community to access education.
reply:

question: D'fhiafraigh Deputy Shónagh Ní Raghallaigh den Aire Oideachais agus Óige her views on the challenges in the system of identifying and assessing children with both dyslexia and autism.
reply:
This government is fully committed to supporting students with special educational needs to fulfil their full potential and the Programme for Government makes a number of commitments to deliver on this objective.
The National Educational Psychological Service (NEPS) is the psychological service of the Department of Education and Youth which provides educational psychological support to primary, post-primary and special schools in Ireland. NEPS does not operate waiting lists -in common with other psychological services and best international practice, NEPS operates on a consultative model of service with assessments only one aspect of the NEPS service.
NEPS encourages schools to support children and young people using the Continuum of Support, whereby school staff use a problem-solving approach, including school screening (assessment) and evidence-based intervention, for children and young people experiencing difficulties in the school context. The response to intervention is monitored and recorded in the Student Support File. The teachers, parents and child are involved in this process. Under this model, a diagnosis is not required for a child or young person to access supports that can be implemented at school level in mainstream classes, such as special education teaching support and special needs assistant (SNA) support.
If a school has concerns that a child or young person is not making reasonable progress following evidence informed support and intervention, the school m

question: D'fhiafraigh Deputy Shónagh Ní Raghallaigh den Aire Oideachais agus Óige the number of assessments completed by NEPS psychologists each year for the past five years that produced a diagnosis of dyslexia.
reply:
I would like to take this opportunity to outline the work of NEPS. All schools have access to:
• General support and advice from an educational psychologist in NEPS, either through the school’s assigned psychologist or through the NEPS Advisory Support Service.
• Support from an educational psychologist in NEPS in the event of a Critical Incident.
• National and Regional Support and Development service for school staff.
• Access for individual casework where a priority need is established to either an educational psychologist in NEPS or a private educational psychologist on the Scheme for Commissioning Psychological Assessments (SCPA) panel.

If a child is not making sufficient progress following appropriate supports and interventions being provided by the school, the school may consider referring the child to NEPS to assist in identifying their needs and determining any additional supports required. Assessment is one aspect of the work carried out by NEPS and it is not always the most appropriate or necessary intervention for every child. The primary focus is on identifying and implementing the supports that will best meet the child's needs and help them make progress in school. question: D'fhiafraigh Deputy Shónagh Ní Raghallaigh den Aire Oideachais agus Óige the CPD resources available to teachers seeking to upskill to support dyslexic students.
reply:

On an annual basis, the department provides funding for two distinct categories of post-graduate programmes for Special Education Teachers:

question: Deputy Michael Healy-Rae asked the Minister for Education and Youth her views on a school bus route (details supplied).
reply:

Under the terms of the Post Primary School Transport Scheme, children are eligible for transport where they reside not less than 4.8 kms from their nearest post primary school/centre as determined by the Department/Bus Éireann, having regard to ethos and language.
Where a child is eligible for transport and the application and payment process has been completed on time, they will get a seat on a school bus service, where a service is available.
Children who are not eligible, but who apply for school transport are considered for spare seats that may exist after eligible children have been facilitated; previously known as concessionary seats.
Because of the nature of transport for non-eligible children and the priority of providing places for eligible children, there may be an excess of demand over supply for non-eligible pupils. In these cases, Bus Éireann will allocate tickets for spare seats using an agreed selection process.
Where practicable, and subject to considerations of cost and logistics, routes are planned to avoid an eligible child having to travel more than 3.2 kms to or from a pick-up/set down point or to have travel and waiting times in excess of 1.5 hours per day. Routes are planned on the basis of the locations of children who are eligible for school transport only.

question: Deputy Séamus McGrath asked the Minister for Education and Youth to provide an update on the building project for a school (details supplied).
reply:
The school referred to by the Deputy was approved to enter my department's pipeline of projects under the Additional School Accommodation (ASA) scheme. The project will provide a five classroom Special Education Needs (SEN) base. The project is devolved to the school authority for delivery.
The Stage 2a developed design report has been submitted to my department. This report is currently under review from a technical and cost perspective.
In June 2026, department officials contacted the school to advise that the project remains under review in the context of NDP parameters and the overall prioritisation of capital investment.
As I am sure you will appreciate, all school buildings, as they progress through the pipeline, must undergo the necessary due diligence in the Infrastructure Guidelines and Capital Works Management Framework.
The timing of a project moving from one stage to the next requires careful planning and takes account of factors such as compliance with all scope, design and cost requirements; timing of affordability; and the prioritisation necessary for the school building programme to remain within agreed annual funding allocations.
I have asked my departments officials to continue their engagement with the school over the coming months and to provide any necessary guidance.

question: Deputy John Lahart asked the Minister for Education and Youth the number of schools nationally and in Dublin, that have not been assigned a dedicated NEPS psychologist for the 2026/2027 school year due to staffing or capacity constraints; and the steps being taken to address current staffing pressures within NEPS.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 388 to 390, inclusive, together.
Each year, NEPS staffing levels are evaluated and capacity to serve schools is established. There is currently a national shortage of suitably qualified educational psychologists which has resulted in vacancies. For the year ahead, NEPS will support schools without an assigned psychologist through the NEPS Advisory Support Service. All schools will continue to have the support of a NEPS educational psychologist in the event of a critical incident as well as access to staff training and support from NEPS.
The NEPS Advisory Support Service has been designed specifically to support schools that are temporarily without an assigned psychologist. Through this service, schools can access responsive support and advice from a NEPS educational psychologist and, where the need is established, can sanction an assessment through the Scheme for the Commissioning of Psychological Assessments (SCPA). Schools can contact the Advisory Support Service as needed throughout the school year.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment the supports currently available to people living alone, older people and low income households to meet the cost of household waste collection; whether he will consider the introduction of a national waiver or support scheme for such households.
reply:
Waste management is a statutory function of local authorities. Under section 60(3) of the Waste Management Act 1996, the Minister is precluded from exercising any power or control in relation to the performance, in particular circumstances, of a local authority's statutory functions under that Act.
There has never been a national waste waiver scheme and the introduction, administration or continuation of any such scheme would be a matter for individual local authorities. Accordingly, persons seeking information on the availability of a waiver scheme in a particular area should contact the relevant local authority directly.
It should also be noted that household waste collection services are provided by private waste collection operators in a competitive market. Charges for waste collection services are therefore matters for individual service providers and their customers, subject to compliance with relevant contract, consumer protection and competition law. The Minister has no statutory role in setting or regulating the prices charged by private waste collection companies.
The National Waste Collection Permit Office has conducted a study on incentivised charging structures in the waste collection market which examines what changes could be made to the permitting system for waste collectors to fully incentivise waste prevention and improve source segregation practices by their customers to minimise their waste collection bills. This study also considers mechanisms for support
