question: Deputy Jen Cummins asked the Minister for Education and Youth her plans to support schools to identify caring-related needs (details supplied); and if young carers can be explicitly included in the revised Wellbeing Policy, with their experiences informing the review.
reply:
The Department is currently reviewing the Wellbeing Policy Statement and Framework for Practice (2019-2025) to inform the development of a successor policy, expected in 2027.
An internal review has been completed, examining progress, challenges and lessons learned.
The ESRI completed a literature review, published in January 2026 “Supporting student wellbeing in school contexts: A narrative review” that identified strengths, areas for improvement and international best practice.
Stakeholder consultation is now underway, including through an independently chaired Advisory Group. Those in care and carers are represented on the advisory group through EPIC.
A dedicated child and youth participation process is well underway across primary and post-primary settings, with a particular focus on ensuring seldom-heard voices are included, including young carers. A direct consultation to ascertain the young carer experience is also planned to help inform the review.
A public consultation survey conducted as part of the review attracted over 13,500 responses. The quantitative and qualitative data from these responses is being analysed and compiled and we hope that the experience of young carers will also be captured within this data.

question: Deputy Jen Cummins asked the Minister for Education and Youth the evidence her Department has that young carers experiences have informed DEIS school improvement planning (details supplied).
reply:
Addressing educational disadvantage in all schools remains a key priority for me as Minister of Education and Youth.
The DEIS Strategy to 2035, its first Implementation plan 2026-2028 and the DEIS Plus scheme were launched earlier this year. The strategy sets out the departments long term vision to address educational disadvantage in all schools to ensure that every child and young person experiencing disadvantage is supported to succeed in their education journey, regardless of their background.
The strategy acknowledges that students at risk of educational disadvantage are present in all schools. It therefore focuses on improving outcomes, encouraging innovation, and ensuring schools can access the right supports when needed. The DEIS Strategy to 2035 sets out actions under the strategic objective 2.2, to develop an agile resource allocation model to support all children and young people at risk of educational disadvantage in all primary and post-primary schools. These actions focus on the continued enhancement of the data available to measure school level disadvantage and for the development of a more flexible resource allocation model that can react to change in school needs and provide the right resources at the right time.
As part of the DEIS programme, schools are required to engage in ongoing planning processes based on identified targets across DEIS themes and integrate with the SSE process.
There are currently no specific arrangements within the Inspectorate's DEIS

question: Deputy Jen Cummins asked the Minister for Education and Youth if her Department will consult young carers on their views on early recognition; and the way in which the framework will assess whether schools are recognising them before attendance or attainment has already suffered.
reply:
Addressing educational disadvantage in all schools remains a key priority for me as Minister for Education and Youth.
The DEIS Strategy to 2035 sets out the departments long term vision to address educational disadvantage in all schools and to ensure that any child or young person experiencing disadvantage is supported to succeed in their education journey, regardless of their background.
A key action under the strategy is the development and implementation of a comprehensive monitoring and evaluation framework to track and measure the impact of the DEIS programme. The framework will build on what we currently use to measure outcomes and impacts, such as literacy and numeracy results, attendance, attainment, and retention data.
It will evaluate the actions outlined in the strategy and support the department in identifying and scaling interventions that are having a positive impact. This will help to ensure that the needs and experiences of all children and young people are reflected in the evaluation of the DEIS programme.
The Department is currently working with the ESRI on the development of this framework, which will be published in the coming months.

question: Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Education and Youth to outline when applications may open for schools for new home school liaison teachers; and the criteria to be used for allocation.
reply:
Addressing educational disadvantage remains a key priority for me as Minister for Education and Youth.
As part of the DEIS Strategy to 2035, a pilot project was recently introduced to extend Home-School-Community-Liaison (HSCL) provision to 130 schools that are in the DEIS Rural band and outside the DEIS programme. This pilot provides an important opportunity to trial the extension of this support to additional schools and to inform future policy development in relation to the scheme.
The HSCL scheme is a core element of the DEIS programme and forms part of the wider Tusla Education Support Service (TESS). HSCL coordinators are teachers assigned to work directly with parents, guardians, school staff and community services to strengthen engagement between home, school and community. The overarching aim of HSCL is to improve attendance, participation and retention, particularly for children and young people experiencing educational disadvantage.
Schools included in the HSCL pilot project were identified using nationally available data relating to concentrations of educational disadvantage. Operational factors, including clustering feasibility and regional capacity requirements, were also considered to support implementation of the pilot at this stage.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Education and Youth following the review of the assistive technology scheme, whether she will provide the findings and outcome of that review; and to detail the actions taken, or proposed, arising from the review, including changes to the scheme eligibility criteria funding or provisions of the devices.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 358, 369 and 383 together.
The Assistive Technology (AT) Scheme is currently in the final stages of review. The review will culminate in the publication of a new circular which will set out the revised arrangements for the scheme. The Department expects to announce the commencement date of the revised scheme shortly.
The key changes arising from the review include a move from the current diagnosis-based approach to a needs-based model of support. This will provide schools with greater autonomy in identifying and determining the assistive technology requirements of their pupils. The revised scheme will also introduce a new online application process which is intended to streamline the application process and significantly reduce processing times.
In addition, it is proposed that funding will issue to schools in advance of equipment purchase. This will enable schools to procure approved equipment more quickly for pupils and will reduce the administrative burden associated with the current reimbursement-based model, whereby schools must first purchase equipment and subsequently seek reimbursement from the Department.
Full details of the revised arrangements will be set out in the new circular when published.
Circular 0010/2013, which governs the Assistive Technology Scheme, sets out the arrangements relating to the ownership, management and transfer of assistive technology equipment provided under the scheme.

reply:

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment the current regulatory requirements on household waste collectors regarding the number and type of bins that must be provided to each household; whether a householder is obliged to accept and pay for a three bin service regardless of the number of occupants in the home or the volume of waste generated.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 38, 40 and 41 together.
Waste management is a statutory executive function of individual local authorities. Under the Waste Management Act, responsibility for the permitting and regulation of waste collection activities rests with the National Waste Collection Permit Office (NWCPO).
The waste collection market is serviced by competing private companies, where prices charged are matters between those companies and their customers, subject to compliance with all applicable legislation, including contract, consumer and competition legislation. The Minister has no power to set prices in a private competitive market. The Department does not hold data on collection charges, broken down by household type.
All waste collectors are required to hold a permit from the NWCPO in order to collect waste. A standard set of conditions are attached to the permits. Under the conditions, collectors must charge fees which encourage their customers to segregate their waste. All permits are available to view on www.nwcpo.ie.
Waste collectors are obliged to provide their customers with a 3-bin system to allow for waste segregation. However, there is no requirement on households to avail of a door-to-door collection service. Where a household chooses not to avail of a collection service, they may home compost, use local waste compactors, bring their waste to a local authority recycling facility (Civic Amenity Site) or bin share, subject to local authority waste bye-la

question: Deputy Peadar Tóibín asked the Minister for Education and Youth the procedures followed when a person enrolled in second-level education is subsequently determined not to be a minor; whether such persons are removed from second-level education; and the number removed in each of the past five years.
reply:
Under the provisions of the Education Act, 1998 the Board of Management is the body charged with the direct governance of a school on behalf of the patron, and the principal is responsible for the day-to-day management of the school.
There is no requirement or procedure that a student cease attending post primary education because they have attained the age of 18. It is not uncommon for students enrolled in post primary schools to reach 18 years of age while in the school, particularly those completing senior cycle education.
The Department does not collect any such data as requested by the Deputy.

question: Deputy Shane Moynihan asked the Minister for Education and Youth the guidance provided to post-primary schools on the use of class periods for students exempt from Irish; and if consideration is being given to issuing further guidance on their appropriate use.
reply:
As the deputy is aware, an exemption from the study of Irish may be granted by school management in the exceptional circumstances outlined in circular 0054/2022 (Primary) and 0055/2022 (Post Primary).
The provision of classes in a specific subject, and the arrangement or timetabling of those subjects are a matter for the management of an individual school.
Section 3 of the Circular 0055/2022 outlines that:
Schools, where appropriate, should take account of the literacy learning needs of students who are exempt from the study of Irish when deploying available special education teaching resources.
Students who are exempt from the study of Irish may also be allowed to substitute another subject, short course or area of learning for Irish. To support inclusive practices, a student who is exempt from the study of Irish should be included in a meaningful way in aspects of Irish language and cultural activities in line with his/her ability and interests.
All children educated in Ireland, including those who have been granted an exemption from the study of Irish, are expected to have had the opportunity to study Irish to an appropriate standard. All students should be encouraged to study the language and achieve a level of personal proficiency that is appropriate to their ability. The granting of an exemption from the study of Irish should therefore not be an obstacle to a student building on their language skills, and these students have the option not to exercise the exemption gran

question: Deputy Pat Buckley asked the Minister for Education and Youth to calculate the true cost of workplace violence in special education including assault leave, ordinary sick leave, substitution, occupational health, healthcare, staff turnover and long-term absence; and to compare it with the cost of prevention.
reply:
As provided for under the Education Act, it is the school/ETB that is the employer of teaching and non-teaching staff in a school/ETB, and not the Department of Education and Youth.
While the Department holds information in relation to the number and duration of absences under the provisions of the sick leave scheme, and other schemes such as the Leave of Absence Following Assault Scheme and the Occupational Injuries Scheme for Teachers, as the Department is not the employer, the Department does not hold detailed information in relation to the cause of the injuries giving rise to these absences.
In addition, as the Department is not the employer, the Department does not hold information in relation to the reason why an employee of a school leaves that employment, and indeed from the perspective of the employer, there is no obligation on a member of staff of a school to provide to their employer a reason for why they are leaving their employment.
In accordance with the Safety, Health and Welfare at Work Act 2005, it is the responsibility of individual school authorities, as employers, to have a safety statement in place in its school and to ensure as far as is reasonably practicable, the safety, health and welfare at work of its employees and those who are in anyway affected by the work activities of the school.
The safety statement should identify potential hazards, assess the risks to health and safety and put appropriate provision in place to safeguard the safety and health

question: Deputy Barry Heneghan asked the Minister for Education and Youth the arrangements available for students who cannot attend school regularly for medical reasons to complete and have their additional assessment components authenticated; whether an alternative process will be available; where this cannot be done through their school; and the guidance that has been provided to schools on such cases.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 320 and 376 together.
The State Examinations Commission (SEC) has statutory responsibility for administering the State examinations and for setting authentication requirements for any coursework components in line with overall examinations and assessment policy.
Prior to the implementation of revised subject specifications and assessment arrangements under the Senior Cycle Redevelopment (SCR) programme, 28 existing Leaving Certificate subjects already included assessment components beyond written examinations, including oral examinations, practical performance tests, and coursework. This variety of formats is being maintained as the SCR programme is implemented.
The policy rationale underpinning expanding Additional Assessment Components (AACs) to all subjects is to reward students for demonstrating a broader range of skills and competencies than can be assessed through terminal written examinations alone; to spread the assessment load experienced by students and to reduce the pressure that students can experience around the written examinations.
To protect examination integrity and ensure inter-candidate equity, the SEC advises that it requires all coursework to be authenticated. Coursework completion and authentication is an ongoing process of engagement and oversight over by class teachers, rather than a single ‘point in time’ engagement. question: Deputy John Connolly asked the Minister for Education and Youth whether the evaluations of the School Transport 2030 pilot schemes operated during the 2024-2025 school year have been completed; if so, when they were completed; and whether the evaluation reports, supporting data and findings will be published.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 370, 371, 373, 374 and 375 together.
The School Transport Scheme is a significant operation managed by Bus Éireann on behalf of the Department of Education and Youth that has expanded significantly over the past six years. In that time, the numbers of children and young people using the service have grown from under 120,000 pupils in 2018 to over 181,000 pupils including over 24,000 pupils with Special Educational Needs in 2025 which equates to an increase of over 50%. Since 2018, investment in the scheme has more than doubled, from €200 million to €537 million.
The School Transport 2030 report was published in early 2024. The recommended changes to the schemes include expansion of the current eligibility criteria, addressing current operational challenges and moving towards better integration with public transport to ensure the best value for money to the Exchequer.
It was outlined at the time the Review was published that the proposed changes to the eligibility criteria would further increase demand for the scheme. Therefore, it was considered prudent to implement the changes on a phased basis.
One of the recommendations of the School Transport 2030 Review was that the Department of Education and Youth, together with Bus Éireann and the Department of Transport should carry out an assessment as to where school transport pilot schemes could be successfully established. This assessment was based on a number of factors, including local evidence

question: Deputy Willie O'Dea asked the Minister for Education and Youth if she is aware that graduates (details supplied) have been informed that their qualification is not recognised by an organisation; and her proposals to assist these graduates.
reply:
The Teaching Council is the body with the statutory authority and responsibility for the regulation of the teaching profession in Ireland including the registration of teachers in the State.
The Teaching Council register teachers under the Teaching Council Act 2001-2015 and in line with the Teaching Council Registration Regulations 2025. As set out in the Schedule of the Regulations, the Council registers teachers under five routes of registration: Route 1 - Primary, Route 2 - Post-primary, Route 3 - Further Education, Route 4 - Other and Route 5 - Student Teacher. The qualification requirements for each route are set out in the Schedule of the Regulations. Per the legislation, my department has no role in the registration of individual teachers.
As the independent regulator of the teaching profession in Ireland, the Teaching Council’s role is to protect the public by promoting and regulating professional standards in teaching. This is carried out through the statutory registration of teachers, ensuring a highly qualified teaching profession whose members meet and uphold high standards of professional competence and conduct.
The qualification requirements for Route 2 (post-primary) can be summarised as follows:
Completion of an undergraduate degree in teacher education, accredited by the Teaching Council which satisfies the requirements for at least one curricular subject:
or
Completion of a post-primary programme of teacher education (ITE) accredited by the Teaching Council

question: Deputy Erin McGreehan asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment the powers available to local authorities to investigate and address air-pollution complaints arising from stationary vehicle exhaust; whether national guidance exists on prolonged engine idling; and whether he will work with the Minister for Transport to establish a clear public complaints procedure and consistent measures to reduce unnecessary idling.
reply:
Under the Air Pollution Act 1987, as amended by the Air Pollution (Amendment) Act 2026, https://www.bing.com/ck/a?!&&p=2bbd86b388bc0e931b9a9c8243194146e45642c84b712c17cd5814c4bd5de7d8JmltdHM9MTc5MTQxNzYwMA&ptn=3&ver=2&hsh=4&fclid=07af993b-fe13-6e27-23e9-8f83ff356fb7&psq=air+pollution+amendment+act+2026&u=a1aHR0cHM6Ly93d3cuaXJpc2hzdGF0dXRlYm9vay5pZS9lbGkvMjAyNi9hY3QvMTQvZW5hY3RlZC9lbi8, local authorities are responsible for “monitoring, reporting, and improving air quality in their area” and for “dealing with complaints about air pollution”. question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Education and Youth whether all primary and post-primary schools have been formally informed of the provisions of Circular 0010/2013, concerning the transfer of assistive technology with a pupil when they change school, including when progressing to post-primary; whether further guidance has issued to schools on this process; and whether she will publish any circular, guidance or communication issued to schools in this regard.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 358, 369 and 383 together.
The Assistive Technology (AT) Scheme is currently in the final stages of review. The review will culminate in the publication of a new circular which will set out the revised arrangements for the scheme. The Department expects to announce the commencement date of the revised scheme shortly.
The key changes arising from the review include a move from the current diagnosis-based approach to a needs-based model of support. This will provide schools with greater autonomy in identifying and determining the assistive technology requirements of their pupils. The revised scheme will also introduce a new online application process which is intended to streamline the application process and significantly reduce processing times.
In addition, it is proposed that funding will issue to schools in advance of equipment purchase. This will enable schools to procure approved equipment more quickly for pupils and will reduce the administrative burden associated with the current reimbursement-based model, whereby schools must first purchase equipment and subsequently seek reimbursement from the Department.
Full details of the revised arrangements will be set out in the new circular when published.
Circular 0010/2013, which governs the Assistive Technology Scheme, sets out the arrangements relating to the ownership, management and transfer of assistive technology equipment provided under the scheme.

question: Deputy Louis O'Hara asked the Minister for Education and Youth whether her Department has plans to establish standalone special educational needs co-ordinator positions within the education system.
reply:

This would include transition planning for the identified students.

question: Deputy Louis O'Hara asked the Minister for Education and Youth whether the current pupil-teacher ratio includes special education teachers; if so, the rationale for their inclusion as special education teachers do not generally teach children within a whole classroom setting.
reply:
The OECD defines the student-teacher (or pupil-teacher) ratio as the number of students enrolled divided by the number of teachers, measured on a full-time equivalent basis. The OECD notes that this indicator reflects the level of teaching resources available to students and should not be confused with average class size.
The key factor for determining the level of mainstream staffing resources provided at individual school level is the staffing schedule for the relevant school year and pupil enrolments on the previous 30 September. The staffing schedule operates as a standardised allocation mechanism, using enrolment bands to determine the number of classroom teaching posts assigned to each school. The primary staffing schedule now operates on a general average of 1 classroom teacher for every 23 pupils. More favourable ratios are implemented for DEIS Urban Band 1 schools. Budget 2021 also introduced a three point retention level on the staffing schedule for schools that might otherwise be at risk of losing a teacher. Primary schools are now staffed at the most favourable level ever seen.
Pupil-teacher ratio includes all teachers allocated to a school as a ratio to the number of pupils enrolled in that school. The latest figures in relation to pupil-teacher ratio shows an improved ratio of pupils to teachers from 16:2 to 12.6 at primary level when comparing the 2014/15 school year to the 2025/26 school year. question: Deputy Richard Boyd Barrett asked the Minister for Education and Youth given that the primary annual census 2026-27 is the first time the State has tried to count the number of children withdrawn from religious instruction, whether the Minister will commit to publishing this data by a set date, and to issuing guidance to schools within this school year in order that these children are no longer left without meaningful teaching during religious instruction.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 350 and 363 together.
My department has included in its annual return from primary schools a question on how many pupils have requests been made to withdraw from religious instruction/formation. This information is of use to my department to indicate the general level of requests to primary schools from parents who have requested that their children attend school without attending Religious Instruction. This information is self-reported and supplied on a voluntary basis from schools and has not been published.
My department has committed to undertaking a consultation process with relevant stakeholders on the development of best practice guidance for primary schools with a denominational ethos in relation to arrangements for facilitating parental requests for their children to attend school without attending religious instruction and work is ongoing in this regard.

question: Deputy Richard Boyd Barrett asked the Minister for Education and Youth whether her Department has issued, or plans to issue, guidance to primary schools on the educational provision and supervision of pupils withdrawn from religious instruction, including during sacramental preparation and school-time religious ceremonies.
reply:
The Education Plan 2025 included a commitment to provide best practice guidance to schools in relation to arrangements to facilitate parental requests for children to attend school without attending religious instruction. Work is underway within my department to develop this guidance.
The guidance is intended to improve consistency across schools and to make expectations clearer for all stakeholders. The planned guidance will focus on how schools can better facilitate requests from parents and provide for a greater consistency of approach across all schools.

question: Deputy Eamon Scanlon asked the Minister for Education and Youth if she will engage with the management of a school (details supplied) in relation to their SNA resource allocation in terms of dealing with pupils with additional needs.
reply:
The National Council for Special Education (NCSE) is the statutory body responsible for the provision of special education and allocating supports for students with special educational needs.
Special Needs Assistants (SNAs) play a key role in the successful inclusion of students with additional and significant care needs in schools to enable them to achieve their best outcomes and reach their full potential.
If a school has a concern with either their SNA allocation for the 2026/27 school year or the outcome of a SNA review/appeal, they should discuss the matter with their NCSE Special Education Needs Organiser (SENO).
In relation to the school referred to by the Deputy the NCSE has advised that they are engaging with the school on the SNA review process.
It is important to note that there have been increases in SNAs in all counties and across all education settings since 2020, including mainstream, special classes and special schools.
SNA posts are allocated to schools as a school-based resource. Principals/board of managements deploy SNAs within schools to meet the care support requirements of the students enrolled whom SNA support has been allocated. This provides schools flexibility in how the SNA support is utilised.
My department and the NCSE are committed to delivering an education system that is of the highest quality and where every child and young person feels valued and is actively supported and nurtured to achieve their full potential.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Education and Youth the maximum timeframe her Department considers acceptable between a child's need for assistive technology being identified and the child receiving the required device; whether her Department has a formal service standard or target for processing assistive technology applications; and the percentage of applications in 2025 and 2026 that were processed within this timeframe.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 349 and 360 together.
The Assistive Technology (AT) Scheme provides funding towards specialised equipment for pupils with special educational needs who require assistive technology to access the curriculum.
There is currently no formal service standard or processing target for applications under the Assistive Technology Scheme. question: Deputy Cian O'Callaghan asked the Minister for Education and Youth to outline, with regard to the primary school survey, the statistical basis and appropriateness of applying a margin of error to a voluntary, self-selected survey; how the Department distinguishes the preferences actually expressed by respondents from assumptions about non-respondents; the reason multiple submissions associated with the same eircode were permitted where the survey was intended to capture one submission per household; and the arrangements in place to ensure the integrity and security of the survey.
reply:
There was no single “required” response rate to make the Primary School Survey results valid; the margin of error provides the necessary context for understanding the results. The school Response Rate (included in the school-specific reports) sets out how many parents/guardians responded to the survey. For example, if a school has children from 100 households with Eircodes included in the department's Primary Online Database, and 40 responded, this is a 40% response rate. The margin of error gives a range around the survey result, showing how much the results might be higher or lower if all parents/guardians of children in a school had responded. If many parents/guardians of children in a school responded to the survey, the result is more reliable and leads to a smaller margin of error. If fewer parents/guardians respond, the result is less certain and leads to a larger margin of error.
The survey was open to all households that have children in primary school and/or have younger children. Parents and guardians inputted their Eircode to complete a survey. The Eircode of the household was used to uniquely count responses. The arrangements for validating survey returns operated after survey returns were received as this facilitated ease of use for survey users. The validation process was designed to deal with any scenarios of multiple returns. question: Deputy Pat Buckley asked the Minister for Education and Youth to establish meaningful national reporting and analysis of assaults, injuries and assault-related absence in special education, including mechanisms for identifying repeated incidents and ensuring that reporting leads to reflection and change.
reply:
As provided for under the Education Act, it is the school/ETB that is the employer of teaching and non-teaching staff in a school/ETB, and not the Department of Education and Youth.
In accordance with the Safety, Health and Welfare at Work Act 2005, it is the responsibility of individual school authorities, as employers, to have a safety statement in place in its school and to ensure as far as is reasonably practicable, the safety, health and welfare at work of its employees and those who are in anyway affected by the work activities of the school.
The safety statement should identify potential hazards, assess the risks to health and safety and put appropriate provision in place to safeguard the safety and health of employees and pupils.
As the Department is not the employer, the Department does not have access to the information set out in the Deputy’s question.
The Department does hold information in relation to the number of applications for leave under the 'Leave of absence following assault' scheme, where a teacher/SNA receives a physical injury during the course of their duty from physical contact from a third party. However, the scheme does not require that there is an intent to cause injury, only that the individual concerned did receive a physical injury arising from physical contact from a third party.
The Department also holds information in relation to the number of applications for leave from teachers under the Occupational Injuries scheme.

question: Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Education and Youth if her attention has been drawn to urgent repairs and upgrades required at a school (details supplied); and the steps she will take to address the fact that these requests have been rejected by her Department to date.
reply:
As the Deputy may be aware, the purpose of the Emergency Works Scheme (EWS) is to provide funding specifically for sudden and unforeseen emergencies, or to provide funding to facilitate inclusion and access for pupils with special needs. It does so by ensuring the availability of funding for urgent works to those schools that are in need of resources as a result of an emergency situation.
An emergency is deemed to be a situation which poses an immediate risk to health, life, property or the environment, which is sudden, unforeseen and requires immediate action, and in the case of a school, if not corrected would prevent the school or part thereof from opening.
The EWS operates on the basis of a minimal scope works to address the emergency situation. The EWS is intended to remedy an emergency situation and usually provides only an interim measure until a permanent solution can be delivered under the Summer Works Scheme (SWS) which deals with upgrade works to the school.
The schools application was unsuccessful as the works outlined were not deemed sudden and unforeseen circumstances, as set out in Circular Letter 0068/2020. The school were advised to revert to the section who delivered the project, in this case the Departments Modular accommodation team.
Following receipt of the school's correspondence, the issues raised were referred to the Department's modular buildings team for clarification. The modular team has confirmed that the doors installed as part of the modular acc

question: Deputy Pat Buckley asked the Minister for Education and Youth to provide ring-fenced funding for additional staffing, specialist input and other control measures identified as necessary through individual and workplace risk assessment in special education.
reply:
The Government’s commitment to special education is demonstrated through the significant investment provided under Budget 2027. A record €3.8 billion has been allocated for special education, including funding for 1,353 additional special education teachers and 2,339 additional Special Needs Assistants (SNAs). This will bring the total dedicated special education workforce across mainstream schools, special classes and special schools to approximately 52,000 staff.
The allocation of special education resources is informed by identified need and is designed to ensure that students receive the appropriate supports in the most suitable educational setting. Schools are supported through a range of staffing and other measures to meet the needs of children and young people with special educational needs.
In addition to expanding staffing capacity, Budget 2027 provides for enhanced supports to schools through investment in a new accredited programme in inclusive education for teachers and increased funding for the Education Therapy Service. This will support the continued rollout of speech and language therapy and occupational therapy services, including their gradual expansion into mainstream schools.
My Department will continue to work closely with schools and education stakeholders to ensure that special education supports and resources are deployed effectively and continue to meet the needs of students and school communities.

question: Deputy Pat Buckley asked the Minister for Education and Youth to create an appropriate leave mechanism for staff employed in special education where occupational health advises that an employee should remain away from a particular working environment while identified workplace safety measures are implemented.
reply:
An Occupational Health Strategy is in place as a supportive resource for teachers. The aim of this strategy is to promote the health of teachers in the workplace, with a focus primarily on prevention rather than cure. The Occupational Health Strategy is comprised of the Employee Assistance Service (EAS) and the Occupational Health Service (OHS).
The OHS is in place to provide employers with occupational health advice in relation to teachers’ medical fitness for work. It incorporates pre-employment health assessments, sickness absence referrals, assessments of medical fitness for work and ill health retirement assessments.
The Employment Equality Acts require employers to take reasonable steps to accommodate the needs of employees and prospective employees with disabilities. Reasonable accommodation typically involves some modification to the tasks/structure of a job or workplace environment, which would enable such an employee to fully perform their work role and enjoy equal employment opportunities. An employer will make reasonable adjustments for teachers who have a disability, or who have acquired a disability, to have reasonable accommodation made to facilitate their return to work. However, employers are not obliged to provide special treatment or facilities if the cost of doing so is excessive or disproportionate. question: Deputy Pat Buckley asked the Minister for Education and Youth to ensure occupational injuries do not ultimately consume an employee's ordinary sick leave entitlement while working in special education.
reply:
Teachers who have been certified as medically unfit for work due to a physical injury, sustained as a result of an accident in the actual discharge of their duties, including approved school activities; which was not due to negligence on the part of the teacher, and by some injury solely attributable to the nature of their duty which has been established by the employer as an Occupational Injury, may qualify for leave with pay where this leave is granted by their employer under the Occupational Injury Scheme for teachers.
The Occupational Injury Leave Scheme for teachers was introduced following engagement by the teacher unions under the auspices of the Teachers Conciliation Council (TCC) and a related adjudication process. The terms and conditions of the non-statutory Occupational Injury Leave Scheme for teachers were agreed with the Education Partners and the Department of Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation following that process and are set out in Circular Letter 0013/2025 titled “Occupational Injury Leave Scheme for Registered Teachers employed in Recognised Primary and Post Primary Schools”.
Subject to the terms and conditions of the Occupational Injury Leave Scheme, a teacher may be granted paid leave up to a maximum of 3 months (92 days) full pay in a rolling 4 year period. question: Deputy John Connolly asked the Minister for Education and Youth the number of post-primary students nationally who were refused school transport in each of the past three school years due to the fact that they were not attending their nearest eligible school; the number of such students in County Galway; and whether this issue is being considered as part of the School Transport 2030 reform programme.
reply:
The School Transport Scheme is a significant operation managed by Bus Éireann on behalf of the Department of Education and Youth.
Under the current terms of the mainstream school transport scheme, children are eligible for transport at post primary level where they reside not less than 4.8 kilometres from and are attending their nearest post primary school/education centre as determined by the department/Bus Éireann, having regard to ethos and language.
Eligible children who complete the application process and pay or enter their medical card details on time will get a seat on a school bus service, if a service is available.
Children who are not eligible for school transport but complete the application and pay or enter their medical card details on time will be considered for any spare seats available after eligible children have been accommodated. These spare seats are called concessionary seats.
Pupils may be deemed as concessionary for not meeting the distance under the scheme or where they are not attending their nearest post primary centre having regard to ethos and language. Therefore, the information requested by the Deputy is not available in that format. Information on the number of on time concessionary pupils who did not receive a ticket (where a service exists) is provided on the attached table.
It was outlined at the time the School Transport Review was published that the proposed changes to the eligibility criteria would further increase demand for the scheme.

question: D'fhiafraigh Deputy Shónagh Ní Raghallaigh den Aire Oideachais agus Óige cad iad a pleananna chun an liúntais le haghaidh múineadh trí mheán na Gaeilge a thabhairt ar ais do mhúinteoirí meánscoile.
reply:
Foráiltear le Comhaontú na Seirbhíse Poiblí 2024 – 2026 go bhféadfaidh fostóirí agus ceardchumainn/comhlachais athruithe breise ar rátaí pá agus/nó ar choinníollacha fostaíochta a idirbheartú suas go 1% ar a mhéad den chostas bunphá, lena n-áirítear liúntais de chineál pá, a bhaineann leis an ngrád, leis an ngrúpa nó leis an gcatagóir fostaí ar leith nó leis an aonad margála ar leith. Féadfaidh go n-áireofar leis sin tograí a bhfuil athruithe ar struchtúir, ar chleachtais oibre nó ar choinníollacha eile seirbhíse i gceist leo.
Roghnaigh Cumann Múinteoirí Éireann (INTO) an Ciste Margála Áitiúla a úsáid chun roinnt éileamh a shocrú de réir théarmaí an Chiste agus laistigh den teorainn cistiúcháin Státchiste atá i bhfeidhm. Leagtar amach i gCiorclán 54/2026 an toradh a comhaontaíodh le INTO i ndáil le roinnt éileamh atá á socrú don earnáil bunscoile.
Ós rud é go bhfuil roinnt ceardchumann ag déanamh ionadaíocht do mhúinteoirí, is faoi gach eagraíocht ionadaíoch atá sé idirbheartú thar ceann a comhaltaí féin.
Ní fhéadfar leasuithe breise ar Théarmaí agus Coinníollacha múinteoirí, lena n-áirítear pá agus liúntais, a bhaint amach ach amháin trí idirchaidreamh agus comhaontuithe cómhargála idir an Rialtas agus na ceardchumainn Seirbhíse Poiblí. Ní fhéadfar athruithe den sórt sin a dhéanamh ach amháin faoi na próisis sin, agus ba ghá don Roinn, don Roinn Caiteachais Phoiblí agus Athchóirithe agus do na ceardchumainn iomchuí mionbhreithniú a dhéanamh ar aon tograí dá leithéid.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Education and Youth the number of applications for assistive technology for children with special educational needs received by her Department in each of the years 2024, 2025 and 2026; the number approved and refused, respectively; the number currently awaiting a decision; the average processing time to sanction; the longest period an application has remained awaiting sanction; the average time between sanction and the child receiving the device; and the number of children currently awaiting assistive technology following a recommendation from the National Council for Special Education.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 349 and 360 together.
The Assistive Technology (AT) Scheme provides funding towards specialised equipment for pupils with special educational needs who require assistive technology to access the curriculum.
There is currently no formal service standard or processing target for applications under the Assistive Technology Scheme. Under the current scheme, applications are assessed by the National Council for Special Education (NCSE) before being submitted to the Department for consideration and decision. Processing times can therefore vary depending on the volume and complexity of applications received.
The Department does, however, prioritise applications relating to pupils in 6th Class who are transitioning to post-primary education, together with applications supported by the Visiting Teacher Service, where appropriate.
The Assistive Technology Scheme is currently in the final stages of review. The revised scheme will introduce a new online application process as part of a needs-based model of support. This is expected to streamline the application process, significantly reduce processing times and enable pupils to access assistive technology supports more quickly following the identification of need.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Education and Youth whether a school may satisfy a parent's exercise of the right under section 30(2)(e) of the Education Act 1998 by requiring a child to remain physically present in the classroom while the instruction to which the parent has objected is delivered; if not, the national guidance that has been issued to schools regarding the physical removal or alternative supervision of a child during such instruction.
reply:
Under the provisions of the Education Act 1998, where schools provide religious instruction, parents or in the case of a student who has reached the age of 18 years, the student, can request that the student attend the school without attending religious instruction in the school. It is expected that this right will be upheld by schools on foot of a parental request.
The manner in which a school ensures that this right is upheld is a matter for the school concerned. Each school must determine the particular arrangements which are most appropriate in its individual circumstances having regard to local issues such as available space, supervision requirements and how the school concerned organises classes etc.
Guidance for good practice is available to schools in the follow-up paper to the Report of the Forum on Patronage and Pluralism in the Primary Sector which was published in 2014. The paper provides an overview of different types of arrangements that schools can put in place to facilitate parents who do not wish for their children to attend religious instruction. The paper encourages school authorities to consider their policies and practices and to review whether they are taking the steps necessary to welcome all pupils and make them feel included.

question: Deputy Pádraig O'Sullivan asked the Minister for Education and Youth the projected 2026 outturn for current expenditure on the education and youth Vote compared with the budget 2026 allocation of €11,475 million; and the reasons for the increase in the 2026 allocation to €12,442 million, by programme, in tabular form.
reply:
The Department of Education and Youth's published gross allocation for 2026 is €14.1 billion, comprising €12.4 billion in current expenditure and €1.7 billion in capital expenditure. This includes temporary funding of €320 million that mainly relates to an additional payroll payment falling due within the 2026 calendar year due to an extra (53rd) Thursday arising in the year. This is a payroll timing-related issue arises periodically, typically every six to seven years, depending on the timing of payroll payment dates and impacts all Departments who administer weekly or bi-weekly payrolls. This issue was known at Budget time and the Department of Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation informed that it would be provided for post Budget as part of the usual Revised Estimates process.
A further €646 million was agreed by Government post Budget to support the continued delivery of high-quality education and youth services, with this increase reflecting a combination of additional funding to meet growing demand across the sector, including special education provision, school transport and pay-related costs.
Details of the Department's 2026 allocation originally approved ('Voted') by Dáil Éireann is set out in the Estimates Volumes that are published on gov.ie.

reply:

question: Deputy Eoin Ó Broin asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment the actions he has taken pursuant to his obligations under section 9 of the Electricity Regulation Act 1999 to satisfy himself that data centre will not pose a risk to the continuity, security and quality of supplies of electricity.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 33 and 43 together.
Section 9 of the Electricity Regulation Act 1999 (as amended) sets out the responsibilities of the CRU with regard to electricity security of supply, which includes ensuring that supply and demand growth remain in balance. CRU have a dedicated email for queries via oireachtas@cru.ie.
EirGrid complement this role in their function as Transmission System Operator (TSO) through developing, managing and operating the transmission grid in Ireland. They balance supply and demand on an on-going basis, while also planning for Ireland’s long-term electricity needs. As part of its role in planning the electricity system, EirGrid publishes an annual All-Island Resource Adequacy Assessment (AIRAA) which provides a forecast for supply and demand on the all-island electricity grid over the next ten years. Ireland’s electricity security of supply is improving year on year. Overall, the AIRAA 2026-35 shows marked progress on the outlook for security of supply over the last five years.
The Government continues to work with electricity system operators to assess the various expected future demands on the system including from economic and population growth, housing, electric vehicle and heat pump targets in addition to data centre growth as part of their network development plans to ensure medium and long term future demands on our electricity system continue to be supported.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Education and Youth if she considers a book (details supplied) for third year junior cycle SPHE, to be appropriate and age-appropriate for students; and if her Department or the NCCA has reviewed its content for suitability for use in schools.
reply:
The Curriculum specification and prescribed material for any subject are determined by the National Council for Curriculum and Assessment (NCCA) – https://ncca.ie/en/.
To support teachers in teaching the curriculum, NCCA publishes online toolkits. The SPHE Toolkits have been developed to assist teachers in teaching Social, Personal and Health Education (SPHE). The resources presented on the toolkit aim to provide a range of relevant materials to support teaching and learning in SPHE. The toolkit states that each resource should be considered with respect to the needs and interests of children, their parents, the wider school community, and a school’s SPHE and RSE policies. The resources listed are not intended as exhaustive or prescriptive as each school will decide what resources are best suited to their needs and their context.
Apart from a small number of prescribed texts at post-primary level, determined by the NCCA, the decisions on which textbooks, programmes and resources, if any, to use in primary and post-primary schools are taken at school level. Any concerns regarding material published in textbooks should be raised with the publisher themselves.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Education and Youth what constitutes “regularly” for the purposes of her Department's requirement that exclusive school uniform supply arrangements should be tendered regularly under Circular 0032/2017; the way in which her Department verifies that schools comply with this provision; and the number of schools that have been found not to comply since the circular was issued.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 326 and 327 together.
Under the Education Act 1998, all recognised schools are managed by school Boards of Management. Individual school authorities are responsible for the drawing up of a school policy in relation to the wearing of uniforms. My department does not engage in procurement on behalf of schools, nor does it supervise school procurement activities. Responsibility for school uniform procurement rests with individual schools and their Boards of Management. Schools are advised to consult with parents and students when drafting a policy on uniforms.
Circular 0032/2017 sets out best practice guidelines and schools should create their uniform policies, and all policies, in consultation with their whole school community. As the Deputy is aware, Circular 0032/2017 is currently being reviewed. In addition to a focus on reducing costs for parents, the review is looking at the comfort and sustainability of school uniforms.
The provision and use of digital devices in post-primary schools is a matter for the board of management, having regard to their unique circumstances, educational programmes and the needs of their students. Schools are best placed to determine how technology can support teaching and learning in their settings, including decisions relating to device usage.

question: Deputy Mary Lou McDonald asked the Minister for Education and Youth to provide an updated timeframe on when the works on a new school build (details supplied) will recommence.
reply:
The new build for Gaelscoil Choláiste Mhuire is a large scale capital project for the construction of a sixteen classroom primary school in Dublin 1.
The building project to complete the new build for Gaelscoil Coláiste Mhuire, Dominick Street is at Stage 3 of the Architectural Planning Process – Tender Action and Award.
The Department can confirm that following a confidential conciliation process concerning all matters in dispute between the Department and the original contractor, the conciliator issued a formal recommendation for the resolution of those disputes, and that recommendation was accepted by both parties.

question: Deputy Niall Collins asked the Minister for Education and Youth the status of an application (details supplied).
reply:
Under the Assistive Technology Scheme, as set out in my Department’s Circular 0010/2013, funding is provided to schools towards the cost of computers and specialist equipment which are required for educational purposes.

question: Deputy Sean Fleming asked the Minister for Education and Youth if there are funding schemes, grants or other avenues of support available for a school (details supplied) in County Laois.
reply:
Supporting special educational needs (SEN) provision in schools is a priority for my department. The furniture and equipment needs of children with special educational needs is highly sensitive and individualised and as a result applications for funding are generally dealt with on a case-by-case basis as opposed to a general level of grant funding.
A school that has an existing or approved SEN classroom can make an application for a sensory room start up grant funding to my department. In order to be considered eligible for this grant the school must meet the following criteria:
The school must have an existing SEN classroom or be in the process of opening one;
The designated sensory room must be separate from the SEN classroom or any other room with its own entry/exit door and accessible from the main corridor, and should not require any major refurbishment. Part of classrooms, sensory spaces, and sensory pods do not qualify for the grant.
It should be noted the school in question received a grant of €7,000 in March 2022 for the provision of a Sensory room. Only one sensory room grant is funded by my department per school.

question: Deputy Barry Heneghan asked the Minister for Education and Youth the arrangements in place for Leaving Certificate students who, due to disability, medical needs or school avoidance, cannot regularly attend school to complete required coursework or additional assessment components; whether alternative arrangements are available to allow these students to complete the assessments; and the way in which she will ensure they are not prevented from taking any specific subject as a result.
reply:

Prior to the implementation of revised subject specifications and assessment arrangements under the Senior Cycle Redevelopment (SCR) programme, 28 existing Leaving Certificate subjects already included assessment components beyond written examinations, including oral examinations, practical performance tests, and coursework. question: Deputy Emer Currie asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment if his Department has assessed the likely impact of the proposed EU own resource based on non-collected waste electrical and electronic equipment, including its potential effect on collection, reuse, repair and recycling, and its interaction with the forthcoming revision of the EU Waste Electrical and Electronic Equipment framework.
reply:
Negotiations on the proposed EU own resource based on non-collected waste electrical and electronic equipment (WEEE) are being led by the Department of Finance as part of the Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF) package. The proposal has both environment and fiscal implications.
The EU framework governing the collection and environmentally sound management of WEEE is also under review, with a legislative proposal expected to be published later this year as part of the EU Circular Economy Act.
I understand that this review will seek to address, inter alia, the need to further incentivise and improve WEEE collection, while also refining the methodology used to calculate collection rates. It is particularly important that the methodology reflects developments such as longer product lifespans and policies promoting reuse and repair. Any assessment of the eventual impact of the proposed own resource, from an environment and circular economy perspective, will need to take account of these developments.
The expected focus on the calculation rate methodology will likely prove significant in underpinning the metric on which the own resource is based. Accurate collection rate reporting will be key to ensuring a level playing field across Member States as well as a consistent and proportionate application of any own resource levy.

question: Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Education and Youth the mechanisms in place to ensure that children with dyslexia and other reading challenges are identified at as early an age as possible.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 317, 318 and 319 together.
The Department of Education and Youth has invested considerably in ensuring that all recognised mainstream schools have been allocated additional special education teaching resources to support children with special educational needs, including students with literacy difficulties.
There are 15,200 special education teachers allocated to primary and post-primary schools to enable them to support children with special educational needs, including those with literacy difficulties.
It is important to note that the majority of students with literacy difficulties currently receive additional teaching support from a special education teacher in a mainstream class.

question: Deputy Eoin Ó Broin asked the Minister for Education and Youth to confirm an appeal regarding teacher allocation has been received from a school (details supplied); if the points outlined in the appeal will be comprehensively considered, taking into account the school's previous enrollment; and the unique experience of the school.
reply:
The key factor for determining the level of staffing resources provided at individual school level is the staffing schedule for the relevant school year and pupil enrolments on the previous 30 September.
The staffing arrangements include a provision whereby schools experiencing rapid increases in enrolment can apply for additional permanent mainstream posts, using projected enrolment. The school referred to by the Deputy has been allocated a post on this basis.
The staffing process also contains an appeals mechanism for schools to submit a staffing appeal to an independent Primary Staffing Appeals Board. One of the appeals criteria is aimed at schools that receive a projected enrolment post but do not meet the required enrolment on 30 September. Such schools may submit an appeal to the October meeting of the Primary Staffing Appeals Board. Information and application forms are available in Circular 0025/2026.

question: Deputy Daniel Ennis asked the Minister for Education and Youth the processes and supports in place to protect a child's right to education in the event that a school does not have enough SNAs to open at regular hours.
reply:
The National Council for Special Education (NCSE) is the statutory body responsible for the provision of special education and allocating supports for students with special educational needs.
Special needs assistants (SNA)s play a central role in the successful inclusion of students with additional and significant care needs in schools. They help ensure that these students can access an education to enable them to achieve their best outcomes and reach their full potential.
SNA posts are allocated to schools as a school-based resource. Principals/board of managements deploy SNAs within schools to meet the care support requirements of the students enrolled whom SNA support has been allocated.?This provides schools flexibility in how the SNA support is utilised.?
If a school has a concern with either their SNA allocation for the 2026/27 school year or the outcome of a SNA review/appeal, they should discuss the matter with their NCSE Special Education Needs Organiser (SENO).
My department and the NCSE are committed to ensuring that sufficient special education placements remain available for students with special educational needs and will continue to review and monitor the situation as to where new specialist provision is required.

question: Deputy Michael Cahill asked the Minister for Education and Youth if she is aware that families attending a school (details supplied) are currently privately funding school transport at significant cost due to the absence of a Bus Éireann school transport service; if her Department has assessed the transport needs of pupils attending the school; whether consideration will be given to establishing a dedicated school transport route or extending an existing route to serve the school.
reply:
The School Transport Scheme is a significant operation managed by Bus Éireann on behalf of the Department of Education and Youth.
The purpose of my Department's School Transport Scheme is, having regard to available resources, to support the transport to and from school of children who reside remote from their nearest school.
Under the terms of the School Transport Schemes, children are eligible for transport at primary level where they reside not less than 3.2 kms from and are attending their nearest national school. At post primary level, they are eligible where they reside not less than 4.8 kms from and are attending their nearest post primary school/education centre. Distance is determined by the Department/Bus Éireann and rules have regard to ethos and language.
Children who are not eligible but who apply for school transport are considered for spare seats that may exist after eligible children have been facilitated; such seats are referred to as concessionary seats.
A minimum number of 10 eligible children residing in a distinct locality, as determined by Bus Éireann, are required before consideration may be given to the establishment or retention of school transport services, provided this can be done within reasonable cost limits.
Bus Éireann has advised that 13 applications have been received from this school for the 26/27 school year, 4 of which are deemed eligible and 9 are not eligible.

question: Deputy Daniel Ennis asked the Minister for Education and Youth to confirm what supports are in place to assist special schools that are understaffed due to leave.
reply:
This government is fully committed to supporting students with special educational needs to fulfil their full potential and the Programme for Government makes a number of commitments to deliver on this objective.
DEY Circular 0054/2019 provides that each employer shall develop and maintain a policy on teacher/special needs assistant (SNA) absences, including non-statutory schemes e.g. Job Sharing, Career Breaks, Unpaid Leave, specific to the needs of the school authority. In drawing up this policy, the welfare and educational needs of the pupils must take precedence over all other considerations and must be in accordance with the rules of the relevant circulars. This policy shall have due regard to the capacity of the school to meet its obligations to its pupils and may therefore apply a limit to the number of teaching and SNA staff that may avail of non-statutory leave schemes at any one time. Employers must consider applications in the context of other statutory and non-statutory leave and must also take into account the availability of an appropriately qualified replacement teacher or SNA.

question: Deputy Seán Crowe asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment to report on the criteria used by the SEAI to prioritise the worst performing homes; and if this includes whether the occupant is suffering from a disability or long-term illness.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 25, 31 and 42 together.
The Warmer Homes Scheme (WHS) aims to improve the energy efficiency and warmth of homes owned by people at risk of energy poverty by providing fully funded retrofits. The scheme is operated by the Sustainable Energy Authority of Ireland (SEAI) on behalf of my Department and is funded through carbon tax revenues and the European Regional Development Fund.
The scheme targets support to those on the lowest incomes who are living in the least efficient homes so that the resources available can have the greatest impact in addressing energy poverty. Over 8,100 homes were upgraded last year, 109% of the annual target.
Applications to the scheme are assessed on the basis of when they first apply to the SEAI. Homes with the worst Building Energy Ratings also known as BER (E, F or G) are then prioritised for works. No other prioritisation takes place under the scheme.
Under the WHS, a pre-works BER is an obligation mandated for EU funding via the ERDF. The BER rating enables the SEAI to prioritise the worst performing homes and it is also key in determining the increase in energy efficiency as a result of the works upon completion.
Over 8,060 upgrades were completed under the scheme to end September 2026, an increase of 34.5% on the same period last year. At the same time, 11,823 applications have been received to the WHS to end September compared to 7,905 in the same time window last year, an increase of 49.6%.

question: Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Education and Youth the position regarding the review of the formal recognition of QQI level 6 qualification for special needs assistants relative to their pay scale and conditions.
reply:

It sets out a clear framework to strengthen and support SNAs through enhanced professional development, greater role clarity, workforce sustainability measures and stronger collaboration across school communities.
The Plan was developed following extensive engagement and consultation with stakeholders across the education sector and sets out high level objectives and policy developments under five key pillars including in the area of learning and development for SNAs.
Currently, the minimum educational requirement for appointment to the post of SNA is set out in Circular 0051/2019 ‘Recruitment and Appointment Procedures for Special Needs Assistants (SNAs). The current requirement is a level 3 qualification on the National Framework of Qualifications (NFQ) or a minimum of three grade Ds in the Junior Certificate or equivalent.
In the research phase of the Plan my department conducted the first national survey of special needs assistants (SNAs). The purpose of the survey which was accessed by more than 13,000 SNAs was to gather information about SNAs and their work to inform the Plan. question: Deputy John Connolly asked the Minister for Education and Youth to provide an update on the engagement between her Department and trade unions representing school secretaries and caretakers.
reply:
School secretaries and caretakers are at the heart of the school and are the key interface between students, parents, school leaders, and other staff. Without them, our schools would be unsustainable. In supporting these vital school staff members, we also support the school community as a whole.
Following intensive and constructive engagement between the Department of Education and Youth and Fórsa trade union at the Workplace Relations Commission (WRC) on the 1st of September 2026, a set of proposals aimed at resolving three elements of the dispute was issued by the WRC. Both parties recommended the WRC’s proposal for acceptance.
The WRC-recommended proposal includes enhanced terms and conditions for secretaries and caretakers including a pay framework for caretakers, bereavement leave and sick leave/acute illness leave for both secretaries and caretakers.
The Department notes the positive outcome of the secretaries’ and caretakers’ vote on the WRC proposal and is committed to working constructively with Fórsa trade union to implement the agreed proposals on a phased basis, as set out in the WRC proposal.
With regards to the claim for a comparable pension entitlement, following hearings in the Labour Court a recommendation was issued by the Court to the parties on 15 July 2026. The Department notes the outcome of the Fórsa ballot on this matter, and it is closely considering the recommendation of the Court and engaging with colleagues in Government as appropriate.

question: Deputy John Connolly asked the Minister for Education and Youth If her Department will review the current conditions pertaining to illness leave for school secretaries employed through her Department.
reply:
My Department is providing a payroll service for school secretaries which are covered under the terms of Department Circular 36/2022. The provision of a payroll service is part of a package agreed with FÓRSA, the trade union representing school secretaries, following a series of engagements at the Workplace Relations Commission (WRC). The agreement includes revised terms and conditions related to salary and leave entitlements.
The revised leave arrangements which have been included in the agreement are set with reference to statutory leave entitlements.
My Department has recently engaged with Fórsa under the auspices of the WRC in relation to the introduction of an acute illness provision for school secretaries covered under the terms of Department Circular 36/2022 and that process is ongoing.

question: Deputy Cian O'Callaghan asked the Minister for Education and Youth to detail the level of oversight her Department has over patron bodies; and the actions her Department can take if a school is not compliant with the Governance Manual for Primary Schools 2023-2027.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 300 and 303 together.
The Education Act, 1998 sets out the key roles and functions that are discharged by patrons and boards of management in the running of schools. Each primary school has a patron which is charged with carrying out the functions and exercising the powers conferred upon a patron under the Act. It is the duty of the patron, for the purposes of ensuring that a recognised school is managed in a spirt of partnership to appoint a board of management. The composition of the board is agreed nationally between patrons of schools, national associations of parents, recognised school management organisations, recognised trade unions and staff associations representing teachers, and the Minister.
The agreed procedures for the appointment of boards of management of primary schools and the rules under which these boards operate are set out in the department’s publication ‘Governance Manual for Primary Schools 2023-2027’. The term of office of the current boards of the circa 3,300 primary schools will expire on 30 November 2027 with new boards being appointed from the 1 December 2027. It is intended that this publication will be reviewed and updated as appropriate by my department in advance of that date in consultation with the relevant education partners at primary level including the National Parents Council. The National Parents Council is the representative organisation for parents of children attending primary school.

reply:

The Department is liaising with the relevant school management bodies to ensure schools are kept informed of developments, as well as planning for the operation of its own key services and those of its aegis bodies with the advice of DPER.

question: Deputy Paul Murphy asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade the reason "high degree of caution" travel advice was issued in relation to Brazil on 2 October 2026; if this was influenced by the decision of the US administration to suspend consular services in Brazil; and if she is concerned that the decision by the US was an attempt to influence the election campaign underway.
reply:
As I’m sure the Deputy is aware, my Department provides travel advice to assist our citizens in respect of more than 200 countries and territories worldwide. This advice provides an objective assessment of the risks our citizens could face while travelling, working, or living overseas, with a view to helping them to make informed decisions linked to their personal security.
The advice also includes a security rating, which represents my Department’s estimation of the relative safety and security of a country at a specific point in time, and is a useful tool in highlighting to a citizen how safe or unsafe a country or territory is to visit.
There are four levels of security status. Currently Brazil is assessed to be at level two, where citizens are advised to exercise a ‘High Degree of Caution’. Countries or territories in this category might have additional risks such as serious crime and/or terrorism, specific targeting of foreigners, disease or extreme weather events. Citizens travelling to this country can expect more or higher risks than they would find in Ireland.
This current security status for Brazil has been in place since November 2021. Travel advice for Brazil is formulated based on consultation with our Embassy in Brasilia, Consulate General in São Paulo, relevant local authorities, and other partners as appropriate.

My department will continue to engage directly with CEIST, as appropriate, throughout this review if further information is required.

reply:

The department is committed to providing funding to recognised primary and post-primary schools in the Free Education Scheme by way of per capita grants. question: Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Education and Youth the position regarding the 72 hours provisions listed in Circular 0071/2011; and the engagement she has had on this matter with trade unions representing special needs assistants.
reply:
As part of the agreement between my department, the relevant unions and school management boards on a standard employment contract for SNA's in 2005, all SNAs are required to be available for a number of days at the start and finish of each school term, not exceeding 12 days in total.
Under the Croke Park Agreement it was agreed to introduce greater flexibility to the use of these 12 days. Accordingly, DEY Circular 71/2011 was issued on 15 December 2011 which outlined that these 12 days now equate to 72 hours (pro-rata for part-time SNAs) to be used by schools as an additional bank of hours to be utilised and delivered outside of normal school opening hours and/or the normal school year.
This time outside of classroom hours (up to a maximum of 72 hours per school year) is used to complete training and upskilling as well as partaking in planning, reviewing and collaboration with colleagues. It allows SNAs to complete these important tasks without taking away from the time spent supporting students during the school day.
As you are aware my department published the first ever SNA Workforce Development Plan (the Plan), in June of this year. The Plan recognises the vital contribution SNAs make to supporting children and young people with special educational needs in our schools.
The Plan sets out high level objectives and policy developments for the SNA workforce under five key pillars. It provides a clear framework to strengthen and support SNAs through enhanced professional dev

question: Deputy Louise O'Reilly asked the Minister for Education and Youth if she will provide an update on the work her Department is undertaking to increase understanding and acceptance of neurodiversity in classrooms.
reply:
Enabling students with special educational needs to receive an education that meets their needs is a priority for this Government. It is also a key priority for me, my department and for the National Council for Special Education (NCSE).
The department has long held the position that children should be educated in the most inclusive environment possible. For the vast majority of children, this means being educated alongside their peers in mainstream schools and classes. To support those who attend mainstream classes, but who may have some additional needs, the department has allocated approximately 15,000 special education teachers to schools to assist them in meeting those needs. There are, however, some children whose needs are at a level of complexity that they cannot have those needs met in a mainstream environment.
Current Department of Education policy is based on a continuum of provision for children and young people with special educational needs, ranging from fulltime placement in mainstream settings to specialist provision, including special schools and classes.
Since 2017, and the introduction of a needs-based approach the Department allocates additional teaching supports directly to schools through the special education teaching (SET) model. This aims to ensure that those with the highest level of need have access to the greatest level of support in a timely and flexible manner, without the requirement for a diagnosis of disability.
