question: Deputy Louise O'Reilly asked the Minister for Education and Youth if all children with additional needs in school have an entitlement to an individual education plan; the scope that exists for parents input on the plan; the frequency with which the plan should be reviewed.
reply:
In December 2024, revised and updated Special Education Teaching Guidelines were issued to all schools to aid them in supporting students with identified special education learning needs.
The guidelines are available at the following link and includes information for both parents/guardian and children and young people on the importance of their input to the student support planning process. www.gov.ie/en/department-of-education/publications/set-guidelines-and-supporting-documentation-to-aid-schools-in-supporting-childrenyoung-people-with-special-education-needs/#primary-schools
The provision of special education teaching support is a collaborative and holistic process, involving parents/guardians, children, teachers and other professionals, where appropriate.
The views and wishes of children are central to planning and decision making in relation to special education provision.
The Student Support Plan is a learning plan which documents the child’s strengths, interests and needs, as well as the priority learning needs that have been agreed as the basis for targets and interventions. Some children may present with many needs, and their priority learning needs should be identified and recorded. These inform the targets, supports and interventions required to remove identified barriers to learning and participation across the curriculum, and in the life of the school community.

question: Deputy Louise O'Reilly asked the Minister for Education and Youth if she has considered the inclusion of a disability awareness module on the school curriculum.
reply:
While there is not a standalone module on ‘disability awareness’, disability, inclusion, equality and respect for diversity are embedded across both the primary and post-primary curriculum.
Primary
The redeveloped Primary Curriculum places a strong emphasis on inclusion and ensuring that every child experiences a sense of belonging and participation in school life. The new Wellbeing specification (including SPHE) includes learning about:
• valuing and respecting all people
• developing empathy and positive relationships
• understanding diversity and inclusion
• promoting a sense of belonging for everyone in the school community.
Post-primary
At junior and senior cycle, subjects which foster students' awareness and promote understanding and empathy towards people experiencing various forms of discrimination include CSPE, SPHE, Religious Education, History and Politics and Society. Students learn about:
• equality and human rights
• diversity and inclusion
• respect for all members of society
• challenging prejudice, discrimination and exclusion
• creating inclusive communities and relationships.
SPHE, for example, can provide a safe, supportive and non-judgemental space where students’ self-awareness and awareness of others can grow, and where they engage in reflection and dialogue, and identify actions they can take to protect and promote their own wellbeing and that of others.

reply:
I wish to thank the Deputy for raising this issue.
The Department of Education and Youth has invested considerably in ensuring that all recognised mainstream schools have been allocated additional special education teaching resources to support children with special educational needs, including students with literacy difficulties.
There are 15,200 special education teachers allocated to primary and post-primary schools to enable them to support children with special educational needs.
It is important to note that the majority of students with literacy difficulties currently receive additional teaching support from a special education teacher in a mainstream class.
This is provided on the basis of the individual student’s learning needs, identified in schools, as opposed to being based on a requirement for a child to have a diagnosis, or an assessment, of a particular disability.
Furthermore, there are four schools dedicated to supporting students with specific learning disability (SLD). There are also fourteen SLD classes in eleven mainstream primary schools located across the country, in counties Dublin, Clare, Louth, Galway, Kerry and Wexford.
However, I recognise that more needs to be done. I am happy to advise that my officials in conjunction with the NCSE are currently at an advanced stage in developing a pilot programme to test best practice and support policy formulation going forward.

question: Deputy Louise O'Reilly asked the Minister for Education and Youth the way in which disability inclusion and awareness is taught to trainee teachers; the number of hours per year of their course that is dedicated to disability training.
reply:
Under Section 38 of the Teaching Council Act, all initial teacher education programmes must be accredited by the Teaching Council for registration purposes. The Council reviewed its policy on standards for programmes of initial teacher education (ITE) and published updated standards in Céim Standards for Initial Teacher Education in October 2020.
The Céim standards require programmes to include foundation studies, professional studies and school placement and are underpinned by seven core elements that underpin all aspects of programme design. Inclusive Education is one of the seven core elements which underpin all aspects of programme design and delivery in accredited ITE programmes.
Céim describes inclusive education as one that ‘includes the fostering of appropriate learning environments, including digital ones, that support the development of student teachers’ ability to provide for the learning needs of all pupils by utilising, for example, a universal design for learning framework’.
The term inclusive education is any aspect of teachers’ learning aimed at:
• Improving their capacity to address and respond to the diversity of learners’ needs,
• Removing barriers to education through the accommodation and provision of appropriate structures and arrangements; and
• Enabling each learner to achieve the maximum benefit from his/her attendance at school.

reply:

It aims to assist teachers, SNAs and others working with children and young people with autism in an education setting to understand their needs so that there can be effective engagement. reply:
This government is fully committed to supporting students with special educational needs to fulfil their full potential and the Programme for Government makes a number of commitments to deliver on this objective.
For special schools and classes, the ratios for teacher to student is grounded in the report of the special education review committee or SERC report from 1993. While this report provides a grounding for the allocation to special schools and classes, the NCSE can also examine the allocations based on the individual needs of the school/class. There are Department circulars / guidelines and NCSE guidelines and processes in place which determine the number of teachers in place to support children with special educational needs.
When a new special school is established, there is an automatic allocation of a minimum of 1 teacher and 2 SNAs per class of 6 children but this is invariably increased based on the profile of needs of the children enrolled. Special schools are resourced by the NCSE based on an annual review of their enrolment and the profile of the children and young people enrolled in them.
A list of all mainstream and special schools is available on my department's website on gov.ie. question: Deputy Louise O'Reilly asked the Minister for Education and Youth the way in which she will ensure that the recommendations in assessment reports for neurodivergent pupils submitted to schools are implemented.
reply:
This government is fully committed to supporting students with special educational needs to fulfil their full potential and the Programme for Government makes a number of commitments to deliver on this objective.
Schools support children and young people using the Continuum of Support, whereby school staff use a problem-solving approach, including school screening (assessment) and evidence-based intervention, for children and young people experiencing difficulties in the school context. For children with additional learning needs, the school will develop a Student Support Plan. This plan outlines:
• The child's strengths, interests, and needs.
• Priority learning goals.
• The supports and interventions that will help the child participate fully in school and make progress in their learning.
The Student Support Plan is developed collaboratively and may involve the child's teacher, parents or guardians, the child themselves, and may include assessment reports from other relevant professionals. If a child is not making sufficient progress following appropriate supports and interventions being provided by the school, the school may consider referring the child to National Educational Psychological Service (NEPS) to assist in identifying their needs and determining any additional supports required.

question: Deputy Seán Ó Fearghaíl asked the Minister for Education and Youth the occupational therapy and speech and language therapy supports allocated under the education therapy service to a school (details supplied); the number of occupational therapists and speech and language therapists assigned to the school; whether such posts are filled and fully operational; the nature and extent of services delivered since the school's inclusion in the education therapy service rollout; and the way in which the education therapy service interacts with children's disability network team services.
reply:
In line with the 2025 Programme for Government, there is a commitment to introduce a national therapy service in education settings. The Education Plan 2025, which was announced on the 19th of June 2025, confirmed Government approval for the establishment of the Education Therapy Service (ETS).
The ETS is an additional support for children with special education needs and has been established as an important support for children and young people in their school environment. The service will include Occupational Therapists and Speech and Language Therapists initially and is delivered by the National Council for Special Education (NCSE). The ETS will be delivered in a complementary manner to existing services and will not replace family centred supports currently provided by existing children’s health and disability services.
In February 2026, my department announced the phased expansion of the ETS starting with in special schools. The expanded service started with an initial 45 special schools in February 2026 and a further 19 in September 2026. It is envisaged therapists will support a cluster of schools. The number of schools a therapist will support in a cluster will be dependent on a number of factors including; geographical location, the demographic and number of students per school.

question: Deputy Claire Kerrane asked the Minister for Education and Youth if she is aware that up to 70 children in the Ballinasloe area are currently without school transport following the withdrawal of private operators from the system; the action her Department will take to ensure all affected children have access to school transport.
reply:
The School Transport Scheme is a significant operation managed by Bus Éireann on behalf of the Department of Education and Youth.
Under the current terms of the mainstream scheme, children are eligible for transport at primary level where they reside not less than 3.2 kilometres from and are attending their nearest national school, and at post primary level where they reside not less than 4.8 kilometres from and are attending their nearest post primary school/education centre as determined by the department/Bus Éireann, having regard to ethos and language.
A minimum number of 10 eligible children residing in a distinct locality, as determined by Bus Éireann, are required before consideration may be given to the establishment of school transport services, provided this can be done within reasonable cost limits.
The scheme is a demand led scheme based on the number of eligible children who apply. It is operated using a mix of Bus Éireann owned vehicles and directly recruited drivers, and private contractors who recruit their own drivers to operate on the scheme. Private operators who are not contracted under the scheme are outside the remit of the Department.
Bus Éireann has advised that there are no operational issues with services operating as part of the school transport scheme in the area referred to by the Deputy. 348 mainstream and 105 SEN pupils have been allocated on school transport services into schools in the area in question for the 2026/27 school year.

question: Deputy Seán Ó Fearghaíl asked the Minister for Education and Youth the current status of the replacement building project for a school (details supplied); whether the project remains approved and fully funded; the stage reached within her Department's building programme; whether the existing planning permission remains valid; the estimated timeline for progression to tender and construction; whether her Department is satisfied that the current accommodation is adequate to meet the educational, care and therapy needs of pupils pending delivery of the new school building.
reply:
The brief for the project referred to by the Deputy is to provide a new 16 classroom Special school including the demolition of some existing buildings. It also includes the retention of an extension completed in 2012.
The major building project for the school is currently at an advanced stage of architectural planning – Stage 2(b) Detailed Design, where the Design Team have secured all statutory approvals and are preparing the suite of tender documents.
My Department remains committed to progressing this matter, and a meeting has been scheduled with the Principal and the relevant Stakeholders for early November.
St Annes is one of the 105 prioritised projects to progress to tender on a rolling basis over the course of 2026 and 2027 and within the context of NDP funding parameters. The timing of project progression will reflect the need to carefully manage the rollout of these projects to construction on a controlled basis to ensure that projects are delivered efficiently, align with the requirements of the Infrastructure Guidelines and Capital Works Management Framework and remain within the parameters of NDP funding.
My Department is committed to supporting the operation of the school system with the necessary infrastructure and facilities for the year ahead.

question: Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment to provide an update on the operation of section 32 of the Circular Economy and Miscellaneous Provisions Act 2022, including the number of local authorities who have availed of its provision and put CCTV into operation.
reply:
Since 15 February 2024, when the relevant provisions of the Circular Economy and Miscellaneous Provisions Act 2022 were commenced, all local authorities have been able to put in place the necessary procedures to facilitate the GDPR-compliant use of CCTV and other mobile recording technologies to combat littering and illegal dumping.
The use of these technologies is an operational matter for each local authority, which must determine the most appropriate enforcement response based on local circumstances and priorities. Accordingly, my Department does not maintain a central record of the number of local authorities that have introduced CCTV schemes under these provisions.
I am aware, however, that Carlow County Council recently secured the first conviction for illegal dumping arising from the GDPR-compliant use of CCTV under the new legislative framework. This represents a significant milestone and demonstrates the effectiveness of these powers in supporting environmental enforcement. Funding for these cameras was secured through the Department’s Anti-Dumping Initiative which has made available some €26 million to local authorities, community groups and other stakeholders since its establishment in 2017.

question: Deputy Niamh Smyth asked the Minister for Education and Youth further to Parliamentary Question No. 67955/26, if she will review the case of a person (details supplied).
reply:
The School Transport Scheme is a significant operation managed by Bus Éireann on behalf of the Department of Education and Youth.
Under the terms of the Post Primary School Transport Scheme, children are eligible for transport where they reside not less than 4.8 kms from their nearest post primary school/centre as determined by the Department/Bus Éireann, having regard to ethos and language.
Where a child is eligible for transport and the application and payment process has been completed on time, they will get a seat on a school bus service, where a service is available.
Children who are not eligible, but who apply for school transport are considered for spare seats that may exist after eligible children have been facilitated; previously known as concessionary seats.
Because of the nature of transport for non-eligible children and the priority of providing places for eligible children, there may be an excess of demand over supply for non-eligible pupils. In these cases, Bus Éireann will allocate tickets for spare seats using an agreed selection process.
Bus Eireann has advised that the family referred to by the Deputy are not eligible for school transport as they are attending their 3rd nearest post primary centre.
Bus Éireann further advise the pupil referred applied and paid on time but was not successful in obtaining a ticket for the current 26/27 school year. The service is operating to capacity, and the pupil cannot be accommodated at this time.

question: Deputy Donna McGettigan asked the Minister for Education and Youth if alternative arrangements can be approved for small schools where existing kitchen facilities do not meet the new requirements for the School Meals Programme; if funding is available to help schools make the necessary adaptations; if the impact of these requirements on small and rural schools has been assessed; and the immediate solution that can be put in place to restore the lunch programme for pupils in a school (details supplied) in County Clare.
reply:
The School Meals Programme, operated by the Department of Social Protection (DSP), provides funding towards the provision of food services to schools and organisations.
The objective of the School Meals Programme is to provide regular, nutritious food to children to support them in taking full advantage of the education provided to them. The programme is an important component of policies to encourage school attendance and extra educational achievement.
My department has in place detailed design guidelines for primary and post primary schools which provide for a standard range of servery and eating facilities in the design of new and refurbished schools.
The provision of hot school meals in schools is not dependent on cooking facilities being available in the school. The scheme is aimed primarily at schools with no onsite cooking facilities.
Each school must identify a supplier who will supply (prepare and deliver) the hot meals in line with the relevant food safety regulations and in compliance with the Healthy Ireland ‘Nutrition Standards for Hot School Meals’.
In circumstances where a primary school is unable to secure a hot meals supplier due its location or facilities and space, it should explore options with local caterers or supermarkets within the area. If a school is still unsuccessful in securing a supplier, they should then try to source a local supplier that could instead provide a cold lunch with drink as an alternative to a hot meal.

reply:
The Department of Education and Youth has invested considerably in ensuring that all recognised mainstream schools have been allocated additional special education teaching resources to support children with special educational needs, including students with literacy difficulties.
There are 15,200 special education teachers allocated to primary and post-primary schools to enable them to support children with special educational needs.
It is important to note that the majority of students with literacy difficulties currently receive additional teaching support from a special education teacher in a mainstream class.
This is provided on the basis of the individual student’s learning needs, identified in schools, as opposed to being based on a requirement for a child to have a diagnosis, or an assessment, of a particular disability.
Furthermore, there are four schools dedicated to supporting students with specific learning disability (SLD). There are also fourteen SLD classes in eleven mainstream primary schools located across the country, in counties Dublin, Clare, Louth, Galway, Kerry and Wexford.
However, I recognise that more needs to be done. I am happy to advise that my officials in conjunction with the NCSE are currently at an advanced stage in developing a pilot programme to test best practice and support policy formulation going forward.

question: Deputy Denise Mitchell asked the Minister for Education and Youth the way in which existing common enrolment systems for primary schools should operate if a change of ethos results in two linked schools having differing patrons; and if there is a best practice guide for schools undergoing a change of patron in terms of whether they should proceed via a phased transition or a whole-of-school transition to the new ethos.
reply:
My department ran the Primary School Survey in November and December 2025 and provided primary schools with their survey results in June 2026. This is a separate process to "enrolment systems for primary schools”.
An enrolment system is an administrative admissions process and is separate from any patronage decision-making arrangements. However, schools are expected to engage with and communicate with their school communities in the normal way regarding any significant changes to admissions arrangements.
As part of the Primary School Survey process, schools have been asked to reflect on their survey results, engage with their school community and inform their patron and my department by 31 October if they request to be included in the first group to change configuration arising from this process.
If a school informs their patron and my department that it wishes to explore a change in configuration, my department will assess the potential outcomes on overall school places in the area.
In relation to a change of ethos to multi-denominational, this can take place all at once, or gradually, starting with younger classes over time.
My department will assign a point of contact to offer guidance, as appropriate, to help schools in considering the practicalities and timeframe for a change in configuration.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment the mechanisms in place to monitor the pricing of household waste collection services; the number of complaints received regarding household waste collection charges in County Cork in each of the years 2024, 2025 and to date in 2026.
reply:
At the outset I would note that responsibility for the policy governing waste collection and pricing of same is under remit of my colleague Minister Darragh O’Brien’s Department of Climate, Energy and the Environment.
For the Deputy’s information, my Department contacted the Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (CCPC), the independent statutory body responsible for enforcing competition and consumer protection law under the remit of my Department.
Based on records held by the CCPC, there were 50 contacts to its consumer helpline relating to waste services between 1 January 2024 and 8 October 2026. The figures are based on callers selecting the "waste services" category when contacting the helpline. As a result, not all contacts necessarily constituted complaints regarding waste collection charges. For instance it should be noted that 3 of the cited 50 cases related specifically to skips.
Where consumers have concerns that consumer protection legislation may have been breached, they may bring the matter to the attention of the CCPC, which assesses such information as part of its enforcement and compliance functions.

question: Deputy Michael Healy-Rae asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment further to his Department's press release, to confirm the timeframe for the publication of the Short-Term Letting and Tourism Bill.
reply:
In April of last year, I obtained Government approval for the general scheme of the Short-Term Letting and Tourism Bill. Upon enactment, the Short-Term Letting and Tourism Bill will provide, for the first time, a comprehensive statutory framework governing the short-term letting sector in Ireland, including the establishment of a national register. The Government approved the Bill for publication on 6 October, representing a significant step towards a more transparent and effectively regulated sector. The Department, in conjunction with the relevant parliamentary offices, is progressing the necessary arrangements for the publication of the Bill. Once published the Bill will then proceed to Second Stage in Dáil Éireann.
This register, which has been broadly welcomed by the tourism sector, will be implemented and managed by Fáilte Ireland. The register will launch on 1 December 2026, with a legal obligation on all operators to register by 31 December 2026. The register will operate in compliance with the EU Short-Term Rental Regulation (EU) 2024/1028, which came into effect on 20 May 2026.
The planning policy framework for short-term letting activity, and all matters relating to planning and local authority resources, fall within the remit of the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage.

question: Deputy Albert Dolan asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment if Government employment or job-creation projections and targets for 2026 to 2030 have been disaggregated by region; to provide by region and year; and to provide the equivalent regional projections or targets underpinning the national planning framework for comparison, in tabular form.
reply:
The National Planning Framework (NPF) establishes overarching spatial objectives for employment growth, including a target to concentrate 50% of future employment growth in Ireland's five cities. However, the revised NPF does not specify quantified employment growth targets for individual regions.
Separately, my Department has undertaken a statistical analysis to examine how projected national employment growth is likely to be distributed regionally. The analysis is anchored to the central scenario in the Department of Finance’s Future Forty framework and extends to 2040. It provides a baseline projection of how regional employment might develop if historical relationships between national and regional employment continue. However, these projections are not Government employment or job-creation targets.
The analysis indicates that employment would grow across all regions, with some concentration in Dublin and the wider eastern region, reflecting the existing scale of these labour markets as well as their projected growth rates. At the same time, most regions exhibit broadly similar growth rates over the projection horizon, and are projected to grow at rates broadly in line with the national average. question: Deputy Richard Boyd Barrett asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment whether he is considering measures to ban a product associated with ineradicable and significant occupational safety risks (details supplied) with regard to his responsibility for workplace safety legislation and in line with a proposal under consideration in California.
reply:
The safety, health and welfare of workers is a priority for my department. There are existing legal obligations under the Safety, Health and Welfare at Work Act 2005 and associated regulations requiring employers to identify, assess and control risks arising from exposure to respirable crystalline silica dust.
In particular, work involving exposure to respirable crystalline silica dust generated by a work process is classified as carcinogenic under the Carcinogens, Mutagens and Reprotoxic Substances (CMRS) Regulations. These Regulations require employers to reduce the use of carcinogenic substances in the workplace, in particular by replacing them, insofar as is technically possible, with a substance, mixture or process which, under its conditions of use, is not dangerous or is less dangerous to employees’ health or safety. Employers are also required to ensure that the level of exposure of employees is reduced to a level as low as technically possible, representing a high duty of care.
The existing framework therefore places significant obligations on employers to prevent or minimise exposure to respirable crystalline silica dust. These include conducting risk assessments, implementing appropriate engineering controls and safe systems of work, using dust suppression techniques such as wet cutting, providing suitable respiratory protective equipment and undertaking health surveillance where appropriate.

question: Deputy Emer Currie asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment for an update on matters raised in correspondence (details supplied).
reply:
The Companies Registration Office (CRO) has advised that it has no statutory power under the Registration of Business Names Act 1963 to remove a person from the register of business names, nor does it have a power to remove or suppress a residential address that has been properly registered under that Act.
Unlike the Companies Act 2014, which contains provisions allowing for the non-disclosure of a company officer's residential address in certain exceptional circumstances, no equivalent provision exists in the Registration of Business Names Act 1963.
Accordingly, there is currently no statutory mechanism available to the Registrar to remove, redact or suppress a residential address from the business names register, including in circumstances where personal safety concerns have been raised. Similarly, the fact that a person who has made a registration of a business name, and who subsequently determines that that registration was not required, does not provide a legal basis for the removal of the registration or the associated address from the register.
My Department is currently developing legislation to repeal and replace the Registration of Business Names Act 1963.

question: Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment his views on whether the right-to-request model is sufficient in the context where an employee's request to work remotely is refused but the WRC cannot examine whether the refusal itself was reasonable.
reply:
Under Part 3 of the Work Life Balance Act 2023, employees are able to refer a dispute to the Workplace Relations Commission (WRC) where an employer fails to fulfil their obligations under the Act. The WRC and the Labour Court can direct employers to comply with the requirements of the Act however, neither the WRC nor the Labour Courts are empowered to assess the merits of the employer’s decision, nor are they empowered to overturn a refusal of remote working. The obligation on the employer is to comply with the procedures set out in the Act.
It is not the Government’s role, nor the role of the Workplace Relations Commission, to effectively assess and direct when employees can or cannot work remotely. Providing a right to request strikes the right balance between flexibility and the need for businesses to remain competitive, profitable and viable.
The Department completed a statutory review of the right to request remote working provisions of the Work Life Balance Act 2023 in March 2024. The report is available on the Department’s website and has been laid before the Houses of the Oireachtas. The review found that, when used, the legislation is operating effectively in practice with the majority of requests to work remotely being either fully or partially approved. While the number of requests made under the legislation is currently low, when employees do avail of their right, the legislation works well. On this basis, amendments to the primary Act are not proposed at this tim

The scheme targets support to those on the lowest incomes who are living in the least efficient homes so that the resources available can have the greatest impact in addressing energy poverty. Over 8,100 homes were upgraded last year, 109% of the annual target.

question: Deputy Paul McAuliffe asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment if he is examining whether consumers should have a statutory right to speak with a human customer service representative, rather than being required to deal exclusively with artificial intelligence or automated systems, when engaging with telecommunications, utility and other essential service providers.
reply:
With the exception of financial products or services, there is currently no general provision in Irish consumer protection law requiring traders to provide consumers with access to a human customer service representative or preventing the use of artificial intelligence, chatbots or other automated systems for customer interactions. The way a trader provides customer service is a commercial decision for the trader.
However, under Part 5 of the Consumer Rights Act 2022, there is certain information which traders must provide to consumers before they enter a contract. This includes information which will allow consumers to contact traders and direct complaints, such as the geographical address at which the trader is established, the trader’s telephone number and the trader’s email address. Where applicable, traders must also provide consumers with information as to their complaint handling policy.
Where a consumer is seeking to exercise their rights under consumer protection law, such as seeking a remedy for a non-conformity with a good or service, they must be able to contact the trader in order to do so. Where a trader fails to facilitate consumers in exercising their statutory rights, this may give rise to issues under consumer protection legislation, depending on the circumstances.

question: Deputy Naoise Ó Muirí asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation when the upgrade works to the playground in the People’s Gardens, Phoenix Park, Dublin 8 are expected to be completed; the length of time the playground is expected to remain closed to the public; the anticipated reopening date; the impact this is having on the local community.
reply:
The Office of Public Works (OPW) is working to ensure the older children's playground in the People's Gardens can re-open as soon as possible.
The closure was necessary for health and safety reasons, due to a collapsed culvert beneath the playground. The cause of the collapse has now been fully investigated and the OPW will publish tender documents for the necessary works in the coming days. It is anticipated that a Contractor will be appointed by mid-December, with works to commence in January.
While it is not possible to give a definitive timescale for completion at this time, every effort is being made to reopen the playground as soon as possible.

question: Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation to list the projects that have been designated under s.20 of the Future Ireland Fund and Infrastructure, Climate and Nature Fund Act 2024.

The Future Ireland Fund and Infrastructure, Climate and Nature Fund Act 2024 established the Infrastructure, Climate and Nature Fund (ICNF).
The criteria under which a project may be designated by a Minister are provided in Section 20 of the Act. These criteria include contributing to or being likely to contribute, either directly or indirectly, to the:
• Reduction of greenhouse gas emissions
• Improvement of water quality
• Achievement of conservation objectives or the improvement of habitats

In addition to the projects listed above, the Minister for Transport has designated MetroLink as an eligible project, while the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment has designated both the Biomethane Programme and the District Heating Programme as relevant projects.
Although these projects will not receive ICNF funding in 2026, it is intended that funding will be provided between 2027 and 2030.

question: Deputy Eoin Hayes asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation the way in which his Department accounts for the difference in the figures in the Expenditure Report released for Budget 2027 between the detailed selected measures totalling just over €1 billion and the allocation for new initiatives totalling over €1.8 billion.
reply:
The Department of Social Protection was allocated €31 billion in Budget 2027, an increase of over €2 billion or 7% on the REV 2026 allocation.
As set out in Table 5 on page 162 of the Budget 2027 Expenditure Report, when account is taken of the net effect of various timing and other adjustments, €1.8 billion is being provided to fund both new and existing policies, including policy adjustments and the expansion of services.
This category reflects increases in the cost of existing services and schemes, including recipient growth on pension and illness, disability and carer schemes due to demographic changes (population growth, ageing) and previous policy expansions.
It also includes funding for new policy changes and service expansions, including those announced on Budget Day, such as broadening eligibility, extending existing supports, or introducing new measures to improve public services.
A selection of the measures provided for under this category are included in Table 4 on page 160 of the Expenditure Report, with the cost of the measures set out totalling over €1 billion in 2027.

question: Deputy Pádraig O'Sullivan asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation the specific savings and efficiency measures each Department will implement in 2027 to meet the expenditure levy totalling €446 million set out in the Budget 2027 Expenditure Report, in tabular form, by Department; and the reason the Department of Education and Youth is not subject to the levy.
reply:
The achievement of value for money in public expenditure is a Government priority, with an agenda for reform and efficiencies established over the past year. Public expenditure must be managed to maximise value for money for the taxpayer and support the delivery of Government priorities within the voted allocation, as outlined in Circular 18/2025 (Value for Money Obligations).
Earlier this year, the Government agreed that additional funding of €646 million would be provided to the Department of Education and Youth in 2026. To accommodate this reprioritisation and deliver on the 2027 ceiling agreed under the Medium Term Fiscal Plan, an Expenditure Levy of €446 million has been reflected in all Budget 2027 funding allocations, with the exception the Department of Education and Youth.
In April, my Department wrote to all other Departments highlighting the Government decision to apply an Expenditure Levy for 2027 and emphasising the need to achieve savings. Given that the levy was applied to offset a permanent increase in the funding allocation for the Department of Education and Youth, no levy was applied to that Department.
In September 2026, I wrote to all Ministers, asking them to identify efficiencies and reforms in the context of the Estimates process for Budget 2027. Reforms and efficiencies were published and are set out in tabular form for each Vote or Vote Group in Part II of the 2027 Expenditure Report, which can be accessed at the following link: assets.gov.ie/static/

reply:
The Infrastructure Guidelines and the Capital Works Management Framework (CWMF) set down the procedures that public bodies who are charged with the delivery of public infrastructure and building projects must follow.
Securing value for money is an ongoing priority for this Government and is at the heart of all decision making, at every stage of a policy or programme lifecycle. Delivering value for money is about securing the efficient and effective use of public resources in the pursuit of better public services, living standards and infrastructure for the people of Ireland. It is not solely concerned with costs and price levels – it also involves the consideration of quality, specialist expertise, and social and environmental impacts.
Under the Infrastructure Guidelines and the CWMF, public works contracts are structured so that risks are allocated to the party best placed to manage and mitigate them.
The CWMF provides a comprehensive suite of standard public works contracts. These contracts clearly define the circumstances in which contractors may be entitled to additional payment and the risks that remain the responsibility of the contractor. Compensation events are limited and are explicitly identified in the contract documentation.
Schedule K17 in the form of tender identifies which classes of events are actually compensation events. Contractor claims are detailed in clause 10.3.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance the assessment that has been undertaken of the distributional impact of local property tax across households according to income, household composition, property ownership; the number of properties owned; and if an assessment has been made of the ability of households to meet increases in LPT.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 183 and 218 together.
Local Property Tax (LPT) was legislated for in 2012 in the Finance (Local Property Tax) Act 2012. On the introduction of the LPT, the Government decided that a liability to the tax should apply to all owners of residential properties based on the market value of the property and with a limited number of reliefs available. This ensures that liable taxpayers are not charged more to account for a shortfall driven by reductions in LPT charges based on other factors, including household composition.
The design of LPT was considered by an interdepartmental group chaired by Dr. Don Thornhill in 2012. In 2019, the tax was subject to a review by an interdepartmental group chaired by the Department of Finance. The distributional impact of LPT according to household composition or property ownership was not examined as part of these reports.
The 2019 review group conducted a distributional impact analysis according to income using the ESRI SWITCH (Simulating Welfare and Income Tax Changes) tax and benefit micro-simulation model. This model was used to compare the impact that different reform scenarios for LPT would have on household incomes relative to a benchmark position where the property value increases but there is no change in the structure of LPT. The results indicate that all scenarios were progressive rather than regressive to varying degrees.

reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 188 and 217 together.
The Help to Buy (HTB) incentive, is a tax-based scheme to assist first-time purchasers with the deposit they need to buy or build a new house or apartment. It also aims to encourage additional supply of new houses by supporting demand.
HTB provides a refund of Income Tax and Deposit Interest Retention Tax (DIRT) paid in Ireland over the previous four years, subject to limits outlined in the legislation.

Additionally, the purchase value/approved valuation of the property must not exceed €500,000. • €30,000; or
• 10 per cent of the purchase price of the new property; or
• the amount of Income Tax and DIRT paid in the four years before application for the relief.
As announced as part of Budget 2027 the maximum amount of the relief, which a can be claimed by a first time purchaser or self builder, increased by €5,000, to €35,000. The change was implemented by way of a Budget night Financial Resolution which took effect from 7 October 2026.

question: Deputy Michael Healy-Rae asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance to review the way in which fuel is taxed in Ireland with a view to reducing the Government take.
reply:
Fuel taxation policy is kept under regular review.
As the Deputy will be aware, during the current fuel crisis, this Government has acted on numerous occasions to shield households and businesses from the worst of the impacts. These actions have included reductions in the excise duty on fuel products, which, from March 2026 to June 2027, will reduce excise revenues by an estimated €1.3 billion.

question: Deputy Michael Healy-Rae asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance that RZL tax should not be applicable to local authorities; and if he will examine this issue (details supplied).
reply:
Finance Act 2021 introduced Part 22A Residential Zoned Land Tax (RZLT) into the Taxes Consolidation Act 1997. RZLT is designed to prompt residential development by owners of land that satisfies the relevant criteria for the tax, that being that the land is zoned for residential or mixed-use (including residential) purposes and that is serviced.
RZLT is an annual tax, calculated at a rate of 3% of the market value of the land within its scope. The tax is due and payable from 2025 onwards in respect of land which satisfied the relevant criteria on 1 January 2022, or in the course of 2022, as where land satisfies the relevant criteria after 1 January 2022, RZLT will be first due in the third year after the year in which it satisfies the relevant criteria. RZLT first arose on 1 February 2025 and the 2026 liability was payable by 23 May 2026, subject to certain exceptions.
The legislation underpinning RZLT provides for a number of exemptions, deferrals and abatements subject to the relevant criteria being met. The legislation does not provide for a specific exemption for local authorities. Local authorities that own land meeting the criteria for RZLT are subject to the tax. It is important to note that, to come within the scope of RZLT, land must be both zoned by the local authority for residential use and serviced. The intention of RZLT is to activate development of this residentially zoned and serviced land to meet critical housing needs.

reply:

Health expenses are defined as “expenses in respect of the provision of health care” and include "expenses representing the cost of maintenance or treatment necessarily incurred in connection with the services of a practitioner". question: Deputy Pearse Doherty asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance to provide details of the changes made to the research and development tax credit regime.
reply:
It is assumed that the Deputy is referring to the changes made to the Research and Development (R&D) tax credit regime as part of Budget 2027.

question: Deputy Pearse Doherty asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance if the increase in rent a room relief is universal or solely for multi-room lets; and the assessment or analysis carried out on the likely impact this will have on rents charged.
reply:
Rent a Room relief was introduced in 2001 as an incentive to encourage individuals to let rooms in their sole or main residence as residential accommodation in order to bring about an increase in the availability of rental accommodation.
To qualify for the exemption, it is necessary for the residential premises to be situated in the State and occupied by the individual as his or her sole or main residence during the tax year. The relief only applies to individuals. It does not apply to companies or partnerships. Nor does it apply to income from the carrying on of a trade, such as the trade of operating a B&B.
Currently, the scheme provides an exemption from Income Tax, PRSI and USC on rent received where a person rents out a room or rooms in his or her principal private residence and the rent received does not exceed €14,000 per year. This figure includes payments for utilities (such as gas and electricity) and any other charges.
The Rent a Room rental income ceiling was last increased in Budget 2017 from €12,000 to €14,000.
Budget 2027 announced an increase in the maximum rental income which can qualify for the relief from €14,000 to €16,000. This revised ceiling will apply to the 2027 year of assessment and subsequent years.
The increased rental income ceiling of €16,000 will apply to all claimants regardless of the number of rooms let or the number of tenants accommodated.

question: Deputy Pearse Doherty asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance if the estimated cost of the CGT changes outlined in budget 2027 of 46.5million first year and 186 million full year are based on CGT for individuals and some corporates in respect of gains on development land solely or if it also includes chargeable gains for corporates; in the case of the former provide a full estimated cost including all chargeable gains for corporates.
reply:
I am advised by Revenue that, in general, capital gains tax (CGT) is chargeable on a gain arising on the disposal of an asset, at the rate of 31% for disposals made on or after 7 October 2026. The chargeable gain is generally the difference between the cost of acquisition of the asset and sales proceeds realised on the disposal of the asset.
Chargeable gains may arise to individuals, non-corporate persons and companies. With the exception of chargeable gains arising on the disposal of development land, companies pay corporation tax on chargeable gains, rather than CGT. As the rates of corporation tax and CGT are different, a chargeable gain which arises to a company is adjusted, such that when the relevant corporation tax rate is applied to the adjusted amount, the result is the same as if the chargeable gain was subject to the relevant CGT rate.
I am further advised by Revenue that the €186 million full year cost outlined in Budget 2027 includes the chargeable gains for corporates. As outlined above, this is payable as corporation tax but is included in the overall estimated CGT costing.

reply:

The revised proposal was agreed in May 2023 when the EU adopted Directive 2023/959. This Directive strengthened rules in relation to the existing EU ETS and made provision for the introduction of a separate but adjacent system for the Buildings, Road Transport and Additional Sectors (ETS2).
Directive 2023/959 provides for Member States who operate a national carbon tax in buildings, road transport and additional sectors to apply for a derogation from obligations under the EU ETS2 once certain criteria are met. The derogation allows a Member State with a national carbon tax rate equivalent or higher than the average ETS2 auction price, in a given reference year, to exempt regulated entities from the obligation to surrender ETS2 allowances between 2027 and 2030.

Subsequently, Ireland secured a derogation which is subject to ongoing review. question: Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance to outline the level of funds currently held in the Climate and Nature Fund.
reply:

Given these annual contributions, and an initial transfer of €2bn from the National Reserve Fund (NRF) in 2024, the Act provides for resourcing of the ICNF of up to €14bn.
Management and investment of the ICNF rests with the National Treasury Management Agency (NTMA), who invest according to the long-term investment strategy. The financial accounts of the ICNF are published in the NTMA’s annual report each year, which are available on the NTMA’s website. reply:

The VAT treatment of goods and services is subject to EU VAT law, with which Irish VAT law is required to comply. VAT is a tax on consumption of goods and services within the EU, and each Member State is obliged to operate its own VAT system in accordance with a common framework of principles and rules that are designed to support coherent application of the tax across the EU, protection of the tax base, and facilitation of trade.
The EU VAT Directive provides that VAT is not charged on goods exported from the Union. In accordance with the Directive Ireland applies its zero rate of VAT to exports outside the EU and to intra-Community supplies of goods. This means that businesses predominantly engaged in making such supplies outside the State would be in a permanent repayment position for VAT. question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance the estimated number of existing investors who will remain subject to deemed disposal following the introduction of the personal investment account announced in Budget 2027; the number facing a deemed disposal charge in 2027; the estimated cost to the Exchequer of extending equivalent treatment to these existing investors.
reply:
The information available to Revenue does not allow them to isolate the tax returned due to the deemed disposal rule from other chargeable events which give rise to a tax liability. Chargeable events include:
• the making of relevant payments;
• the redemption of the investment;
• the transfer by an investor of their investment; and
• the ending of an eight-year period following the acquisition of the investment and then every eight years thereafter (deemed disposal).
Therefore, it is not possible to directly identify the tax revenue arising from the application of the deemed disposal rule. This is because investment funds and life companies are not obliged to report the category of chargeable event that the exit tax relates to at the time of making payment to Revenue. This strong uptake demonstrates that householders continue to recognise the benefits of investing in solar PV.
In the run-up to Budget 2027 (and as part of the broader work of the National Energy Affordability Task Force), I delivered a suite of enhanced SEAI energy upgrade grants to help households and businesses reduce energy costs and move away from volatile, imported fossil fuels. The package of measures includes a new grant for battery storage systems and expanded eligibility for solar PV and solar thermal grants. question: Deputy Séamus McGrath asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance the timeline for the application of the derelict property tax; and when the digitally accessible online register will be activated.
reply:
The introduction of a new Derelict Property Tax (DPT) forms part of the ‘Delivering Homes, Building Communities 2025-2030’ housing plan. The tax will be collected by the Revenue Commissioners and will be based on registers of derelict properties that are compiled and maintained by local authorities.
In its first year of operation, the tax will apply to towns and cities which were recorded as having populations of 4,000 or greater in Census 2022. In the second year of operation, the tax will expand to towns with populations of 2,000 or greater.
DPT will be legislated for as part of Finance (No. 2) Bill 2026. Local authorities will conduct visual surveys of the designated towns and cities under the tax and place derelict properties that they identify on a derelict property register. They key timelines for the first liability year for DPT are as follows:
• 1 January to 31 August 2027: Local authorities inspect the relevant towns and identify derelict properties.
• 1 September 2027: Preliminary registers of derelict properties are published.
• 1 September 2027 to 30 November 2027: Property owners can seek review of inclusion on register.
• 1 September 2027 to 29 February 2028: Local authorities decide on reviews.
• 28 February 2028: Final registers of derelict properties published and Revenue pay and file window opens.
• 23 June 2028: First pay and file deadline.

question: Deputy Emer Currie asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance if he will progress the aligning of the substantial shareholding exemption with the existing dividend participation exemption as part of the upcoming Finance Bill.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 191 and 201 together.
Ireland’s corporation tax approach has been consistent for many years – a low rate on a broad base, providing stability and certainty for businesses. This approach has provided businesses with a clear and reliable framework within which to plan and invest, contributing to Ireland’s success in attracting multinational enterprises. Ireland remains committed to a tax system that is both competitive and internationally respected.
The Participation Exemption for Foreign Dividends regime was introduced in Finance Act 2024. The exemption, which applies simplifies the double tax relief system and enhances Ireland’s attractiveness for multinational businesses. The exemption is available, subject to conditions, in respect of distributions received from qualifying subsidiaries in EEA and treaty partner jurisdictions and jurisdictions that have imposed a non-refundable withholding tax on the distribution.

question: Deputy Emer Currie asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance whether as part of the Government’s planned holistic review of enterprise taxation in 2027, he will include a review of the taxation of residential landlords, with a view to recognising landlords as businesses for taxation purposes.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 190 and 219 together.
As announced Budget 2027, a holistic assessment of Ireland’s enterprise support regime including grant schemes and tax incentives available to businesses will be undertaken. Further detail on this review will be announced in due course.
I expect that the assessment will examine the full range of enterprise supports, including grant schemes, tax incentives and business development programmes currently available.
It is not intended to include the taxation of the residential rental market in this assessment. The taxation of rental income was considered by my Department as part of the 2022 Tax Strategy Group process. (Further details set out in chapter 7 of the "Property-Related Tax Issues Tax Strategy Group – 22/04 July 2022" paper, available at the following link: https://assets.gov.ie/static/documents/tsg-22-04-property-related-tax-issues-4b78c888-4c5a-4642-9f8b-5a28c181ee1a.pdf).
My Department continues to monitor all aspects of the property market, and I will continue to work with my colleagues in Government to ensure that any further interventions in the housing market are appropriately calibrated, represent the best use of public resources and boost the supply of housing in both the public and private sectors.

reply:
The Solar PV for the Medically Vulnerable Scheme is a targeted scheme for the installation of solar photovoltaic (PV) panels for customers/households who are registered on the life support category of the Priority Services Register. These homes have a dependence on electrically powered equipment, including medical equipment, life protecting devices and assistive technologies such as dialysis machines and respirators. As such, these households may have a higher energy demand than the average user and this scheme is designed to go some way towards helping to reduce those energy costs.
The scheme is operated by the Sustainable Energy Authority of Ireland (SEAI) in conjunction with energy suppliers and is open to all suppliers who wish to participate, with each energy supplier contacting their own eligible customers directly, in line with the work plans for their solar PV installers.
The scheme is energy supplier-led, meaning each energy supplier is responsible for contacting their own eligible customers directly. Government, through the SEAI, funds each energy supplier for the installations they provide to their eligible customers.
It is important to note that suppliers, who manage the administrative aspects of the scheme under the SEAI, issue offers to eligible homeowners. Each participating supplier received an allocated amount of funding under their Memorandum of Understanding with the SEAI and contacts eligible households in batches, based on operational capacity.

question: Deputy Louis O'Hara asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance if there are planned changes to the disabled drivers and disabled passengers scheme in 2027, following the publication of Budget 2027.
reply:
My Department and I share concerns that the Disabled Drivers and Disabled Passengers Scheme or DDS is no longer fit-for-purpose. The Government has now agreed to commence from early 2027 the Department of Transport’s Vehicle Adaptation Scheme (VAS). The VAS will provide direct financial assistance to all individuals with qualifying vehicle adaptation needs to meet the costs of those adaptations. The VAS will improve individuals’ functional mobility that in turn can contribute to better social and economic opportunities.
The Disabled Drivers and Disabled Passengers Scheme (DDS) remains with the Department of Finance and will be kept under review. Learning from the commencement and initial operation of the VAS will further inform reform options for the DDS.
As the Deputy will be aware, when this government took office, we committed to a step change in the delivery of supports and services for people with disability and their families.
Budget 2027 delivers significant progress for disabled children and adults, bringing the budget to over €4 billion for the first time.
This funding will be vital in delivering the National Human Rights Strategy for Disabled People. The commitment to develop a new scheme by the Department of Transport, and in this context review the Disabled Drivers and Disabled Passengers Scheme, are strong commitments in this strategy.

question: Deputy Denise Mitchell asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance the regulatory or other protections which apply to investors where the underlying investment company has entered liquidation and the firm that advised or serviced the investment has also entered liquidation.
reply:
The Central Bank of Ireland is the independent regulator for financial services and it determines what measures or actions need to be taken in relation to any potential, or actual, wrongdoing by regulated financial service providers.
European and Irish legislation requires the regulation of financial services firms providing investment services in relation to investment products. The law lists the various types of regulated investment services and investment. Regulated firms may also sell investment products which are not specifically mentioned in the law (i.e. unregulated products). Where they do so, certain investor protections, which apply to regulated activities do not apply.
The Central Bank recently reviewed the Consumer Protection Code (CPC) and this included a review of the rules around the sale of unregulated products by regulated entities. As part of the review, the Central Bank held a public consultation, and changes came into effect in March 2026.
Under the Code’s Standards for Business, firms are required to ensure that all information they provide to customers is presented in a way that seeks to effectively inform the customer.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance if his Department has assessed the distributional impact of LPT according to household composition, including households with dependent children and households without dependent children; and if consideration has been given to incorporating household composition or ability to pay into the calculation of LPT liability.
reply:

On the introduction of the LPT, the Government decided that a liability to the tax should apply to all owners of residential properties based on the market value of the property and with a limited number of reliefs available. This ensures that liable taxpayers are not charged more to account for a shortfall driven by reductions in LPT charges based on other factors, including household composition.
The design of LPT was considered by an interdepartmental group chaired by Dr. Don Thornhill in 2012. question: Deputy Tom Brabazon asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance the total amount of interest on late payment of tax charged and collected by the Revenue Commissioners, broken down by tax head, in each of the past five years in tabular form; if his Department or the Revenue Commissioners have undertaken research or analysis into the reasons taxpayers fail to discharge their tax liabilities by the relevant payment deadlines; and if so, if he will provide the findings of any such research.
reply:

Revenue has confirmed that the levying of interest on late payment of tax is a statutory charge prescribed in legislation that must be factored into any phased payment agreement or debt collection/enforcement action. I am satisfied that collection of interest by Revenue is a key element in reflecting the value of money forgone by the Exchequer where a taxpayer does not pay what is due on time in accordance with the law. question: Deputy Erin McGreehan asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance whether his Department has assessed the introduction of an electric vehicle salary sacrifice scheme, similar to that operating in the United Kingdom; the findings of any such assessment, including the implications for benefit-in-kind taxation and the Exchequer; whether he plans to introduce such a scheme.
reply:
Section 121 of the Taxes Consolidation Act (TCA) 1997 provides that where a car is made available for the private use of an employee then the employee is chargeable to BIK. Where such a benefit is provided for an employee by his or her employer, the employer is required to include that notional payment as part of the employee’s emoluments and to deduct tax via the PAYE system accordingly.
A CO2-based BIK regime for employer provided vehicles became effective from 1 January 2023. From that date the taxable BIK amount is based on the car’s original market value (OMV) and the annual business kilometres driven, with new CO2 emissions-based bands determining whether a standard, discounted, or surcharged rate applies. The number of mileage bands was also reduced from five to four.
Battery Electric Vehicles (BEVs) and plug in hybrids benefit from a preferential rate of BIK, while fossil-fuel vehicles are subject to higher BIK rates. This new structure with CO2-based discounts and surcharges is designed to incentivise employers to provide employees with low-emission cars. This brought the taxation of employer provided cars into step with other CO2-based motor taxes as well as with the long-established CO2-based vehicle BIK regimes in other EU Member States.
Furthermore, there is a BIK exemption on the installation of an EV charging facility by an employer at the home of a director or employee, subject to certain conditions.

question: Deputy Erin McGreehan asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance whether his Department has assessed the combined impact of income tax, USC, PRSI and the withdrawal of income-related supports on the financial benefit to working households of additional earnings; whether measures to address abrupt eligibility thresholds are being considered with the relevant Departments.
reply:
As part of the Budgetary process, officials in my Department conduct a distributional analysis of all the changes made to the welfare and tax system. This analysis is carried out using the ESRI’s SWITCH model, which accounts for the interaction between policy changes, and the impact that these have on households. The results of this assessment are published each year in the Beyond GDP document.
The Department of Finance also works closely with other Departments to ensure that budgetary measures do not create unintended interactions that discourage individuals from taking on additional work. For example, the Tax Policy Changes Book, produced by Department officials, examines how changes to selected Department of Social Protection payments affect the effective marginal tax rates faced by workers across different income levels.
These considerations are also reflected in policy. Budget 2027, for instance, raised the 2 per cent threshold for USC to account for the increase in the minimum wage. This was done to ensure that part-time workers on minimum wage continue to face a low marginal tax rate on any additional hours worked. Similarly, the Working Family Payment thresholds were also increased, allowing low-income families to work additional hours while continuing to receive income support from the state.

question: Deputy Barry Ward asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance if he will ensure that online retailers within the European Union apply the appropriate VAT rate when selling products to Irish consumers, including the 0% VAT rate that applies to certain items such as children’s clothes.
reply:
I am advised by Revenue that the VAT rating of goods and services is subject to EU VAT law, with which Irish VAT law is obliged to comply. In general, the EU VAT Directive provides that all goods and services are liable to VAT at the standard rate, unless they are exempt from VAT or fall within the categories of goods and services listed in Annex III of the EU VAT Directive, to which Member States are permitted to apply lower VAT rates subject to certain rules.
The EU VAT Directive allows that a Member State may be permitted to maintain a historic VAT treatment, subject to strict conditions, including that the scope of its historic treatment is not expanded. On this basis, Ireland retains its long-standing application of the zero VAT rate to the supply of certain children's clothing not exceeding the size “appropriate to children of average build of 10 years of age”.
I understand from Revenue that, in the practical administration of the measure, the zero rate applies to clothing, specifically designed for children, in sizes up to and including 32-inch chest, 26-inch waist and 152cm height. Clothing for persons above 10 years, and clothing in excess of these sizes is liable to VAT at the standard rate currently 23%. Also, in accordance with the legislation, if clothing is not described, labelled, marked or marketed on the basis of age or size then the standard rate of VAT applies.

reply:

The Part 16 reliefs are designed to help small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) attract equity-based risk finance investment from individual investors by allowing those investors to claim income tax relief on qualifying investments.
The Part 16 reliefs are State aid that come under the terms of the EU General Block Exemption Regulation (GBER).
I am advised by Revenue, that a qualifying investor must subscribe for eligible shares in a qualifying company. The investment can be made directly in the company by an individual or, in the case of EII, directly by a Designated Investment Fund (DIF) or indirectly by a Qualifying Investment Fund (QIF).
Relief is given by allowing the individual investor to claim a deduction from their total income of a proportion of the amount of their investment for the year of assessment in which the shares are issued. In line with the parameters required by GBER, the proportion of the investment that can be deducted varies from 50% to 125% of the amount invested depending on the type of investment made and on whether the investment was made directly by the individual or a DIF, or indirectly by a QIF. question: Deputy Barry Heneghan asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance the steps being taken to broaden participation in the employment investment incentive scheme among ordinary taxpayers, including through designated investment funds with lower minimum subscriptions.
reply:
The Employment Investment Incentive (EII) provides an incentive for investment in certain SMEs. The EII provides income tax relief (between 20% and 50%) for individuals who purchase shares in qualifying trading companies. The relief aims to encourage individuals to provide equity-based finance to trading companies, to assist those companies to raise finance thereby allowing them to expand and create or retain jobs.
The incentive operates under the EU State aid framework the General Block Exemption Regulation (GBER).
As indicated in the Budget speech, the EII will be extended in their current format by a further period to be determined once the GBER has been adopted.
The European Commission is reviewing the GBER, in line with the EU’s Competitiveness Compass and the Clean Industrial Deal. The aim is to cut red tape and promote necessary investments, while keeping a level playing field in the Single Market. A final draft of the revised GBER is expected before the end of the year and will be effective 1 January 2027.
Once the new GBER is adopted, further potential amendments will be examined in the context of Budget 2028.
With regard to question Designated Investment Funds, I am advised by Revenue that a Designated Investment Fund (DIF) is a type of investment fund that is established for the sole purpose of investing in qualifying companies under the EII scheme and has been designated as a DIF by Revenue for the purposes of Part 16. reply:

However, Part 16 TCA 1997 provides for a mechanism whereby a company that wishes to raise investment under EII may, in advance of issuing a Statement of Qualification (SOQ) to investors, make an application to Revenue to request confirmation of compliance with certain eligibility conditions. question: Deputy Barry Ward asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance the position regarding the review of the Local Property Tax system that would allow for a reduction for people on a State pension or other social welfare payment.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 166 and 167 together.
On the introduction of the Local Property Tax (LPT), the Government decided that a liability to the tax should apply to all owners of residential properties with a limited number of reliefs. Limiting the exemptions or reductions available allows the rate to be kept low for property owners who do not qualify for such relief. There is no specific provision for a reduction in LPT for those in receipt of the State pension or other social welfare payments under the Finance (Local Property Tax) Act 2012 (as amended). However, homeowners in receipt of social welfare payments may be entitled to an exemption or deferral subject to meeting the qualifying conditions.
The LPT legislation provides for the possibility of deferring the charge to LPT in certain circumstances to assist individuals who may have difficulty paying the tax. A qualifying person may opt to defer, or partially defer, payment of the tax. Where a person qualifies for a full deferral, 100% of the liability can be deferred. Where a person qualifies for partial deferral, then 50% of the liability can be deferred. The balance of 50% of the tax must be paid. The deferred tax remains as a charge on the property and must be paid before a sale or transfer can be completed. Interest is charged at 3% per annum on the deferred amount.

question: Deputy Sinéad Gibney asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance to provide a schedule of EU Presidency events being hosted by his Department broken down by the name of the event, location, date, and State agencies or other Departments involved in the organising of the event; and cost or budgeted cost of same, including costs borne by State agencies under its aegis, in tabular form.
reply:
The rotating Presidency of the Council of the European Union is a core institutional requirement of EU membership. Assuming responsibility for organising ministerial and official-level meetings facilitates negotiations between Member States and supports the effective functioning of the Council’s legislative and policy agenda. On this basis, the Government committed in the Programme for Government to resource and deliver a successful EU Presidency. Significant planning and inter-departmental engagement have taken place to ensure costs are managed across all expenditure headings. Prudent financial planning will continue to ensure value for money.
The Revised Estimates for 2026, published in December 2025, included allocations to individual Government Departments for the requirements of the EU Presidency. This included an allocation of €4,083,000 for the Department of Finance. The overall estimated pay costs of €3,438,000 cover the additional temporary staffing need in Brussels and in Ireland to deliver on the Council’s legislative and policy agenda and to support policy and operational planning. The overall estimated non-pay costs of €645,000 are being used for costs associated with organising Presidency-related events in Ireland and to cover the costs of Presidency associated official travel.
At all times value for money is pursued.

question: Deputy Barry Ward asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance the position regarding any research specifically carried out by his Department into the removal of the deemed disposal rule in the context of investment funds.
reply:
The final report of the Funds 2030 Review, Funds Sector 2030: A Framework for Open, Resilient and Developing Markets Final Report, made recommendations regarding the taxation of investments. It noted that changes to the deemed disposal rule require guardrails to protect the Exchequer and ensure that appropriate tax is paid.
Developing such guardrails requires careful consideration to ensure that any changes strike a balance between supporting retail investment while retaining necessary anti-avoidance protections and considering changes in the investment landscape since its introduction in Finance Bill 2006.
In addition, for every Budget, the cost to the Exchequer of different polices must be considered in the context of the agreed Budget package, and there is an immediate Exchequer impact from removing deemed disposal, notwithstanding the potential for more tax to be paid at a future date.
As outlined in the Roadmap for the Taxation of Retail Investment, published 31 August, measures of this nature are considered as part of the annual budgetary process and any decision has to consider the Budget ceilings agreed by Government, and the range of options across the entire tax system.
A key aspect of the Roadmap is the inclusion of key parameters of the proposed new investment account, acknowledging the need for industry to understand how the account is intended to operate. question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Transport if his Department was consulted before a company (details supplied) stated publicly that it will remain at Tivoli until 2045; if his Department has engaged with the Department of Housing, Local Government and Heritage on the impact of that position on housing delivery at Tivoli.
reply:
The Tivoli site was identified in the Land Development Agency (LDA) Report on Relevant Public Lands 2023 and 2025. It is classified as a 'Class 3 Site', i.e. a long-term, significantly constrained site, with potential to deliver between 4,830 – 6,510 homes.

I trust that this clarifies this matter for you.

reply:

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Transport the total legal costs incurred by a company (details supplied) including costs awarded against the company; when his Department was first informed of those proceedings; and if his Department was advised at any stage of the likely outcome of the case.
reply:
