question: Deputy Colm Burke asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine the action his Department is taking to ensure that the IT issue affecting non-productive investment applications received under the ACRES and ACRES-CP scheme for 2025 from applicants who transferred to a registered farm partnership during the scheme and who cannot submit a claim for their 2025 application.
reply:
The Agri-Climate Rural Environment Scheme, or ACRES, is the current agri-climate environment measure provided under the 2023-2027 CAP Strategic Plan (CSP). There are two approaches within ACRES namely ACRES General and ACRES Co-Operation.
Non-Productive Investments (NPIs) are actions that are available to participants in the Co-operation approach of ACRES to directly address environmental issues on the farm, thereby increasing the farmer's capacity to improve field scores through appropriate management, as well as to contribute to wider environmental objectives.
There are a number of steps in the processing of NPI payments. Initially applications for NPIs are made on behalf of a participant by their advisor in an NPI-Annual Works Plan (AWP). All applications are screened by the local Co-Operation Team and decision letters will follow to advise if the actions within the AWP have received approval or not.
Approved actions may then be implemented by the participants, and the details can then be submitted to the NPI claims system.
It is important to note that there is no obligation on a participant to carry out an approved action, and the claim serves as confirmation from the participant that the action has been implemented. Once a claim is submitted, NPI payment may then issue.
To date almost €9.7 million has issued in NPI payments to farmers with almost 98% of 2023 AWP claims and nearly 93% of 2024 AWP claims paid.

question: Deputy Shónagh Ní Raghallaigh asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine his plans to strengthen the protection of animals transported across Europe in line with the latest scientific evidence; and to support a transition away from long-distance live transport.
reply:
In December 2023, the EU Commission published a legislative proposal for new rules on the protection of animals during transport, to replace the current EU Regulation (EC) No 1 of 2005 protection of animals during transport and related matters in the context of the EU’s Farm to Fork Strategy.
Ireland is strongly committed to improving animal welfare standards during transport and supports the revision of the EU Regulation for this sector.
Ireland demands the highest standards of animal welfare at every stage of the animal’s life, including during transport. Ireland has continuously reinforced its practical, administrative, and legislative measures to protect the welfare of animals during transport, often going beyond the minimum requirements of EU law, for example in terms of extra space for calves, more frequent driver retraining and stricter policies on temperature conditions during transport.
Ireland is currently chairing the EU Council Working Party on this proposal as part of its Presidency of the EU Council from 1 July to 31 December 2026. In this context Ireland is working to reach a consensus on this proposal on behalf all Member States.
Ireland has chaired three EU Council Working Party meetings on this proposal since our tenure commenced. The Irish Presidency team is treating this file as a matter of priority.

question: Deputy Paula Butterly asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine if he will consider extending any existing or future fuel support schemes to include hydrotreated vegetable oil (HVO), noting that while reliefs have been provided in respect of petrol and diesel, many tractors and agricultural machinery are capable of operating on HVO; whether he has examined the potential environmental and economic benefits of supporting the use of HVO in the agricultural sector.
reply:
My Department has introduced the Fuel Income Support Scheme as a targeted income support to assist farmers and agricultural/forestry contractors facing unprecedented increases in fuel costs.
Separate schemes have been put in place to support fishers and specialist horticultural growers.
The fuel income support is targeted towards farmers and agricultural/forestry contractors who have and will continue to use Marked Gas Oil (MGO), which is the predominant fuel used in the agricultural and forestry sectors at present.
As announced in the Budget, I am pleased to have secured agreement on the extension to the end of this year of the important fuel supports schemes provided for farmers and agricultural contractors, fishermen and women and horticulture producers impacted by higher fuel prices. The allocation of €31.2 million to cover the five months August to December 2026 for these supports will be rapidly implemented by my Department.

I have no plans no plans to amend the eligibility criteria for the scheme at this point to include Hydrotreated Vegetable Oil (HVO).

question: Deputy Richard Boyd Barrett asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine whether he will consider a report (details supplied) as regards the relationship between State procurement and agricultural emissions, and develop similar proposals.
reply:
The report referenced by the Deputy refers to School Meals. My Department has responsibility for implementing the EU School Scheme in Ireland. The EU School Scheme is implemented in Ireland through the Food Dudes Programme and the School Milk Scheme. The main objective of the Scheme is to increase fruit, vegetables and milk consumption amongst schoolchildren in recognition of the fact that across all Member States children are consuming less than the recommended amounts as per the WHO guidelines.
The EU Commission published proposals in July 2025 to amend Council Regulation (EU) No 1308 of 2013 which provides the basis for the EU School Scheme (School Fruit & Vegetables and Milk). These proposals which include reference to giving priority to products where origin is in the EU and with high environmental sustainability standards are currently being discussed at EU level. Any future schemes under this Regulation will be informed by the outcome of these discussions.
In addition to my Department’s school schemes, the School Meals Programme falls under the responsibility of my colleague the Minister for Social Protection.

question: Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science to outline Ireland's investment in supercomputing facilities; and the plans to further expand such operations.
reply:
I am deeply committed to advancing national investments in supercomputing facilities, ensuring both the timely delivery of planned infrastructure and the strategic scoping of complementary solutions.
In 2022, after a competitive selection process at EU level, Ireland was awarded €20 million by the EuroHPC Joint Undertaking (JU) for the co-funding of the mid-range supercomputer CASPIr. Following the favourable opinion from a ministerially-appointed Expert Panel and the National Development Plan (NDP) review in 2025, CASPIr procurement commenced earlier this year. question: Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science to outline Ireland's strategy to play a significant role in the development of robotics; and the plans to increase the number of graduates operating in this space.
reply:
The development and adoption of robotics across the economy is a cross-Government matter involving enterprise, innovation and industrial policy. Demand for robotics-related skills is closely linked to broader trends in digitalisation, automation and advanced manufacturing. Research undertaken through the skills forecasting system, including work by the Skills and Labour Market Research Unit and Future Skills Ireland, consistently highlights growing demand for high-level engineering, automation, digital and artificial intelligence (AI) skills across the economy. Recent analysis also points to increasing demand for AI and advanced technology capabilities, reflecting the continuing transformation of industry and workplaces.
Ireland's tertiary education system provides a strong range of programmes relevant to robotics. At undergraduate level, disciplines such as mechatronic engineering, automation engineering, robotics and automation, electronic engineering, computer engineering and related STEM fields are delivered across a number of higher education institutions and technological universities. In addition, specialised postgraduate programmes, including robotics and intelligent manufacturing, support the development of advanced technical expertise. Further Education and Training provision, including through apprenticeships, micro-credentials and upskilling programmes, also contributes to meeting emerging skills needs in this area.

question: Deputy Barry Heneghan asked the Minister for Health the assessment that has been made of the impact of delays in Cross-Border Directive reimbursements on patients, including those who have borrowed to fund treatment or delayed further treatment while awaiting reimbursement; the additional staffing and resources provided to address the backlog; the measures being taken to reduce processing times; and whether a target date has been set for returning to the stated aim of processing completed applications within 30 working days;.
reply:
The Cross Border Directive (CBD) allows public patients to access necessary healthcare, which they would have been entitled to access in the public healthcare service in Ireland, in another EU or EEA country. The patient pays upfront for the treatment and is reimbursed upon return to Ireland.
The HSE is responsible for the operation of the Cross Border Directive and has a dedicated office for that purpose.
The continued growth in use of the scheme has placed additional demands on the HSE CBD office and given rise to a build-up of applications. The increased activity is evidenced by the number of treatments reimbursed increasing by approx. 75% between 2020 and 2024.
It is important that this service operates in a responsive way and that reimbursement applications are processed within a reasonable timeframe. The HSE advises it usually aims to repay patients within 30 working days of receipt of all completed documents. The HSE advise the CBD office is currently processing applications received in early April 2026. A 6-month delay for reimbursement is clearly unacceptable. To address this the HSE has advised my Department that additional resources are being assigned to manage this increase in demand with the aim of restoring processing times to expected levels. I have set the HSE a specific target of getting back to the 30-day target by the end of 2026.

The budgetary allocation for TAMS 3 is spread across all eleven sub schemes and it is therefore not possible to allocate a budget to each of the eleven schemes individually.
In respect of the TAMS 3 Solar Capital Investment scheme (SCIS) this measure was launched on 22 February 2023. It is supporting farmers to transition to renewable energy sources, reducing dependence on fossil fuel based energy.
The solar scheme is ring fenced with its own investment ceiling of €90,000, and grant aided at the enhanced rate of 60%.

question: Deputy Barry Heneghan asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine the work his Department is undertaking to protect Ireland’s native and solitary bee populations; whether it is supporting or engaging with online platforms and citizen-science initiatives that allow the public to record, monitor and support native bee populations; and whether further support for such initiatives is being considered.
reply:
My Department is committed to protecting Ireland’s native bees, including solitary bees, through support for habitat improvement, scientific monitoring and public participation.
A central element of this work is our support for the All-Ireland Pollinator Plan, delivered in partnership with the National Biodiversity Data Centre (NBDC) and other bodies. The new Plan, covering 2026 to 2030, was launched in July. My Department is funding two Farmland Pollinator Officers throughout this period to help farmers implement practical, evidence-based measures. These will contribute to the Plan’s ambition to provide food and shelter for pollinators every 200 meters, particularly benefiting solitary bees with limited foraging ranges.
My Department also supports pollinator habitats through the CAP Strategic Plan. ACRES actions, including planting new hedgerows, establishing grass margins and planting traditional orchards, help provide food and habitats for native bees. Such actions not only support the National Pollinator plan but will contribute to delivery on Ireland Nature Restoration plan.
We have funded the Protecting Farmland Pollinators European Innovation Partnership and the Great Yellow Bumblebee Project. These projects have supported practical conservation on farms and helped develop approaches to improving pollinator habitats.

question: Deputy Martin Kenny asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine if his Department has put forward a proposal on the definition of an active farmer as part of the CAP negotiations; and if he will give an update on discussions around the active farmer definition.
reply:
The Irish Presidency has proposed a definition of an “active farmer” as part of the negotiations on the post-2027 Common Agricultural Policy (CAP). The proposal was developed following consultation with each Member State and with the European Commission.
The proposed definition is intended to provide for continuity and consistency with the current approach, allowing Member States flexibility to take account of different farming structures and circumstances.
There has been broad support from Member States for the proposed definition. There are still some issues to be resolved, including in relation to which interventions the definition should apply to, and whether its application should be mandatory or voluntary for Member States.
The Irish Presidency will continue to work with Member States and the European Commission over the coming weeks to resolve these remaining issues, and to develop a definition that will gain the required support among Member States.
In the meantime, negotiations on all aspects of the proposed CAP Regulation are continuing in accordance with the principle that nothing is agreed until everythig is agreed.

question: Deputy Jennifer Whitmore asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine the measures his Department is taking to increase food security in Ireland in view of the huge impact that changes to weather patterns have.
reply:
Ireland is one of the most food secure countries in the world, ranking second of 113 countries assessed for food security in the Global Food Security Index. Furthermore, the most recent Teagasc Sustainability Report finds that Irish dairy, cattle, tillage and sheep farms produce protein sufficient to meet the requirements of over 36 million people (or 30 million people on a net basis).
Nonetheless, recent extreme weather events challenge established assumptions on food security. My Department's Climate Change Sectoral Adaptation Plan (2025 to 2030) provides the strategic framework for strengthening resilience across the agriculture, forestry and seafood sectors. The current plan represents the most comprehensive climate adaptation assessment undertaken to date of climate risks affecting the sectors under the Department's remit and reflects the findings of Ireland's National Climate Change Risk Assessment (NCCRA).
These risks span a wide range of issues including flooding, prolonged wet periods, drought, water availability, animal health and welfare, soil degradation, infrastructure resilience, biosecurity, forestry impacts, coastal change, supply chain disruption and food system resilience.

question: Deputy Danny Healy-Rae asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine for updates on the fuel subsidy support schemes.
reply:
My Department has introduced the Fuel Income Support Scheme as a targeted income support to assist farmers and agricultural/forestry contractors facing unprecedented increases in fuel costs.
Separate schemes have been put in place to support fishers and specialist horticultural growers.
Applications under the scheme closed on June 2nd and payments commenced on July 22nd. To date 31,025 applicants have received payments totalling €26.52 million. It is expected that the total final payments under this scheme will be approximately €27 million.
Incomplete payments are due to a number of issues. For certain cases my Department is waiting on further information from applicants to allow them to be set-up on payment systems or a request has been made for further evidence, for example fuel receipts. As information is supplied cases are being cleared and payments will continue to be made on a weekly basis.
As announced in the Budget, I am pleased to have secured agreement on the extension to the end of this year of the important fuel supports schemes provided for farmers and agricultural contractors, fishermen and women and horticulture producers impacted by higher fuel prices. The allocation of €31.2 million to cover the five months August to December 2026 for these supports will be rapidly implemented by my Department.

question: Deputy Tony McCormack asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine the progress that has been made in reducing the administrative and regulatory burden on farmers; the further simplification measures that are being considered at national and EU level; and the timeframe for their implementation.
reply:
As President of the AGRIFISH Council during Ireland’s Presidency of the Council of the European Union, I continue to engage actively and constructively in negotiations concerning CAP post-2027 to ensure that the agri-food sector in Ireland and Europe continues to benefit from an ambitious, workable and adequately funded CAP that balances economic, social, and environmental sustainability and underpins food security.
While it is my Department's responsibility to ensure that funding provided by European taxpayers is properly administered, it is also the case that the regulation associated with farming has become increasingly complex and there is scope for simplification of the Common Agricultural Policy.
Farmers need rules that are clear, proportionate and capable of being implemented effectively on the ground. In recent years, simplification of the Common Agricultural Policy has been a key focus for my Department and significant progress has been made on reducing the burden for farmers to-date:
• In 2024, the European Commission introduced changes to the CAP regulations to reduce the administrative burden for farmers. These changes included an exemption from controls and penalties under the CAP conditionality for the 20,000 farmers in Ireland farming on less than ten hectares.

question: Deputy Jennifer Whitmore asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine the measures his Department is taking to address the expected increase in grocery prices towards the end of 2026, given warnings (details supplied) that continued inflation of over 3% will put pressure on food prices.
reply:
As Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine, I have no role in determining or intervening in prices for agri-food commodities at farm gate or retail level.
Ireland's participation in the EU Single Market and Common Agricultural Policy remains the key instrument to ensure the EU’s food security and to support a food system which is economically, socially and environmentally sustainable.
While market prices are a matter between suppliers and buyers, my Department continues to administer support payments via Ireland's CAP Strategic Plan and other supports as required, and continues to monitor developments in agricultural input and output prices on an ongoing basis.
We have also provided signficant supports as part of Budget 2027 to help support critical parts of the food supply chain with increased costs experienced in recent months.
The Central Statistics Office (CSO) reports monthly on the Agricultural Output Price Index, which tracks the prices paid to farmers for their produce, and the Agricultural Input Price Index, which tracks the prices paid by farmers for purchases of goods and services. These prices are sensitive to geopolitical and global economic trends and shocks and have experienced considerable volatility in recent years.
I acknowledge the exceptional pressures our primary producers and food business face due to cost increases and moderations in prices received in recent months, while at the same time many consumers are facing higher grocery bills.

question: Deputy Colm Burke asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine to provide an update on the Protection of the Native Irish Honey Bee Bill 2021; and when the scientific research report issued to his Department in December 2024 will be published.
reply:
The Protection of the Native Irish Honey Bee Bill 2021, a Private Members Bill, which seeks to ban the importation of non-native honey bees is currently before Dáil Éireann, Second Stage. Progression of the Bill through Dáil Éireann is subject to the procedures of the Oireachtas.
Following legal advice in relation to the Protection of the Native Irish Honey Bee Bill 2021, my Department procured independent scientific evidence and in October 2023, a contract was signed with the National University of Ireland, Galway for the provision of research services on the native Irish honey bee (Apis mellifera mellifera).
The research work concluded, and the research report was subsequently evaluated by an external expert. Following the completion of the evaluation, the research service provider was afforded the opportunity to respond to the evaluator’s comments and these comments were received in September 2025. My Department is currently finalising the overall response to the report and I intend to bring this evaluation to the attention of Government in the near future.

question: Deputy Ruth Coppinger asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine if he will confirm if fox cub hunting is prohibited under animal welfare regulations; and if he will support a ban on the practice.
reply:
Animal welfare is a key priority for me as Minister and for the Government. My Department has lead policy responsibility within government for animal welfare and takes this matter most seriously.
I am committed to the policy that animal welfare standards are vigorously applied in a fair and even-handed manner and remain committed to the continued robust enforcement of the Animal Health and Welfare Act 2013, which provides a modern framework for regulating and applying standards in the area of animal health and welfare.
On the general matter of hunting, a detailed debate was held during the passage of the Animal Health and Welfare Act 2013 and the Dáil decided to allow the continuation of fox hunting in accordance with an appropriate code of conduct. On 28th May 2025, a Private Members Bill to ban fox hunting was introduced. It proceeded to a second stage reading on 17th December 2025, where it was opposed.
Section 25 of the Animal Health & Welfare Act 2013 allows for the establishment of codes of practice and for the adoption of codes published by other persons for the purposes of providing practical guidance relating to any aspect of the Act, including fox hunting. Voluntary codes of practice have been established by the Hunting Association of Ireland which detail the conduct to be adhered to in respect of the hunting of foxes and the treatment of the animal during the hunt. question: Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine if he is satisfied with the functioning of the Rásaíocht Con Éireann Traceability System, particularly in relation to the tracking of dogs after they are retired.
reply:
Rásaíocht Con Éireann (RCÉ) is a commercial state body, established under the Greyhound Industry Act, 1958, chiefly to control greyhound racing and to improve and develop the greyhound industry. RCÉ is a body corporate and a separate legal entity to the Department of Agriculture, Food and the Marine.
Since 2020 my Department has ringfenced 10% of the Fund allocation to RCÉ for welfare including integrity. Each year RCÉ has significantly exceeded the 10% requirement in its budget allocation towards welfare including integrity. A key priority of the board of RCÉ is the continued expansion of the Care and Welfare initiatives which include a range of measures.
RCÉ has informed my Department that the Rásaíocht Con Éireann Traceability System (RCÉTS) continues to play an important role in supporting the traceability, accountability and welfare oversight of racing greyhounds.
RCÉTS was introduced in January 2021 and as of June of this year, 64,676 greyhounds were subject to traceability. The system was specifically designed to capture key life events for racing greyhounds, including microchipping, registration, racing activity, changes of ownership, location changes, export, retirement, rehoming and end-of-life notifications.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration further to Parliamentary Question No. 68776/26 of 29 September 2026, which did not address the matters, the date on which officials were asked to examine the confidentiality provisions of the International Protection Acts 2015 and 2026; whether terms of reference were set; whether any paper or submission has been prepared; whether the Attorney General has been consulted; the target date for proposals; and whether the outcome will be published.
reply:
As set out in my replies of 16 September 2026 and 29 September 2026, the principle of confidentiality is a fundamental element of asylum law and is reflected both in the Asylum Procedures Regulation and in domestic legislation, namely the International Protection Act 2015, which applies to applications made before 12 June 2026, and the International Protection Act 2026, which applies to applications made on or after that date.
I have asked my officials to examine this matter with a view to determining whether the provisions of those Acts relating to the publication of information that is likely to lead members of the public to identify a person as an applicant for international protection, without that person's consent, can be amended or clarified to provide greater flexibility regarding what may be reported in the media, particularly in the context of reporting on a person of interest in a criminal investigation.
This examination is ongoing within my Department, with a view to developing a legislative proposal that complies with the Asylum Procedures Regulation, which is binding on Ireland as a matter of EU law, as well as with other international instruments in the field of asylum law to which Ireland is a party.
As regards timing, I have asked my officials to bring forward proposals at an early date.

question: Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the rationale for subhead 1(k) of head 9 of the general scheme of the Irish Nationality and Citizenship (Amendment) Bill 2026 which permissions the Minister intends to prescribe under subhead 1(k) of head 9; and the assessment that was made of head 4's effect on children born in Ireland after commencement.
reply:
The Government recognises and values the significant contribution that migrants make to Irish society, communities and the economy.
The Programme for Government contains a commitment to continue to implement a firmer and more sustainable migration system which protects the integrity of the State's immigration framework. In that context, the General Scheme of the Irish Nationality and Citizenship Bill 2026 proposes a number of reforms to the citizenship process.
Existing policy is that time spent residing in Ireland on temporary permissions and other ad-hoc schemes, including time spent in the State on the basis of temporary protection under the Temporary Protection Directive is not reckonable for naturalisation purposes. The legislation will be clarified to reflect this position.
Head 9 sets out the categories of residence permission that may be reckonable for the purposes of satisfying the proposed residence requirement for naturalisation. Subhead (1)(k) provides a regulation-making power that would enable the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration to prescribe additional classes of permission as reckonable residence where this is considered appropriate having regard to the purposes of the Act and evolving immigration arrangements. question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the status of the proposal to demolish the old Cork prison on Rathmore Road, Cork; whether a decision has been made following the 84 submissions received by 3 July 2026; whether any alternative sites have been assessed for the proposed expansion of Cork Prison; and he will make a statement on the matter.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 241, 243 and 244 together.
Government has allocated funding for a significant building programme across the prison estate. As part of this, I have secured a record capital investment of €67.9 million for 2026, as part of a total investment of €528 million from 2026 to 2030, of which €495 million is being invested in building projects to increase prison capacity. This reflects the Government’s commitment to increase prison capacity and modernise the estate in line with population growth, with an overall target of delivering over 1,500 spaces by 2031.
The Cork Prison extension is an important element of the prison building programme. The project aims to redevelop the site of the former Cork Prison and provide approximately 330 additional prison spaces, including accommodation for around 100 women and 230 men.
There is a critical need for additional prison accommodation in Cork for people from the county. As of 7 October, 57 prisoners from Cork were being accommodated on mattresses on the floor in Cork Prison. In addition, on 17 June, 16 female prisoners with Cork city/county addresses were being accommodated in Limerick Prison, while a further 34 male prisoners were accommodated in other prisons due to capacity constraints at Cork Prison. The final capacity to be delivered through the project will be determined through the detailed design process, with overall project costs to be confirmed following completion of the construction tender process.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the estimated cost and number of prison spaces of the proposed extension to Cork prison on the site of the old Cork prison; the planning timeline.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 241, 243 and 244 together.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration further to Parliamentary Question No. 68475/26 of 29 September 2026, the current ownership of lands at Kilworth, County Cork, transferred from the Department of Defence to his Department in 2006 for the purpose of a new prison; if the lands were transferred back to the Department of Defence or another body, the date and reason; if the lands remain held by his Department or the Irish Prison Service; the reason they were not included in the reply to Parliamentary Question No. 68475/26.
reply:
I am informed by the Irish Prison Service that, between 2006 and 2010, consideration was given to the development of a new prison facility at Kilworth, Co. Cork, on a portion of a larger site owned by the Department of Defence.
As part of this process, the Irish Prison Service commissioned a preliminary assessment of the suitability of the site. This work included a range of surveys and assessments, including in respect of archaeology, flora and fauna, roads and infrastructure, and topography. I am informed that expenditure of approximately €64,000 was incurred in respect of these assessments during 2007 and 2008.
While agreement in principle had been reached regarding the transfer of a portion of the site to the Irish Prison Service, the transfer did not ultimately proceed and the proposed development at Kilworth was not progressed.
Accordingly, no site at Kilworth was transferred to the Irish Prison Service or my Department for the purposes of the proposed prison development, and the project did not proceed.
As the lands were not owned or otherwise held by my Department or by any body and agency under the aegis of my Department, they were not included in the response to Parliamentary Question No. 68475/26.

question: Deputy Mattie McGrath asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine if his Department has considered the use of native rare cattle breeds, such as Dexter cattle, for conservation grazing on upland and mountainous areas, including Slievenamon, as a means of reducing excessive vegetation growth and mitigating wildfire risk; and if grants or support schemes are available, or are being considered, to assist farmers and landowners in undertaking such conservation grazing projects.
reply:
My Department recognises the potential role of appropriately managed conservation grazing in maintaining upland habitats, supporting biodiversity and controlling vegetation growth. Appropriate livestock grazing can also reduce the accumulation of combustible vegetation and contribute to mitigating wildfire risk as part of wider land management.
Native rare breeds are an important part of Ireland’s agricultural heritage and a valuable genetic resource. My Department recognises Dexter, Droimeann, Irish Moiled and Kerry cattle as native rare bovine breeds. Each is supported by an approved breeding programme operated by its recognised breed society in accordance with EU Animal Breeding Regulations.
My Department provides annual grants to eligible organisations to assist in conserving Irish rare breed farm animals. These grants support activities such as DNA analysis, promotion and equipment purchase. Funding is also available to organisations under the Genetic Resources Grant Aid Scheme for projects supporting the conservation and sustainable use of genetic resources for food and agriculture.
Hardy, smaller cattle breeds, such as Dexter cattle, may be suitable for conservation grazing where their characteristics match the terrain, vegetation and habitat management objectives. For upland and mountainous areas, including Slievenamon, suitability would need to be assessed locally. reply:

It is a central priority for me that Ireland's immigration system is robust and rules-based. Effective enforcement of our immigration laws, including the implementation of deportation orders, is essential to maintaining confidence in the integrity of the system and ensuring that our legislation is applied consistently.
Deportations are often costly and complex to carry out. Consequently, voluntary return is the preferred option wherever possible. reply:
It is estimated that up to 70% of the prisoner population have addiction issues. A multi-disciplinary, multi-layered approach includes opioid substitution treatment, counselling, harm reduction initiatives, peer-support programmes, psychoeducational services delivered through prison education units, and podcasts provided through the prison television channel. Assessment and intervention is provided by nurses, general practitioners, pharmacists, and psychologists, supported by in-reach addiction counselling services delivered by Merchants Quay Ireland (MQI), Recovery College, and AA and NA meetings.

question: Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration when the Government will ratify and implement OPCAT.
reply:
Ireland ratified the UN Convention against Torture in 2002 and signed the Optional Protocol to the convention (OPCAT) in 2007. The OPCAT obliges signatory states to establish a system of inspections of all places where persons can be detained, to be carried out by inspection bodies to be known as National Preventive Mechanisms.
The Inspection of Places of Detention Bill will provide the legislation necessary for Ireland to ratify the OPCAT. The Bill is on the priority for publication list and my Department is working with the Office of Parliamentary Counsel towards publication in 2026.
The legislation will provide for the designation of a single National Preventive Mechanism (NPM) to visit and inspect all places of detention in the Justice Sector and for Government Ministers in other sectors to appoint appropriate NPMs for any places of detention that may lie within their remit.
The existing post of Inspector of Prisons will be replaced by a new post of Chief Inspector of Places of Detention to take on the role of NPM for the Justice sector to include prisons, Garda stations, the courts and vehicles used for the transport of prisoners by the Irish Prison Service and Gardaí. The new Chief Inspector will have a mandate to monitor a person’s entire journey through detention, from being placed in a Garda vehicle, through their time in a custody (Garda and court), on remand and, if sentenced, into a term of imprisonment.
The OPCAT will be ratified after the legislation is passed b

reply:

The EU-Mercosur Trade Agreement has been applied on a provisional basis since 1st May 2026. While the Council of the EU voted by Qualified Majority Voting to grant authority to the Commission to apply the agreement on a provisional basis, Ireland did not support that vote.
Earlier this year, the European Parliament approved a motion to refer the EU-Mercosur Agreement to the Court of Justice of the European Union. reply:

Suspected fraud can be reported in a variety of ways. The Department provides a dedicated service on its website to enable reports to be made. A concerned member of the public can also write to the Department or telephone with information.
All reports are received on an anonymous and confidential basis. The report received provides a ‘trigger’ for the instigation of a review of a specific entitlement and further investigation may occur if it is considered to be warranted. In addition, there are many situations where the information provided about a person may not constitute fraud and may already be known or may be permitted under the terms of a particular scheme.

question: Deputy Louis O'Hara asked the Minister for Social Protection whether his Department has plans to review the current means assessment for the working family payment including whether any income from the child support payment should be included in the means assessment.
reply:
The Child Support Payment is a supplement paid on a primary payment to support with the cost of raising children. Most weekly social welfare payments include a Child Support Payment in respect of each qualified child up to the age of 18, which is extended to encompass older children to age 22 under certain circumstances.
The Working Family Payment is a weekly, tax-free payment available to employees with children. It gives extra financial support to families with children with rates depending on their incomes and family size. The rate of Working Family Payment is determined as 60% of the difference between the household income and the threshold for that family size. A Child Support Payment is not paid as a supplement to the Working Family Payment.
In cases where a family on Working Family Payment is also in receipt of another social welfare payment, the amount of the payment, including any Child Support Payment, is included in the means assessments for Working Family Payment. This ensures that the full household income is considered when determining the rate of Working Family Payment.

question: Deputy Richard Boyd Barrett asked the Minister for Social Protection whether he is able to offer any discretion regarding the allowable time spent in education or training for carers every week, to account for situations such as an individual (details supplied).
reply:

To qualify for Carer's Allowance, Carer's Benefit or the Carer's Support Grant, the carer must provide full-time care and attention. A carer is considered to be providing full-time care and attention to a relevant person, where the number of hours providing such care is not less than 35 hours in a period of seven consecutive days, and care is provided on any five days, whether consecutive or not, within a period of seven consecutive days.

My Department has a culture of continuous improvement when it comes to providing schemes to support farmers, and the systems used to access them.
For example, earlier this year, my Department launched the “MyAgFood” portal MyAgfood.ie which is the Department’s new digital platform and provides the gateway for access to all of its online services with a core focus on enhancing our customers’ user experience by meeting t

question: Deputy Michael Cahill asked the Minister for Social Protection to ensure the substantial rise in the income disregarded for the means testing of carers allowance in 2026, and all subsequent years is abolished.
reply:
Carer’s Allowance is the main income support for carers, with 112,000 people receiving the payment at an estimated cost of over €1.4 billion this year. The primary objective of the payment is to provide an income support to people whose earning capacity is substantially reduced because they cannot work full-time due to their caring responsibilities.
The Programme for Government commits to significantly increasing the income disregards for Carer’s Allowance, with a view to phasing out the means test during the lifetime of this Government.
We are well on our way to achieve this commitment and the changes announced as part of Budget 2027 shows the Government's determination to further deliver to carers.
Budget 2026 is the Government's second Budget, and during that period we have increased the income disregard for single carers by €525 and by €1,050 for carers who part of a couple, an increase of 84%. Since June 2022, changes to the disregards have resulted in cumulative increases of almost 246%.
From July 2026, we increased the weekly income disregard by 60% from €625 to €1,000 for a single person, and from €1,250 to €2,000 for carers who are part of a couple. These disregards are now by far the highest in the social welfare system.
These changes mean that a carer in a two-adult household with an income of €110,000 can retain their full Carer’s Allowance payment and receive a partial payment with a household income up to €139,000. Some 2,700 carers received an increase in their

question: Deputy John Lahart asked the Minister for Social Protection the financial supports, grants, or exceptional needs payments are available to families caring for an 18-year-old who is terminally ill.
reply:
Families caring for a person who is terminally ill face significant challenges. The Department of Social Protection provides a range of income supports that may be available to support them.
Depending on the individual circumstances of the case, a family caring for an 18-year-old who is terminally ill may qualify for supports including Carer's Allowance, Carer's Benefit and/or the Carer's Support Grant. Expenditure on caring income supports in 2026 is estimated at over €2.2 billion.
Carer's Allowance is a weekly social welfare payment for people who provide full-time care and attention to someone who needs support due to age, disability, or a physical or mental illness. There are currently over 112,000 carers receiving this payment. As part of Budget 2027, the maximum weekly rate of Carer's Allowance will increase by €10 from January 2027. In addition, the weekly income disregards for Carer's Allowance will increase to €1,150 for a single person and €2,300 for a couple, allowing carers to earn more while retaining entitlement to the payment. Under current arrangements, a carer in a two-adult household with an income of €110,000 can retain their full Carer’s Allowance payment and receive a partial payment with a household income up to €139,000. The income thresholds will increase further from July 2027.

question: Deputy Aidan Farrelly asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage the number of protected disclosures received by his Department in each of the years 2019 to date in 2026, in tabular form; if an external contractor has been engaged regarding a protected disclosure over that time period; if so, the cost of same; and the number of protected disclosures that were rejected, accepted and that remain under review for the time period in question.
reply:
Details on the number and status of protected disclosures received by my Department in each year from 2019 to 2025 is published in the Department's Protected Disclosures Annual Reports, which are available on my Department's website here: www.gov.ie/en/department-of-housing-local-government-and-heritage/collections/protected-disclosures-annual-reports/.
My Department is fully compliant with the requirements of the Protected Disclosures Act 2014, as amended by the Protected Disclosures (Amendment) Act 2022. question: Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage the measures currently in place for the process of local authorities taking in charge housing estates or roads that are not currently in public ownership; and the actions that have been or are being taken in 2026 to address this challenge.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 214 and 216 together.
The legislative process for the taking in charge of housing estates by local authorities is set out in section 180 of the Planning and Development Act 2000. The prescribed process applies to residential developments consisting of two or more dwellings that have been granted planning permission under section 34 of the Act.
Under section 180 (1) of the Act of 2000, the planning authority is obliged to initiate the taking in charge process where requested by either the developer or the majority of owners of the dwellings in the estate in question. This is subject to the development being completed to the satisfaction of the authority and in accordance with the permission and any conditions attached thereto.
To conclude the taking in charge process, where the development has been deemed to have been satisfactorily completed, a local authority is required to make a declaration under section 11 of the Roads Act following a proposal by the executive. The making of such a declaration, which effectively confirms that the authority is prepared to take over responsibility for the ongoing maintenance of the public works elements of the estate, is a reserved function of the elected members of a local authority.
Therefore, the decision to take any particular estate or estates in charge is ultimately one for the elected members of the local authority who, by way of declaration made under the Roads Act, will make such a decision. The Dep

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage further to Parliamentary Question No. 65798/26 of 1 October 2026, which stated that a Child Rights Impact Assessment was undertaken in developing the Child and Family Homelessness Action Plan, whether the assessment will be published; if not, the reason.
reply:
Addressing child and family homelessness is a key priority for Government. I recognise that the experience of homelessness for a child goes beyond housing alone and requires a response across Government. Our housing Plan, Delivering Homes, Building Communities, commits to the development of a Child and Family Homelessness Action Plan.
Development of the Plan has brought together key stakeholders to drive the continued focus on preventing children and families entering emergency accommodation, providing enhanced supports for children experiencing homelessness, as well as measures to accelerate exits and reduce the time spent by children and their families in homeless emergency accommodation. As part of its development, a Child Rights Impact Assessment was undertaken to ensure that consideration of children's rights was embedded in the Plan. The Assessment will be published shortly following publication of the Plan.

question: Deputy Jennifer Whitmore asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage to share the link for the national online GIS platform that his Department has developed to map the locations and relevant details of community support centres across the country.
reply:
Following Storm Éowyn, my Department, through the National Directorate for Fire & Emergency Management, undertook a review of the National Emergency Coordination Group (NECG) response. The review was circulated to the Government Task Force on Emergency Planning, chaired by the Department of Defence, and subsequently submitted to Government. The review has since been published and is available on my Department's website.
A key recommendation arising from the review, and a priority for my Department, was the further development of Community Hubs, now known as Community Support Centres (CSCs). In collaboration with the Local Government sector, guidance has been developed to support the identification of suitable premises and the activation of CSCs where required during emergency events.
This approach has already proven effective in practice. Community Support Centres were successfully activated in Donegal following Storm Amy and in Aughrim and Enniscorthy following Storm Chandra, providing practical assistance and support to affected communities.
Community Support Centres serve as an important focal point during emergencies, providing access to essential supports such as phone charging facilities, refreshments, welfare assistance, and reliable, up-to-date information and advice for the public.
To support this initiative nationally, 572 locations have been identified to date as potential Community Support Centres. My Department has developed a national GIS-based platform to map C

question: Deputy Matt Carthy asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage if he will consider introducing a grace period or flexibility mechanism for self-builders under the temporary development contribution waiver scheme whose homes are currently under construction and well-advanced but face missing the 31 December 2026 completion deadline due to documented trade and construction delays.
reply:
In the first instance, the management and delivery of the development contribution scheme waiver is a matter for the local authorities concerned, and Local Authority officials will determine locally if a waiver applicant has complied with the terms and conditions of the scheme.
On foot of requests received from the Local Government Sector, my Department recently issued guidance to assist with the cessation of the Development Contribution Levy Scheme waiver. For most developments, the submission of a valid Certificate of Compliance on Completion under the Building Control Regulations will provide an indication of dwelling completion but the local authority can also determine an appropriate standard of completion.
The guidance also states that the deadline for the lodgement of a Certificate of Compliance on Completion on the Building Control Management System (BCMS) to comply with the terms and conditions of the waiver scheme will be the 31 December 2026. There is provision for the Building Control Authority to allow for follow-up queries and clarification.

question: Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine the position regarding any proposals to provide multiannual funding for animal welfare organisations to allow for longer term planning; and his views on whether these organisations are sufficiently funded to deal with their work loads.
reply:
Animal welfare is a key priority for me as Minister and for the Government.
Considerable funding is provided to support, eligible, animal welfare charities, nationwide, through the annual Animal Welfare Grant Programme, which is administered by my Department.
Each year my Department invites eligible animal welfare charities to submit a funding application, under the Animal Welfare Grants Programme. To qualify, applicants must meet specified requirements, which are clearly set out in the application process.
This application process is robust and comprehensive. Applicants are asked to provide information on their activities, including reporting specific data and metrics, with successful applicants allocated funding on the basis of objective criteria which are reviewed on an annual basis.
The awards support a wide range of criteria and can include the numbers of animals assisted, re-homing figures, the provision of education and knowledge sharing to the public on animal welfare and responsible pet ownership, helping to raise animal welfare standards. Veterinary inspection results are also taken into consideration when grant amounts are determined.
In December 2025, I provided funding of almost €6.5 million to 94 animal welfare charities throughout the country, this figure represents the highest allocation of funding awarded under the Animal Welfare grants programme, greatly exceeding the Programme for Government commitment to double the €2.4 million of funding available to anim

reply:
I refer to my reply to Dáil Question No. 74 of 23 September 2026 which sets out the position as it relates to employees who transferred to Uisce Éireann from local authorities.
I have no function in relation to the pension arrangements of the other bodies referred to in the Question.

question: Deputy Darren O'Rourke asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage if he plans to extend the first home scheme to second-hand houses.
reply:
The First Home Scheme is a shared equity scheme designed to help bridge the gap between a purchaser’s deposit and mortgage, and the price of their new home, within price ceilings established across the country. First time buyers, Fresh Start applicants and those who wish to build their first home are eligible to apply.
The First Home Scheme Designated Activity Company (DAC) is responsible for the operation and management of the First Home Scheme on behalf of its shareholders - the State, Allied Irish Bank, Bank of Ireland and Permanent TSB.
In relation to the use of the Scheme for second hand homes, the DAC introduced the Tenant Home Purchase Product in April 2023. This Product allows tenants to purchase their current rental property where they have received a Notice of Termination because the landlord is selling the property.

question: Deputy Charles Ward asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage the average waiting time currently experienced by applicants under the defective concrete blocks grant scheme for the scheduling and completion of core testing, broken down by local authority area; and if homeowners participating in the defective concrete blocks grant scheme who miss a scheduled core testing appointment are placed at the bottom of the waiting list for testing; if not, the procedures that apply where an appointment is missed, cancelled or requires rescheduling; and whether discretion is exercised in cases involving illness, family emergencies or other exceptional circumstances.
reply:
The Remediation of Dwellings Damaged by the use of Defective Concrete Blocks Act 2022 as amended by the Act of 2025 sets out the framework under which the Grant Scheme which provides grant funding to people whose homes have been affected by Defective Concrete Blocks (DCB) operates.
Under the terms of the Scheme the Housing Agency acts as agent on behalf of the local authorities. Once a home has met the damage threshold for entry to the Scheme, the Housing Agency works with Chartered Engineers from an approved framework to help assess applications. This assessment includes surveys, sampling, testing and the categorisation of dwellings under the Scheme. Based on these evaluations, the Housing Agency then determines the appropriate remediation option and grant amount.
For further information regarding waiting times for core testing and the operational procedures that apply, the Deputy may wish to contact the Housing Agency directly at the specific email address established to deal with queries from public representatives: publicreps@housingagency.ie.

question: Deputy Charles Ward asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage when he expects to introduce the regulations necessary to operationalise the application for review of approved remediation option provided for under section 23 of the Defective Concrete Blocks (Amendment) Act 2025; the reasons for the delay in commencing these provisions; whether a draft of the proposed regulations has been prepared; and the anticipated application process for homeowners seeking a review.
reply:
The Remediation of Dwellings Damaged by the use of Defective Concrete Blocks Act 2022 as amended by the Act of 2025 sets out the framework under which the Grant Scheme which provides grant funding to people whose homes have been affected by Defective Concrete Blocks (DCB) operates.
A number of amendments contained in the Amendment Act of 2025 came into operation on 25 February 2026 and further provisions commenced on 27 May 2026.
Upon commencement of Section 17 of the Act of 2025, homeowners who received a determination under the previous standard (I.S. 465:2018) that is not the demolition of the relevant dwelling and either have not started works or paused works as of 6 November 2024 will be able to apply for a review of the approved remediation option.
Work is ongoing on the drafting of these regulations that will contain the process for homeowners. A commencement date for these provisions will be determined as soon as possible, following which homeowners will be able to submit an application through their designated local authority.

question: Deputy Seán Kyne asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage his views that there should be a moratorium on new solar developments pending the publication of solar farm guidelines.
reply:
In line with commitments in the Programme for Government 2025, my Department is working with the Department of Climate, Energy and the Environment (DCEE), which holds policy responsibility for renewable energy matters, in respect of the introduction of a number of National Planning Statements related to Ireland's Climate Action Plan target to increase the share of electricity generated from renewable sources up to 80% in 2030. This includes the preparation of a National Planning Statement for solar energy development.
Further to the commencement of Chapter 3 of Part 3 of the Planning and Development Act 2024 on 2 October 2025, provisions for National Planning Statements have been introduced to replace the provisions for Ministerial guidelines issued under section 28 of the Planning and Development Act 2000. All existing Section 28 guidelines will, over time, be revoked and replaced with new National Planning Statements. Any current section 28 guidelines will however remain in force until revoked or replaced by a corresponding National Planning Statement. The timing of the issuing of National Planning Statements will be based on Government priorities.
In respect of sectoral national planning statements in particular there is also an important role for the relevant policy Department in collaborating with my Department on the development of these National Planning Statements. In that context, my Department is working closely with the DCEE as the Department with policy responsibi

question: Deputy Conor D. McGuinness asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage the reason the national standard operating procedure for the Irish Fire Service is that the fire service do not routinely call An Garda Síochána to every report of a fire they receive.
reply:
The provision of a fire service within its functional area, including the establishment and maintenance of a fire brigade, the assessment of fire cover needs and the provision of fire station infrastructure, is a statutory responsibility of each individual local authority under the Fire Services Acts 1981 & 2003. My Department supports fire authorities through the development of national policy and legislation, the provision of a central training programme, the issuance of operational guidance and support on related matters, and through capital funding for equipment and priority infrastructure projects.
Local authority fire services do not routinely notify or request the attendance of An Garda Síochána for every emergency call received. Garda involvement is generally required only where specific circumstances arise. The attendance of An Garda Síochána is determined in accordance with inter-agency arrangements and based on the operational assessment and professional judgement of the fire service Incident Commander at the scene of an emergency. Such circumstances may include incidents requiring the establishment of safety cordons, the protection of emergency personnel, multi-agency emergency coordination, incidents involving fatalities or serious injuries, suspected criminal activity, or any situation where evidence may need to be preserved.
The Incident Commander has responsibility for assessing conditions at an incident and determining what additional resources may be require

question: Deputy Séamus McGrath asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage the estimated cost of repair works cost in relation to bonfires in each local authority area, in the past 12 months.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 199 and 200 together.
The provision of a fire service in its functional area, including the establishment and maintenance of a fire brigade, the assessment of fire cover needs and the provision of fire station premises, is a statutory function of individual fire authorities under the Fire Services Acts, 1981 & 2003. My Department supports fire authorities through setting general policy, providing a central training programme, issuing guidance on operational and other related matters, and by providing capital funding support for equipment and priority infrastructural projects.
My Department does not receive reports on incidents involving bonfires specifically. However, it does collect annual fire statistics from fire authorities, including information on the locations and causes of fires. These records are published annually as part of the Department's fire and emergency incident statistics and can be accessed at: www.fireireland.ie/fire-safety/fire-statistics/.
The National Directorate for Fire & Emergency Management (NDFEM), within my Department, does not maintain records relating to damage arising from bonfires, associated remediation works, or the costs incurred in undertaking such works. Responsibility for recording any such damage, remediation measures or related expenditure rests with the relevant local authority or other agency with responsibility for the affected area, as appropriate.

question: Deputy Jennifer Whitmore asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine the measures his Department is taking to insulate households from the expected increase in grocery prices towards the end of 2026 and start of 2027, in view of warnings (details supplied) that inflation will put pressure on food prices.
reply:
As Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine, I have no role in determining or intervening in prices for agri-food commodities at farm gate or retail level.
Ireland's participation in the EU Single Market and Common Agricultural Policy remains the key instrument to ensure the EU’s food security and to support a food system which is economically, socially and environmentally sustainable.
While market prices are a matter between suppliers and buyers, my Department continues to administer support payments via Ireland's CAP Strategic Plan and other supports as required, and continues to monitor developments in agricultural input and output prices on an ongoing basis.
We have also provided signficant supports as part of Budget 2027 to help support critical parts of the food supply chain with increased costs experienced in recent months.
The Central Statistics Office (CSO) reports monthly on the Agricultural Output Price Index, which tracks the prices paid to farmers for their produce, and the Agricultural Input Price Index, which tracks the prices paid by farmers for purchases of goods and services. These prices are sensitive to geopolitical and global economic trends and shocks and have experienced considerable volatility in recent years.
I acknowledge the exceptional pressures our primary producers and food business face due to cost increases and moderations in prices received in recent months, while at the same time many consumers are facing higher grocery bills.

reply:

However, as the table attached shows, almost 7,000ha of new forests have been created since 2023 and I am confident that these would not have been planted without the afforestation supports offered through the current Forestry Programme.
The Forest Road Scheme has provided grants to forest owners to facilitate the construction of over 215 kilometres of forest roads. The Scheme provides opportunities for forest owners to create and improve access to forests to facilitate maintenance, recreation, harvesting and the monitoring and protection of forests.

The Programme also provides a mechanism to support forest owners with the restoration of their forests after adverse events such as disease or storms. Since 2023, site clearance grants have been paid for over 3,200 hectares of forests impacted by ash dieback. question: Deputy Seán Ó Fearghaíl asked the Minister for Education and Youth further to Parliamentary Question No. 67853/26 if she will outline the specific educational placement and support options currently available to the child concerned; if a suitable school place has been identified for the 2026/27 school year; if not, the steps being taken to secure an appropriate placement, and the timeframe within which the child's family can expect a resolution.
reply:

The National Council for Special Education (NCSE) has advised that the local special educational needs organiser (SENO) is working closely with the student’s family regarding options for school placements and other special education supports for the coming school year.

question: Deputy Seán Ó Fearghaíl asked the Minister for Education and Youth if she will intervene in the case of a child (details supplied) without a primary school place following the disallowance of a Section 29 appeal, resulting in significant transport and financial difficulties for the family; and the actions she is taking to secure a suitable school place locally or within a reasonable distance of the family home.
reply:
My department’s main responsibility is to ensure that schools in an area can, between them, cater for all pupils seeking school places in the area.
Parents have the right to choose which school to apply to and where the school has places available for the relevant year, the student should be admitted. However, in schools where there are more applicants than places available, a selection process will be necessary. This selection process and the enrolment policy on which it is based must be non-discriminatory and must be applied fairly in respect of all applicants. However, this may result in some students not obtaining a place in the school of their first choice.
Tusla Education Support Service (TESS) is the agency which can assist parents who are experiencing difficulty in securing a school place for their child. TESS advise the parents to make applications to both local schools and schools outside of their locality.
TESS have advised that the parents may contact the local regional office directly, and they can assist this parent with a referral to the service, from which support will be given regarding same. The contact details for this area are 01 5252166 or by email tess.dml@tusla.ie.

question: Deputy Matt Carthy asked the Minister for Education and Youth if emergency capital funding will be fast-tracked for a school in County Cavan (details supplied); and if the ongoing plumbing and electrical deterioration caused by severe overcrowding will be addressed.
reply:
The purpose of the Emergency Works Scheme (EWS) is to provide funding specifically for unforeseen emergencies. It does so by ensuring the availability of funding for urgent works to those schools that are in need of resources as a result of an emergency situation.
An emergency is deemed to be a situation which poses an immediate risk to health, life, property, or the environment, which is sudden, unforeseen and requires immediate action, and in the case of a school, if not corrected would prevent the school or part thereof from opening.
The EWS operates on the basis of the minimal scope of works required to remedy an emergency situation. The EWS usually provides an interim solution until such time as a comprehensive solution can be provided under the Summer Works Scheme (SWS).
The purpose of the Climate Action Summer Works Scheme (CASWS) is to enable individual school authorities to undertake small-scale building works on a devolved basis that, ideally, can be carried out during the summer months or at other times that avoid disrupting the operation of the school. The CASWS operates on a multi-annual basis across a number of categories of works.
It is envisaged that approvals in any given year will involve a spread of categories rather than the traditional single category at a time. This is aimed at managing market capacity and maximising value for money opportunities for school authorities.

question: Deputy Louis O'Hara asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine to provide an update on the implementation of the recommendations contained within the report of the Commission on Generational Renewal in Farming.
reply:
Supporting young farmers and facilitating generational renewal is a priority of mine and critical to ensure a bright future for the agri-food sector. The challenge of generational renewal in farming is widely recognised at both national and EU level. It is important that we have skilled, innovative young farmers coming into the sector to secure a viable and sustainable future for Irish farming. We recognised the need to consider whether existing supports are having the desired effect, and how supports might best be configured for the future. Farm succession is a complex issue and there are many factors that impact farmers’ decisions and that is why the Commission on Generational Renewal in Farming was established.

question: Deputy Richard Boyd Barrett asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine whether he will support the replacement of Sitka spruce plantations with native forestry, particularly where the former is growing on drained bogs and there are major climate gains to be realised by rewetting them.
reply:
My Department controls the felling and replanting of forests, primarily using the statutory based felling licence process. Where an applicant wishes to change species from the first rotation where Sitka spruce was planted and replant with native forests, this would generally be fully supported by my Department.

My Department’s ‘Felling and Reforestation Policy’ document sets out numerous reforestation objectives supported by my Department ranging from Conifer Forest for Wood Production to Reforestation for Biodiversity and Water Protection. Depending on site suitability, a landowner may select the objective which best suits their own management objective. The document also states that permanent forest removal may be considered where there is an over-riding environmental consideration such as protecting habitats and species listed as qualifying interests within Special areas of Conservation or Special Protection Areas.

Action 43 of the Forest Strategy Implementation Plan supports “habitat restoration measures for forests on peatlands based on the best available science”.

My Department’s Climate Resilient Reforestation scheme provides eligible landowners with grant aid to convert conifer forest to a native woodland mix. reply:

Under the Education Act 1998, all recognised schools are managed by school Boards of Management. Individual school authorities are responsible for the drawing up of a school policy in relation to the wearing of uniforms. Decisions on changes to school uniform polices are a matter for schools at local level. Schools are advised to consult with parents and students when drafting a policy on uniforms.
Ultimately, decisions on school uniforms are a matter for individual schools and Boards of Management.

question: Deputy Aidan Farrelly asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment the number of protected disclosures received by his Department in each of the years 2019 to 2026 to date, in tabular form; if an external contractor has been engaged regarding a protected disclosure over that time period; if so, the cost of same; and the number of protected disclosures that were rejected, accepted and that remain under review for the time period in question.
reply:
The Protected Disclosures Act 2014, www.irishstatutebook.ie/eli/2014/act/14/enacted/en/html, as amended by the Protected Disclosures (Amendment) Act 2022, www.irishstatutebook.ie/eli/2022/act/27/enacted/en/index.html, provides a framework for workers to report relevant wrongdoing and protects them from penalisation for doing so. My Department is committed to providing a clear, accessible and confidential process through which workers can raise concerns, and to ensuring that reports received are assessed and followed up in a fair, proportionate and timely manner and in accordance with the law.
Every report of potential wrongdoing received in the manner prescribed under the Act is considered in line with the provisions of the Act, the Department’s own Policy on Protected Disclosures and the Department of Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation’s Statutory Guidelines for public bodies and prescribed persons. Following assessment, reports may be closed, referred to another relevant procedure , or they may require further follow-up or investigation.
Section 22(5) of the Protected Disclosures Act 2014 requires public bodies to provide an annual summary of the number of protected disclosures received during the preceding year, and any actions taken, if any, as a result of those disclosures. All of the reports for the Department of Enterprise, Tourism and Employment are available online at www.enterprise.gov.ie/en/publications/protected-disclosure

question: Deputy Michael Murphy asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment the measures being taken under the Action Plan to Promote Collective Bargaining to address circumstances where workers have chosen trade union representation but an employer declines to engage in collective bargaining or recognise that representation; if he is satisfied that the voluntary framework is sufficient to deliver a meaningful increase in collective bargaining coverage; if specific criteria or benchmarks have been established for assessing the effectiveness of that approach; and if legislation will be considered where voluntary engagement does not deliver progress.
reply:
Under Irish law, workers are free to join and participate in trade unions, and existing industrial relations legislation provides a range of mechanisms, through the Workplace Relations Commission (WRC) and the Labour Court, to address disputes where collective bargaining does not take place. Moreover, while employers are not legally required to recognise trade unions for collective bargaining purposes, employees may avail themselves of the statutory industrial relations machinery in circumstances where collective bargaining arrangements are not in place, including the services of the Workplace Relations Commission and the Labour Court.
The agreed Action Plan on Collective Bargaining seeks to address barriers to collective bargaining through a combination of measures rather than through any single mechanism. These include improving the capacity of trade unions and employer representative bodies to engage effectively; promoting awareness and good practice; examining workplace access; reviewing relevant legal protections for workers and trade union representatives; and strengthening the evidence base on collective bargaining coverage. The combined measures in the Action Plan, supported by close engagement with ICTU and Ibec to identify and understand the most significant barriers, have the potential to deliver meaningful and lasting progress. question: Deputy Michael Murphy asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment if, in the context of the Action Plan to Promote Collective Bargaining 2026–2030, he intends to introduce measures to provide trade unions with reasonable access to workplaces for the purposes of communicating with and representing workers; the current status of discussions with ICTU and Ibec on this matter; the timeframe for their conclusion; and if he will consider legislation should agreement not be reached.
reply:
Ireland's Action Plan to Promote Collective Bargaining, developed through the Labour Employer Economic Forum (LEEF) Technical Sub-Group comprising Department officials, ICTU and Ibec, seeks to strengthen the environment for collective bargaining through a range of practical measures, including ongoing engagement with the social partners on issues relevant to collective bargaining and workplace dialogue.
As part of the implementation process, the issue of workplace access is being considered by the Sub-Group alongside other priority matters under the Plan and those discussions are ongoing. Importantly, the existing Code of Practice on the Duties and Responsibilities of Employee Representatives provides that employee representatives should be granted reasonable access to workplaces where they represent trade union members and where access is necessary to enable them to carry out their representative functions. Consideration of workplace access under the Action Plan will have regard to this existing framework.
Since the launch of the Action Plan, six dedicated meetings have taken place between Department officials, ICTU and Ibec to oversee implementation and consider proposals and actions to support collective bargaining. Engagement on a number of issues remains ongoing and no final position has yet been reached on all measures under consideration.
