question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment if he has received representations or data from the CCPC on consumer complaints relating to shelf price labelling where the displayed price applies only to loyalty app members; and whether current price display rules require such conditions to be clearly shown on shelf labels.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 152, 153 and 154 together.
The Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (CCPC) is the independent statutory body responsible for enforcing competition and consumer protection law under the remit of my Department. I have consulted the CCPC in relation to the issues raised.
The CCPC is aware of concerns regarding app-based and loyalty scheme pricing models, particularly where some consumers may not have regular access to the internet or do not wish to participate in a loyalty programme.
In general, businesses in Ireland are free to set the prices they charge and may offer discounts to members of loyalty schemes as part of their commercial strategy. There is currently no requirement under competition or consumer protection law for retailers to charge members and non-members of loyalty schemes the same price.
The CCPC notes that some grocery retailers provide a range of options for consumers to participate in loyalty schemes, including smartphone applications and physical loyalty cards.
Retailers must, however, comply with consumer protection law, including requirements to display prices and discounts clearly and accurately. Consumers must be provided with clear and unambiguous pricing information so that they can make informed purchasing decisions, including where a discounted price is conditional on membership of a loyalty scheme.
The CCPC actively monitors compliance with these requirements and takes enforcement action where breaches are

question: Deputy Cian O'Callaghan asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment whether there are sufficient protections, safeguards or expectations around how employment permit sponsorship is communicated to migrant workers on time-limited immigration permissions, particularly where a worker may reasonably believe for several months that an application is progressing and is only informed close to the expiry of their permission that the employer will not proceed.
reply:
The employment permits legislation governs the making and assessment of employment permit applications submitted to the Department. Where an employer indicates to an individual that they may support or submit an employment permit application but subsequently decides not to proceed before an application is made, that decision does not fall within the scope of the employment permits legislation.
The circumstances outlined in the question appear to relate to a person who is already present in the State on a time-limited immigration permission which is approaching expiry. The granting, renewal of immigration permissions are matters for the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration. Individuals who have concerns regarding their immigration status should engage with that Department at the earliest opportunity.

question: Deputy John Lahart asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation the timeline for completion of the Whitechurch flood alleviation scheme; if he is aware that some residents have just completed works on their homes almost nine months after the flooding and some are just returning to their homes following the flooding (details supplied).
reply:
The Whitechurch Stream Flood Alleviation Scheme (Whitechurch Stream FAS) is being progressed by South Dublin County Council with funding provided by the Office of Public Works (OPW), as part of the Government's commitment to support the delivery of flood relief schemes under the National Development Plan. The Scheme consists of river bank improvements, flood defence walls, increasing wall heights, the removal or replacement of low-level bridges, and the provision of trash screens. The Scheme is expected to provide flood protection from the Whitechurch Stream for some 52 residential and commercial properties when complete.
The construction of the Whitechurch Stream FAS is being undertaken by the OPW's direct labour force, with approximately 77% of the linear meters of flood defences completed to date. The substantial completion date for the Whitechurch Stream FAS is programmed for the end of 2026. Temporary flood defences will remain in place for the remaining duration of the construction phase, and will be rechecked for effectiveness ahead of all forecast flood events.
South Dublin County Council, that has responsibility for flood emergency response and planning, has advised that it will provide sandbags to local residents for flood mitigation, in advance of any future forecast flood events pending the scheme's completion.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation the total legal costs, including solicitors' and counsel fees, incurred by Government Departments and public bodies in defending complaints and proceedings under the Protected Disclosures Acts 2014 to 2022, at the Workplace Relations Commission, the Labour Court and the superior courts, from 2014 to date, by year and by body, in tabular form; if this information is collated centrally; and if not, the reason therefor.
reply:
I thank the Deputy for the question.
The information requested is not held or collated centrally by my Department.
The Protected Disclosures Act 2014, as amended, requires public bodies to report annually on specified information relating to protected disclosures. Information published by public bodies in relation to protected disclosures is available through their annual reporting arrangements and on their respective websites.
The Act does not require the central collection or publication of information on any legal costs, including solicitors' and counsel fees, incurred in defending complaints or proceedings under the Protected Disclosures Act before the Workplace Relations Commission, the Labour Court, or the courts.
Decisions relating to the management of litigation, including whether to defend complaints or proceedings under the Protected Disclosures Act and any associated legal costs are matters for the individual Government Department or public body concerned, having regard to the particular circumstances of each case.

Deputy Colm Burke asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation when a primary care centre in Cork city Mayfield/Ballyvolane will be granted a Section 50 Licence, from the OPW, for an access crossing a stream so that the infrastructure project can proceed.
reply:
Section 50 consent under the Arterial Drainage Act 1945, as amended is required from the Commissioners of Public Works in Ireland by bodies proposing to carry out construction or alteration works on bridges and culverts.
A Section 50 application for a proposed project at Ballyhooly Primary Care Centre was received on behalf of Horganlynch Consulting Engineers by the OPW in November 2025. The Office of Public Works (OPW) completed its initial review of the application, and made a number of requests for further information in relation to the proposed project over the intervening period. This application was subsequently approved by the OPW with letter of consent issued to the applicant's agent on the 6th October 2026.
The OPW's assessment under Section 50 is concerned solely with the flood risk from the proposed works. Any plans for the progression of construction or alteration works on bridges and culverts, through the Planning and Development Acts, are matters for the relevant Local Authority.

reply:

question: Deputy Michael Cahill asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine to ensure that CAP is adequately funded and that leader is included and adequately funded.
reply:
Discussions on the overall EU budget for the post-2027 CAP form part of negotiations on the broader Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF), or EU budget, for 2028–2034. The MFF is negotiated by Finance Ministers and will ultimately be agreed by Heads of State and Government at the European Council.

Member State Agriculture Ministers have been clear that the future CAP must be adequately funded if it is to continue to support viable farm incomes, food production and food security, to contribute to the development of rural areas, and to enable farmers to contribute to environmental and climate objectives.

The CAP budget must be considered in the context of the wider negotiations on the next EU Multiannual Financial Framework. Heads of State and Government must ultimately agree on a balanced outcome across all EU budgetary headings that will support the delivery of CAP and other EU objectives.

LEADER is provided for as a mandatory intervention in the proposed CAP Regulation. This means that Member States will be required to provide support for LEADER under their future plans. Funding for LEADER will be provided from the general National and Regional Partnership Plan (NRPP) allocation, outside the amount ring-fenced for CAP. The level of funding will be determined through the wider funding negotiations during the development of Member State NRP plans.

reply:

question: Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation further to Parliamentary Question No. 352 of 21 October 2025, whether, when his Department commissioned the "Review of MyGovID on eIDAS Level of Assurance" in 2024, it was aware that the firm engaged had worked on the design, delivery and operation of MyGovID; the way in which the independence of the review was assured; and whether any re-evaluation recommended by that review has since been carried out.
reply:
The Office of the Government Chief Information Officer (OGCIO) within my Department commissioned a review of MyGovID's alignment with eIDAS Levels of Assurance following a competitive procurement process conducted in 2023. Four companies were invited to submit quotations for the review.
None of the four companies invited to participate in the procurement process had been involved in the design, delivery or operation of MyGovID. Following an evaluation of the responses received against the criteria established for the competition, Deloitte Belgium was selected to undertake the review.
While MyGovID was originally developed by Deloitte Ireland, Deloitte Belgium had no involvement in the design, delivery or operation of the MyGovID service. The independence of the review was assured through the competitive procurement process and the evaluation of tender submissions against the requirements established for the competition.
The review examined the alignment of MyGovID with the eIDAS framework and made a number of observations and recommendations. The findings of the review have informed the Department's broader consideration of matters relating to digital transformation, digital public services and developments in the area of digital identity.
No separate re-evaluation of the type conducted in 2024 has been commissioned since the completion of that review.

question: Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance if consideration will be given to including second hand properties as part of the help to buy scheme.
reply:
The Help to Buy (HTB) incentive, is a tax-based scheme to assist first-time purchasers with the deposit they need to buy or build a new house or apartment. It also aims to encourage additional supply of new houses by supporting demand.
HTB provides a refund of Income Tax and Deposit Interest Retention Tax (DIRT) paid in Ireland over the previous four years, subject to limits outlined in the legislation.
The level of support available to first time buyers under the HTB scheme, is whichever is the lesser of:
• €35,000 (from Budget 2027); or
• 10 per cent of the purchase price of the new property; or
• the amount of Income Tax and DIRT paid in the four years before application for the relief.
For a property to qualify for the HTB scheme, it must be new or converted for use as a dwelling, having not previously been used as a dwelling. Additionally, the purchase value/approved valuation of the property must not exceed €500,000.
Based on the latest available data (31 August 2026), the scheme has supported over 69,000 individuals or couples to buy or build their own home.
In relation to second-hand properties, an increase in the supply of new housing remains a priority aim of Government policy. The HTB scheme is specifically designed to support the demand for affordable new build homes so as to encourage the construction of an additional supply of such properties.

All these systems operate under human supervision at every decision point. They assist professional judgment rather than replace it.

question: Deputy Conor Sheehan asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance the reason early years educators and school-age childcare practitioners are excluded from Revenue’s flat rate expense allowance registry; the details of any recent reviews conducted by his Department or Revenue into Section 114 of the Taxes Consolidation Act 1997 regarding modernising this registry for low-paid sectors; and if he intends to update the tax code to include early years professionals.
reply:
The flat rate expense (“FRE”) regime is operated by Revenue on an administrative basis where both a specific commonality of expenditure exists across an employment category and the statutory requirement for the tax deduction as set out in section 114 of the TCA 1997 is satisfied, namely, that the expenses are wholly, exclusively and necessarily incurred in the performance of the duties of the office or employment by the employee concerned and that such expenses are not reimbursed by his or her employer.
The FRE regime was established to apply a uniformity of approach to tax deductibility for expenses of large groups of employees and to facilitate ease of administration for both Revenue and employees. The expense should apply to all employees in that category and not be discretionary.
I am informed by Revenue that the FRE regime and individual FREs are kept under review to ensure they remain justified, appropriate to current employment practices and consistent with the statutory requirements for deductibility.
In addition, Revenue advised that it considers FRE applications where a large number of employees incur broadly identical qualifying expenses which are not reimbursed by their employer. Applications are only accepted once they are made by the representative bodies in the employment sectors concerned and are based on the specific commonality of expenses within the employment category and compliance with the strictly applied statutory requirement for a tax deduction.

question: Deputy Denise Mitchell asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance if he will consider the introduction of an 8% Section 481 uplift for all productions filming outside the main production hub within the Dublin Metropolitan Area incorporating Ashford.
reply:
Finance Act 2018 introduced a short-term, tapered regional uplift under the Section 481 Film tax credit for productions being made in areas designated under the State aid regional guidelines (among other criteria).
As the regional uplift was an approved State aid, any restoration of the uplift would require approval from the European Commission. It is worth noting that the Section 481 Film tax credit is explicitly linked to the promotion of Irish or European culture.
While the uplift was not a Regional Aid measure, it operated by reference to the regional aid map in force at the time it was introduced. A new regional aid map, covering a significantly smaller geographic area, came into effect in April 2021; consequently, it is not expected that such an approach would be viable for a future relief to support activities outside the main Dublin production hub.
Since the expiration of the Regional Uplift, Government supports for audio-visual productions have been considerably enhanced and broadened. There are no geographic restrictions on the availability of these supports, so they are available to projects taking place in all regions of the State.
For example, the Scéal Uplift was introduced as part of Finance Act 2024 to provide for an uplift of 8 per cent to the existing Film Tax Credit rate of 32 per cent for small-to-medium sized productions with a maximum qualifying expenditure of €20 million where certain additional cultural criteria are also met. question: Deputy Pádraig O'Sullivan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of persons held in prison pending deportation in 2025 and 2026 to date; and the median length of that detention.
reply:
A deportation order is a legal order to leave the State. If a person does not remove themselves from the State following the issuance of a deportation order, they will be removed. The enforcement of deportation orders is an operational matter for the Garda National Immigration Bureau (GNIB).
If a person has not complied with their requirement to present to GNIB or has not left the State, they may be detained under Section 5 of the Immigration Act 1999 for up to 56 days for the purpose of ensuring their deportation from the State. An application to extend this period of detention must be made to the District Court. Alternatives to detention are widely used where they are deemed appropriate.
Under the European Communities (Free Movement of Persons) Regulations 2015, which transposes the Free Movement Directive (Directive 2004/38/EC) into Irish law, orders can be made for both the removal and exclusion of citizens of the European Union, European Economic Area and Switzerland.
Such orders are made after a full assessment of a person’s individual circumstances and can be made on the grounds of public policy, public security or public health; legally, such orders must not be disproportionate and an individual assessment of factors such as length of residence in the country, integration (e.g. work history), age, health etc. must be carried out.
This year, 3,538 deportation orders have been signed up to 2 October, while 1,809 people have had their departure from the State confirmed.

I am advised that a design team has been appointed to prepare the Strategic Assessment and Preliminary Business Case for the proposed project. This work is being undertaken in accordance with the Infrastructure Guidelines and will define the scope, scale and requirements of the project, while assessing its feasibility, affordability and value for money.
The Preliminary Business Case will examine both current and future operational requirements and identify the accommodation needed to support the effective delivery of court services in Portlaoise into the future. The assessment will provide the evidence base necessary to inform the next stage of project development and decision making.

question: Deputy Seán Kyne asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration for an update on Ireland's operation and implementation of the EU Migration and Asylum Pact.
reply:
The International Protection Act 2026 gives effect to the EU Migration and Asylum Pact and came into effect on 12 June 2026.
The Pact provides for a fair, sustainable and efficient asylum procedure. This will be achieved through greater convergence in asylum practices across the EU, including standardised processing times for decisions: six months for a standard procedure, three months for accelerated and border procedures, and two months for inadmissible cases.
The Department undertook significant preparation prior to commencement, developing and resourcing new processes and procedures to ensure readiness for the new timelines required under the Pact. The new system has been in place for almost four months and is operating as intended.
At the front end of the process, screening, registration and pathway allocation are functioning effectively, with statutory timelines being met and cases successfully channelled into the appropriate procedural pathways. Early data also suggests that screening under the new framework is being successfully operationalised at scale, with 2,427 applicants for international protection commencing screening and 2,113 completing screening between 12 June and 23 September 2026.
The Pact has strengthened our ability to establish identity and assess vulnerabilities at an early stage. Enhanced screening measures, improved document verification capabilities, and more effective use of electronic evidence are supporting more robust and informed decision-maki

question: Deputy Mark Ward asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration when there will be a roll out of a new youth justice strategy; and the priorities his Department will focus on.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 44 and 75 together.
The Government’s approach to tackling youth offending is primarily through youth diversion and early intervention. The core exchequer and dormant account funding allocation for youth justice measures has almost doubled since 2020, standing at a record €43 million.
The Youth Justice Strategy 2021-2027 emphasises early intervention, prevention, family support and community engagement. It targets behavioural change so the cycle of offending by young people is broken. It follow operates a graduated response, ranging from diversion to detention. As offending increases in severity, so too does the criminal justice response to address youth crime.
The Government has fulfilled its commitment in the Youth Justice Strategy to ensure the availability of YDPs throughout the State. Every young person in Ireland now has access to a youth diversion service.
An evaluation of the YDPs was commissioned in 2022 and published in June 2023 concluding that YDPs are performing well in many areas that are known to impact positively on reducing crime and reoffending.
There has been an estimated 20% reduction in youth offences referred to An Garda Síochána between 2020 and 2025; with this decrease taking place during a period of population growth in the 12-17 cohort. Youth Diversion Projects work with more than 4,500 young people each year, resulting in thousands of young people diverted from criminal pathways, which then leads to fewer victims and

question: Deputy Matt Carthy asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration when he expects to publish the draft National Migration and Integration Strategy; and if it will include consideration of an all-island approach to the management of migration.
reply:
The Programme for Government contains a commitment to publish a National Migration and Integration Strategy setting out how the Government intends to respond to the demands and opportunities facing Ireland's society and economy over the next decade.
My Department is currently working collaboratively with a wide range of Government Departments to develop this Strategy, with the aim of publishing Ireland's first overarching, whole-of-government National Migration and Integration Strategy in the coming months.
The scope of the Strategy will include issues such as social impacts, labour market needs, legal pathways, international education and planning for public service provision, including housing, among other migration-related issues. While the Strategy cannot extend beyond matters within the State's control, it will recognise the importance of Irish migration policy accounting for developments elsewhere, including in Northern Ireland and the Common Travel Area generally, as well as migration policy development within the European Union. This is particularly important in protecting the Common Travel Area and ensuring the free movement of citizens between Ireland and the United Kingdom.
To support this work, a Strategic Migration Policy Group (SMPG) was established in December 2024. The Group now comprises ten Government Departments meeting at senior official level.
Each Department is in a position to convey the perspectives of the agencies under its remit, which have also prov

question: Deputy Naoise Ó Muirí asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the categories of harmful and violent material that will be covered by the forthcoming legislation criminalising the possession, production, and distribution of extreme pornography; and to provide an update on the proposed scope of the legislation.
reply:
In July, I secured Government approval to draft legislation to criminalise the possession, production and distribution of extreme or violent pornography, addressing a significant gap in Irish law. Such material is having a harmful impact, particularly on young people, and is distorting healthy sexual development and contributing to misogynistic attitudes.
The proposed offences will criminalise extreme or violent pornographic material, including depictions of rape or violence causing serious harm to a person and depictions of bestiality or necrophilia. It is intended to set out specific categories of such extreme or violent content, which will be defined during the drafting process.
In developing this proposal, my Department has considered a range of sources, including the Resolution 1835 (2011) of the Council of Europe Parliamentary Assembly on violent and extreme pornography and a review of approaches in other jurisdictions. All of these sources have informed development of the proposal to date. The specifics of the approach will be further examined, with the benefit of advice from the Office of the Attorney General. The timeline will depend on completion of drafting, the publication of the Bill and its subsequent passage through the Oireachtas.

question: Deputy Ruairí Ó Murchú asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration to provide an update on the progress being made to resolve the solicitors' dispute over the introduction of the new criminal legal aid scheme.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 33 and 70 together.
The reform of the criminal legal aid fee structure in the District Court is designed to improve efficiencies, reduce unnecessary adjournments, simplify the administration of criminal legal aid, speed up case resolution and enable faster payments to practitioners through the repeal of previous regulations and the provision of new regulatory arrangements.
Since the commencement of the new system, and as of 2 October, almost 2,400 new certificates (invoices for payment) for legal aid have issued with an approximate total value of €1.25 million in the District Court alone.
It should be noted that, under the Criminal Justice (Legal Aid) Act 1962, it is the courts, through the judiciary, that are responsible for the granting of legal aid. My Department has no involvement in the granting of free legal aid or the assignment of solicitors. These matters are handled entirely by the courts. Under the Courts Service Act 1998, the management and administration of the courts is a matter for the Courts Service, while the allocation of court business, the scheduling of cases and the management of court lists are matters for the Judiciary, in particular the Presidents of the Courts.

question: Deputy Aindrias Moynihan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the current position regarding Garda recruitment and retention for County Cork; the measures being taken to ensure adequate policing resources for rural Ireland.
reply:

Garda funding has increased by more than €500 million since 2020, with a record Budget 2026 allocation of €2.74 billion to ensure An Garda Síochána has the personnel, equipment and resources necessary to meet policing demands across the country.

A fourth group will attest from the College next week and there will be a fifth group attesting from the Garda College before the end of the year.
The allocation of each intake of newly attested probationer Gardaí is considered by the Commissioner in the context of the overall operational needs and policing priorities of the organisation, whilst also having regard to the resourcing requirements of each Garda Division. It is also important to note that the allocation of Probationer Gardaí is one part of the overall picture. Another part is the transfer of serving Gardaí to their preferred location which is facilitated by the attestation and allocat

question: Deputy Paul Lawless asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the reason he overturned in excess of 500 deportation orders last year.
reply:
It is a central priority for me that Ireland’s immigration system is robust and rules based. The enforcement provisions of our immigration laws, including deportation orders, are an essential component of an effective system and help to ensure public confidence in the fair and consistent application of our legislation.
Deportations are often costly and complex to carry out. Where a person does not remove themselves from the State following the making of a deportation order, they may be removed. My Department has taken significant steps to strengthen immigration enforcement measures and increase the number of removals.
The number of deportation orders signed in 2024 (2,403) represented an increase of 180% compared with 2023 (857). In 2025, 4,700 deportation orders were signed, an increase of 96% compared with 2024. As of 2 October 2026, 3,538 deportation orders have been signed.
In 2024, 1,122 people departed the State through various mechanisms, including enforced deportation and voluntary return. In 2025, the departure of 2,111 people was confirmed through these pathways, an increase of 88% compared with 2024. As of 2 October 2026, 1,809 people have departed the State through these pathways.
Section 3(11) of the Immigration Act 1999, as amended, provides that a deportation order may be revoked and my Department receives submissions from people seeking that this provision be invoked.
In assessing such submissions, consideration is given to whether there is compelling new info

question: Deputy Naoise Ó Cearúil asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the measures being taken by his Department and An Garda Síochána to prevent and reduce anti-social behaviour in communities; and the initiatives currently in place to address issues such as public disorder, dangerous driving, and the misuse of fireworks.
reply:
This Government is committed to building stronger, safer communities across the country.
As Minister, my role is to ensure that the Garda Commissioner has the resources that he needs to tackle crime. Record funding and efforts to prioritise recruitment have ensured that there is a strong pipeline of Garda recruits in place. Garda funding has increased by over €500 million since 2020, and groups of over 200 trainees are now regularly entering and attesting from the Garda College. I can assure the Deputy that I will continue to engage with the Commissioner to ensure that he has the resources that he needs to tackle crime in all of our communities.
The Policing, Security and Community Safety Act 2024, which I commenced in 2025, provides for the establishment of 36 Local Community Safety Partnerships within each local authority area.
Local Community Safety Partnerships (Safety Partnerships) represent a significant step towards a more collaborative, responsive, and locally driven model of public safety. They bring together a broad range of relevant stakeholders to address community safety issues in their area.
Safety Partnership members include residents, local councillors, community representatives, business and education representatives, and a range of public services including the HSE, Tusla, An Garda Síochána and the local authority.
Each Safety Partnership will focus on concerns identified and prioritised by local people and are mandated to consult with their local community

question: Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the position regarding any allowances being considered for people legally resident in Ireland and in the process of meeting the requirements for Irish citizenship in the context of imminent changes in citizenship requirements.
reply:
The Government recognises and values the significant contribution that migrants make to Irish society, communities, and the economy.
The Programme for Government contains a commitment to continue to implement a firmer and more sustainable migration system which protects the integrity of the State's immigration framework. In that context, the General Scheme of the Irish Nationality and Citizenship Bill 2026 proposes a number of reforms to the citizenship process.
Citizenship represents the fullest expression of membership of Irish society and it is important that the legislative framework governing access to citizenship is robust, fair and sustainable.
The proposed changes do not seek to restrict integration or exclude migrants from Irish society. Rather, they are intended to ensure that citizenship reflects a genuine and lasting connection to Ireland, an understanding of the State and its institutions, and an ongoing commitment to Irish society.
While the proposals may affect the timeframe within which some individuals become eligible to apply for citizenship, they do not affect a person's entitlement to reside, work, study, establish a business or establish a life in Ireland in accordance with the terms of their immigration permission.

question: Deputy Darren O'Rourke asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration for an update on his plans for Thornton Hall; and projected timeframe for same.
reply:
I am acutely aware of the capacity constraints in our prisons and the challenges faced by those who work and live in our prisons as a result.
The Irish Prison Service (IPS) must accept into custody all people committed to prison by the courts and has no control over the numbers committed to custody at any given time. Since 2024, 292 spaces have been constructed across the prison estate, with 126 delivered in 2024, 106 in 2025 and 60 constructed so far in 2026. question: Deputy Seán Kyne asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the status of the rollout and establishment of community safety partnerships nationwide and, in particular, in Galway city and Galway county; the progress made to date in replacing joint policing committees; and if he is satisfied that community safety partnerships are delivering improved outcomes for community engagement and local safety.

Safety Partnerships are independent, community-led bodies mandated to design tailored safety plans based on local priorities. Drawing together the collective resources of partners at the table, they will ensure interventions are delivered proactively by the service best placed to deliver it and in a joined up, integrated way with other services. question: Deputy Ruairí Ó Murchú asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the current average processing times for international protection applicants; and the progress being made to reduce the processing times for international protection applicants.
reply:
It is a central priority for me that Ireland’s immigration system is robust and rules based.
There has been a significant increase in investment in the international protection system over the last number of years which, combined with digitisation and process re-engineering, has facilitated a major increase in processing capacity and demonstrates a strong commitment to reducing cases on hand.
In 2025, the International Protection Office (IPO) delivered over 20,200 first instance decisions compared to approximately 14,100 in 2024: a 44% increase. IPAT more than doubled the number of appeals closed from 3,100 in 2024 to nearly 6,300 in 2025. This year, as of 30 September 2026, International Protection Appeal Tribunal (IPAT) has already closed 6,898 appeals exceeding the number of total appeals completed in 2025.
As the Deputy will be aware, the International Protection Act 2026 (IP Act 2026) gives effect to the EU Migration and Asylum Pact and came into effect on 12 June 2026.
The Pact provides for a fair, sustainable, and efficient asylum procedure. This will be achieved through greater convergence in asylum practices across the EU, including standardised processing times for decisions: six months for a standard procedure, three months for accelerated and border procedures, and two months for inadmissible cases.

question: Deputy Matt Carthy asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration whether the Government remains committed to implementing the multi-agency competent authority model for the national referral mechanism established under the Criminal Law (Sexual Offences and Human Trafficking) Act 2024; and if not, the reasons for that decision.
reply:
The Government remains committed to strengthening the National Referral Mechanism (NRM), including through the expansion of the multi-agency competent authority model, and to ensuring that victims of human trafficking are identified and referred to appropriate supports as effectively and as early as possible. The NRM already operates on a multi-agency basis, with Departments, State agencies and other organisations identifying and referring potential victims. Under the current arrangements, An Garda Síochána is responsible for the formal identification of victims.
Part 3 of the Criminal Law (Sexual Offences and Human Trafficking) Act 2024 provides for the formal identification function to be extended beyond An Garda Síochána to other designated bodies. Detailed implementation planning has identified practical and operational issues concerning the implementation and sequencing of these arrangements, including their interaction with broader State structures and processes. There is also a need to ensure appropriate alignment with changes across the migration and international protection systems.
In light of these issues, a phased approach is being taken to assigning formal identification responsibilities to the additional competent authorities on an administrative basis, while referral procedures related to the existing NRM are strengthened and the designated bodies put in place the necessary operational arrangements.

reply:

The Youth Justice Strategy 2021-2027 emphasises early intervention, prevention, family support and community engagement. It targets behavioural change so the cycle of offending by young people is broken. It follow operates a graduated response, ranging from diversion to detention. As offending increases in severity, so too does the criminal justice response to address youth crime.
The Government has fulfilled its commitment in the Youth Justice Strategy to ensure the availability of YDPs throughout the State. Every young person in Ireland now has access to a youth diversion service.
An evaluation of the YDPs was commissioned in 2022 and published in June 2023 concluding that YDPs are performing well in many areas that are known to impact positively on reducing crime and reoffending.
There has been an estimated 20% reduction in youth offences referred to An Garda Síochána between 2020 and 2025; with this decrease taking place during a period of population growth in the 12-17 cohort. question: Deputy Paula Butterly asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if he will provide an update on the progress of sentencing reform legislation contained in the programme for Government.
reply:
In January 2026, I secured cabinet approval for the drafting of a Judicial Council (Amendment Bill) and to publish the General Scheme. As the Deputy will be aware, the Judicial Council was established in 2019 to promote judicial independence as well as to ensure public confidence in the administration of justice. The Council is an independent body whose members are all of the judges in Ireland.
A key aim of the Bill is to ensure that the process for the adoption of Personal Injuries Guidelines is more transparent and comprehensive. It provides for a mechanism for the Judicial Council to reconsider revised Personal Injuries Guidelines, should the Oireachtas not approve the Guidelines presented to them. The Bill’s provisions in this regard also include procedural amendments regarding Sentencing Guidelines to align with the Supreme Court judgement in the Delaney case.
The General Scheme also provides for the Programme for Government commitment to empower the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration to ask the Judicial Council to draw up sentencing guidelines for a particular crime area, within a certain timeframe. It also requires the Council to comply with such a request.

question: Deputy Edward Timmins asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the measures that have been taken to reduce the value of contracts with IPAS providers; and the plans for the future of same.
reply:
My Department is taking action across all aspects of international protection accommodation to improve value for money, strengthen governance and compliance, and renegotiate contracts with providers.
A range of updated and strengthened systems and procedures have been put in place and are already having an impact, including processes for appraisal, validation, contracting and payments.
A new rate-card pricing structure was introduced in May 2025 and has been applied to all new or renewing contracts. The rate card is considered commercially sensitive as it is used in live negotiations, but it functions as a bench-mark rate across various types of accommodation and is being used to renegotiate rates on renewal, and to define rates for any new contracts.
Implementation of this rate card has resulted in over €162 million in projected savings on contract values across 259 centres per annum.
In addition to seeking better value through applying the rate card, my Department has also increased inspections and compliance activities over the last year or more, and 43 IPAS accommodation contracts have been terminated since the beginning of 2025.
The allocation for IPAS accommodation and supports for 2025 was €1.27 billion and this reduced to €1.1 billion for accommodation and supports in 2026.

question: Deputy Matt Carthy asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration his plans to reform the operation of the in-camera rule in family law proceedings.
reply:
Ensuring transparency and promoting a greater understanding of the family law system is critical to maintaining and building trust in it. At the same time, those who seek the assistance of the courts in resolving their family justice disputes need to be assured that their privacy, and that of their children, will be maintained at what can be a very difficult time. In recognising the need for a balance between these two positions, the Family Justice Strategy commits to undertaking a review of the operation of the in-camera rule in family law proceedings.
Further to this commitment, an independent research report, entitled The Operation of the In Camera Rule in Family Law Proceedings, was published in 2025. The extensive report contains 21 detailed recommendations. Officials from my Department are currently considering the findings and recommendations of the report in the context of developing policy proposals for reform. Officials are also examining how family court proceedings operate in other jurisdictions, to see what can be learned from them.
Following on from the findings of the report, I commissioned the Child Law Project to deliver the Family Law Reporting Project. The first volume of case reports was published by my Department on the 19 August 2026. Previously there was no comprehensive system in Ireland for regularly and systematically reporting on private family law proceedings. Officials in my Department and An Garda Síochána are now moving from proof-of-concept to the establishment of a full programme for the procurement and implementation of a National Body Worn Camera solution with a secure local Digital Evidence Management solution.

question: Deputy James Geoghegan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if he will provide an update on the new framework for the authorisation and operation of CCTV schemes through Part 5 of the Garda Síochána (Recording Devices) Act 2023.
reply:
CCTV in public places has a role in giving people a greater sense of security. Whilst the use of CCTV by An Garda Síochána and Local Authorities can have great merit, its use can have a direct impact on the human rights of individuals. Therefore, its installation and operation must be carefully planned and its use competently managed, ensuring compliance with data protection law and regulations.
The Garda Síochána (Recording Devices) Act 2023 was enacted on 5 December 2023. Part 5 of the Act, which relates to public CCTV, was not commenced at that time as it required the completion of operational guidelines and further legislative changes. The enactment of the Garda Síochána (Recording Devices) (Amendment) Act 2026 in July 2026 and the recent completion of the Garda CCTV Code of Practice means that Part 5 of the Act will be commenced in the coming weeks.
The commencement of Part 5 will establish a new statutory framework for the authorisation and operation of public CCTV schemes, repealing Section 38 of the Garda Síochána Act 2005.

reply:
Munster Technological University (MTU) is an autonomous institution and is responsible for the management of its own academic affairs, including the content of its programmes. Accordingly, neither I nor my Department has a role in determining these matters.

While a once-off arrangement was facilitated with Teagasc for certain students who entered the programme in 2019 and 2020, this was an exceptional accommodation for those cohorts and did not constitute Green Certificate equivalence for the programme itself. In seeking to assist the students concerned, MTU explored with Teagasc whether an alternative bridging pathway could be made available. Following consideration of the proposal, Teagasc advised that it could not be accommodated within the existing eligibility, quality assurance and validation requirements applying to the Green Certificate.

question: Deputy Jen Cummins asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science the number of students that have been accepted into a course in Ireland but have been unable to commence due to being denied a visa over the last five years, in tabular form.
reply:
As autonomous bodies, higher education institutions are responsible for their own admissions processes, including the issuing of offers and the receipt of acceptances of applicants. My Department does not collect data on individual applicants who accept offers but do not ultimately take up their place.
Decisions relating to visas and immigration permissions are matters for the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration. Information on visa applications and refusals is therefore held by that Department.

reply:
Higher Education Institutions (HEIs) are autonomous under legislation and manage their own academic affairs including admissions procedures. The Central Applications Office (CAO) is an independent body established by the HEIs whose function is to process applications for undergraduate courses on behalf of the HEIs. Neither I nor my Department have a role in the operation of the CAO, and information on applications is held by the CAO and the HEIs.
While the CAO publishes a certain amount of data each year on applications, it is not published at individual course level and therefore the data requested on the applicant figures for the pharmacy degree programme at University College Cork for the 2026/27 academic year is not available. Given the capacity limits on this course, and the high CAO points required for entry, it is highly likely that there were more applications to this course than places available.
Arrangements are in place within the CAO system to ensure that applicants who secure an improved grade following a Leaving Certificate appeal can be considered for subsequent CAO offer rounds. Where places remain available, or where additional capacity arises, eligible applicants may receive a revised offer in later rounds. Most applicants who receive an improved grade on appeal are accommodated through these processes in the current academic year.

question: Deputy Pádraig Rice asked the Minister for Health in the absence of statutory regulation of psychologists, if any interim protections exist for patients; and if consideration has been given to a proposal (details supplied).
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 327 and 334 together.
As the Deputy will be aware, CORU is Ireland's multi-profession health and social care regulator. CORU’s role is to protect the public by regulating the health and social care professions designated under the Health and Social Care Professionals Act 2005 (as amended).
The Psychologists Registration Board (PSRB) was established in 2017. The work of the PSRB includes setting the Standards of Proficiency for entry to its register and Criteria for Education and Training Programmes, establishing a Code of Professional Conduct and Ethics that registrants must adhere to, and approving and monitoring education and training programmes.
The PSRB’s statutory remit is to ensure the competence of registrants to practice safely in any setting where they engage with vulnerable service users. This is inextricably bound with its legal object and remit to ensure protection of the professional title; namely, that all who use the protected title of psychologist have the same threshold knowledge, skills and competence to ensure a consistent, safe level of practice.
Regulating a new profession is a complex and lengthy process, requiring careful consideration and preparatory work to ensure that it is effective in protecting the public. Psychology has been a uniquely challenging profession to regulate due to the diversity of its specialisms and the fact that there is no common education pathway or standards for entry to the profession.

question: Deputy Mairéad Farrell asked the Minister for Health whether the free HRT Scheme will be extended to cover hormone replacement therapy for patients with congenital or permanent endocrine conditions, including testosterone replacement for Klinefelter syndrome.
reply:
The HSE has statutory responsibility for decisions on the pricing and reimbursement of medicines. This arises from the Health (Pricing and Supply of Medical Goods) Act 2013.
Reimbursement is for licenced indications which have been granted marketing authorisation by the European Medicines Agency (EMA) or the Health Products Regulatory Authority (HPRA). Pharmaceutical companies must apply to the HSE for reimbursement.
Under the Free Hormone Replacement Therapy (HRT) arrangement, which came into effect on 1 June 2025, where a woman has been prescribed a HRT product on the reimbursement list by her healthcare provider for the purpose of alleviating the symptoms associated with all stages of menopause, the cost of the HRT medications or products, and the dispensing fees will be met by the State.
This measure is intended to support the management of the symptoms of menopause and, therefore, relates to the provision of treatment for a specific medical condition/life stage i.e. menopause. HRT is the most commonly used treatment for managing symptoms of menopause and has shown to be the most effective intervention.
Menopause has been highlighted as a key priority area by the Women’s Health Taskforce. It is a key action in the Women’s Health Action Plans. A number of measures have been implemented in recent years to improve the experience of menopause for women in Ireland, including this HRT arrangement.

With the 2026 plan, we will continue to build upon the progress delivered to date under the multi annual action plan approach, moving towards the ultimate vision of a public healthcare service in which everyone has timely access to high-quality scheduled care, where and when they need it.

question: Deputy Réada Cronin asked the Minister for Health the measures being taken to reduce overcrowding and improve patient flow at Naas General Hospital.
reply:
Improving patient flow and reducing overcrowding in emergency departments remains a key priority for Government, my Department and the HSE.
The HSE's Urgent and Emergency Care (UEC) Operational Plan sets out a range of measures to improve access to urgent and emergency care services and patient flow across the healthcare system. These measures focus on four key areas: hospital avoidance, emergency department operations, in-hospital care delivery and discharge management.
The HSE and my Department are focused on actions which include increasing alternatives to hospital attendance and admission, improving patient flow through acute hospitals, reducing delayed transfers of care, enhancing discharge processes, and expanding models of care that support patients to receive treatment in the most appropriate setting. A particular focus remains on reducing delayed transfers of care through improved integration and coordination between hospital and community services.
The HSE is also continuing to expand Acute Virtual Ward services, which support suitable patients to receive hospital-level care in their own homes while increasing available capacity within acute hospitals. Acute Virtual Wards are a key component of the national urgent and emergency care programme.
As this PQ refers specifically to Naas General Hospital, I will refer it to the HSE for more specific local measures that are being undertaken.

question: Deputy David Cullinane asked the Minister for Health the number of hospital-initiated scheduled care cancellations by month in the year to date, by hospital, appointment or procedure type and reason, in tabular form.
reply:
I fully acknowledge the distress and inconvenience for patients and their families when hospital appointments are cancelled, particularly in the case of clinically urgent procedures.
While every effort is made to avoid cancellation or postponement of planned procedures, the Health Service Executive (HSE) has advised that planned procedures and operations can be postponed or cancelled for a variety of reasons including capacity issues due to increased unscheduled care demand.
Patient safety remains at the centre of all hospital activity and elective care scheduling. To ensure services are provided in a safe, clinically aligned and prioritised way, hospitals follow HSE clinical guidelines and protocols.
Cancelled hospital procedures/appointments are, where appropriate, rescheduled as early as possible with priority given to patients requiring time-sensitive and urgent treatment. Patients that are cancelled are rescheduled with the next available appointment based on their clinical prioritisation, with urgent patients prioritised for access.

question: Deputy Tony McCormack asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration his plans to implement the recommendations of the Cost of Business Advisory Forum report that come under the remit of his Department.
reply:
The Cost of Business Advisory Forum was established by the Department of Enterprise, Tourism and Employment as a priority commitment in the Programme for Government, noting the increased costs faced in recent years, particularly by small businesses. The Forum’s key objective was to examine and identify the concerns of enterprise regarding the impact of the rising cost of doing business in Ireland through structured engagement between enterprise representative bodies, from various sectors, alongside Government Departments and State agencies.
On 28 August 2026, the Forum published its final report, which was informed by extensive stakeholder input and cross-government collaboration. The report identifies six key themes affecting businesses and sets out 63 recommendations focused on price transparency, switching and access, regulatory reform and simplification, and targeted measures to address bottlenecks.
The Department of Enterprise is currently engaging with my Department regarding the feasibility of the Report’s recommendations. However, a number of reforms relevant to the issues identified in the Report are already being progressed.
In terms of insurance, last year the Government unveiled its new Action Plan on Insurance Reform with a range of priorities aimed at lowering insurance premiums. question: Deputy Mairéad Farrell asked the Minister for Health the action the HSE and the HPRA are taking on the current supply shortage of budesonide orodispersible tablets in the State.
reply:
The Health Products Regulatory Authority (HPRA), as the competent authority in Ireland for coordinating the management of medicine shortages, has advised that it has received no notifications indicating a current supply interruption affecting Jorveza (budesonide orodispersible tablets).
Ireland has a multi-stakeholder Medicines Shortages Framework, operated by the HPRA, through which the Department of Health, the Health Service Executive (HSE), the HPRA and other stakeholders work together to help prevent and mitigate medicine shortages and minimise any impact on patients.
Marketing authorisation holders are required to report actual and anticipated medicine shortages to the HPRA. Where a shortage is reported, details are assessed by the HPRA and published on its publicly available medicines shortages database.
Patients who are experiencing difficulty obtaining their medication should consult their healthcare professional, such as their GP or pharmacist.

The Government’s approach to tackling youth offending is primarily through youth diversion and early intervention. The core exchequer and dormant account funding allocation for youth justice measures has almost doubled from 2020 to 2026, standing at a record €43 million. The budget allocated increased from over €34 million in 2024 to over €40 million in 2025 and to €43 million in Budget 2026. Funding for 2027 will be allocated through the normal budgetary cycle.

question: Deputy Michael Healy-Rae asked the Minister for Health if health insurance companies are allowed to change their plans and/or benefits after a person has signed up with them.
reply:
As Minister for Health, I am responsible for the legal framework governing the health insurance market in Ireland. This is a voluntary market that operates under the principles of community rating, open enrolment, lifetime cover and minimum benefits. These protections are designed to support fairness and keep health insurance as affordable as possible for all consumers.
Private health insurers operate as commercial entities and may introduce, withdraw or amend health insurance plans and benefits, subject to compliance with the requirements of health insurance legislation.
A customer whose policy is mid-term will not ordinarily experience changes to their premium until renewal, and any changes to price or benefits must be clearly set out in the renewal notice.
The Health Insurance Act 1994 (Minimum Benefit) Regulations 1996 require insurers to provide a minimum level of cover to every insured person, regardless of what insurance policy has been purchased.
Private health insurers operate as commercial entities within a competitive market and, beyond the minimum requirements set out in legislation, may determine the range of products and services they offer. Insurers may withdraw, reduce or restructure benefits, provided they comply with the Minimum Benefit Regulations.

question: Deputy Paul McAuliffe asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if he plans to increase targeted allocations through the community safety fund to certain parts of the country, given the increase in gangland criminal activity in certain parts of the country in recent years.
reply:
The Community Safety Fund redirects proceeds of crime seized by the Criminal Assets Bureau (CAB) and An Garda Síochána back into communities. First opened in 2022, this annual fund reallocates these criminal proceeds so that they are used to develop positive programmes that strengthen local communities, support vulnerable groups, engage young people and help prevent crime.
Last month, I announced the allocation of €4.84 million through the Community Safety Fund to 56 community safety projects nationwide. This is over double the number of projects funded by the first Community Safety Fund in 2022.
This year’s allocation is a 10% increase on the €4.4 million awarded in 2025, and a 146%, or €2.84 million increase on the funding allocated to the first Community Safety Fund in 2022.
These projects will deliver tangible benefits across Ireland and demonstrate my commitment to ensuring that the proceeds of crime are used to create safer, stronger and more inclusive communities.
The Funding Call document, which is available online, outlined the criteria used to assess applications, including the degree to which the planned outcomes meet the goals of the scheme and its strategic objectives; the overall strength of the project proposal having regard to the planned activities; and financial management, governance, and value for money.

question: Deputy Joe Neville asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the measures that have been implemented by An Garda Síochána to de-escalate incidents of young adults video-recording themselves driving the wrong way down motorways, as occurred recently.
reply:
The Department of Culture, Communications and Sport has primary responsibility for Online Safety, including the sharing of videos in which young adults record themselves driving the wrong way down motorways.
The Online Services and Media Regulation Act was introduced and Coimisiún na Meán established, by that Department, to regulate online media, including enforcing rules about how online services or platforms should deal with harmful and illegal content on their services.
Coimisiún na Meán introduced and enforces a binding online safety code for video-sharing platforms, which set out obligations for online services to protect users from and tackle the availability of defined categories of harmful online content.
Coimisiún na Meán is also key to the enforcement of the Digital Services Act (DSA) in Ireland. The DSA is EU-wide legislation which requires online services to take steps to make the internet safer for users by addressing harmful or illegal content on their sites.
The Government remains committed to ensuring that An Garda Síochána has the resources, equipment and legislative framework necessary to carry out its policing functions.
An updated Spontaneous Pursuits Policy was issued by An Garda Síochána in late 2024 to provide guidance to Garda personnel to evaluate the risks associated with pursuits.
The Garda Commissioner has confirmed that Garda pursuit training, a specialist capability being introduced for the first time, will commence before the end of year.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Health the steps being taken to address the gap in pay, mileage and conditions between home support workers directly employed by the HSE and those employed by approved private providers delivering HSE funded hours; whether any provision will be made in Budget 2027 for this purpose.
reply:
Approximately 70% of exchequer funded home support in Ireland is delivered by the private and voluntary sectors via a procurement arrangement known as the Authorisation Scheme. The Authorisation Scheme provides a framework to enable regions to deliver home support services to its service users through a standardised commissioning model with a national hourly rate in place with providers across Ireland. There are agreed premium rates outside of core hours and for 30 minute calls.
The Authorisation Scheme was one of the key recommendations of the Strategic Workforce Advisory Group, the ‘SWAG’, which was established to address the issues facing frontline workers in home support and nursing homes. It was established in August 2023 and has delivered on significant reforms to the sector including payment for travel time for home support providers and paying carers the National Living Wage at a minimum.
As the HSE has operational responsibility for the management and delivery of health services nationally, any funding requests from such organisations seeking additional funding must be submitted to the HSE for consideration.
Addressing pay, mileage and conditions of home support workers is an operational matter, I have therefore asked the Health Service Executive to respond to the Deputy directly on these issues as soon as possible.

From the 1st October 2026, omaveloxolone (Skyclarys®) is approved to be added to the list of reimbursable items under the High-Tech Drug Arrangements for the treatment of Friedreich’s ataxia in adults and adolescents aged 16 years and older. Prescribing of omaveloxolone (Skyclarys®) is through the High-Tech Hub and will be restricted to designated approved consultants.
As this is an operational matter, I have asked the Health Service Executive to respond to the Deputy directly, as soon as possible.

question: Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration to outline public information campaigns planned to raise awareness of NIS2, particularly for businesses and organisations impacted.
reply:
The NIS2 Directive aims to enhance and strengthen cyber security and resilience across a number of critical sectors including energy, transport, water, healthcare and digital infrastructure.
Work is close to finalisation on the drafting of the National Cyber Security Bill, which will transpose the NIS2 Directive and establish Ireland’s National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) on a statutory basis, and will be published shortly. This legislation is a priority for myself and this Government and I hope to be in a position to notify transposition of the NIS2 Directive by the end of 2026.
The NCSC is engaging with its constituents and stakeholders to ensure the requirements of the Bill are communicated ahead of time and has produced resources and guidance for entities that fall within the scope of NIS2. The NCSC has also prepared a media campaign for launch when the bill is enacted.
Some of the resources and guidance currently available to entities on the NCSC website includes:
• Draft Risk Management Measures and the Cyber Fundamentals (CyFun) framework, both designed to help organisations comply with NIS2 requirements.
• Guidance on Cyber Governance for Management Board Members in NIS2 Entities. This new resource is specifically designed to support Management Board members fulfil their leadership responsibilities and protect the continuity of essential services with confidence.
• A ‘NIS2 Quick Reference Guide’ and associated FAQ page.

question: Deputy Eoin Ó Broin asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality if the home support policy with the eligibility and prioritisation criteria promised in the Action Plan for Disability Services 2024–2026 has been published; and if age-based exclusions are consistent with the policy.
reply:
A key programme of reform is ongoing in the home support sector, encompassing disability, older persons and mental health services. The programme has a vision at its centre of an equitable, person-centred, and enabling home support service that enhances service user and staff experience. The reform programme is being led by the Department of Health and the HSE, in conjunction with the Department of Children, Disability and Equality.
A crucial element of the home support reform programme is the development of a regulatory framework for home support providers. This work is being led by the Department of Health, and the Department of Children, Disability and Equality has been engaging with them on all elements of the framework that impact disability services.
The home support regulatory framework comprises:
- primary legislation providing for the licensing and regulation of public and private home support providers;
- secondary legislation (regulations) establishing the minimum requirements with which home support providers must comply; and
- National Standards currently under development by the Health Information and Quality Authority (HIQA) to support progressive quality improvements in home support service provision across the sectors.
The primary legislation underpinning the framework, the Health (Amendment) (Home Support Providers) Act 2026, was enacted on 1 July 2026.

question: Deputy Tom Brabazon asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration whether, further to the provisions of the Children Act 2001, he will consider introducing legislation providing criminal liability for a parent or guardian where it can be established that a wilful or reckless failure to exercise reasonable care or control has contributed to antisocial or criminal behaviour by a child under 18 years.
reply:
The Government recognises the critical role that strong family relationships and effective parental supervision play in preventing youth offending.
The role of parental supervision orders, which are already provided for under the Children Act 2021 and other parental measures, will be further considered in the development of a new Youth Justice Strategy over the coming year.
The Government’s approach to tackling youth offending is primarily through youth diversion and early intervention, and the budget allocation for youth justice measures has almost doubled since 2020, standing at €43 million for 2026.
The Youth Justice Strategy 2021-2027 emphasises early intervention, prevention, family support and community engagement. It targets behavioural change so that the cycle of offending by young people is broken.
The Departments of Health and Children, Disability and Equality play important roles and deliver a number of parental and child interventions and supports. For example, the HSE has responsibility for delivering Parenting Capacity Assessments, and Tusla has responsibility for child interventions and related parental supports.
It is important to recognise that our existing Youth Justice Strategy has been successful in diverting children who have engaged in criminal or anti-social behaviour away from the Criminal Justice system and towards more positive pro-social behaviour and life choices.

question: Deputy Aindrias Moynihan asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine to outline his engagements with the distillery industry in the establishment of a clear farm to bottle providence model for Irish Whiskey, ensuring a clear link between Irish land, Irish farmers and Irish grain.
reply:
The public consultation on the Irish Whiskey Technical File has only recently closed and over the course of the consultation, approximately 200 submissions were received. I was pleased to see the broad level of public engagement from across the spirit drink industry and beyond.
In relation to a farm to bottle providence model, there are several distilleries operating this model in Ireland. This option is open to all distilleries and there are obvious benefits that they can highlight as part of their marketing.
I have made it clear that I am committed to promoting the use of Irish grain in the distilling industry. I have stressed this in my meetings with the Drinks industry and have asked my Department to explore options as part of a wider review. I continue to support new market development and market access efforts for our quality, sustainable food and drink products including Irish whiskey.
My Department is now in the process of reviewing the submissions received from the public consultation.
Over the coming weeks and months my Department will engage with key stakeholders and experts on the proposals. Once the proposed amendments have been reviewed and assessed, then the process of updating the product specification including any required European Commission approval will begin.
I will ask my officials to closely examine any request that strengthens the promotion of Irish Grain and how those asks can fit within the rules that govern the spirit GI regulations.

question: Deputy Pearse Doherty asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine the reason a compliance notice issued requiring a consignment to be re-dispatched to a third country after a container was inspected at Dublin Port, released and delivered to its owner home in County Donegal, when a phytosanitary certificate e16 was submitted to Revenue as part of a Transfer of Residence application.
reply:
My Department carries out Sanitary and Phytosanitary (SPS) checks on certain goods and machinery imported into the EU from third countries at designated Border Control Posts (BCPs). Used machinery must be accompanied by a valid phytosanitary certificate where required. In this case, there were concerns regarding the validity of the phytosanitary certificate presented at documentary inspection. This is being investigated further.
Following the issuing of a compliance notice, the consignment was released from Customs control in error.
My Department undertook a review of the case and concluded that local engagement with the importer was the appropriate course of action while the matter is investigated. In this context, my Department has since withdrawn the compliance notice while this process is ongoing.

question: Deputy John Paul O'Shea asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine the additional funding he will provide under the farm safety scheme for farmers in Cork to upgrade livestock handling facilities and farmyards; and the way in which he will ensure smaller family farms can access these supports.
reply:
The Targeted Agricultural Modernisation Scheme (TAMS 3) provides grants to farmers to build and/or improve a specified range of farm buildings and equipment on their holdings. Overall, the scheme has proved very popular, with an unprecedented level of applications received.
The Farm Safety Capital Investment Scheme is a measure in TAMS 3, which provides an incentive to farmers to avail of investments to improve their own safety and that of their farm. This scheme includes a number of investment items such handling equipment, tank covers, pens and bale slicers, all of which make the day to day running of a small family farm safer and more efficient.
I have ensured that 100% of valid applications submitted under the FSCIS continue to be approved including those from Cork farmers, supporting farmers in improving their own safety and that of their farm.
In addition, the current TAMS 3 ranking and selection criteria ensure that farmers with smaller holdings, regardless of their location, are treated more favourably than those with larger farm holdings. For example, a maximum of 20 marks is allocated to farmers with five hectares declared on their Basic Income Support for Sustainability (BISS) application, with the marks decreasing as the size of the holding increases, thus ensuring that smaller farms can be ranked higher than large enterprises, and are therefore more likely to be selected.

question: Deputy John Paul O'Shea asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine the measures he is taking to protect the viability of dairy, beef and sheep farms in Cork in light of high production costs; and the additional supports he plans to introduce for family farms as part of Budget 2027.
reply:
The agri-food sector has demonstrated its ongoing adaptability and resilience despite numerous uncertainties and economic pressure in recent years. The Government continues to provide strong support to farmers via Ireland’s €10.3 billion CAP Strategic Plan, as well as other national sectoral schemes. In 2025, €244 million worth of CAP funding was provided to farmers in Cork.
I am conscious of the exceptional cost pressures family farms are facing at present. I introduced the Fuel Income Support Scheme as a targeted income support, alongside the fuel excise and levy reductions and delay of Carbon Tax increases introduced by Government. To date total payments of €26.52m have been made under the Fuel Income Support Scheme, with over 31,000 farmers and contractors paid.
Regarding any extension of excise reductions, taxation policy is the responsibility of my colleague the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance. In advance of the budget, I work closely with him on taxation issues relating to the agri-food sector, considering a range of proposals. I also work closely with the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation on expenditure proposals. Working across Government, we will continue to keep developments in global energy markets under close review and remain ready to respond as circumstances evolve.

question: Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine whether or not the native Irish honey bee is under threat; and if he will make a statement on the matter:.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 219 to 221, inclusive, together.
The movement of bees within the European Union is governed by Regulation (EU) 2016/429 (the Animal Health Law) which is supplemented by Commission Implementing and Delegated Regulations (Regulation (EU) 2020/688 and 2021/403). These EU regulations contain specific provisions to safeguard the health of bees located in the territory of the Union.
The Protection of the Native Irish Honey Bee Bill 2021, a Private Members Bill, which seeks to ban the importation of non-native honey bees is currently before Dáil Éireann, Second Stage. Progression of the Bill through Dáil Éireann is subject to the procedures of the Oireachtas.
Following legal advice in relation to the Protection of the Native Irish Honey Bee Bill 2021, my Department sought tenders for research services to provide independent scientific evidence in the form of a comprehensive assessment of the threat to the Native Irish honey bee Apis mellifera mellifera and the impact upon biodiversity and the ecosystem from the introgression/crossing/cross-breeding of the native Irish Honey Bee with non-native species based on the most reliable scientific data available. In October 2023, a contract was signed with the National University of Ireland, Galway for the provision of research services on the native Irish honey bee (Apis mellifera mellifera).
