question: Deputy Gillian Toole asked the Minister for Social Protection if a comprehensive review of the social welfare system is to be carried out to ensure capacity for all requirements including migration reforms and to ensure fairness, equity and transparency.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 386 and 417 together.
The social protection system comprises of over 100 schemes administered by my Department that provide a wide range of income and employment supports.
Many of these schemes operate in line with specific legislation, eligibility criteria, income thresholds or means tests, and operating guidelines.
My Department regularly reviews its schemes and policies to ensure that they continue to provide effective support and respond to changing demographic, social and economic conditions.
In doing so, we consider submissions from our regular engagement with community and voluntary organisations, including through our bi-annual meetings with the Community and Voluntary Pillar, our annual flagship Social Inclusion Forum, the Carers, and Pre-Budget Forums, and our quarterly Disability Consultative Forum, as well as our public consultation processes.
We consider the engagement we have with other Government Departments, as well as data and research from, for example, my Department's Social Impact Assessments, the Central Statistics Office, the Vincentian MESL Research Centre's Minimum Essential Standard of Living which my Department funds, and international sources such as Eurostat and the OECD. In addition, the Department has a poverty research contract with the ESRI, and occasionally awards contracts to consultancy firms, such as Indecon who are currently researching low hours workers.
Customer feedback is also very important in reviewin

question: Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Social Protection if it is possible to introduce a reduced rate of employers' PRSI for employees under the age of 24, to incentivise the employment of young people.
reply:
In general, the issue of targeted supports to incentivise the employment of young people is a matter for the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment. However, the following is the position with regards to employer PRSI.
The main finding of the latest Actuarial Review of the Social Insurance Fund was that the Fund will experience significant long term sustainability challenges. It is in this regard that the previous Government agreed to a series of annual incremental increases in all PRSI rates, including employer PRSI, up to and including 2028. A further evaluation of the position of the Fund will be held after the completion of the next Actuarial Review next year.
It is in this context that there are no proposals, nor has consideration has been given to reduce the employer PRSI rate for employees of any age group. However, in recognition of the pressures faced by businesses, the Government agreed, in Budget 2026, to increase the employer PRSI threshold from €527 to €552 per week, effective from 1 January 2026. This will ensure that employers with full time employees on the national minimum wage or employees with earnings under €552 per week will attract the lower employer PRSI rate of 9%.
Any further changes to the PRSI employer rates or threshold would have to be considered in a budgetary context, taking account of the economic circumstances and with a view to the sustainability of the Social Insurance Fund.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Social Protection whether consideration has been given to a waste collection support for State pensioners living alone, in view of annual minimum bin charges exceeding one week's pension.
reply:
The matter of waste collection charges is the responsibility of my colleague the Minister for the Environment, Climate and Communications. The waste management market in Ireland is now serviced by private companies, where prices charged are matters between those companies and their customers, subject to compliance with all applicable environmental and other relevant legislation, including contract and consumer legislation.
However, my Department does provide Additional Needs Payments as part of the Supplementary Welfare Allowance scheme for people who have essential expenses, which they cannot meet from their own resources.
The decision process involves consideration of the need presented and the ability of the person and their household to meet that need. This entails an assessment, as opposed to a specific means test, of an applicant’s weekly household income, their savings and investments, their outgoings and the type of assistance needed. Other State supports that may already be available to the person are also considered. This ensures that support is provided to people with the greatest financial need.
Any person who considers that they may have an entitlement to an Additional Needs Payment is encouraged to contact their local community welfare service. There is a National Community Welfare Contact Centre in place - 0818-607080 - which will direct callers to the appropriate office. In addition, applications can be made online via www.mywelfare.ie.

question: Deputy John Connolly asked the Minister for Social Protection when the comprehensive review of means testing within the social protection system commenced; the status of that review; when he expects the review to be completed and its finding published; and the reasons for the length of time taken to complete the review.
reply:
The Programme for Government commits to carry out a comprehensive review of means tests across the social welfare system taking into account the Report on Means Testing by the Joint Oireachtas Committee on Social Protection. My Department is conducting a review of means testing within the social protection system.
The aim is to examine various means-tested schemes and identify any issues related to their respective means tests. With over 140 schemes and services, many of which are means-tested, this is a complex and detailed task.
It is my intention that the review's findings will inform decisions regarding potential changes to means testing in future Budgets.
The review is currently with senior management of the Department for review and I expect that it will be submitted to me shortly.
Due to the complexity of the review, I will carefully and thoroughly evaluate it to determine the best way to utilise its findings and identify those that may warrant further consideration.
However, any prospective changes to means-testing arrangements will need to be evaluated and considered within the overall policy and budgetary context.

reply:

question: Deputy Peadar Tóibín asked the Minister for Social Protection the proportion of the total social welfare overpayments raised in each of the years 2016 to 2025 that was attributable to proven fraud, customer error and official or administrative error respectively; and the monetary value associated with each category.
reply:

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Social Protection if she will review the treatment of inherited capital in the means test for disability allowance where the recipient has a lifelong disability and the inheritance is intended to fund their long-term care and independent living; the number of recipients whose payment was reduced or ceased due to inherited capital in each of the past three years.
reply:
Disability Allowance is my Department's primary disability related social assistance scheme. It is a means-tested payment for people with a disability who are aged between 16 and 66. In order to be eligible, the disability must have continued for at least one year or be expected to continue for at least one year.
In addition, the person must be substantially restricted from doing work that would otherwise be suitable for a person of their age, experience, and qualifications. Eligibility for the payment is also subject to a habitual residency requirement.
Social welfare legislation provides that, for means-tested social assistance schemes, all income and assets belonging to the claimant, and their spouse or partner, where applicable, is assessable. This recognises the fact that couples operate as a single household and can share living expenses in a manner not available to a single person.
The purpose of a means test is to ensure that scarce resources are directed to those with the greatest need and it supports an economically sustainable and socially equitable allocation of scarce resources
Disability Allowance has one of the highest capital disregards operated by my Department. A recipient can have up to €50,000 in savings and still receive the full rate of payment. reply:
All 3,200 primary schools and 550,000 children are eligible for hot school meals. Across all meal types there some 3,700 schools and 682,000 children are eligible for support. This equates to the distribution of up to 3.4 million school meals per week.

question: Deputy Paul Lawless asked the Minister for Social Protection if he is aware of the difficulties being experienced by families who are being refused fuel allowance on household means grounds where adult children remain living in the family home due to the lack of affordable rental accommodation and housing options; whether consideration is being given to amending the means assessment for fuel allowance in such cases.
reply:
The criteria for Fuel Allowance are framed in order to direct the limited resources available to the department in as targeted a manner as possible. To qualify for the Fuel Allowance payment, a person must satisfy all the qualifying criteria.
Fuel Allowance operates as part of an overall system of social protection supports which provides assistance payments based on a system of means testing. The means test ensures that the recipient has a verifiable income need and that resources are targeted to those who need them most.
For those who apply and are aged 66 or over, only the means of the applicant and, if applicable, their spouse, civil partner or cohabitant is included when assessing means for Fuel Allowance purposes. However, the normal household composition criteria apply.
A change in the qualifying criteria such as including adult children who are in employment and not in receipt of a qualifying social protection payment, would have to be considered in the context of scheme policy and budgetary negotiations. Disregarding a household member who is not reliant on long term social protection payments and who is in employment would change the targeted nature of the scheme.

question: Deputy Jen Cummins asked the Minister for Social Protection the specific action he is taking to move school meals (details supplied) towards a model where meals are cooked from fresh raw ingredients from scratch in one kitchen, and away from the current predominant ‘assembly and reheat’ model used in the Irish school meal programme.

The recently published Report on Nutrition Review of the Hot School Meals Scheme examined the different catering systems in operation. question: Deputy Seán Ó Fearghaíl asked the Minister for Social Protection If he will address the concerns raised in correspondence details attached regarding the financial difficulties experienced by households where a person remains unable to return to work following cancer treatment and is approaching the end of their illness benefit entitlement.
reply:
Illness Benefit is the primary short term income support provided by my Department to those who are unable to work due to illness of any type and who are covered by social insurance. Eligibility for Illness Benefit depends on the person’s PRSI record and class. It is available for up to two years for people who have the required social insurance contributions under PRSI class A, E, H or P.
Where a person exhausts their entitlement to payment of Illness Benefit and is expected to remain unfit to attend work for a further period of at least 12 months, they have the option of making an application for Invalidity Pension, which is another social insurance scheme paid from the Social Insurance Fund. Eligibility is based on PRSI contributions and medical condition. To qualify, the person must have been incapable of work for at least 12 months and be likely to be incapable of work for at least another 12 months or they must be permanently incapable of work.
Where a person is in a position to return to work to some degree following a period of at least six months in receipt of Illness Benefit they may be eligible for Partial Capacity Benefit. A person may qualify for Partial Capacity Benefit if their restriction on capacity for work is assessed as moderate, severe, or profound. The rate of payment made is dependent on the level of restriction determined in the medical assessment. Where this is deemed to be mild, the person is not eligible for payment. question: Deputy Mairéad Farrell asked the Minister for Social Protection if his attention has been drawn to pension entitlements for staff in voluntary residential and aftercare services, which have been effectively frozen since the financial collapse; if he is aware of the serious recruitment and retention challenges this has created within the sector which may leave voluntary care services at risk of closure; and if he will consider providing entitlement for voluntary social care staff to the State pension scheme.
reply:
The Department of Social Protection is responsible for the State pension system, which is made up of the social insurance-based State Pension (Contributory) and the means tested State Pension (Non-Contributory).
Employees in voluntary residential and aftercare services are covered by the social insurance system according to the PRSI class applicable to their employment. Employees who pay full-rate PRSI may qualify for the State Pension (Contributory) and other social insurance benefits, subject to the relevant qualifying conditions.
The State Pension (Contributory) is not means tested and may be paid alongside earnings or an occupational pension. Where a person does not qualify for the contributory pension, or qualifies only at a reduced rate, they may apply for the State Pension (Non-Contributory), subject to the relevant means and residency conditions.
State pension entitlement is separate from occupational pension provision. My Department has no role in determining occupational pension arrangements for employees of voluntary organisations or in extending membership of a public service pension scheme to a particular group of voluntary-sector employees.

question: Deputy Pat Buckley asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment for an immediate national moratorium on grid connections for data centres.
reply:
Data centres are fundamental to Ireland’s position as a leading global hub for digital and technology-driven enterprise. They form a critical part of the State’s digital infrastructure, supporting activities including cloud computing, artificial intelligence, financial services and public sector digital services. Their economic footprint is substantial with €104 billion in gross value added (around 20% of Ireland’s economy) enabled by data-centre-dependent sectors, approximately 183,000 people working in Ireland’s ICT sector and around 19,500 jobs directly in data centre construction and operations.
While data centres are large energy users, unlike other European countries that have heavy-industry bases, Ireland’s industrial electricity demand is primarily concentrated in our digital economy. This is our core energy-intensive industry. The Government is committed to delivering a balanced approach to facilitate the sustainable growth of data centres, whilst achieving the twin objective of decarbonisation and digitalisation and ensuring overall energy security and affordability for consumers and businesses.
The Large Energy User Action Plan (LEAP), published in January 2026, sets out a ‘plan-led’ approach for very large and energy intensive investments which, due to their scale and energy consumption, benefit from coordinated national infrastructure planning. question: Deputy John McGuinness asked the Minister for Social Protection if entitlement to a State Pension (Non-Contributory) for a person (details supplied) will be reviewed; and if the information provided in this case will be accepted as sufficient to continue the payment.
reply:
The person concerned was awarded State pension non-contributory from their 66th birthday in 2007.
State pension non-contributory is a means tested scheme. Assessable means include cash income, foreign pensions, the value of any property/land (excluding a person’s own home) and the value of any savings and investments which a person or their spouse, civil partner or cohabitant may have.
Where land is leased, the means assessment is based on the persons net income from the lease, calculated by deducting allowable expenses from the gross rental income. Where land is neither farmed nor leased and is not otherwise productively used, it is assessed on its capital value in accordance with the statutory means test provisions applicable to state pension non-contributory.

question: Deputy John McGuinness asked the Minister for Social Protection if retired nurses that paid a D stamp during their employment will be given the same pension entitlements as nurses that now pay an A stamp under a revised arrangement, particularly those that applied at the time to change to the A stamp; and if the matter will be considered as part of budget 2027.
reply:
The State Pension (Contributory) is funded through contributions paid to the Social Insurance Fund, whereas public service occupational pensions are provided for under the terms and conditions of employment. Matters relating to public service pension entitlements, including pension rates and increases, are a matter for the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation.
To qualify for the State Pension (Contributory), a person must be aged 66 or older, have entered the social insurance system 10 years before they draw down their State Pension (Contributory), and have paid a minimum of 520 qualifying contributions. In general, qualifying contributions are contributions paid at the full rate of social insurance, including Class A contributions paid by employees and Class S contributions paid by self-employed contributors.

Consequently, such contributors paid less in social insurance contributions in return for fewer social insurance benefits. My Department regularly reviews its schemes and policies to ensure that they continue to provide effective support and respond to changing demographic, social and economic conditions.

question: Deputy Ciarán Ahern asked the Minister for Social Protection the reason founders of social enterprises established as companies limited by guarantee may be classified as self-employed and required to pay Class S PRSI, despite being paid through payroll, holding no shares in the organisation and being accountable to a voluntary board of directors; if this classification excludes them from MyFutureFund; the steps available to correct an inappropriate classification; and if he will review the rules in order that social enterprise founders are supported to save for retirement rather than penalised for establishing organisations they do not own.
reply: The correct insurability of a person who is a founder of a social enterprise which is established as a company limited by guarantee will depend on the facts and circumstances of the engagement. In general, workers who are engaged on a contract of service (employee) basis and who are the beneficial owner of a company or who are able to control 50 per cent or more of the ordinary share capital of the company which they work for are required to pay class S PRSI in accordance with Paragraph 7 of Part 2 of Schedule 1 of the SWCA 2005. As CLG’s do not have any share capital, Scope Section make decisions on the correct classification of workers engaged by a CLG on a case-by-case basis, in accordance with Social Welfare legislation and the Code of Practice on Determining Employment Status. It is open to any individual seeking a decision regarding their own insurability to apply to Scope Section for a formal decision at any time.

question: Deputy Catherine Callaghan asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage whether he is satisfied that communities affected by strategic infrastructure developments, SIDs, have adequate opportunities to participate in the planning process; and if he will outline any proposals to enhance public participation.
reply:
Section 37E of the Planning and Development Act 2000, as amended (Act of 2000) sets out the public participation procedure in relation to Strategic Infrastructure Development (SID). Specifically section 37E(3)(a)(ii) of the Act of 2000 requires newspaper notices for SID specifying the times and places at which, and the period (not being less than 6 weeks) during which, a copy of the application and the environmental impact assessment report may be inspected free of charge or purchased on payment of a specified fee (which fee shall not exceed the reasonable cost of making such copy), section 37E(3)(a)(iii) of the Act of 2000 invites the making, during such period, of submissions and observations by the public to An Coimisiún Pleanála (the Commission).
Additionally, section 134 of the Act of 2000 provides the Commission may in its absolute discretion, hold an oral hearing of an application for SID under section 37E of the Act of 2000. These provisions ensure public participation in applications for SID and these will be maintained when the Planning and Development Act 2024 is commenced.

A sanction may include one, or all of the following: a written caution; a direction to pay a financial penalty of up to €15,000; and a direction to pay RTB investigation costs up to €15,000.
The Investigations and Sanctions Unit can initiate an investigation either as a result of information received from members of the public or as a result of information gathered from records that the RTB has access to under the RTA. If a member of the public has information about an alleged instance of Improper Conduct, they can contact the Investigations and Sanctions Unit at investigations@rtb.ie.

question: Deputy Pa Daly asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage if he will ask Met Éireann to examine whether the existing weather monitoring network adequately captures localised wind speeds and severe weather conditions in the Laune Valley and Killorglin area, particularly given the surrounding mountainous topography.
reply:
Met Éireann’s key mission is to monitor, analyse and predict Ireland's weather, flooding, and climate, and to provide Irish society and decisionmakers with information to protect life and property.
In keeping with this mission, Met Éireann carries out forecast verification to evaluate the performance of its forecasts compared to the actual observed conditions. This is carried out across Met Éireann’s entire forecast area on an ongoing basis. Findings from these evaluations are used in the refinement of Met Éireann’s weather models and to help inform the development of its observation networks countrywide.

question: Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage when Ireland’s draft nature restoration plan submitted to the European Commission on 1 September 2026 will be made publicly available.
reply:
The EU Nature Restoration Law (NRL) entered into force on 18 August 2024. It sets out a framework for EU Member States to restore nature, with binding targets for the restoration of a wide range of ecosystems including rivers, forests, oceans, urban and agricultural areas, as well as protected habitats and species. Ireland had until 1 September 2026 to submit a draft National Restoration Plan to the EU Commission, setting out how we intend to achieve these legally binding targets.
The draft National Restoration Plan (NRP) template was submitted to the European Commission on the 1 September 2026. The draft NRP template is very technical. An accessible version of the draft NRP submitted to the European Commission along with a detailed guide is currently being drafted and will be made publicly available once complete.
In early 2027 the EU Commission will submit formal feedback on the NRP, and the draft NRP will be revised based on this feedback. In September 2027, the final National Restoration Plan template will be submitted to the EU Commission.

reply:

The 2011 Regulations prescribe maximum net income limits for each local authority, in different bands according to the area concerned, with income being defined and assessed according to a standard Household Means Policy.
The Policy provides for a range of income disregards and local authorities also have discretion to disregard income that is once-off, temporary or short-term in nature and which is outside the regular pattern of a person’s annual income. The income bands are expressed in terms of a maximum net income threshold for a single-person household, with an allowance of 5% for each additional adult household member, subject to a maximum allowance under this category of 10% and separately a 2.5% allowance for each child.

question: Deputy Pa Daly asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage if consideration will be given to installing an automatic weather station or other appropriate monitoring equipment in the lower foothills of the MacGillycuddy’s Reeks, County Kerry to improve monitoring of local wind conditions in the Laune Valley and Killorglin area.
reply:
Met Éireann’s key mission is to monitor, analyse and predict Ireland's weather, flooding, and climate, and to provide Irish society and decisionmakers with information to protect life and property.
Met Éireann’s observation networks are a vital component in the delivery of this mission. Met Éireann manages a broad range of observation networks including weather stations, climate stations, rainfall stations, weather radars and environmental samplers. The location and density of these networks is governed by a range of complex factors including forecast and operational impact, climate requirements, site suitability and representativeness, amongst a range of others. Met Éireann is continuously developing and enhancing its observation networks countrywide. Careful consideration is and will be given to locations where additional monitoring will be beneficial to Met Éireann’s mission.

question: Deputy Duncan Smith asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage if there are plans for lands (details supplied) purchased by the Land Development Agency; when is it planned these lands will be developed and approximately; and the number of homes planned for these lands.
reply:
The Land Development Agency (LDA) plays a key role in the delivery of new housing under the Government’s Housing Plan, Delivering Homes, Building Communities.
The Agency is actively developing housing on State lands and market acquired lands and working in partnership with local authorities to develop large scale mixed tenure schemes of starter homes for purchase and rent, along with social housing on local authority owned sites.
The 86-hectare site at Lissenhall, Swords, Co. Dublin was acquired by the LDA from the National Asset Management Agency (NAMA) in October 2025. The land, which includes the proposed MetroLink Estuary terminus, has the potential to deliver c.6,000 homes, alongside new commercial and community amenities.
The LDA is a statutory body under the aegis of my Department and in line with section 12(4) of the Act is independent in the performance of its functions.
It may be helpful to note that arrangements have been put in place by my Department to ensure that public bodies under its aegis have a dedicated email address in place to facilitate the provision of information directly to members of the Oireachtas. This provides a speedy, efficient and cost effective system to address queries directly to the relevant bodies. In this regard, the LDA can be contacted by emailing oireachtas@lda.ie.

reply:
A key priority under the Governments Starter Homes Programme is the scaling up of the delivery of affordable Starter Homes for purchase, aimed at first time buyers and some fresh start applicants, through the local authorities and the Land Development Agency. reply:

The Planning and Development (Funfairs and Fairground Equipment) Regulations 2025 set out the requirements relating to applications for, and the granting of, a certificate of safety for fairground equipment.
Section 487 of the Planning and Development Act 2024 provides that a person who organises a funfair or owns fairground equipment shall not make available for public use any fairground equipment unless a valid certificate of safety has been granted in respect of that equipment. reply:

The Vacant Property Refurbishment Grant, funded under the Croí Cónaithe Towns Fund, has been a key measure in addressing vacancy and dereliction across the country.
The Vacant Property Refurbishment Grant provides a grant of up to €50,000 to support the refurbishment of vacant properties for occupation as a principal private residence and for properties which will be made available for rent. A top-up grant of up to €20,000 is available where the property is confirmed to be derelict, bringing the total grant available for a derelict property up to a maximum of €70,000. In order to qualify for the grant, the property must be vacant for two years or more at the time of application.
To the end of Q2 2026, over 18,800 applications have been received, over 14,300 approved, with more than 6,300 grants paid out following completion of works, totalling almost €349 million.
The maximum grant amounts were increased in May 2023 from €30,000 to €50,000 for the Vacant Property Refurbishment Grant and from €50,000 to €70,000 for homes considered derelict.
In conjunction with the Vacant Property Refurbishment Grant, other supports and grants may be used supporting bringing these vacant and derelict properties into use as homes.

question: Deputy Sean Fleming asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage to provide the list of household income thresholds for people who want to enter a mortgage to rent agreement, by county.
reply:
The Mortgage to Rent (MTR) scheme is targeted at households in mortgage arrears who have had their mortgage position deemed unsustainable by their lender under the Mortgage Arrears Resolution Process. In order for a borrower to qualify for the MTR scheme, the mortgage, property and household must meet detailed eligibility criteria. One of the requirements of the scheme is that the household must qualify for social housing support.
Applications for social housing support are assessed by the relevant local authority, in accordance with the eligibility and need criteria set down in section 20 of the Housing (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 2009 and the associated Social Housing Assessment Regulations 2011, as amended.
The 2011 Regulations prescribe maximum net income limits for each local authority, in different bands according to the area concerned, with income being defined and assessed according to a standard Household Means Policy. Local authorities have discretion to disregard income that is once-off, temporary or short-term in nature and which is outside the regular pattern of a person’s annual income. Local authorities have no discretion to exceed the limits applying to their administrative areas.
A table setting out the details of the three bands and the limits currently applicable in each local authority area is available on my Department's website on the following link:
www.gov.ie/en/publication/04c69-social-housing-support-table-of-income-limits/.

question: Deputy Seán Ó Fearghaíl asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage if he is aware of the concerns raised in correspondence (details supplied) regarding the decision not to provide an increased local property tax allocation to Kildare County Council for 2027; and the measures under consideration to address the long-standing funding deficit faced by Kildare County Council and ensure that it is adequately resourced to meet growing service demand.
reply:
The 2027 Local Property Tax (LPT) allocations are based on the best available information available at the time they were determined. The latest data from Revenue indicates that the expected yield for the 2026 liability year is approximately €605 million, which is €20 million lower than the original estimate of €625 million.
In light of this revised forecast, the Government's priority was to maintain local authority funding at existing levels rather than reduce baselines or LPT allocations for 2027. Accordingly, it was decided that 2027 allocations would remain unchanged and that the increases provided in 2026 would be carried forward.
While the final outturn may change before year-end, should the LPT yield remain below earlier projections, local authority allocations will still be maintained in full. Any funding shortfall will be met from Departmental resources. The latest LPT yield position will be reviewed again in advance of determining allocations for 2028.
It is also important to note that local authorities gained significantly from changes to baselines which ensured the sector fully benefited from the uplift arising from the 2026 LPT revaluation. These changes, along with increases in surplus LPT retained, resulted in an increase of more than €85 million in total own-use funding across the sector in 2026 compared to the previous year.
Kildare County Council, in particular, has seen a substantial increase in its LPT funding in recent years. This reflects a combination o

question: Deputy William Aird asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment to confirm whether that the scrappage scheme relating to old boilers not only applies to replacement with heat pumps, but also replacement with pellet and wood gasification boilers.
reply:
My Department funds a number of grant schemes, administered by the Sustainable Energy Authority of Ireland (SEAI), to support homeowners in improving the energy efficiency of their properties. These schemes focus on measures that reduce energy use, lower energy costs and cut carbon emissions. Grant supports for wood pellet stoves are not available under the SEAI residential energy upgrade schemes.
The boiler scrappage scheme forms part of a wider package of measures which I announced on 29 September and was developed through the National Energy Affordability Taskforce to help households and businesses reduce energy costs and move away from volatile, imported fossil fuels. The measures include enhanced supports for households at risk of energy poverty, medically vulnerable customers, lower-income homeowners and renters to help ensure that those who need support most can access the benefits of lower energy bills. The package also substantially boosts support for solar installations for business, as well as other energy efficiency measures.
The new €2,000 boiler scrappage scheme will immediately further support the switch from fossil fuel heating systems in eligible homes when installing heat pumps. From end January 2027 the grant is scheduled to be expanded to support eligible homes to install efficient electric heating or to connect to district heating systems.

question: Deputy Cian O'Callaghan asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage his Department's plans to ensure that every local authority home still without attic, cavity or any other suitable insulation has it installed; and his plans to boost the BER rating for all local authority homes to at least a B rating.
reply:
Since 2013, my Department's Energy Efficiency Retrofit Programme (EERP) has supported the retrofit of 85,292 local authority owned social homes requiring insulation and energy efficiency upgrades, with more than €0.5 billion provided to local authorities to support these works in the period to end 2025.
A revised EERP, introduced in 2021, is targeting the retrofit of 36,500 local authority homes by end 2030 to a post works Building Energy Rating (BER) equivalent of the previous B2 standard (125 kWh/m²/year), with no plans at present to expand this target. Eligible works include insulation upgrades, including attic and cavity wall insulation where appropriate, replacement of windows and doors, heat pump installation and associated works. Since 2021, over 11,000 social homes have been upgraded with support from my Department of approximately €342.3 million.
Funding and output targets under the EERP are determined annually through the Estimates process. For 2026, an allocation of €140 million has been provided for the programme, representing an increase of over 50% on the previous year and supporting the retrofit of approximately 3,500 local authority homes.
Having regard to the quantum of new build social homes delivered in recent years, those expected to be delivered by the end of the decade, and the successful delivery of target under the EERP, I expect at least 70% of local authority social homes will have achieved an A or B BER by 2030.

question: Deputy Robert O'Donoghue asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage the details of the formal complaints mechanisms available to residents of emergency accommodation where they have concerns regarding the conduct of accommodation providers or staff (details supplied); if complaints can be made directly to the relevant local authority, the regional homeless executive or his Department; the procedure for investigating such complaints; the expected timeframe for a response; and whether complaints are recorded centrally.
reply:

Statutory responsibility in relation to the provision of homeless accommodation and related services rests with individual local authorities.

Details on the operation of homeless services are a matter for individual local authorities in consultation with the Management Group of the relevant regional joint Homelessness Consultative Forum.

Details of the process are available at the following link: www.homelessdublin.ie/homeless/advice/make-a-complaint. Where a resident of emergency accommodation outside the Dublin region wishes to make a complaint, it should be submitted directly to the relevant local authority in the first instance.

question: Deputy Danny Healy-Rae asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage to consider reviewing the current mandatory retirement age of 62 for retained fire fighters (details supplied).
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 355 and 356 together.
The Courts, Civil Law, Criminal Law and Superannuation (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 2024 amended, among other matters, the law in relation to the age at which certain public servants are required to retire.
Part 11 of the Act provided the then Minister for Public Expenditure National Development Plan Delivery and Reform (M/PENDR), to make orders, enabling line ministers – Justice, Defence, and Housing – to make regulations regarding the retirement age of uniformed services. My predecessor made these regulations in August 2024, with the consent of then M/PENDR, raising the mandatory retirement age to 62.
Given this was addressed two years ago, in consultation with fire service staff representative organisations, there are no plans to revisit this matter presently.

reply:
Responsibility for the proper maintenance, repair, upgrade or replacement of a domestic wastewater treatment system (DWWTS), including the associated costs, rests with the system owner. The DWWTS Grant Scheme provides targeted financial support in specific exceptional circumstances.

question: Deputy Rory Hearne asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage the number of HAP tenancies registered to cost-rental properties with an approved housing body or a local authority as a landlord.
reply:
Cost Rental is a new form of housing tenure in Ireland, only established in 2021, where the tenant pays a rent which is set to cover the cost of delivering, managing, and maintaining the home. Cost Rental is intended for people in the middle-income cohort, who do not qualify for social housing, but who may be facing acute affordability pressures on the private rental market.
Eligibility for tenancies in Cost Rental homes is primarily determined by the net household income (less income tax, PRSI, USC, and pension contributions) of applicants, which is assessed at the point of application. The net household income limits are €66,000 for Cost Rental homes in Dublin, and €59,000 elsewhere.
More than 6,600 new Cost Rental homes were delivered by the end of Q1 2026, and there is a substantial pipeline of future developments in place.
Section 34 of the Affordable Housing Act 2021 specifies that Cost Rental tenants are eligible to seek HAP support in certain circumstances. This applies if they experience a sudden and unexpected fall in income, are within the local authority qualifying thresholds for social housing, and if they have been availing of a current Cost Rental tenancy agreement over a continuous period for more than 6 months.
The latest data available covers the period up to end Q1 2026. The table below shows the number of HAP tenancies registered to Cost Rental properties as of end Q1 2026.

reply:
The National Broadband Plan (NBP) is the Government’s initiative to deliver high?speed broadband to all premises in Ireland. In addition, Ireland's Digital Connectivity Strategy published in December 2022, sets out a number of targets including that all Irish households and businesses will be covered by a Gigabit network no later than 2028.
The Department does not have any regulatory oversight on the issue outlined in the question, but a citizen has the right to raise an issue to ComReg, the regulator on the matter.
However, the Department is aware that such issues do arise, and that often the issue is that the communication cables that need to be replaced to establish connectivity are directly encased in the concrete forming the public footpath. As outlined in my answer to Question No. 557 of 16 June 2026, my Department is continuing to monitor the upgrades by commercial operators to ensure any unnecessary barriers to their investment are addressed so that the risk of areas not being upgraded to a gigabit broadband services is mitigated.
My Department is investigating all potential scenarios for these gigabit challenged areas, including the issue of Direct Buried Leads (DBL), for why commercial operators may be prevented from upgrading their networks to gigabit broadband. It should be noted that DBLs are one of a number of scenarios that may make these network upgrades challenging for commercial operators.

question: Deputy Seán Ó Fearghaíl asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment With regard to energised grid-scale Li-BESS installations in the State, which body is statutorily responsible for inspecting and enforcing operational safety after an installation is energised; and under what legislative powers those functions are exercised.
reply:
A number of Government Departments, State bodies and public authorities have specific roles regarding the safety and regulation of lithium-ion battery electricity storage systems (Li-BESS) in Ireland and these agencies are best served to deal with the elements that are under their respective remits.
In July 2024, my Department published the Electricity Storage Policy Framework for Ireland. Chapter 4 of the Policy Framework provides an overview of the safety and regulatory regime in place for grid scale electricity storage systems, outlining the roles and remits of the relevant bodies.
All batteries in Ireland are manufactured, sold and operated in line with relevant EU regulation and standards. This includes safety testing, certification and labelling for the marketing and the putting into service of batteries used in grid-connected electrical storage systems.
EU Regulation (2023/1542) – ‘Concerning Batteries & Waste Batteries’, sets out the homogenisation of electricity storage standards and classification as well as the safety testing and certification requirements relevant to grid-connected Battery Electricity Storage Systems (BESS).

question: Deputy Pa Daly asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment whether consideration will be given to reviewing the pre-2006 eligibility requirement under the warmer homes scheme, given that a person whose home was built in 2007 may otherwise meet the qualifying criteria but is excluded solely on the basis of the year the property was built.
reply:
The Warmer Homes Scheme (WHS) aims to improve the energy efficiency and warmth of homes owned by people at risk of energy poverty by providing fully-funded retrofits. The scheme is operated by the Sustainable Energy Authority of Ireland (SEAI) on behalf of my Department and is funded through the carbon tax revenues and the European Regional Development Fund.
The WHS is available to owner-occupied properties, based on the householder being in receipt of certain Department of Social Protection income supports. The scheme targets support to those on the lowest incomes who are living in the least efficient homes so that the resources available can have the greatest impact in addressing energy poverty.
The year of build requirement is in place as homes constructed after 2006 are generally more energy efficient than those built before then due to the energy performance requirements of the 2003 Building Regulations. The scheme targets support to those most in need and living in the least efficient homes so that the resources available can have the greatest impact on homes in or at risk of energy poverty.
The demand for WHS is very high with the existing year of build criteria, with over 11,000 homes waiting to be allocated to a contractor and applications up 52% at end August this year compared to the same period last year.

Each piece of coursework presented for assessment to the SEC must be the candidate’s own, individual work completed in full compliance with the SEC’s Coursework Rules and Procedures. The rules for the completion, authentication and submission of Coursework apply to the eight new Coursework AACs for first examination in 2027, including Physics and Chemistry. reply:

reply:

question: Deputy Conor Sheehan asked the Minister for Education and Youth when the long-promised guidance for policies regarding code of behaviours in primary schools will be published.
reply:
Under section 23 of the Education (Welfare) Act 2000, the Board of Management of each school must prepare and make available a code of behaviour for its students. A code of behaviour specifies the standards of behaviour that shall be observed by each student. The current guidelines to schools on developing a code of behaviour issued from the National Educational Welfare Board in 2008.
The review and updating of the 2008 ‘Developing a code of behaviour guidelines for schools’ is an action in Cineáltas: Action Plan on Bullying. Tusla Education Support Service (TESS) are leading to update the code and to reflect current Department of Education and Youth policies and procedures for schools.
A steering group chaired by TESS was formed and its membership comprised of representatives from the management bodies, unions (teaching and student), parents’ representative body along with officials from my department. A structured systematic consultation processes took place which included children and young people. The updated Code of Behaviour guidelines are nearing finalisation. The rollout of the new Guidelines will be led by TESS and will include supports for schools to assist them in updating their current codes.

question: Deputy Pa Daly asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment further to Parliamentary Question No. 2954/24, the number of local authorities that have a waste disposal waiver scheme in place; if he does not have this information, the reason; the options that are available to them.
reply:
Waste management is a statutory function of local authorities. Under section 60(3) of the Waste Management Act 1996, the Minister is precluded from exercising any power or control in relation to the performance, in particular circumstances, of a local authority's statutory functions under that Act.
The Department does not maintain information on the number of local authorities that operate waste disposal or waste collection waiver schemes. There has never been a national waste waiver scheme and the introduction, administration or continuation of any such scheme is a matter for the local authority concerned. Accordingly, persons seeking information on the availability of a waiver scheme in a particular area should contact the relevant local authority directly.
It should also be noted that household waste collection services are provided by private waste collection operators in a competitive market. Charges for waste collection services are therefore matters for individual service providers and their customers, subject to compliance with relevant contract, consumer protection and competition law. The Minister has no statutory role in setting or regulating the prices charged by private waste collection companies.

question: Deputy Paul Nicholas Gogarty asked the Minister for Education and Youth the latest date during the calendar year by which schools are sent details of in-service dates for the following school year; whether there is any requirement for schools to inform parents of such dates well in advance so as to plan ahead.
reply:
My department provides a range of high-quality models of teacher professional learning to teachers and school leaders through Oide, the national network of Education Support Centres and appropriate groups, bodies and institutions who design, develop and deliver programmes.
The volume and nature of professional learning provision in any academic year is dependent upon needs identified in relation to curricular reform, implementation of priority educational policies/strategies, and the target cohorts of teachers involved.
School closure is approved where it is considered necessary and where it is intended that all relevant teachers will attend, such as professional learning for the national implementation of new or revised curricula or specifications, for example the redeveloped primary curriculum and senior cycle redevelopment. The sanction of whole school closure days is carefully considered by my Department to ensure that the benefits to pupils and students from teachers receiving the professional learning outweighs any disruption to their time in school.
There may also be benefits to the quality of education provided in a school when teachers and school leaders can engage in professional learning as a whole school team and subsequently translate their learnings into their everyday practice in that school.

reply:
The waste collection market is serviced by competing private companies, where prices charged are matters between those companies and their customers, subject to compliance with all applicable legislation, including contract, consumer and competition legislation. The Minister has no power to set prices in a private competitive market.
The National Waste Collection Permit Office (NWCPO) has conducted a study on incentivised charging structures in the waste collection market. This study also considers mechanisms for supports in relation to households disposing of medical incontinence products based on international practice.
Recommendations will be considered in conjunction with outcomes from the feasibility study into transitioning our national waste collection from its current competitive licensing system to a franchise model which has recently been completed. Both will inform the development of the next iteration of the Waste Action Plan for a Circular Economy (WAPCE).
The Department has previously engaged with relevant public bodies, including the Department of Social Protection, and representative organisations with respect to the waste disposal costs for incontinence wear, and further engagement will be undertaken in the context of updating the WAPCE in the coming months.

question: Deputy Paul Lawless asked the Minister for Education and Youth the policies and procedures governing the recovery of payroll overpayments arising from Departmental error in cases where the employee acted in good faith and had no knowledge that an overpayment was occurring; and is she will make a statement on the matter.
reply:
I wish to advise the Deputy that, while overpayments may occasionally occur, officials of the Department do not have discretion to waive or write off an overpayment where the recipient was not responsible for the error that gave rise to it.
Government Departments and Offices are required to pursue the recovery of all overpayments and to put appropriate repayment arrangements in place, regardless of how the overpayment arose.
The Department of Education and Youth's policy and procedures governing the recovery of salary and pension overpayments are set out in Circular 0084/2015. This circular provides that overpayments should be repaid as soon as practicable and outlines the repayment options available to affected individuals.
The Department of Public Expenditure and Reform Circular 07/2018 notes that Departments and Offices are under an obligation to seek to recover the amount of the overpayment and to correct the mistake in the disbursement of public monies, subject to relevant procedures and practices in Government accounting. Staff members/former staff members/pensioners have a reciprocal obligation to repay.
I can advise the Deputy that officials in the NTS Payroll Section of my Department have engaged directly with the Secretary concerned to explain the position and to explore a repayment arrangement that is manageable and seeks to minimise the financial impact on the individual as far as possible.

question: Deputy Paul Lawless asked the Minister for Education and Youth if her attention has been drawn to the case of a person (details supplied) who has been notified of a payroll overpayment due to an administrative error by her Department, in this case the employee's payslips did not record the number of hours worked; if this matter has been taken into account in assessing the overpayment.
reply:
I wish to advise the Deputy that the employee concerned has been contacted directly by officials of my Department and has been provided with written confirmation of the overpayment, including the breakdown of how the overpayment arose and the period to which it relates.
The Department assesses all payroll overpayments on the basis of the available payroll and employment records. In this case, the circumstances surrounding the overpayment, including the information available to the employee through their payslips and payroll records, have been taken into account as part of the Department's engagement with the employee.
Department officials remain available to engage with the employee to clarify any aspect of the overpayment calculation, discuss the breakdown provided, and address any questions she may have in relation to the matter.

question: Deputy Paul Lawless asked the Minister for Education and Youth to clarify the arrangements that apply where a school secretary payroll overpayment remains outstanding when a person retires, specifically whether a remaining balance can be recovered from a person's pension payments; to further clarify whether outstanding overpayment debt is written off in the event of the death of the person concerned, or if recovery is pursued against the estate:.
reply:
I wish to advise the Deputy that the recovery of payroll overpayments is managed in accordance with the Department's Overpayments Policy as set out in Circular 0084/2015.
Where a payroll overpayment remains outstanding on the retirement of a school secretary, recovery arrangements will be considered in line with the provisions of the Circular and the particular circumstances of the case. Where an individual has no entitlement to a pension payable by or through my Department, the outstanding overpayment cannot be recovered from pension payments.
In the event of the death of a person with an outstanding overpayment balance, the debt is not automatically written off. In accordance with the Department's Overpayments Policy and established legal principles, any outstanding amount may be pursued as a debt of the deceased person's estate and addressed as part of the administration of that estate, subject to the relevant legal requirements.
The Department seeks to ensure that the recovery of overpayments is undertaken in a fair, reasonable and proportionate manner, having regard to the circumstances of each individual case and the requirements of Circular 0084/2015.

question: Deputy Tom Brabazon asked the Minister for Education and Youth whether she will review Circular 0029/2010 and the current arrangements for the award of incremental salary credit to registered teachers, with a view to allowing relevant and verifiable teaching service in recognised or established private schools outside the European Union to be reckonable for incremental credit; and whether she is aware of the financial impact the current restriction can have on qualified teachers returning to Ireland after teaching abroad.

question: Deputy Aengus Ó Snodaigh asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment the steps being taken to assist families with children or adults who have special needs resulting in very high waste management bin charges (details supplied); and if he spoken with the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality on the need to address this matter.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 24 and 25 together.
The waste collection market is serviced by competing private companies, where prices charged are matters between those companies and their customers, subject to compliance with all applicable legislation, including contract, consumer and competition legislation. The Minister has no power to set prices in a private competitive market.
The National Waste Collection Permit Office (NWCPO) has conducted a study on incentivised charging structures in the waste collection market. This study also considers mechanisms for supports in relation to households disposing of medical incontinence products based on international practice.
Recommendations will be considered in conjunction with outcomes from the feasibility study into transitioning our national waste collection from its current competitive licensing system to a franchise model which has recently been completed. Both will inform the development of the next iteration of the Waste Action Plan for a Circular Economy (WAPCE).
The Department has engaged with relevant public bodies and representative organisations with respect to the waste disposal costs for incontinence wear and and further engagement will be undertaken in the context of updating the WAPCE in the coming months.

question: Deputy Pádraig Rice asked the Minister for Education and Youth whether her attention has been drawn to the number of schools that cater for students with additional needs that have had to independently fundraise for school buses for vital transport; and whether funding will be made available to assist schools in acquiring these buses.
reply:
The School Transport Scheme is a significant operation managed by Bus Éireann on behalf of the Department of Education and Youth.
The purpose of the Department's School Transport Scheme is, having regard to available resources, to support the transport to and from school of children who reside remote from their nearest school.
The National Council for Special Education acts in an advisory role to the Department on the suitability of placements for children with special educational needs. Under the terms of the School Transport Scheme for Children with Special Educational Needs, the Department will consider the report of the Special Education Needs Organiser (SENO). School transport is provided to children with special educational needs who are attending the nearest school to their place of residence that is or can be resourced to meet their educational needs, as identified by the SENO.
Bus Éireann manages the operation of the school transport scheme on behalf of the Department which includes the procurement tender process to include services provided by contractors under the scheme.
The provision of funding to schools to purchase vehicles for their own use is not a feature of the School Transport Scheme.

question: Deputy Darren O'Rourke asked the Minister for Education and Youth if the serious issues of intergenerational drug use, poverty and intergenerational trauma associated with drug feuds and drug intimidation were not considered when assessing schools in the Rathmullan area of Drogheda for inclusion in the DEIS plus programme; if not, the reason; and if she will commit to ensuring these factors are considered, possibly by way of narrative/qualitative submissions from school leaders and others, into the future.
reply:

The DEIS Plus scheme, launched as part of the DEIS Strategy to 2035, represents the most significant expansion of targeted supports since the establishment of the DEIS programme.
DEIS Plus provides enhanced, evidence-based supports to schools with the highest concentrations of children and young people at risk of educational disadvantage. Schools were identified through a nationally consistent, data-based model that draws on a range of indicators associated with persistent and intergenerational disadvantage. Following the conclusion of the identification and appeals processes, 129 schools were identified for inclusion in the DEIS Plus scheme.
The DEIS Plus identification model was developed and refined as part of the introduction of the scheme, drawing on the most up-to-date data available and an assessment of indicators of concentrated and persistent disadvantage over a three-year period. The identification model is underpinned by a range of administrative data on every child and young person enrolled in primary and post-primary school. This data includes:

question: Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Minister for Education and Youth if she plans to seek increases in capitation for primary schools in Budget 2027.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 235 and 236 together.
The Government is committed to increasing funding to support schools and the Programme for Government commits to increasing capitation funding to schools of all types to ensure that schools can meet the elevated day-to-day running costs.
This commitment builds on the progress made in recent years. The Department of Education and Youth has secured €39 million in Budget 2026 towards increased capitation funding for primary, post-primary and special schools to provide additional financial support towards their running costs. This will see an increase in the standard capitation rates paid to schools of €50 per pupil for primary schools from €224 to €274 and of €20 per student for post-primary schools from €386 to €406.

These increases will take effect from September 2026. This funding will benefit schools around the country in managing their day-to-day running costs.

question: Deputy Seán Ó Fearghaíl asked the Minister for Education and Youth If, having regard to concerns raised in correspondence (details supplied), she will outline the actions being taken by her Department and the National Council for Special Education to secure an appropriate school placement for a child with significant additional needs who, despite applications to a special school and all suitable special classes available, remains without a school place.
reply:
The National Council for Special Education (NCSE) is the statutory body responsible for the provision of special education and allocating supports for students with special educational needs.
The NCSE has advised that the local special educational needs organiser (SENO) is working closely with the family of the student named regarding options for school placements and other special education supports for the coming school year.
Parents may apply to enrol their child in a school of their choosing and where the school has places available for the relevant year, the student should be admitted. However, in schools where there are more applicants than places available, a selection process will be necessary. This selection process and the enrolment policy on which it is based must be non-discriminatory and must be applied fairly in respect of all applicants. Nonetheless, it may result in some students not obtaining a place in the school of their first choice.
My department and the NCSE are committed to delivering an education system that is of the highest quality and where every child and young person feels valued and is actively supported and nurtured to achieve their full potential.

reply:

My department’s general approach is to support schools at their existing location as best as possible which may involve modernisation of existing facilities and provision of additional capacity where necessary. In this regard, the Department provided additional capacity at the school through a significant modular accommodation project that was completed in November 2024. question: Deputy Séamus McGrath asked the Minister for Education and Youth the position regarding the commitment in the programme for Government to reduce the pupil-teacher ratio.
reply:
Under the Programme for Government, there is a commitment to reduce the general primary pupil : teacher ratio to 19:1 over the lifetime of the Government and to introduce targeted measures for schools with very large classes. This builds on substantial progress already made.
The primary staffing schedule has improved from an average allocation ratio of 26:1 five years ago to 23:1 for the current school year, the lowest ever at primary level. Average class sizes have fallen from 24.1 to 21.9 pupils, while the overall pupil : teacher ratio improved from 15:1 in 2019/20 to 12.6:1 in 2025/26, comparing favourably with the OECD average of 14:1. More favourable staffing arrangements also apply in DEIS Urban Band 1 schools.
I am conscious of the importance of continuing to reduce class sizes and improve teacher allocations at primary level. Any further measures, including proposals for additional teaching posts, will be considered in the context of the annual budgetary process and Programme for Government commitments.

question: Deputy Louise O'Reilly asked the Minister for Education and Youth if she is aware that removing a teacher from a school (details supplied) will result in a 50% increase in class sizes from 22 students to 33 students; if she is aware of concerns of parents about the ensuing detrimental impacts on the education and wellbeing of their children; if she is aware of the impact this will have on autistic students; if she is aware this goes against the Government commitments to reduce class sizes; if she will address this and ensure all current teaching posts are retained.
reply:
The key factor for determining the level of staffing resources provided at individual school level is the staffing schedule for the relevant school year and pupil enrolments on the previous 30 September.
The staffing arrangements include a provision whereby schools experiencing rapid increases in enrolment can apply for additional permanent mainstream posts, using projected enrolment. In order to qualify for such a post, the school's projected enrolment must be at least 23 pupils more than the previous September.
The school referred to by the Deputy has been allocated a post on this basis, having advised of an expected enrolment of 273 pupils. The school has been advised that to retain the post, an enrolment of 272 is required on 30 September.
The staffing process also contains an appeals mechanism for schools to submit a staffing appeal to an independent Primary Staffing Appeals Board. One of the appeals criteria is aimed at schools that receive a projected enrolment post but do not meet the required enrolment on 30 September. Such schools may submit an appeal to the October meeting of the Primary Staffing Appeals Board. Information and application forms are available in Circular 0025/2026. The closing date for receipt of applications is Tuesday 13 October.

question: Deputy Michael Cahill asked the Minister for Education and Youth the number of teachers on the primary school main panel in County Kerry at the commencement of the 2026-2027 school year; the number of permanent vacancies available to those teachers (details supplied).
reply:
At primary level, panel arrangements are a long standing feature of the redeployment process. Schools are required to fill their vacancies from the Main Redeployment Panel. Once all teachers on the Main Panel have been redeployed, permanent vacancies are offered to teachers on the Supplementary Redeployment Panel, comprised of eligible fixed-term (temporary/substitute) and part-time teachers. At that point, fixed-term vacancies may be advertised through open competition.
Of the 17 teachers placed on the Kerry Main Redeployment Panel, ten were redeployed permanently to other schools, three were reinstated into positions in their own schools, two took maternity leave exemptions from the panel and the remaining two chose to leave the panel for personal reasons.

question: Deputy Niamh Smyth asked the Minister for Education and Youth if she will review the case of a person (details supplied); the status of the school bus ticket application; and if the matter will be reconsidered given the exceptional circumstances.
reply:
The School Transport Scheme is a significant operation managed by Bus Éireann on behalf of the Department of Education and Youth.
Under the terms of the Post Primary School Transport Scheme, children are eligible for transport where they reside not less than 4.8 kms from their nearest post primary school/centre as determined by the Department/Bus Éireann, having regard to ethos and language.
Where a child is eligible for transport and the application and payment process has been completed on time, they will get a seat on a school bus service, where a service is available.
Children who are not eligible, but who apply for school transport are considered for spare seats that may exist after eligible children have been facilitated; previously known as concessionary seats.
Because of the nature of transport for non-eligible children and the priority of providing places for eligible children, there may be an excess of demand over supply for non-eligible pupils. In these cases, Bus Éireann will allocate tickets for spare seats using an agreed selection process.
Bus Eireann has advised that the pupil referred to by the Deputy is not eligible for school transport as they are attending their 3rd nearest post primary centre.
Bus Éireann further advise the pupil referred applied and paid on time but was not successful in obtaining a ticket for the current 2026/27 school year. The service is operating to capacity, and the pupil cannot be accommodated at this time.

question: Deputy Jennifer Whitmore asked the Minister for Education and Youth the date on which the policy of automatically including special class provision in all new school builds was first adopted; whether the policy was approved by Government decision, departmental instruction, NCSE recommendation or school design guidance; and if she will share the relevant documentation.
reply:

question: Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Education and Youth the position regarding any engagement she has had with unions representing teachers with a view to preventing their planned strike actions (detail supplied).
reply:
The Department notes that members of Fórsa, SIPTU and the AHCPS commenced industrial action on 30 September 2026, and that members of INTO and ASTI commenced industrial action from Monday, 5 October 2026. question: Deputy Mattie McGrath asked the Minister for Education and Youth her views on the convention on Education and the panel discussion on school values and culture; the reason for no involvement from the Catholic Church or religious bodies on the panel considering the number of schools in the State under their patronage; the way the panellists were selected; the people that selected the panellists; her views on there being no representatives from the Catholic Church when discussing school values and culture when Educate together were represented.
reply:
The Convention on Education was established to deliver on a Programme for Government commitment to hold a Convention bringing together all stakeholders in Education. An independent Chair of the Convention was appointed in July 2025 and is supported in this important work by five Deputy Chairs who lead the four groups that comprise the Convention:
• Children and young people.
• Parents and guardians.
• School employees and early years educators.
• Education stakeholders.
The 150 individuals selected to be participants in the Convention each bring a unique voice and perspective to the proceedings.
The Chair and Deputy Chairs are also supported by a Convention secretariat, who are appointed to advise in their fields of expertise and who support the Chairs and Deputy Chairs in safeguarding the integrity of the Convention’s work.
The agenda for the Convention on Education was approved by Government in April of this year and provides a framework to guide discussions over the Convention sessions.
To ensure the independence of the Convention process decisions on the format of the meetings and panellists who speak at the Convention are made by the Chair, Deputy Chairs and Secretariat.
I understand that participants are hearing from contributors from a diversity of backgrounds, beliefs and perspectives, on a variety of topics over the course of the four Convention weekends. This will help inform their deliberations to make recommendations on the future of our education system.

question: Deputy Emer Currie asked the Minister for Education and Youth to consider carrying out a similar initiative as the Primary School Survey to survey communities on secondary school provision.
reply:

The Primary School Survey gathered the views of parents of children currently attending primary school and parents of children yet to enter the school system. It explored preferences regarding language of instruction (education through Irish or English), school patronage/ethos and single-sex or co-educational school provision.
In early June, my department issued primary schools with their school-specific results and explanatory information. Boards of Management have been asked to engage with their communities and to inform their patron and my department by 31 October 2026 if they request to be included in the first group of schools to change configuration arising from this process.

A pilot phase of the Schools Energy Inventory project was completed with support from the European Investment Bank Advisory Hub programme. This was completed in December 2022 and included 601 schools across five Counties, Kildare, Meath, Offaly, Wexford and Wicklow.
Funding was subsequently secured under the REPowerEU programme to complete this work for all remaining schools in 2025 and 2026.
The programme is a very cost-effective approach for delivering an energy & condition asset rating system for the entire school estate and is hosted on the Department’s Geographic Information System (GIS). It has significant advantages in that rather than producing individual standalone ratings and reports it can collectively capture the range of relevant issues for analysis centrally by the Department.
The innovative approach of bringing energy and condition data together in the one survey database will facilitate future prioritisation of decarbonisation and investments in the school estate, enabling identification and targeted development of future school sector energy and decarbonisation programmes that will reduce overall reliance on fossil fuels and accelerate the deployment of renewable energy.
The school to which the Deputy refers was surveyed last year.
