question: Deputy Denise Mitchell asked the Minister for Education and Youth if there are plans for her Department to allow for the recognition of certified teaching experience from established schools outside the EU.
reply:
The criteria for the award of incremental credit are set out in the Department’s Circulars 10/2001, for primary teachers, and 29/2007 and 29/2010, for post-primary teachers. The criteria for the award of incremental credit to recognised teachers were agreed under the auspices of the Teachers Conciliation Council (TCC).
These circulars provide for the award of incremental credit in respect of overseas teaching service, both within and outside the EU. Where a school satisfies the criteria set out in the circulars to have service at that school recognised for incremental credit, an award of incremental credit can be made. There is no contractual entitlement to incremental credit.
Criteria such as whether the school is subject to state funding, which can be of relevance when examining claims relating to private teaching schools, and the length of time the school has been in existence, must be satisfied for service at that school to be recognised for incremental credit.
Where schools do not satisfy the required criteria, then service at that school cannot be considered towards incremental credit. Teachers must be on the Department of Education’s teacher payroll or teaching in an Education and Training Board school before an application can be processed.
The criteria for the award of incremental credit for teachers are subject to review by way of an incremental credit committee, which is a sub-committee of the Teachers Conciliation Council, and which meets on an ongoing basis.

question: Deputy Emer Currie asked the Minister for Education and Youth if any communication has been issued to a school (details supplied) regarding an application for a new school building.
reply:
I would like to confirm to the Deputy that an acknowledgement was issued to the school in question on the 13/05/2026, confirming that their application for a new school building was received by my department's Strategic Infrastructure Appraisal Section.
Updates on this matter have also been provided in response to representations made on behalf of the school by public representatives.
It should also be noted that applications for large scale projects require detailed analysis in line with public Infrastructure Guidelines and must consider a wide range of factors including the school’s accommodation requirements, the condition of existing accommodation, site constraints, available accommodation capacity across schools in the area, school building projects already in train, projected demand for places in the school planning area, timing of requirements, value for money, and affordability within NDP funding envelopes.
It is in this context that the school's application will be considered and in due course a decision on this application will be communicated directly to the school authority.

question: Deputy Mattie McGrath asked the Minister for Education and Youth the supports and services each school will lose in circumstances (details supplied); the supports that would be available from her Department to support such a merge; the position with regard to the re-deployment of staff including principal, teachers and support staff; and the procedure for the school community to follow in this instance.
reply:

It explored preferences regarding school ethos, co-educational or single-sex provision and language of instruction (Irish or English).
In early June, my department issued primary schools with their school-specific results and explanatory information, marking the next stage in the process of engaging school communities on the future direction of their schools.

question: Deputy Cathal Crowe asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment the way in which Ireland is engaging with the European Commission's Sovereign Cloud Framework, and the proposed Cloud and AI Development Act.
reply:
The key objective of the European Commission’s proposed Cloud and AI Development Act (CADA) is to ensure that the EU has sufficient cloud computing, AI and data processing capacity to support future economic growth, innovation and public services. The Commission considers these technologies to be increasingly strategic assets, underpinning critical sectors such as healthcare, energy, communications, financial services and public administration.
The Sovereign Cloud Framework is a key pillar of the CADA proposal and will require careful examination as the file develops.
My Department is responsible for co-ordinating the file at a Government level, and is taking steps to gather views and analyse the potential implications of the proposal. A public consultation took place between the 14th August and the 18th September, and responses are being assessed. An Inter-Departmental steering group has been established, and relevant and affected Government Departments, agencies and regulatory bodies have been notified and are being consulted.
As the Member State holding the Presidency of the Council of the European Union, Ireland's first responsibility is to progress the EU agenda and to act as an honest broker in respect of ongoing negotiations at EU level.
In relation to CADA, our primary role has been to progress technical and policy-level discussions and to develop a clear understanding of Member States' views on the file. This includes facilitating constructive discussions to clarify

question: Deputy Donna McGettigan asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment when Section 888 of the Company Act 2014 will be commenced (details supplied).
reply:
Section 888 of the Companies Act 2014 provides that documents may be authenticated in a prescribed manner other than by signature or seal. This enabling provision provides flexibility to accommodate alternative methods of authentication as business practices and technology evolve, including the use of electronic signatures where prescribed. This section was commenced by the Companies Act 2014 (Commencement) Order 2015 (S.I. No. 169 of 2015), together with the majority of the other provisions of that Act.
I understand that a large number of filings with the Companies Registration Office (CRO) may currently be authenticated using ROS (Revenue Online Signature) without the need for a wet signature. This functionality covers many of the most common activities such as the filing of annual returns and the changing of directors and their details. The Registrar of Companies periodically reviews and updates the forms that may be submitted electronically on the Companies Online Registration Environment (CORE).
I am informed by the Registrar that a review of current arrangements will be undertaken by the CRO in the context of the forthcoming implementation of the EU Digital Identity wallet.

question: Deputy Peadar Tóibín asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment the steps being taken by his Department to assist Irish small and medium-sized enterprises that are required to register with multiple authorities across the European Union in order to sell and distribute goods to customers in other Member States; if he has assessed the cumulative cost of such registration and compliance requirements for small businesses; and if he will raise this matter at EU level with a view to reducing administrative burdens on SMEs.
reply:
My Department is actively working with fellow Member States and the European Commission to remove the many practical barriers to selling and operating across Europe that are holding back Irish businesses, in particular Irish SMEs, and European growth. Through the full implementation of the EU’s Single Market Strategy, we are collectively aiming at delivering on one seamless Single Market, rather than the experience of 27 different regulatory regimes that often confront companies seeking to scale across Europe.
The Irish Presidency of the EU is seeking to advance a range of initiatives introduced under the Single Market Strategy, aimed at addressing regulatory fragmentation across Member States and in particular what the European Commission has identified as the “Terrible Ten” most impactful or burdensome Single Market barriers.
These include the Simplification Omnibus packages, the proposals for EU Inc and a European Business Wallet, as well as other key priority initiatives set out under the more integrated Single Market pillar of the One Europe One Market Roadmap.
This work is being supported domestically through a new implementation framework for Single Market rules, on which my Department is leading, and which was established by the Government in May of this year.
This new implementation framework is promoting greater whole of Government implementation of Single Market rules through a dedicated "Single Market Office" in the Department of Enterprise, Tourism and Employment

question: Deputy John Connolly asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment whether his Department, the AI Office of Ireland, or any agency under his remit has assessed recent reports concerning autonomous artificial intelligence systems allegedly engaging in cyberattack-related activities (details supplied); the implications such developments may have for Ireland's national policy on artificial intelligence governance and risk management; the engagement that has taken place with relevant cybersecurity authorities on emerging AI-enabled threats.
reply:
The AI Office of Ireland was established on 31 July 2026 and is developing the systems, expertise, relationships and organisational capacity required to carry out its functions under the EU AI Act.
During this establishment phase, the AI Office is engaging with relevant competent authorities and stakeholders to support the effective implementation of the EU AI Act in Ireland, including where responsibilities overlap.
The EU AI Act establishes a risk-based regulatory framework for AI. The AI Office’s role concerns the implementation, coordination and oversight functions assigned to it under that framework. Operational cybersecurity and the protection of critical infrastructure remain the responsibility of the relevant authorities.
As the relevant provisions of the EU AI Act become applicable, the AI Office will continue to develop coordination arrangements so that matters within the remit of more than one authority can be addressed through the appropriate channels.
The EU AI Act, adopted in 2024, provides safeguards for safety and fundamental rights while supporting innovation and the uptake of AI. Its provisions are becoming applicable in phases, enabling national and EU authorities to supervise and enforce the regulatory framework.
The Regulation of Artificial Intelligence Act 2026 commenced in July 2026, giving effect in Ireland to the EU AI Act and establishing the national framework for its implementation.
Under the EU AI Act, the European Commission’s AI Office is respon

question: Deputy Ruth Coppinger asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment to legislate for the provision of a guaranteed right for paid bereavement leave for those who have experienced a loss of a family member.
reply:
There is currently no form of statutory bereavement leave in Ireland. Bereavement leave is normally addressed through employment contracts and can be negotiated between employers and employees when entering into contracts of employment. Employers may also grant bereavement leave at their discretion if their employees suffer the bereavement of close family members.
The introduction of any new form of broad-based employment rights or leave entitlements require careful consideration to ensure that the needs of employees are adequately met and to assess impacts for employers. There is currently no commitment in the Programme for Government to introduce bereavement leave for the loss of a family member.

question: Deputy Naoise Ó Cearúil asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment the progress made to date in implementing Ireland's National AI Strategy; the actions completed, underway and outstanding.
reply:
Government published a new National Digital & AI Strategy, Digital Ireland – Connecting our People, Securing our Future, in February this year. It provides a clear roadmap for strengthening Ireland’s digital and AI capabilities in the years ahead, recognising digital competitiveness and innovation as a cornerstone of our economic resilience.
Containing 20 high-level objectives and 90 specific deliverables, the Strategy reflects the breadth of the Governments ambition across a range of areas, from public services, digital infrastructure and cyber security to enterprise innovation, digital regulation, online safety and skills.
The Strategy adopts a whole-of-Government approach, recognising that AI is a cross-cutting technology that has implications across a broad range of sectors. As such, sectoral AI policy issues are the responsibility of each relevant line department.
The Department of the Taoiseach leads the overall implementation of the Strategy and monitors progress across departments through a quarterly Implementation Group. Updates on deliverables are reported to the Senior Officials Group on Digital Issues, supported by the Department of the Taoiseach's Economic Development and Digital Unit, which in turn reports to the Cabinet Committee on Economy and Investment.
My Department's key priorities in the Strategy are to strengthen Ireland's position as a leading location for global technology companies, AI and digital start-ups, and applied AI innovation and accelerating

question: Deputy Naoise Ó Cearúil asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment the key challenges identified in increasing the adoption of artificial intelligence technologies among businesses and public bodies, including skills, regulatory and infrastructure constraints.
reply:
My Department closely monitors AI adoption across enterprises, with recent research pointing to rapid progress in AI adoption in Ireland. CSO data shows that over 20% of enterprises used AI in 2025, up from 15% in 2024, while the European Commission's 2025 Digital Decade Report indicates that Irish SMEs continue to outperform the EU average in digitalisation, with digital intensity reaching 71% compared with an EU average of 62%.
As part of a joint research programme with the ESRI, a recent study examined the factors influencing AI adoption among Irish micro, small and medium-sized enterprises. The research highlights the significant opportunities associated with AI adoption, while identifying knowledge-related barriers as a key factor affecting uptake among firms. Access to finance, security concerns and skills shortages were also found to influence firms' future investment intentions.
Analysis from UCD's Working in Ireland Survey 2025 showed that although AI adoption among workers is substantial and above EU averages, uptake varies significantly by education, occupation, gender, income and firm size.
The Expert Group on Future Skills Needs (EGFSN) report published last week, projects shortages of digital specialists as demand for digital specialists continues to grow strongly across all sectors.
This body of research highlights the importance of increasing awareness of the benefits of AI, investing in skills and implementing a strong regulatory environment.

These supports are intended to help small businesses improve productivity, adopt new technologies, enhance sustainability and remain competitive, and are therefore available to small businesses across a broad range of sectors including retail.

question: Deputy Aengus Ó Snodaigh asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment to list the cultural institutions, if any, including museums, galleries, libraries, archives, theatres, concert halls, bands, ensembles, and performing companies, operated or hosted by his Department and public bodies or semi-State companies under his Department's remit, identifying the State funding provided for these institutions each year for the past ten years; where they are based; and the number of personnel dedicated to them.
reply:
Neither the Department of Enterprise, Tourism and Employment nor the bodies under its remit operate or host cultural institutions such as museums, galleries, libraries, archives, theatres, concert halls, bands, ensembles or performing companies.
Fáilte Ireland supports tourism development in Ireland in a number of ways, which include supports for visitor attractions, festivals, heritage projects and tourism experiences that enhance Ireland’s appeal to domestic and international visitors. However, it does not operate or manage cultural institutions of the type referred to.
Responsibility for Ireland's national cultural institutions, including museums, galleries, libraries, archives, theatres and concert halls, falls under the remit of the Department of Culture, Communications and Sport. As such the above question should be addressed to my colleague Patrick O'Donovan T.D., Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport.

question: Deputy Catherine Callaghan asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment if he will review and remove the quota restrictions that apply to the issuing of employment permits for meat processing operatives, in view of the ongoing labour shortages reported by the meat processing sector; the measures he will take to ensure that processors can access an adequate workforce to maintain production levels and protect jobs throughout the agri-food supply chain.
reply:
My Department keeps the occupations for employment permits under regular review to ensure it remains responsive to labour market needs. The review process involves a public consultation inviting stakeholder submissions, consideration of research undertaken by the Expert Group on Future Skills Needs and the Skills and the Labour Market Research Unit in SOLAS.
The most recent review of the occupation lists commenced last summer with an open public consultation attracting a wide range of stakeholder submissions. The outcome was published on 26th May, giving approval for 32 changes to eligibility for roles for employment permits. The review report can be accessed on the Department's website at: https://enterprise.gov.ie/en/publications/employment-permits-occupations-lists-report-of-the-review-2025.html.
As part of that review process, I provided an additional quota of 1,000 permits for the meat processor role, recognising ongoing recruitment difficulties and workforce shortages within the sector. Where a quota expires, an employment permit cannot be granted for that role.
The review process determines where adjustments are appropriate based on evidence, guided by the principles of sustainable adjustable economic migration. It is a delicate balancing act, with recommendations reached through the participation and contributions of the Interdepartmental Group on Economic Migration Policy, which includes representatives of key Government Departments, including the Department of Agric

question: Deputy Jennifer Whitmore asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation if his Department will consider extending pay parity for public service pensions in payment beyond June 2026.
reply:
As Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation, I have overarching responsibility for public service pension policy, including in relation to pension increases in the public service.
Pensions in payment under the Single Public Service Pension Scheme are adjusted in line with increases in the Consumer Price Index (CPI), as provided for under section 40 of the Public Service Pensions (Single Scheme and Other Provisions) Act 2012.
Pension increase policy for "pre-existing" schemes is decided by ministerial discretion, as provided for under the Pension (Increase) Act 1964; the 1964 Act does not prescribe a methodology for how these increases should apply.
As the Deputy may be aware, the most recent method of post-retirement pension adjustment for retirees of pre-existing (pre-2013) public service pension schemes is known as ‘pay parity’. This method of pension adjustment was agreed by Government in respect of the Public Service Agreement 2024-2026, which expired at the end of June.
Under the policy of pay parity, in general, a salary increase awarded to serving public servants will be passed through to the pensions of those persons who have retired on an equivalent grade and pay scale point. I will consider future pension increase provisions, and whether pay parity will continue to apply, once further public service pay increases have been scheduled.

question: Deputy Naoise Ó Cearúil asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation the principal barriers identified by Government Departments and agencies to the implementation of digital transformation projects and artificial intelligence initiatives.
reply:
As Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation, I have responsibility for leading the Government’s public service transformation and digitalisation agenda. My department provides the overarching policy framework through Better Public Services 2030 and leads the Digital Public Services Plan 2030, working with Departments and public service bodies to develop more integrated, accessible and user-centred services. This includes supporting shared digital infrastructure, stronger data foundations and the responsible adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) across the public service. Individual Departments and public service bodies remain responsible for implementing digital and AI initiatives within their own remits and governance arrangements.
My department has taken a proactive and coordinated approach to supporting the responsible and effective adoption of Artificial Intelligence (AI) across the Public Service, realising that one of the primary barriers to effective AI deployment is often knowing where to start and how to begin designing and implementing effective and safe applications. A key part of this was the publication of the ‘Guidelines for the Responsible Use of Artificial Intelligence in the Public Service’ in May 2025, which provides clear information on government’s principles for responsible AI, a decision framework for evaluating the potential use of AI, a responsible AI canvas tool to be used at planning stage, and an A

question: Deputy Cathal Crowe asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation if his Department plans to publish a national sovereign cloud strategy for the public sector and critical national infrastructure; and the way in which it will address strategic dependence on non-EU cloud providers.
reply:
My Department, through the Office of the Government Chief Information Officer (OGCIO) and the Office of Government Procurement (OGP) divisions, has published a range of guidance to support the safe and appropriate adoption of cloud services across the Public Service. This includes the Cloud Computing Advice Notes, together with Cloud Services Procurement Guidance. These documents provide guidance on governance, security, procurement, risk management, data protection, and data sovereignty considerations when public bodies are determining how and where their information and workloads should be processed.
My Departments approach is to support public service organisations in making informed, risk-based decisions regarding cloud adoption, while ensuring compliance with applicable Irish and European legislation, including data protection, cybersecurity and resilience requirements. The OGCIO guidance recognises the growing importance of issues such as data sovereignty and strategic control of digital assets and requires these matters to be considered as part of cloud adoption and procurement decisions.
We are mindful of the need to address potential strategic dependencies within digital infrastructure. Public service bodies are therefore encouraged to consider matters such as vendor lock-in, portability of data and services, contractual safeguards, business continuity, resilience, multi-cloud and hybrid-cloud approaches, and compliance with evolving European regulatory frameworks wh

question: Deputy Cathal Crowe asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation if future ICT procurement frameworks will include explicit evaluation criteria covering European providers, open-source solutions, interoperability, vendor lock-in and cloud sovereignty where appropriate.
reply:
The Office of Government Procurement, a Division within my Department, operates as a Central Purchasing Body (CPB) establishing Framework Agreements and Dynamic Purchasing Systems for commonly required goods and services across a range of categories of expenditure including ICT. There are presently 11 different central procurement arrangements available to public sector bodies for commonly required ICT equipment, solutions and services.
The establishment of a national level framework is a significant undertaking. OGP Framework Agreements are established based on public sector bodies needs and market capabilities and are a key instrument in delivering value for money, promoting SME access to Government contracts as well as incorporating horizontal policy considerations.
The development of new ICT frameworks by the Office of Government Procurement entails extensive consultation with key stakeholders to determine the required scope of the arrangement, relevant policy considerations, statutory obligations and appropriate selection and evaluation criteria for awarding contracts, which would fulfil the common ICT requirements of public sector bodies, subject always to abiding by the key principles of transparency, equal treatment and proportionality.
When establishing its central procurement arrangements, the Office of Government Procurement adheres to the prevailing public procurement regulations and all applicable legislation. It should also be noted that the Office of Government

question: Deputy Cathal Crowe asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation the investment or policy support planned for Irish and European cloud, cybersecurity, open-source and digital public infrastructure providers, to ensure Ireland is not only a consumer of digital infrastructure but also contributes to European capability.
reply:
The recently published European Technological Sovereignty Package provides a framework for strengthening European capacity, reducing strategic dependencies and accelerating the digital and AI transformation of the Single Market.
This package was published by the European Commission on 3 June 2026. It comprises four interrelated initiatives:
• the proposed Cloud and AI Development Act, or CADA;
• the proposed Chips Act 2.0;
• the EU Open Source Strategy; and
• the Strategic Roadmap for Digitalisation and AI in the Energy Sector.
Together, these measures are intended to strengthen Europe’s capabilities across the digital technology stack, from semiconductors and computing infrastructure to software, cloud services and artificial intelligence. They also complement existing European initiatives, including AI Factories and AI Gigafactories.
Specifically, the Cloud and AI Development Act (CADA) is intended to ensure that the European Union has sufficient cloud, artificial intelligence and data-processing capacity to support future economic growth, innovation and the delivery of public services. These technologies increasingly underpin critical sectors, including healthcare, energy, communications, financial services and public administration.
Ireland continues to engage with European Union initiatives relating to cloud computing, digital sovereignty, and data governance. As previously outlined to the Dáil, Ireland has contributed to the development of European cloud policy and cont

question: Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation the governance framework under which the Accelerating Infrastructure Taskforce operates, including whether the Code of Practice for the Governance of State Bodies applies to the taskforce and whether a register of members’ interests and potential conflicts of interest is maintained.
reply:
The Accelerating Infrastructure Taskforce was established in May 2025 following Government agreement on 15 April 2025. It is a non-statutory Taskforce established to support my Department in its increased infrastructure functions, including supporting the Department’s programme of reform to unblock barriers and accelerate infrastructure delivery.
The Taskforce is a non-statutory advisory group. It is not a commercial or a non-commercial State body and, as such, the Code of Practice for the Governance of State Bodies does not apply to it.
The Taskforce operates under published Terms of Reference that define its role and functions. Membership of the Taskforce and records of meetings are published on my Department’s website. Functions of the Taskforce include: providing strategic guidance and expert input on measures to accelerate infrastructure delivery, advising on the identification of significant barriers to infrastructure delivery, providing advice on the development of focused, high-impact reform actions and overseeing the implementation of those actions.
Members have been advised in writing by my Department that they are responsible for declaring any actual or potential conflict of interest arising in relation to matters on the Taskforce’s agenda.

question: Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation the process and criteria used for the selection and appointment of each member of the Accelerating Infrastructure Taskforce, including whether the positions were advertised or otherwise subject to an open selection process; the body or person responsible for selecting each member; and the basis on which each member was considered suitable for appointment.
reply:
The Accelerating Infrastructure Taskforce was established in May 2025. This followed Government agreement on 15 April 2025 to the creation of a Taskforce, along with the identification by Government of the skills necessary for the group.
The Taskforce is a non-statutory group established to support my Department in its increased infrastructure functions, including supporting the Department’s programme of reform to unblock barriers and accelerate infrastructure delivery. The Taskforce replaced the Project Ireland Delivery Board.
There are twelve members of the Taskforce, six independent experts, experienced in infrastructure delivery, combined with six ex-officio members. I chair meetings of the Taskforce.
Of the ex-officio members, four are the heads of the commercial semi-states at the frontline of critical infrastructure development, specifically ESB Networks, the Land Development Agency, Uisce Éireann and the National Transport Authority. The two remaining ex-officio members were selected to represent the local Government sector, given the key role played by that sector in planning and development approvals for essential projects and the chair of the Major Projects Advisory Group, which assesses all major Exchequer infrastructure projects.
The six independent experts were selected by identifying senior level executives, current and retired, with experience of operations in Ireland that required significant infrastructure delivery, along with executives of planning / constr

question: Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation the amount of remuneration and expenses paid to each individual member of the Accelerating Infrastructure Taskforce since their appointment, showing the amount paid to each member separately and distinguishing between fees, travel expenses and other expenses.
reply:

Four categories of fixed annual fees were established for both Commercial and non-Commercial boards. The applicable Category of fee for each State Board is generally determined by reference to the remuneration of the head/CEO of the State Body which the State Board oversees. The framework is also used to ensure appropriate fees to other standing bodies, including for example the Senior posts Remuneration Committee (SPRC).

Specifically, this means that members of the Accelerating Infrastructure Taskforce are eligible for annual payments of €7,695 as well as expenses incurred in attendance at meetings.
My Department is currently finalising the information requested on the specific payments made to members of the Taskforce to date, with input from the National Shared Services Office. I propose to take Questions Nos. 149, 150, 151, 152, 153, 154, 155, 156, 157 and 158 together.
I would like to thank the Deputy for her questions.
The Protected Disclosures Act 2014, as amended, provides a comprehensive statutory framework for the protection of reporting persons who make protected disclosures. question: Deputy Barry Ward asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance the action he is taking in relation to the proposal from an organisation (details supplied) introduce a permanent 8% Section 481 regional uplift for productions filming outside the Dublin Metropolitan Area.
reply:
Finance Act 2018 introduced a short-term, tapered regional uplift under the Section 481 Film tax credit for productions being made in areas designated under the State aid regional guidelines (among other criteria).
As the regional uplift was an approved State aid, any restoration of the uplift would require approval from the European Commission. It is worth noting that the Section 481 Film tax credit is explicitly linked to the promotion of Irish or European culture.
While the uplift was not a Regional Aid measure, it operated by reference to the regional aid map in force at the time it was introduced. A new regional aid map, covering a significantly smaller geographic area, came into effect in April 2021; consequently, it is not expected that such an approach would be viable for a future relief to support activities outside the main Dublin production hub.
Since the expiration of the Regional Uplift, Government supports for audio-visual productions have been considerably enhanced and broadened. There are no geographic restrictions on the availability of these supports, so they are available to projects taking place in all regions of the State.
For example, the Scéal Uplift was introduced as part of Finance Act 2024 to provide for an uplift of 8 per cent to the existing Film Tax Credit rate of 32 per cent for small-to-medium sized productions with a maximum qualifying expenditure of €20 million where certain additional cultural criteria are also met. question: Deputy Albert Dolan asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance the measures currently being considered to reduce the cost of hydrotreated vegetable oil (HVO) for consumers; whether an assessment has been undertaken of the potential environmental benefits of increased HVO usage as a substitute for conventional diesel; and if he will consider introducing taxation, excise or other support measures to reduce the price differential between HVO and diesel in order to encourage greater uptake and support emissions reductions.
reply:
The Mineral Oil Tax treatment of biofuels, including HVO, already financially incentivises biofuels over fossil fuels such as diesel. Under section 100(5) of Finance Act 1999 (as amended), biofuels which are produced from biomass qualify for relief from the carbon component of MOT (Carbon Tax), thus incentivising the uptake of more sustainable and renewable fuels. In the case of blended fuels, the biofuel relief applies to the biofuel portion. The effective MOT rates on biofuels, along with comparable MOT rates for fossil fuels, such as auto-diesel, are published on Revenue’s website at www.revenue.ie/en/companies-and-charities/excise-and-licences/mineral-oil-tax/liquid-substitute-fuels/index.aspx.
The rate of the carbon tax relief for biofuels such as HVO used in place of auto diesel is currently c. 23 cents per litre on a VAT inclusive basis.
As biofuels are relieved of the carbon component of MOT, they are not impacted by annual carbon tax increases. I am advised by Revenue that in 2025 the tax forgone under the MOT biofuel relief is estimated at approximately €80 million. This estimate is based on an analysis of MOT returns data across all fuel types and a breakdown in respect of specific biofuels, such as HVO, is not available.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance the number of complaints received by the Financial Services and Pensions Ombudsman relating to residential mortgages held by non-bank loan owners or serviced by credit servicing firms, in each of the years 2024, 2025 and to date in 2026; the number of those returned or not accepted on procedural grounds.
reply:
The Financial Services and Pensions Ombudsman (FSPO) advises that the categorisation of data sought by the Deputy is not readily available.
The FSPO advises that complaints may be categorised as ‘compliance incomplete’ if the internal dispute resolution process was not initiated with the provider, if there was information outstanding from the complainant that was necessary for the FSPO to be able to assess or progress the complaint, or if the complainant did not respond when contacted, following multiple attempts to contact them.
For all mortgages, the number categorised as 'compliance incomplete' was 156 in 2024, 109 in 2025 and 59 to date in 2026.
More information on complaints is published by the FSPO annually in its Overview of Complaints.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance whether the Department has received correspondence regarding the return of mortgage complaints by the Financial Services and Pensions Ombudsman on signature grounds; the number of such representations received in 2026; the action taken in response.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 127, 130, 135, 138 and 145 together.
The Financial Services and Pensions Ombudsman (FSPO) provides an independent, fair, impartial, confidential and free service to resolve complaints by consumers about the conduct of a regulated financial service providers and pension providers.
The FSPO is independent in the performance of its functions. Due to their independence, I have no role, as Minister for Finance, in its day-to-day operations or decision-making functions.
The statutory functions of the FSPO are governed by the provisions of the Financial Services and Pensions Ombudsman Act 2017 (as amended).
The FSPO advises that where a complaint is submitted on behalf of co-complainants by an authorised third-party representative, the FSPO must ensure that all co-complainants are:
• represented by that third party,
• aware of the complaint to the FSPO, and
• consent to the complaint to the FPSO, including confirmation that they are aware of how it will process their personal data, and of the consequences of a legally binding decision by the Ombudsman.
The FSPO accepts electronically signed or hand (‘ink’) signed FSPO complaint forms, where the signatures have been applied individually to the complaint form by each co-complainant.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance the protections that apply to borrowers whose residential mortgages are transferred between non-bank loan owners or credit servicing firms, including under the Consumer Protection Code, the Code of Conduct on Mortgage Arrears and the Consumer Protection (Regulation of Credit Servicing Firms) Act 2018; whether a complaint lodged with the Financial Services and Pensions Ombudsman against the original loan owner continues against the new owner following a transfer; and if he will make statement on the matter.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 143 and 144 together.
Central Bank of Ireland regulated entities have the general right to assign or sell their entitlements and rights under a credit agreement, or a portfolio of agreements, to another entity.
In such a situation the new entity acquires the rights and benefits of the mortgage provider.
Such a transaction does not change the terms of the underlying credit contract and the benefits, rights and obligations of both the mortgage provider and mortgage holder as set out in the mortgage contract remain in place.
If a lender sells a mortgage to another entity, the new legal owner must be regulated by the Central Bank of Ireland, and the mortgage holder continues to be protected by the Consumer Protection Code. Rights under the Code, including the right of an internal appeal, do not change.
Recent legislative and regulatory reforms have strengthened protections for mortgage holders, supported by Government-funded assistance services for those experiencing mortgage difficulties.
The regulatory framework for non-bank lenders ensures that borrowers receive the same consumer protections regardless of whether they deal with a bank, retail credit firm, or credit servicing firm. The Consumer Protection Code remains the foundation of this framework and requires firms to act in their customers' best interests at all times.

question: Deputy Shane Moynihan asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance the manner in which the Financial Services and Pensions Ombudsman gives effect, when investigating complaints concerning mortgages and other consumer financial services, to rights arising under Council Directive 93/13/EEC on unfair terms in consumer contracts; whether complaints alleging breaches of rights arising under that Directive are assessed by reference to the relevant EU consumer-protection requirements.
reply:
As Minister for Finance, I have no role in the day-to-day operations or decision making process of the independent Financial Services and Pensions Ombudsman (FSPO).
The FSPO advises that each complaint dealt with through its formal investigation process, which may require a legally binding decision, is adjudicated based on the merits of the complaint.
Subject to the aspect of the complaint falling within its jurisdiction, the FSPO takes into account, as relevant, a range of national and EU legislation and case law, including legislation and case law on unfair terms, when adjudicating on matters in dispute between consumers and financial services providers and pension providers.
The FSPO notes that the Unfair Contract Terms Directive (EEC) 93/13 was initially transposed into Irish Law by virtue of the European Communities (Unfair Terms in Consumer Contracts) Regulations 1995 (as amended) (the 1995 Regulations). This measure was repealed by the current transposing measure, Part 6 of the Consumer Rights Act 2022, which came into force on 29 November 2022. The 1995 Regulations continue to apply to contracts concluded before 29 November 2022 while the Consumer Rights Act 2022 applies to contracts concluded after this date.

question: Deputy Shane Moynihan asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance the manner in which the Financial Services and Pensions Ombudsman gives effect to Article 8 of Directive 2013/11/EU concerning the making available of the outcome of an ADR procedure within 90 calendar days of receipt of the complete complaint file, subject to the provisions applying to highly complex disputes; when a complaint file is considered complete for this purpose; whether complainants are notified of that date.
reply:
The Financial Services and Pensions Ombudsman (FSPO) advises that it takes into account as relevant a range of national and EU legislation and case law, when adjudicating on matters in dispute between consumers and financial services providers and pension providers.
The latest FSPO data notes that the average resolution time was 8.3 months for all complaints that closed in 2025.
The FSPO's Dispute Resolution Service (mediation) closed 2,586 complaints in 2025. Mediation is an informal process and is generally concluded before a complete complaint file, (as would be required in the formal investigation processes), being received by the FSPO. The table below details the time taken from receipt to closure of complaints within the DRS (mediation) section in 2025.
Where early interventions through initial assessment process or through the mediation process do not resolve the dispute, the FSPO formally investigates the complaint and issues a decision that is legally binding on both parties, subject only to an appeal to the High Court.
These more complex complaints, including those requiring a formal adjudication, can longer to resolve, as given their legally binding nature, due process must be followed.

question: Deputy Louise O'Reilly asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance if he will consider introducing legislation so that the bereaved partner’s contributory pension does not reduce the tax credits or tax rate band of a working recipient (details supplied); if he will consider treating this pension in the same way as other social welfare payments that are exempt from income tax; if the Government is currently reviewing the tax treatment of the bereaved partner’s contributory pension; the reason this particular social welfare payment continues to be taxable while a number of other social welfare payments are exempt.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 119 and 122 together.
It is a general principle of taxation that all income, from whatever source, is income for tax purposes and this includes amounts paid to an individual by the Department of Social Protection (DSP), unless specifically exempted by legislation.
Section 19 of the Taxes Consolidation Act 1997 (TCA 1997) provides that income from offices or employments, and from annuities, pensions or stipends payable out of State funds, is within the charge to tax under Schedule E.
In addition, section 126(2) TCA 1997 specifically provides that payments made under the Bereaved Partner’s (Contributory) Pension are deemed to be emoluments to which Chapter 4 of Part 42 (Collection and recovery of income tax on certain emoluments (PAYE system)) applies. Accordingly, and as is the case with other long-term Department of Social Welfare (DSP) payments for example, the State Pension (Contributory or Non-Contributory), Jobseeker’s Benefit, and Illness Benefit, the Bereaved Partner’s (Contributory) Pension is subject to tax under Schedule E.
While Bereaved Partner’s (Contributory) Pension is subject to Income Tax, it is exempt from USC and PRSI.
The Bereaved Partner’s (Contributory) Pension is paid gross to the recipient by the DSP. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance the estimated annual contribution by Ireland to the EU budget under the European Commission's proposal for the Multiannual Financial Framework 2028 to 2034, compared with the annual contribution under the current framework, in tabular form; his Department's estimate of the contribution should the proposal be reduced by several hundred billion euros.
reply:
As the Deputy will be aware, negotiations are ongoing at EU-level on the Commission’s proposal for the next Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF), which will cover the years 2028 to 2034.
Ireland assumed its role as Presidency of the Council of the European Union earlier this year. As Presidency, we are committed to progressing negotiations on the next MFF and will continue to engage with Member States as we work towards our shared goal of reaching an agreement by the end of the year.
Ireland’s EU budget contributions for the years 2028-34 will depend on the outcome of these negotiations: namely, the volume of the agreed budget for the years in question, and any changes to the EU budget’s revenue system, or own resources. question: Deputy Ryan O'Meara asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance if his Department have considered tax reliefs for private gyms, similar to those introduced for hospitality; if further consideration has been given to the introduction of a tax relief for gym and pool memberships to encourage uptake.
reply:
As the Deputy will be aware, the Programme for Government, Securing Ireland’s Future, contains a commitment to “consider measures, in conjunction with the Department of Finance, to encourage gym membership and active participation in sport and exercise.”
The tax code already provides for a number of fitness-based measures more generally i.e. the Cycle to Work Scheme and the Accelerated Capital Allowances scheme for Childcare facilities and Fitness Centres which encourages employers to develop childcare facilities and fitness centres onsite for their employees. Furthermore, the private gym sector already receives tax-based public support through a reduced rate of VAT of 9 per cent on membership fees. It is estimated that this reduced rate saves private gym operators and gym members in the order of approximately €30 million per annum.
An exemption from Income Tax and Corporation Tax applies for the income of certain bodies established for the purpose of the promotion of athletic or amateur games or sports where it can be shown to the satisfaction of Revenue that such income is applied solely for those purposes. Any income received and availing of the relief by the sports body must be used for the purpose of promoting the game or sport.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance the estimated loss to the Exchequer from illegal cigarettes and illegal roll-your-own tobacco, respectively, in each of the years 2020 to 2025, as estimated by the Revenue Commissioners in the Illegal Tobacco Products Research Survey; the proportion of cigarettes consumed in the State that were illegal, legal non-Irish duty paid and Irish duty paid, respectively, in each of those years.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 110, 111, 112, 113, 114 and 115 together.
Smoking is the leading cause of preventable death in Ireland and remains one of the biggest avoidable health risks in Irish society. This is a significant public health concern for successive Governments who have committed to reducing the prevalence of smoking, particularly among younger people. A key element of the Government’s multi-faceted policy approach to achieve this is our commitment to high taxation of tobacco, which has been implemented through successive annual tax increases. A high tax strategy for tobacco is strongly endorsed by the World Health Organisation and was also supported by the Commission on Taxation and Welfare in its comprehensive review of Ireland’s tax and social welfare systems, which recognised tobacco tax as a behavioural tax directed at supporting public health and explicitly endorsed “using tobacco taxation to fight tobacco consumption”.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance if he will consider introducing a specific capital acquisitions tax exemption or enhanced threshold for inheritances received by persons with a lifelong disability or permanent incapacity; the number of such beneficiaries who paid CAT in each of the past five years.
reply:
The Capital Acquisitions Tax Consolidation Act 2003 (CATCA 2003) contains a number of exemptions from Capital Acquisitions Tax (CAT) for gifts and inheritances taken by individuals who are incapacitated by reason of physical or mental infirmity. The principal exemptions relevant to such individuals are outlined below.
Section 84 CATCA 2003 provides a specific exemption from CAT for a gift or inheritance taken exclusively to cover the “qualifying expenses” of an individual who is permanently incapacitated by reason of mental or physical infirmity. “Qualifying expenses” are expenses relating to medical care, including hospital charges, doctors’ fees, medicines and other pharmaceutical costs, together with the cost of maintenance relating to medical care. For the exemption to apply, the individual must be permanently incapacitated by reason of mental or physical infirmity, the benefit must be provided exclusively to meet qualifying expenses, and there must be clear evidence from the disponer (the person making the gift or bequest), whether by will or otherwise, that the benefit is provided solely for these purposes. Further information on this exemption is available in Capital Acquisitions Tax Manual Part 22, which can be found on the Revenue website at: www.revenue.ie/en/tax-professionals/tdm/capital-acquisitions-tax/cat-manual/part-09-exemptions/section-84-exemption-relating-to-qualifying-expenses-of-incapacitated-individuals.pdf.

question: Deputy Séamus McGrath asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance if he will consider allowing medical expenses to qualify for tax relief at the higher rate of tax given this existed prior to 2009.
reply:
Section 469 of the Taxes Consolidation Act 1997 provides for tax relief where an individual proves that he or she has incurred costs in respect of qualifying health expenses.
Only "health expenses" incurred in the provision of “health care”, which has been carried out or advised by (in certain circumstances) a practitioner, will qualify for tax relief.
Health care is defined as the “prevention, diagnosis, alleviation or treatment of an ailment, injury, infirmity, defect or disability”.
Health expenses are defined as “expenses in respect of the provision of health care” and may include, but are not limited to, the following
• the services of a practitioner,
• diagnostic procedures carried out on the advice of a practitioner,
• maintenance or treatment necessarily incurred in connection with the services of a practitioner or diagnostic procedures carried out on the advice of a practitioner, and
• drugs or medicines supplied on the prescription of a practitioner.
A practitioner is defined as "any person who is:
• registered in the register established under section 43 of the Medical Practitioners Act 2007,
• registered in the register established under section 26 of the Dentists Act, 1985, or,
• in relation to health care provided outside the State, entitled under the laws of the country in which the care is provided to practice medicine or dentistry there".

question: Deputy Naoise Ó Muirí asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance for an update on the RZLT exemption which has been in place for the past two years; if he has considered continuing the exemption for 2027.
reply:
Finance Act 2021 introduced Part 22A Residential Zoned Land Tax (RZLT) into the Taxes Consolidation Act 1997. RZLT is designed to prompt residential development by owners of land that satisfies the relevant criteria for the tax, that being that the land is zoned for residential or mixed-use (including residential) purposes and that is serviced.
RZLT is an annual tax, calculated at a rate of 3% of the market value of the land within its scope. The tax is due and payable from 2025 onwards in respect of land which satisfied the relevant criteria on 1 January 2022, or in the course of 2022, as where land satisfies the relevant criteria after 1 January 2022, RZLT will be first due in the third year after the year in which it satisfies the relevant criteria. RZLT first arose on 1 February 2025 and the 2026 liability was payable by 23 May 2026, subject to certain exceptions.
The legislation underpinning RZLT provides for a number of exemptions, deferrals and abatements subject to the relevant criteria being met. The legislation does not provide for a specific exemption for farms. Landowners including farmers, who own land meeting the criteria for RZLT are subject to the tax. It is important to note that, to come within the scope of RZLT, land must be both zoned by the local authority for residential use and serviced. The intention of RZLT is to activate development of this residentially zoned and serviced land to meet critical housing needs.

question: Deputy Séamus McGrath asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance if he would consider introducing tax relief for PAYE individuals who engage the services of an accountant for the purposes of their tax return and incur fees.
reply:
I am advised by Revenue that no deduction or relief is available against employment income except to the extent expressly permitted by the Tax Acts. The legislation governing the deductibility of expenses from employment income is contained in section 114 Taxes Consolidation Act 1997 (“TCA 1997”). To qualify for tax relief under this section, the expenses must be wholly, exclusively and necessarily incurred in the performance of the duties of the relevant employment.
The provisions of section 114 TCA 1997 are strictly applied, with a body of case law supporting the interpretation and application of this section. Under this section, the expense must be incurred in the actual performance of the duties of the office or employment or as a direct consequence of those duties and should not arise because of the personal circumstances or preference of the individual. Accountancy fees incurred solely for personal tax compliance, do not meet the test of wholly, exclusively and necessarily incurred in the performance of the duties of the employment. This means that such expenses are not deductible against employment income.

question: Deputy Séamus McGrath asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance to consider removing VAT on sunscreen products to make them more affordable and encourage use given their importance for skin cancer prevention.
reply:
As the Deputy may be aware, the setting of VAT rates is subject to the terms of the EU VAT Directive, which Irish VAT law must comply. Generally, it is held that all goods and services are subject to VAT at the standard rate, unless they are included in a list of categories under Annex III of the Directive, in which case either a reduced rate or exemption may be applied.
It is my understanding that there was engagement on this issue with the European Commission in 2023, and clarity was sought on whether the text of Annex III of the VAT Directive which refers to pharmaceutical products could be understood to include sun protection products.
Unfortunately, the European Commission confirmed the position that it was not possible for sunscreen products to be considered as pharmaceutical products as they are deemed to be classed as a product in the category of cosmetic or toilet preparations.
In those circumstances the Commission advised that a reduced rate cannot be applied to sun protection products such as sunscreen.
In the broader context of the Annex III of the VAT Directive, I have been advised that an agreement was reached to amend and expand its scope in April of 2022. These changes to the VAT Directive, which require unanimity among Member States were negotiated over a four-year period.
It is my understanding that no further changes to Annex III of the VAT Directive are expected.

question: Deputy James O'Connor asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade her response to recent Russian hybrid attacks against the European Union and its Member States.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 47 and 90 together.
The Government has strongly condemned Russia’s attempted drone attack at Leipzig airport in August.
This activity is part of a clear trend. It forms part of a broader, coordinated, and long-standing hybrid campaign aimed at threatening and undermining the security, resilience and democratic foundations of the EU, its Member States and its partners.
In response to the Leipzig incident, I expressed my full solidarity with Germany, and with all Member States affected by Russia’s reckless and increasingly frequent hybrid attacks. I discussed the issue with the HRVP, Kaja Kallas, and my German and other EU counterparts at the meeting of EU Foreign Ministers I hosted in Druid's Glen in early September.
The Ambassador of the Russian Federation was summoned by senior officials of the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade on 3 September to hear expression of Ireland’s strong condemnation. Ireland is extremely concerned at the continued increased in hybrid activity. Russia’s actions threaten the security of EU citizens, as well as regional stability and international peace.
We support the full use of all tools available to prevent, deter, and respond to Russia’s hybrid activities, including through sanctions.

question: Deputy Brendan Smith asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade for a report on her attendance at the recent British-Irish Association annual conference.
reply:
I attended the annual British Irish Association conference in Oxford on 4 September which was held under Chatham House rules.
I was pleased to deliver opening remarks and to participate in an interactive question and answer session with participants. In my remarks, I spoke about how relations across these islands are being reshaped by the changes we are seeing in the international environment and the shared challenges these changes present us all.
I recalled the ambitious agenda for bilateral relations between the Irish and UK government, in the shape of the UK-Ireland Joint Statement.
I also spoke about our work to unlock the full potential of the Good Friday Agreement through the work of the North South bodies and through the Shared Island Initiative. I discussed the implementation of the Joint Framework on Legacy, which we agreed with the UK Government last year.
I am pleased that this year the BIA was once more designated as a Strategic Partner of the Reconciliation Fund which will provide funding of €50,000 per year for the next three years.
The BIA conference remains as an important event in the calendar of British-Irish relations which promotes mutual understanding and good relations between the people of our islands, and with a valuable focus on Northern Ireland.

question: Deputy Sinéad Gibney asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade the actions she and her Department have taken diplomatically at EU and UN level to pursue global action on climate commitments and the Paris Agreement following the heatwaves, flooding, and other extreme weather events globally in recent months.
reply:
This year has seen devastating heatwaves, floods, droughts and storms affecting communities across every region of the world. The summer wildfires in Europe and the recent devastation in Nepal are stark reminders that climate change is not a future threat but a present reality, underscoring the urgency of global action.
At EU and UN level, Ireland continues to advocate for ambitious implementation of the Paris Agreement and stronger international action to address the effects of climate change. As EU Presidency, Ireland is leading engagement with EU Member States, the European Commission and international partners in advance of COP31 in Antalya in November. We are working to build consensus around outcomes on emissions reduction, adaptation, climate finance and loss and damage, with the objective of keeping the Paris Agreement's 1.5°C goal within reach.
At the United Nations, including during UN General Assembly High-Level Week, we have engaged with UN partners, fellow Member States and vulnerable countries on preparations for COP31. Ireland consistently advocates for the prioritisation of adaptation finance for Least Developed Countries and Small Island Developing States, with a particular emphasis on grant-based support.
This is reflected across Ireland's own international climate finance with, 89% of which supports adaptation, helping vulnerable communities to strengthen their resilience and prepare for a changing climate.

question: Deputy Sinéad Gibney asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade the steps her Department is taking to reach the 0.7% goal for overseas development aid; and the engagements she has had with other EU member states on increasing their aid budgets.
reply:
The Government remains committed to the United Nations target to provide 0.7% of Gross National Income (GNI) in Official Development Assistance (ODA). reply:

Overall, we expect to host more than 270 Presidency events in Ireland, with approximately a quarter of these taking place regionally. question: Deputy Paul Murphy asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade to report on her Department's engagements, if any, with the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration in relation to the Ireland-Palestine scholarship programme which the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade co-administers; if she believes the programme has been undermined by the refusal of visas to Palestinian students offered places under the programme.

Visa policy is a matter for the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration, which assesses each visa application on its own merits.

question: Deputy Duncan Smith asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade if Ireland will increase foreign aid in budget 2027.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 52 and 80 together.
The Government remains committed to the UN target to provide 0.7% of Gross National Income (GNI) in Official Development Assistance (ODA). This commitment was reaffirmed in A Better World, Ireland's International Development Policy and in the Programme for Government, which commits to increases in ODA, towards the 0.7% target.

question: Deputy Shane Moynihan asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade if she will provide an update on the British Government's response to the State's ongoing request for full disclosure and access to all relevant documents concerning the Dublin and Monaghan bombings of 17 May 1974.
reply:
This year marks the 52nd anniversary of the Dublin Monaghan bombings. My thoughts are first and foremost with the families who continue to seek the truth of what happened to their loved ones on that day and it was important to me that my Department was represented at the commemoration on Talbot Street in May.
In relation to contact with the British Government, I have spoken with the new Secretary of State for Northern Ireland, Christ Bryant MP, a number of times since his appointment in July.
We have discussed our key priorities for Northern Ireland in the months ahead, particularly the need to progress the implementation of the Joint Framework on the Legacy of the Troubles, agreed last year by the two Governments. Reciprocal co-operation is at the heart of the Joint Framework, which commits the British Government to provide "cooperation to Ireland for investigations, inquiries and inquests" in this jurisdiction.
The Government has long-standing requests in place to allow access by an independent, international judicial figure to all original documents held by the British Government relating to the Dublin and Monaghan bombings. These requests arise from successive all-party motions adopted by this House.

question: Deputy Darren O'Rourke asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade the way in which she has raised the issue to advance the case for Irish reunification internationally.
reply:
The position of the Government on Irish re-unification is determined by Article 3 of the Constitution, as amended by the people in 1998 to incorporate the framework set out in the Good Friday Agreement.
The Programme for Government states clearly that this Government is committed to the unity of the Irish people. This can only be achieved through a sustained focus on and investment in reconciliation. We remain steadfast in implementing the Good Friday Agreement in full and supporting the functioning of all of its institutions.
In my discussions with international partners, I am heartened that there is a continued interest in the peace process and on furthering reconciliation in Northern Ireland today.
Securing the peace through the Good Friday Agreement would not have been possible without the support of those international partners.
Our commitment to unlocking the full potential of the Agreement, includes addressing the legacy of the Troubles and through the Shared Island Initiative, to which we have allocated €2 billion through to 2035. Our whole-of-government approach is building a more connected, prosperous and reconciled island for people North and South. In the event of a future referendum, we will make all necessary preparations within the terms of the Constitution and the principles and procedures of the Agreement.

question: Deputy Cathy Bennett asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade if she will consider opening a passport office in the North.
reply:
The Passport Online service offers citizens the ability to apply online for their passport 24 hours a day, 7 days a week. Over 97% of all passport applications are now made through Passport Online which is available to 100% of all applicants globally. It is worth noting that just 1% of passports issue through the public counter in Dublin.
Demand for passports from citizens resident in Northern Ireland remains steady. To date in 2026, over 97% of applications from citizens resident in Northern Ireland have been made through Passport Online, compared with 91% in 2025.
Last December, the Passport Service launched a new Passport Assist Service to support citizens who do not wish to use Passport Online channel and assist them to make a paper passport application. Citizens can call the dedicated Passport Assist number to receive a personalised paper form, along with a bespoke list of documents required, which they can post back to the Passport Service through their local post office. This all-island service has enhanced the paper application route by offering direct assistance to citizens.
In terms of any proposed additional passport office, there are considerable financial implications to consider. The Passport Service estimates the initial capital cost of opening an office in Northern Ireland, including purchasing and installing new printer and mailing machine, to be approximately €5.3 million. reply:

I am very concerned by the resumption of hostilities between Iran and the United States, following the expiry of the negotiating period provided for under the 17 June Memorandum of Understanding. Ireland has consistently maintained that the best way forward is a return by both sides to meaningful, good-faith negotiations aimed at restoring regional peace and stability.
I have remained in contact with my counterparts on the confict in the Gulf, including during High Level Week at the United Nations General Assembly in New York last week. The situation in the region was also discussed at the EU informal Foreign Affairs Council meeting in Wicklow in September. Last week, in New York, I joined over 80 countries in issuing a statement condemning Iran's continued attacks on its neighbours and on international shipping.
Attacks by Iran risk further undermining regional stability. Ireland calls on all parties to exercise restraint and uphold international law, including the protection of civilians and civilian infrastructure. Any loss of civilian life through conflict is unacceptable and must be avoided. We extend our sympathy to the families of those who have lost loved ones.

question: Deputy Naoise Ó Muirí asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade if her Department has been in contact with Irish citizens in Turkey, following the recent crackdowns.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 29, 46 and 75 together.
I am deeply concerned about recent measures, including legal proceedings and arrests, against LGBTIQ+ organisations and persons in Türkiye. As an EU candidate country, member of the Council of Europe, and a party to international human rights instruments, Türkiye is expected to uphold the highest democratic standards and to ensure the respect of fundamental rights for all, including for LGBTIQ+ persons.
Every person, regardless of sexual orientation, gender identity, or any other characteristic, is entitled to equality, dignity and the full enjoyment of their human rights. The promotion and protection of the rights of LGBTIQ+ persons is a domestic and foreign policy priority for Ireland, and this is reflected in our campaign for membership of the UN Human Rights Council, where defending the rights of LGBTIQ+ persons is one of our five thematic priorities.
Ireland continues to support initiatives in the EU and other international fora which promote and protect the rights of LGBTIQ+ people, and which condemn violence and discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity. Ireland stands in full solidarity with LGBTIQ+ persons and their allies in Türkiye. As part of ongoing bilateral engagement, Ireland raises human rights issues, including regarding LGBTIQ+ persons, with the Turkish authorities.

reply:

Supporting the most vulnerable remains at the heart of this new strategy, as is our commitment to partner with Irish communities overseas to promote our culture, music, identity and sport, and to showcase the values of a modern and diverse Ireland to a global audience.
We also address the particular challenges facing those who are considering emigrating, those who are newly arrived abroad and those looking to return.
The strategy recognises the real appetite among the diaspora for supporting our trade and economic priorities. We will step up our engagements to embrace these influential networks and vital insights in support of accessing new markets, securing Foreign Direct Investment and driving job creation and innovation.

question: Deputy Seán Ó Fearghaíl asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade the way in which she is promoting diplomatic and trade relations with Barbados.
reply:

question: Deputy Seán Kyne asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade if her Department has assessed whether Ireland is out of step with other European Union member states in not maintaining a trade or representative office in Taiwan; and if consideration has been given to reopening an Irish Trade and Cultural Office in Taipei to strengthen economic, trade, cultural and links with Taiwan.
reply:
Ireland, along with our EU partners, adheres to the One China Policy. This means that we recognise the People's Republic of China as the sole legal government of China, and that we do not have diplomatic relations with Taiwan. However, the absence of diplomatic of relations does not preclude the development of economic, cultural and people-to-people connections.
My Department has never maintained an office in Taipei. IDA Ireland, the agency responsible for attracting foreign direct investment to Ireland, previously had an office in Taipei but it was closed in 2011 solely based on business reasons. IDA Ireland now manages the Taiwanese market from its Singapore office, and Enterprise Ireland, the agency responsible for enterprise development, manages the market from its office in Hong Kong.
I am aware that some EU Member States have trade offices in Taipei, and I note that the EU has maintained its European Economic and Trade Office in Taipei since 2003. However, it is important to note that decisions on the opening of new offices by the Government are taken on the basis of need and how best to promote our own interests abroad rather than to match the approach of other countries.
There are currently no plans to establish a trade and cultural office in Taipei. The establishment of new offices is always kept under review. The opening of new offices is a resource-intensive process. Decisions are evaluated on the basis of a number of factors, including cost-benefit considerations

question: Deputy Ruairí Ó Murchú asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade to provide an update on her recent engagements regarding the EU-Israel Association Agreement; and the possible sanctions to be taken against Israel on the basis of its actions against the Palestinian people.
reply:
The Israel-Palestine conflict, and the defence of the two-State solution, is a key priority during our Presidency. We are working to ensure that focus is maintained on the dire humanitarian needs in Gaza and the appalling situation in the West Bank.
In particular, we are continuing to press for appropriate action in response to egregious Israeli breaches of international law, human rights and democratic principles. The situation in Gaza and the West Bank was discussed at the Informal Meeting of EU Foreign Ministers that I hosted in Wicklow on 1-2 September.
Ireland’s long-standing position is that the EU-Israel Association Agreement should be suspended, or at a minimum that the trade elements should be suspended. A number of other Member States have supported Ireland’s call for stronger collective EU action, and this is a call that Ireland will continue to make.
In addition, while we have moved ahead at the national level with our own Israeli Settlements Act, Ireland continues to lead the call for an EU-wide prohibition on trade with Israeli settlements. The Government remains clear that collective action at the EU level is the strongest and most effective route to prohibit trade with Israeli settlements.
I have repeatedly called for the European Commission to bring forward proposals in this regard, on the basis of the EU's Common Commercial Policy, to ensure the EU is in compliance with its international obligations.
I am disappointed that the Commission has not come forward

question: Deputy Paul Murphy asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade to report on her recent meeting with a company (details supplied) and its relevance to Ireland's foreign affairs and trade policy in relation to AI, digital deregulation and big tech.
reply:
Last week, I travelled to New York to attend the UN General Assembly High Level Week during which AI was a prominent theme this year. In relevant engagements I highlighted the opportunity provided by the AI Summit in Ireland later this year.
While in New York there, I also undertook a programme to promote trade and economic links. These engagements were an opportunity to focus on Ireland’s trade and investment relationship with the United States at a time of significant change and uncertainty in the international trading environment.
